AI.result: Ukrainian shows 68-121% token overhead on modern tokenizers and 220% on cl100k. Overhead negatively correlates with Cyrillic vocabulary allocation but not statistically significantly (rho = -0.536, p = 0.215, n = 7). LLMLingua-2 reduces Ukrainian input length by 47-49% with no value loss among 80 retrievable cases. The balanced BPE tokenizer reduces the held-out UK/EN ratio from 2.22x to 1.30x. Romanization increases token counts by 2-19% on most tokenizers. Tokenization efficiency favors the script more prevalent in web training data.
AI.conclusion: Training data allocation is a contributing factor to Cyrillic tokenization overhead. Mitigation is feasible at both inference time (via compression techniques like LLMLingua-2) and at tokenizer design time (via balanced byte-level BPE training). Script prevalence in web data drives tokenization efficiency disparities across languages.

title: SchemaRouter: Field-Aware Tool Routing for Efficient Heterogeneous Agentic RAG
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Code, benchmark, and fixtures: https://github.com/JDeun/SchemaRouter_research
summary:
Heterogeneous agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems increasingly orchestrate external APIs, internal databases, vector stores, and graph stores. Exposing all tool descriptions to an LLM agent, or selecting tools only by vector similarity, causes two costly failures: over-fetching, which increases payload size, token use, and latency, and under-fetching, which omits fields needed to answer the query.
  We present SchemaRouter, a lightweight routing layer that represents tools, endpoints, parameters, response fields, domain concepts, units, provenance, and license policies as a schema graph. Given a query, SchemaRouter emits an executable tool plan specifying which tools to call and which fields to retrieve. A small LLM extracts intent, concepts, and source constraints, while field selection is deterministic over the graph through intent-group projection and concept-field matching with an alias layer.
  On a materials-science benchmark of 110 queries, SchemaRouter achieves answer accuracy of 0.71, matching fetch-everything within overlapping confidence intervals and exceeding prompt-all's 0.66, though their intervals overlap. It uses 227 retrieved-context tokens versus 2,066 for fetch-everything and achieves 2.7x lower end-to-end latency than prompt-all. It also obtains the best tool-exact rate of 0.93 and parameter validity of 1.0. SchemaRouter grounds provenance and license information in 62 percent of answers, compared with approximately 0 percent for all baselines.
  We also find that minimizing selected-field count is counterproductive: it reduces answer accuracy to 0.56 with negligible token savings, while recall-preserving projection restores top accuracy. SchemaRouter improves efficiency, schema-size-independent scaling, and verifiable provenance/license-grounded answering at competitive accuracy.

AI.tldr: SchemaRouter is a lightweight routing layer for heterogeneous agentic RAG systems that represents tools and their metadata as a schema graph. It uses a small LLM for intent extraction plus deterministic graph-based field selection to emit executable tool plans. On a materials-science benchmark, it matches fetch-everything in accuracy (0.71) while using ~90% fewer retrieved-context tokens (227 vs 2,066) and achieving 2.7x lower latency than prompt-all, with strong tool-exact rate (0.93), parameter validity (1.0), and provenance/license grounding (62%).
AI.motivation: Existing heterogeneous RAG systems that orchestrate multiple tools (APIs, databases, vector stores, graph stores) suffer from two costly routing failures: over-fetching (excessive payload size, token use, and latency) and under-fetching (missing fields needed to answer the query). Prior tool-selection approaches relying on vector similarity or exposing all tool descriptions to the LLM are insufficient for both efficiency and completeness.
AI.method: SchemaRouter builds a schema graph representing tools, endpoints, parameters, response fields, domain concepts, units, provenance, and license policies. Given a query, it uses a small LLM to extract intent, concepts, and source constraints, then deterministically performs field selection via intent-group projection and concept-field matching with an alias layer, emitting an executable tool plan that specifies which tools to call and which fields to retrieve.
AI.result: On a 110-query materials-science benchmark: answer accuracy 0.71 (matching fetch-everything, exceeding prompt-all's 0.66), 227 retrieved-context tokens vs 2,066 for fetch-everything, 2.7x lower end-to-end latency than prompt-all, best tool-exact rate 0.93, parameter validity 1.0. Provenance/license grounded in 62% of answers vs ~0% for baselines. Minimizing selected-field count hurts accuracy (0.56) with negligible token savings; recall-preserving projection restores top accuracy.
AI.conclusion: SchemaRouter demonstrates that a schema-graph-based routing approach with deterministic field selection can achieve competitive accuracy while dramatically improving efficiency (token usage, latency), providing schema-size-independent scaling, and uniquely enabling verifiable provenance and license-grounded answering. The finding that naive field-count minimization is counterproductive highlights the importance of recall-preserving projection in schema-based routing.

title: Text-Guided Visual Dependency Graph Learning with Cross-Modal Attention Priors
summary: Estimating interpretable conditional-dependence structures from multimodal visual-linguistic features remains largely unexplored. We propose CM-GLasso (Cross-Modal Graphical Lasso), a framework that bridges vision-language representation learning and sparse Gaussian Graphical Models. CM-GLasso introduces three key components: (i) a text visualization strategy that renders class-attribute descriptions as images and processes them through the same SigLIP-2 vision encoder as natural images, yielding prototype-indexed patch-level attention footprints in a shared feature coordinate system; (ii) a cross-attention distillation mechanism that condenses high-dimensional patches into a small set of semantic graph nodes, whose attention-footprint similarities yield cross-modal structural priors for non-uniform L1 penalization; (iii) a joint ADMM formulation that estimates shared and class-specific precision components within a single convex objective, avoiding the need to first estimate and then decompose separate class-wise graphs. The learned sparse graph topologies directly support a parameter-free, precision-based classification rule and a lightweight topology-aware segmentation head. Extensive experiments on eight benchmarks demonstrate that CM-GLasso achieves competitive or superior performance compared with strong feature-based and task-specific baselines. Under the matched controlled protocol, it attains the highest average classification accuracy (91.97%) and the highest segmentation mIoU among the controlled baselines on VOC (74.75%) and ADE20K (64.01%), while also yielding explicit sparse conditional-dependence graphs with common-specific decomposition.

AI.tldr: CM-GLasso is a novel framework that bridges vision-language representation learning with sparse Gaussian Graphical Models, estimating interpretable conditional-dependence structures from multimodal visual-linguistic features. It introduces text-to-image visualization, cross-attention distillation for graph node construction, and a joint ADMM-based convex optimization for shared and class-specific precision matrices. It achieves state-of-the-art or competitive results on eight benchmarks, with top classification accuracy (91.97%) and segmentation mIoU on VOC (74.75%) and ADE20K (64.01%) under controlled protocols.
AI.motivation: Estimating interpretable conditional-dependence structures from multimodal visual-linguistic features remains largely unexplored. Existing approaches lack a principled way to model sparse dependencies across modalities while maintaining interpretability, and typically require separate estimation then decomposition of class-wise graphs.
AI.method: CM-GLasso consists of three key components: (i) a text visualization strategy that renders class-attribute descriptions as images and processes them through the same SigLIP-2 vision encoder as natural images, yielding prototype-indexed patch-level attention footprints in a shared feature space; (ii) a cross-attention distillation mechanism that condenses high-dimensional patches into a small set of semantic graph nodes, whose attention-footprint similarities provide cross-modal structural priors for non-uniform L1 penalization; (iii) a joint ADMM formulation that estimates shared and class-specific precision components within a single convex objective. The learned sparse graph topologies enable a parameter-free, precision-based classification rule and a lightweight topology-aware segmentation head.
AI.result: Experiments on eight benchmarks show CM-GLasso achieves competitive or superior performance against strong feature-based and task-specific baselines. Under the matched controlled protocol, it achieves the highest average classification accuracy (91.97%) and the highest segmentation mIoU among controlled baselines on VOC (74.75%) and ADE20K (64.01%), while also producing explicit sparse conditional-dependence graphs with common-specific decomposition.
AI.conclusion: CM-GLasso demonstrates that coupling multimodal representation learning with sparse Gaussian Graphical Models yields both strong task performance and interpretable graph structures. The joint convex formulation overcomes limitations of prior two-stage approaches, and the resulting precision-based classifier and topology-aware segmentation head show broad applicability across classification and dense prediction tasks.

title: Selective Cross-View Consistency for World Action Models: Held-Out Viewpoint Robustness Without Test-Time Camera Information
summary: World action models (WAMs) jointly denoise future video frames and robot actions, and the video prior is expected to generalize their control. Camera viewpoint change remains one of their hardest perturbation axes. We study a question specific to this model class: when training with same-state cross-view image pairs, on which output coordinates should a consistency loss be imposed? The WAM denoising target mixes view-covariant coordinates, namely the predicted future scene, with view-invariant coordinates, namely the action chunk, future proprioception, and value. We show that consistency applied to the covariant block is provably harmful, shrinking legitimate view-specific content to a fraction $1/(1+4λ)$ of its true value, and we verify this shrinkage law in controlled experiments. Selective cross-view consistency (SCVC) therefore constrains only the invariant block, requires no camera labels, extrinsics, depth, or view synthesis at training or test time, and leaves the deployment interface unchanged. We introduce a carve-and-hold-out evaluation protocol on the LIBERO-Plus camera track that separates a distribution-matched ceiling from genuine interpolation and extrapolation to held-out viewpoints, with a matched pair-trained control isolating the effect of the consistency term from pair exposure. On held-out orbital viewpoints beyond the training envelope, SCVC improves closed-loop success over the matched control by 12.2 points (95% CI [7.4, 17.0]; +15.5, CI [11.7, 19.4], under an independent second seed) -- an effect two further camera axes replicate -- while interpolation within the envelope shows no gain in either seed (-1.2 and -4.3 points) and in-distribution competence is preserved (-0.6, -0.2). We also report a cross-backbone audit showing that published camera-robustness numbers are confounded by wrist-camera pose stability.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates where consistency loss should be applied when training world action models (WAMs) with cross-view image pairs. It proves that applying consistency to view-covariant (scene) coordinates is provably harmful, shrinking legitimate content by 1/(1+4λ), and proposes Selective Cross-View Consistency (SCVC) that constrains only view-invariant coordinates (actions, proprioception, value), requiring no camera labels or extrinsics. SCVC improves closed-loop success on held-out camera viewpoints by ~12-15 points while preserving in-distribution performance.
AI.motivation: World action models (WAMs) struggle with camera viewpoint changes, one of their hardest perturbation axes. The authors seek to determine the correct output coordinates for enforcing cross-view consistency when training with same-state cross-view image pairs, since naive consistency on all outputs may be harmful.
AI.method: The authors theoretically analyze the WAM denoising target which mixes view-covariant (predicted scene) and view-invariant (action, proprioception, value) coordinates. They prove consistency on the covariant block shrinks legitimate view-specific content to 1/(1+4λ) of its true value, and verify this shrinkage law experimentally. They propose SCVC which constrains only the invariant block, requiring no camera labels, extrinsics, depth, or view synthesis. They introduce a carve-and-hold-out evaluation protocol on LIBERO-Plus with matched pair-trained controls, and conduct a cross-backbone audit for confounds.
AI.result: On held-out orbital viewpoints, SCVC improves closed-loop success by 12.2 points (95% CI [7.4, 17.0]; +15.5 under a second seed) over the matched control, replicated across two further camera axes. Interpolation within the training envelope shows no gain (-1.2, -4.3 points), and in-distribution competence is preserved (-0.6, -0.2). The shrinkage law 1/(1+4λ) is verified in controlled experiments, and a cross-backbone audit reveals published camera-robustness numbers are confounded by wrist-camera pose stability.
AI.conclusion: Cross-view consistency for WAMs should be applied only to view-invariant outputs, not to covariant scene predictions, since consistency on covariant coordinates is provably harmful. SCVC provides camera-robust generalization without requiring any camera geometry information, and evaluation protocols must account for confounds like wrist-camera pose stability when reporting camera robustness claims.

title: A Social Media Analysis of Discourse on the Israel--Palestine Conflict on Telegram
summary: Social media has become a central arena in which armed conflicts are contested, yet the pro-Israel and pro-Palestine communities on Telegram, whose broadcast architecture yields an unusually direct record of deliberate political communication, have not been systematically compared at scale. This study presents a multi-method computational analysis of 87,617 messages from sixteen Telegram channels, eight pro-Israel and eight pro-Palestine, spanning May 2021 to June 2026 and covering multiple conflict escalations. It combines sentiment analysis, three stance detection methods drawn from distinct paradigms (keyword matching, zero-shot DeBERTa via natural language inference, and a fine-tuned BERTweet model), and a framing analysis, all evaluated against 736 manually annotated messages. The fine-tuned model performed best (72.1% accuracy, 0.721 macro F1 under 5-fold cross-validation), outperforming both label-free baselines by 8 to 11 points; the baselines stalled in the low-to-mid 60s, indicating a hard ceiling for stance detection not adapted to in-domain language. The central finding emerges only when sentiment, stance, and framing are read together: the two communities deploy the same death- and victim-related vocabulary in opposite emotional registers, pro-Israel channels predominantly neutral and report-style, pro-Palestine channels markedly more negative, consistent with writing from the distinct discourse positions of acting party and affected party.

AI.tldr: A multi-method computational analysis of 87,617 messages from 16 Telegram channels (8 pro-Israel, 8 pro-Palestine) between May 2021 and June 2026 reveals that both communities use identical death- and victim-related vocabulary but in opposite emotional registers—pro-Israel channels are neutral and report-style while pro-Palestine channels are markedly more negative—reflecting their discursive positions as acting party versus affected party.
AI.motivation: Social media has become a critical arena for contesting armed conflicts, yet the pro-Israel and pro-Palestine communities on Telegram—whose broadcast architecture provides an unusually direct record of deliberate political communication—have never been systematically compared at scale. This gap motivates a large-scale, multi-method comparative analysis of both communities across multiple conflict escalations.
AI.method: The study analyzes 87,617 messages from sixteen Telegram channels (eight per community) spanning May 2021 to June 2026. It employs sentiment analysis, three distinct stance detection methods (keyword matching, zero-shot DeBERTa via natural language inference, and a fine-tuned BERTweet model), and framing analysis, all validated against 736 manually annotated messages with 5-fold cross-validation.
AI.result: The fine-tuned BERTweet model achieved the best performance (72.1% accuracy, 0.721 macro F1), outperforming both label-free baselines by 8–11 points; the baselines stalled in the low-to-mid 60s, demonstrating a hard ceiling for stance detection not adapted to in-domain language. The central finding is that both communities share the same death- and victim-related vocabulary but with opposite emotional registers: pro-Israel channels are predominantly neutral and report-style, while pro-Palestine channels are markedly more negative.
AI.conclusion: The emotional asymmetry between the two communities is not attributable to vocabulary differences but to divergent discourse positions—pro-Israel channels write from the standpoint of the acting party (neutral, reportorial), while pro-Palestine channels write from the standpoint of the affected party (emotionally negative). This finding underscores the necessity of integrating sentiment, stance, and framing analyses to uncover latent communicative patterns in conflict-related social media.

title: RIACT: A Responsible AI System for Personalized Study Habit Tracking and Early Burnout Signal Detection in University Students
comment: 11 pages. Also available on EdArXiv: https://doi.org/10.35542/osf.io/94hr5_v1
summary: Student burnout is highly prevalent in higher education, with reported rates ranging from 12% to over 70% and consistently exceeding those of the working population - yet it is typically identified only retrospectively, after academic decline has already occurred. A contributing factor is that students have little structured visibility into their own study behaviour, and existing productivity tools record activity without interpreting it. This paper presents RIACT (Record, Insight, Analyze, Coach, Track), a web-based application that combines structured study session logging with a hybrid AI architecture to surface personalized insights and early burnout signals. Students log sessions by location and time; the system computes net focus time by accounting for breaks, detects burnout signals through transparent, deterministic rules operating on week-over-week behavioural comparisons, and uses a large language model - constrained to a fixed output schema - to contextualize patterns and generate personalized recommendations. The design embeds responsible AI principles throughout: warnings are governed by auditable rules rather than model judgement, all output is framed as an observation rather than a diagnosis and data collection is limited to self-logged behavioural fields. We describe the system's design rationale, situate it within the literature on student burnout and explainable AI in education and propose an evaluation framework for validating its behavioural signals against established burnout instruments.

AI.tldr: RIACT is a web-based application combining structured study session logging with a hybrid AI architecture (deterministic rules + LLM) to provide students with personalized insights and early burnout signals, grounded in responsible AI principles.
AI.motivation: Student burnout is highly prevalent (12-70%+) and exceeds working population rates, yet is typically only identified retrospectively after academic decline. Students lack structured visibility into their own study behavior, and existing productivity tools record activity without interpreting it.
AI.method: RIACT combines structured study session logging (by location and time) with a hybrid AI architecture: (1) deterministic, auditable rules compute net focus time and detect burnout signals via week-over-week behavioral comparisons; (2) a large language model constrained to a fixed output schema contextualizes patterns and generates personalized recommendations. Design embeds responsible AI principles: auditable rules for warnings rather than model judgment, outputs framed as observations rather than diagnoses, and data limited to self-logged behavioral fields.
AI.result: The paper describes the system's design rationale and situates it within literature on student burnout and explainable AI in education, and proposes an evaluation framework for validating its behavioral signals against established burnout instruments.
AI.conclusion: RIACT addresses the gap between activity recording and interpretation in study tools by pairing transparent rule-based burnout detection with LLM-based contextualized recommendations, with a proposed evaluation framework to validate its behavioral signals against established burnout instruments.

title: ViTexSZ: Heterogeneous Vision-Text Knowledge Distillation for EEG Seizure Detection
summary: Automated seizure detection from electroencephalography (EEG) is essential for continuous neurological monitoring, particularly for subclinical epileptic seizures that may exhibit only subtle electrographic changes. Existing time-series methods are often designed for fixed EEG channel configurations, thereby limiting their applicability to heterogeneous EEG recordings with irregular channel layouts. Although visual and language modeling offer promising alternatives, aligning heterogeneous EEG representations with clinical semantics remains challenging. We introduce ViTexSZ, a heterogeneous Vision-Text knowledge distillation framework for EEG seizure detection. ViTexSZ converts EEG recordings into structured waveform images and introduces a query-based multi-channel alignment module that maps source-dependent visual features into a unified token space. A heterogeneous teacher further integrates the aligned EEG representations with clinical prompts through a multimodal large language model, associating high-level clinical semantics with seizure-related evidence. Vision-text knowledge distillation then transfers the teacher representations to a lightweight student during detection. Experiments on four EEG seizure datasets demonstrate the generalizability of ViTexSZ across both subclinical and general seizure detection scenarios, achieving the highest accuracy on all datasets and relative improvements of up to 12.9% over the second-best baselines, showing its effectiveness.

AI.tldr: ViTexSZ is a heterogeneous Vision-Text knowledge distillation framework for EEG seizure detection that converts EEG into waveform images, aligns multi-channel visual features into a unified token space, integrates clinical semantics via a multimodal LLM teacher, and distills knowledge to a lightweight student, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy across four seizure datasets with up to 12.9% relative improvement.
AI.motivation: Automated EEG seizure detection is critical for continuous neurological monitoring, especially for subclinical seizures with subtle electrographic changes. However, existing time-series methods assume fixed EEG channel configurations and struggle with heterogeneous recordings having irregular layouts. While visual and language models offer alternatives, aligning heterogeneous EEG representations with clinical semantics remains a significant challenge.
AI.method: ViTexSZ converts EEG recordings into structured waveform images and introduces a query-based multi-channel alignment module that maps source-dependent visual features into a unified token space. A heterogeneous teacher integrates aligned EEG representations with clinical prompts through a multimodal large language model to associate high-level clinical semantics with seizure-related evidence. Vision-text knowledge distillation then transfers teacher representations to a lightweight student during detection.
AI.result: Experiments on four EEG seizure datasets demonstrate the generalizability of ViTexSZ across both subclinical and general seizure detection scenarios. The method achieves the highest accuracy on all datasets with relative improvements of up to 12.9% over the second-best baselines.
AI.conclusion: ViTexSZ effectively addresses heterogeneous EEG seizure detection by combining vision-text knowledge distillation with multimodal LLM-based clinical semantic alignment, demonstrating robust generalization across diverse seizure types and datasets.

title: Tolerance-Dependent Inspection Disagreement Between a Fixed CMM and a Portable Articulated-Arm CMM
summary: Fixed coordinate measuring machines (CMMs) and portable articulated-arm CMMs are often assigned to the same inspection task, but their nominal accuracy specifications do not show whether a change of instrument will preserve the disposition of a part. The question is not simply how far the two results differ, but whether that difference crosses the tolerance boundary. We examined this issue with recorded measurements of cylindrical, cubic, and spherical features under nominal 20 °C and 30 °C conditions. Repeated records and two roughness profiles without sufficient acquisition information were removed, leaving six dimensional and four form profiles. For each dimensional feature, the distances of the two system means from nominal define the exact tolerance interval in which the systems receive opposite direct labels. The fixed-CMM stream was approximately 11.2 μm higher than the articulated-arm stream at both conditions. All four form profiles fell on opposite sides of the recorded 10 μm upper limit. The dimensional disagreement intervals also overlapped strongly; their mean widths were 6.573 μm at 20 °C and 4.995 μm at 30 °C. The results clarify why an average difference between instruments is not, by itself, a measure of substitution risk. The proposed tolerance map identifies the feature-tolerance combinations for which instrument choice can change the recorded inspection label and, therefore, where a controlled equivalence study and a task-specific uncertainty budget are needed before substitution.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether substituting fixed coordinate measuring machines (CMMs) for portable articulated-arm CMMs preserves part disposition under tolerance limits, using dimensional and form measurements of cylindrical, cubic, and spherical features at 20°C and 30°C. Results show the fixed-CMM stream runs ~11.2 μm higher, all form profiles cross the 10 μm upper limit, and dimensional disagreement intervals (mean widths 6.573 μm at 20°C and 4.995 μm at 30°C) overlap strongly—demonstrating that average differences alone do not indicate substitution risk. The proposed tolerance map identifies feature-tolerance combinations where instrument choice can flip inspection labels, guiding where equivalence studies and task-specific uncertainty budgets are required.
AI.motivation: Fixed CMMs and portable articulated-arm CMMs are often assigned interchangeably to the same inspection task, yet nominal accuracy specifications do not reveal whether switching instruments changes part disposition relative to tolerance boundaries. The core question is not simply the magnitude of measurement difference but whether that difference crosses the tolerance limit.
AI.method: Recorded measurements of cylindrical, cubic, and spherical features were collected under nominal 20°C and 30°C conditions using both instrument types. After removing repeated records and two roughness profiles lacking acquisition information, six dimensional and four form profiles remained. For each dimensional feature, distances of the two system means from nominal defined the tolerance interval where opposite direct labels occur. Mean differences and disagreement interval widths were computed at both temperature conditions.
AI.result: The fixed-CMM stream was approximately 11.2 μm higher than the articulated-arm stream at both conditions. All four form profiles fell on opposite sides of the 10 μm upper limit. Dimensional disagreement intervals overlapped strongly, with mean widths of 6.573 μm at 20°C and 4.995 μm at 30°C.
AI.conclusion: An average difference between instruments is not by itself a measure of substitution risk. The proposed tolerance map identifies feature-tolerance combinations where instrument choice can change the recorded inspection label, indicating where controlled equivalence studies and task-specific uncertainty budgets are needed before instrument substitution.

title: Mitigating Bias in Large Vision-Language Models via Counterfactual Ensemble Decoding
summary: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across a wide range of tasks; however, they often inherit social biases from their training data, resulting in biased behavior when processing portraits from different social groups. Existing debiasing approaches typically compare token probabilities between the original and biased generations during decoding, but they are fundamentally limited by their reliance on a single, stereotyped viewpoint and fail to account for the diversity of social perspectives. Inspired by the social science principle that diversity fosters fairness, we propose Counterfactual Ensemble Decoding (CED), a novel framework that constructs multi-group counterfactual perspectives within the visual representation space and integrates them during decoding to promote equitable model behavior. CED first performs counterfactual steering in the visual space by identifying semantic directions associated with each social group and generating counterfactual representations along these directions, thereby offering diverse perspectives that disrupt stereotypical narratives. During decoding, CED locates the decoder layer exhibiting the greatest divergence among these perspectives and ensembles their token distributions using uncertainty-aware weights, prioritizing high-confidence tokens from different groups to yield a more balanced probability distribution that guides fairer generation. Extensive experiments on three social bias evaluation benchmarks demonstrate that \tool achieves substantial improvements over leading baselines, reducing bias by up to 47.97% across scenarios involving occupations, descriptors, and persona traits. Moreover, CED also preserves the core capabilities of the original model with minimal degradation.

AI.tldr: CED is a novel framework that constructs multi-group counterfactual perspectives in visual representation space and ensembles them during decoding to reduce social biases in LVLMs, achieving up to 47.97% bias reduction while preserving core model capabilities.
AI.motivation: Existing debiasing approaches for LVLMs rely on comparing token probabilities between original and stereotyped generations, which is fundamentally limited by dependence on a single stereotyped viewpoint and fails to account for the diversity of social perspectives.
AI.method: CED first performs counterfactual steering in visual space by identifying semantic directions for each social group and generating counterfactual representations along those directions, creating diverse perspectives. During decoding, it locates the decoder layer with the greatest divergence among these perspectives and ensembles their token distributions using uncertainty-aware weights, prioritizing high-confidence tokens from different groups to produce a balanced probability distribution.
AI.result: On three social bias evaluation benchmarks, CED reduces bias by up to 47.97% across occupations, descriptors, and persona traits, surpassing leading baselines while causing minimal degradation to the original model's core capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Grounding in the social science principle that diversity fosters fairness, CED demonstrates that constructing and ensembling multi-group counterfactual visual perspectives effectively mitigates social bias in LVLMs without significantly sacrificing performance.

title: There Is No Neutral Harness: Modern LLM Leaderboards Are Manufactured by Config-Fragile Items
summary: Multiple-choice benchmarks fix the questions and the correct answers, but not the harness: the order of the options, the wording of the prompt, and whether a language model's answer is read from generated text or from per-option likelihoods. Work on this harness sensitivity reports it as aggregate score variance, leaving unexamined which items the variance falls on and whether they are the items that separate one model from the next. We treat the evaluation harness of large language models (LLMs) as an independent variable and resolve its effect to single items. We introduce the \textit{fragility grid}: 12 open-weight instruction-tuned LLMs from 4 families answer the same 3{,}679 items from 4 benchmarks (ARC, HellaSwag, MMLU, TruthfulQA) under 26 equally defensible harness configurations, recording one correctness bit for every model, item, and configuration. The comparison is matched, since the items, the weights, and the greedy decoding stay fixed while only the harness varies. Under the grid a model's score is a band rather than a point: gemma4-31b scores between 31 and 89 percent depending only on the harness. Three results follow. On the items that two adjacent models both answer stably the pair is tied, and config-fragile items carry 95.7 percent of a pair's gap on average. Four of the 12 models reach rank one under some configuration, so the harness selects the winner. Item discrimination, the property that benchmark-compression methods maximize, correlates with fragility at 0.28 (95 percent CI 0.25 to 0.30), so compression keeps the fragile items rather than removing them. The scoring choice, not the option order that protocols usually fix, is the load-bearing axis. We release the per-item records and the analysis script, from which every number regenerates on a CPU in seconds, and we position the fragility grid as a check a leaderboard can run before it reports an order.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the "fragility grid": a matched, per-item analysis of how evaluation harness choices (option order, prompt wording, scoring method) affect LLM benchmark results. 12 models, 3,679 items, 26 harness configurations show that model scores are bands, not points, harness configuration can select the winner, fragile items dominate model-pair gaps, and benchmark compression methods retain fragile items.
AI.motivation: Prior work treats harness sensitivity as aggregate score variance, without examining which specific items are affected or whether harness-induced variance lands on items that actually separate competing models. This obscures whether reported leaderboard rankings are robust to arbitrary evaluation-harness choices.
AI.method: The authors construct a "fragility grid": 12 open-weight instruction-tuned LLMs from 4 families evaluated on 3,679 items from 4 benchmarks (ARC, HellaSwag, MMLU, TruthfulQA) under 26 equally defensible harness configurations. The design is matched—items, weights, and greedy decoding are fixed, with only the harness varying—yielding one correctness bit per model, item, and configuration, enabling per-item resolution of harness effects.
AI.result: Model scores form bands rather than points (gemma4-31b ranges from 31 to 89 percent depending on harness). Stably answered items between adjacent model pairs are ties, and config-fragile items carry 95.7% of a pair's score gap on average. Four of 12 models can reach rank one under some configuration. Item discrimination correlates with fragility at 0.28 (95% CI 0.25–0.30), meaning compression methods keep fragile items. The scoring choice (likelihood vs. generated text) is the load-bearing axis, not option order.
AI.conclusion: Harness configuration is a decisive variable in LLM evaluation that must be accounted for before reporting leaderboard orders. The authors release per-item records and analysis scripts so all numbers regenerate on a CPU in seconds, and position the fragility grid as a standard check before rankings are published.

title: BIMScript: Material-Aware Structured Scene Programs for BIM Ingestion
comment: Project Page: see https://bimscriptworld.github.io/BIMScript/ ; to be published in ECCV 2026 TwinWorld Workshop
summary: Structured-language models such as SceneScript reconstruct a scene as a short program of parametric commands, an inherently editable and semantically explicit representation. We ask three questions that stand between such models and their most compelling application, automated ingestion of existing buildings into BIM tools, studied here on synthetic scans: \emph{what} is the scene made of, \emph{how fast} can it be produced, and \emph{exactly where} is each element. BIMScript answers all three within one grammar. First, we extend the layout language with per-element \emph{material} and \emph{condition} attributes, supervised by a vision-language-model material-passport corpus we build over 100k synthetic scenes (1.9M pseudo-labeled elements), and route image appearance to the material tokens through a lifted-feature point encoder. Second, we show that autoregressive decoding of these programs is dominated not by compute but by kernel-launch and host-synchronization overhead, and remove it with an output-exact CUDA-graph decoder (1.9 vs 6.4\,ms/step, $3.4\times$) plus a grammar-parallel, tolerance-verified draft-and-verify scheme that exploits the deterministic entity schema. Third, we address the model's 5cm token-grid granularity with training-free geometric snapping and a hybrid discrete--continuous decoder head that regresses a sub-bin offset, and measure how much of the residual error each recovers. Because each command maps one-to-one onto a native Revit object, we validate direct ingestion into a BIM authoring tool end to end with a working add-in and its IFC4 export, and the same program's language form is designed to support LLM-driven, sustainability-aware reasoning over the built asset.

AI.tldr: BIMScript is a structured-language scene reconstruction model that outputs parametric programs of commands, addressing three challenges for automated BIM ingestion: scene content (what materials/conditions elements have), speed (overcoming autoregressive decoding overhead with CUDA graphs and a draft-and-verify scheme, 3.4x faster), and geometric accuracy (overcoming 5cm token-grid granularity with geometric snapping and a hybrid discrete-continuous decoder head). The system is validated end-to-end via direct ingestion into Revit with IFC4 export.
AI.motivation: Structured-language scene models like SceneScript produce editable, semantically explicit program representations, but their most compelling application—automated ingestion of existing buildings into BIM tools—is blocked by three gaps: no material/condition semantics per element, slow decoding bottlenecked by kernel-launch overhead rather than compute, and coarse token-grid geometric precision (5cm).
AI.method: (1) Extends the layout language with per-element material and condition attributes, trained on a VLM-generated material-passport corpus over 100k synthetic scenes (1.9M pseudo-labeled elements), using a lifted-feature point encoder to route image appearance to material tokens. (2) Removes decode overhead with an output-exact CUDA-graph decoder (1.9 vs 6.4 ms/step, 3.4x) plus a grammar-parallel, tolerance-verified draft-and-verify scheme exploiting the deterministic entity schema. (3) Addresses 5cm quantization with training-free geometric snapping and a hybrid discrete-continuous decoder head regressing sub-bin offsets.
AI.result: CUDA-graph decoding achieves 1.9 ms/step vs 6.4 ms/step baseline (3.4x speedup). A working Revit add-in validates direct end-to-end ingestion of synthetic scenes into BIM authoring tools with IFC4 export. The language form also supports LLM-driven, sustainability-aware reasoning over built assets.
AI.conclusion: BIMScript demonstrates that a single, unified grammar can address scene content, production speed, and geometric precision for automated BIM ingestion, validated with a working Revit add-in and IFC4 export, positioning structured-language scene models as a practical path to building digital twins.

title: Mamba-based Selective State Space Modeling Improves the Accuracy-Complexity Tradeoff of SmolVLA Vision-Language-Action Experts
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models face a crucial tradeoff between their task success rate and the policy-call frequency. Executing a single action per inference ($N=1$) enables accurate robot control but comes at the cost of huge compute time overheads, making real-time implementation infeasible. On the other hand, executing longer action horizons before replanning ($N\gg1$) reduces compute complexity, but inevitably degrades the system's success rate. In order to improve the VLA accuracy-complexity tradeoff, this paper investigates Mamba's selective state-space modeling as an alternative to causal self-attention within the action expert of the popular SmolVLA model, widely used as a reference model for its highly accurate yet low complexity nature. We evaluate both the Mamba- and Transformer-based experts on the widely-adopted LIBERO benchmark suites across three execution horizons $N\!\in\!\{1,25,50\}$, respectively corresponding to high, moderate and low compute complexities. Our results remarkably show that the advantage of the Mamba expert increases with the execution horizon, indicating significant success retention under long execution horizons $N = 50$ and $N = 25$. When $N = 50$ actions are executed before replanning (i.e., corresponding to feasible real-time deployment), the Mamba expert outperforms the Transformer baseline by $7.8\%$. In addition, when $N = 25$ actions are executed before replanning, our Mamba expert outperforms the Transformer baseline by $3.7\%$. Finally, under per-action replanning ($N=1$), our Mamba variant matches the Transformer-based mean success rate while significantly reducing the overall model parameter complexity by $24\%$ thanks to Mamba's compute-efficient nature.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates using Mamba's selective state-space modeling as an alternative to causal self-attention in the action expert of the SmolVLA model to improve the accuracy-complexity tradeoff. Across three execution horizons (N=1, 25, 50) on LIBERO benchmarks, the Mamba expert shows increasing advantage with longer horizons, outperforming the Transformer baseline by 7.8% at N=50, 3.7% at N=25, and matching it at N=1 while reducing parameter complexity by 24%.
AI.motivation: VLA models face a fundamental tradeoff between task success rate and policy-call frequency. Executing one action per inference (N=1) is accurate but computationally infeasible for real-time deployment, while longer action horizons (N≫1) reduce compute but degrade success rates. The paper aims to improve this accuracy-complexity tradeoff.
AI.method: The paper replaces the causal self-attention mechanism with Mamba's selective state-space modeling within the action expert of the SmolVLA model. Both Mamba- and Transformer-based experts are evaluated on the LIBERO benchmark suites across three execution horizons N ∈ {1, 25, 50}, corresponding to high, moderate, and low compute complexities.
AI.result: The Mamba expert's advantage increases with execution horizon. At N=50 (feasible real-time deployment), Mamba outperforms the Transformer baseline by 7.8%. At N=25, Mamba improves by 3.7%. At N=1, Mamba matches the Transformer's mean success rate while reducing model parameter complexity by 24%.
AI.conclusion: Mamba's selective state-space modeling provides a superior accuracy-complexity tradeoff for VLA action experts, particularly excelling at long execution horizons where real-time deployment is feasible, while also offering significant parameter efficiency gains at low horizons without sacrificing accuracy.

title: Agentic Security: A Systematization of Tools, Failure Modes, and Design Laws for LLM-Driven Penetration Testing
summary: Agentic security uses large-language-model (LLM) agents to plan, dispatch, and interpret security tools. As these systems move from demonstrations to deployed products, practitioners repeatedly encounter the same operational failures. We systematize these failures through a hands-on evaluation of ten widely used static, dynamic, cloud, orchestration, and AI red-teaming tools for unattended pipelines. We introduce a four-dimensional Integration Friction Index that separates one-time engineering cost from recurring organisational, legal, and maintenance cost. We then derive quantitative regularities that explain recurring failure modes. Modelling an agentic security system as stochastic LLM policies wrapped by a deterministic mediator, we show that long-lived sessions lose resident evidence with phase count, while short-lived sub-agents extend the usable horizon according to the compression ratio between raw evidence and its summary. We show that a two-stage verdict cascade multiplies scorer likelihood ratios, but provides little benefit when scorer errors correlate. We show that treating unevaluable outcomes as attack failures biases downstream measurements toward evasive and severe responses. We formulate planner-versus-worker model routing as a knapsack problem and derive a closed-form execution cap for heavy-tailed tools, eta* = alpha v/c. Finally, we show why scope and budget enforcement cannot be delegated to system prompts: prompts do not constrain what actually executes. Inspectra, our implemented platform, serves as a worked instantiation, with mechanisms labelled shipped, partial, or planned, including those that did not work.

AI.tldr: This paper systematizes operational failures in agentic security systems through hands-on evaluation of ten security tools. It introduces a four-dimensional Integration Friction Index, derives quantitative regularities explaining recurring failure modes, and presents Inspectra, an implemented platform serving as a worked instantiation.
AI.motivation: As LLM-agent-based security systems move from demonstrations to deployed products, practitioners consistently encounter the same operational failures. These failures have not been systematically analyzed, motivating the authors to systematize recurring issues through hands-on evaluation.
AI.method: The authors conduct a hands-on evaluation of ten widely used security tools (static, dynamic, cloud, orchestration, and AI red-teaming) for unattended pipelines. They introduce a four-dimensional Integration Friction Index separating one-time engineering cost from recurring organizational, legal, and maintenance cost. They model agentic security systems as stochastic LLM policies wrapped by a deterministic mediator, and derive quantitative regularities for failure modes: resident evidence loss with session length, two-stage verdict cascades as likelihood ratio multiplication, unevaluable outcome bias, planner-versus-worker routing as a knapsack problem with closed-form execution cap eta* = alpha v/c, and scope/budget enforcement limitations of system prompts.
AI.result: The authors derive several quantitative regularities: long-lived sessions lose resident evidence with phase count while short-lived sub-agents extend usable horizon according to compression ratio; two-stage verdict cascades multiply scorer likelihood ratios but provide little benefit when errors correlate; treating unevaluable outcomes as failures biases measurements toward evasive/severe responses; derive closed-form execution cap eta* = alpha v/c for heavy-tailed tools; and show system prompts cannot enforce scope/budget constraints on actual execution. They implement Inspectra as a worked instantiation.
AI.conclusion: Agentic security failures are systematizable and quantifiable. The Integration Friction Index separates cost dimensions, and the derived regularities provide predictive models for failure modes. Inspectra demonstrates both what works and what does not in practice, labeling mechanisms as shipped, partial, or planned.

title: Spyre-Accelerated Retrieval-Augmented Generation on IBM LinuxONE: A Cloud-Native Architecture for Secure, High-Throughput Enterprise AI Inference
summary:
Running large language models inside enterprise environments has always bumped up against a practical wall: the data lives in one place, the AI horsepower sits somewhere else, and moving sensitive records between the two creates real headaches around latency, security, and regulatory exposure. IBM's Spyre accelerator PCIe inference card built for LinuxONE and the broader IBM Z family changes that equation.
  In this paper we lay out a six-subsystem RAG architecture that runs entirely on IBM LinuxONE, using Spyre for generative inference, the Telum II on-chip accelerator for lightweight classification tasks, and Red Hat OpenShift for container orchestration. Every piece of the pipeline from query intake through vector retrieval, prompt assembly, LLM inference, compliance filtering, and response delivery stays within a single LinuxONE system, so sensitive data never has to leave the hardware perimeter.
  We walk through the design choices behind each subsystem, dig into the Spyre compilation and serving stack, explain how LinuxONE's Secure Execution technology extends confidential-computing guarantees to AI workloads, and benchmark the architecture against cloud-GPU and on-premises alternatives. Early analysis points to end-to-end RAG latencies under two seconds and up to a 20x reduction compared to off-platform inference, all while keeping the strong encryption and auditability posture that regulated industries actually need.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a six-subsystem RAG architecture running entirely on IBM LinuxONE using the Spyre accelerator for LLM inference, Telum II for classification, and OpenShift for orchestration, keeping all data within a single hardware perimeter. Benchmarks suggest sub-two-second end-to-end latencies and up to 20x reduction versus off-platform inference.
AI.motivation: Enterprises face challenges deploying LLMs in regulated environments where sensitive data cannot leave their infrastructure due to latency, security, and regulatory concerns. Traditional cloud-GPU inference requires moving data off-premises, creating friction in confidential or regulated industries.
AI.method: The authors design a six-subsystem RAG pipeline (query intake, vector retrieval, prompt assembly, LLM inference, compliance filtering, response delivery) all hosted on IBM LinuxONE, using Spyre for generative AI inference, Telum II's on-chip accelerator for lightweight classification tasks, and Red Hat OpenShift for orchestration. They detail the Spyre compilation/serving stack and leverage LinuxONE Secure Execution for confidential-computing guarantees.
AI.result: Early analysis shows end-to-end RAG latencies under two seconds and up to a 20x reduction compared to off-platform inference alternatives, while maintaining the strong encryption and auditability posture required by regulated industries. Benchmarks compare against cloud-GPU and on-premises alternatives.
AI.conclusion: The architecture demonstrates that enterprise-grade RAG workloads can run entirely within a single LinuxONE system, eliminating the need to move sensitive data off-premises while achieving competitive performance—making it a viable alternative to cloud-GPU deployments for regulated industries.

title: Beyond Visual Similarity: Entity-Aligned Retrieval for Knowledge-Based Visual Question Answering
summary: Knowledge-Based Visual Question Answering (KB-VQA) relies on retrieving external information to answer queries involving long-tail entities. However, existing retrieval pipelines predominantly employ CLIP-style dual encoders, which prioritize surface-level visual similarity over entity-level semantic alignment. This paradigm often fails when semantically identical concepts exhibit large visual variations or when distinct entities appear visually similar. To address this, we propose KBMR, the first MLLM-based embedding retriever tailored for KB-VQA. Leveraging the robust autoregressive capabilities of MLLMs, KBMR maps images into a semantic space that better preserves concept identity. To tackle the challenge of noisy supervision in Wikipedia-scale retrieval, we introduce an MLLM-based semantic discriminator that generates continuous entity-consistency weights. These weights guide a novel continuous semantic distillation objective, enabling effective hard negative sampling and soft supervision beyond rigid binary labels. Extensive experiments demonstrate that KBMR significantly outperforms CLIP baselines, yielding up to a 14.7% improvement in retrieval Recall@1 and a 9.4% gain in end-to-end VQA accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/realHarryX/KBMR.

AI.tldr: KBMR is the first MLLM-based embedding retriever for Knowledge-Based Visual Question Answering, addressing the failure of CLIP-style dual encoders in long-tail entity retrieval. It leverages MLLMs' autoregressive capabilities for semantic alignment, and introduces an MLLM-based semantic discriminator with continuous entity-consistency weights to guide a novel continuous semantic distillation objective, achieving up to 14.7% improvement in retrieval Recall@1 and 9.4% gain in end-to-end VQA accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing KB-VQA retrieval pipelines use CLIP-style dual encoders that prioritize surface-level visual similarity over entity-level semantic alignment, failing when semantically identical concepts exhibit large visual variations or distinct entities appear visually similar—a critical limitation for long-tail entity queries.
AI.method: KBMR is an MLLM-based embedding retriever that leverages the autoregressive capabilities of MLLMs to map images into a semantic space preserving concept identity. It also introduces an MLLM-based semantic discriminator generating continuous entity-consistency weights, which guide a novel continuous semantic distillation objective for effective hard negative sampling and soft supervision beyond rigid binary labels.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show KBMR significantly outperforms CLIP baselines, achieving up to 14.7% improvement in retrieval Recall@1 and a 9.4% gain in end-to-end VQA accuracy.
AI.conclusion: KBMR demonstrates that MLLM-based retrieval with continuous semantic distillation effectively addresses the entity-level alignment shortcomings of CLIP-style encoders in KB-VQA, providing a new paradigm for long-tail knowledge retrieval.

title: Position: Robot Privacy as Embodied Boundary Work. Connecting Capabilities, Contexts, and Design Responses in Everyday Robotics
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Accepted for publication in UbiComp Companion '26
summary: Robots are increasingly entering everyday environments where privacy is shaped not only by data practices, but also by spatial, bodily, social, and relational boundaries. Their embodied capabilities allow them to reshape these boundaries through situated action, challenging privacy framings centered on data flows, interface settings, or one-time consent. Prior work has examined robot privacy through sensing, data collection, telepresence, transparency, consent, bystander awareness, and multi-stakeholder governance. Building on this work, we propose embodied boundary privacy as a capability-by-context framing for examining how physically present robots may reshape privacy boundaries in situated interaction. Specifically, this framing organizes privacy risks across seven robot capabilities and five deployment contexts, asking how embodied capabilities enable boundary crossings and how situated contexts shape who is affected, how these crossings are interpreted, and when they become contested. We use this perspective to outline design and research implications for embodied privacy mechanisms, including boundary checkpoints, viewpoint-aware sensing control, remote-presence disclosure, object- and body-level access rules, constraints on socially persuasive privacy influence, and local interruption rights. We encourage HRI research, design, and governance to treat robot movement, orientation, proximity, object access, remote presence, and social expression as privacy-relevant actions whose meaning depends on context.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an "embodied boundary privacy" framework for understanding how physically present robots reshape privacy boundaries in situated interaction, organizing privacy risks across seven robot capabilities (movement, orientation, proximity, object access, remote presence, social expression, and sensing) and five deployment contexts, then outlining design implications such as boundary checkpoints, viewpoint-aware sensing control, and local interruption rights.
AI.motivation: Existing privacy framings centered on data flows, interface settings, or one-time consent inadequately address how robots' embodied capabilities reshape spatial, bodily, social, and relational privacy boundaries through situated action in everyday environments.
AI.method: The authors synthesize prior work on robot privacy (sensing, data collection, telepresence, transparency, consent, bystander awareness, multi-stakeholder governance) and propose a capability-by-context framing, organizing privacy risks across seven robot capabilities and five deployment contexts to examine boundary crossings and their contextual interpretation.
AI.result: The framework yields design and research implications for embodied privacy mechanisms, including boundary checkpoints, viewpoint-aware sensing control, remote-presence disclosure, object- and body-level access rules, constraints on socially persuasive privacy influence, and local interruption rights.
AI.conclusion: HRI research, design, and governance should treat robot movement, orientation, proximity, object access, remote presence, and social expression as privacy-relevant actions whose meaning is fundamentally context-dependent.

title: CyrillicQA: The Influence of Phonetically Encoded Secret Language on LLM Performance
comment: 4 pages, in English; 4 pages, in German (original); German version originally published in: Rüdian, S. (2026). Prompt-Engineering in Education (1st ed., pp. 39-42). Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21413892
summary: Due to the selection of their training data, large language models (LLMs) perform best on standard-language inputs from languages using the Latin alphabet with large speaker populations, while disadvantaging other language varieties. Nevertheless, they can also be a versatile tool for preserving precisely such endangered languages. But do they also possess the necessary creativity and capacity for abstraction to decode phonetically encoded language the same way humans do?

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can decode phonetically encoded endangered languages, given that their training data biases them toward dominant, Latin-alphabet, high-resource languages.
AI.motivation: LLMs underperform on low-resource and endangered language varieties due to training data selection biases, yet they could serve as tools for language preservation. The question is whether they possess the creativity and abstraction capacity to decode phonetically encoded language like humans do.
AI.method: The abstract does not detail the experimental methodology, but presumably involves testing LLMs on tasks that require decoding phonetically encoded endangered language inputs and comparing their performance to human abilities.
AI.result: The abstract does not report specific results, leaving the answer to the posed research question open.
AI.conclusion: The paper explores the dual nature of LLMs: biased against endangered languages yet potentially useful for their preservation, specifically questioning their capacity for phonetic decoding akin to human cognition.

title: Hate Speech Classification In Roman Urdu: A Comparative Study On Parameter Efficient Fine-Tuning And Prompt Engineering
summary: Due to the widespread accessibility of the internet and social media, toxic and hateful con-tent has grown exponentially, causing significant distress and negative societal impacts. Ro-man Urdu, a low-resource language used in Pakistan and among Urdu-speaking communities worldwide, presents additional challenges because of its informal grammar, inconsistent sen-tence structures, and multiple variations in word spellings. This research aims to identify the most effective techniques for hate speech classification in such low-resource settings with limited data. To address this, the study investigates and compares the latest approaches, in-cluding prompt tuning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) using LoRA, and prompt en-gineering, under various experimental configurations. To achieve this objective, four exper-iments were designed. The first experiment involved direct inferencing with LLMs without any fine-tuning, to evaluate how well these models understand Roman Urdu in a zero-shot setting, especially given limited data. The second experiment utilized parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) with LoRA, which updates only a small subset of parameters, thereby reducing computational cost. The third experiment explored prompt tuning with both mixed and manually crafted prompts, using very small sets of training examples relative to the entire dataset, making it computationally efficient as well. Finally, the fourth experiment applied prompt engineering through zero-shot and few-shot learning, relying solely on care-fully designed instruction prompts for classification without further training.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates effective hate speech classification techniques for Roman Urdu, a low-resource language, by comparing prompt tuning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) with LoRA, and prompt engineering across four experimental configurations using limited data.
AI.motivation: Toxic and hateful content on the internet has grown exponentially, and Roman Urdu—a low-resource language with informal grammar and inconsistent spelling—presents unique challenges for hate speech classification. The research aims to identify the most effective techniques for classification in such low-resource settings with limited data.
AI.method: Four experiments were designed: (1) zero-shot direct inferencing with LLMs without fine-tuning; (2) parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) using LoRA, which updates only a small subset of parameters; (3) prompt tuning with mixed and manually crafted prompts using very small training sets; and (4) prompt engineering via zero-shot and few-shot learning with carefully designed instruction prompts, requiring no further training.
AI.result: The abstract does not report specific experimental results or performance metrics, as it focuses on the experimental design and methodological comparison across the four approaches.
AI.conclusion: The paper aims to determine which approach—prompt tuning, PEFT with LoRA, or prompt engineering—performs best for hate speech classification in Roman Urdu under data-scarce, low-resource conditions, balancing computational efficiency with classification effectiveness.

title: Multi-Scale Fruit Capsules: Dilated Convolutions and Dynamic Routing for In-the-Wild Explainable Fruit Recognition
summary: The same fruit appears in a bunch, unpicked, peeled, bagged in plastic, or sliced on a dish, so automated fruit classification in the wild (AFCW) must absorb wide intra- class and narrow inter-class variability in shape, size, colour and texture. Convolutional networks route information through pooling, which discards the pose and location of the region of interest and therefore generalises poorly across these presentations. We propose FruitCapsNet, a capsule network whose Fruit Capsules replace the standard convolutional front end with dilated convolutions: the receptive field grows exponentially at constant parameter cost, so each capsule encodes multi-scale context before dynamic routing resolves part whole spatial agreement. Hyper-parameters, including the dilation factor, are selected by Bayesian optimisation rather than grid search. On three public datasets (SMP, FruitsGB, Fruits-360) and a new 19-class, 10,639-image in-the-wild dataset (PD-19), FruitCapsNet exceeds ten fine-tuned transfer-learning backbones at one-third the depth, with the largest margin (+2.7% over the nearest competitor) on the hardest set. Grad-CAM saliency propagated from the DigitCaps layer shows that the improvement comes from attributing decisions to whole-fruit regions rather than to object edges, giving post-hoc evidence that the gain is not a dataset artefact.

AI.tldr: FruitCapsNet, a capsule network with dilated convolutions replacing the standard conv front end, improves automated fruit classification in the wild by encoding multi-scale context before dynamic routing. It outperforms ten fine-tuned transfer-learning backbones on three public datasets and a new in-the-wild dataset (PD-19), with hyper-parameters tuned via Bayesian optimization.
AI.motivation: Fruit classification in the wild faces wide intra-class and narrow inter-class variability due to differing presentations (bunched, peeled, bagged, sliced). Standard convolutional networks use pooling that discards spatial information such as pose and location, leading to poor generalization across these varied presentations.
AI.method: FruitCapsNet replaces the standard convolutional front end with dilated convolutions so that the receptive field grows exponentially at constant parameter cost, allowing each capsule to encode multi-scale context before dynamic routing resolves part-whole spatial agreement. Hyper-parameters, including the dilation factor, are selected via Bayesian optimization instead of grid search.
AI.result: On three public datasets (SMP, FruitsGB, Fruits-360) and a new 19-class, 10,639-image in-the-wild dataset (PD-19), FruitCapsNet exceeds ten fine-tuned transfer-learning backbones at one-third the depth, with the largest margin (+2.7% over the nearest competitor) on the hardest set. Grad-CAM saliency propagated from the DigitCaps layer confirms improvements come from attributing decisions to whole-fruit regions rather than object edges.
AI.conclusion: The improvement from FruitCapsNet is attributed to whole-fruit region decisions rather than object edges, providing post-hoc evidence that the gain is not a dataset artifact. The approach offers better accuracy at significantly reduced model depth compared to transfer-learning backbones.

title: Social Graph Mamba: Forecasting Pedestrian Movements Based on Social Context
summary: Forecasting pedestrian motion has always been fundamental for autonomous navigation in crowded environments. While attention-based methods achieve strong performance, they suffer from quadratic computational complexity in modeling social interactions, limiting scalability. Additionally, the existing methods often achieve high accuracy on prediction benchmarks at the individual level, but fail to fully capture the natural movement behaviors of crowds in real-world scenarios, particularly group structures. In this study, we propose Social Graph Mamba (SGM), a novel architecture that replaces attention-based social reasoning with Selective State Space Models (SSMs) operating on dynamically constructed interaction graphs. SGM introduces a dynamic interaction graph with social triplet factorization to decompose crowd interactions sequentially, and a community-aware module to effectively discover group structures via differentiable MinCut optimization and conditions both the embedding space and multi-modal decoder on group membership. Our experiments on standard benchmarks (ETH/UCY, SDD) demonstrate competitive performance with linear sequence complexity compared to quadratic attention-based methods. We further validate SGM in physical robot experiments by integrating predicted trajectories into a Social Force Model (SFM) for real-world implementation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Social Graph Mamba (SGM), a novel architecture for pedestrian trajectory forecasting that replaces quadratic-complexity attention-based social interaction modeling with linear-complexity Selective State Space Models (SSMs) on dynamically constructed interaction graphs. SGM incorporates social triplet factorization for sequential crowd interaction decomposition and a community-aware module using differentiable MinCut optimization to discover group structures, conditioning both the embedding space and multi-modal decoder on group membership. Experiments on ETH/UCY and SDD benchmarks show competitive performance with linear sequence complexity, and the method is validated in physical robot experiments via integration with a Social Force Model.
AI.motivation: Existing attention-based pedestrian trajectory prediction methods achieve strong accuracy but suffer from quadratic computational complexity in social interaction modeling, limiting scalability. Additionally, current methods often capture individual-level accuracy but fail to model natural crowd movement behaviors, particularly group structures, in real-world scenarios.
AI.method: SGM replaces attention-based social reasoning with Selective State Space Models (SSMs) operating on dynamically constructed interaction graphs. It introduces (1) a dynamic interaction graph with social triplet factorization to decompose crowd interactions sequentially, and (2) a community-aware module that discovers group structures via differentiable MinCut optimization, conditioning both the embedding space and multi-modal decoder on group membership.
AI.result: Experiments on standard benchmarks (ETH/UCY, SDD) demonstrate competitive prediction performance with linear sequence complexity compared to quadratic attention-based methods. The approach is also validated in physical robot experiments by integrating predicted trajectories into a Social Force Model (SFM) for real-world implementation.
AI.conclusion: SGM demonstrates that SSM-based architectures on dynamic interaction graphs can achieve competitive pedestrian trajectory forecasting performance while offering linear computational complexity, and can effectively capture group structures in crowd motion for practical robot navigation applications.

title: Forgotten in Weights, Recovered by Tools: Agentic Tool Unlearning for LLM Agents
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as tool-augmented agents, where responses can depend on tool calls and external observations rather than model parameters alone. This creates an evaluation mismatch for LLM unlearning: previous unlearning methods may suppress direct parametric recall, but an agent can still recover the same forget target through tools such as web search, retrieval, or database lookup. We identify this failure mode as tool-mediated recovery and study agentic tool unlearning, which aims to reduce both parametric recall and tool-mediated recovery while preserving normal tool use for retained knowledge. To address this challenge, we propose Agentic Tool Unlearning (ATU), a two-stage framework. The first stage applies parametric knowledge unlearning to suppress direct recall, while the second stage performs trajectory-level reinforcement learning in simulated tool-augmented environments to penalize target-seeking tool behavior and final-answer leakage. Experiments on RWKU and MUSE across different LLM architectures show that ATU achieves a better balance between target forgetting and retained utility, making unlearning more robust under tool-augmented agent deployment.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a novel failure mode in LLM unlearning called "tool-mediated recovery," where tool-augmented agents can recover forget targets through external tools even after parametric unlearning. The authors propose Agentic Tool Unlearning (ATU), a two-stage framework combining parametric knowledge unlearning with trajectory-level reinforcement learning in simulated tool environments to reduce both direct recall and tool-mediated recovery while preserving utility for retained knowledge. Experiments on RWKU and MUSE show ATU achieves a better forget-retain balance.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed as tool-augmented agents where responses depend on tool calls and external observations. Previous unlearning methods only suppress parametric recall but fail to prevent agents from recovering forget targets through tools like web search, retrieval, or database lookup, creating an evaluation mismatch.
AI.method: ATU is a two-stage framework. Stage one applies parametric knowledge unlearning to suppress direct recall. Stage two performs trajectory-level reinforcement learning in simulated tool-augmented environments to penalize target-seeking tool behavior and final-answer leakage.
AI.result: Experiments on RWKU and MUSE across different LLM architectures demonstrate that ATU achieves a better balance between target forgetting and retained utility under tool-augmented agent deployment.
AI.conclusion: Tool-augmented deployment introduces new unlearning challenges beyond direct parametric recall; trajectory-level reinforcement learning can make unlearning more robust to tool-mediated recovery while preserving normal tool use for retained knowledge.

title: The Abstention Protocol: RCA for Clos Fabrics
comment: Presented at Usenix OSDI 2026. 17 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables
summary:
Root cause analysis (RCA) in large datacenter networks is challenging because telemetry is noisy, partial, and asynchronous. Score-based approaches degrade under these conditions, often yielding unstable or incorrect attributions.
  We present \textsc{CoreSec}, a production RCA system that replaces weighted fusion with a PAM-style abstention algebra. Telemetry agents are composed using control flags that yield deterministic decisions and explicit abstention when evidence is ambiguous. CoreSec combines this algebra with topology-aware configurations that capture failure surfaces across Clos fabrics and converge monotonically as evidence accumulates.
  Deployed at hyperscale, CoreSec provides stable and explainable RCA behavior across diverse environments without retuning. Our experience shows that structured composition with abstention forms a practical foundation for automated RCA in real-world cloud networks.

AI.tldr: CoreSec is a production root cause analysis (RCA) system for hyperscale datacenter networks that replaces score-based weighted fusion with a PAM-style abstention algebra. It uses control flags for deterministic decisions and explicit abstention under ambiguity, combined with topology-aware configurations that capture failure surfaces in Clos fabrics. Deployed at hyperscale, it provides stable and explainable RCA without retuning.
AI.motivation: Traditional score-based RCA approaches degrade under realistic telemetry conditions in large datacenter networks, which are noisy, partial, and asynchronous, leading to unstable or incorrect root cause attributions.
AI.method: CoreSec replaces weighted fusion with a PAM-style abstention algebra. Telemetry agents are composed using control flags that produce deterministic decisions and explicit abstention when evidence is ambiguous. This algebra is combined with topology-aware configurations designed to capture failure surfaces across Clos fabrics, with monotonic convergence as evidence accumulates.
AI.result: Deployed at hyperscale, CoreSec demonstrates stable and explainable RCA behavior across diverse environments without requiring retuning, validating structured composition with abstention as a practical approach for automated RCA in real-world cloud networks.
AI.conclusion: Structured composition with abstention forms a practical and effective foundation for automated root cause analysis in real-world cloud networks, outperforming score-based approaches in stability and explainability under noisy, partial, and asynchronous telemetry conditions.

title: Tomatoes, Potatoes, and Onions: Questioning the Need for Faces in Face Presentation Attack Detection
summary: Face presentation attack detection (PAD) is traditionally formulated as a face-specific problem, although many of the visual artifacts introduced by print, replay, and recapture processes are not inherently tied to facial appearance. In this work, we investigate whether transferable PAD representations can be learned without using faces during downstream PAD training. To this end, we introduce TPO, a controlled face-free presentation attack dataset consisting of bona fide, print, and replay recordings of, almost randomly chosen, tomatoes, potatoes, and onions acquired under protocols that closely mirror conventional face PAD datasets. Using a foundation-model-based PAD architecture, we demonstrate that a detector trained on TPO achieves an average AUC of 92.70% across four standard cross-dataset face PAD benchmarks, outperforming training on synthetic faces and remaining competitive with models trained on real face datasets. Conversely, models trained on face PAD datasets transfer consistently above chance to TPO, suggesting that the learned representations capture characteristics of the presentation process rather than object semantics. Furthermore, incorporating TPO into conventional face PAD training consistently improves cross-dataset performance under fixed optimization budgets, indicating that face-free data provides complementary information rather than simply additional training samples. Finally, representation and frequency analyses provide further evidence that transferable PAD representations cannot be explained by a single spectral artifact but instead encode richer presentation cues shared across object categories. Together, these results provide empirical evidence that transferable presentation attack representations can be learned independently of facial content, opening new opportunities for privacy-preserving and identity-independent PAD development.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TPO, a face-free presentation attack dataset of tomatoes, potatoes, and onions, demonstrating that transferable PAD representations can be learned without facial content. A detector trained on TPO achieves 92.70% average AUC across four face PAD benchmarks, outperforming synthetic-face training and remaining competitive with real-face-trained models, while also providing complementary information when combined with face data.
AI.motivation: Face presentation attack detection is traditionally treated as a face-specific problem, yet many print/replay/recapture artifacts are not inherently facial.
