AI.method: TASSO combines two complementary techniques: (1) subspace learning via a sequence of task-specific low-rank projectors applied to latent representations before cross-entropy optimization, and (2) geometry-aware knowledge distillation using a geodesic-distance-based loss that distills knowledge from the previous-task model while preserving latent space geometry. These techniques avoid unnecessary parameter updates along full embedding dimensions and focus learning on task-specific manifolds.
AI.result: Experiments with the CLIP vision language model on multi-domain task incremental and class incremental learning benchmarks show clear improvements over state-of-the-art methods in mitigating catastrophic forgetting and preserving zero-shot capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Focusing on task-specific low-dimensional manifolds and maintaining latent space geometry via geodesic-based distillation significantly reduces both catastrophic forgetting and zero-shot degradation, providing a robust paradigm for continual learning with VLMs.

title: Model-Free Adaptive Parameter Tuning for Efficient Multi-Robot Warehouse Operations
summary: Robotic Fulfillment Centers (FCs) store inventory on shelves (pods) arranged in dense blocks. Retrieving a target pod that is buried deep in a block requires moving obstructing pods out of the way (i.e., digout). Multi-robot planners use parameterized cost functions to control digout behavior, producing a spectrum of strategies: at one extreme, obstructing pods are sent to other blocks (using more robots in travel lanes); at the other, pods are shuffled within the block (avoiding lane congestion but increasing extraction time). Each point on this spectrum has different downstream consequences for floor congestion and throughput. The optimal operating point depends on the specific facility configuration and shifts with operational conditions such as varying station demand and congestion patterns, making offline tuning impractical. We present an adaptive parameter tuning framework based on Extremum Seeking Control (ESC) that continuously adjusts planner parameters in response to measured throughput. ESC performs model-free optimization by perturbing parameters with sinusoidal dither signals and correlating perturbations with performance changes to estimate gradients, making it robust to the multi-minute delayed effects and credit assignment challenges inherent in large FC operations. Simulation studies demonstrate that the adaptive policy improves upon fixed policies across several conditions. We observe an improvement in throughput by an average of 5.0% across map and robot fleet size variations, and by 8.4% under dynamic operating conditions. This work eliminates manual parameter provisioning and enables real-time adaptation, providing a self-tuning paradigm for FC storage operations.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an adaptive parameter tuning framework based on Extremum Seeking Control (ESC) for multi-robot planning in Robotic Fulfillment Centers. The framework continuously adjusts planner parameters (that control pod digout behavior trade-offs) in response to measured throughput, achieving 5.0% average throughput improvement across facility configurations and 8.4% under dynamic operating conditions, eliminating manual parameter provisioning.
AI.motivation: Robotic Fulfillment Centers require tuning parameterized cost functions that control pod digout behavior, producing a spectrum of strategies (from sending obstructing pods to other blocks to shuffling within a block). The optimal operating point depends on facility configuration and shifts dynamically with station demand and congestion, making offline tuning impractical and creating a need for automated, real-time adaptation.
AI.method: The method uses Extremum Seeking Control (ESC), a model-free optimization technique that continuously perturbs planner parameters using sinusoidal dither signals and correlates perturbations with performance (throughput) measurements to estimate gradients. ESC is robust to multi-minute delayed effects and credit assignment challenges inherent in large FC operations, enabling real-time adjustment of digout parameters without requiring a system model.
AI.result: Simulation studies show the adaptive policy outperforms fixed policies: throughput improves by an average of 5.0% across map and robot fleet size variations, and by 8.4% under dynamic operating conditions.
AI.conclusion: The work eliminates manual parameter provisioning for digout behavior and enables real-time adaptation, providing a self-tuning paradigm for FC storage operations that is robust to changing operational conditions.

title: Evaluation Awareness in Language Models: Representation, Verbalization, and Control
comment: The first two authors contributed equally
summary: Both capability and safety benchmarks rest upon the assumption that the behavior of language models undergoing a test is informative about their behavior in deployment. This assumption can fail, should models infer that they are being evaluated and condition their response on such context. This hypothesis, termed ``evaluation awareness'', has been observed in frontier and open-weight language models alike. We provide a systematic study of this phenomenon, by probing for it across six language models (from four families and three sizes) and three metrics. More precisely, we examine whether (i) being under evaluation is linearly represented within the models' activations space, (ii) it is verbalized in their output tokens (as scored by an LLM-as-judge), and (iii) steering causally affects their behavior. For the open-checkpoint Olmo models, we further test these measures at every training stage. In doing so, we report that evaluation awareness is linearly decodable from the residual streams of every model (best AUROC $\geq 0.7$). By contrast, these representations align only in part with verbalization: their correlations and mutual information are nonzero in some settings, yet vary substantially across models, layers, and readout choices. Nevertheless, steering along probe-derived directions can shift the verbalization scores. Finally, a comparison across the Olmo checkpoints reveals that evaluation awareness is already present within base models, becomes amplified throughout the stages of supervised fine-tuning, and remains stable thereafter---unlike the effects of steering, that grow more pronounced at every successive training stage. These results show the need for evaluations to account for the disjunction between what models represent internally, what they verbalize, and their steering.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically studies "evaluation awareness" in language models—the phenomenon where models infer they are being evaluated and condition their responses accordingly. Across six LMs and three metrics, the authors find evaluation awareness is linearly decodable from residual streams in all models (AUROC ≥ 0.7), but its verbalization correlates only partially with internal representations. Steering along probe-derived directions shifts verbalization scores. In Olmo checkpoints, evaluation awareness emerges in base models, is amplified by supervised fine-tuning, and stabilizes thereafter, while steering effects grow at each training stage.
AI.motivation: Capability and safety benchmarks assume that model behavior during testing is representative of deployment behavior. This assumption can break if models detect they are being evaluated and adapt their responses. Since evaluation awareness has been observed but not systematically characterized, the authors investigate whether it is internally represented, verbalized, and causally steerable across models.
AI.method: The authors probe six language models (four families, three sizes) using three complementary metrics: (i) linear probing of activation spaces for evaluation-related representations (AUROC-based decoding), (ii) LLM-as-judge scoring to measure whether evaluation awareness is verbalized in output tokens, and (iii) causal steering along probe-derived directions to test behavioral effects. For Olmo open-checkpoint models, they additionally measure all three metrics at every training stage to track the developmental trajectory.
AI.result: Evaluation awareness is linearly decodable from residual streams of every model (best AUROC ≥ 0.7). However, internal representations align only partially with verbalization—correlations and mutual information are nonzero in some settings but vary substantially across models, layers, and readout choices. Steering along probe-derived directions does shift verbalization scores. Across Olmo checkpoints, evaluation awareness is present in base models, amplified by supervised fine-tuning, and stable thereafter, whereas steering effects grow stronger at every successive training stage.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight a disjunction between what models represent internally, what they verbalize, and how steering affects them. This has important implications for benchmark validity: evaluations must account for evaluation awareness and the gaps between internal representation, verbalization, and steerability when interpreting model performance.

title: Let Credit Follow Computation: Architecture-Aware Credit Transport for Large Language Model Reinforcement Learning
summary: Credit assignment in large-language-model reinforcement learning (LLM RL) can be separated into three objects: evidence about success, a transport operator that converts this evidence into token-level advantages, and an update geometry that turns advantages into policy changes. Recent work has greatly improved evidence, sampling, and update geometry, but the transport operator is usually architecture-agnostic. Fixed-discount GAE applies a stationary geometric kernel along token time; group-relative methods broadcast an outcome statistic across an entire response. Neither operator represents the trajectory-specific computation used by the Transformer policy itself. We introduce computation-conditioned credit transport (CCT), a general framework in which a detached statistic of the behavior policy's internal computation parameterizes the causal kernel that transports downstream value through a rollout. Our concrete algorithm, CompPO, maps native attention concentration to a bounded per-token retention gate, uses the gate in both the one-step bootstrap and a path-dependent generalized-advantage trace (Comp-GAE), and co-designs a transport-aligned critic (TAC) that reuses the actor's hidden states and routing information without a second same-scale Transformer. The task reward and clipped PPO policy objective remain unchanged; a constant gate recovers fixed-coefficient GAE. Across five Qwen3-4B seeds, CompPO reaches 61.4% final held-out accuracy (95% CI [60.8,62.0]) versus 53.8% [52.9,54.7] for tuned GRPO. Neither Comp-GAE with a standard critic (55.2%) nor TAC with a fixed gate (56.4%) matches the full model (interaction +2.4 [1.9,2.9]). Shuffle and position controls confirm trajectory-specific alignment; CompPO is stable in 10/12 PPO-grid runs versus 3/12. Frozen evaluation improves over GRPO by 4.3 and 3.9 greedy pass@1 macro points on Qwen3-4B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces computation-conditioned credit transport (CCT), a framework that uses the Transformer policy's own internal computation to parameterize the credit-assignment kernel in LLM RL. Its concrete algorithm CompPO maps attention concentration to a per-token retention gate used in a path-dependent GAE (Comp-GAE) with a transport-aligned critic (TAC), significantly improving over GRPO across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Recent advances in LLM RL have improved evidence, sampling, and update geometry for credit assignment, but the transport operator—which converts evidence into token-level advantages—remains architecture-agnostic. Fixed-discount GAE and group-relative methods apply static kernels that do not represent the trajectory-specific computation performed by the Transformer policy itself.
AI.method: CCT uses a detached statistic of the behavior policy's internal computation to parameterize the causal kernel transporting downstream value through a rollout. CompPO maps native attention concentration to a bounded per-token retention gate, used in both the one-step bootstrap and a path-dependent generalized-advantage trace (Comp-GAE). It also co-designs a transport-aligned critic (TAC) that reuses the actor's hidden states and routing information, avoiding a second same-scale Transformer. The task reward and clipped PPO policy objective remain unchanged; a constant gate reduces to fixed-coefficient GAE.
AI.result: Across five Qwen3-4B seeds, CompPO reaches 61.4% final held-out accuracy vs. 53.8% for tuned GRPO. Ablations confirm both components matter: Comp-GAE with standard critic (55.2%) and TAC with fixed gate (56.4%) both underperform the full model (interaction +2.4). Shuffle and position controls confirm trajectory-specific alignment. CompPO is stable in 10/12 PPO-grid runs vs. 3/12. Frozen evaluation improves over GRPO by 4.3 (Qwen3-4B) and 3.9 (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) greedy pass@1 macro points.
AI.conclusion: Making the credit-transport operator computation-conditioned—tied to the policy's own internal attention dynamics—substantially improves sample efficiency, stability, and final performance in LLM RL, demonstrating the value of co-designing the transport operator with the architecture rather than relying on architecture-agnostic kernels.

title: DamageScope: Vision-Language Retrieval at Scale for Disaster Damage Assessment from Satellite Imagery
summary: Timely and accurate assessment of property damage is critical following natural disasters. Traditional on-site inspections are labor-intensive, costly, and often pose safety risks. Advances in satellite imagery and vision-language models (VLMs) enable scalable remote damage assessment; however, integrating VLMs into large-scale Earth observation pipelines presents challenges in computational efficiency, data organization, and information retrieval. To address these challenges, we present DamageScope, a retrieval-augmented framework that combines satellite imagery with Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and Large Language Models (LLMs) to automate property damage analysis. Built on a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework, DamageScope extracts structured visual representations from satellite imagery to support interactive natural language queries for damage assessment. To address scalability, we introduce a novel multi-vector embedding-based clustering algorithm that outperforms traditional single-vector embedding approaches while reducing indexing time by up to 14x. Furthermore, a dual-store data architecture minimizes LLM API calls, reducing both operational cost and response latency by up to approximately 3x. By effectively balancing scalability and operational efficiency, DamageScope provides a robust and practical solution for real-world damage assessment tasks.

AI.tldr: DamageScope is a retrieval-augmented framework that combines satellite imagery with VLMs and LLMs to automate property damage assessment, featuring a multi-vector embedding-based clustering algorithm that reduces indexing time by up to 14x and a dual-store data architecture that cuts LLM API costs and latency by up to ~3x.
AI.motivation: Traditional on-site property damage inspections after natural disasters are labor-intensive, costly, and risky. While satellite imagery and VLMs enable scalable remote assessment, integrating VLMs into large-scale Earth observation pipelines faces challenges in computational efficiency, data organization, and information retrieval.
AI.method: DamageScope builds on a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework that extracts structured visual representations from satellite imagery to support interactive natural language queries. It introduces a novel multi-vector embedding-based clustering algorithm for scalability and a dual-store data architecture to minimize LLM API calls, balancing scalability and operational efficiency.
AI.result: The multi-vector embedding-based clustering algorithm outperforms traditional single-vector embedding approaches while reducing indexing time by up to 14x. The dual-store data architecture reduces operational cost and response latency by up to approximately 3x.
AI.conclusion: DamageScope provides a robust, scalable, and cost-effective practical solution for real-world property damage assessment by effectively balancing scalability and operational efficiency in large-scale Earth observation pipelines.

title: GOLEM: Modular Humanoid Autonomy Towards Electric Vehicle Battery Disassembly
summary: Disassembling end-of-life electric vehicle (EV) battery packs is dull and dangerous work, performed almost entirely by humans. We present GOLEM (Generalized Open Library of Embodied Modules), an end-to-end, open-source system architecture for EV battery disassembly with the Unitree H1-2 humanoid robot in which walking, manipulation, dynamic stability, navigation, and spatial memory are independent modules with abstract interfaces, so that methods are easily developed, interchanged, and compared. GOLEM is deployed as a Docker-based ROS 2 abstraction in which MuJoCo and IsaacLab digital twins expose interfaces matching the physical robot. GOLEM's composability and per-module customization enable development and demonstration of humanoid EV battery disassembly, from simulation to reality. GOLEM provides fair comparison between humanoid modules, enabling evaluation as a capability ladder, in which one module is characterized at a time and added as a rung: LiDAR-inertial navigation places the robot within 13.0cm of a 6m goal; a learned standing controller recovers from external disturbances that sampling-based lower-body MPC does not; and grasping loosened fasteners from a real Hyundai Ioniq 5 pack degrades from 97% tethered to 87% free-standing to 37% under navigation-induced pose variance. Source code is available at the project page https://golem-humanoid.github.io

AI.tldr: GOLEM is an open-source, modular ROS 2-based system architecture for autonomous EV battery disassembly using the Unitree H1-2 humanoid robot, with interchangeable modules for walking, manipulation, stability, navigation, and spatial memory validated from simulation to reality.
AI.motivation: EV battery disassembly is currently performed almost entirely by humans despite being dull and dangerous. There is a need for a robotic system capable of performing this task safely, while enabling modular development and fair comparison of individual capabilities.
AI.method: GOLEM employs an end-to-end open-source architecture on the Unitree H1-2 humanoid robot, where walking, manipulation, dynamic stability, navigation, and spatial memory are independent modules with abstract interfaces. It uses Docker-based ROS 2 with MuJoCo and IsaacLab digital twins matching the physical robot's interfaces. Modules are evaluated as a "capability ladder," characterizing one module at a time.
AI.result: LiDAR-inertial navigation achieves 13.0cm accuracy to a 6m goal; a learned standing controller outperforms sampling-based lower-body MPC in recovering from external disturbances; grasping loosened fasteners from a real Hyundai Ioniq 5 pack degrades from 97% (tethered) to 87% (free-standing) to 37% (under navigation-induced pose variance).
AI.conclusion: GOLEM demonstrates successful humanoid robot EV battery disassembly from simulation to reality, providing composability and per-module customization with a capability-ladder evaluation framework for fair module comparison. Source code is publicly available.

title: No One Model Catches Every Harm: Benchmarking Content Moderation Across Safety Scenarios
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, yet they remain vulnerable to generating harmful content. From adversarial jailbreaks that bypass safety filters to implicit hate that evades detection, the range of risks these models pose continues to grow. While both specialized content moderators and general-purpose LLMs are being used as safety layers, the question of which model is best suited for which type of harmful content remains unanswered. We present the most comprehensive evaluation of LLM safety capabilities to date, systematically testing \textbf{53} models across \textbf{11} datasets that we organize into four distinct categories. Our evaluation under both prompt-only and prompt-response settings uncovers critical blind spots: large frontier models that lead on one category fall significantly behind smaller, specialized alternatives on others, and real-world conversational safety remains largely unsolved across all model families. These findings challenge the assumption that scale alone ensures safety, and provide the community with a structured framework for informed model selection.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive evaluation of 53 LLMs across 11 safety datasets organized into four categories, testing both prompt-only and prompt-response settings, revealing that large frontier models do not consistently outperform smaller specialized models in safety, and that conversational safety remains largely unsolved.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in real-world applications but remain vulnerable to generating harmful content through adversarial jailbreaks and implicit hate. While both specialized content moderators and general-purpose LLMs are used as safety layers, there is no systematic answer to which model is best suited for which type of harmful content. This gap motivates the need for a comprehensive, structured evaluation.
AI.method: The study conducts a large-scale systematic evaluation of 53 models across 11 datasets, organized into four distinct categories of harmful content. Each model is tested under two settings: prompt-only (assessing the model's response to a harmful prompt) and prompt-response (evaluating the model as a safety layer judging a prompt-response pair).
AI.result: The evaluation uncovers critical blind spots: large frontier models that lead on one safety category fall significantly behind smaller, specialized alternatives on other categories. Real-world conversational safety remains largely unsolved across all model families, challenging the assumption that scale alone ensures safety.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide the community with a structured framework for informed model selection, demonstrating that model scale is not a sufficient predictor of safety performance and that task-specific considerations must guide the choice of safety model.

title: Quantifying geographic domain shift to decouple the geospatial transferability of human mobility flow generation models
summary: Human mobility serves as an essential proxy for understanding social, economic, and environmental dynamics in urban systems. Geospatial transferability, which measures a model's capability in a new location or unseen region, is a critical dimension for comparing different human mobility generation models. However, few studies have studied the intrinsic characteristics of geospatial transferability. To this end, this study systematically investigates the geospatial transferability of four representative human mobility generation models using a large-scale benchmark dataset of census tract level commuting flows across 2265 counties in the United States. Inspired by the domain adaptation theory in machine learning, we introduce geographic domain shift to describe the intrinsic differences in geographic feature distributions and spatial structures between source and target regions, which may jointly affect model transferability. Moreover, we propose two metrics, mutual information and spatial shift, to quantify the geographic domain shift. To examine their associations with model transferability, we employ linear mixed-effects regression to analyze the associations between geographic domain shifts and transferability. Our results reveal substantial spatial heterogeneity and asymmetry in transfer performance across regions. Both information shift and spatial shift exhibit statistically significant and complementary explanatory power. This indicates that geospatial transferability depends not only on model design but also on intrinsic geographic differences. These findings provide a novel methodological framework for evaluating and improving the geospatial transferability of human mobility generation models and support more robust and fair human mobility data synthesis across diverse regions. It also offers insights on spatial transferability for GeoAI model development.

AI.tldr: This study systematically investigates the geospatial transferability of four human mobility generation models using commuting flow data across 2,265 U.S. counties, introducing geographic domain shift (quantified via mutual information and spatial shift metrics) to explain why model performance varies across regions.
AI.motivation: Geospatial transferability—a model's ability to generalize to unseen regions—is critical for human mobility generation models, yet few studies have examined its intrinsic characteristics or the underlying geographic factors that drive transfer performance.
AI.method: The authors benchmark four human mobility generation models on census tract level commuting flows across 2,265 U.S. counties. Inspired by domain adaptation theory, they introduce the concept of geographic domain shift and propose two metrics—mutual information (information shift) and spatial shift—to quantify intrinsic differences in feature distributions and spatial structures between source and target regions. Linear mixed-effects regression is used to analyze associations between these domain shifts and model transferability.
AI.result: Substantial spatial heterogeneity and asymmetry in transfer performance across regions were found. Both information shift and spatial shift exhibit statistically significant and complementary explanatory power for model transferability, indicating that transfer performance depends on both model design and intrinsic geographic differences.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide a novel methodological framework for evaluating and improving geospatial transferability of human mobility generation models, support more robust and fair mobility data synthesis across diverse regions, and offer insights for spatial transferability in GeoAI model development.

title: presto: Efficient, Training-free, and Open-world Object Placement via Imaginary Search
summary: Object placement is critical in image composition, requiring spatially and semantically coherent positioning of objects within diverse scenes. Existing approaches typically rely on hand-crafted rules or supervised learning on limited datasets, which restricts their generalization and interpretability, especially in open-world scenarios involving novel objects and scenes. In this work, we reformulate open-world object placement as a heuristic search task guided by reasoning from a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM). We introduce \textsf{presto}, a zero-shot, training-free framework that operates within an imaginary action space to iteratively refine object position and scale. Our coarse-to-fine search strategy ensures fast convergence, and we evaluate two decision-making variants: Metric-guided Selection and MLLM-as-a-judge. Experiments across multiple benchmarks show that \textsf{presto}~achieves state-of-the-art performance, particularly in previously unseen, open-world settings. Human studies further reveal that the MLLM-as-a-judge variant produces more perceptually coherent placements than metric-driven approaches, highlighting a gap between standard evaluation metrics and human visual judgment.

AI.tldr: Presto is a zero-shot, training-free framework for open-world object placement that reformulates the task as heuristic search guided by a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM), iteratively refining object position and scale through a coarse-to-fine strategy. It achieves state-of-the-art results across benchmarks, particularly in unseen open-world scenarios, with the MLLM-as-a-judge variant producing more perceptually coherent placements than metric-driven methods.
AI.motivation: Existing object placement methods rely on hand-crafted rules or supervised learning on limited datasets, restricting generalization and interpretability in open-world scenarios involving novel objects and scenes.
AI.method: Presto reformulates object placement as a heuristic search task in an imaginary action space, guided by MLLM reasoning. It uses a coarse-to-fine search strategy for fast convergence and evaluates two decision-making variants: Metric-guided Selection and MLLM-as-a-judge.
AI.result: Presto achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks, especially in open-world settings. Human studies show the MLLM-as-a-judge variant yields more perceptually coherent placements than metric-driven approaches, revealing a gap between standard metrics and human visual judgment.
AI.conclusion: Presto demonstrates that reasoning-based heuristic search with a multimodal LLM can effectively handle open-world object placement without training, and that MLLM-based judgment better aligns with human perceptual preferences than traditional metric-driven evaluation.

title: Model-Based Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Task Assignment Under Distribution Shifts
summary: Heterogeneous multi-robot service systems must assign requests to compatible robots, construct feasible schedules, and adapt as new tasks arrive online. Historical data can help anticipate future demand, but relying too heavily on inaccurate predictions can degrade performance under distribution shifts. We develop a prediction-aware adaptive rollout framework for heterogeneous multi-robot task assignment with scheduled and real-time requests. The problem is formulated as a finite-horizon stochastic dynamic program incorporating robot-task compatibility, ordered service requirements, routing constraints, service windows, and end-of-horizon return requirements. The proposed policy evaluates current assignments using sampled future request scenarios while restricting immediate commitments to requests already observed. To enable online use, the framework combines pruned candidate controls, wait actions, and an interaction-aware base policy for efficient future-cost estimation. Robustness to forecast error is provided by adaptively reweighting predicted requests based on recent prediction mismatch and selectively re-optimizing assigned but unstarted requests. We also introduce a historical-data-driven procedure for selecting the heterogeneous fleet composition before deployment. In a case study using real nursing-task requests from hospital inpatient floors, the proposed approach achieves near-complete service and reduces serviced-request wait times relative to reactive, token-passing, prediction-positioning, and myopic greedy baselines, with the largest improvements in tail-delay metrics.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a prediction-aware adaptive rollout framework for heterogeneous multi-robot task assignment with both scheduled and real-time requests, formulated as a finite-horizon stochastic dynamic program. The framework uses sampled future request scenarios, adaptively reweights predictions based on forecast error, and includes a data-driven fleet composition selection procedure. Case study on hospital nursing-task requests shows near-complete service and reduced wait times versus multiple baselines.
AI.motivation: Heterogeneous multi-robot service systems face the challenge of assigning requests to compatible robots while adapting to online task arrivals. Historical data can inform demand prediction, but over-reliance on inaccurate predictions degrades performance under distribution shifts. There is a need for a framework that leverages predictions while remaining robust to forecast error.
AI.method: The problem is formulated as a finite-horizon stochastic dynamic program incorporating robot-task compatibility, ordered service requirements, routing constraints, service windows, and end-of-horizon return requirements. The proposed policy evaluates current assignments using sampled future request scenarios while limiting immediate commitments to observed requests. Online use is enabled via pruned candidate controls, wait actions, and an interaction-aware base policy for future-cost estimation. Robustness is achieved through adaptive reweighting of predicted requests based on recent prediction mismatch and selective re-optimization of assigned but unstarted requests. A historical-data-driven procedure selects the heterogeneous fleet composition before deployment.
AI.result: In a real nursing-task request case study from hospital inpatient floors, the proposed approach achieves near-complete service and reduces serviced-request wait times relative to reactive, token-passing, prediction-positioning, and myopic greedy baselines, with the largest improvements in tail-delay metrics.
AI.conclusion: The prediction-aware adaptive rollout framework effectively balances the use of historical demand predictions with robustness to forecast errors, delivering superior service performance in realistic heterogeneous multi-robot settings, particularly improving worst-case wait times.

title: Lexical Coupling in GUI Element Grounding: Sentence Embeddings Track Labels across Mobile and Web
summary: GUI grounding evaluations that expose UI elements as text metadata often treat high instruction-element embedding similarity as evidence of semantic grounding. Across three mobile and web benchmarks, we show that this interpretation is frequently confounded by visible-label recovery. Lexical baselines remain competitive at top-1, label-poor targets remain weak for text-only methods, and encoder top-1 hits are predictable from lexical rank, candidate-pool size, and label type. We evaluate each action as a same-screen ranking task, comparing five off-the-shelf single-vector encoders with lexical baselines. Encoders recover some lexical misses, but deployable fusion gains are much smaller than target-aware oracle gains. These findings show that embedding-based evaluations can conflate visible-label recovery with semantic GUI grounding. Embedding-based evaluations should therefore report lexical baselines, label-type stratification, and deployable-fusion diagnostics. Our released repository provides analysis scripts and detexted per-step panels: https://github.com/qijia123/lexical-coupling-release.

AI.tldr: GUI grounding evaluations that use text metadata and embedding similarity are often confounded by visible-label recovery rather than true semantic grounding. Lexical baselines are competitive at top-1, label-poor targets remain weak, and encoder hits are predictable from lexical rank, pool size, and label type. The paper recommends reporting lexical baselines, label-type stratification, and deployable-fusion diagnostics.
AI.motivation: To expose that embedding-based GUI grounding evaluations can conflate visible-label recovery with genuine semantic grounding, thereby leading to inflated claims of capability.
AI.method: Across three mobile and web benchmarks, each action is evaluated as a same-screen ranking task. Five off-the-shelf single-vector encoders are compared with lexical baselines, and analyses examine top-1 hits, label-poor targets, lexical rank predictability, candidate-pool size, and label type, along with oracle versus deployable fusion gains.
AI.result: Lexical baselines remain competitive at top-1; label-poor targets are weak for text-only methods; encoder top-1 hits are predictable from lexical rank, candidate-pool size, and label type. Encoders recover some lexical misses, but deployable fusion gains are much smaller than target-aware oracle gains.
AI.conclusion: Embedding-based evaluations can conflate visible-label recovery with semantic GUI grounding. Evaluations should report lexical baselines, label-type stratification, and deployable-fusion diagnostics. The repository provides analysis scripts and detexted per-step panels.

title: A Reproducible, License-Aware Distillation Recipe for CPUDeployable Safety Classification
summary: Deploying a safety layer for large language models on commodity hardware is constrained by the guards available to do it: current open guard models hold between 1 and 9 billion parameters, are oriented toward the graphics processing unit, and answer in seconds per request on a central processing unit. This paper presents a reproducible, license-aware knowledge-distillation recipe addressing that constraint. A strong open guard labels a corpus of roughly 97,000 prompts, drawn from 24 public datasets, into seven safety categories aligned to a public hazard taxonomy, and a fleet of small students spanning lexical, shallow, encoder and generative architectures is trained to reproduce that signal. The corpus is partitioned at the license boundary, so that a deployable and a research model differ only in their training data and the cost of that restriction becomes measurable. Every model is scored against an independent gold benchmark of 6,361 rows over four slices, labeled apart from the teacher and including a slice of harmless prompts that makes over-defense measurable. The distilled students match the teachers on adversarial text within overlapping confidence intervals and reduce false alarms on harmless prompts, the smallest generative student reaching 3.8% against 4.8% for the 8-billion-parameter teacher, while the encoder classifies in roughly 24 ms per request on CPU. Per-class rebalancing is the only decisive ingredient of the recipe. No superiority over the distilled guards is claimed; on the clean reference slice they remain ahead.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a reproducible, license-aware knowledge distillation recipe for creating small guard models for LLM safety on commodity CPU hardware. A strong open teacher model labels ~97k prompts from 24 public datasets into seven safety categories, and a fleet of small student models (lexical, shallow, encoder, generative) are trained to reproduce the signal. The corpus is partitioned at the license boundary. Students match the teacher on adversarial text while reducing false alarms on harmless prompts, with the smallest generative student at 3.8% false alarm (vs 4.8% for the 8B teacher) and the encoder achieving ~24 ms/request on CPU.
AI.motivation: Deploying safety layers for LLMs on commodity hardware is constrained because current open guard models hold 1–9 billion parameters, are GPU-oriented, and answer in seconds per request on CPU. There is a need for small, fast, CPU-friendly safety classifiers.
AI.method: A strong open guard model labels a corpus of ~97,000 prompts from 24 public datasets into seven safety categories aligned to a public hazard taxonomy. A fleet of small student models spanning lexical, shallow, encoder, and generative architectures is trained to reproduce the teacher signal via knowledge distillation. The corpus is partitioned at the license boundary so a deployable and a research model differ only in training data, making the cost of license restrictions measurable. Models are scored against an independent gold benchmark of 6,361 rows over four slices, including harmless prompts to make over-defense measurable.
AI.result: Distilled students match the teacher on adversarial text within overlapping confidence intervals and reduce false alarms on harmless prompts. The smallest generative student reaches 3.8% false alarms vs 4.8% for the 8B teacher. The encoder model classifies in roughly 24 ms per request on CPU. Per-class rebalancing is the only decisive ingredient of the recipe.
AI.conclusion: The distilled guards are not claimed to be superior overall—on the clean reference slice the teachers remain ahead—but they offer competitive safety classification with substantially reduced latency and hardware requirements, enabling deployment on commodity CPU hardware.

title: Extending the Horizon of Early Diagnosis: Lung Cancer Prediction with Vision Transformers
summary: Lung cancer remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, and early diagnosis is critical for improving survival. However, early-stage malignancies can be subtle on chest X-rays, creating challenges for radiologists. This study evaluates Vision Transformers (ViTs) for predicting lung cancer one to two years before clinical diagnosis. We analyzed 259,361 chest X-rays from 91,020 imaging studies at the Jamaica Plains VA Hospital in Boston, MA. The dataset showed extreme class imbalance, approximately 1:150 cancer to non-cancer, which was addressed using hybrid under- and over-sampling and class-weighted loss optimization. Three ViT configurations were evaluated: a model trained from scratch, an ImageNet-pretrained model, and a Corona-pretrained model fine-tuned on the lung cancer dataset. Transfer learning improved performance, with pretrained models exceeding the scratch baseline by 6-10 percentage points in AUC and about 10-12 percent in balanced accuracy. ImageNet-pretrained models showed the most stable overall performance, while Corona-pretrained models achieved higher sensitivity in some settings but greater variability. Moderate resampling ratios, including 1:1 undersampling and 1.5:2 oversampling, provided favorable trade-offs between sensitivity, precision, and computational efficiency, reducing runtime by up to 70 percent without major performance loss. These findings demonstrate the potential of ViTs for early lung cancer risk prediction from routine chest X-rays. Although performance remains below clinical deployment thresholds, the results support further development of ViT-based triage systems to flag high-risk patients for earlier evaluation.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates Vision Transformers (ViTs) for predicting lung cancer 1-2 years before clinical diagnosis using 259,361 chest X-rays from 91,020 studies. Extreme class imbalance (~1:150) was handled via hybrid resampling and class-weighted loss. Pretrained ViTs (ImageNet and Corona) outperformed scratch models by 6-10 AUC points. Moderate resampling ratios reduced runtime by up to 70% without major performance loss, demonstrating potential for ViT-based early lung cancer triage systems, though performance remains below clinical deployment thresholds.
AI.motivation: Early-stage lung cancer is often subtle on chest X-rays, making early diagnosis challenging for radiologists. Since early detection is critical for survival, there is a need for automated methods that can predict lung cancer risk from routine imaging before clinical diagnosis.
AI.method: The study analyzed 259,361 chest X-rays from 91,020 imaging studies at Jamaica Plains VA Hospital. Extreme class imbalance (~1:150) was handled using hybrid under- and over-sampling combined with class-weighted loss optimization. Three ViT configurations were compared: training from scratch, ImageNet-pretrained fine-tuning, and Corona-pretrained fine-tuning. Various resampling ratios (including 1:1 undersampling and 1.5:2 oversampling) were evaluated for performance and computational trade-offs.
AI.result: Pretrained models outperformed the scratch baseline by 6-10 percentage points in AUC and about 10-12 percent in balanced accuracy. ImageNet-pretrained models showed the most stable overall performance, while Corona-pretrained models achieved higher sensitivity in some settings but with greater variability. Moderate resampling ratios reduced runtime by up to 70% without major performance loss.
AI.conclusion: ViTs demonstrate potential for early lung cancer risk prediction from routine chest X-rays, capable of predicting cancer 1-2 years before clinical diagnosis. Although performance remains below clinical deployment thresholds, the results support further development of ViT-based triage systems to flag high-risk patients for earlier evaluation.

title: Betting for Sim-to-Real Performance Certificates
summary: Consider a typical test of a robot system: one observes a sequence of outcomes concerning some aspect of interest (crash or no crash, tracking error, time to completion), and reports a mean (crash risk, average error, mean time to completion) and, more importantly, an interval guaranteed to contain that mean at a prescribed confidence, referred to as a performance certificate. Given expensive real-world trials, the sample size is therefore small, and the certificate is often loose. Now consider the same procedure, except that before each real outcome is revealed, the operator ``peeks'' at a large bank of simulated results, and places a bet on where the real outcome will land. As the real outcomes settle the bets, the operator gains or loses wealth. One's ``trust'' over simulators also shifts within the portfolio. This paper develops that idea into a sim-to-real betting certificate framework with three contributions: (i) An algorithm that links a scalable bank of simulators to effective bets, and the accumulated betting wealth to the certificate. (ii) A proof that the returned certificate is anytime valid, covering the true mean with the prescribed probability, using any simulator bank. (iii) The guaranteed wealth-regret bounds yield configuration principles for the proposed algorithm and simulator bank design to deliver tight certificates. Experiments across synthetic distributions and real-world robot tests, covering both replayed standardized testing outcomes and online runtime evaluation, show the proposed method narrows the certificate by $51.6\%\pm16\%$ against classic and state-of-the-art baselines, and by $32.26\%\pm8\%$ in the extremely limited-sample regime ($\leq30$ samples).

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a sim-to-real betting certificate framework that uses a portfolio of simulators to place bets on real-world outcomes, accumulating wealth that tightens confidence intervals for performance certificates. The method provably maintains anytime validity and demonstrates 51.6% certificate narrowing over baselines, with 32.26% improvement in extremely limited-sample regimes.
AI.motivation: Real-world robot testing is expensive, yielding small sample sizes and loose performance certificates (confidence intervals on means). The paper seeks to leverage the abundance of cheap simulation data to tighten these certificates without sacrificing statistical validity.
AI.method: The framework connects a scalable bank of simulators to a betting strategy: before each real outcome, bets are placed based on simulator predictions, and accumulated betting wealth is linked to the certificate width. Includes an algorithm for portfolio-based betting, a proof of anytime validity for any simulator bank, and wealth-regret bounds that guide algorithm and simulator bank configuration.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic distributions and real-world robot tests (replayed standardized testing and online runtime evaluation) show the method narrows certificates by 51.6%±16% against classic and state-of-the-art baselines, and by 32.26%±8% in the extremely limited-sample regime (≤30 samples).
AI.conclusion: Incorporating simulator information through a betting framework enables significantly tighter and still anytime-valid performance certificates for robot systems, even with very few real-world trials.

title: More Computational Resources Do Not Ensure Higher Scholarly Impact: Evidence from Leading NLP Conference Papers
summary: Computational resources are increasingly central to NLP research, but how closely reported GPU capability aligns with scholarly impact remains unclear. We analyze 13,921 ACL, EMNLP, and NAACL main-conference papers published between 2020 and 2025, using GPU resources as our operational measure of computational resources. From full texts, we extract GPU models and counts, standardize each paper's largest reported configuration into a comparable hardware-capability measure, and link these data to citation, award, topic, and institutional metadata. GPU reporting became more common but remained incomplete, while reported capability increased mainly through newer hardware generations and medium-scale multi-GPU configurations. Resource concentration substantially exceeded impact concentration: the annual top 20% of GPU-quantifiable papers accounted for 83.9%-89.9% of reported GPU capability, but only 27%-32% of citations and 20%-33% of paper awards. In adjusted models, a tenfold increase in aggregate reported GPU capability was associated with a 3.52-percentage-point increase in within-NLP topic-year citation percentile, but increased model R^2 by only 0.0042. GPU count showed more consistent positive associations with citation and award outcomes than newer hardware generation. Overall, reported GPU resources are associated with scholarly impact but provide little standalone explanation of research influence.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes 13,921 ACL/EMNLP/NAACL papers (2020-2025) to examine the relationship between reported GPU resources and scholarly impact. It finds that GPU reporting is incomplete but increasing, resource concentration greatly exceeds impact concentration, and while GPU capability is positively associated with citations/awards, it explains very little variance in research influence.
AI.motivation: Computational resources are increasingly central to NLP research, yet it remains unclear whether reported GPU capability actually aligns with scholarly impact. The authors aim to quantify this relationship using a large corpus of NLP conference papers.
AI.method: The authors collect 13,921 ACL, EMNLP, and NAACL main-conference papers from 2020-2025. They extract GPU models and counts from full texts, standardize each paper's largest reported configuration into a hardware-capability measure, and link these to citation, award, topic, and institutional metadata. They then analyze concentration patterns and fit adjusted regression models to assess associations between GPU capability and impact metrics.
AI.result: GPU reporting became more common but remained incomplete. Reported capability increased primarily through newer hardware generations and medium-scale multi-GPU setups. The top 20% of GPU-quantifiable papers accounted for 83.9%-89.9% of reported GPU capability but only 27%-32% of citations and 20%-33% of awards. A tenfold increase in aggregate GPU capability was associated with only a 3.52-percentage-point increase in citation percentile, with model R^2 increased by just 0.0042. GPU count showed stronger associations with outcomes than newer hardware generation.
AI.conclusion: Reported GPU resources are positively associated with scholarly impact but provide little standalone explanatory power for research influence. Resource concentration far exceeds impact concentration, and GPU count is a more consistent predictor of impact than hardware generation.

title: Robust Lightweight Deep Learning Models for Oral Cancer Screening
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, Paper accepted for the 6th International Conference on AI-ML Systems, 2026
summary: Oral cancer is a leading cause of mortality in low-to-middle-income countries, where a shortage of specialists delays diagnosis. While point-of-care screening via smartphones offers a scalable solution, developing robust AI for resource-constrained settings poses significant challenges, including class imbalance in training data, variable data quality, and computational constraints on edge devices. In this paper, we present the optimisation of lightweight deep learning models for smartphone-based oral cancer screening. Using a diverse, multi-centre retrospective dataset of approximately 30,000 images acquired over a decade, we systematically evaluate state-of-the-art convolutional, transformer, and hybrid architectures. Through rigorous pipeline ablation, we demonstrate that directly optimising hybrid architectures for the edge strictly outperforms computationally heavy paradigms, such as large models or knowledge distillation. Furthermore, interpretability analysis and simulated noise-stress tests revealed that the system anchors on clinical features and remains robust to unstructured sensor noise, despite vulnerabilities to impulse bit errors. In the held-out test set, our optimised MobileViTv2 models achieved an average sensitivity of 83.2 $\pm$ 1.5% and an average specificity of 86.0 $\pm$ 0.8%, with the best model exhibiting 87.4% sensitivity, 86.5% specificity, and a critical negative predictive value of 97.2% with reference to specialist labels. These results confirm that with targeted architectural selection and streamlined optimisation, interpretable and robust lightweight AI models exhibit high potential for edge deployment to enable automated triage in primary care settings.

AI.tldr: This paper optimizes lightweight deep learning models (MobileViTv2) for smartphone-based oral cancer screening, achieving 83.2% sensitivity and 86.0% specificity on a ~30,000 image multi-centre dataset, demonstrating that directly optimizing hybrid edge architectures outperforms heavy paradigms like large models or knowledge distillation.
AI.motivation: Oral cancer is a leading cause of mortality in low-to-middle-income countries due to specialist shortages and delayed diagnosis. While smartphone-based point-of-care screening offers a scalable solution, developing robust AI for resource-constrained settings faces challenges including class imbalance, variable data quality, and computational constraints on edge devices.
AI.method: The authors systematically evaluate convolutional, transformer, and hybrid architectures on a diverse multi-centre retrospective dataset of ~30,000 oral images collected over a decade. They perform rigorous pipeline ablations comparing lightweight edge-optimized hybrid models against computationally heavy paradigms including large models and knowledge distillation. They also conduct interpretability analysis (saliency on clinical features) and simulated noise-stress tests (unstructured sensor noise and impulse bit errors).
AI.result: On the held-out test set, optimized MobileViTv2 models achieved average sensitivity of 83.2±1.5% and specificity of 86.0±0.8%. The best model achieved 87.4% sensitivity, 86.5% specificity, and a critical negative predictive value of 97.2%. The system anchored on clinical features and remained robust to unstructured sensor noise, though vulnerable to impulse bit errors.
AI.conclusion: Targeted architectural selection and streamlined optimization of lightweight hybrid models produce interpretable and robust AI that outperforms heavier computational paradigms, showing high potential for edge deployment to enable automated triage in primary care settings in resource-constrained regions.

title: Perturb the Thought, Not the Pixels: Latent-Space Rollout Diversification for Reinforcement Learning of Vision-Language Models
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves the reasoning ability of vision-language models (VLMs), and diversifying the rollouts within each optimization group amplifies its gains. Existing approaches diversify through decoding temperature or pixel-space image distortion; we ask whether the perturbation belongs in the model's latent space instead. We introduce Noise-Contrastive GRPO (NC-GRPO), which injects scale-calibrated Gaussian noise into the last hidden layer of the prompt-encoding pass for half of each rollout group, branching those rollouts from a displaced departure state. Branches that reach the answer despite the displacement are reinforced over those derailed by it, converting sensitivity at the branch point into policy-gradient signal; the objective, reward, and inference protocol are untouched. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B trained on Geometry3K, NC-GRPO significantly improves out-of-domain mathematical reasoning over vanilla GRPO across five held-out benchmarks (pooled McNemar $p \le 0.001$) while also improving in-domain accuracy and hallucination robustness -- the latter an axis on which image-space noise regresses even while posting a larger OOD average on perception-heavy benchmarks. Mechanism ablations indicate that independent stochastic diversity, not noise budget or direction, is the active ingredient, and a noise-scale study exposes a dial between reasoning specialization and general capability. NC-GRPO is designed to be modality-agnostic and integrates into a standard RLVR pipeline as a ~50-line change to the inference engine.

AI.tldr: NC-GRPO injects scale-calibrated Gaussian noise into the last hidden layer of the prompt-encoding pass to create latent-space-branched rollouts for RLVR, improving out-of-domain mathematical reasoning, in-domain accuracy, and hallucination robustness of VLMs over vanilla GRPO without changing the objective, reward, or inference protocol.
AI.motivation: Existing RLVR diversification strategies rely on decoding temperature or pixel-space image distortion, which either don't explore diverse reasoning paths effectively or can regress on hallucination robustness. The authors hypothesize that perturbation should instead occur in the model's latent space to better exploit the diversity-amplification effect of RLVR.
AI.method: NC-GRPO injects scale-calibrated Gaussian noise into the last hidden layer during the prompt-encoding pass for half of each rollout group, creating a displaced departure state for branched rollouts. Branches reaching the correct answer are reinforced over derailed ones, converting sensitivity at the branch point into policy-gradient signal. The objective, reward, and inference protocol are unchanged; it is a ~50-line modification to the inference engine.
AI.result: On Qwen2.5-VL-7B trained on Geometry3K, NC-GRPO significantly improves out-of-domain mathematical reasoning over vanilla GRPO across five held-out benchmarks (pooled McNemar p ≤ 0.001), while also improving in-domain accuracy and hallucination robustness. Image-space noise regresses on hallucination robustness despite stronger OOD averages on perception-heavy benchmarks. Ablations show independent stochastic diversity—not noise budget or direction—is the active ingredient, and a noise-scale study reveals a trade-off between reasoning specialization and general capability.
AI.conclusion: Latent-space noise injection is a more effective and safer diversification mechanism for RLVR than pixel-space distortion, improving both reasoning and robustness. NC-GRPO is modality-agnostic, minimally invasive, and exposes a dial between specialization and general capability via noise scale.

title: Force/Torque-Based Kinematic Adaptation for Robotic Manipulation Tasks
summary: Contact-rich robotic manipulation requires an accurate model of the kinematic relationship between a robot's joints and the task features it senses. This relationship is rarely known exactly: it changes with each tool the robot picks up and shifts, sometimes almost instantaneously, as contact modes change --- especially for multi-fingered hands that make and break contact at points that are not exactly prescribed, as in full-hand grasping. This paper develops an adaptive scheme that estimates that relationship online, using only joint-angle sensing and a wrist-mounted force/torque sensor, with no exteroceptive measurement of the tool tip. We derive a provably stable kinematic update law that identifies the kinematics of an unknown tool from force/torque feedback alone, and prove stability of both the rigid case and the case with a compliance controller as an inner loop. We show that identification is confined to the directions the motion excites --- so that, for example, a tool's length is unobservable under a rigid insertion push, while a compliant loop's passive yielding partially excites it; and that with a second-order admittance the compliant certificate holds unconditionally in continuous time. We also pose the combined control and estimation problem as a Quadratic Program (QP): the formulation yields the prediction term of the update law exactly but, instructively, cannot reproduce the tracking adaptation term. We validate the scheme in simulation on a peg-in-hole insertion. This work is the first step in a research program aimed at factoring manipulation learning into a task policy which can be learned in isolation of the robot, for instance by reinforcement learning, and an adaptive kinematic component that adapts online to the particular robot, hand, or tool in use.

AI.tldr: This paper develops an adaptive kinematic identification scheme for contact-rich robotic manipulation that estimates the joint-to-task-feature kinematic relationship online using only joint-angle sensing and wrist-mounted force/torque feedback, without exteroceptive tool-tip measurement. The authors prove stability of the update law for both rigid and compliant-controlled cases, analyze observability limits (identification confined to motion-excited directions), and validate the method in peg-in-hole insertion simulations.
AI.motivation: Contact-rich manipulation requires accurate kinematic models of the joint-to-task-feature relationship, but this relationship is rarely known exactly—it changes with each tool, hand, or contact mode, and can shift almost instantaneously during full-hand grasping or multi-fingered manipulation. Existing approaches relying on exteroceptive measurement of the tool tip are impractical in many settings, motivating the need for an online adaptive estimation scheme using only joint-angle and force/torque sensing.
AI.method: The paper derives a provably stable kinematic update law that identifies the kinematics of an unknown tool from force/torque feedback alone. It proves stability for both the rigid case and the case with a compliance controller as an inner loop. The combined control and estimation problem is also posed as a Quadratic Program (QP), which yields the prediction term of the update law exactly but cannot reproduce the tracking adaptation term. Stability is analyzed in continuous time, including a second-order admittance formulation with an unconditional compliant certificate.
AI.result: The authors prove that identification is confined to the directions the motion excites—for example, a tool's length is unobservable under a rigid insertion push, whereas a compliant loop's passive yielding partially excites it. The QP formulation exactly reproduces the prediction term of the update law but cannot reproduce the tracking adaptation term. The scheme is validated in simulation on a peg-in-hole insertion task.
AI.conclusion: This work is the first step toward factoring manipulation learning into a task policy learned in isolation of the robot (e.g., via reinforcement learning) and an adaptive kinematic component that adapts online to the specific robot, hand, or tool in use. The provably stable adaptive scheme provides a foundation for future work on separating task and embodiment-specific learning in manipulation.

title: MCite-RL: Towards Reliable Multimodal RAG via Citation-enhanced Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with visual citation is crucial for ensuring the traceability and verifiability of MLLMs. However, current RAG and SFT-based methods struggle to achieve robust cross-modal reasoning, causing imprecise visual citations or decoupling between the citation and the generated answers. To address these limitations, we propose MCite-RL, a citation-enhanced agentic reinforcement learning framework designed for reliable multimodal RAG. MCite-RL introduces an Agentic Refinement module for visual citation that employs iterative retrieval, reasoning, and recursive cropping to progressively narrow the search space, transforming citation into a dynamic, evidence-driven reasoning process rather than a static step. Furthermore, we incorporate a Citation-enhanced Reward mechanism that integrates both process-level and outcome-level feedback within a reinforcement learning paradigm to jointly optimize answer accuracy and source traceability. Extensive experiments on benchmarks such as Wiki-VISA, FinRAGBench-V, and MMLongBench-Doc demonstrate that MCite-RL effectively achieves the joint optimization of citation precision and answer quality.

AI.tldr: MCite-RL is a citation-enhanced agentic reinforcement learning framework for multimodal RAG that uses iterative retrieval, reasoning, and recursive cropping (Agentic Refinement) plus process/outcome-level reward feedback to jointly optimize answer accuracy and visual citation precision.
AI.motivation: Current RAG and SFT-based methods for multimodal RAG with visual citation struggle with robust cross-modal reasoning, leading to imprecise visual citations or a disconnect between citations and generated answers.
AI.method: MCite-RL introduces (1) an Agentic Refinement module that uses iterative retrieval, reasoning, and recursive cropping to progressively narrow the search space, making citation an evidence-driven reasoning process; and (2) a Citation-enhanced Reward mechanism integrating process-level and outcome-level feedback within a reinforcement learning paradigm to jointly optimize answer accuracy and source traceability.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on Wiki-VISA, FinRAGBench-V, and MMLongBench-Doc demonstrate that MCite-RL achieves joint optimization of citation precision and answer quality.
AI.conclusion: MCite-RL effectively addresses the limitations of existing methods by transforming visual citation into a dynamic, evidence-driven reasoning process and jointly optimizing both citation precision and answer quality through reinforcement learning.

title: Data-Driven Dynamic Algorithm Dispatch with Large Language Models
comment: 3 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at the 2025 IEEE High Performance Extreme Computing Conference (HPEC). Outstanding Short Paper Award
summary: We introduce a large language model (LLM)-driven approach for generating dynamic algorithmic dispatch heuristics in high-performance linear algebra. By combining prompt engineering with LLaMA 3 and a curated performance database, the model learns to synthesize selection heuristics that exploit structural patterns to identify fast algorithmic choices. A case study on LU factorization demonstrates the model's ability to replicate expert-designed strategies. This work, developed as part of the DARPA-MIT SmartSolve project, highlights the promise of LLMs for algorithmic discovery and the development of more adaptive, fast linear algebra software.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an LLM-driven approach for generating dynamic algorithmic dispatch heuristics in high-performance linear algebra, using LLaMA 3 with prompt engineering and a curated performance database to synthesize selection heuristics that identify fast algorithmic choices. A case study on LU factorization shows the model can replicate expert-designed strategies, and the work is part of the DARPA-MIT SmartSolve project.
AI.motivation: High-performance linear algebra requires efficient algorithmic dispatch—selecting the right algorithm for a given problem based on structural patterns. Manually designing these dispatch heuristics is labor-intensive and requires expert knowledge, motivating the need for automated approaches.
AI.method: The approach combines large language models (LLaMA 3) with prompt engineering and a curated performance database. The LLM is trained/generated to synthesize selection heuristics that exploit structural patterns in inputs to identify fast algorithmic choices, validated through a case study on LU factorization.
AI.result: The case study on LU factorization demonstrates the LLM's ability to replicate expert-designed dispatch strategies, showing the feasibility of LLM-driven algorithmic heuristic generation for linear algebra.
AI.conclusion: LLMs show promise for algorithmic discovery and the development of more adaptive, fast linear algebra software, as demonstrated in the DARPA-MIT SmartSolve project context.

title: Semantic Slots for Video Object-Centric Learning
summary: Video Object-Centric Learning (OCL) has traditionally focused on refining the encoder architecture to ensure temporal consistency. In this paper, we argue that the primary bottleneck lies in the decoder. We show that traditional decoders force slots to be spatially anchored, hindering their ability to adapt to motion. We propose SemanticSlots, which uses a Transformer-based decoder that leverages image context, relieving slots from encoding boundary precision and spatial location. This allows slots to function as semantic queries that are inherently object position invariant, retrieving matching features rather than memorizing coordinates. More importantly, this property allows slots computed from a single frame to decompose subsequent video frames, eliminating the need for complex temporal predictors or auxiliary temporal losses. Results on YouTube-VIS show that SemanticSlots improves upon VideoSAUR by 31 points in mBO and outperforms current state-of-the-art methods by 21 points, achieving 86.6% ARI and 62.8% mBO.

AI.tldr: SemanticSlots argues that the decoder, not the encoder, is the primary bottleneck in video object-centric learning. By using a Transformer-based decoder that treats slots as semantic, position-invariant queries, it eliminates the need for temporal predictors while achieving state-of-the-art performance on YouTube-VIS (86.6% ARI, 62.8% mBO).
AI.motivation: Traditional video OCL research focuses on refining encoder architectures for temporal consistency, but the authors argue the true bottleneck is the decoder. Conventional decoders force slots to be spatially anchored, which limits their ability to handle object motion and adaptation across frames.
AI.method: SemanticSlots introduces a Transformer-based decoder that leverages image context, freeing slots from encoding boundary precision and explicit spatial location. This enables slots to act as semantic, object position-invariant queries that retrieve matching features rather than memorize coordinates. A key property is that slots computed from a single frame can decompose subsequent video frames, removing the need for complex temporal predictors or auxiliary temporal losses.
AI.result: On YouTube-VIS, SemanticSlots improves upon VideoSAUR by 31 points in mBO and outperforms state-of-the-art methods by 21 points, achieving 86.6% ARI and 62.8% mBO.
AI.conclusion: The decoder is the primary bottleneck in video OCL, and rethinking it as semantic query-based retrieval—rather than spatial anchoring—enables more compact models with superior performance and simpler architecture by removing temporal machinery entirely.

authors: Ruan Rithelle Chagas de Faria Carminati
title: Why Personalization Matters: Cross-Subject Challenges in EMG-IMU-based HRI Activity Recognition
comment: Data collection was approved by the Federal University of Technology-Paraná Ethics Committee (CAAE 91430125.0.0000.0177). The MAGIC-HRI (Multimodal Activity, Gesture, and Intention Collection for HRI) dataset is available at [https://github.com/ruancarminati/MAGIC-HRI-V01.git](https://github.com/ruancarminati/MAGIC-HRI-V01.git). This paper will be presented at IEEE RO-MAN 2026
summary: This paper investigates wearable-based recognition of human activities and gestures to support Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) in object-handover and assembly-like scenarios. Electromyography (EMG) and Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) signals were collected using a Myo armband, culminating in a novel dataset introduced as MAGIC-HRI (Multimodal Activity, Gesture and Intention Collection) with a large taxonomy of 53 movement classes, including Brazilian Sign Language (LIBRAS) numbers (0-9), hand gestures, object/tool handover actions (pick up/give/hold), tool-manipulation tasks, and generic assembly/idle motions, collected from 11 participants with 10 samples per class (530 samples per participant). Signals are segmented by detecting muscle activation via an EMG energy envelope, then processed using sliding windows; time- and frequency-domain features are extracted. Multiple classical classifiers are tuned via cross-validated grid search, with Random Forest as the strongest baseline. A Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) protocol reveals a large generalization gap, indicating substantial subject dependence. A personalized adaptation experiment suggests that injecting a small number of samples from a new user can markedly improve recognition. Overall, the study contributes a broad, HRI-driven multimodal dataset, a rigorous evaluation emphasizing generalization, and practical evidence that personalization is likely required for robust deployment in practical HRI.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MAGIC-HRI, a novel multimodal dataset (EMG+IMU via Myo armband) for wearable-based human activity and gesture recognition in HRI object-handover and assembly scenarios, containing 53 movement classes from 11 participants. Using an EMG-energy-envelope segmentation pipeline with sliding windows and classical classifiers, Random Forest emerges as the strongest baseline. LOSO evaluation reveals a large generalization gap across subjects, while a personalization experiment shows that injecting a small number of new-user samples significantly improves recognition, indicating personalization is necessary for robust HRI deployment.
AI.motivation: To support Human-Robot Interaction in object-handover and assembly tasks by providing a broadly-taxonomized multimodal dataset and a rigorous evaluation framework for wearable-based activity and gesture recognition, while identifying the critical challenge of subject dependence that impedes practical deployment.
AI.method: EMG and IMU signals are collected via a Myo armband from 11 participants across 53 movement classes. Signals are segmented by detecting muscle activation through an EMG energy envelope, then processed using sliding windows; time- and frequency-domain features are extracted. Multiple classical classifiers are tuned via cross-validated grid search, and evaluation uses Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) plus a personalized adaptation experiment with small numbers of new-user samples.
AI.result: Random Forest performs as the strongest classical baseline. LOSO evaluation shows a substantial generalization gap, evidencing significant subject dependence. A personalized adaptation experiment demonstrates that adding a small number of samples from a new user markedly improves recognition accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The study contributes a broad HRI-driven multimodal dataset with 53 classes, a rigorous generalization-focused evaluation, and practical evidence that personalization is likely essential for robust, reliable deployment of wearable-based activity recognition in real-world HRI scenarios.

title: Convergence in Science, Divergence in Religion: Calibrated Framing Differences Across Wikipedia's Language Editions
summary: When Wikipedia's language editions describe the same concept, how differently do they frame it? Prior work measures coverage gaps between editions; we measure framing distance for matched concepts. We analyze 2,799 valid articles from 3,000 possible concept-language observations, spanning 150 Wikidata-anchored concepts, 20 language editions, 4 domains, and a calibration set. Raw embedding distances reflect both content differences and how well the encoder aligns each language pair. Even among calibration concepts with stable cross-cultural denotations (e.g., chemical elements, numbers, colors), the largest language-pair mean distance is 3.6 times the smallest, and distances are typically smaller within language families. We define a baseline-adjusted distance (calibrated distance): the distance between two language versions of a concept minus the mean distance for calibration concepts in the same language pair. This adjustment substantially reduces pair-specific alignment differences and the language-family pattern. Across three multilingual encoders (LaBSE, multilingual MPNet, and CMLM), scientific articles align more closely than calibration articles, and all three rank religion first and science/technology last. Concept-level rankings are highly consistent across encoders (Spearman rho=0.75-0.79 for MPNet and CMLM relative to LaBSE). Religion lies significantly above the calibration baseline under LaBSE. Within politics, divergence concentrates on concepts such as censorship and refugee, while democracy and human rights are among the most aligned. Code, data, and per-language-pair calibration baselines are released.\footnote{https://github.com/hhchen1105/cross-linqual-concept}

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a framing distance metric to measure how differently Wikipedia language editions frame the same concept. Using 2,799 articles across 150 concepts, 20 languages, and 4 domains, the authors propose a calibration baseline-adjusted distance that removes language-pair-specific encoder alignment artifacts. They find scientific articles align most closely, religion diverges most, and consensus across multilingual encoders is high.
AI.motivation: Prior work on multilingual Wikipedia has focused on coverage gaps (whether concepts exist across editions), but has not systematically quantified framing differences—i.e., how differently language editions present the same concept when it does exist in both. This paper addresses that gap.
AI.method: The authors collect 2,799 matched articles across 20 language editions for 150 Wikidata-anchored concepts across 4 domains plus a calibration set. They compute embedding distances between language versions of the same concept using three multilingual encoders (LaBSE, multilingual MPNet, CMLM). They define calibrated distance as the raw embedding distance minus the mean calibration-concept distance for the same language pair, which corrects for encoder language-pair alignment quality.
AI.result: Raw distances show significant language-pair alignment artifacts and language-family patterns. Calibrated distance substantially reduces these. Across all encoders, science/technology articles align most closely and religion diverges most. Concept rankings are highly consistent across encoders (Spearman rho=0.75-0.79 relative to LaBSE). Religion is significantly above the calibration baseline under LaBSE. Within politics, censorship and refugee show greatest divergence, while democracy and human rights are most aligned.
AI.conclusion: Calibrated distance is an effective measure for cross-lingual framing analysis that controls for encoder alignment biases. Framing differences vary systematically by domain and concept, with culturally-dependent topics showing greater divergence. The released code, data, and per-language-pair calibration baselines enable reproducible cross-lingual framing research.

title: K-Bench: measuring model performance on real scientific agent requests
summary: Benchmarks for scientific artificial intelligence are mostly written to be scored: multiple-choice questions, curated agent tasks with reference solutions, or simulators with a known generative structure. Real scientific requests arrive differently. They are underspecified, they carry attachments, and lack ground truth. We report K-Bench 01, an evaluation built from first-turn requests sampled from live user traffic on K-Dense Web and run end to end by nine frontier models in identical sandboxes, yielding 1,602 completed agent runs. Three blinded language-model judges scored every run against an eight-dimension rubric.
