On a rubric whose 8-anchor instructs judges that a domain scientist would accept the work with minor edits, no model clears the line under all three judges. gpt-5.6-sol has the highest pooled mean, 8.04, but its 95% interval [7.80, 8.23] spans the threshold, and two of the three judges rank claude-opus-5 first instead. We therefore report the ordering of systems as the reproducible quantity, the absolute level as an attribute of the instrument, and the top of the table as unresolved. Across all 39,934 scored judgments -- the eight dimension scores plus a holistic overall for each assessment, excluding not-applicable cells -- 47.6% fall below the 8-point threshold. Difficulty is not uniform across the rubric: scientific accuracy averages 6.22 against 7.33 for communication, on identical denominators and in the same direction within every one of the nine models. The single leading failure tag is overclaiming, on 31.4% of assessments. We argue that the informative quantity for scientific agents is not a leaderboard position but the joint distribution of what was delivered, what was claimed, and what artifacts were produced.

AI.tldr: K-Bench 01 evaluates nine frontier AI models on 1,602 real, underspecified scientific agent tasks sampled from live user traffic on K-Dense Web, scored by three blinded LLM judges on an eight-dimension rubric. No model reliably clears the bar a domain scientist would accept the work with minor edits: gpt-5.6-sol leads with pooled mean 8.04 but its confidence interval spans the threshold, and judges disagree on the top model. Scientific accuracy (6.22 avg) lags communication (7.33 avg) across all models, overclaiming is the dominant failure (31.4%), and 47.6% of all scored judgments fall below the 8-point threshold. The authors argue that reproducibility of relative ordering, not absolute leaderboard position, is the informative quantity.
AI.motivation: Existing scientific AI benchmarks are written to be scored (MCQs, curated agent tasks, simulators with known structure), but real scientific requests are underspecified, carry attachments, and lack ground truth. There is a gap between benchmark performance and real-world scientific usefulness that needs to be measured.
AI.method: First-turn requests are sampled from live user traffic on K-Dense Web and run end to end by nine frontier models in identical sandboxes, producing 1,602 completed agent runs. Three blinded language-model judges score every run against an eight-dimension rubric with an 8-anchor that signals a domain scientist would accept the work with minor edits. A pooled analysis over 39,934 scored judgments (eight dimensions plus holistic overall, excluding not-applicable) is performed.
AI.result: No model clears the 8-point acceptance threshold under all three judges. gpt-5.6-sol has the highest pooled mean (8.04) but its 95% interval [7.80, 8.23] spans the threshold, while two of three judges rank claude-opus-5 first. 47.6% of all scored judgments fall below the threshold. Scientific accuracy averages 6.22 versus 7.33 for communication across identical denominators and consistently within all nine models. Overclaiming is the leading failure tag, present on 31.4% of assessments.
AI.conclusion: The paper argues that the informative quantity for scientific agents is not a leaderboard position but rather the joint distribution of what was delivered, what was claimed, and what artifacts were produced. Relative system ordering should be reported as the reproducible result, with the absolute score level treated as an attribute of the evaluation instrument itself.

title: SketchFlow: Zero-Shot Vector Sketch Generation via GMM Prior Flow in CLIP Latent Space
comment: Accepted to SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 Conference Papers. 16 pages
summary: Vector sketches remain one of the most concise and immediate mediums for abstract human expression. However, generating high-quality vector strokes that exhibit human-like drawing styles remains an open challenge due to the severe scarcity of fine-grained, high-quality text-to-sketch paired data. Existing text-conditioned generation methods often rely on unstable, time-consuming optimization or struggle to generalize to unseen categories in a zero-shot manner. To address these limitations, we present SketchFlow, a novel generative framework rooted in Optimal Transport (OT) theory and flow matching. By leveraging pre-trained CLIP models to bypass labor-intensive image-level text annotations, we formulate cross-modal alignment as a continuous mapping problem directly within the CLIP latent space. To bridge the inevitable modality gap between discrete text concepts and continuous sketch features, we first inject noise into discrete category embeddings to construct a continuous Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) prior. We then utilize an Optimal Transport Conditional Flow Matching (OT-CFM) model to learn a deterministic vector field mapping from this continuous GMM prior to the target sketch feature distribution. Finally, a Hybrid Diffusion Decoder, fusing 1D U-Net and Transformer architectures, is designed to decode these features into fast and high-fidelity stroke trajectories. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SketchFlow substantially outperforms existing baselines in visual quality and adherence to natural human drawing styles. Furthermore, our geometry-preserving framework demonstrates promising local zero-shot synthesis for prompts beyond the QuickDraw training vocabulary, including unseen concept labels and semantic modifiers, while enabling smooth, continuous semantic interpolation between distinct concepts. Source code is available at: https://github.com/QiuHong-1202/SketchFlow.

AI.tldr: SketchFlow is a novel generative framework for high-quality vector sketch generation that leverages Optimal Transport theory and flow matching, combined with pre-trained CLIP models to bypass text-to-sketch paired data requirements. It constructs a continuous Gaussian Mixture Model prior by injecting noise into discrete category embeddings, uses OT-CFM to learn a vector field mapping, and employs a Hybrid Diffusion Decoder (1D U-Net + Transformer) for fast, high-fidelity stroke trajectory generation. The framework demonstrates state-of-the-art visual quality, adherence to human drawing styles, and zero-shot generalization to unseen categories with smooth semantic interpolation.
AI.motivation: Vector sketches are a concise medium for abstract human expression, but generating high-quality human-like vector strokes remains challenging due to the severe scarcity of fine-grained text-to-sketch paired data. Existing text-conditioned methods either rely on unstable, time-consuming optimization processes or fail to generalize to unseen categories in a zero-shot manner.
AI.method: SketchFlow consists of three key components: (1) leveraging pre-trained CLIP models to formulate cross-modal alignment as a continuous mapping problem directly in CLIP latent space, avoiding labor-intensive image-level text annotations; (2) injecting noise into discrete category embeddings to construct a continuous Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) prior, bridging the modality gap between discrete text concepts and continuous sketch features; (3) using an Optimal Transport Conditional Flow Matching (OT-CFM) model to learn a deterministic vector field mapping from the GMM prior to target sketch features, followed by a Hybrid Diffusion Decoder combining 1D U-Net and Transformer architectures for fast, high-fidelity stroke trajectory decoding.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show SketchFlow substantially outperforms existing baselines in visual quality and adherence to natural human drawing styles. The geometry-preserving framework demonstrates promising local zero-shot synthesis for prompts beyond the QuickDraw training vocabulary, including unseen concept labels and semantic modifiers, while enabling smooth, continuous semantic interpolation between distinct concepts.
AI.conclusion: SketchFlow provides an effective and efficient solution for text-conditioned vector sketch generation by combining Optimal Transport theory, flow matching, and CLIP-based cross-modal alignment, achieving superior quality and zero-shot generalization capabilities while avoiding the need for expensive paired data.

title: OpenSCvx: An Open-Source Modular and Extensible Nonlinear Trajectory Planning Package
summary: Trajectory optimization computes dynamically feasible motions that enable autonomous systems to accomplish complex tasks while satisfying operational and environmental constraints. This tutorial presents OpenSCvx, an open-source Python framework that bridges the gap between high-level problem specification and efficient numerical optimization. Rather than requiring users to derive solver-specific mathematical formulations, OpenSCvx provides a symbolic modeling interface that automatically constructs and solves trajectory optimization problems from modular descriptions of objectives, dynamics, and constraints. Beyond simplifying problem formulation, OpenSCvx supports (i) continuous-time constraint modeling, (ii) temporal and logical specifications, (iii) automatic vectorization for scalable and batched optimization, and (iv) a modular architecture that enables new algorithms, models, and solver backends to be incorporated with minimal effort. These capabilities allow researchers and practitioners to rapidly prototype, solve, and extend state-of-the-art trajectory optimization methods.

AI.tldr: This tutorial presents OpenSCvx, an open-source Python framework for trajectory optimization that provides a symbolic modeling interface, automatically constructing and solving optimization problems from modular descriptions of objectives, dynamics, and constraints without requiring solver-specific formulations.
AI.motivation: There is a gap between high-level problem specification and efficient numerical optimization in trajectory optimization. Users typically need to derive solver-specific mathematical formulations, which is time-consuming and error-prone.
AI.method: OpenSCvx provides a symbolic modeling interface with four key capabilities: (i) continuous-time constraint modeling, (ii) temporal and logical specifications, (iii) automatic vectorization for scalable and batched optimization, and (iv) a modular architecture enabling easy integration of new algorithms, models, and solver backends.
AI.result: OpenSCvx enables researchers and practitioners to rapidly prototype, solve, and extend state-of-the-art trajectory optimization methods by automatically constructing optimization problems from modular problem descriptions.
AI.conclusion: OpenSCvx bridges the gap between problem specification and numerical optimization, making trajectory optimization more accessible and extensible for autonomous systems research and practice.

title: Do Large Language Models Perform Well on Comprehending Poetic Logic in Modern Chinese Poetry?
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved significant progress across a wide range of natural language processing (NLP) tasks, yet their ability to understand literary texts, particularly modern Chinese poetry, remains largely unexplored. The unique literary characteristics of modern Chinese poetry necessitate a distinct form of reasoning for effective comprehension. Unlike conventional texts that convey clear information, the unique "poetic logic" of modern Chinese poetry requires a holistic reasoning approach that goes beyond superficial semantic analysis to be understood. However, current evaluation paradigms largely ignore this critical dimension. To address this gap, we propose Peony, the first benchmark specifically designed for evaluating the poetic logic of modern Chinese poetry. We define poetic logic as four tasks across three levels, namely stanza, line, and imagery, and systematically evaluate and analyze six mainstream LLMs based on Peony. We evaluate these models under both non-thinking and thinking configurations. The experimental results reveal the limitations of current LLMs in understanding the poetic logic of modern Chinese poetry and validate the effectiveness and necessity of Peony. Our data and code will be available.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Peony, the first benchmark specifically designed to evaluate LLMs' understanding of poetic logic in modern Chinese poetry, defining four tasks across three levels (stanza, line, imagery) and systematically evaluating six mainstream LLMs under both non-thinking and thinking configurations.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation paradigms overlook the unique "poetic logic" of modern Chinese poetry, which requires holistic reasoning beyond superficial semantic analysis. Despite LLMs' progress in NLP, their ability to understand literary texts, particularly modern Chinese poetry, remains largely unexplored.
AI.method: The paper proposes Peony, a benchmark that defines poetic logic as four tasks across three levels (stanza, line, imagery), and systematically evaluates six mainstream LLMs under both non-thinking and thinking configurations.
AI.result: Experimental results reveal the limitations of current LLMs in understanding the poetic logic of modern Chinese poetry, and validate the effectiveness and necessity of the Peony benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The Peony benchmark addresses a critical gap in evaluating LLMs' literary comprehension by providing the first dedicated framework for assessing poetic logic in modern Chinese poetry, with data and code made publicly available.

title: Generate in the Chart, Not on the Boundary: Function-Symbol Grounding for Hard Constraints in LTN-GANs
summary: Logic Tensor Network-Enhanced Generative Adversarial Networks (LTN-GANs) inject background knowledge by grounding each logical axiom as a predicate and training the generator to raise its satisfaction, a fuzzy truth value in $[0,1]$. Previous LTN-GAN work grounded every constraint this way, at the predicate level, and improved constraint satisfaction. A predicate, however, only scores a sample, so it cannot embed hard structural constraints, rules such as orderings, positivity, and definitional identities that must hold in every generated sample. In this work, we investigate grounding each axiom as a function symbol inside the LTN framework. We compare against the state-of-the-art alternative, a constraint layer that clamps each violating sample onto the feasible boundary and so produces outputs that are always valid. Our investigation shows that a valid sample is not always a realistic one. An inequality is not merely satisfied or violated. It holds by a margin, and a faithful generator should also reproduce the margin's real distribution. We find that the resolution ratio $R$, the data's scale over the margin's spread, is a diagnostic, computable before training, of which constraints a chosen grounding can learn. When $R$ is large, the predicate receives no learning signal, the clamp pushes every sample onto the boundary, and the margin distribution is lost while every standard metric still looks fine. A function symbol avoids both failures, computing the constrained variable rather than scoring it. Together the function symbols form a chart, a coordinate system inside the feasible region, where every sample is valid by construction and the margin is learned like any other quantity.

AI.tldr: LTN-GANs are extended by grounding logical axioms as function symbols rather than predicates, creating a chart/coordinate system inside the feasible region where every generated sample is valid by construction and margin distributions are learned faithfully, avoiding the failures of predicate-level grounding and constraint-layer clamping.
AI.motivation: Predicate-level grounding of constraints in LTN-GANs can only score samples and cannot embed hard structural constraints (orderings, positivity, definitional identities) that must hold in every generated sample. Existing alternatives like constraint layers that clamp samples to the feasible boundary produce valid but unrealistic outputs, losing the margin distribution of constraints.
AI.method: Grounds each logical axiom as a function symbol inside the LTN framework instead of a predicate. Function symbols compute constrained variables rather than scoring them, forming a chart (coordinate system) inside the feasible region. Introduces the resolution ratio R (data scale over margin spread) as a pre-training diagnostic for whether a chosen grounding can learn a constraint.
AI.result: When R is large, predicate-based grounding receives no learning signal and clamp-based approaches push all samples onto the boundary, losing the margin distribution while standard metrics still appear fine. Function-symbol grounding avoids both failures by construction, ensuring valid samples while learning the margin distribution like any other quantity.
AI.conclusion: Function-symbol grounding is superior to predicate grounding for hard structural constraints in LTN-GANs, and the resolution ratio R serves as a useful diagnostic for determining constraint learnability before training. A valid sample is not necessarily a realistic one—constraint satisfaction must consider the margin distribution.

title: Emotion Intensity Matters: Generating Realistic Expressions in Virtual Humans with CVAEs
summary: Generating expressive facial behavior in virtual humans (VHs) remains a central challenge in affective computing and character animation. This paper presents a novel approach based on Conditional Variational Autoencoders (CVAEs), trained on real human facial expression data, to synthesize controllable emotional expressions at varying intensities. Using a dataset comprising six basic emotions represented at two intensity levels (low and high), we train a CVAE model to generate synthetic facial expression data while preserving semantic consistency with real human expressions. Despite the limited amount of training data (only 7,680 facial expression samples), the proposed approach learns meaningful latent representations and generates coherent emotional variations. Our method enables control over emotional intensity, making it suitable for animating virtual characters without requiring actor performances or manual artistic intervention. Our research aimed to evaluate whether the method (CVAE) preserves the characteristics associated with the different intensity levels present in the dataset. Results show that the proposed model preserves key expressive characteristics across intensity levels while supporting generalization across emotional intensity levels, contributing to the creation of emotionally expressive virtual characters from relatively small datasets.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a CVAE-based approach trained on real human facial expression data to synthesize controllable emotional expressions at varying intensity levels for virtual humans. Despite using a small dataset (7,680 samples of six basic emotions at low/high intensity), the model learns meaningful latent representations, preserves expressive characteristics across intensity levels, and enables emotional intensity control without actor performances or manual artistic intervention.
AI.motivation: Generating expressive facial behavior in virtual humans remains a central challenge in affective computing and character animation, particularly when aiming for controllable emotional expressions without relying on actor performances or manual artistic intervention.
AI.method: The approach uses a Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) trained on a dataset of six basic emotions at two intensity levels (low and high), comprising 7,680 real human facial expression samples. The CVAE learns latent representations conditioned on emotional categories and intensity to synthesize coherent emotional variations while preserving semantic consistency.
AI.result: The CVAE model learns meaningful latent representations and generates coherent emotional variations despite limited training data. Results show the model preserves key expressive characteristics across intensity levels and supports generalization across emotional intensity levels.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CVAE method effectively enables controllable emotional expression synthesis for virtual characters from relatively small datasets, contributing to emotionally expressive VHs without requiring actor performances or manual artistic input.

title: Lifelong Robot Recomposition via Persistent Categorical Modeling for Unified Task-Driven Co-Design, Verification, and Planning
summary: Robotic systems are traditionally designed and deployed in static configurations, with assumptions made at design-time becoming immutable constraints during runtime. This design-then-deploy paradigm produces performant systems under narrow operating conditions, but renders robots brittle when qualities of themselves, their tasks, or their environments unexpectedly change. We address this challenge with a compositional framework that formalizes robotic systems as abstract circuits within a strict symmetric monoidal category, in which design and runtime composition of hardware, software, and behavior are synthesized simultaneously via an SMT-based solver, with monoidal functors projecting the system into lifecycle-specific views and free symbolic variables simultaneously solving for parameters and entire component specifications within larger compositions. This persistent model also supports queries a long-lived system needs beyond plan existence across its entire lifecycle, including mapping Pareto fronts over candidate compositions, diagnosing why a composition has become infeasible, finding its minimal restoration, and reconfiguring with limited change to the deployed system. We evaluate against official implementations of optimal numeric, stream-based, and SMT-based planners all measured onboard a deployed robot and demonstrate the approach end-to-end in a search-and-rescue scenario in which the robot recognizes when it has become unfit and synthesizes and assumes new holistic configurations to restore operation. We release our solver and supporting software open-source.

AI.tldr: A compositional framework formalizes robotic systems as abstract circuits in a strict symmetric monoidal category, using SMT-based synthesis to simultaneously design and runtime-compose hardware, software, and behavior, with monoidal functors and free symbolic variables enabling lifecycle-wide queries such as Pareto front mapping, infeasibility diagnosis, minimal restoration, and reconfiguration. Evaluated against official optimal planners on a deployed robot in a search-and-rescue scenario.
AI.motivation: Traditional design-then-deploy robotic systems are brittle when system, task, or environmental qualities change at runtime, because design-time assumptions become immutable constraints. There is a need for a framework that supports both design-time and runtime composition of robotic systems holistically.
AI.method: A compositional framework that (1) formalizes robotic systems as abstract circuits within a strict symmetric monoidal category, (2) synthesizes design and runtime composition of hardware, software, and behavior simultaneously via an SMT-based solver, (3) uses monoidal functors to project systems into lifecycle-specific views, and (4) uses free symbolic variables to solve for parameters and entire component specifications within larger compositions.
AI.result: Evaluation against official implementations of optimal numeric, stream-based, and SMT-based planners onboard a deployed robot, plus an end-to-end search-and-rescue demonstration where the robot detects its own unfitness and synthesizes new holistic configurations to restore operation. Software released open-source.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables persistent, lifecycle-spanning queries beyond plan existence—mapping Pareto fronts over candidate compositions, diagnosing infeasibility, finding minimal restorations, and reconfiguring with limited change—demonstrating that robotic systems can maintain operation through autonomous holistic self-reconfiguration under changing conditions.

title: Training a Knowledge Base: Supervised Structure Learning for Agent-Curated Document Stores
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to IEEE BigData 2026
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation treats the document store as a frozen input, and the systems that instead let an agent curate one never measure what curation does to the store. We invert the framing: the knowledge base is the model. A training agent answers a supervised question against the current store, is shown the gold, then edits the store; an unchanged reader is later examined on a frozen snapshot under a fixed action budget. Where offline graph construction is unsupervised, (question, answer) pairs are our labels -- and that supervision is what makes the structure cheap. Per point of corpus indexed it returns 1.6x the action saving and 1.8x the accuracy of an unsupervised entity index covering everything, using 1,913 links against its 196,112. On questions the store trained on, an unchanged reader spends 31% fewer actions at higher accuracy, and the result reproduces on an official PhantomWiki generation whose questions we did not write. To measure how far this reaches we introduce a key-coverage gradient, a probe varying how much of a question the training set touched, replacing a train/test split's pass/fail with a decay curve. Generalization proves endpoint-dependent: accuracy carries to unseen questions (+0.167 F1 where both of a question's keys were indexed, +0.100 where one was, zero where neither) while the action saving stays on trained questions. Because that decay is indexed by coverage rather than by novelty, more training extends it -- and the store is undertrained, not saturated: coverage grows linearly in new questions and stops the moment training repeats them, so a hundred questions reach a quarter of the corpus and four times as many would close the gap.

AI.tldr: This paper inverts the standard retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framing by treating the knowledge base as the model itself. A training agent edits the document store using supervised (question, answer) pairs, and an unchanged reader is later evaluated on a frozen snapshot. This supervised curation produces 1.6x action savings and 1.8x accuracy per point of corpus indexed compared to an unsupervised entity index, while using only 1,913 links versus 196,112. The authors introduce a key-coverage gradient to measure generalization decay, finding that accuracy generalizes to unseen questions based on key coverage while action savings remain on trained questions. The store is shown to be undertrained rather than saturated, with coverage growing linearly in new questions.
AI.motivation: Standard RAG treats the document store as a frozen input with no feedback loop, while existing agent-curated systems never measure what curation actually does to the store. The paper inverts the framing to make the knowledge base itself the model, using supervised (question, answer) pairs as labels to guide store editing — where prior offline graph construction was entirely unsupervised.
AI.method: A training agent answers a supervised question against the current store, is shown the gold answer, then edits the store. An unchanged reader is later evaluated on a frozen store snapshot under a fixed action budget. The authors introduce a key-coverage gradient, a probe that varies how much of a question the training set touched, replacing a binary train/test split with a decay curve. Generalization is measured as a function of key coverage (both, one, or neither of a question's keys indexed).
AI.result: Per point of corpus indexed, the method returns 1.6x the action saving and 1.8x the accuracy of an unsupervised entity index covering everything, using only 1,913 links versus 196,112. On trained questions, an unchanged reader spends 31% fewer actions at higher accuracy, and results reproduce on an official PhantomWiki generation. Accuracy generalizes: +0.167 F1 where both keys were indexed, +0.100 where one was, zero where neither. Action savings remain on trained questions. Coverage grows linearly in new questions and stops when training repeats, so a hundred questions reach a quarter of the corpus.
AI.conclusion: Generalization is endpoint-dependent: accuracy transfers to unseen questions proportional to key coverage, while action savings are confined to trained questions. Because decay is indexed by coverage rather than novelty, more training extends it — the store is undertrained, not saturated. Increasing from a hundred questions toward four times that number would close the coverage gap.

title: Semantic Compression Trees: Multi-Resolution Knowledge Retrieval via Hierarchical Semantic Residuals
summary:
Retrieval-augmented generation relies mostly on flat, fixed-granularity indexes: documents are cut into uniform chunks and retrieved by similarity, discarding the hierarchical structure of the source. We introduce Semantic Compression Trees (SCT), a hierarchical index in which each node stores only its semantic residual -- the information it adds beyond its parent -- and retrieval proceeds by progressive descent from the root, so that per-query cost is governed by tree depth rather than collection size.
  We evaluate on QASPER (50 papers, 173 questions) under two protocols differing only in whether the benchmark supplies the relevant document, with bootstrap confidence intervals and paired significance tests throughout. The results are mixed and we report them as such. When the document is given, SCT with a zero-LLM extractive compressor matches dense retrieval on answer quality (0.274 vs. 0.277 F1, $p = 0.37$) using 30% fewer context tokens and no LLM calls to build the index, and residual storage beats storing full summaries at each node (0.274 vs. 0.205, $p < 0.001$). Increasing the collection fifty-fold multiplies flat retrieval's per-query scoring work by 48.9x and SCT's by 6.4x.
  Progressive descent itself is not supported. Retrieving the same residuals without the tree performs identically when the document is given ($p = 0.27$), and descent is substantially worse when the system must select the document (0.122 vs. 0.165, $p < 0.001$). Routing accuracy localises the cause: descent selects the correct paper 20.2% of the time against 39.3% for flat retrieval, because that choice is made from the root residual, the most compressed node in the tree. We conclude that the residual representation is worth keeping and top-down routing is not.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Semantic Compression Trees (SCT), a hierarchical retrieval index where each node stores only the semantic residual beyond its parent, with retrieval by progressive descent. Evaluation on QASPER shows mixed results: residual representation helps (matches dense retrieval with 30% fewer tokens when the document is given), but top-down routing hurts document selection accuracy significantly (20.2% vs 39.3% correct paper selection).
AI.motivation: Standard RAG uses flat, fixed-granularity chunk indexes that discard the hierarchical structure of source documents, leading to inefficient retrieval that scales with collection size rather than tree depth.
AI.method: SCT builds a hierarchical index where each node stores only its semantic residual (information beyond its parent), and retrieval proceeds by progressive descent from the root, making per-query cost depend on tree depth instead of collection size. Evaluated under two protocols (document given vs. document selection required) on QASPER with bootstrap confidence intervals and paired significance tests.
AI.result: With document given: SCT with zero-LLM extractive compressor matches dense retrieval (0.274 vs 0.277 F1, p=0.37) using 30% fewer context tokens; residual storage beats full summaries (0.274 vs 0.205, p<0.001). Scaling collection 50x: flat retrieval work grows 48.9x vs 6.4x for SCT. However, progressive descent is not supported — without hierarchical routing, identical performance when document given (p=0.27), and descent is substantially worse when document selection is required (0.122 vs 0.165, p<0.001) due to poor routing accuracy (20.2% vs 39.3% correct paper selection) caused by decisions made from the most compressed root residual.
AI.conclusion: The residual representation is a worthwhile contribution, but top-down routing as implemented does not work well; the authors honestly report mixed results rather than overclaiming success.

title: StereoDiffuer: Diffusion-based Progressive Geometry Modeling with Saliency Attention Perception for Stereo Matching
comment: 17 pages, 9 figures, and 11 tables. Accepted by Signal Processing: Image Communication
summary: With the advance of deep neural networks, the quality of disparity maps obtained through stereo matching has steadily improved. However, existing stereo matching methods still struggle to preserve fine-grained geometric details, resulting in blurred edges and over-smoothed predictions in challenging regions. To address these limitations, we propose StereoDiffuer, an iterative diffusion-based stereo matching framework that explicitly models geometric details and progressively refines disparity estimates. The framework incorporates a Saliency Attention Perception (SAP) module to extract salient geometric cues, including object boundaries, thin structures, and sharp edges. Confidence-guided SAP features are combined with the initial disparity estimate to condition an iterative denoising diffusion process, which corrects residual disparity errors and restores geometric details suppressed during cost-volume regularization and upsampling. Experimental results on the Scene Flow and KITTI benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework and its competitive performance relative to the compared stereo matching methods.

AI.tldr: StereoDiffuser is an iterative diffusion-based stereo matching framework that explicitly models fine-grained geometric details using a Saliency Attention Perception (SAP) module, combining confidence-guided salient geometric cues with initial disparity estimates to condition a denoising diffusion process that corrects residual errors and restores edges and structures suppressed during cost-volume regularization and upsampling.
AI.motivation: Existing stereo matching methods, despite steady quality improvements from deep neural networks, still fail to preserve fine-grained geometric details, producing blurred edges and over-smoothed predictions in challenging regions.
AI.method: The framework proposes StereoDiffuser, an iterative diffusion-based approach featuring a Saliency Attention Perception (SAP) module that extracts salient geometric cues (object boundaries, thin structures, sharp edges). Confidence-guided SAP features are fused with initial disparity estimates to condition an iterative denoising diffusion process that progressively corrects residual disparity errors and restores suppressed geometric details.
AI.result: Experimental results on the Scene Flow and KITTI benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework and its competitive performance relative to compared stereo matching methods.
AI.conclusion: The diffusion-based iterative refinement conditioned on salient geometric cues effectively addresses edge blurring and over-smoothing in stereo matching, achieving competitive results on standard benchmarks.

title: In-Situ Reconstruction of the International Space Station Using 3D Gaussian Splatting and Astrobee
summary: This article presents a novel 3D reconstruction and mapping of the interior of the International Space Station (ISS) using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). Using existing grayscale images from the Astrobee free-flying robot dataset, we construct a full 3D splat of the ISS' Kibō or Japanese Experiment Module (JEM). 3DGS has in recent years shown promise in providing novel view synthesis of scenes captured from many images or videos, this article applies this approach to human spaceflight systems. We compare our 3DGS architecture to existing methods such as Nerfacto and TensoRF and show that reconstruction improves the state-of-the-art in both scene quality and rendering speed. We show that with as little as 500 in-situ images, a high-fidelity map can be constructed using Astrobee's Navigation Camera (NavCam) during free-flight in the JEM. These reconstructions could enable free-flyers to rapidly create and update interior maps for intra-vehicular habitats like the ISS.

AI.tldr: This paper applies 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to reconstruct the interior of the ISS Japanese Experiment Module (Kibō) using grayscale images from the Astrobee free-flying robot, achieving state-of-the-art scene quality and rendering speed compared to Nerfacto and TensoRF, even with as few as 500 images from the NavCam.
AI.motivation: The need for rapid, high-fidelity 3D mapping and reconstruction of intra-vehicular habitats like the ISS to enable free-flying robots to create and update interior maps autonomously.
AI.method: The authors apply 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to existing grayscale images captured by the Astrobee free-flying robot's Navigation Camera (NavCam) to construct a full 3D splat of the ISS Kibō module (JEM). They benchmark their architecture against existing methods (Nerfacto and TensoRF) for scene quality and rendering speed.
AI.result: The 3DGS-based reconstruction outperforms Nerfacto and TensoRF in both scene quality and rendering speed. A high-fidelity map can be constructed from as few as 500 in-situ grayscale images captured during free-flight in the JEM.
AI.conclusion: 3DGS is a promising approach for real-time, rapid 3D mapping of human spaceflight habitats, enabling free-flyers like Astrobee to efficiently construct and update interior maps for intra-vehicular environments.

title: GUI-Primitives: Diagnosing Spatial Reasoning Failures in Vision-Language GUI Grounding
summary: Computer-use agents ground natural-language instructions in screenshots to locate interface elements, yet existing benchmarks do not isolate whether models bind relational language to the correct element. We introduce GUI-Primitives, a 994-item benchmark of contrastive instruction pairs over seven spatial relations in graphical user interfaces (left/right, above/below, containment, alignment, proximity, list ordinal, occlusion). Each pair holds the screenshot and anchor fixed while changing the relation expression, so the correct target moves between two designated candidates. Five annotators validate a 196-item subset ($κ= 0.94$ well-formedness; $κ= 0.79$ target selection). Nineteen vision-language models reach at most $32\%$ strict point-in-box accuracy. Because models emit unconstrained coordinates, we classify each prediction by the candidate region it falls within. Predictions fall outside both candidates on $60-92\%$ of items. Conditional on falling within a candidate region, target selection reaches 0.82-0.90 for horizontal position, vertical position, proximity, and list ordinal, but does not differ significantly from 0.50 for containment and occlusion: most failures reflect candidate localization rather than relation understanding. Across ten models, benchmark accuracy correlates with ScreenSpot-Pro accuracy (Spearman $ρ= +0.74$), an exploratory association at this sample size. Marking the two designated candidates raises selection accuracy by 35--57 percentage points, an oracle diagnostic that supplies the candidate set rather than a deployable method. We release the benchmark, predictions, and code.

AI.tldr: GUI-Primitives is a 994-item benchmark of contrastive instruction pairs testing whether vision-language models can bind spatial relational language to correct interface elements in screenshots. Nineteen VLMs achieve at most 32% strict point-in-box accuracy; most failures stem from candidate localization rather than relation understanding, with weak performance (chance-level) on containment and occlusion relations.
AI.motivation: Existing computer-use benchmarks do not isolate whether models genuinely bind relational language (e.g., "left of," "above," "containing") to the correct interface element. The authors aim to disentangle whether failures arise from relation understanding versus candidate localization.
AI.method: Constructs 994 contrastive instruction pairs over seven spatial relations (left/right, above/below, containment, alignment, proximity, list ordinal, occlusion), holding screenshots and anchors fixed while varying the relation expression so the correct target moves between two candidates. Five annotators validate subsets (κ=0.94 well-formedness, κ=0.79 target selection). Nineteen VLMs are evaluated with strict point-in-box accuracy and a relaxed candidate-region classification, plus an oracle diagnostic that marks candidate regions.
AI.result: Maximum strict accuracy is 32%. Predictions fall outside both candidates on 60-92% of items. Conditional on falling within a candidate, accuracy is 0.82-0.90 for horizontal/vertical position, proximity, and list ordinal, but not significantly different from 0.50 for containment and occlusion. Benchmark accuracy correlates with ScreenSpot-Pro (ρ=+0.74). Marking candidates raises selection accuracy by 35-57 points.
AI.conclusion: Most model failures on GUI grounding reflect candidate localization rather than relational language understanding. However, containment and occlusion relations are genuinely not understood, even when localization is satisfied. The candidate-marking oracle is a diagnostic for isolating relation understanding, not a deployable solution.

title: SAEM: Stage-Aware Expert Management for Memory-Efficient MoE Inference in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
comment: Extended version of the paper accepted at DAC 2026. Extends the conference version with evaluations on AIME 2024 and GPQA-Diamond and a prediction-oracle upper-bound analysis
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting improves LLM reasoning by decomposing complex problems into intermediate steps, but its sequential nature increases decoding latency and memory usage. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale capacity through sparse expert activation, yet their full expert weights often exceed GPU memory and require costly GPU-CPU transfers. Existing runtimes treat all tokens uniformly, overlooking a key structural property of CoT traces: consecutive reasoning stages exhibit coherent and predictable expert activation patterns. Ignoring this stage-level regularity leads to inefficient caching and unnecessary data movement. We propose SAEM, a stage-aware MoE inference runtime that detects reasoning stage boundaries and exploits stage-level activation coherence to guide expert placement. SAEM combines stage-aware caching, expert-aligned token repacking, and in-situ CPU execution to reduce data transfer and kernel fragmentation. On mathematical and scientific reasoning workloads, SAEM achieves an average 1.33x throughput improvement over the strongest state-of-the-art caching and offloading baselines under constrained GPU memory, rising to 1.54x when calibration data matches the workload, demonstrating the effectiveness of stage-aware, locality-driven MoE inference for CoT reasoning.

AI.tldr: SAEM is a stage-aware MoE inference runtime that detects reasoning stage boundaries in chain-of-thought traces and exploits stage-level expert activation coherence to guide expert placement, caching, token repacking, and CPU execution, achieving up to 1.54x throughput improvement over state-of-the-art baselines under constrained GPU memory.
AI.motivation: CoT prompting improves LLM reasoning but increases decoding latency and memory usage; MoE models scale capacity via sparse expert activation but their full expert weights exceed GPU memory, requiring costly GPU-CPU transfers. Existing runtimes treat all tokens uniformly, overlooking the structural property that consecutive reasoning stages in CoT traces exhibit coherent and predictable expert activation patterns, leading to inefficient caching and unnecessary data movement.
AI.method: SAEM combines three key techniques: (1) stage-aware caching that exploits stage-level activation coherence for expert placement decisions, (2) expert-aligned token repacking to reduce kernel fragmentation, and (3) in-situ CPU execution to minimize data transfer. The runtime detects reasoning stage boundaries in CoT traces and uses this stage-level regularity to guide memory management and scheduling decisions.
AI.result: On mathematical and scientific reasoning workloads, SAEM achieves an average 1.33x throughput improvement over the strongest state-of-the-art caching and offloading baselines under constrained GPU memory, rising to 1.54x when calibration data matches the workload.
AI.conclusion: Stage-aware, locality-driven MoE inference is effective for CoT reasoning, demonstrating that exploiting reasoning-stage expert activation coherence significantly improves throughput in memory-constrained settings.

title: The Plan, Not the Decoder: Diagnosing and Repairing Compositional Failure in Reasoning-Augmented Text-to-Image Generation
summary: Reasoning-augmented text-to-image models such as GoT-R1 emit an explicit textual plan - object names, attributes, and bounding boxes - before generating image tokens. When such a model fails a compositional prompt, is the plan wrong, or is the plan right and the decoder unfaithful? Because the plan is machine-readable it can be edited before decoding, which makes the two separable. We first validate the ruler. Swapping the two bounding boxes inside the model's own chain demonstrably flips the generated layout: detector-based accuracy falls 0.75 -> 0.48 (p<1e-3), while a widely used VQA-based spatial metric rises. A five-rater human study agrees with the detector on 81% of items and with the VQA judge on 57%. All spatial results therefore use geometric scoring. Under sound measurement the decoder is a faithful executor: 94% of generated layouts realize the planned relation, and object-box binding survives reordering of the plan's object segments. The planner is the bottleneck. It writes wrong relations for phrasing-dependent reasons - 98% accuracy on "left" against 54% on "right" for semantically identical layouts, a raster-order bias we isolate with a mention-order control - and cluttered geometry that the decoder faithfully reproduces. Editing the plan therefore fixes the image without retraining: symbolic verification with resampling gives +5.0 points (p<1e-3), minimal in-place repair +6.0 (p=.02), rewriting only box geometry +10.7 (p<1e-4), and replacing the plan outright +13.3 (p=1e-4). Gains are indifferent to the plan's prose style and to its likelihood under the planner, but not to its geometry. Modular planner-decoder designs are therefore viable, provided the plan is internally consistent: box-text contradictions induce object duplication and identity fusion. We release the plan-fidelity evaluation protocol, all plans, and 12k generated images.

AI.tldr: This paper separates planning from decoding in reasoning-augmented text-to-image models by editing the machine-readable plan before decoding. Using detector-based geometric scoring, the authors show the decoder is a faithful executor (94% layout fidelity), while the planner is the bottleneck—exhibiting biases like asymmetric "left"/"right" accuracy (98% vs 54%) and cluttered geometry. Editing plans fixes images without retraining, with gains up to +13.3 points, but box-text contradictions cause object duplication and identity fusion.
AI.motivation: When reasoning-augmented text-to-image models fail compositional prompts, it is unclear whether the textual plan is wrong or the decoder is unfaithful. Since the plan is machine-readable and editable before decoding, the authors aim to disentangle these two failure sources and determine where the bottleneck lies.
AI.method: The authors validate a measurement "ruler" by swapping bounding boxes in the model's own chain and comparing detector-based accuracy against a VQA-based metric, with a five-rater human study adjudicating. They then use geometric scoring to test decoder faithfulness (layout realization and object-box binding under plan reordering), and separately probe planner errors via mention-order controls. Finally, they test plan editing strategies (symbolic verification with resampling, in-place repair, rewriting box geometry, replacing the plan) without retraining.
AI.result: Swapping boxes flips layout (detector accuracy 0.75→0.48, p<1e-3); human raters agree with the detector 81% vs. 57% with VQA. The decoder is faithful: 94% of layouts realize the planned relation and binding survives reordering. The planner is the bottleneck: "left" accuracy is 98% vs 54% for "right" (raster-order bias), and cluttered geometry is reproduced faithfully. Plan editing improves compositional accuracy: +5.0 (resampling), +6.0 (in-place repair), +10.7 (box geometry rewrite), +13.3 (full plan replacement). Gains depend on geometry, not prose style or planner likelihood. Box-text contradictions cause object duplication and identity fusion.
AI.conclusion: Modular planner-decoder designs are viable provided the plan is internally consistent. The decoder is a faithful executor; the planner is the primary failure source. Plan editing without retraining is an effective fix, and the authors release the plan-fidelity evaluation protocol, all plans, and 12k generated images.

title: Towards insect-like distributed proprioception in actuators and appendages for flapping-wing insect-scale aerial robots
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, this work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Modern flapping-wing insect-scale air vehicles display agility similar to that of their insect counterparts; however, these impressive maneuvers are only possible with off-board sensors like optical tracking cameras. In this manuscript, we introduce two embedded proprioceptive sensors for insect-scale aerial robots: thin film piezoelectric polymers integrated directly into a driving actuator and a pitching hinge which track stroke and pitch angle, respectively. We fabricate the aforementioned size-agnostic mechanically intelligent structures (sensor-actuator, sensor-flexure) using laminate stack fabrication methods. Chirp experiments with our sensors integrated into an insect-size flapping-wing robot show accurate tracking of stroke (RMSE = 0.44 deg) and pitch (RMSE = 2.44 deg) angles in the relevant frequency range. As the first step towards demonstrating the utility of these sensors for enabling numerous onboard autonomy applications, including closed-loop wingbeat control and sensor fusion with existing insect-scale sensor suites for more accurate proprioception and localization, we show one application for each sensor. The proprioceptive hinge enables collision detection, reducing the chance of permanent damage if the robot's wing collides with an object. The proprioceptive actuator enables asynchronous flapping, which is hypothesized to increase adaptability and efficiency in insects and robots alike. A microrobot equipped with our proprioceptive actuator allows us to test these hypotheses with potential for improving flapping aerial robot performance. We foresee proprioceptive sensors having an important role in progressing both the fields of insect-scale aerial robots and robo-physics due to the bio-inspired nature and high integration level of our sensors.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces two embedded proprioceptive sensors for insect-scale flapping-wing aerial robots: a thin-film piezoelectric sensor-actuator that tracks wing stroke angle, and a piezoelectric sensor-flexure that tracks pitch angle. Both are fabricated using laminate stack methods and demonstrated on an insect-size robot with high accuracy (stroke RMSE = 0.44°, pitch RMSE = 2.44°). Two applications showcase utility: collision detection via the proprioceptive hinge, and asynchronous flapping via the proprioceptive actuator.
AI.motivation: Insect-scale flapping-wing air vehicles achieve impressive agility but currently depend on off-board sensors (e.g., optical tracking cameras) for such maneuvers. There is a need for embedded proprioceptive sensing to enable onboard autonomy, closed-loop control, and improved sensor fusion for these micro-robots.
AI.method: The authors integrate thin-film piezoelectric polymers directly into a driving actuator and a pitching hinge of an insect-scale flapping-wing robot. These size-agnostic, mechanically intelligent structures (sensor-actuator and sensor-flexure) are fabricated using laminate stack fabrication. Chirp experiments are used to validate their sensing accuracy for stroke and pitch angles across relevant frequencies.
AI.result: The sensors achieve accurate tracking of stroke angle (RMSE = 0.44°) and pitch angle (RMSE = 2.44°) in the relevant frequency range. Two application demonstrations are provided: the proprioceptive hinge enables collision detection to prevent permanent wing damage, and the proprioceptive actuator enables asynchronous flapping behavior.
AI.conclusion: The embedded proprioceptive sensors represent a significant step toward onboard autonomy for insect-scale aerial robots, with applications in closed-loop wingbeat control, sensor fusion, and collision avoidance. The bio-inspired, highly integrated nature of these sensors is expected to advance both insect-scale aerial robotics and robo-physics.

title: PUMA: A Polish Benchmark for Culturally Grounded Multimodal Understanding
summary: Large language models are increasingly moving beyond text processing, adding support for other modalities such as images and audio. While text understanding and generation have been extensively studied, multimodal data processing capabilities, particularly in the context of cultures and languages other than English, have not yet been evaluated comprehensively. In this paper, we propose PUMA (Polish Unified Multimodal Assessment), a novel benchmark of 900 hand-crafted tasks designed to probe the limits of multimodal models in the Polish cultural and linguistic context. The dataset evaluates both cultural understanding and practical skill in processing text, images, audio, and visually rich documents. Our extensive evaluation of frontier commercial models, open-weights models, and specialized smaller systems highlights a significant performance gap. While top commercial models achieve high scores in visual question answering, most models struggle with complex audio or document understanding. We open-source our evaluation framework to advance localized multimodal AI research.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces PUMA (Polish Unified Multimodal Assessment), a benchmark of 900 hand-crafted tasks evaluating multimodal LLMs in the Polish cultural and linguistic context across text, images, audio, and visually rich documents. Evaluation of frontier commercial, open-weights, and specialized models reveals a significant performance gap, particularly in complex audio and document understanding tasks.
AI.motivation: Multimodal capabilities of LLMs have expanded beyond text to images and audio, yet these capabilities have not been comprehensively evaluated for non-English languages and cultures. The authors aim to fill this gap by assessing multimodal models in the Polish context.
AI.method: The authors construct PUMA, a benchmark comprising 900 hand-crafted tasks targeting both cultural understanding and practical multimodal skill in Polish. The dataset covers text, images, audio, and visually rich documents, and is used to evaluate frontier commercial models, open-weights models, and specialized smaller systems.
AI.result: Top commercial models achieve high scores on visual question answering, but most models struggle significantly with complex audio or document understanding, revealing a notable performance gap across different modalities and model categories.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark highlights the need for more research and development in localized multimodal AI, and the authors open-source their evaluation framework to support advancement in this area.

title: Measuring Activation Control in Large Language Models
summary: Safe deployment of increasingly capable models will likely come to rely on latent-space monitoring as a complement to behavioral evaluations, especially when evaluation-aware models exhibit scheming or deception. However, if models can also control their own activations, deception could extend into the latent space itself. With this in mind, we introduce the Activation Controllability Benchmark to quantify the extent to which models can modulate their residual stream via natural-language instruction. Across model families and capability levels, we find that most LLMs can control the direction and magnitude of their residual stream activations with some degree of temporal resolution, though performance varies considerably across models. In simple tasks, this level of control can evade activation-based monitoring methods (including linear probes, natural language autoencoders, activation oracles, and the Jacobian lens), albeit imperfectly. These results suggest that control over the activation space itself could become a confound for monitoring as introspective capabilities increase; therefore, we recommend that frontier labs and evaluators track activation controllability in future models.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Activation Controllability Benchmark to measure how well LLMs can modulate their own residual stream activations via natural-language instructions. Results show most models can control activation direction, magnitude, and temporal resolution, and such control can partially evade activation-based monitoring methods.
AI.motivation: As models become more capable, monitoring methods relying on latent-space analysis may be vulnerable if models themselves can manipulate their activations. This is especially concerning for evaluation-aware models that may engage in scheming or deception, where such manipulation could extend to the latent space, confounding safety monitoring.
AI.method: The authors design the Activation Controllability Benchmark, which quantifies a model's ability to modulate its residual stream via natural-language instructions. They assess control over activation direction, magnitude, and temporal resolution across multiple model families and capability levels, and test whether such control evades several monitoring methods including linear probes, natural language autoencoders, activation oracles, and the Jacobian lens.
AI.result: Most LLMs can modulate their residual stream activations with some temporal resolution, though performance varies across models. On simple tasks, this level of control can evade activation-based monitoring methods, though evasion is imperfect.
AI.conclusion: Activation-space controllability could become a confound for latent-space monitoring as models' introspective capabilities grow. The authors recommend that frontier labs and evaluators track activation controllability in future models.

title: Calibrate What You SHIP: Post-Selection Risk Control for Verifier-Guided Text-to-Image Generation
summary: Verifier-guided text-to-image systems increasingly use test-time search to select, refine, or stop among multiple candidates, yet release thresholds are often calibrated on individual images. This creates a candidate-to-policy calibration mismatch: search changes both which prompts receive an output and which candidate is released, so candidate-level risk control need not imply control of released-output risk. We formalize this estimand shift through prompt reweighting and within-prompt selection, and introduce SHIP, Selection-aware Held-out calibration of Inference Policies. SHIP runs or replays the complete deployed policy on held-out prompts, evaluates the image it actually releases using an independent target judge, and selects the most permissive threshold whose risk upper bound satisfies a prescribed budget. For replayable policies with a prespecified threshold grid, simultaneous confidence control provides finite-sample validity. Experiments across fixed, sequential, and adaptive T2I inference procedures show that policy-level calibration recovers lower-risk operating points while exposing policy-dependent tradeoffs among risk, coverage, and compute. On GenEval2 with FLUX at N=16, a pooled-candidate threshold yields released risk 0.310, whereas SHIP reduces it to 0.162. Across 200 cached-stream splits, the fixed-grid certificate has no target crossing. Reliable inference-time scaling therefore requires calibrating the output distribution induced by the complete deployed policy.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a calibration mismatch in verifier-guided text-to-image systems where thresholds calibrated on individual candidates fail to control risk of the actual released output after test-time search. The authors introduce SHIP (Selection-aware Held-out calibration of Inference Policies), which calibrates the complete deployed policy by running/replaying it on held-out prompts, evaluating released images with an independent judge, and selecting the most permissive threshold with a valid risk upper bound via simultaneous confidence control. Experiments show SHIP reduces released risk from 0.310 to 0.162 on GenEval2/FLUX and produces valid certificates across cached-stream splits.
AI.motivation: Test-time search in text-to-image systems changes both which prompts receive output and which candidate is released, yet thresholds are typically calibrated on individual candidate images. This candidate-to-policy calibration mismatch means candidate-level risk control does not guarantee control of released-output risk—a formal estimand shift that existing calibration approaches fail to address.
AI.method: SHIP formalizes the estimand shift through prompt reweighting and within-prompt selection. It runs or replays the complete deployed policy on held-out prompts, evaluates the actual released image using an independent target judge, and selects the most permissive threshold whose risk upper bound satisfies the prescribed budget. For replayable policies with a prespecified threshold grid, simultaneous confidence control (e.g., multiple testing corrections) guarantees finite-sample validity.
AI.result: Across fixed, sequential, and adaptive T2I inference procedures, policy-level calibration recovers lower-risk operating points while exposing policy-dependent tradeoffs among risk, coverage, and compute. On GenEval2 with FLUX at N=16, a pooled-candidate threshold yields released risk 0.310, while SHIP reduces it to 0.162. Across 200 cached-stream splits, the fixed-grid certificate has no target crossing.
AI.conclusion: Reliable inference-time scaling in text-to-image generation requires calibrating the output distribution induced by the complete deployed policy, not individual candidates. Policy-level calibration (SHIP) provides finite-sample risk guarantees and exposes important tradeoffs between risk, coverage, and compute that candidate-level calibration misses.

title: Safety-Critical Bilateral Teleoperation for Omnidirectional Aerial Manipulation Using Force-Sensorless Haptic Feedback
comment: 8 pages, 10 figures. Accepted to the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: This paper presents a safety-critical bilateral teleoperation framework for omnidirectional aerial manipulators that integrates visual and force-sensorless haptic wrench feedback. Unlike existing approaches that either rely on onboard force/torque sensors or use model-dependent wrench estimates, which may become unreliable under model uncertainties or induce unintended feedback during free-flight, our method implements a hierarchical safety filter based on control barrier functions to avoid such limitations. The safety filter, being the key contribution, explicitly accounts for tracking errors arising from physical interaction between the aerial manipulator and its surroundings while enforcing thrust limits, a factor overlooked despite its critical importance for flight safety. This safety filter adjusts the command from the operator to ensure safe and stable aerial manipulation and avoid motor saturation. The adjustment made by the filter is mapped to haptic feedback, which is intuitive to the operator and conveys information on physical interaction and impending motor saturation. By actual experiments with a hexarotor-based omnidirectional aerial manipulator, we demonstrate that the proposed method avoids haptic feedback during free-flight, provides directionally consistent feedback under physical interaction, and can be operated for diverse manipulative tasks. Moreover, an ablation study further shows that the saturation filter improves interaction stability by explicitly preventing motor saturation and informing the operator of corrective actions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a safety-critical bilateral teleoperation framework for omnidirectional aerial manipulators that uses a hierarchical control barrier function-based safety filter to provide haptic wrench feedback without force/torque sensors. The filter explicitly accounts for tracking errors from physical interaction while enforcing thrust limits, and maps its corrective adjustments to intuitive haptic feedback. Experiments on a hexarotor platform validate that the method avoids haptic feedback during free-flight, provides directionally consistent feedback during interaction, and improves stability via saturation prevention.
AI.motivation: Existing teleoperation frameworks for aerial manipulators either rely on onboard force/torque sensors or use model-dependent wrench estimates that become unreliable under model uncertainties or induce unintended haptic feedback during free-flight. A safety-critical approach that avoids these limitations is needed.
AI.method: The method implements a hierarchical safety filter based on control barrier functions (CBFs) that explicitly accounts for tracking errors arising from physical interaction between the aerial manipulator and its environment while enforcing thrust limits. The filter adjusts operator commands to ensure safe and stable operation, and the adjustments are mapped to haptic feedback conveying physical interaction and impending motor saturation information.
AI.result: Actual experiments with a hexarotor-based omnidirectional aerial manipulator demonstrate that the proposed method avoids haptic feedback during free-flight, provides directionally consistent feedback under physical interaction, and supports diverse manipulative tasks. An ablation study confirms the saturation filter improves interaction stability by explicitly preventing motor saturation and informing the operator of corrective actions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CBF-based safety filter with sensorless haptic feedback provides a practical and reliable teleoperation solution for aerial manipulation, improving safety and interaction stability by preventing motor saturation while maintaining intuitive operator feedback.

title: HiDiffTIR: Hierarchical Difficulty-Aware Policy Optimization for Multi-Turn Tool-Integrated Reasoning
summary: Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) is a fundamental capability for LLM agents to solve complex tasks by interacting with external tools iteratively. Reinforcement Learning (RL) has become the dominant paradigm for enabling this capability. However, existing approaches typically assign uniform trajectory-level advantages and treat all correct tool calls equally, ignoring the varying difficulty and learning value across trajectories and reasoning steps. This can lead to imprecise learning signals that do not adequately distinguish between trivial and challenging tool-use patterns. To address this limitation, we propose HiDiffTIR, a Hierarchical Difficulty-aware policy optimization framework for multi-turn TIR. HiDiffTIR performs difficulty-aware credit assignment at both trajectory and turn levels, enabling the policy to focus on more informative trajectories and harder reasoning steps. Notably, this fine-grained optimization is achieved without additional supervision, relying solely on group-level statistics derived from standard RL rollouts. Extensive experiments on three tool-using benchmarks demonstrate that HiDiffTIR consistently improves multi-turn TIR performance and tool invocation accuracy over strong RL baselines, highlighting the necessity of difficulty-aware credit assignment for effective policy optimization in tool-integrated LLM agents.

AI.tldr: HiDiffTIR is a hierarchical difficulty-aware RL framework for tool-integrated reasoning that performs credit assignment at both trajectory and turn levels, enabling policies to focus on more informative trajectories and harder reasoning steps without additional supervision, improving multi-turn TIR performance and tool invocation accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing RL approaches for Tool-Integrated Reasoning assign uniform trajectory-level advantages and treat all correct tool calls equally, ignoring varying difficulty and learning value across trajectories and reasoning steps, leading to imprecise learning signals that fail to distinguish trivial from challenging tool-use patterns.
AI.method: HiDiffTIR performs difficulty-aware credit assignment at both trajectory and turn levels, using only group-level statistics derived from standard RL rollouts without additional supervision, enabling the policy to focus on more informative trajectories and harder reasoning steps in multi-turn TIR.
AI.result: Experiments on three tool-using benchmarks show HiDiffTIR consistently improves multi-turn TIR performance and tool invocation accuracy over strong RL baselines.
AI.conclusion: Difficulty-aware credit assignment is necessary for effective policy optimization in tool-integrated LLM agents, and hierarchical structuring of learning signals improves both performance and tool-use accuracy.

title: From Mastery Profile to Simulated Response: Stochastic Student Knowledge Graphs (SSKG) for Faithful LLM Student Simulation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate students at different mastery levels. These simulations can generate synthetic training data and stress-test tutoring systems. However, common prompt-based approaches leave the answer decision to the LLM, which tends to perform according to its built-in capabilities even when instructed to simulate a student with low mastery. As a result, these approaches may have difficulty distinguishing students with low and high levels of mastery. We demonstrate this limitation using 379 College Board-calibrated SAT Algebra items and five archetypal mastery profiles. Three LLMs from three vendors (Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, Claude Haiku 4.5, and GPT-5.4-mini) achieve 96.8-100% accuracy across all profiles. To address this limitation, we introduce a method grounded in a Stochastic Student Knowledge Graph (SSKG). A curriculum knowledge graph (CKG) is extracted from an open algebra textbook, and each SAT solution is decomposed into a chain of required triples. The SSKG assigns a mastery probability to each triple, which is sampled to determine question correctness. An LLM then generates a first-person rationale consistent with the outcome. The simulation reduces accuracy to 44.1-85.2% across profiles and produces a clear monotone mastery gradient.

AI.tldr: LLMs used to simulate students at different mastery levels tend to perform according to their built-in capabilities regardless of instructed mastery, achieving 96.8-100% accuracy on SAT Algebra items across five archetypal profiles. To fix this, the authors introduce a Stochastic Student Knowledge Graph (SSKG) method that decomposes SAT solutions into required knowledge-graph triples, assigns mastery probabilities to each triple, and samples to determine correctness. This reduces accuracy to 44.1-85.2% with a clear monotone mastery gradient.
AI.motivation: Prompt-based approaches for simulating low-mastery students fail because LLMs default to their own capabilities, making it difficult to distinguish between low and high mastery levels—a critical limitation for generating synthetic training data and stress-testing tutoring systems.
AI.method: A Stochastic Student Knowledge Graph (SSKG) grounded in a Curriculum Knowledge Graph (CKG) extracted from an open algebra textbook. Each SAT solution is decomposed into a chain of required triples, mastery probabilities are assigned to each triple and sampled to determine question correctness, and an LLM generates a first-person rationale consistent with the outcome. Tested on 379 College Board-calibrated SAT Algebra items with five archetypal mastery profiles across three LLMs (Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-5.4-mini).
AI.result: Prompt-based approaches achieve 96.8-100% accuracy across all mastery profiles, demonstrating poor discrimination. The SSKG-based approach reduces accuracy to 44.1-85.2% across profiles and produces a clear monotone mastery gradient, successfully distinguishing between different levels of student mastery.
AI.conclusion: The SSKG-based approach provides a more realistic and controllable method for simulating students at varied mastery levels than naive prompt-based prompting, enabling better differentiation of student abilities and more useful synthetic data generation.

title: Fidelity-Diversity-Consistency (FDC): Data Pruning for Remote Sensing Change Detection
summary: Despite the success of data pruning (DP) in reducing training data sizes and improving downstream model performance in classification and segmentation tasks, its potential in remote sensing change detection remains unexplored. For the first time, we benchmark six representative DP methods across building- and forest-change datasets, CNN- and transformer-based models, and three pruning budgets, and show that existing baselines yield no reliable advantage over random selection. Notably, even the strongest evaluated baseline, Feature Diversity, is matched or exceeded by $\sim$33\% of randomly sampled subsets. To understand the underlying mechanism, we conduct a systematic regression study over 540 randomly sampled data subsets, characterizing each with four descriptors covering label statistics, image diversity, and feature-space geometry. Random Forest models show that \emph{change distribution fidelity} is the most prominent factor in determining the quality of change detection data subsets, a property absent from the existing pruning literature. Our analyses further show that pixel-wise image diversity and label-feature consistency are secondary factors. We translate these findings into Fidelity-Diversity-Consistency (FDC), a simple two-stage pruning method that shows consistent improvements over existing baselines across change detection benchmarks and backbones, especially at lower pruning ratios. Code is available at \href{https://github.com/ddydyd32/fidelity-diversity-consistency}{https://github.com/ddydyd32/fidelity-diversity-consistency}.

AI.tldr: This paper is the first to benchmark data pruning (DP) methods for remote sensing change detection. It shows that six existing DP baselines offer no reliable advantage over random selection on building- and forest-change datasets. Through regression analysis over 540 random data subsets, the authors identify change distribution fidelity as the most critical factor for subset quality. They propose Fidelity-Diversity-Consistency (FDC), a two-stage pruning method that consistently outperforms existing baselines, especially at lower pruning ratios.
AI.motivation: Data pruning has been successful in classification and segmentation tasks, but its potential in remote sensing change detection remains unexplored. This paper seeks to fill that gap by benchmarking existing DP methods and understanding what actually drives subset quality in the change detection context.
AI.method: The authors benchmark six representative DP methods across two change detection datasets (building and forest), CNN- and transformer-based backbones, and three pruning budgets. They conduct a systematic regression study over 540 randomly sampled data subsets, characterizing each with four descriptors (label statistics, image diversity, and feature-space geometry). Random Forest models are used to identify which descriptors most influence change detection subset quality. Based on these findings, they design FDC, a two-stage pruning method incorporating fidelity, diversity, and consistency.
AI.result: Existing DP baselines show no reliable advantage over random selection in change detection; even the strongest baseline (Feature Diversity) is matched or exceeded by ~33% of random subsets. Regression analysis reveals change distribution fidelity is the most dominant factor, with pixel-wise image diversity and label-feature consistency as secondary factors. The proposed FDC method achieves consistent improvements over existing baselines across benchmarks and backbones, particularly at lower pruning ratios.
AI.conclusion: Change distribution fidelity is a unique and critical property for data pruning in change detection that is absent from existing pruning literature. The FDC method successfully translates this insight into a practical pruning approach that yields consistent performance gains over prior baselines.

title: CounterAlign: Counterfactual Supervision for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are typically trained with behavior cloning (BC) on expert demonstrations. However, BC provides only positive supervision for expert actions, without explicit negative supervision indicating which actions are instruction-inconsistent or otherwise inappropriate. Reinforcement learning (RL) can provide such corrective signals, but often relies on externally specified rewards or curated non-expert data, both of which are costly to obtain in robotics. We show that offline RL for VLA models need not rely on curated non-expert trajectories: successful expert demonstrations alone can be transformed into dense corrective supervision through instruction relabeling. Specifically, by pairing expert actions with mismatched alternative instructions, we synthesize counterfactual instruction-observation-action tuples from the dataset and combine them with adversarial discriminator training to learn an instruction-grounded reward model for offline RL, without collecting additional rollouts or annotations. On the robustness-focused LIBERO-PRO benchmark, our method improves robustness to object position and task perturbations over a strong state-of-the-art baseline. It also outperforms competitive baselines in real-robot experiments on the TX-G2 (compatible with AGIBot G2). More broadly, our results suggest that, for data-constrained VLA learning, extracting denser supervision from each demonstration can complement collecting additional data.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a method to extract dense corrective supervision for offline RL of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models without curated non-expert data, by relabeling instructions on expert demonstrations to create counterfactual training tuples and using adversarial discriminator training to learn an instruction-grounded reward model. The method improves robustness on LIBERO-PRO and outperforms baselines in real-robot experiments.
