AI.motivation: VLA models are typically trained with behavior cloning, which only provides positive supervision on expert actions without explicit negative signals for instruction-inconsistent actions. While RL can provide corrective supervision, it often requires costly externally specified rewards or curated non-expert data in robotics settings.
AI.method: The method synthesizes counterfactual instruction-observation-action tuples by pairing expert actions with mismatched (alternative) instructions from the existing dataset. These synthetic negatives are combined with adversarial discriminator training to learn an instruction-grounded reward model, enabling offline RL without additional rollouts, annotations, or curated non-expert trajectories.
AI.result: The method improves robustness to object position and task perturbations over a strong state-of-the-art baseline on the LIBERO-PRO benchmark, and outperforms competitive baselines in real-robot experiments on the TX-G2 platform (compatible with AGIBot G2).
AI.conclusion: For data-constrained VLA learning, extracting denser supervision from each demonstration—via instruction relabeling and counterfactual training—can complement collecting additional data, suggesting a more efficient path to robust policy learning.

title: The Chase Is the Curriculum, the Capture Anchors the Credit: Pursuit-Evasion Self-Play for Zero-Data LLM Reasoning
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has become the dominant recipe for improving large language model reasoning, yet it presumes large human-curated task collections. Zero-data self-play removes this dependency, but existing methods vet learnability only by probing candidates and rejecting post hoc, never learning where along an environment's difficulty axis to place a task, and credit the solver with sparse terminal rewards alone. We recast zero-data self-play as a pursuit-evasion game: in LURE, an LLM evader positions tasks along each environment's difficulty axis to stay one step ahead of a planner-executor pursuer that hunts it down through verifiable interaction. The evader is trained on a capture-frontier reward that peaks when the solver captures it on exactly half of its rollouts, turning barely catchable into a learned positioning strategy rather than a hand-tuned rejection band. The pursuer earns capture-anchored dense process credit, in which monotone verifier progress is group-normalized jointly with the terminal capture under a round-anchored KL that keeps the co-evolution stable. Across three verifiable reasoning environments and three backbone families, LURE outperforms advanced baselines under unified/specialist settings, while the unified model attains stronger aggregate OOD zero-shot accuracy than all trained baselines across nine held-out benchmarks from three task families.

AI.tldr: LURE recasts zero-data self-play for LLM reasoning as a pursuit-evasion game where an evader positions tasks along a difficulty axis to stay just ahead of a solver, trained with a capture-frontier reward, while the solver earns capture-anchored dense process credit under round-anchored KL for stability. This outperforms baselines across three verifiable reasoning environments and three backbone families.
AI.motivation: Existing reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards relies on large human-curated task collections, while zero-data self-play methods only probe candidates and reject them post hoc, failing to learn where along a difficulty axis to place tasks and giving solvers only sparse terminal rewards.
AI.method: LURE frames zero-data self-play as a pursuit-evasion game. An LLM evader positions tasks along each environment's difficulty axis to stay one step ahead of a planner-executor pursuer. The evader is trained on a capture-frontier reward that peaks when the solver captures it on exactly half of its rollouts. The pursuer receives capture-anchored dense process credit, where monotone verifier progress is group-normalized jointly with terminal capture under a round-anchored KL to maintain co-evolution stability.
AI.result: Across three verifiable reasoning environments and three backbone families, LURE outperforms advanced baselines under unified and specialist settings. The unified model attains stronger aggregate OOD zero-shot accuracy than all trained baselines across nine held-out benchmarks from three task families.
AI.conclusion: Turning bare catchability into a learned positioning strategy rather than a hand-tuned rejection band enables effective zero-data self-play for improving LLM reasoning without human-curated task collections.

title: Context as an Environment: Programmatic Context Management for Long-Horizon Agents
summary: LLM agents increasingly take on long-running tasks whose history grows far beyond a single model context window. Existing approaches compress earlier interactions or extract selected information into fixed memory representations, committing to what to preserve before future needs are known. We present Scroll, a context manager that treats each agent session as an executable Session Environment. The environment is backed by an append-only Event Log and a sandboxed, persistent Python kernel. The kernel maintains a typed namespace across model calls, allowing tool outputs, retrieved history, and derived state to be bound to variables rather than serialized into the prompt at each call. Model-written code searches, materializes, and transforms session state through exec; only explicitly printed projections enter the model's working view for the next call. Context management thus becomes a programming task that inherits the improving coding abilities of LLMs, while the Event Log preserves lossless historical ground truth. As the working view approaches its budget, stale spans are evicted but remain recoverable: an eviction index keeps compact landmarks tied to exact Event Log addresses, so that the agent navigates directly to evicted regions instead of searching the full log. With Qwen3.8-Max as the backbone, Scroll achieves 94.8% on LongMemEval_S; 73.1% on BEAM_10M, surpassing the best published memory system by 5.1 points; and 86.7% on LOCA_256K, exceeding the best published long-horizon agent by 37.4 points.

AI.tldr: Scroll is a context manager that models agent sessions as executable Session Environments backed by an append-only Event Log and a persistent Python kernel, allowing context management to be framed as a programming task. It achieves state-of-the-art results on LongMemEval_S (94.8%), BEAM_10M (73.1%), and LOCA_256K (86.7%), significantly outperforming prior memory systems and long-horizon agents.
AI.motivation: LLM agents performing long-running tasks accumulate histories that exceed a single context window. Existing approaches compress interactions or extract fixed memory representations, committing to what to preserve before future needs are known—a fundamental limitation that Scroll aims to overcome.
AI.method: Scroll treats each agent session as an executable Session Environment with: (1) an append-only Event Log preserving lossless historical ground truth; (2) a sandboxed, persistent Python kernel maintaining a typed namespace across model calls, binding tool outputs and derived state to variables rather than serializing them into prompts; (3) model-written code that searches, materializes, and transforms session state via exec, with only printed projections entering the model's working view; and (4) an eviction index with compact landmarks tied to exact Event Log addresses for direct navigation to evicted regions.
AI.result: Using Qwen3.8-Max as the backbone, Scroll achieves 94.8% on LongMemEval_S, 73.1% on BEAM_10M (surpassing the best published memory system by 5.1 points), and 86.7% on LOCA_256K (exceeding the best published long-horizon agent by 37.4 points).
AI.conclusion: By reframing context management as a programming task that leverages LLMs' improving coding abilities, Scroll provides lossless history retention and efficient eviction-recovery, achieving superior performance on long-horizon and memory-intensive benchmarks compared to existing approaches.

title: Learning to Look Again: Loss-Gap Supervision for Free-form Crop Routing in Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) fail many detail-centric questions for a concrete reason: the answer is visible in the image, yet lost after the image is compressed into a low-resolution global view. Allocating more visual tokens to every query improves some OCR and document cases, but it spends computation indiscriminately and can disturb tasks that rely on global context. We propose GapSight, a framework for learning visual re-reading: a VLM first takes a global glance, then selectively returns to a free-form region when the question calls for local evidence. The supervision comes from the target model's own failure signal. Offline, we compare answer loss or multiple-choice option margin under a global-only view and candidate crop-augmented views; crops that improve the target answer become model-specific review labels. A lightweight free-form crop router distills these labels into a one-shot inference policy that predicts whether to review, expected utility, and a continuous crop box from the global state. Across LLaVA-1.5-7B, InternVL2.5-8B, and Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct, GapSight improves the Base no-zoom baseline on six benchmarks spanning OCR, documents, charts, infographics, VStarBench, and MME-RealWorld-Lite. On InternVL2.5-8B, GapSight raises the six-benchmark average from 52.25 to 64.29, above CropVLM (57.16), ViCrop (55.84), and ZoomRefine (54.43). Mechanism analyses show that the router rescues concrete wrong answers, adapts its action rate by task, and forms a favorable token-performance profile. These results position loss-gap supervision as a practical route to teaching VLMs when and where to look again.

AI.tldr: GapSight is a framework that teaches VLMs to selectively "re-read" local image regions by learning from the target model's own failure signals, improving performance on detail-centric benchmarks without indiscriminately allocating more tokens.
AI.motivation: VLMs fail detail-centric questions because answers are visible in the image but lost after compression into low-resolution global views. Naively allocating more visual tokens to every query wastes computation and can disturb tasks relying on global context.
AI.method: GapSight uses a two-stage approach: (1) offline, it compares answer loss or multiple-choice option margin under global-only views versus candidate crop-augmented views, using crops that improve the target answer as model-specific review labels; (2) a lightweight free-form crop router distills these labels into a one-shot inference policy that predicts whether to review, expected utility, and a continuous crop box from the global state.
AI.result: Across LLaVA-1.5-7B, InternVL2.5-8B, and Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct, GapSight improves the Base no-zoom baseline on six benchmarks (OCR, documents, charts, infographics, VStarBench, MME-RealWorld-Lite). On InternVL2.5-8B, the six-benchmark average rises from 52.25 to 64.29, outperforming CropVLM (57.16), ViCrop (55.84), and ZoomRefine (54.43).
AI.conclusion: Loss-gap supervision provides a practical route for teaching VLMs when and where to re-examine image regions, as the router rescues concrete wrong answers, adapts action rates by task, and achieves a favorable token-performance trade-off.

title: Vision Guided Target Conditioned Control for Autonomous Excavation
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at ISCSIC 2026
summary: Autonomous excavation requires an intelligent control system that can convert spatial work intent into coordinated bucket motion under contact-rich soil interaction. This paper presents a target-conditioned intelligent control framework for autonomous excavation in a physics-based deformable-soil simulation workflow. An image-aligned target mask serves as a visual spatial command for the desired digging region, while a mask-conditioned Action Chunking Transformer maps multi-view RGB observations, proprioception, and the target mask to temporally extended joystick commands. To reduce target-ignoring behavior, demonstrations are organized with paired-condition supervision, where the same or closely matched scene is demonstrated with different target masks and corresponding action chunks. The framework is evaluated through both a diagnostic manipulation task and an excavation simulation benchmark with single-scoop and sequential pile-clearing protocols. In manipulation, target success is 4\% for no-condition ACT, 63\% for non-paired mask-conditioned ACT, and 96\% for paired-condition mask-conditioned ACT. In sequential pile clearing, paired-condition mask-conditioned ACT removes 76.8\% of the pile versus 27.4\% and 15.7\% for the two baselines, with 91.0\% human-normalized efficiency. The results show that visual target conditioning, paired demonstration structure, and action-chunk control form a practical cyber-physical simulation pipeline for excavator automation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a target-conditioned intelligent control framework for autonomous excavation, using an image-aligned target mask as a visual spatial command and a mask-conditioned Action Chunking Transformer that maps multi-view RGB, proprioception, and the target mask to temporally extended joystick commands. The framework achieves 96% target success in manipulation and 76.8% pile removal with 91.0% human-normalized efficiency, significantly outperforming baselines.
AI.motivation: Autonomous excavation requires an intelligent control system capable of converting spatial work intent into coordinated bucket motion under contact-rich soil interaction, which is challenging due to the complexity of soil dynamics and the need for precise spatial targeting.
AI.method: The framework uses an image-aligned target mask as a visual spatial command for the desired digging region, and a mask-conditioned Action Chunking Transformer that maps multi-view RGB observations, proprioception, and the target mask to temporally extended joystick commands. Demonstrations are organized with paired-condition supervision, where the same or closely matched scene is demonstrated with different target masks and corresponding action chunks to reduce target-ignoring behavior. Evaluation is conducted in both a diagnostic manipulation task and an excavation simulation benchmark with single-scoop and sequential pile-clearing protocols.
AI.result: Target success: 4% for no-condition ACT, 63% for non-paired mask-conditioned ACT, and 96% for paired-condition mask-conditioned ACT. Sequential pile clearing: 76.8% of pile removed by paired-condition mask-conditioned ACT versus 27.4% and 15.7% for the two baselines, with 91.0% human-normalized efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Visual target conditioning, paired demonstration structure, and action-chunk control form a practical cyber-physical simulation pipeline for excavator automation, demonstrating that the proposed framework effectively bridges spatial intent and coordinated excavation actions.

title: BanglaVeilGuard: Cross-Script Safety Benchmarking and Lightweight Guardrails for Bangla Large Language Models
comment: Accepted at the 4th International Conference on Computing Advancements (ICCA 2026). 8 pages
summary: Bangla large language model (LLM) safety is difficult to evaluate with English-centric or standard-script benchmarks because Bangla users routinely write across scripts, spellings, code-mixed forms, and regional registers. This paper presents BanglaVeilGuard, a compact Bangla-first safety benchmark and lightweight prompt guard for six language forms: standard Bangla, Romanized Bangla, Banglish, code-mixed Bangla--English, noisy Bangla, and dialectal Bangla. The benchmark contains 2,366 quality-filtered prompts and a held-out 354-prompt evaluation split spanning unsafe, safe, and safe-sensitive requests. BanglaVeilGuard uses non-destructive multi-view normalization with a prompt-risk classifier and thresholded pre-generation gate, allowing it to screen prompts for heterogeneous target models without changing their weights. Across target-model families, guarded runs reduce attack success under deterministic response scoring from 93.8--100.0\% to 6.3\% for Claude Opus 4.8, BanglaLLama, and TituLLM; TigerLLM-1B with BanglaVeilGuard achieves 78.2\% accuracy with 8.8\% ASR. The prompt guard also attains 88.5\% unsafe recall, substantially above the evaluated prompt-only guard baselines. The main remaining cost is over-refusal on dialectal and noisy benign prompts, revealing a concrete safety-helpfulness frontier for Bangla LLM deployment.

AI.tldr: BanglaVeilGuard is a compact Bangla-first safety benchmark and lightweight prompt guard covering six Bangla language forms (standard, Romanized, Banglish, code-mixed, noisy, dialectal), reducing attack success rates from 93.8-100% to 6.3% across target LLMs while achieving 88.5% unsafe recall.
AI.motivation: English-centric benchmarks fail to evaluate Bangla LLM safety because Bangla users write across multiple scripts, spellings, code-mixed forms, and regional registers, leaving Bangla LLMs largely unprotected.
AI.method: BanglaVeilGuard uses a 2,366-prompt benchmark (354 held-out) spanning six Bangla language forms, combined with non-destructive multi-view normalization, a prompt-risk classifier, and a thresholded pre-generation gate that screens prompts without altering target model weights.
AI.result: Guarded runs reduce attack success from 93.8-100% to 6.3% for Claude Opus 4.8, BanglaLLama, and TituLLM; TigerLLM-1B achieves 78.2% accuracy with 8.8% ASR; the guard attains 88.5% unsafe recall, surpassing prompt-only guard baselines.
AI.conclusion: BanglaVeilGuard demonstrates a practical safety guard for multilingual and code-mixed Bangla deployment, with the main remaining trade-off being over-refusal on dialectal and noisy benign prompts—revealing a concrete safety-helpfulness frontier for Bangla LLMs.

title: From Association to Causation: Improving Retrieval Precision of Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Causal Relations and an Attention Mechanism
comment: 16 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables, 1 algorithm. Code available at https://github.com/Silk-Road/causal-rag-rerank
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds LLM generation on retrieved documents, but the standard terminal retrieval stage--dense-vector similarity, optionally followed by reranking--often returns documents that share keywords with the query without containing the needed information, a failure mode that grows with the knowledge base. We trace it to a conceptual gap: similarity captures only associational relations, whereas the documents that matter are linked to the query causally. We model the terminal retrieval stage with a causal graph grounded in Reichenbach's common cause principle: the keywords shared by the query and a retrieved document form a latent common cause A, and the document's residual keywords form a latent set B linking the document to the ideal output. Since a retrieved document is a collider (A -> d <- B), retrieval itself opens an associational path between the query and B, which licenses a training-free, attention-style re-scoring rule: the cosine similarity between the query embedding and the weighted centroid embedding of B. Unlike causality-enhanced RAG variants that model causal relations inside the knowledge content, our graph models the causal structure of the retrieval process itself. On a real 471-document enterprise knowledge base, the method promotes a relevant guideline from rank 6 to the top 3; on a controlled diagnostic corpus reproducing the keyword-stuffing regime, it improves the mean target rank from 2.88 to 1.25, while a trained cross-encoder reranker barely helps (2.63). Conversely, on three BEIR benchmarks the score underperforms the similarity baseline, delineating the applicability boundary: the method guards the keyword-stuffing regime of growing proprietary knowledge bases and complements neural rerankers; a corpus-level calibration gate selects the correct regime with >= 95% reliability. A fully local testbed demonstrates deployability.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a conceptual gap in RAG's terminal retrieval stage: dense similarity captures associational relations while relevant documents are causally linked to the query. The authors model retrieval with a causal graph based on Reichenbach's common cause principle, treating retrieved documents as colliders, and propose a training-free attention-style re-scoring rule using cosine similarity between query and the centroid embedding of residual keywords (B). The method improves retrieval on keyword-stuffing regimes (enterprise KB and diagnostic corpus) but underperforms on BEIR benchmarks, with a calibration gate selecting the correct regime at ≥95% reliability.
AI.motivation: Standard RAG terminal retrieval (dense-vector similarity plus optionally reranking) often returns documents that share keywords with the query but lack the needed information—a failure mode that worsens as knowledge bases grow. The authors trace this to a conceptual gap: similarity captures only associational relations, whereas relevant documents are causally linked to the query.
AI.method: The authors model the terminal retrieval stage with a causal graph grounded in Reichenbach's common cause principle. Shared keywords between query and retrieved document form a latent common cause A, and the document's residual keywords form a latent set B linking the document to the ideal output. Since a retrieved document is a collider (A → d ← B), retrieval opens an associational path between query and B, licensing a training-free, attention-style re-scoring rule: cosine similarity between the query embedding and the weighted centroid embedding of B.
AI.result: On a real 471-document enterprise knowledge base, the method promotes a relevant guideline from rank 6 to top 3. On a controlled diagnostic corpus reproducing the keyword-stuffing regime, mean target rank improves from 2.88 to 1.25, while a trained cross-encoder reranker barely helps (2.63). On three BEIR benchmarks, the score underperforms the similarity baseline, delineating the applicability boundary. A corpus-level calibration gate selects the correct regime with ≥95% reliability.
AI.conclusion: The method guards the keyword-stuffing regime of growing proprietary knowledge bases and complements neural rerankers rather than replacing them. A fully local testbed demonstrates deployability, and the corpus-level calibration gate ensures correct regime selection with high reliability.

title: LiteEvent-AE: Lightweight Autoencoder for Event-Based Vision on Low-Latency Energy-Constrained Edge Devices
summary: Event-based vision has emerged as a promising paradigm for energy-aware artificial intelligence (AI), offering sparse, low-latency visual signals that reduce redundant data processing and support sustainable edge computing. However, the asynchronous and noise-prone nature of event streams creates challenges for conventional deep learning models, which are often too computationally intensive for low-power embedded platforms. This work presents a compact and configurable event-driven autoencoder that efficiently compresses neuromorphic data while preserving essential spatiotemporal structure for downstream inference. The architecture integrates lightweight convolutional encoding with robust performance under adaptive event thresholding and a minimal classifier head, enabling substantial reductions in computational cost without degrading recognition fidelity. Extensive evaluations on the Smart Event Face Dataset (SEFD) and Event-Based Crossing Dataset (EBCD) show that the proposed framework achieves competitive or superior accuracy compared to YOLOv9 while requiring up to 35.6$\times$ fewer parameters. To assess real-world sustainability, the model is deployed on resource-constrained hardware: a Raspberry Pi 4B and a NVIDIA Jetson Nano. On NVIDIA Jetson Nano, it delivers real-time throughput of 44.8 FPS. On a Raspberry Pi 4B CPU, the 50\% autoencoder classifier consumes 16.19 J for the evaluated inference workload, corresponding to approximately 726.3$\times$ lower energy consumption than YOLOv9 under the same evaluation protocol. These results demonstrate the potential of compact event-driven models to advance environmentally conscious, low-power AI systems for high-speed perception in autonomous, mobile, and embedded computing environments.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a compact, configurable event-driven autoencoder that compresses neuromorphic data while preserving spatiotemporal structure for downstream inference. The approach achieves competitive accuracy vs. YOLOv9 with up to 35.6× fewer parameters, real-time throughput of 44.8 FPS on Jetson Nano, and ~726.3× lower energy consumption than YOLOv9 on a Raspberry Pi 4B CPU.
AI.motivation: Event-based vision offers energy-efficient, sparse visual signals, but its asynchronous, noise-prone nature challenges conventional deep learning models that are too computationally intensive for low-power embedded platforms. There is a need for compact models that can process neuromorphic data efficiently on resource-constrained devices.
AI.method: The architecture combines lightweight convolutional encoding with a minimal classifier head in an autoencoder framework, designed to compress event streams while preserving essential spatiotemporal structure. It is configurable via adaptive event thresholding and evaluated on the Smart Event Face Dataset (SEFD) and Event-Based Crossing Dataset (EBCD).
AI.result: The model achieves competitive or superior accuracy compared to YOLOv9 with up to 35.6× fewer parameters. Deployed on NVIDIA Jetson Nano, it delivers real-time throughput of 44.8 FPS. On Raspberry Pi 4B CPU, the 50% autoencoder classifier consumes 16.19 J, corresponding to ~726.3× lower energy than YOLOv9 under the same protocol.
AI.conclusion: Compact event-driven models demonstrate significant potential for advancing environmentally conscious, low-power AI systems for high-speed perception in autonomous, mobile, and embedded computing environments.

title: Vision-Guided Morphing Quadcopter for Multi-Geometry Payload Transport through Narrow Passages
summary: Aerial payload transport using multirotor unmanned aerial vehicles is challenging because payload geometry, contact interaction, grasp stability, flight control, and narrow-passage traversal are strongly coupled during pickup and transport. Object-specific grippers often cannot adapt their footprint or grasp geometry when the payload shape or passage width changes. This paper presents a vision-guided morphing quadcopter for multi-geometry payload transport through narrow passages. The proposed platform uses four hybrid arm-leg structures that function as both landing supports and grasping members. A centrally placed actuator drives a tendon-based morphing mechanism, enabling all four arms to synchronously retract or expand for object grasping, footprint reduction, and post-transport release. Onboard vision estimates the payload geometry and passage width, while endpoint force feedback is used to confirm grasp contact during payload engagement. A phase-wise mission planner, PID-based flight stabilization, and morphology-adaptive grasp controller are implemented in a MuJoCo simulation environment. The framework is evaluated using box, cylindrical, and spherical payloads, representing flat-faced, rolling-curved, and fully curved contact conditions. Across the three cases, the simulated system completes the pickup-transport-release sequence with a maximum RMS position error of 0.31 m, a final drop-zone error below 0.18 m, a compact grasp footprint of 0.09-0.21 m2, and a footprint reduction of 75.0-89.7 percent. The results demonstrate that a single-actuator morphing quadcopter can adapt its grasp footprint for the transport of payloads with different geometries while reducing its overall footprint for narrow-passage traversal.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a vision-guided morphing quadcopter with four hybrid arm-leg structures driven by a single tendon-based actuator for transporting multi-geometry payloads (box, cylindrical, spherical) through narrow passages. Evaluated in MuJoCo simulation, the system achieves a compact grasp footprint of 0.09-0.21 m², footprint reduction of 75.0-89.7%, a maximum RMS position error of 0.31 m, and final drop-zone error below 0.18 m across the pickup-transport-release sequence.
AI.motivation: Conventional aerial payload transport with multirotor UAVs is challenging due to strong coupling between payload geometry, contact interaction, grasp stability, flight control, and narrow-passage traversal. Object-specific grippers cannot adapt their footprint or grasp geometry when payload shape or passage width changes, creating a need for a morphology-adaptable platform.
AI.method: The proposed system uses four hybrid arm-leg structures that serve as both landing supports and grasping members. A single centrally placed actuator drives a tendon-based morphing mechanism for synchronized arm retraction/expansion. Onboard vision estimates payload geometry and passage width, while endpoint force feedback confirms grasp contact. A phase-wise mission planner, PID-based flight stabilization, and morphology-adaptive grasp controller are implemented in MuJoCo simulation.
AI.result: The framework was evaluated with box, cylindrical, and spherical payloads. The simulated system completed the pickup-transport-release sequence with a maximum RMS position error of 0.31 m, a final drop-zone error below 0.18 m, a compact grasp footprint of 0.09-0.21 m², and a footprint reduction of 75.0-89.7% across the three cases.
AI.conclusion: A single-actuator morphing quadcopter can effectively adapt its grasp footprint for transporting payloads of different geometries while reducing its overall footprint for narrow-passage traversal, demonstrating the viability of morphology-adaptive aerial manipulation for heterogeneous payload transport.

title: Modeling Claim Dependency Structure for Patent Litigation Prediction with Graph Attention Networks
summary: Patent litigation imposes substantial costs on firms and distorts R&D incentives, making early risk identification a practically important task. While prior work has applied BERT-based models to patent claim text, two fundamental limitations remain: flat sequence encoding loses the dependency structure between independent and dependent claims that legally determines patent scope, and feeding the entire claim set to a single encoder discards legally critical text. A six-model ablation on 1.34 million USPTO utility patents confirms that per-claim encoding, graph connectivity, attention, and Attentional Aggregation each provide independent, additive predictive value. We propose ClaimGAT, a Graph Attention Network that encodes each claim independently, constructs a directed claim dependency graph, processes it with GATConv layers, and aggregates independent claims via Attentional Aggregation to yield both a litigation risk score and claim-level gate weights that enable post-hoc structural analysis. ClaimGAT achieves an AUC-ROC of 0.818 and a lift of 4.89x at the top 10%, using only information observable at the time of patent grant. It reveals a tendency in high-risk patents for structural selection and content sensitivity to diverge, a pattern consistent with defensive claim drafting.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ClaimGAT, a Graph Attention Network for early patent litigation risk prediction that encodes each claim independently, models the directed dependency structure between claims via a graph, and aggregates independent claims with attentional mechanisms. Evaluated on 1.34 million USPTO utility patents, it achieves an AUC-ROC of 0.818 and 4.89x lift at the top 10%, outperforming flat BERT-based baselines and revealing structural patterns consistent with defensive claim drafting.
AI.motivation: Patent litigation imposes substantial costs on firms and distorts R&D incentives, making early risk identification practically important. Prior BERT-based approaches suffer from two fundamental limitations: flat sequence encoding ignores the legal dependency structure between independent and dependent claims, and feeding the entire claim set to a single encoder discards legally critical text.
AI.method: ClaimGAT encodes each claim independently with BERT-style encoding, constructs a directed claim dependency graph reflecting legal claim relationships (independent vs. dependent claims), processes this graph with GATConv layers to propagate structural information, and aggregates independent claims via Attentional Aggregation. This yields both a litigation risk score and claim-level gate weights for post-hoc structural analysis. A six-model ablation validates that per-claim encoding, graph connectivity, attention, and Attentional Aggregation each contribute independent, additive predictive value.
AI.result: ClaimGAT achieves an AUC-ROC of 0.818 and a lift of 4.89x at the top 10% using only information observable at patent grant time. The ablation on 1.34 million USPTO utility patents confirms that all four design components (per-claim encoding, graph connectivity, attention, and Attentional Aggregation) provide independent additive value. Analysis reveals that high-risk patents exhibit divergence between structural selection and content sensitivity, consistent with defensive claim drafting patterns.
AI.conclusion: Modeling the legal dependency structure between patent claims through graph attention networks significantly improves early litigation risk prediction over flat sequence encoding approaches. The claim-level gate weights enable post-hoc structural analysis, and the observed divergence between structural and content signals in high-risk patents provides interpretable insights into defensive claim drafting strategies.

title: ATHENA: Knowledge-guided agentic neural architecture search for AutoFormer-based electronic health record modeling
summary: Transformer-based models are widely used for clinical prediction from electronic health records (EHRs), yet their architectures still require substantial manual tuning, and the optimal configuration may vary across tasks and hospitals. Neural architecture search (NAS) automates architecture design, but conventional methods are computationally costly for Transformer-based EHR models. Recent large language model (LLM)-guided NAS methods reduce manual search design but typically conduct each search independently, without reusing architecture knowledge across hospitals. In this study, we propose ATHENA (Agentic Transfer across Hospitals for EHR Neural Architecture Search), a knowledge-guided agentic NAS framework for Transformer-based EHR modeling. ATHENA uses a weight-sharing supernet that is pretrained once per hospital, allowing candidate architectures to be instantiated as inherited subnetworks and evaluated through fine-tuning rather than independent pretraining. It also incorporates a two-layer cross-hospital architecture prior. The first layer retrieves high-performing architecture examples from source sites based on task descriptors, while the second estimates the effects of architectural components using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based meta-regression. These priors guide a multi-agent LLM search together with validation feedback from the target hospital. Across six clinical prediction tasks and two independent health systems, ATHENA matches or outperforms four NAS baselines in 9 of 12 hospital-task evaluations at a search budget of 30. It also shows more consistent architecture selection across repeated searches. ATHENA provides a practical approach for reducing manual architecture tuning in Transformer-based EHR modeling. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/GatorAIM/ATHENA.

AI.tldr: ATHENA is a knowledge-guided agentic neural architecture search (NAS) framework for Transformer-based EHR prediction models. It uses a weight-sharing supernet pretrained once per hospital, a two-layer cross-hospital architecture prior, and multi-agent LLM search to automate architecture design while reusing knowledge across hospitals. It matches or outperforms four NAS baselines in 9 of 12 hospital-task evaluations.
AI.motivation: Transformer-based EHR models require substantial manual architecture tuning, and the optimal configuration varies across tasks and hospitals. Conventional NAS is computationally costly for such models, and existing LLM-guided NAS methods conduct each search independently without reusing architecture knowledge across hospitals, leading to redundant computational effort and inconsistent search quality.
AI.method: ATHENA proposes a three-part approach: (1) a weight-sharing supernet pretrained once per hospital, allowing candidate architectures to be instantiated as inherited subnetworks and fine-tuned (avoiding independent pretraining); (2) a two-layer cross-hospital architecture prior, where the first layer retrieves high-performing architecture examples from source sites using task descriptors and the second estimates component effects via SHAP-based meta-regression; (3) a multi-agent LLM search guided by these priors and validation feedback from the target hospital.
AI.result: Across six clinical prediction tasks and two independent health systems, ATHENA matches or outperforms four NAS baselines in 9 of 12 hospital-task evaluations at a search budget of 30. It also shows more consistent architecture selection across repeated searches compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: ATHENA provides a practical approach for reducing manual architecture tuning in Transformer-based EHR modeling by enabling cross-hospital knowledge transfer in NAS, achieving competitive performance with greater consistency and lower computational cost. Code is publicly available.

title: SpatialDiff: 3D-Aware Object Movement via Implicit Spatial Modeling
summary: Recent advances in image editing allow impressive manipulation of objects, existing methods still struggle to handle spatial movement in complex scenes, such as objects span different depth layers or are partially occluded. Most image editing methods focus solely on prior information from 2D datasets, emphasizing planar features while lacking support for spatial structures. Even approaches that incorporate explicit positional information fail to capture true 3D spatial relationships, thus limiting accurate object movement in complex scenes. In this paper, we present SpatialDiff, a method that effectively captures 3D spatial structures, enabling precise and consistent object movements in complex scenes. Our core innovations are twofold: (1) Implicit 3D Spatial Modeling, which introduces 3D prior knowledge and enables the model to internally build a comprehensive understanding of the three-dimensional spatial structure; and (2) Global Spatial Supervision, which constrains the latent spatial features to enable the model to perceive changes in object spatial positions caused by editing operations. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly improves the accuracy and fidelity of spatial movement in complex scenes.

AI.tldr: SpatialDiff is a method for image editing that captures 3D spatial structures to enable precise and consistent object movement in complex scenes involving multiple depth layers or partial occlusions. It introduces implicit 3D spatial modeling with 3D prior knowledge and global spatial supervision that constrains latent spatial features to perceive positional changes.
AI.motivation: Existing image editing methods struggle with spatial movement in complex scenes because they rely primarily on 2D dataset priors, emphasizing planar features without support for spatial structures. Even methods incorporating explicit positional information fail to capture true 3D spatial relationships, limiting accurate object movement in scenes with depth layers or occlusions.
AI.method: SpatialDiff comprises two core innovations: (1) Implicit 3D Spatial Modeling, which incorporates 3D prior knowledge so the model can internally build a comprehensive understanding of three-dimensional spatial structure; and (2) Global Spatial Supervision, which constrains latent spatial features to allow the model to perceive changes in object spatial positions resulting from editing operations.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate that SpatialDiff significantly improves the accuracy and fidelity of spatial object movement in complex scenes compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: By integrating implicit 3D spatial modeling and global spatial supervision, SpatialDiff enables precise and consistent object movement in complex scenes, addressing limitations of 2D-prior-based image editing approaches.

title: An Interpretable Deep Learning Framework for Material Perception and Classification from Multisensory Tactile Data
summary: Human tactile perception relies on complex multisensory cues. Yet the relationship between tactile signals and perceptual representations remains poorly understood, limiting the integration of touch in digital environments and human-like robotic perception. To address this gap, we developed a computational framework comprising three interconnected deep learning models that map multisensory touch data to material perception, without relying on hand-crafted features. The models represent progressively different routes from tactile signals to material class: from low-level interaction signals to perceptual attribute distributions (Model 1), from predicted attribute distributions to material classification (Model 2), and directly from tactile signals to material categories, bypassing intermediate representations (Model 3). By combining deep learning with Integrated Gradients, the framework achieved high accuracy while offering interpretability, revealing which sensory modalities most strongly drive its decisions. Our results show that deep learning can approach near-perfect material classification when unconstrained by intermediate perceptual stages, but matching human-like performance is harder once those stages are modeled explicitly. Notably, thermal cues emerged as particularly informative across all models, providing robust signals for material differentiation. The results offer a computational account of how tactile signals lead to material perception and show how interpretable deep learning can both approach human-level performance and reveal cues that robotic and haptic systems need to incorporate.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a computational framework of three interconnected deep learning models that map multisensory tactile data to material perception without hand-crafted features, achieving high accuracy and interpretability via Integrated Gradients, with thermal cues emerging as the most informative modality.
AI.motivation: The relationship between tactile signals and perceptual representations is poorly understood, limiting the integration of touch in digital environments and human-like robotic perception.
AI.method: A framework of three deep learning models: Model 1 maps tactile signals to perceptual attribute distributions, Model 2 maps predicted attribute distributions to material classification, and Model 3 maps tactile signals directly to material categories. Integrated Gradients is used for interpretability.
AI.result: Deep learning achieves near-perfect material classification without intermediate perceptual stages, but performance drops when intermediate perceptual stages are modeled. Thermal cues are the most informative modality across all models.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a computational account of tactile-to-material perception, showing that interpretable deep learning can approach human-level performance and reveal which sensory cues robotic and haptic systems need to incorporate.

title: EDGE: Experience-Distillation for Guided Exploration in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning with outcome-based objectives such as GRPO enables LLM-based agents to solve complex, long-horizon tasks, yet the reusable exploration patterns embedded in interaction trajectories are largely discarded after a single policy update. Existing experience-augmented approaches retrieve historical guidance at inference time, but they apply experiences without accounting for the policy's evolving capability and create persistent dependencies on external retrieval. We propose EDGE (Experience-Distillation for Guided Exploration), a framework that treats retrieved experiences as temporary training-time scaffolds and progressively internalizes their benefits into the parametric policy. Concretely, EDGE partitions each rollout group into experience-conditioned and experience-free trajectories to estimate and admit only positive marginal gains without extra sampling, then distills the induced behavior into the base policy via a reverse-KL objective on its own empirical support. A co-evolutionary experience bank further synthesizes guidance from emerging failure modes and prunes obsolete entries as the policy evolves. On ALFWorld and WebShop, EDGE improves over GRPO by 8.3 and 12.5 success-rate points at the 7B scale and retains 96.0% of its scaffolded performance when external experiences are removed at inference time. The code is available at https://github.com/xvolcano02/EDGE.

AI.tldr: EDGE is a framework that treats retrieved experiences as temporary training-time scaffolds for RL-based LLM agents, progressively distilling their benefits into the parametric policy via positive marginal-gain filtering and reverse-KL distillation, with a co-evolutionary experience bank. It improves over GRPO by 8.3 and 12.5 success-rate points on ALFWorld and WebShop at 7B scale, retaining 96% of scaffolded performance when experiences are removed at inference.
AI.motivation: Reusable exploration patterns in interaction trajectories are discarded after a single policy update in outcome-based RL (e.g., GRPO). Existing experience-augmented approaches retrieve historical guidance at inference time without accounting for the policy's evolving capability and create persistent dependencies on external retrieval.
AI.method: EDGE partitions each rollout group into experience-conditioned and experience-free trajectories to estimate and admit only positive marginal gains without extra sampling, then distills induced behavior into the base policy via a reverse-KL objective on its own empirical support. A co-evolutionary experience bank synthesizes guidance from emerging failure modes and prunes obsolete entries as the policy evolves.
AI.result: On ALFWorld and WebShop, EDGE improves over GRPO by 8.3 and 12.5 success-rate points at the 7B scale and retains 96.0% of its scaffolded performance when external experiences are removed at inference time.
AI.conclusion: EDGE demonstrates that treating experiences as temporary training-time scaffolds rather than permanent inference dependencies effectively internalizes their benefits into the parametric policy, eliminating external retrieval dependencies while improving performance over standard RL baselines.

title: Ask or Answer: A Decision Framework for Multi-Turn Health Misinformation Intervention
summary: Correcting health misinformation in dialogue requires more than producing a factual rebuttal: users differ in what they know, what they believe, and what they need to hear, so an effective intervention often depends on first asking the right clarifying question. Yet existing methods either respond immediately or probe indiscriminately, treating clarification as either unnecessary or always beneficial. We propose Reward-Optimized Probe-and-Respond (RO-PnR), a framework that learns when asking is worth its cost. At each turn, RO-PnR chooses between probing for more information and committing to a final correction, guided by a turn-level reward that weighs the expected gain from probing against its interaction cost. To capture how user heterogeneity affects probing value, we model each simulated user with a latent state along health literacy and belief commitment. Experiments show that RO-PnR achieves the highest cost-adjusted utility across three health-misinformation datasets and three base models, using 30% fewer turns than always-probe baselines.

AI.tldr: RO-PnR is a framework that learns when to ask clarifying questions versus when to deliver a final correction in health-misinformation dialogue, optimizing the trade-off between information gain and interaction cost.
AI.motivation: Users differ in knowledge, beliefs, and needs when it comes to health misinformation; existing methods either respond immediately (treating clarification as unnecessary) or probe indiscriminately (treating it as always beneficial), neither of which is optimal.
AI.method: The framework uses a turn-level reward that weighs expected gains from probing against interaction costs. It models each simulated user with a latent state along two dimensions: health literacy and belief commitment, enabling heterogeneous probing value.
AI.result: RO-PnR achieves the highest cost-adjusted utility across three health-misinformation datasets and three base models, while using 30% fewer turns than always-probe baselines.
AI.conclusion: Cost-aware, selective probing is both more efficient and more effective than indiscriminate probing or immediate rebuttals in health-misinformation correction dialogues.

title: DefaultShift: Auditing Semantic Default Shift in Accelerated Text-to-Image Models
summary: Few-step text-to-image models increasingly replace slower generators, yet acceleration can silently change distributions over unspecified attributes even when individual outputs remain plausible and aligned. We call these distributions semantic defaults and their change under replacement semantic default shift. Existing quality, preference, and diversity evaluations do not test whether a replacement preserves its reference model's semantic defaults. We introduce DefaultShift, a paired audit that labels repeated samples with closed semantic vocabularies, measures probability-mass movement, and separates interpretable ranking from confirmatory cross-fit inference. Across 14 reference and replacement pairs, adjusted color discrepancies range from 0.054 to 0.303 with recipe-specific directions. A 1,000-image human audit reproduces the ordering. We further introduce DefaultShift-Select, an offline calibration method that reduces human-measured shift by 10.3 percent to 35.1 percent across Turbo, DMD2, and FLUX without material quality loss. Under balanced evaluation, selected data recover 4.3 accuracy points and 7.5 worst-group points over uncalibrated replacement data. DefaultShift makes semantic preservation under acceleration measurable and actionable.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces DefaultShift, a paired audit that measures semantic default shift when fast text-to-image generators replace slower reference models. It quantifies distribution changes over unspecified semantic attributes using closed vocabularies, validates findings with human audits, and proposes DefaultShift-Select, an offline calibration method reducing human-measured shift by 10.3%-35.1% without quality loss.
AI.motivation: Few-step text-to-image models accelerate generation but silently alter distributions over unspecified semantic attributes (called semantic defaults), even when individual outputs remain plausible. Existing evaluations (quality, preference, diversity) do not test whether a faster replacement preserves the reference model's semantic defaults.
AI.method: DefaultShift uses paired auditing that labels repeated samples with closed semantic vocabularies, measures probability-mass movement across attributes, and separates interpretable ranking from confirmatory cross-fit inference. DefaultShift-Select is an offline calibration method applied to generated data before deployment.
AI.result: Across 14 reference and replacement pairs, adjusted color discrepancies range from 0.054 to 0.303 with recipe-specific directions; a 1,000-image human audit reproduces the ordering. DefaultShift-Select reduces human-measured shift by 10.3%-35.1% on Turbo, DMD2, and FLUX, recovering 4.3 accuracy points and 7.5 worst-group points over uncalibrated data under balanced evaluation.
AI.conclusion: DefaultShift makes semantic preservation under acceleration measurable and actionable, providing both a diagnostic framework for detecting semantic default shift and a calibration technique to mitigate it in few-step text-to-image generators.

title: CIDER: Continual Interactive Distillation for Embodied Reinforcement Learning
summary: Human-in-the-loop real-world reinforcement learning enables rapid acquisition of effective robotic manipulation policies for individual tasks, often within tens of minutes. Yet it remains unclear how to extend this paradigm to continual learning, where a single policy must acquire new skills without losing previously learned behaviors. Existing real-world continual learning methods do not explicitly constrain prior behaviors, leading to severe catastrophic forgetting. We introduce Continual Interactive Distillation for Embodied Reinforcement Learning (CIDER), a continual reinforcement learning framework that freezes the accumulated historical policy as a teacher before learning each new task and interleaves task learning with distillation-based retention. We further introduce gradient routing to separate the gradients used for acquiring new tasks from those used for preserving prior behaviors. We evaluate our method with a single shared actor on six real-world household and industrial manipulation tasks. Interactive Distillation maintains high measured success on previously learned tasks across our six-task real-robot sequence while acquiring each new task in 10 to 20 minutes, whereas every baseline forgets at least one previous task. Additional ablations reveal the key design choices that govern the tradeoff between stability and plasticity in real-world continual reinforcement learning.

AI.tldr: CIDER is a continual reinforcement learning framework for real-world robotic manipulation that freezes prior policies as a teacher and interleaves task learning with distillation-based retention, enabling acquisition of new skills while preserving previously learned behaviors across six real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing human-in-the-loop real-world RL methods work well for single tasks but fail to extend to continual learning scenarios. Current continual learning approaches for real-world robotics do not explicitly constrain prior behaviors, leading to catastrophic forgetting when a single policy must acquire new skills without losing previously learned ones.
AI.method: CIDER freezes the accumulated historical policy as a teacher before learning each new task, and interleaves new task learning with distillation-based retention. It introduces gradient routing to separate gradients used for acquiring new tasks from those used for preserving prior behaviors, decoupling the stability-plasticity tradeoff.
AI.result: CIDER maintains high success rates on previously learned tasks across a six-task real-robot sequence while acquiring each new task in 10-20 minutes. All baselines forget at least one previous task, demonstrating CIDER's superior stability. Ablations reveal key design choices governing the stability-plasticity tradeoff.
AI.conclusion: CIDER effectively enables continual learning in real-world embodied RL by separating gradient pathways for task acquisition and behavior retention, achieving both stability (no catastrophic forgetting) and plasticity (rapid new skill acquisition).

title: Bulbul: A Dataset for Dialectal Arabic Speech Recognition
summary: Arabic automatic speech recognition (ASR) faces unique challenges due to diglossia, extensive regional dialect variation, and limited speech resources. Existing speech datasets often focus on single dialects or large-scale broadcast/web data, leading to trade-offs between linguistic diversity and annotation quality. We present BULBUL, a multi-dialect Arabic ASR dataset collected from 275 speakers in 11 Arab countries. BULBUL includes structured dialect and sub-dialect coverage, as well as recordings of classical Arabic and modern standard Arabic spoken by participants in their native dialectal accents to support accent-aware modeling. The quality of the recordings was ensured through a two-level human verification process. We further benchmark a range of recent ASR systems, establishing strong baselines for modern dialectal and accented Arabic ASR.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces BULBUL, a multi-dialect Arabic ASR dataset collected from 275 speakers across 11 Arab countries, featuring structured dialect/sub-dialect coverage, classical and modern standard Arabic recordings in native dialectal accents, two-level human quality verification, and benchmarks for modern ASR systems.
AI.motivation: Arabic ASR faces challenges from diglossia, regional dialect variation, and limited speech resources. Existing datasets create trade-offs between linguistic diversity and annotation quality—either focusing on single dialects or leveraging large-scale broadcast/web data at the expense of quality.
AI.method: The authors created BULBUL, a multi-dialect Arabic ASR dataset with 275 speakers from 11 Arab countries. It includes structured dialect and sub-dialect coverage, recordings of classical Arabic (CA) and modern standard Arabic (MSA) spoken in native dialectal accents for accent-aware modeling, and employs a two-level human verification process to ensure recording quality. They benchmarked several recent ASR systems on this dataset.
AI.result: The paper establishes strong baselines for modern dialectal and accented Arabic ASR by benchmarking a range of recent ASR systems on the BULBUL dataset.
AI.conclusion: BULBUL addresses the diversity-quality trade-off in Arabic ASR datasets by providing broad dialectal coverage with verified annotation quality, enabling accent-aware modeling and serving as a benchmark resource for dialectal Arabic ASR research.

title: ECHO: A Cognitively Inspired, Auditable Memory Plane for Long-Horizon Agents
summary: Long-horizon agents need memory that identifies relevant experience, resolves revisions, and exposes checkable provenance. We present ECHO (Embodied Context and History Orchestration), an auditable memory architecture and service prototype inspired by episodic encoding, consolidation, contextual reinstatement, reconsolidation, and executive control. This is functional inspiration, not neural equivalence; the empirical analysis focuses on retrieval and context construction. Development runs reach 96.29% Hit@10 and 73.64% turn Recall@5 on 1,536 LoCoMo category 1-4 questions, and 97.60% Hit@10, 88.84% turn Recall@5, and 88.71% session Recall@5 on all 500 LongMemEval-S questions. A five-history BEAM gate fails, and in a separate matched 91-question QA sample Mem0 OSS scores 64.84% versus ECHO's 41.76% (exact McNemar p = 0.00107), with a history-cluster interval crossing zero. A post-hoc audit found source-specific phrases in the query-expansion rules. Although no gold answer field entered the runtime, expansion-enabled retrieval scores are therefore descriptive development measurements, not independent confirmation.

AI.tldr: ECHO is an auditable memory architecture for long-horizon agents inspired by cognitive memory processes (episodic encoding, consolidation, reinstatement, reconsolidation, executive control). It achieves strong retrieval performance on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S benchmarks, but the authors explicitly flag that their query-expansion rules contained source-specific phrases found via post-hoc audit, meaning the reported scores are descriptive development measurements rather than independent confirmation.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon agents require memory systems that can identify relevant past experience, handle revisions/updates to stored information, and expose verifiable provenance for auditability—capabilities standard memory designs lack.
AI.method: ECHO takes functional inspiration (not neural equivalence) from episodic encoding, consolidation, contextual reinstatement, reconsolidation, and executive control to build an auditable memory architecture and service prototype. The paper evaluates retrieval and context construction empirically on LoCoMo (1,536 category 1-4 questions) and LongMemEval-S (500 questions), compares against Mem0 OSS on a matched 91-question QA sample, and tests a five-history BEAM gate. A post-hoc audit examines query-expansion rules for contamination.
AI.result: ECHO reaches 96.29% Hit@10 and 73.64% turn Recall@5 on LoCoMo; 97.60% Hit@10, 88.84% turn Recall@5, and 88.71% session Recall@5 on LongMemEval-S. The five-history BEAM gate fails. In the matched 91-question sample, Mem0 OSS scores 64.84% vs ECHO's 41.76% (exact McNemar p=0.00107), with a history-cluster interval crossing zero. Post-hoc audit found source-specific phrases in query-expansion rules.
AI.conclusion: Although no gold answer field entered the runtime, because source-specific phrases were found in the query-expansion rules, the expansion-enabled retrieval scores must be treated as descriptive development measurements rather than independent confirmation. The architecture shows promise but requires re-evaluation with contamination-free expansion rules.

title: HP-UniIF: Hierarchical Prompt Learning for Unified Image Fusion
summary: General image fusion seeks to integrate complementary information from multiple source images, yet real-world applications often require a single system to support heterogeneous fusion, degradation restoration, and task-oriented perception simultaneously. Existing unified frameworks struggle with these orthogonal objectives, resulting in entangled representations and degraded performance across subtasks. We propose HP-UniIF, a unified vision framework that leverages diffusion priors to bridge heterogeneous fusion, visual restoration, and downstream perception. To address the limited adaptability of diffusion models to domain-, degradation-, and task-level objectives within one pipeline, HP-UniIF introduces a depth-wise hierarchical conditional modulation strategy that decouples these objectives across network stages. Task prompt modulation at bottleneck layers adapts the backbone to different fusion paradigms, the degradation prompt router at shallow layers injects degradation-aware constraints for local restoration, and the application prompt bank at decoding stages aligns generation with downstream tasks. This hierarchical design enables HP-UniIF to produce visually faithful results while preserving task-relevant semantics. Extensive experiments across multiple fusion tasks, diverse degradations, and various downstream applications demonstrate the superior performance of HP-UniIF.

AI.tldr: HP-UniIF is a unified vision framework using diffusion priors to simultaneously handle heterogeneous image fusion, degradation restoration, and task-oriented perception via a depth-wise hierarchical conditional modulation strategy that decouples these objectives across network stages.
AI.motivation: Real-world applications require a single system to support heterogeneous fusion, degradation restoration, and task-oriented perception simultaneously, but existing unified frameworks struggle with these orthogonal objectives, resulting in entangled representations and degraded performance across subtasks.
AI.method: HP-UniIF leverages diffusion priors and introduces a depth-wise hierarchical conditional modulation strategy: (1) task prompt modulation at bottleneck layers adapts the backbone to different fusion paradigms, (2) a degradation prompt router at shallow layers injects degradation-aware constraints for local restoration, and (3) an application prompt bank at decoding stages aligns generation with downstream tasks.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across multiple fusion tasks, diverse degradations, and various downstream applications demonstrate the superior performance of HP-UniIF, producing visually faithful results while preserving task-relevant semantics.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchical design of HP-UniIF successfully decouples orthogonal objectives (domain-, degradation-, and task-level) within a single diffusion-based pipeline, enabling a unified framework that excels at both visual fidelity and downstream task alignment.

title: Stakeholder Insights for Designing In-Home Social Robots for Dementia Disorientation Detection and Caregiver-Aware Intervention
summary: Disorientation is a common and distressing experience for people living with dementia. It often manifests as confusion about time, place, or personal context. These episodes can increase anxiety, agitation, and safety risks, especially for persons with dementia (PwDs) who live independently at home. While assistive technologies have explored reminders, monitoring, and activity support, little research has explored how socially assistive robots can support the detection and management of disorientation in everyday living contexts. Hence, disorientation detection and intervention remain under-examined as socio-technical challenges. We conducted 14 semi-structured interviews with dementia caregivers and practitioners, including family and professional caregivers, occupational therapists, mental health practitioners, dementia nurse practitioners, and well-being and technology leads. The findings reveal that recurrent and fluctuating. It often emerges through behavioural cues such as repeated questioning, inappropriate activity timing and disrupted daily routines. Caregivers described orientation as emotionally charged, and direct correction may increase distress. The participants were generally receptive to robotic assistance when framed as supportive rather than corrective. Based on the insights, we identify essential design implications for socially assistive robots that provide context-aware orientation support, integrate into daily routines and support caregivers through timely escalation.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates disorientation in people living with dementia at home through 14 semi-structured interviews with caregivers and practitioners. It identifies behavioral cues of disorientation, highlights the emotionally charged nature of orientation correction, and proposes design implications for socially assistive robots that provide context-aware, supportive orientation assistance integrated into daily routines.
AI.motivation: Disorientation is a common and distressing experience for PwDs living independently at home, yet detection and management of disorientation remain under-examined as socio-technical challenges. Little research has explored how socially assistive robots can support disorientation detection and intervention in everyday living contexts.
AI.method: Conducted 14 semi-structured interviews with dementia caregivers and practitioners, including family and professional caregivers, occupational therapists, mental health practitioners, dementia nurse practitioners, and well-being and technology leads. Thematic analysis of qualitative interview data.
AI.result: Disorientation emerges through behavioral cues such as repeated questioning, inappropriate activity timing, and disrupted daily routines. Orientation is emotionally charged, and direct correction may increase distress. Participants were receptive to robotic assistance when framed as supportive rather than corrective.
AI.conclusion: The study identifies essential design implications for socially assistive robots that provide context-aware orientation support, integrate into daily routines, and support caregivers through timely escalation.

title: ToSCA: Leveraging Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning on Temporal and Strategic Abstractions of Conversational Agents
summary: Humans have multiple levels of temporal abstractions on daily interaction and thinking, such as concept perception and strategic planning. Inspired by this nature, we propose a two-level hierarchical reinforcement learning (RL) framework for conversational agents, bridging the gap between previous token-level or utterance-level RL methods. Developed on a two-level MDP, the token-level response decoding is conditioned on the utterance-level action, the explicit textual strategies. Based on theoretical derivation and efficiency consideration, we use DQN to solve the high-level critic and PPO to solve the low-level actor-critic. To further alleviate the reward sparsity and facilitate the convergence, we also design the dual-granularity reward mechanism, in which the utterance-level satisfaction score is integrated with token-level intrinsic motivation and K-L penalty. Experiments on both daily and emotional support conversations show that our method outperforms versatile baselines in strategy determination and response quality. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/AaronJi/ToSCA.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes ToSCA, a two-level hierarchical reinforcement learning framework for conversational agents that bridges token-level and utterance-level RL. It conditions token-level response decoding on utterance-level explicit textual strategies, using DQN for the high-level critic and PPO for the low-level actor-critic, along with a dual-granularity reward mechanism to address reward sparsity.
AI.motivation: Humans utilize multiple levels of temporal abstraction in daily interaction and thinking (e.g., concept perception and strategic planning). Previous RL methods for conversational agents operate only at token-level or utterance-level, missing the hierarchical nature of natural conversation.
AI.method: A two-level hierarchical RL framework built on a two-level MDP: token-level response decoding is conditioned on utterance-level actions (explicit textual strategies). DQN solves the high-level critic while PPO solves the low-level actor-critic, based on theoretical derivation and efficiency considerations. A dual-granularity reward mechanism integrates an utterance-level satisfaction score with token-level intrinsic motivation and KL penalty to alleviate reward sparsity and facilitate convergence.
AI.result: Experiments on both daily and emotional support conversation datasets show the method outperforms versatile baselines in both strategy determination and response quality.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchical RL approach effectively bridges token-level and utterance-level RL for conversational agents, improving strategy selection and response generation quality across different conversation domains.

title: What Does CLIP Learn for Regional Geolocalization? Probing Visual Cues and Scene Configuration After Adaptation
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, 9 tables. Manuscript under review
summary: Large collections of street-view imagery provide rich visual information about urban environments, but extracting fine-grained geographic information from such data remains challenging. In particular, fine-grained regional geolocalization is challenging because nearby areas often share coarse geographic cues. We study regional geolocalization within a metropolitan area and ask whether pretrained CLIP features are sufficient for regional discrimination, and what visual information supports performance after adaptation. Using 9,085 street-view images from eight Greater Los Angeles regions, we compare zero-shot CLIP, frozen-encoder readouts, partial encoder updating, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), and full fine-tuning. Frozen readouts remain near the 39.03% zero-shot accuracy, whereas encoder adaptation achieves 75.94-82.10%. Full fine-tuning also reduces the mean distance to the predicted region center from 12.30 km to 3.86 km. We probe these gains through semantic cue removal, appearance reduction using edge maps and blur, and scene-configuration disruption using patch scrambling. Adapted models achieve higher edge and blur accuracy and switch 42.92-45.56% of predictions after scrambling, compared with 10.79-14.60% for frozen methods. However, adaptation does not improve the fraction of performance retained after appearance reduction, while vegetation and sky remain influential. A Caltech101 control further shows that scrambling sensitivity is not unique to geolocalization. Overall, encoder adaptation substantially improves nearby-region discrimination and is associated with greater sensitivity to intact scene configuration, without evidence that coarse structure alone becomes sufficient for prediction. These conclusions concern viewpoint variation near known locations rather than geographically disjoint generalization.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates fine-grained regional geolocalization within a metropolitan area using street-view imagery, comparing zero-shot CLIP, frozen-encoder readouts, partial encoder updating, LoRA, and full fine-tuning on 9,085 images from eight Greater Los Angeles regions. Encoder adaptation methods achieve 75.94-82.10% accuracy versus 39.03% zero-shot, and full fine-tuning reduces mean distance to predicted region center from 12.30 km to 3.86 km. Adaptation improves sensitivity to intact scene configuration (42.92-45.56% prediction switches after scrambling) and edge/blur accuracy, though vegetation and sky remain influential.
AI.motivation: Extracting fine-grained geographic information from street-view imagery remains challenging because nearby areas share coarse geographic cues. The authors aim to determine whether pretrained CLIP features are sufficient for regional discrimination within a metropolitan area and what visual information supports performance after adaptation.
AI.method: Using 9,085 street-view images from eight Greater Los Angeles regions, the authors compare five approaches: zero-shot CLIP, frozen-encoder readouts, partial encoder updating, LoRA, and full fine-tuning. They probe adaptation gains through semantic cue removal, appearance reduction via edge maps and blur, and scene-configuration disruption via patch scrambling, with a Caltech101 control.
AI.result: Frozen readouts stay near 39.03% zero-shot accuracy, while encoder adaptation achieves 75.94-82.10%. Full fine-tuning reduces mean distance to predicted region center from 12.30 km to 3.86 km. Adapted models achieve higher edge and blur accuracy and switch 42.92-45.56% of predictions after scrambling versus 10.79-14.60% for frozen methods. Adaptation does not improve performance retention after appearance reduction, and vegetation and sky remain influential.
AI.conclusion: Encoder adaptation substantially improves nearby-region discrimination in metropolitan geolocalization and is associated with greater sensitivity to intact scene configuration, without evidence that coarse structure alone becomes sufficient for prediction. The findings concern viewpoint variation near known locations rather than geographically disjoint generalization.

title: SAFE-G: Structure-aware Faithful Evidence-guided Generation for Knowledge-based Visual Question Answering
summary: Knowledge-based Visual Question Answering (KB-VQA) aims to answer queries that necessitate reasoning over external knowledge sources beyond the visual content. Typically, current methods fuse multimodal features to retrieve external information, subsequently leveraging Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to derive answers from the retrieved evidence. However, these methods often struggle to capture structural associations within complex contexts to effectively filter noise. Furthermore, they frequently fail to ensure that the reasoning process remains strictly faithful to the retrieved evidence. To address these challenges, we propose SAFE-G, a Structure-Aware Faithful Evidence-guided Generation framework, which enables precise evidence localization and trustworthy reasoning. Specifically, we first employ a coarse-grained hybrid search fusing visual and textual modalities to recall candidate documents, and subsequently implement a structure-aware fine-grained graph retrieval that captures structural dependencies to filter noise and pinpoint precise evidence. Moreover, we introduce a reinforcement learning (RL) strategy with an evidence-grounded reward that assigns credit to correct answers only when the selected evidence is correct. This strict alignment constraint compels the model to anchor its response in the retrieved context, effectively enhancing its capability to locate evidence via multimodal features and perform faithful reasoning. Extensive experiments on the Encyclopedic-VQA and InfoSeek benchmarks demonstrate that SAFE-G outperforms prior methods by a margin of 8.9% and 3.5%, substantially enhancing the overall reasoning accuracy. Our source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/MINE-USTC/SAFE-G.

AI.tldr: SAFE-G is a Structure-Aware Faithful Evidence-guided Generation framework for KB-VQA that uses coarse-to-fine retrieval (hybrid search + structure-aware graph retrieval) and a reinforcement learning strategy with evidence-grounded rewards to ensure faithful reasoning over retrieved evidence, achieving 8.9% and 3.5% improvements over prior methods on Encyclopedic-VQA and InfoSeek benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current KB-VQA methods struggle with (1) capturing structural associations within complex contexts to effectively filter retrieval noise, and (2) ensuring the reasoning process remains strictly faithful to retrieved evidence, leading to hallucinated or unsupported answers.
AI.method: SAFE-G employs a two-stage retrieval pipeline: first, a coarse-grained hybrid search fusing visual and textual modalities recalls candidate documents; second, a structure-aware fine-grained graph retrieval captures structural dependencies to filter noise and localize precise evidence. Additionally, a reinforcement learning strategy with an evidence-grounded reward is introduced, which assigns credit only when both the selected evidence and answer are correct, forcing the model to anchor responses in retrieved context.
AI.result: SAFE-G outperforms prior methods by 8.9% on Encyclopedic-VQA and 3.5% on InfoSeek benchmarks, substantially improving overall reasoning accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The combination of structure-aware graph retrieval for precise evidence localization and RL-based evidence-grounded alignment for faithful reasoning effectively addresses both noise filtering and reasoning faithfulness challenges in KB-VQA.

title: Design of a Human-Assistance Robot System with Contextual Action Recognition
comment: Published in Automation 2025: Recent Advances in Automation, Robotics and Measurement Techniques, Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems, vol. 1687, Springer Nature, 2025. DOI: 10.1007/978-3-032-08359-3_16
summary: This paper presents a conceptual design for a proactive human assisting robot system capable of recognizing human activities and responding proactively. The system leverages contextual human activity recognition to interpret human actions across diverse contexts, while behavior trees are utilized to define dynamic and interpretable robot behaviors. We outline the system architecture, incorporating contextual human action recognition (HAR), behavior trees (BTs), and ROS, using the Spot robot platform as a representative example.
