We explain how HAR enables the robot to provide proactive assistance, discuss its limitations, and introduce methodologies for contextual HAR to address these limitations, thereby enhancing the robot's decision-making in complex human activity scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a conceptual design for a proactive human-assisting robot system that combines contextual human activity recognition (HAR) with behavior trees (BTs) on the ROS framework, using the Spot robot as a representative platform to enable dynamic and interpretable proactive assistance.
AI.motivation: To enable robots to proactively assist humans, they must accurately interpret human activities in diverse contexts. Standard human activity recognition approaches have limitations in complex scenarios, motivating the need for contextual HAR integrated with a flexible robot behavior framework.
AI.method: The system architecture integrates three key components: contextual human action recognition (HAR) to interpret human actions across diverse contexts, behavior trees (BTs) to define dynamic and interpretable robot behaviors, and ROS as the middleware. The Spot robot platform is used as a representative deployment example.
AI.result: The paper outlines the system architecture and explains how contextual HAR enables proactive assistance, discusses limitations of standard HAR, and introduces methodologies for contextual HAR to enhance robot decision-making in complex human activity scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Contextual human activity recognition combined with behavior trees provides a viable approach for enhancing robot proactive assistance capabilities, improving decision-making in complex human activity situations.

title: Machine learning and digital pragmatics: Which word category influences emoji use most?
summary: This study examines the performance of the state-of-the-art MARBERT model in identifying the lexical/pragmatic category associated with emoji use on X within a digital pragmatics approach (DPA). A net corpus of 15856 Colloquial Arabic (CA) posts containing emojis was collected from X using Python. The texts were tokenized and normalized into 4 lexical categories, namely noun_norm, verb_norm, adj_norm, and adverb_norm, and 2 pragmatic/structural categories, question_norm and exclamation_norm. MARBERT was finetuned and optimized to identify which category scores standard metrics more, hence associated with emoji use, while binary logistic regression was used to examine which category is statistically associated with emoji occurrence. Findings unveil that nouns dominate the corpus in normalized frequency (M = 0.675, SD = 0.161), followed by verbs (M = 0.083, SD = 0.100). However, verbs have the strongest influence of emoji use indicated by verb density (\b{eta} = 0.821, p = .001, 95% CI [0.332, 1.309]). The study concludes that in digital pragmatics of CA on X, emoji use association with lexical/pragmatic category can be explained by a hybrid approach of computational, statistical, and pragmatic methods, reflecting the interaction among machine learning, linguistic/lexical features, contextual representation, and pragmatic communication.

AI.tldr: This study investigates how the MARBERT model and binary logistic regression identify lexical/pragmatic categories associated with emoji use in Colloquial Arabic posts on X. Nouns dominate in frequency, but verbs have the strongest statistical influence on emoji occurrence, within a hybrid digital pragmatics approach.
AI.motivation: To understand which lexical/pragmatic categories are most associated with emoji use in Colloquial Arabic on social media (X), using a digital pragmatics approach that integrates computational, statistical, and pragmatic methods.
AI.method: A corpus of 15,856 Colloquial Arabic posts containing emojis was collected from X using Python. Texts were tokenized and normalized into 4 lexical categories (noun, verb, adj, adverb) and 2 pragmatic/structural categories (question, exclamation). MARBERT was fine-tuned to identify which category scores standard metrics more (associated with emoji use), while binary logistic regression examined statistical associations with emoji occurrence.
AI.result: Nouns dominate the corpus in normalized frequency (M = 0.675, SD = 0.161), followed by verbs (M = 0.083, SD = 0.100). However, verbs have the strongest statistical influence on emoji use (verb density: β = 0.821, p = .001, 95% CI [0.332, 1.309]).
AI.conclusion: Emoji use association with lexical/pragmatic categories in Colloquial Arabic on X can be explained through a hybrid approach combining computational, statistical, and pragmatic methods, reflecting the interaction among machine learning, linguistic/lexical features, contextual representation, and pragmatic communication.

title: Physics-Knowledge-Guided Hybrid Neural Learning for Arctic Sea Ice Concentration Evolution and Short-Range Prediction
summary: Accurate modeling of sea ice concentration (SIC) evolution is essential for polar climate assessment and short?range sea ice prediction. Numerical and data-driven approaches constitute major foundations for SIC modeling, but the former often require complex parameterizations and substantial compu?tation, whereas the latter rarely encode physical dependencies explicitly. This study presents the Physics-Informed Hybrid Ice Model (PIHIM), a differentiable data-driven hybrid ice model for daily SIC evolution that organizes its network structure according to the physical dependencies encoded in the sea ice continuity equation and explicitly accounts for dynamical transport, ther?modynamically driven areal growth and loss, and unresolved local processes. PIHIM preserves the representation capacity of deep learning while providing a process-decomposed formulation of ice displacement, freeze-melt areal change, and local error closure. Two evaluation settings are adopted: reanalysis-forced simulation examines SIC evolution stability under reanalysis forcing, and forecast-forced prediction assesses short-range performance un?der forecast-forced conditions, with reanalysis and observational SIC serving as verification references. Results indicate enhanced ice-edge preservation and error-growth control in reanalysis?forced simulation, while PIHIM retains measurable short-range prediction skill under forecast-forced conditions. Our code will be made publicly available after the paper is accepted.

AI.tldr: PIHIM is a differentiable data-driven hybrid ice model that organizes its network architecture according to the physical dependencies of the sea ice continuity equation, explicitly decomposing dynamical transport, thermodynamic areal change, and local error closure for daily sea ice concentration evolution.
AI.motivation: Numerical models for sea ice concentration require complex parameterizations and substantial computation, while data-driven approaches rarely encode physical dependencies explicitly. There is a need to combine the representation capacity of deep learning with physically meaningful structure to improve SIC modeling.
AI.method: The Physics-Informed Hybrid Ice Model (PIHIM) is a differentiable data-driven model whose network structure follows the physical dependencies in the sea ice continuity equation. It explicitly decomposes SIC evolution into: (1) dynamical transport, (2) thermodynamically driven areal growth/loss, and (3) unresolved local processes (local error closure). Two evaluation settings are used: reanalysis-forced simulation and forecast-forced prediction, verified against reanalysis and observational SIC.
AI.result: PIHIM shows enhanced ice-edge preservation and error-growth control in reanalysis-forced simulation, while retaining measurable short-range prediction skill under forecast-forced conditions.
AI.conclusion: The physics-informed hybrid approach effectively bridges numerical and data-driven SIC modeling by providing a process-decomposed, differentiable formulation that balances physical interpretability with deep learning flexibility.

title: FlashReg: GPU-Accelerated 3-Clique Point Cloud Registration for Real-Time Correspondence-to-Pose Estimation
summary: Graph-based point cloud registration achieves high robustness by identifying geometrically consistent correspondence sets, but constructing second-order compatibility graphs and enumerating candidate cliques remain compute- and memory-intensive. This work presents FlashReg, a GPU-oriented correspondence-to-pose estimator that avoids materializing the dense scored second-order graph. Its Fast First- and Second-Order Graph (FFSOG) construction builds a capacity-bounded sparse second-order graph directly from the binary first-order graph. A dataflow-optimized three-node clique (3-clique) search then selects pivots from compact per-row candidate pools and enumerates triples through sorted sparse-neighborhood intersections. Across indoor and outdoor benchmarks, FlashReg reduces correspondence-to-pose latency by 2--3x relative to TurboReg at comparable registration recall, while using about 50% of its peak allocated tensor memory on an embedded GPU. These results make FlashReg suitable as a high-throughput registration backend within onboard perception pipelines.

AI.tldr: FlashReg is a GPU-oriented correspondence-to-pose estimator for point cloud registration that avoids materializing dense second-order compatibility graphs. It uses a Fast First- and Second-Order Graph construction to build capacity-bounded sparse second-order graphs from binary first-order graphs, plus a dataflow-optimized three-node clique search. It achieves 2-3x lower latency than TurboReg at comparable recall while using ~50% of the peak tensor memory on an embedded GPU.
AI.motivation: Graph-based point cloud registration achieves high robustness through geometrically consistent correspondence sets, but constructing second-order compatibility graphs and enumerating candidate cliques is compute- and memory-intensive, limiting its use in resource-constrained onboard perception systems.
AI.method: FlashReg introduces (1) a Fast First- and Second-Order Graph (FFSOG) construction that builds a capacity-bounded sparse second-order graph directly from the binary first-order graph without materializing dense scored graphs, and (2) a dataflow-optimized 3-clique search that selects pivots from compact per-row candidate pools and enumerates triples via sorted sparse-neighborhood intersections. The entire pipeline is GPU-oriented.
AI.result: Across indoor and outdoor benchmarks, FlashReg reduces correspondence-to-pose latency by 2-3x relative to TurboReg at comparable registration recall, while using about 50% of its peak allocated tensor memory on an embedded GPU.
AI.conclusion: FlashReg demonstrates that high-throughput, memory-efficient graph-based point cloud registration is achievable on embedded GPUs, making it suitable as a registration backend in onboard perception pipelines.

title: DELTA: Deformable Elevation-Based Local Terrain Attention Encoder for Sparse-Terrain Quadrupedal Locomotion
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to the 2027 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA 2027). This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Stable quadrupedal locomotion on sparse terrain requires selecting state-relevant terrain evidence for precise foot placement. Model-based foothold planners provide precise foothold selection but rely heavily on explicit model assumptions. Recent attention-based map encoding (AME) studies show that end-to-end reinforcement learning (RL) can learn implicit foothold guidance. However, the computational cost of dense AME encoding grows with map resolution, limiting its scalability to fine-grained sparse terrain. We propose DELTA, a Deformable Elevation-Based Local Terrain Attention encoder. DELTA predicts state-conditioned sampling locations, forms terrain evidence tokens from adaptive local elevation patches, and attends only to a fixed-size token set. With fixed sampling and patch settings, DELTA's encoder cost is independent of map resolution. Experiments show that DELTA achieves final traversal performance comparable to AME at the standard resolution while improving learning efficiency. This fixed encoder cost enables the use of higher-resolution terrain maps, improving traversal on fine-grained sparse terrain. DELTA also demonstrates strong generalization to unseen mixed evaluation courses composed of continuous and discrete terrain elements. Beyond simulation, DELTA demonstrates successful sim-to-real transfer on RAIBO2. Analysis of the learned sampling offsets and attention weights shows that DELTA samples steppable regions and attends to terrain evidence relevant to future touchdowns without foothold labels or attention supervision.

AI.tldr: DELTA is a Deformable Elevation-Based Local Terrain Attention encoder that enables scalable, resolution-independent terrain encoding for quadrupedal locomotion on sparse terrain via end-to-end RL, achieving performance comparable to attention-based map encoding (AME) at standard resolution while improving learning efficiency, supporting higher-resolution maps, generalizing to unseen terrain combinations, and demonstrating successful sim-to-real transfer on RAIBO2.
AI.motivation: Traditional model-based foothold planners require explicit model assumptions, while attention-based map encoding (AME) in end-to-end RL suffers from computational costs that grow with map resolution, limiting scalability to fine-grained sparse terrain where precise foot placement is critical.
AI.method: DELTA predicts state-conditioned sampling locations, forms terrain evidence tokens from adaptive local elevation patches, and attends only to a fixed-size token set. This makes encoder cost independent of map resolution with fixed sampling and patch settings.
AI.result: DELTA achieves traversal performance comparable to AME at standard resolution with improved learning efficiency. Its fixed encoder cost enables higher-resolution terrain maps, improving traversal on fine-grained sparse terrain. It generalizes to unseen mixed evaluation courses and demonstrates successful sim-to-real transfer on RAIBO2. Analysis shows DELTA learns to sample steppable regions and attend to terrain evidence relevant to future touchdowns without explicit foothold labels or attention supervision.
AI.conclusion: DELTA provides a scalable and efficient terrain encoding solution for quadrupedal locomotion on sparse terrain, enabling resolution-independent computation, better performance on fine-grained terrain at higher resolutions, strong generalization, and successful real-world deployment, all without requiring foothold labels or attention supervision.

title: Align, Unify, Suppress, Route: A Coherentist View of Transformer Computation
summary: Mechanistic interpretability has identified transformer circuits, but lacks a shared vocabulary for describing how their functions compose across tasks and architectures. We introduce Coherentist Probabilistic Compositionalism (CPC), an interpretive framework that grounds transformer computation in coherentist theories of interpretation and describes it through four operator roles. Alignment identifies candidate relations, unification integrates supporting information, suppression reduces incompatible alternatives, and routing carries selected information to the output. Across 15 models from five architecture families, the suppression, unification, and routing weight-space signatures correlate with held-out activation-level role measures above random baselines. Suppression is more stable across tasks than unification. Ablating alignment heads reduces downstream suppressive activity beyond a random-head control in 10 models, but similar effects on no-conflict prompts indicate a general upstream dependency, not contradiction-specific coupling. Explicit contradictions significantly shift a layerwise coherence proxy in 14 models; after removing shared residual covariance, the gap has the predicted direction in every model. Base and instruction-tuned variants preserve induction-head score structure ($r{\geq}0.98$) without a consistent shift of operator signatures towards later layers. These results support CPC as a shared vocabulary for comparing transformer mechanisms while showing that their depth and geometric expression remain architecture-specific.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Coherentist Probabilistic Compositionalism (CPC), an interpretive framework that grounds transformer computation in coherentist theories of interpretation and describes it through four operator roles: alignment, unification, suppression, and routing. Across 15 models from five architecture families, weight-space signatures of these operators correlate with activation-level role measures above random baselines. Suppression is more stable across tasks than unification. Ablation studies show alignment-head removal reduces downstream suppressive activity but also affects no-conflict prompts, indicating a general upstream dependency. Explicit contradictions shift a layerwise coherence proxy in 14 models with the predicted direction in all models after removing shared residual covariance. The framework serves as a shared vocabulary for comparing transformer mechanisms while showing that their depth and geometric expression remain architecture-specific.
AI.motivation: Mechanistic interpretability has identified transformer circuits but lacks a shared vocabulary for describing how their functions compose across tasks and architectures. The authors aim to provide a unified interpretive framework grounded in coherentist theories of interpretation to enable cross-architecture comparison.
AI.method: CPC defines four operator roles (alignment, unification, suppression, routing). The framework is tested across 15 models from five architecture families by measuring weight-space signatures of these operators and correlating them with activation-level role measures. Ablation studies on alignment heads and analysis of explicit contradiction prompts examine layerwise coherence proxies, with shared residual covariance removed for control.
AI.result: Suppression, unification, and routing weight-space signatures correlate with activation-level role measures above random baselines. Suppression is more stable across tasks than unification. Alignment-head ablation reduces suppressive activity in 10 models but also affects no-conflict prompts. Explicit contradictions shift the layerwise coherence proxy in 14 models, with the predicted direction in every model after covariance removal. Base and instruction-tuned variants preserve induction-head score structure (r≥0.98) without consistent shift of operator signatures.
AI.conclusion: CPC provides a valid shared vocabulary for comparing transformer mechanisms across architectures, though the depth and geometric expression of these operators remain architecture-specific. The framework supports meaningful cross-model comparison of interpretability findings while highlighting that architectural details still matter.

title: HIRA: A Human-in-the-Loop Retrieval-Augmented Cascade for Document Classification in Regulated Industries
summary:
Document classification in regulated industries is constrained by data residency, limited cold-start labels, scarce review capacity, and costly model-governance procedures. We present HIRA, a training-free, on-premises retrieval-augmented cascade for document classification in regulated deployments that combines BM25 over OCR text, dense text embeddings, and image-level representations through validation-calibrated weighted reciprocal-rank fusion. Confident documents are classified directly by retrieval; uncertain or visually confusable documents are passed to a locally hosted LLM verifier, which receives the OCR text, retrieved exemplars, label descriptions, and confusion-specific terms. When the verifier remains uncertain, the document is sent to human review. Each correction is stored as a margin-weighted retrieval exemplar and updates a Dirichlet-smoothed confusion graph, letting the system improve without updating model weights.
  On a private 80-class trade-finance corpus, HIRA processes the full 30,233-document production stream while requesting human correction for only 1,945 documents (6.4%), improving Macro-F1 from 0.6218 to 0.8548. On the corrected Tobacco-3482 benchmark, HIRA reaches 0.9423 Macro-F1 with a locally hosted DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B verifier, 17.4 percentage points above the zero-shot LLM baseline, while invoking the verifier for only about 40% of documents and reducing LLM calls by approximately 60%. With 518 human corrections (24.8% of the pool), HIRA matches the fully labelled pool oracle, in which all 2,086 pool documents are indexed with their ground-truth labels. These results show that selective human feedback and retrieval-memory adaptation can be a practical alternative to repeated model retraining for long-tail document classification in regulated deployments.

AI.tldr: HIRA is a training-free, on-premises retrieval-augmented cascade system for document classification in regulated industries. It combines BM25, dense text embeddings, and image representations via weighted reciprocal-rank fusion; routes uncertain documents to a locally hosted LLM verifier and then to human review. It improves Macro-F1 from 0.6218 to 0.8548 on a private 30,233-document trade-finance corpus (6.4% human review rate) and reaches 0.9423 Macro-F1 on Tobacco-3482 with ~60% reduction in LLM calls, matching the fully-labeled pool oracle with only 24.8% human corrections.
AI.motivation: Regulated industries face multiple constraints for document classification: data residency requirements prevent cloud-based solutions, cold-start scenarios have limited labeled data, human review capacity is scarce, and model governance procedures make retraining costly. Existing approaches rely on repeated retraining, which is impractical under these constraints.
AI.method: HIRA is a training-free cascade pipeline: (1) retrieval layer combining BM25 over OCR text, dense text embeddings, and image-level representations fused via validation-calibrated weighted reciprocal-rank fusion; (2) confident documents classified directly by retrieval; (3) uncertain documents passed to a locally hosted LLM verifier that receives OCR text, retrieved exemplars, label descriptions, and confusion-specific terms; (4) remaining uncertainty routed to human review; (5) each correction stored as a margin-weighted retrieval exemplar and updates a Dirichlet-smoothed confusion graph, enabling improvement without model weight updates.
AI.result: On a private 80-class trade-finance corpus (30,233 documents), HIRA improves Macro-F1 from 0.6218 to 0.8548 while requesting human correction for only 6.4% of documents. On Tobacco-3482, HIRA reaches 0.9423 Macro-F1 with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B verifier—17.4 points above zero-shot LLM baseline—while invoking the verifier on only ~40% of documents and reducing LLM calls by ~60%. With 518 human corrections (24.8% of the pool), HIRA matches the fully-labeled pool oracle.
AI.conclusion: Selective human feedback combined with retrieval-memory adaptation (margin-weighted exemplars and Dirichlet-smoothed confusion graphs) is a practical and effective alternative to repeated model retraining for long-tail document classification in regulated deployments, achieving substantial accuracy gains with minimal human review and no model weight updates.

title: Through the Schrödinger Bridge: Benchmarking Antemortem Image Restoration from Postmortem Autolysis to Enhance Forensic Diagnostics
summary: Forensic histopathology, essential for determining cause of death and disease diagnosis, is severely impeded by postmortem autolysis, i.e., an irreversible, stochastic degradation process that distorts tissue morphology and introduces diagnostic subjectivity, thereby underscoring the value of restoring autolyzed images to a diagnostically plausible, pre-autolysis state for improving objectivity in forensic practice. This restoration task is fundamentally challenging due to the large, non-deterministic morphological changes caused by autolysis and the infeasibility of pixel-wise paired data, which invalidates assumptions underlying supervised and cycle/structure-consistent unpaired translation methods. To address this, we formalize forensic histopathology autolysis restoration as a new task: under unpaired supervision, transform postmortem images with severe autolysis into diagnostically meaningful ``antemortem'' representations. We contribute AutoPath, the first homologous yet unpaired dataset for this problem, constructed by splitting specimens into adjacent tissue blocks---one processed immediately, the other exposed to induce autolysis---yielding nearly ten thousand $10\times$ patches from 69 cases with varying liver conditions. We further frame the problem as a Schrödinger Bridge between the autolyzed and non-autolyzed distributions, offering a principled approach to modeling stochastic, severe morphological degradation. Critically, we demonstrate the misalignment of generic image-level generative metrics (e.g., FID) with diagnostic utility and propose a forensically grounded, slide-level diagnostic distribution consistency evaluation. Overall, this work establishes a reproducible benchmark (encompassing task definition, a real-world dataset, and an evaluation methodology) toward rigorous and practically meaningful progress in autolysis restoration for forensic pathology.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces AutoPath, the first unpaired dataset for forensic histopathology autolysis restoration, and frames the task as a Schrödinger Bridge problem to transform severely autolyzed postmortem images into diagnostically meaningful antemortem representations. The authors also propose a forensically grounded, slide-level diagnostic distribution consistency evaluation, demonstrating that generic image-level metrics (e.g., FID) misalign with diagnostic utility, thereby establishing a reproducible benchmark encompassing task definition, dataset, and evaluation methodology.
AI.motivation: Forensic histopathology is impeded by postmortem autolysis—an irreversible, stochastic degradation process that distorts tissue morphology and introduces diagnostic subjectivity. Restoring autolyzed images to a pre-autolysis state could improve objectivity, but this is fundamentally challenging because of large non-deterministic morphological changes and the infeasibility of pixel-wise paired data, which invalidates supervised and cycle/structure-consistent unpaired translation assumptions.
AI.method: The authors formalize autolysis restoration as a new task under unpaired supervision, constructing AutoPath—a homologous yet unpaired dataset created by splitting specimens into adjacent tissue blocks (one processed immediately, the other exposed to induce autolysis), yielding ~10,000 10x patches from 69 cases with varying liver conditions. They frame the problem as a Schrödinger Bridge between autolyzed and non-autolyzed distributions to model stochastic severe morphological degradation, and propose a forensically grounded, slide-level diagnostic distribution consistency evaluation.
AI.result: The paper demonstrates that generic image-level generative metrics (e.g., FID) are misaligned with diagnostic utility, and provides a new evaluation methodology grounded in forensic diagnostic distribution consistency at the slide level. It also contributes the first homologous yet unpaired dataset (AutoPath) for this problem.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes a reproducible benchmark—covering task definition, a real-world dataset, and an evaluation methodology—toward rigorous and practically meaningful progress in autolysis restoration for forensic pathology.

title: Ludi${}_{\scriptscriptstyle 0.1}$: An Agentic System for Socially Intelligent Robots
summary: Robot foundation models have substantially advanced perception and control, but natural human-robot collaboration requires more than executing isolated commands. A robot must recognize ambiguity, maintain context across turns, communicate its intentions, and revise ongoing behavior as the user's intent changes. We present $\scriptstyle\mathsf{Ludi}_{\scriptscriptstyle 0.1}$, an agentic system for socially intelligent robots that integrates interactive speech, multimodal reasoning, memory, navigation, and learned manipulation. Its decision-making core is a fine-tuned vision-language model trained on multi-turn interaction traces spanning ambiguous requests, clarifications, corrections, interruptions, mixed social and task dialogue, and multi-step tasks. A purpose-built harness manages the model-tool interaction loop, while specialized navigation and manipulation policies execute physical skills. Ludi${}_{\scriptscriptstyle 0.1}$ demonstrates a practical path toward fluid human-robot collaboration today while producing the multimodal interaction traces needed to develop a more deeply integrated foundation model for robots and people.

AI.tldr: Ludi0.1 is an agentic system for socially intelligent robots that integrates interactive speech, multimodal reasoning, memory, navigation, and learned manipulation, enabling fluid multi-turn human-robot collaboration through a fine-tuned vision-language model trained on interaction traces.
AI.motivation: Natural human-robot collaboration requires more than executing isolated commands; robots must handle ambiguity, maintain context across turns, communicate intentions, and adapt to changing user intent, which existing robot foundation models do not adequately address.
AI.method: Ludi0.1 uses a fine-tuned vision-language model as its decision-making core, trained on multi-turn interaction traces covering ambiguous requests, clarifications, corrections, interruptions, mixed social/task dialogue, and multi-step tasks. A purpose-built harness manages the model-tool interaction loop, while specialized navigation and manipulation policies execute physical skills.
AI.result: Ludi0.1 demonstrates a practical path toward fluid human-robot collaboration, and produces multimodal interaction traces needed for developing a more deeply integrated foundation model for robots and people.
AI.conclusion: The system shows that socially intelligent human-robot collaboration is achievable today by combining an agentic VLM core with specialized physical skill policies, while generating the training data necessary for future, more integrated foundation models.

title: Real-TurnTurk: A Multimodal Turkish Corpus for Turn-Taking Prediction
comment: Accepted to INTCEC 2026. This is the author's pre-print version. The final authenticated version will be available through the conference proceedings
summary: Turn-taking is a basic organizational feature of human conversation and remains difficult to model in natural, synchronous dialog systems. While existing research has explored multimodal approaches and large language models for turn-ending prediction, there is a lack of naturalistic conversational corpora specifically addressing turn-taking dynamics in Turkish. This study introduces a multimodal Turkish conversational dataset of unscripted dyadic interactions, comprising synchronized front-facing video, per-speaker audio channels that allow overlapping speech to be attributed to individual speakers, and time-aligned transcriptions. Turn-taking prediction is formulated as a binary classification problem, and a Genetic Algorithm (GA) is employed to optimize interpretable decision rules derived from visual, acoustic, and linguistic features. A hybrid AND-OR rule representation is adopted in the proposed framework to represent the alternative cue combinations that precede a turn transition.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the first multimodal Turkish conversational dataset for studying turn-taking dynamics, comprising unscripted dyadic interactions with synchronized video, per-speaker audio, and aligned transcriptions. Turn-ending prediction is framed as binary classification using a Genetic Algorithm to optimize interpretable AND-OR hybrid decision rules combining visual, acoustic, and linguistic cues.
AI.motivation: Turn-taking remains difficult to model in natural synchronous dialog systems. While multimodal and LLM-based approaches exist for turn-ending prediction, there is a lack of naturalistic conversational corpora specifically addressing turn-taking dynamics in Turkish, motivating the creation of a new dataset and prediction framework.
AI.method: A multimodal Turkish conversational dataset is constructed from unscripted dyadic interactions featuring synchronized front-facing video, per-speaker audio channels enabling attribution of overlapping speech, and time-aligned transcriptions. Turn-taking prediction is cast as binary classification, and a Genetic Algorithm optimizes interpretable decision rules from visual, acoustic, and linguistic features using a hybrid AND-OR rule representation to model alternative cue combinations preceding turn transitions.
AI.result: The paper presents a novel multimodal Turkish conversational corpus and a GA-based interpretable rule optimization framework for turn-ending prediction using hybrid AND-OR decision rules over multimodal cues.
AI.conclusion: The study addresses the gap in naturalistic Turkish turn-taking corpora and proposes an interpretable multimodal prediction approach, offering an alternative to black-box models for turn-ending classification in dialog systems.

title: Hints, Critics, and Teachers: Prior Injection for Sparse-Reward RL in Vision-Language Math Reasoning
summary: Reinforcement learning for vision-language math reasoning starves under sparse reward: on a pool of 20,830 visual-math problems where Qwen2-VL-2B answers 3.6% of rollouts correctly, 85-97% of GRPO rollout groups are entirely wrong and contribute zero gradient. We train eleven methods under identical conditions in this regime, each injecting a different prior: text (reference-solution hints), distribution (on-policy distillation from a 7B teacher), and value (a value-pretrained critic with an MSE or HL-Gauss categorical loss). A prior helps exactly when it is delivered: the six arms whose prior effectively reaches the policy separate with no overlap from the remaining five -- the no-prior baseline and four arms whose prior is teacher-capped, gated away, or lost to a mis-parameterized critic -- both on the pooled in-domain metric and on cross-domain transfer (DynaMath). The central finding, however, concerns evaluation: one slice of the in-domain pool -- long used as this project's general-distribution check -- anti-correlates with genuine cross-domain transfer (Spearman rho = -0.74, n = 11 arms, permutation p = 0.011), while the hardest in-domain slice predicts it closely (rho = +0.89, p < 0.001). We attribute the inversion to a near-chance multiple-choice subset that rewards models for not having changed; read through it, the best cross-domain method looked mediocre and the worst looked like the champion. Among the methods, hint-guided exploration -- not UFT's auxiliary loss -- drives hint gains, and replacing the critic's MSE loss with HL-Gauss cross-entropy is worth +14.4 points in-domain. All accuracies are blind-judged, with paired exact tests.

AI.tldr: In the sparse-reward regime of reinforcement learning for vision-language math reasoning (where Qwen2-VL-2B solves only 3.6% of 20,830 problems and 85-97% of GRPO groups are entirely wrong), the authors train eleven methods under identical conditions with different priors (text hints, distribution distillation, and value-pretrained critics). A prior helps exactly when it reaches the policy. Crucially, they find that one in-domain evaluation slice anti-correlates with genuine cross-domain transfer (Spearman rho = -0.74), while the hardest slice predicts transfer closely (rho = +0.89), revealing an evaluation-metric inversion driven by a near-chance multiple-choice subset. Hint-guided exploration and HL-Gauss critic loss (worth +14.4 points) are key contributions.
AI.motivation: RL for vision-language math reasoning suffers from sparse rewards: with only 3.6% correct rollouts, most GRPO groups contribute zero gradient. The authors aim to understand which priors help under this starvation regime and to expose a hidden evaluation pitfall—an in-domain evaluation slice that actively misleads cross-domain transfer assessment.
AI.method: Eleven methods are trained under identical conditions, each injecting a different prior: text-based (reference-solution hints), distribution-based (on-policy distillation from a 7B teacher), and value-based (a value-pretrained critic with MSE or HL-Gauss categorical loss). Methods are compared on a pooled in-domain metric and cross-domain transfer to DynaMath, with slice-specific analyses and blind-judged exact-test accuracies.
AI.result: The six arms whose prior effectively reaches the policy separate with no overlap from the remaining five. One in-domain slice anti-correlates with cross-domain transfer (rho = -0.74, p = 0.011) while the hardest slice predicts it (rho = +0.89, p < 0.001). Hint-guided exploration (not UFT's auxiliary loss) drives hint gains, and HL-Gauss cross-entropy beats MSE by +14.4 points in-domain.
AI.conclusion: Prior effectiveness is conditional on successful delivery to the policy; evaluation design is as critical as training method. The near-chance multiple-choice slice can invert method rankings entirely—the best cross-domain method can look mediocre and the worst can look like the champion—so hardest-slice and cross-domain metrics should be preferred over easy multiple-choice checks.

title: PatchGate: Narrowing the Verbalization Gap with Intrinsic Object Inventories in Frozen Vision-Language Models
comment: 31 pages, 9 figures. Code will be available
summary: Reliable image captioning in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) requires captions to be both precise and complete, avoiding unsupported object mentions while covering visible objects. Existing training-free methods primarily address the former requirement, suppressing unsupported object words by intervening on model-predicted mentions during generation. Because they operate only on objects the model is already likely to mention, visible objects omitted from the output remain difficult to recover. We propose PatchGate, a training-free framework that extracts prompt-free object evidence intrinsic to a frozen VLM before generation and uses it to narrow the gap between an intrinsic object set and final object mentions. In the first stage, Visual Evidence eXtraction (VEX) reads patch-level lexical evidence from the latter half of LM decoder layers and constructs an image-conditioned object set without any task prompt. In the second stage, Visual-Evidence Inclusion-Exclusion Decoding (VIED) uses this object evidence to calibrate decoding logits, promoting evidence-supported but under-verbalized objects and suppressing weakly supported but over-verbalized objects. On AMBER, PatchGate improves both sides of object-level reliability, increasing visible-object coverage from 49.4 to 56.0 (+13.4%) and reducing object hallucination by lowering CHAIR from 7.5 to 6.6 (-12.0%), without external detectors or fine-tuning and with one extra forward pass.

AI.tldr: PatchGate is a training-free framework that extracts prompt-free visual object evidence from a frozen VLM's decoder layers before generation and uses it to calibrate decoding logits, simultaneously improving visible-object coverage and reducing object hallucination in image captioning.
AI.motivation: Existing training-free methods for reliable image captioning suppress unsupported object words by intervening on model-predicted mentions during generation, but since they only operate on objects the model is already likely to mention, visible objects omitted from the output remain difficult to recover—leaving the completeness side of object-level reliability largely unaddressed.
AI.method: PatchGate has two stages: (1) Visual Evidence eXtraction (VEX) reads patch-level lexical evidence from the latter half of LM decoder layers and constructs an image-conditioned object set without any task prompt; (2) Visual-Evidence Inclusion-Exclusion Decoding (VIED) uses this object evidence to calibrate decoding logits, promoting evidence-supported but under-verbalized objects and suppressing weakly supported but over-verbalized objects.
AI.result: On AMBER, PatchGate improves visible-object coverage from 49.4 to 56.0 (+13.4%) and reduces object hallucination by lowering CHAIR from 7.5 to 6.6 (-12.0%), without external detectors or fine-tuning and with one extra forward pass.
AI.conclusion: PatchGate demonstrates that prompt-free intrinsic visual evidence extracted from a frozen VLM can effectively narrow the gap between an intrinsic object set and final object mentions, addressing both precision (hallucination reduction) and completeness (coverage improvement) of object-level captioning reliability in a training-free manner.

title: Inferring Action from Future Latent State for Robotic Manipulation
summary: World-Action Models (WAMs) build robot control on video-generation backbones, which jointly predict dense future visual trajectories and robot actions. We argue that video generation is an unnecessary intermediate objective for world-action modeling. For robotic manipulation, the goal of a world model is not to reproduce how the world looks at every intermediate moment, but to predict the state that the world will reach after an action is executed. The intermediate frames only describe the visual transition between physical states, which consumes substantial model capacity and computation, but do not directly specify the physical outcome that the robot action is intended to produce. In this paper, we propose DELE-w0.5, which infers robot actions from predicted future states without relying on video generation. Concretely, DELE-w0.5 infers the action sequence from its corresponding compact future latent state. The future latent state captures the action-relevant physical outcome of robot interaction and serves as an explicit bridge between world modeling and action generation. The core design principle of DELE-w0.5 is to model how the physical world changes under robot actions, rather than how its visual appearance evolves frame by frame. This formulation removes the high-dimensional visual redundancy introduced by dense video representations, and it therefore enables cheaper training and low-latency inference. Across 480 real-robot trials on four long-horizon manipulation tasks, our DELE-w0.5 achieves the best performance among all compared policies, attaining 62.5 overall full-task success and 81.3 macro ordered-stage progress, outperforming the strongest baseline by 47.5 and 30.7 percentage points, respectively.

AI.tldr: DELE-w0.5 proposes a World-Action Model that skips video generation entirely, instead inferring robot actions directly from compact future latent states that capture action-relevant physical outcomes. This removes visual redundancy, enabling cheaper training and faster inference, achieving 62.5% full-task success across 480 real-robot trials on four long-horizon manipulation tasks, outperforming the strongest baseline by 47.5 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Video generation is an unnecessary intermediate objective for world-action modeling in robotics. Predicting intermediate frames consumes substantial model capacity and computation, but does not directly specify the physical outcome the robot action is intended to produce. The goal of a world model for manipulation should be predicting the physical state after an action, not reproducing visual appearance at every intermediate moment.
AI.method: DELE-w0.5 infers action sequences from compact future latent states that capture action-relevant physical outcomes, serving as an explicit bridge between world modeling and action generation. Instead of modeling dense visual transitions frame-by-frame, it models how the physical world changes under robot actions, removing high-dimensional visual redundancy.
AI.result: Across 480 real-robot trials on four long-horizon manipulation tasks, DELE-w0.5 achieves the best performance among all compared policies: 62.5% overall full-task success and 81.3% macro ordered-stage progress, outperforming the strongest baseline by 47.5 and 30.7 percentage points respectively.
AI.conclusion: Modeling physical state changes rather than visual appearance evolution is a more effective formulation for world-action models in robotic manipulation, delivering superior performance while enabling cheaper training and low-latency inference.

title: Spine-Branch Coordination for Multi-agent Computer Use
summary: Computer use agents (CUAs) are increasingly deployed as multi-agent systems that decompose a task into multiple subtasks executed across parallel virtual machines (VMs). However, a critical physical bottleneck is that the state of two VMs cannot be merged. Previous systems handle this ad-hoc rather than treating it as a first-class concern. We propose Spine-Branch Coordination for multi-agent computer use, a framework that decomposes a task into a "spine-branch" graph, where the spine carries the main task flow with continuous VM state and branch tasks execute in parallel to collect information the spine needs to complete the task. Branch VMs are discarded once their tasks finish, so no VM merging ever occurs. Experiments show that on 200 long-horizon tasks from Odysseys and across three CUA backbones, Spine-Branch improves success rate over the baseline system by 6.0% to 16.5%, while reducing per-task cost by 34% to 70%, indicating that explicitly modeling VM-state merging constraint enables multi-agent computer use to scale efficiently.

AI.tldr: Spine-Branch Coordination is a framework for multi-agent computer use that decomposes tasks into a spine-branch graph, where the spine maintains continuous VM state and parallel branches collect information without requiring VM merging. It improves success rates by 6.0–16.5% while reducing costs by 34–70% across three CUA backbones on 200 long-horizon tasks.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent computer use systems decompose tasks across parallel virtual machines, but VMs cannot be merged—a critical physical constraint that previous systems handle ad-hoc rather than treating as a first-class design concern.
AI.method: The framework decomposes a task into a spine-branch graph: the spine carries the main task flow with continuous VM state, while branch tasks execute in parallel on separate VMs to gather information needed by the spine. Branch VMs are discarded upon completion, eliminating any need for VM merging.
AI.result: On 200 long-horizon tasks from the Odysseys benchmark across three CUA backbones, Spine-Branch improves success rate over the baseline by 6.0% to 16.5% and reduces per-task cost by 34% to 70%.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling the VM-state merging constraint as a first-class concern enables multi-agent computer use systems to scale efficiently, demonstrating that architectural design aligned with physical system constraints yields both better performance and lower cost.

title: VisAdj: Learning Adjacency Matrices from Node-Link Images
summary: Learning adjacency matrices from node-link images is a fundamental problem for recovering structured graph information from visual observations. Existing methods typically rely on fixed KNN-based heuristics for candidate edge selection and fail to capture dependencies among edges. To overcome these limitations, we propose VisAdj, a new framework for topology-aware adjacency prediction. VisAdj introduces an attention-sparse neighbor sampler to adaptively select a high-recall set of candidate node pairs and performs joint edge inference using a line-graph transformer that treats candidate edges as tokens and explicitly models dependencies among incident edges. Extensive experiments on synthetic graphs, road networks, and vessel images demonstrate that VisAdj consistently outperforms existing baselines by clear margins.

AI.tldr: VisAdj is a framework for predicting adjacency matrices from node-link images, using an attention-sparse neighbor sampler for adaptive candidate edge selection and a line-graph transformer for joint edge inference that captures dependencies among edges, outperforming baselines on synthetic graphs, road networks, and vessel images.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for learning adjacency matrices from node-link images rely on fixed KNN-based heuristics for candidate edge selection and fail to capture dependencies among edges, limiting their accuracy in recovering structured graph information from visual observations.
AI.method: VisAdj introduces (1) an attention-sparse neighbor sampler that adaptively selects a high-recall set of candidate node pairs, and (2) a line-graph transformer that treats candidate edges as tokens and explicitly models dependencies among incident edges for joint edge inference.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on synthetic graphs, road networks, and vessel images demonstrate that VisAdj consistently outperforms existing baselines by clear margins.
AI.conclusion: VisAdj provides an effective topology-aware approach for adjacency prediction by combining adaptive candidate edge selection with explicit modeling of inter-edge dependencies, achieving superior performance across diverse graph-structured visual domains.

title: Towards Alias-Free 4D Gaussian Representations with Motion-Aware Filtering
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. Project Page: https://maaf-4dgs.github.io/
summary: Novel-view synthesis of dynamic scenes, crucial for AR/VR applications, remains a challenging problem. Recent methods adapt representations like 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) for dynamic scenes by incorporating time as the fourth dimension (4D representations). These 4D representations still suffer from aliasing artifacts, especially when generating novel views from divergent viewpoints (zoom-in/zoom-out operations). While using 3D smoothing filters like those proposed in Mip-Splatting might seem like a possible solution, they fail to account for local motion and also exhibit aliasing. To address this, we propose a motion-aware 3D smoothing filter specifically designed for 4D representations. Our approach adapts the filter strength based on local motion information, effectively mitigating aliasing without compromising rendering quality. This is achieved by estimating the joint density function of time and focal-to-depth ratio using a non-parametric estimation method. During inference, we sample from this joint distribution to determine the appropriate smoothing filter. This flexible strategy can be integrated with various 4D representations. Our evaluations on standard datasets demonstrate superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a motion-aware 3D smoothing filter for 4D dynamic scene representations (e.g., dynamic 3DGS/NeRF) to mitigate aliasing artifacts when rendering novel views from divergent viewpoints. The filter strength is adaptively adjusted based on local motion by estimating the joint density of time and focal-to-depth ratio via non-parametric estimation, and can be integrated into various 4D representations.
AI.motivation: Dynamic scene novel-view synthesis suffers from aliasing artifacts, especially for zoom-in/zoom-out operations from divergent viewpoints. Existing solutions like Mip-Splatting's 3D smoothing filters are designed for static scenes and fail to account for local motion, thus still producing aliasing in 4D representations.
AI.method: A motion-aware 3D smoothing filter is designed for 4D representations. The filter strength is adaptively determined based on local motion information. This is achieved by estimating the joint density function of time and focal-to-depth ratio using a non-parametric estimation method, and sampling from this joint distribution during inference to set the appropriate smoothing filter. The approach is representation-agnostic and can be integrated with various 4D techniques.
AI.result: Evaluations on standard benchmarks demonstrate superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods in mitigating aliasing while preserving rendering quality.
AI.conclusion: The proposed motion-aware smoothing filter effectively addresses aliasing in dynamic 4D scene representations by incorporating local motion cues, achieving better novel-view synthesis quality without compromising rendering fidelity, and offering a flexible solution applicable across different 4D representations.

title: EndoNav: Semantic-to-Geometric Grounding for Language-Guided Robotic Endoscopic Examination
summary: Minimally invasive procedures performed within confined anatomical spaces depend on continuous endoscopic visualization. Current robotic endoscope systems can stabilize or reposition an endoscope, but they do not possess relevant context to provide effective visualization assistance. We present EndoNav, an anatomy-grounded natural-language framework that translates high-level surgeon commands into autonomous endoscopic visualization behaviors within patient-specific sinonasal anatomy. Spoken surgeon commands are transcribed and interpreted by an endoscopic viewpoint agent conditioned on a patient-specific anatomical scene representation. Rather than generating robot motion directly, the viewpoint agent generates structured visualization objectives that are converted into target viewpoints and inspection trajectories, which are then executed through geometry-constrained endoscope motion planning and joint-space control. We evaluate EndoNav using a structured three-pass sinus examination across three CT-derived anatomical models. For one cadaveric specimen, autonomous visualization is compared with sinus examinations performed by two resident surgeons. EndoNav achieved mean visualization IoUs of 87.04% and 84.37% relative to the two surgeon examinations, compared with an inter-surgeon IoU of 87.44%, while recovering 92.91% and 93.20% of surgeon-observed anatomical surfaces, respectively. These results demonstrate the feasibility of grounding high-level anatomical commands into patient-specific geometric objectives and translating them into anatomically constrained robotic visualization behaviors.

AI.tldr: EndoNav is an anatomy-grounded natural-language framework for autonomous robotic endoscope visualization in sinonasal surgery. It translates high-level surgeon voice commands into structured visualization objectives via a viewpoint agent conditioned on patient-specific anatomical scenes, then executes them through geometry-constrained motion planning. Evaluated on sinus examinations across three CT-derived models, it achieved mean visualization IoUs of 87.04% and 84.37% relative to two resident surgeons (vs. inter-surgeon IoU of 87.44%), recovering over 92% of surgeon-observed surfaces.
AI.motivation: Current robotic endoscope systems can stabilize or reposition an endoscope but lack contextual understanding to provide effective visualization assistance during minimally invasive procedures in confined anatomical spaces. There is a need for systems that can interpret high-level clinical intent and autonomously execute anatomically appropriate visualization behaviors.
AI.method: EndoNav comprises four components: (1) speech transcription of surgeon commands, (2) an endoscopic viewpoint agent conditioned on a patient-specific anatomical scene representation that translates commands into structured visualization objectives (not direct robot motion), (3) conversion of these objectives into target viewpoints and inspection trajectories, and (4) geometry-constrained endoscope motion planning with joint-space control. It was evaluated using a structured three-pass sinus examination protocol across three CT-derived anatomical models, including a cadaveric comparison against two resident surgeons.
AI.result: EndoNav achieved mean visualization IoUs of 87.04% and 84.37% relative to the two resident surgeon examinations, compared to an inter-surgeon agreement IoU of 87.44%. It recovered 92.91% and 93.20% of surgeon-observed anatomical surfaces respectively, demonstrating performance approaching human inter-surgeon consistency.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate the feasibility of grounding high-level anatomical commands into patient-specific geometric objectives and translating them into anatomically constrained robotic visualization behaviors, suggesting a viable path toward context-aware autonomous endoscopic assistance in sinonasal surgery.

title: Semantic Reasoning Denoising: Correcting Language Model Reasoning with Semantic Operators
summary: Large language models can produce fluent reasoning traces whose local semantic errors propagate to an incorrect conclusion, while unconstrained self-correction may preserve, amplify, or introduce errors. Existing diffusion language models provide iterative refinement, but usually define noise as token masking or replacement rather than as errors in the reasoning process. We present Semantic Reasoning Denoising (SRD), an operatorized Markov denoising method for natural-language reasoning trajectories. SRD represents semantic noise with executable error operators that describe the error type, its location, and the corrupted and repaired propositions. Composing these operators constructs progressively noisier states. During training, the model learns to identify the semantic noise active in the current trajectory and to reconstruct the paired adjacent lower-noise state. During inference, noise-level-aware denoising repeatedly predicts an inverse operator and checks whether it is applicable, so each executed update makes a localized move toward a stable trajectory. Across six in-domain benchmarks spanning mathematics, code, knowledge, and commonsense, SRD improves the strongest same backbone baseline by 3.2 points on average. On seven cross-dataset transfer targets, it remains competitive with Llama-3-8B-Instruct and improves the strongest Qwen3-8B baseline average by 2.9 points. Analyses of noise sources, objectives, and denoising depth further show that structured semantic-noise prediction and iterative operator execution are central to the improvement.

AI.tldr: SRD is an operatorized Markov denoising method for natural-language reasoning that represents semantic noise via executable error operators, learns to identify and reverse such noise during training, and iteratively applies verified inverse operators at inference to correct reasoning trajectories, improving strong same-backbone baselines by 3.2 points on in-domain benchmarks and 2.9 points over the strongest Qwen3-8B baseline on cross-dataset transfer.
AI.motivation: LLMs produce fluent reasoning traces where local semantic errors propagate to incorrect conclusions, and unconstrained self-correction can preserve, amplify, or introduce errors. Existing diffusion language models offer iterative refinement but define noise as token masking/replacement rather than semantic errors in reasoning, motivating a denoising framework that targets reasoning-level noise specifically.
AI.method: SRD models semantic noise using executable error operators that encode the error type, location, and corrupted/repaired propositions. Composing these operators builds progressively noisier training states. The model learns to identify the active semantic noise and reconstruct the adjacent lower-noise state. At inference, noise-level-aware denoising iteratively predicts an inverse operator, verifies its applicability before execution, and applies localized updates toward a stable trajectory.
AI.result: SRD improves the strongest same-backbone baseline by 3.2 points on average across six in-domain benchmarks (mathematics, code, knowledge, commonsense). On seven cross-dataset transfer targets, it stays competitive with Llama-3-8B-Instruct and improves the strongest Qwen3-8B baseline by 2.9 points on average.
AI.conclusion: Structured semantic-noise prediction and iterative operator execution are central to performance gains, as shown by analyses of noise sources, objectives, and denoising depth. SRD demonstrates that treating reasoning errors as executable semantic operators within a Markov denoising framework is effective for improving reasoning trajectory quality.

title: Beyond Success and Failure: Length-Aware Contrastive Learning for GUI Agents
summary: Graphical User Interface (GUI) agents powered by Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown strong potential for automating tasks across diverse digital environments, where reinforcement learning (RL) has become a dominant training paradigm. However, widely used methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) suffer from reward-gradient misalignment, leading to inefficient and unstable optimization. Recent work addresses this issue by reformulating RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) as contrastive or classification-based objectives, which improve stability by eliminating problematic gradient behaviors. Despite this progress, existing contrastive RLVR methods rely primarily on outcome-level supervision and fail to capture fine-grained differences in trajectory quality within the same outcome category. In this paper, we propose Length-Aware Contrastive Learning for GUI Agents (LACL-GUI), a contrastive RLVR framework that incorporates trajectory-level quality signals into policy optimization. LACL-GUI introduces structured preferences within both successful and failed trajectories, encouraging concise successful executions and differentiating failure quality based on divergence from successful trajectories, while preserving optimization stability. Experiments on GUI agent benchmarks show that LACL-GUI provides more effective learning signals and consistently improves agent performance over prior methods, highlighting the value of trajectory-level supervision in contrastive RLVR.

AI.tldr: LACL-GUI is a contrastive RLVR framework that incorporates trajectory-level quality signals into policy optimization for GUI agents, using length-aware structured preferences to differentiate trajectory quality within success and failure categories, improving learning efficiency and stability over prior methods.
AI.motivation: Existing contrastive RLVR methods for GUI agents rely primarily on outcome-level supervision and fail to capture fine-grained differences in trajectory quality within the same outcome category, limiting the effectiveness of learning signals.
AI.method: LACL-GUI introduces structured preferences within both successful and failed trajectories, encouraging concise successful executions and differentiating failure quality based on divergence from successful trajectories, while preserving optimization stability through a contrastive RLVR formulation.
AI.result: Experiments on GUI agent benchmarks demonstrate that LACL-GUI provides more effective learning signals and consistently improves agent performance over prior methods.
AI.conclusion: The results highlight the value of trajectory-level supervision in contrastive RLVR, suggesting that fine-grained quality signals within outcome categories can substantially enhance GUI agent training.

title: Towards Bitstream-corrupted Harsh Visual Understanding: Through Bitstream Language Modeling as Robust Semantic Priors
summary: Bitstream-corrupted Harsh Visual Understanding (BcHVU) aims to understand harshly degraded videos originally decoded from a severely corrupted bitstream in real-world multimedia communication. The ill-posed nature of BcHVU poses a major challenge for existing vision models, as even subtle bitstream corruption can lead to irreversible pixel distortion and significant semantic loss. To address these challenges in BcHVU, we propose Bitstream Language Modeling as Robust Semantic Priors (BLMSP), a framework for learning and injecting bitstream-native semantic cues. Our proposed BLMSP framework learns to extract bitstream-native semantic cues by bitstream language modeling, and leverages them as priors by injecting into off-the-shelf vision models of BcHVU tasks. Specifically, we present a Video Bitstream Byte Model (VBBM) that integrates byte-level modeling and cross-codec semantic distillation, enabling it to interpret robust semantics from byte sequences in multiple corrupted bitstream formats. The learned bitstream semantics are leveraged as robust priors and fused into BcHVU model backbones for improving the quality of video restoration, captioning, and human pose estimation. To train BLMSP, we construct a large-scale multi-source Corrupted-bitstream Harsh-video Paired (CHP) dataset containing 607k corrupted bitstream segments and 287k paired harsh video clips. Extensive experimental results show that the learned bitstream priors improve video restoration, captioning, and human pose estimation by 2.51 dB in PSNR, 0.20 in CIDEr, and 0.18 in PCK@0.2 on average, respectively. These results demonstrate that corrupted bitstream can serve as robust semantic priors in solving pixel distortion and semantic loss in BcHVU.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces BLMSP, a framework that learns robust semantic priors from corrupted bitstreams via bitstream language modeling, and injects them into off-the-shelf vision models to address Bitstream-corrupted Harsh Visual Understanding (BcHVU). A Video Bitstream Byte Model (VBBM) extracts semantics from byte sequences across codecs, supported by a large-scale CHP dataset, improving video restoration, captioning, and human pose estimation.
AI.motivation: BcHVU tasks face ill-posed challenges where even subtle bitstream corruption causes irreversible pixel distortion and significant semantic loss, which existing vision models cannot handle effectively. There is a need for robust semantic priors derived directly from corrupted bitstreams to mitigate these degradations.
AI.method: BLMSP comprises two stages: (1) bitstream language modeling, where a Video Bitstream Byte Model (VBBM) performs byte-level modeling and cross-codec semantic distillation to interpret robust semantics from byte sequences across multiple corrupted bitstream formats; (2) prior injection, where learned bitstream semantics are fused into off-the-shelf vision model backbones for BcHVU tasks. Training uses a large-scale Corrupted-bitstream Harsh-video Paired (CHP) dataset with 607k corrupted bitstream segments and 287k paired harsh video clips.
AI.result: The learned bitstream priors improve video restoration by 2.51 dB in PSNR, captioning by 0.20 in CIDEr, and human pose estimation by 0.18 in PCK@0.2 on average, demonstrating that corrupted bitstreams can serve as robust semantic priors for BcHVU.
AI.conclusion: Corrupted bitstreams, rather than being discarded, contain valuable native semantic cues that can serve as robust priors to address pixel distortion and semantic loss in harsh video understanding tasks. The BLMSP framework and CHP dataset provide a practical solution for real-world multimedia communication scenarios.

title: Contact-Rich Robotic Manipulation in Construction via Zero-Shot Learning: A Diffusion Policy-Guided Adaptive Control
summary: Construction robotics and automation offer promising means of improving productivity, alleviating workforce shortages, and reducing workers' exposure to physically demanding tasks. However, reliable contact-rich robotic assembly remains challenging under tight tolerances, fabrication inaccuracies, and uncertain contact dynamics. To address this challenge, we present a framework coupling diffusion policies trained on simulation-generated pose and force/torque data with an L1-inspired adaptive controller that corrects policy-predicted actions online to compensate for unmodeled contact dynamics. We benchmark the framework against baselines in timber joinery, pipe fitting, and sequential full-scale truss assembly. It achieves 100% success on single-task assemblies and 90-100% success across sequential truss assembly subtasks, with lower, more stable contact forces than the baselines. By enabling zero-shot sim-to-real transfer for force-aware contact-rich assembly, the framework reduces costly, labor-intensive real-world data collection for policy training and advances scalable, robust automation of multistage assembly, motivating extension to broader contact-rich manipulation tasks in construction.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a framework combining diffusion policies trained on simulated pose and force/torque data with an L1-inspired adaptive controller for contact-rich robotic assembly in construction. It achieves 100% success on single-task assemblies and 90-100% on sequential truss assembly, with lower and more stable contact forces than baselines, while enabling zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
AI.motivation: Construction robotics face significant challenges in contact-rich assembly due to tight tolerances, fabrication inaccuracies, and uncertain contact dynamics. Reliable assembly remains difficult, and collecting real-world training data is costly and labor-intensive.
AI.method: The framework couples diffusion policies trained on simulation-generated pose and force/torque data with an L1-inspired adaptive controller. The controller corrects policy-predicted actions online to compensate for unmodeled contact dynamics.
AI.result: The framework was benchmarked in timber joinery, pipe fitting, and sequential full-scale truss assembly. It achieves 100% success on single-task assemblies and 90-100% success across sequential truss assembly subtasks, with lower and more stable contact forces than baseline methods.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables zero-shot sim-to-real transfer for force-aware contact-rich assembly, reduces costly real-world data collection, and advances scalable robust automation of multistage construction assembly, motivating extension to broader contact-rich manipulation tasks.

title: RAG Collapse: LLM Responses Collapse When Retrieved Documents Are Self-Authored
summary: LLM responses are based on the internet (via training or RAG), and AI is now used to generate a significant amount of content online (Paredes et al., 2026), creating the potential for a self-reinforcing feedback loop. Prior work has shown that when LLMs are recursively trained on their own output, they experience model collapse (Shumailov et al., 2024): responses become less diverse, and eventually no longer resemble the original training data. In this paper, we show that a similar collapse occurs if LLM-based AI systems retrieve references they authored using a search tool. We call this RAG collapse. We conduct extensive experiments with three types of simulations of AI systems retrieving references they generated, using three model families, and 1,019 information-seeking prompts, totaling 1,528 simulations and over one million LLM API calls, and find that 79.6% (1,216/1,528) of simulations end in collapse. Surprisingly, even a single self-authored reference can trigger collapse because the LLM disproportionately cites its own content. This self-bias persists even after controlling for reference quality.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that RAG collapse—a failure mode analogous to model collapse—occurs when LLM-based systems retrieve and cite references they themselves authored via search tools. Across 1,528 simulations with three model families and 1,019 prompts, 79.6% of simulations end in collapse, and even a single self-authored reference can trigger it due to a disproportionate self-citation bias that persists even when controlling for reference quality.
AI.motivation: As AI-generated content proliferates online, LLM systems that retrieve information through search tools may increasingly retrieve references authored by themselves or other AI systems, creating a self-reinforcing feedback loop analogous to model collapse observed in recursive training. Prior work established model collapse from training on self-generated data, but the analogous risk in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems had not been systematically studied.
AI.method: The authors conducted extensive simulations of AI systems retrieving references they generated, using three model families and 1,019 information-seeking prompts. A total of 1,528 simulations and over one million LLM API calls were executed. They also performed controlled experiments to isolate the effect of a single self-authored reference and to test whether self-citation bias persists after controlling for reference quality.
AI.result: 79.6% (1,216/1,528) of simulations ended in collapse. Notably, even a single self-authored reference can trigger RAG collapse because LLMs disproportionately cite their own content. This self-bias persists even after controlling for reference quality, indicating a systematic preference for self-citation rather than a quality-based explanation.
AI.conclusion: RAG collapse is a real and prevalent failure mode in AI-assisted search systems, driven by an inherent self-citation bias in LLMs. This poses a significant risk to information quality and diversity as AI-generated content becomes more common online, and suggests the need for safeguards in retrieval-augmented systems.

title: GameXpert-Bench: How Far Are Coding Agents from Expert Game Development?
summary: Recent large language models (LLMs) can operate as coding agents that build complete games from natural language requests. Game development is especially demanding because program logic, visual and audio content, interfaces, interaction and playability must function together in one executable artifact. Measuring this capability therefore requires evaluation of both game product and the development process. Existing benchmarks often assess the game development capabilities of LLMs by evaluating the final artifact or an isolated development stage. Our analysis of complete human-agent development trajectories identifies three stages that together span the lifecycle of game development with a coding agent: initial game generation, bug diagnosis and repair, and optimization over multiple turns. Therefore, we introduce GameXpert-Bench, which operationalizes the three lifecycle stages as three complementary benchmark tracks. GameGen evaluates complete game creation from a single request in an empty workspace. GameFix evaluates diagnosis and repair when defects are reported or left for the agent to discover. GameOpt evaluates cumulative optimization through request chains seeded by real development trajectories between users and agents. We evaluate each track using live game interaction, deterministic behavioral tests, or final product criteria with regression checks. The suite contains 97 generation tasks across 11 genres; 100 repair tasks from 50 game levels verified by humans, each with 19-27 injected bugs; and 17 optimization chains with six turns and 102 requests. Across the three tracks, current agents are more reliable at producing playable foundations and implementing explicit requirements than at discovering defects, verifying runtime behavior, and preserving functionality across changes.

AI.tldr: Introduces GameXpert-Bench, a three-track benchmark (GameGen, GameFix, GameOpt) for evaluating LLM coding agents across the complete game development lifecycle: generation, bug repair, and multi-turn optimization.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks evaluate LLM game development capabilities on either the final artifact or an isolated development stage, failing to capture the full lifecycle. Complete human-agent development trajectories reveal three stages—initial generation, bug diagnosis/repair, and optimization—that together span the game development process, motivating a more comprehensive benchmark.
AI.method: GameXpert-Bench operationalizes three lifecycle stages as three tracks: GameGen (complete game creation from a single request), GameFix (diagnosis and repair of reported or agent-discovered defects), and GameOpt (cumulative optimization through multi-turn request chains from real trajectories). Evaluation uses live game interaction, deterministic behavioral tests, and final product criteria with regression checks. The suite contains 97 generation tasks across 11 genres, 100 repair tasks across 50 human-verified levels with 19-27 injected bugs each, and 17 optimization chains with six turns and 102 requests.
AI.result: Current agents are more reliable at producing playable foundations and implementing explicit requirements than at discovering defects, verifying runtime behavior, and preserving functionality across changes.
AI.conclusion: GameXpert-Bench reveals systematic weaknesses in LLM coding agents for game development, particularly in defect discovery, runtime verification, and functionality preservation during iterative optimization, highlighting areas needing improvement for real-world game development assistance.

title: FIRM-Video: Check Before You Score for Reliable Text-to-Video Reward Modeling
summary: Reliable reward models are essential for text-to-video evaluation and alignment. However, the trade-off between evaluation accuracy and inference efficiency places high demands on the quality of training supervision. Existing approaches often rely on holistic judges with fixed rubrics or open-ended reasoning, leading to incomplete inspection, unfaithful justification, and entangled attribution. We introduce FIRM-Video, a unified checklist-driven data construction framework based on a check-before-score principle: construct dimension-specific checklists, verify each criterion against temporal visual evidence, and aggregate only verified decisions. For Instruction Following, FIRM-Video decomposes prompts into weighted atomic requirements; for World Coherence, it constructs prompt-calibrated, target-specific checks grounded in visible entities and actions; and for Perceptual Quality, it applies a generic taxonomy of visual defects. The verified criteria and scores are further transformed into natural-language analyses for end-to-end reward modeling. Subsequently, we construct FIRM-Video-90K with 88,044 dimension-specific instances from 29,348 videos, and introduce FIRM-Video-Bench with 750 point-wise human annotations across 250 videos. The Qwen3-VL-based FIRM-Video-8B achieves the best overall MAE on FIRM-Video-Bench while consistently delivering the highest VBench Total, Quality, and Semantic Scores in Best-of-8 sampling across three video generators.

AI.tldr: FIRM-Video introduces a unified checklist-driven data construction framework for text-to-video reward modeling, based on a check-before-score principle that decomposes prompts into atomic requirements, constructs temporal-visual-evidence-verified checklists across three dimensions (Instruction Following, World Coherence, Perceptual Quality), and aggregates verified decisions into natural-language analyses for end-to-end reward training. The resulting FIRM-Video-8B model achieves state-of-the-art MAE on the proposed FIRM-Video-Bench and highest VBench scores in Best-of-8 sampling across three video generators.
AI.motivation: Existing text-to-video reward models rely on holistic judges with fixed rubrics or open-ended reasoning, which suffer from incomplete inspection, unfaithful justification, and entangled attribution when balancing evaluation accuracy with inference efficiency. A more structured, verifiable supervision signal is needed.
