AI.method: FIRM-Video constructs dimension-specific checklists following a check-before-score principle: (1) Instruction Following decomposes prompts into weighted atomic requirements; (2) World Coherence builds prompt-calibrated, target-specific checks grounded in visible entities and actions; (3) Perceptual Quality applies a generic taxonomy of visual defects. Each criterion is verified against temporal visual evidence, and only verified decisions are aggregated. The verified criteria and scores are transformed into natural-language analyses for end-to-end reward model training. A dataset (FIRM-Video-90K) and benchmark (FIRM-Video-Bench) are constructed.
AI.result: FIRM-Video-90K contains 88,044 dimension-specific instances from 29,348 videos; FIRM-Video-Bench has 750 point-wise human annotations across 250 videos. The Qwen3-VL-based FIRM-Video-8B achieves the best overall MAE on FIRM-Video-Bench and consistently delivers the highest VBench Total, Quality, and Semantic Scores in Best-of-8 sampling across three video generators.
AI.conclusion: The checklist-driven, evidence-verified supervision approach effectively addresses the limitations of holistic judging, yielding a reward model that is both more accurate in evaluation and more effective for text-to-video alignment across multiple generators.

title: Meta-Ctrl: Guaranteed Plan Generation by Decoupling Syntactic and Semantic Constraints
summary: LLMs generate fluent plans for robots but routinely violate the syntactic and se8mantic constraints they must satisfy to execute, and existing remedies trade formal guarantees against plan quality: soft methods (affordance scoring, grounded decoding) give no guarantee, while symbolic planners (LLM+P) discard the LM's commonsense. We propose \textbf{Meta-Ctrl}, a constrained-decoding framework that guarantees the encoded constraints while preserving the base LM's plan quality. Meta-Ctrl introduces \emph{meta-tokens}---a compact vocabulary of grounded actions---enforcing syntax at the token level and semantics (preconditions, goals, ordering) at the action level, an exact factorization that cuts the memory of constrained decoding from over 107TB to under 2GB. With it, a small open-weight LM becomes competitive where it otherwise sits at the bottom of the leaderboard: on WAH-NL under the LoTa-Bench protocol it reaches the highest reported subgoal success rate, exceeding GPT-4's, with consistent gains across the Embodied Agent Interface. We further demonstrate it on a real tabletop robot, where every generated plan satisfies its preconditions and goals by construction. Project website: https://meta-ctrlg.github.io/.

AI.tldr: Meta-Ctrl is a constrained-decoding framework for LLM-based robot planning that guarantees syntactic and semantic constraints while preserving plan quality. It uses meta-tokens (a compact vocabulary of grounded actions) to enforce syntax at token level and semantics at action level, with an exact factorization reducing memory from over 107TB to under 2GB. A small open-weight LM becomes highly competitive, achieving the highest subgoal success rate on WAH-NL under LoTa-Bench, exceeding GPT-4.
AI.motivation: LLMs generate fluent robot plans but routinely violate syntactic and semantic constraints required for execution. Existing remedies trade formal guarantees against plan quality: soft methods (affordance scoring, grounded decoding) provide no guarantees, while symbolic planners (LLM+P) discard the LM's commonsense.
AI.method: Meta-Ctrl introduces meta-tokens, a compact vocabulary of grounded actions, to enforce syntax at the token level and semantics (preconditions, goals, ordering) at the action level. It uses an exact factorization that reduces the memory cost of constrained decoding from over 107TB to under 2GB.
AI.result: A small open-weight LM becomes competitive where it previously sat at the bottom of the leaderboard. On WAH-NL under the LoTa-Bench protocol it reaches the highest reported subgoal success rate, exceeding GPT-4, with consistent gains across the Embodied Agent Interface. It is also demonstrated on a real tabletop robot where every generated plan satisfies preconditions and goals by construction.
AI.conclusion: Meta-Ctrl demonstrates that constrained decoding can provide formal guarantees while preserving LLM plan quality, making small open-weight models competitive with (or superior to) much larger models through efficient constraint enforcement.

title: LLM assisted writing deserves empirical evaluation
summary: LLM-assisted writing is often treated as a detection problem, as it raises questions about clarity, integrity, equity, and evaluation. An analysis of 69,209 Health Informatics papers links it to more focused presentation, broader citation practices, and more globally distributed authorship. These patterns do not prove better science, but they support evaluating manuscripts by scholarly quality and accountability rather than by tool use.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes 69,209 Health Informatics papers to show that LLM-assisted writing is linked to more focused presentation, broader citation practices, and more globally distributed authorship—suggesting manuscripts should be evaluated by scholarly quality and accountability rather than by tool use.
AI.motivation: LLM-assisted writing is often treated as a detection problem, raising concerns about clarity, integrity, equity, and evaluation in academic publishing.
AI.method: Analysis of 69,209 Health Informatics papers examining patterns associated with LLM-assisted writing.
AI.result: LLM-assisted writing is associated with more focused presentation, broader citation practices, and more globally distributed authorship.
AI.conclusion: These patterns do not prove better science, but they support evaluating manuscripts by scholarly quality and accountability rather than by tool use.

title: LLM4LLM: Bridging Kernel Benchmarks and Real Deployment via Closed-Loop Agentic Optimization
summary: Large language models have become increasingly capable agents for low-level code and kernel optimization, but isolated kernel benchmarks provide only a proxy for the deployment behavior that matters in language-model inference. We identify a benchmark-to-deployment gap: candidate kernels that appear correct and fast in standalone harnesses can exhibit different performance, safety, or phase behavior after integration into a real inference workload. We introduce LLM4LLM, a deployment-aware closed-loop optimization framework that starts from a target inference script, extracts phase-aware optimization tasks, searches with an experience-guided episodic agent, and accepts patches through in-model validation. Across ten language-model inference workloads on A100 and H100 GPUs, LLM4LLM improves end-to-end latency for every evaluated model, achieving 3.91$\times$/6.98$\times$ geometric-mean speedups on A100/H100; as supporting kernel-level evidence, it also attains up to 2.745$\times$ GeoMean speedup on KernelBench Level 2.

AI.tldr: LLM4LLM is a deployment-aware closed-loop optimization framework that uses large language models to optimize code and kernels within real inference workloads, achieving 3.91x/6.98x geometric-mean end-to-end speedups on A100/H100 GPUs across ten language-model inference workloads, while also attaining up to 2.745x speedup on KernelBench Level 2.
AI.motivation: Isolated kernel benchmarks provide only a proxy for real deployment behavior in language-model inference. Candidate kernels that appear correct and fast in standalone harnesses can exhibit different performance, safety, or phase behavior once integrated into actual inference workloads, creating a benchmark-to-deployment gap.
AI.method: LLM4LLM is a deployment-aware closed-loop optimization framework that: (1) starts from a target inference script, (2) extracts phase-aware optimization tasks, (3) searches with an experience-guided episodic agent, and (4) accepts patches through in-model validation.
AI.result: Across ten language-model inference workloads on A100 and H100 GPUs, LLM4LLM improves end-to-end latency for every evaluated model, achieving 3.91x/6.98x geometric-mean speedups on A100/H100; it also attains up to 2.745x GeoMean speedup on KernelBench Level 2.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating and optimizing LLM-generated kernels in the context of real inference deployments (rather than isolated benchmarks) is both necessary and effective for achieving meaningful end-to-end performance gains.

title: BC-IHV: Conditioning the Color Space for Stable Rectified-Flow Low-Light Enhancement
summary: Low-light image enhancement (LLIE) must correct ambiguous exposure without overwriting structure already supported by the input. Generative transport can model exposure ambiguity; however, its flexibility may also alter observable geometry and chromatic content. Moreover, fixed invertible color coordinates are usually treated only as representations, although their inverse mappings reshape the RGB-domain gradients received by the enhancement network. To address these issues, we propose Structure-Anchored Rectified Flow (SA-RF), which maintains correspondence through separate chromaticity/intensity stems, a scale-matched condition pyramid, and HybridAda. HybridAda assigns location-specific retrieval to spatial cross-attention and global exposure modulation to pooled AdaLN. We further introduce BC-IHV, a learnable Box--Cox polar color space whose analytically invertible intensity mapping controls the inverse-gradient dynamic range through a single exponent. This allows the representation to balance dark-range expansion and gradient conditioning instead of adopting a fixed linear or logarithmic law. Experiments on three LOL benchmarks, blind image-quality evaluation, and cross-dataset tests demonstrate consistent reconstruction and perceptual advantages over the sota. Controlled studies further support the effectiveness of both the proposed framework and color representation.

AI.tldr: SA-RF is a low-light image enhancement framework using rectified flow with separate chromaticity/intensity stems, a scale-matched condition pyramid, and HybridAda (location-specific spatial cross-attention + pooled AdaLN). It introduces BC-IHV, a learnable Box-Cox polar color space whose invertible intensity mapping controls inverse-gradient dynamic range. Results show consistent SOTA improvements on LOL benchmarks, blind IQA, and cross-dataset tests.
AI.motivation: LLIE must correct ambiguous exposure without altering structure already present in the input. Generative transport can model exposure ambiguity but may distort geometry and chromatic content. Additionally, fixed invertible color coordinates are treated only as representations, ignoring that their inverse mappings reshape the RGB-domain gradients received by the enhancement network.
AI.method: SA-RF maintains correspondence through separate chromaticity/intensity stems, a scale-matched condition pyramid, and HybridAda—assigning location-specific retrieval to spatial cross-attention and global exposure modulation to pooled AdaLN. BC-IHV is a learnable Box-Cox polar color space whose analytically invertible intensity mapping controls the inverse-gradient dynamic range via a single exponent, balancing dark-range expansion and gradient conditioning.
AI.result: Experiments on three LOL benchmarks, blind image-quality evaluation, and cross-dataset tests demonstrate consistent reconstruction and perceptual advantages over the state-of-the-art. Controlled studies validate both the framework and the color representation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed SA-RF framework with the learnable BC-IHV color space provides a principled way to handle exposure ambiguity in LLIE while preserving structure, and achieves superior performance over existing methods.

title: BehaviorWorldGen: Closing the Loop between Action Models and World Simulators via Controllable Behavior-Aware Structured World Generation
summary: Modern driving action models are increasingly improved in a self-improvement loop, where a learned world simulator imagines future observations and the resulting data is fed back to refine the action model. However, the bottleneck of this loop lies in the simulators' inability to generate behaviorally plausible responses by surrounding agents, making generated data both unrealistic in interaction and imbalanced in distribution. We introduce BehaviorWorldGen, a framework that closes the loop between action models and world simulators through controllable behavior-aware structured world generation. Its core component is BehaviorFlow, a meta-action-conditioned traffic-flow model that injects interpretable behavior controls and jointly generates multi-agent rollouts. BehaviorFlow realizes the specified agent behaviors while allowing surrounding vehicles to respond to the ego and to one another. The resulting rollouts are rendered by a world simulator into realistic multi-view observations, which are paired with corrected interaction-aware trajectories for action-model refinement. Since BehaviorWorldGen uses structured trajectories as the interface between its modules, it is compatible with diverse action models and world simulators. Experiments on world generation, scene extrapolation, and policy refinement demonstrate consistent improvements, with the largest benefits concentrated on difficult interactive scenarios.

AI.tldr: BehaviorWorldGen is a framework that closes the loop between driving action models and world simulators through controllable behavior-aware structured world generation, using BehaviorFlow—a meta-action-conditioned traffic-flow model—to inject interpretable behavior controls and jointly generate multi-agent rollouts for realistic, interaction-aware data augmentation.
AI.motivation: Existing self-improvement loops for driving action models are bottlenecked by world simulators that fail to generate behaviorally plausible responses from surrounding agents, resulting in unrealistic interactions and imbalanced data distributions.
AI.method: BehaviorWorldGen combines BehaviorFlow (a meta-action-conditioned traffic-flow model that injects interpretable behavior controls and jointly generates multi-agent rollouts) with a world simulator that renders rollouts into realistic multi-view observations, paired with corrected interaction-aware trajectories for action-model refinement. Structured trajectories serve as the interface between modules for compatibility.
AI.result: Experiments on world generation, scene extrapolation, and policy refinement show consistent improvements, with the largest gains concentrated on difficult interactive scenarios.
AI.conclusion: BehaviorWorldGen effectively addresses simulator limitations by enabling controllable, behavior-aware world generation that produces realistic interactive data, thereby improving action-model refinement especially in challenging driving scenarios.

title: SSE-Bio: A Structured Self-Evolving Agent with Agentic Retrieval Policy for Multi-Hop Biomedical Reasoning
summary: Biomedical multi-hop question answering (QA) requires models to connect evidence across intermediate entities such as diseases, drugs, proteins, and phenotypes. Existing agents typically rely on static retrieval workflows or coarse-grained prompt rewriting, which can lead to instruction drift when reasoning procedures need to be updated. We propose SSE-Bio, a structured self-evolving agent with an agentic retrieval policy for multi-hop biomedical reasoning. Instead of globally rewriting agent instructions, SSE-Bio maintains a structured state, selectively retrieves knowledge triplets and prior templates through a trainable proxy policy, and improves its reasoning memory through fine-grained template editing. To optimise retrieval decisions, we introduce a proxy-training strategy based on group relative policy optimization, where the proxy is improved through decision-contrastive groups over alternative retrieval choices. Experiments on three biomedical multi-hop QA benchmarks show that SSE-Bio consistently outperforms existing baselines, achieving an improvement of 6.56 absolute points over the strongest self-evolving baseline on BioHopR.

AI.tldr: SSE-Bio is a structured self-evolving agent with an agentic retrieval policy for multi-hop biomedical question answering. It maintains a structured state, selectively retrieves knowledge triplets and prior templates via a trainable proxy policy (optimized with group relative policy optimization), and improves reasoning through fine-grained template editing. It outperforms baselines across three biomedical multi-hop QA benchmarks, with a 6.56 absolute point improvement over the strongest self-evolving baseline on BioHopR.
AI.motivation: Existing biomedical multi-hop QA agents rely on static retrieval workflows or coarse-grained prompt rewriting, which suffer from instruction drift when reasoning procedures need to be updated. Connecting evidence across intermediate entities (diseases, drugs, proteins, phenotypes) requires more adaptive and fine-grained retrieval control.
AI.method: SSE-Bio employs a structured state that avoids global instruction rewriting. It uses a trainable proxy policy for selective retrieval of knowledge triplets and prior templates, enabling agentic retrieval decisions. The proxy is optimized via group relative policy optimization (GRPO) using decision-contrastive groups over alternative retrieval choices. Reasoning memory is improved through fine-grained template editing.
AI.result: SSE-Bio consistently outperforms existing baselines on three biomedical multi-hop QA benchmarks, achieving a 6.56 absolute point improvement over the strongest self-evolving baseline on BioHopR.
AI.conclusion: Structured, self-evolving agents with agentic retrieval policies and proxy-based optimization provide a more effective alternative to static retrieval workflows and coarse-grained prompt rewriting for multi-hop biomedical reasoning, enabling better adaptation and instruction-update resilience.

title: AI Watchdog: Agent Interfaces for Detecting and Defending Against Manipulative Dark Patterns in AI Conversations
summary: Conversational AI increasingly shapes consequential decisions, yet users have limited support for recognizing and resisting manipulation. We present AI Watchdog, a browser-based agent interface that monitors live conversations, detects five dark-pattern categories, including sycophancy, brand bias, anthropomorphization, sneaking, and harmful generation, and alerts users when they occur. Its open-weight turn-level classifier supports independent deployment and a path toward local inference, preserving user privacy while remaining separate from the conversational AI. We evaluated AI Watchdog in a preregistered, five-condition between-subjects experiment (N = 150) comparing a no-intervention control with four configurations varying nudge timing (prebunking vs. just-in-time) and engagement mode (without vs. with cognitive forcing). Results show that participants rarely flagged manipulative turns across all conditions, and post-task awareness did not differ significantly across groups. However, just-in-time warnings without cognitive forcing were the only intervention to significantly reduce compliance with AI-steered recommendations containing dark patterns, lowering compliance from 71.7% to 53.7%, an 18 percentage-point reduction. Exploratory analyses further showed that lower misinformation susceptibility was associated with greater flagging but not lower compliance, while higher AI trust was associated with greater compliance and lower reported awareness. Together, these findings suggest that explicit recognition of conversational dark patterns and behavioral resistance to AI steering may be distinct outcomes, motivating further investigation of timely, low-friction defensive interfaces.

AI.tldr: AI Watchdog is a browser-based interface that monitors live conversational AI exchanges, detecting five dark-pattern categories (sycophancy, brand bias, anthropomorphization, sneaking, harmful generation) and alerting users. A preregistered five-condition experiment (N=150) found that only just-in-time warnings without cognitive forcing significantly reduced compliance with AI-steered recommendations (71.7% to 53.7%). Users rarely flagged manipulative turns, and explicit recognition of dark patterns and behavioral resistance appear to be distinct outcomes.
AI.motivation: Conversational AI increasingly influences consequential decisions, but users lack adequate support for recognizing and resisting manipulation embedded in AI-generated dialogue.
AI.method: Developed AI Watchdog, a browser-based agent interface with an open-weight turn-level classifier that detects five dark-pattern categories. Conducted a preregistered, five-condition between-subjects experiment (N=150) comparing a no-intervention control with four configurations varying nudge timing (prebunking vs. just-in-time) and engagement mode (without vs. with cognitive forcing).
AI.result: Participants rarely flagged manipulative turns across all conditions; post-task awareness did not differ significantly across groups. However, just-in-time warnings without cognitive forcing significantly reduced compliance with AI-steered recommendations from 71.7% to 53.7%. Lower misinformation susceptibility was associated with greater flagging but not lower compliance; higher AI trust was associated with greater compliance and lower reported awareness.
AI.conclusion: Explicit recognition of conversational dark patterns and behavioral resistance to AI steering may be distinct outcomes. Timely, low-friction defensive interfaces show promise for reducing behavioral compliance, motivating further investigation of this design direction.

title: GaussVid: Sparse-View Gaussian Splatting with 3D-Aware Video Diffusion Priors
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has achieved remarkable success in novel view synthesis; however, reconstructions under sparse views often exhibit noticeable artifacts. While recent video diffusion models provide strong spatio-temporal priors for 3DGS restoration, directly fine-tuning them for restoration is suboptimal, as they lack awareness of the underlying multi-camera geometry, resulting in multi-view inconsistencies. In this work, we propose a novel 3D-aware video restoration framework designed to enhance the quality of sparse 3DGS reconstruction. Specifically, we construct a large-scale 3DGS video dataset to enable specialized fine-tuning. To bridge the gap between 2D video generation and 3D multi-view constraints, we introduce a camera-conditioned geometric prior. By using the first and last frames as boundary anchors and encoding the corresponding camera relationships, we explicitly inject spatial structure into the video generation pipeline. This boundary-anchored, camera-aware prior guides the network toward geometrically grounded restoration that remains coherent across viewpoints. Extensive experiments show that, among video-prior restoration methods, our approach attains the best pixel- and structure-level fidelity (PSNR/SSIM) and improves multi-view consistency, while remaining competitive in perceptual quality (LPIPS).

AI.tldr: A 3D-aware video restoration framework enhances sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructions by injecting camera-conditioned geometric priors (boundary-anchored, camera-aware) into a video diffusion model fine-tuned on a large-scale 3DGS video dataset, achieving state-of-the-art pixel/structure fidelity and multi-view consistency.
AI.motivation: Sparse-view 3DGS reconstructions suffer from noticeable artifacts. Existing video diffusion models offer strong spatio-temporal priors but lack multi-camera geometry awareness, leading to multi-view inconsistencies when directly fine-tuned for restoration.
AI.method: (1) Construct a large-scale 3DGS video dataset for specialized fine-tuning; (2) Introduce a camera-conditioned geometric prior that uses first and last frames as boundary anchors encoding camera relationships; (3) Explicitly inject spatial structure into the video generation pipeline to guide geometrically grounded, multi-view-coherent restoration.
AI.result: Among video-prior restoration methods, the approach achieves the best PSNR/SSIM, improves multi-view consistency, and remains competitive in LPIPS perceptual quality.
AI.conclusion: The boundary-anchored, camera-aware prior effectively bridges 2D video generation with 3D multi-view constraints, providing a practical solution for high-quality sparse-view 3DGS restoration.

title: DreamMimic: Learning Visuomotor Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation via World Model
summary: Vision-based whole-body loco-manipulation on humanoid robots is challenging due to partial observability, contact-rich dynamics, and the difficulty of learning long-horizon behaviors from high-dimensional visual inputs. We present \href{https://github.com/DreamMimic/DreamMimic}{DreamMimic}, a framework that distills privileged teacher policies into vision-based humanoid controllers via world-model-assisted distillation. Instead of using a Dreamer-style RSSM for planning, we repurpose it to learn predictive latent dynamics that serve as both a representation space and an action-conditioned multi-step supervision signal, while exposing compact predictive features to the student policy to reduce long-term drift. Beyond standard reconstruction objectives for proprioceptive and visual observations, we add auxiliary prediction heads for privileged state, contact, object state, and reward estimation. These heads provide additional supervision related to agent--object interaction and task progress, encouraging the latent representation to retain signals that are useful for contact-rich loco-manipulation. We further introduce Performance-Conditioned Guidance (PCG), a reward-driven adaptive distillation schedule that computes performance scores for both teacher and student to dynamically balance guidance and exploration. PCG prevents both premature teacher annealing and excessive teacher interference in challenging visual settings. Experiments on OMOMO and BEHAVE show improved tracking-based loco-manipulation performance over strong vision-based baselines, without exposing online privileged interaction states to the student at deployment. Qualitative simulations further examine morphology and simulator changes. These results suggest that world models can provide a useful mechanism for stabilizing visual policy distillation in contact-rich humanoid behaviors.

AI.tldr: DreamMimic is a framework that distills privileged teacher policies into vision-based humanoid controllers using world-model-assisted distillation, repurposing a Dreamer-style latent dynamics model to provide representation and supervision signals, alongside a Performance-Conditioned Guidance schedule for adaptive distillation.
AI.motivation: Vision-based whole-body loco-manipulation on humanoid robots is challenging due to partial observability, contact-rich dynamics, and difficulty of learning long-horizon behaviors from high-dimensional visual inputs.
AI.method: The framework repurposes a Dreamer-style RSSM for predictive latent dynamics rather than planning. It serves as both a representation space and an action-conditioned multi-step supervision signal. Compact predictive features are exposed to the student policy to reduce long-term drift. Auxiliary prediction heads for privileged state, contact, object state, and reward estimation provide additional supervision. A Performance-Conditioned Guidance (PCG) schedule computes performance scores for teacher and student to dynamically balance guidance and exploration during distillation.
AI.result: Experiments on OMOMO and BEHAVE show improved tracking-based loco-manipulation performance over strong vision-based baselines, without exposing online privileged interaction states to the student at deployment. Qualitative simulations further examine morphology and simulator changes.
AI.conclusion: World models can provide a useful mechanism for stabilizing visual policy distillation in contact-rich humanoid behaviors.

title: Lexical Perturbations Disrupt LLM Reasoning: An Empirical Study of Attention Diversion
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 (Main Conference). 9 pages main text, 12 figures, 20 tables
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve strong reasoning performance, but their robustness to realistic lexical corruption remains poorly understood. We evaluate four open-weight instruction-tuned models and frontier models across four reasoning benchmarks under keyboard noise, character swaps, and filler insertion. Character-level perturbations substantially degrade accuracy, especially on multi-step reasoning tasks, while filler insertion has little effect. We trace this asymmetry to Attention Diversion: lexical corruption fragments subword tokenization, and the resulting fragments attract disproportionate attention mass, concentrated in middle and final transformer layers. Length-matched controls confirm that fragmentation, not prompt length, drives the loss. A factorial intervention then shows why the damage is hard to undo: fragmentation corrupts token content and attention allocation together, and the two are coupled. Restoring clean attention while the content remains corrupted is actively harmful, restoring content alone is insufficient, and only restoring both recovers a substantial share of the gap. This coupling explains why inference-time strategies, including chain-of-thought prompting, spell-checking, self-repair, and stronger repair models, fail to consistently recover performance: each addresses one channel at a time. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Jiaqian-Janelle/Attention-Diversion

AI.tldr: LLMs are vulnerable to lexical corruption (keyboard noise, character swaps, filler insertion), which degrades reasoning performance primarily on multi-step tasks. The damage stems from "Attention Diversion"—fragmented subword tokenization attracts disproportionate attention mass in middle/final layers—and is hard to undo because token content corruption and attention misallocation are coupled; fixing only one is insufficient or even harmful.
AI.motivation: LLMs achieve strong reasoning but their robustness to realistic lexical corruption is poorly understood; the paper aims to characterize degradation patterns and explain why inference-time repair strategies fail.
AI.method: Evaluates four open-weight instruction-tuned models and frontier models on four reasoning benchmarks under keyboard noise, character swaps, and filler insertion; uses length-matched controls, attention analysis (tracing Attention Diversion across layers), and factorial interventions (restoring content and/or attention independently) to test causal coupling.
AI.result: Character-level perturbations significantly reduce accuracy, especially on multi-step reasoning; filler insertion has little effect. Fragmentation (not length) drives loss. Restoring attention alone while content is corrupted is harmful; restoring content alone is insufficient; only restoring both recovers substantial performance. Inference-time strategies (CoT, spell-checking, self-repair, stronger repair models) fail because they address only one channel at a time.
AI.conclusion: Lexical corruption degrades LLM reasoning through a coupled mechanism of token content corruption and attention diversion, explaining the failure of single-channel repair strategies and pointing toward the need for interventions that jointly restore both.

title: MemGuard: Persisting Verifier Signals for LLM-Agent Memory Governance
summary: LLM agents are moving from single-prompt use to long task streams in which reusable memory becomes a core capability for terminal, software-engineering, and web tasks. Such memory is useful only when stored experience remains reliable across hundreds of interactions, but two failure modes break that assumption in practice. The first is unreliable admission: failed trajectories,accidental successes, and misleading observations enter memory because they appear relevant, then mislead later decisions. The second is memory drift: long-running banks accumulate duplicate, stale, and conflicting records that retrieval alone cannot repair. MemGuard's key distinction is to treat verifier output not as a one-shot filter, but as persistent lifecycle metadata. It converts multi-criteria score-token verification into reward, confidence, label, and uncertainty descriptors that are attached to every candidate before activation and reused during retrieval, conflict resolution, summarization, and archival. We evaluate MemGuard on Terminal-Bench 2.0, SWE-Bench Verified, WebArena, and Mind2Web across four backbones, comparing against four memory baselines plus a verifier-only control under matched runtime budgets. Averaged over five seeds, MemGuard achieves the best success metric and lowest average steps in all 16 backbone-benchmark settings, improving over ReasoningBank, the strongest prior baseline among the memory methods we evaluate, with a largest gain of 7.9 success-rate points on WebArena, 5.6 step-success-rate points on Mind2Web, and 2.4-3.5 points on terminal and software-engineering benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/whyyyyy123/MemGuard.

AI.tldr: MemGuard is a memory management framework for LLM agents that treats verifier output as persistent lifecycle metadata, converting multi-criteria score-token verification into reward, confidence, label, and uncertainty descriptors attached to each memory candidate. It addresses two key failure modes—unreliable admission (bad trajectories entering memory) and memory drift (duplicate/stale/conflicting records accumulating)—by reusing verifier descriptors during retrieval, conflict resolution, summarization, and archival. Evaluated on Terminal-Bench 2.0, SWE-Bench Verified, WebArena, and Mind2Web across four backbones, MemGuard outperforms baselines in all 16 backbone-benchmark settings, with gains up to 7.9 success-rate points.
AI.motivation: LLM agents increasingly need reusable memory for long task streams (terminal, software-engineering, web tasks), but existing memory systems fail due to unreliable admission (failed or misleading trajectories entering memory) and memory drift (duplicate, stale, conflicting records accumulating that retrieval cannot repair).
AI.method: MemGuard treats verifier output as persistent lifecycle metadata rather than a one-shot filter. It converts multi-criteria score-token verification into reward, confidence, label, and uncertainty descriptors attached to every candidate before activation, and reuses these descriptors during retrieval, conflict resolution, summarization, and archival to maintain memory reliability.
AI.result: On Terminal-Bench 2.0, SWE-Bench Verified, WebArena, and Mind2Web across four backbones, MemGuard achieves the best success metric and lowest average steps in all 16 backbone-benchmark settings, averaged over five seeds. It improves over ReasoningBank (strongest prior memory baseline) with gains of 7.9 success-rate points on WebArena, 5.6 step-success-rate points on Mind2Web, and 2.4-3.5 points on terminal/software-engineering benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Persistent verifier-derived lifecycle metadata is a principled and effective approach to maintaining reliable agent memory, significantly outperforming prior memory baselines and verifier-only controls across diverse benchmarks and backbones without consuming additional runtime budget.

title: Frame-Level Evaluation in Weakly Supervised Video Anomaly Detection Mostly Measures Video-Level Ranking
summary: Weakly supervised video anomaly detectors are trained with video-level labels but are commonly evaluated as temporal localizers using Micro-AUROC or AP over pooled test frames. Because these metrics compare frames from different videos, a detector can score well by separating videos without accurately ordering moments within them. We exactly decompose Micro-AUROC by video identity into Within-AUROC for temporal ordering within videos and Cross-AUROC for comparisons across videos. Across ShanghaiTech, XD-Violence, and UCF-Crime, only 0.071-0.388% of comparisons between anomalous and normal frames occur within the same video. When both classes remain distributed across V videos, this share decreases as O(1/V), a benchmark property we call temporal dilution. We train anomaly video binary classifiers under the same video-level supervision and repeat each video score across all frames. These video-constant outputs reach 81.40-97.18 Micro-AUROC despite having no within-video variation. Across 72 controlled runs, replacing every frame score with its video mean preserves a median 98.6% of the Micro-AUROC margin above chance. The same empirical pattern holds for author-released outputs and for XD-Violence under its official AP evaluation. A detector can therefore achieve a high pooled score even when it assigns the same score to every moment within each video.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a critical flaw in evaluating weakly supervised video anomaly detectors: common pooled metrics like Micro-AUROC and AP are dominated by cross-video comparisons rather than within-video temporal ordering. The authors show that video-constant outputs (same score for all frames in a video) can achieve high scores, demonstrating that these benchmarks do not meaningfully measure temporal localization ability.
AI.motivation: Weakly supervised video anomaly detectors are trained with video-level labels but evaluated as temporal localizers using pooled frame-level metrics. The authors hypothesize that these metrics may not actually measure temporal ordering within videos, since they compare frames across different videos where the class distribution is heavily skewed.
AI.method: The paper decomposes Micro-AUROC by video identity into Within-AUROC (temporal ordering within videos) and Cross-AUROC (comparisons across videos). They quantify the share of same-video comparisons across multiple benchmarks, derive the temporal dilution property O(1/V), and run controlled experiments training video-level classifiers with video-constant frame outputs.
AI.result: Only 0.071-0.388% of anomalous-normal frame comparisons occur within the same video on ShanghaiTech, XD-Violence, and UCF-Crime. Video-constant outputs achieve 81.40-97.18 Micro-AUROC with no within-video variation. Replacing frame scores with video means preserves a median 98.6% of the margin above chance across 72 runs. The pattern holds for author-released outputs and official AP evaluation on XD-Violence.
AI.conclusion: Pooled frame-level metrics (Micro-AUROC, AP) are insufficient for evaluating temporal anomaly localization because they are dominated by cross-video separation. A detector can achieve high scores without any within-video temporal discriminative ability, questioning the validity of standard evaluation protocols in this area.

title: Beyond Instance Slots: Semantically Rich World Models for Physical Interaction Planning
summary: World models for physical interaction are typically trained to predict future observations or latent features; however, a planning-oriented model must answer a fundamentally different question: whether a candidate action produces a task-consistent future while preserving essential relations.Monolithic state representations obscure the underlying entities, while standard instance-level object slots merely identify \emph{what} is present without specifying \emph{what role} each entity plays in the task context. To bridge this gap, we present the Semantically Rich World Model (SR-WM), a task-conditioned world model structured around five functional roles: gripper, target, goal, relation, and phase.Within SR-WM, a visual entity encoder extracts soft entity hypotheses from pretrained patch features, allowing segmentation masks to serve as optional proposal priors without mandating them as required state representations or inference inputs.A role binder subsequently maps these hypotheses to task-specific roles, while an action-conditioned dynamics model predicts role transitions alongside fine-grained semantics, including grasp/contact, predicate establishment, relation preservation, fixture state, and phase change.Crucially, this unified role state grounds downstream multi-candidate action generation, stage-aware reranking, and violation-aware suffix resampling.Our comprehensive evaluation protocol spans all four LIBERO simulation suites, cross-suite transfer, perception diagnostics, and action-sensitivity analysis.Ultimately, this formulation transforms object-centric prediction into a semantic interface linking visual dynamics with planning-oriented decision making.

AI.tldr: SR-WM is a task-conditioned world model structured around five functional roles (gripper, target, goal, relation, phase) that transforms object-centric prediction into a semantic interface for planning-oriented decision making in physical manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Standard world models predict future observations or latent features, but planning requires answering whether a candidate action produces a task-consistent future. Monolithic state representations and instance-level object slots fail to capture the role each entity plays in the task context.
AI.method: SR-WM uses a visual entity encoder to extract soft entity hypotheses from pretrained patch features (with optional segmentation mask priors), a role binder to map hypotheses to task-specific roles, and an action-conditioned dynamics model predicting role transitions alongside fine-grained semantics (grasp/contact, predicate establishment, relation preservation, fixture state, phase change). This role state grounds multi-candidate action generation, stage-aware reranking, and violation-aware suffix resampling.
AI.result: Evaluated comprehensively across all four LIBERO simulation suites, cross-suite transfer, perception diagnostics, and action-sensitivity analysis.
AI.conclusion: The role-structured formulation transforms object-centric prediction into a semantic interface linking visual dynamics with planning-oriented decision making.

title: The Collaboration Tax: How Much LLM Multi-Agent Systems Pay to Coordinate
summary: Multi-agent systems built from large language models are deployed widely, yet how much performance is lost when two LLMs must coordinate rather than act alone remains unclear. We formulate the collaboration tax as the team-decentralisation loss of a two-player cooperative game with private information, with two propositions characterising its sign and its equivalence to a max-superadditivity violation. We operationalise this definition on 32 solo-tractable tasks grouped by source of grounding friction and measure it on 11 models from 7 providers. The tax is structured along two no-exception axes: a category ordering across every model and a monotonic decrease with capability. The proximate mechanism is not a reasoning deficit but a four-stage conversational cascade in which agents make ungrounded claims, fail to query the partner, skip integrating both views, and accept the answer without re-derivation. The tax is mechanically predictable from conversation features and partly tractable: a prompt intervention targeting all four stages closes a substantial fraction of the gap, with the dominant bottleneck differing across categories. In heterogeneous pairs the tax is pulled toward the stronger partner rather than the additive midpoint, empirically realising the max-superadditivity violation predicted by our framework. Together these results recast collaboration in LLM systems as a measurable, predictable, and partly tractable cost.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes the "collaboration tax" in LLM multi-agent systems—the performance loss when two LLMs coordinate rather than act alone—as a team-decentralisation loss in a two-player cooperative game. It characterizes this tax via two propositions, measures it across 32 tasks, 11 models, and 7 providers, reveals structured axes (category ordering, capability monotonicity), identifies a four-stage conversational cascade as the proximate mechanism rather than reasoning deficits, shows the tax is predictable and partly tractable via a prompt intervention, and demonstrates that heterogeneous pairs are pulled toward the stronger partner (max-superadditivity violation).
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems are widely deployed, yet the cost of coordination between LLMs relative to solo performance remains unmeasured and poorly understood. The paper aims to formalize and empirically quantify this collaboration tax to better understand where and why performance is lost in LLM collaboration.
AI.method: The authors formulate the collaboration tax as the team-decentralisation loss of a two-player cooperative game with private information, deriving two propositions on its sign and equivalence to a max-superadditivity violation. They operationalize this on 32 solo-tractable tasks grouped by source of grounding friction, measuring across 11 models from 7 providers. They analyze the proximate conversational mechanism via a four-stage cascade, test a prompt intervention targeting all four stages, and examine heterogeneous pairs.
AI.result: The tax is structured along two no-exception axes: a category ordering consistent across every model and a monotonic decrease with capability. The proximate mechanism is a four-stage conversational cascade (ungrounded claims, failure to query, skipping integration, accepting answers without re-derivation), not a reasoning deficit. The tax is mechanically predictable from conversation features and partly tractable—the prompt intervention closes a substantial fraction of the gap. In heterogeneous pairs, the tax is pulled toward the stronger partner, empirically realizing the predicted max-superadditivity violation.
AI.conclusion: Collaboration in LLM systems can be recast as a measurable, predictable, and partly tractable cost. The findings provide a formal and empirical foundation for understanding and mitigating coordination losses in multi-agent LLM deployments.

title: HiMA-MDD: A Hierarchical Multi-Agent Harness for Interpretable Multimodal Depression Detection in Clinical Interviews
summary: Depression assessment from multimodal clinical interviews requires integrating dispersed evidence from multiple symptoms into a coherent PHQ-8 profile. This process is hierarchical: relevant evidence is often sparse and context-dependent within local question-answer exchanges, multiple exchanges jointly support symptom-level judgments, and the final assessment depends on the coherence of the complete symptom profile. Existing LLM systems either process interviews holistically or distribute work across generic agent roles; neither design necessarily provides an explicit orchestration mechanism that coordinates evidence access, item-score authority, bounded feedback, and state recording across these levels. To address this gap, we introduce HiMA-MDD, a hierarchical multi-agent harness that aligns this assessment hierarchy with three agent layers. After non-agentic preprocessing constructs context-preserving multimodal QA units, Layer 1 identifies candidate QA-to-item relations and supports bounded item-grounded evidence routing. Layer 2 assigns symptom groups to operational factor specialists, with one specialist responsible for each provisional item score. Layer 3 audits the complete provisional profile, requests at most one round of targeted revision, and reconstructs the verified PHQ-8 profile. This layered design naturally yields a Hierarchical Evidence Trace, preserves all intermediate evidence, judgments, and revisions for auditability. The final item scores then deterministically produce the total score and screening decision. Using Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct as the harness backbone, our experiments on E-DAIC demonstrate that HiMA-MDD outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: HiMA-MDD is a hierarchical multi-agent framework for depression assessment from multimodal clinical interviews that explicitly orchestrates evidence access, item-score authority, bounded feedback, and state recording across three agent layers, outperforming SOTA methods on E-DAIC.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM systems for depression assessment either process interviews holistically or use generic agent roles, lacking an explicit orchestration mechanism that coordinates evidence access, item-score authority, bounded feedback, and state recording across the hierarchical levels of the assessment process (local QA exchanges → symptom-level judgments → global PHQ-8 profile).
AI.method: HiMA-MDD introduces a three-layer hierarchical multi-agent harness aligned with the assessment hierarchy. Non-agentic preprocessing constructs context-preserving multimodal QA units. Layer 1 identifies candidate QA-to-item relations and performs bounded item-grounded evidence routing. Layer 2 assigns symptom groups to operational factor specialists, each responsible for a provisional item score. Layer 3 audits the complete provisional profile, requests at most one round of targeted revision, and reconstructs the verified PHQ-8 profile. The design produces a Hierarchical Evidence Trace preserving all intermediate evidence for auditability, with final item scores deterministically yielding total score and screening decision. The harness uses Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct as the backbone.
AI.result: Experiments on the E-DAIC dataset demonstrate that HiMA-MDD outperforms compared state-of-the-art methods for depression assessment from multimodal clinical interviews.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchical multi-agent orchestration design with explicit evidence routing, specialized item-score authority, bounded revision, and auditable state tracing provides an effective approach for coherent PHQ-8 profiling from multimodal clinical interviews.

title: GuardPaint:SpeculativeSafetyDecodingforText-to-ImageGeneration
summary:
Text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models offer powerful visual generation, but their controllability creates a critical safety challenge: adversarial prompts can steer the denoising trajectory toward policy-violating content such as explicit nudity or graphic violence. Existing safeguards mostly act before generation through prompt filtering or after generation through image classification, leaving the diffusion process itself unguarded and often yielding only refusal rather than safe visual repair.
  We introduce GuardPaint, a speculative decoding framework for safe T2I generation that intervenes inside the diffusion trajectory without modifying the base model. A lightweight auditor monitors intermediate images, localizes unsafe regions, and triggers surgical inpainting repair only where needed. Candidate repairs are generated by a policy-aligned inpainter and selected through a guarded tournament that accepts edits only when they improve policy compliance while preserving prompt fidelity and perceptual quality.
  Across five jailbreak families SneakPrompt, MMA, PGJ, DACA, and RABell and UNet/flow-matching models including SD~1.5, SDXL, SD~3.5, and FLUX.1-dev. GuardPaint reduces attack success and harmful generations with minimal degradation to image quality, prompt fidelity, and benign behavior.
  Content warning: This paper contains examples involving nudity and violence that some readers may find disturbing, distressing, or offensive.

AI.tldr: GuardPaint is a speculative decoding framework that safely intervenes inside the diffusion trajectory of text-to-image models by using a lightweight auditor to detect and surgically repair policy-violating content, without modifying the base model.
AI.motivation: Adversarial prompts can steer T2I diffusion models toward policy-violating content, and existing safeguards only act before (prompt filtering) or after (image classification) generation, leaving the diffusion process itself unguarded and typically producing refusals rather than safe visual repair.
AI.method: GuardPaint operates inside the diffusion trajectory without modifying the base model. A lightweight auditor monitors intermediate images, localizes unsafe regions, and triggers surgical inpainting repairs only in those regions. Candidate repairs are generated by a policy-aligned inpainter and selected via a guarded tournament that accepts edits only when they improve policy compliance while preserving prompt fidelity and perceptual quality.
AI.result: Across five jailbreak families (SneakPrompt, MMA, PGJ, DACA, RABell) and UNet/flow-matching models (SD 1.5, SDXL, SD 3.5, FLUX.1-dev), GuardPaint reduces attack success and harmful generations with minimal degradation to image quality, prompt fidelity, and benign behavior.
AI.conclusion: GuardPaint demonstrates that in-generation safety intervention via speculative decoding and surgical inpainting is an effective approach to safeguarding T2I diffusion models, achieving both policy compliance and preservation of benign generation quality without modifying the base model.

title: TONAV: Task-Oriented Navigation and Action-Velocity Chunk Learning for Articulated Object Quadrupedal Mobile Manipulation
comment: The project page is at https://haochen611.github.io/TONAV
summary: Quadruped mobile manipulation requires two tightly coupled capabilities: reaching manipulation-ready configurations and maintaining stable contact throughout articulated-object interaction. However, existing methods often terminate navigation near the target, leaving a gap between reachability and manipulation readiness, while tracking lag, motion jitter, and contact instability limit continuous interaction. To address these challenges, we present TONAV, a unified framework integrating task-oriented navigation with action-velocity chunk learning. First, we introduce a position-velocity-coupled teleoperation framework that explicitly captures motion dynamics to improve master-follower consistency and collect smooth, temporally consistent demonstrations. Next, task-oriented navigation leverages vision-language reasoning to decompose high-level instructions into executable subgoals and adaptively refine the robot base toward a manipulation-ready configuration. Finally, action-velocity chunk learning jointly models joint positions and their temporal transitions under velocity supervision, enabling smooth and stable sustained-contact manipulation. Real-world experiments across diverse articulated-object tasks demonstrate that TONAV achieves higher success rates in both task-oriented navigation and complete mobile manipulation, mitigating the navigation-manipulation gap and improving continuous-contact interaction. The project page is at https://haochen611.github.io/TONAV.

AI.tldr: TONAV is a unified framework for quadruped mobile manipulation that integrates task-oriented navigation with action-velocity chunk learning, addressing the gap between navigation and manipulation readiness and improving continuous-contact interaction during articulated-object tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing quadruped mobile manipulation methods terminate navigation near targets, creating a gap between reachability and manipulation readiness, while tracking lag, motion jitter, and contact instability limit continuous interaction during articulated-object manipulation.
AI.method: TONAV consists of three key components: (1) a position-velocity-coupled teleoperation framework that captures motion dynamics for smooth, temporally consistent demonstrations; (2) task-oriented navigation using vision-language reasoning to decompose high-level instructions into executable subgoals and refine the robot base to a manipulation-ready configuration; (3) action-velocity chunk learning that jointly models joint positions and temporal transitions under velocity supervision for smooth sustained-contact manipulation.
AI.result: Real-world experiments across diverse articulated-object tasks demonstrate that TONAV achieves higher success rates in both task-oriented navigation and complete mobile manipulation, mitigating the navigation-manipulation gap and improving continuous-contact interaction.
AI.conclusion: TONAV effectively unifies task-oriented navigation and action-velocity chunk learning to enable smoother, more reliable quadruped mobile manipulation of articulated objects, with code and project details publicly available.

title: How Agents Represent Humans: Human-Directed Stereotypes in an Open Agent Social Network
summary: LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed in persistent social environments, where generated claims can be posted, replied to, remembered, and reused. We study human-directed stereotypes on Moltbook, an open agent-native social platform, asking how agents construct humans as a social category. For this human-target analysis, we introduce an annotation framework with four evaluative dimensions---morality, friendliness, competence, and autonomy---and a second-stage subtype scheme for descriptive \textit{other} attributions. We find that competence dominates human-directed evaluations, while many \textit{other} attributions describe humans as epistemic, cultural, or embodied subjects. We further examine how these human representations appear in human--agent narrative contexts and platform-level circulation. As an auxiliary comparison, we analyze agent-internal community feedback through behavioral host affinity. Rather than reproducing the stable insider--outsider rejection often observed in human online communities, Moltbook feedback patterns are better explained by exposure, author visibility, and content selection. These findings suggest that bias in agent societies should be studied not only as isolated model output, but also as a discourse process.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes how LLM-based agents on an open agent-native social platform called Moltbook construct humans as a social category, using an annotation framework with four evaluative dimensions (morality, friendliness, competence, autonomy) and a subtype scheme for "other" attributions. It finds competence dominates human-directed evaluations, examines how these representations circulate in agent narratives and platform-level discourse, and shows that feedback patterns are better explained by exposure/visibility/content selection than rigid insider-outsider dynamics.
AI.motivation: As LLM-based agents are deployed in persistent social environments where their claims can propagate and be remembered, it becomes critical to understand how these agents stereotype and construct human groups as social categories—an underexplored form of bias in agent societies.
AI.method: The authors study human-directed stereotypes on Moltbook using a novel annotation framework with four evaluative dimensions (morality, friendliness, competence, autonomy) plus a second-stage subtype scheme for descriptive "other" attributions. They analyze human-agent narrative contexts, platform-level circulation of human representations, and agent-internal community feedback via behavioral host affinity.
AI.result: Competence dominates human-directed evaluations from agents, while many "other" attributions characterize humans as epistemic, cultural, or embodied subjects. Moltbook feedback patterns are better explained by exposure, author visibility, and content selection rather than the stable insider-outsider rejection dynamics typical of human online communities.
AI.conclusion: Bias in agent societies should be studied not merely as isolated model output but as a discourse process, given how stereotypes circulate and are shaped by platform-level dynamics in persistent social environments.

title: From Solver Feedback to Faithful Plans: Multi-Role Reinforcement Learning for Symbolic Planning
summary: Reliable planning requires converting natural-language instructions into executable symbolic specifications, yet large language models remain brittle without costly PDDL annotations and may exploit solver success in semantically unfaithful ways. We study how to learn faithful natural-language-to-PDDL formalization using only solver feedback, without human-written demonstrations. We propose a solvergrounded multi-role reinforcement learning framework where a single language model acts as an Actor, Judge, and Editor for generation, verification, and repair. The Actor proposes PDDL specifications, the Judge provides a solver-calibrated quality signal, and the Editor performs bounded diagnostic-conditioned refinement. On PlanBench, our method improves average success from 35.5% for LLM+P to 70.8%, achieves 66.3% faithful success, and reduces semantic drift to 6.4%. These results show that organizing solver feedback into generation, verification, and repair roles enables more scalable and faithful annotation-free symbolic planning

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a solver-grounded multi-role reinforcement learning framework where a single language model acts as Actor, Judge, and Editor to learn faithful natural-language-to-PDDL formalization using only solver feedback, achieving 70.8% average success (up from 35.5%) and 66.3% faithful success on PlanBench.
AI.motivation: Large language models are brittle at converting natural-language instructions into executable PDDL specifications without costly PDDL annotations, and may exploit solver success in semantically unfaithful ways, necessitating a method to learn faithful formalization without human demonstrations.
AI.method: A solver-grounded multi-role reinforcement learning framework where a single language model plays three roles: the Actor proposes PDDL specifications, the Judge provides a solver-calibrated quality signal, and the Editor performs bounded diagnostic-conditioned refinement for generation, verification, and repair.
AI.result: On PlanBench, the method improves average success from 35.5% (LLM+P baseline) to 70.8%, achieves 66.3% faithful success, and reduces semantic drift to 6.4%.
AI.conclusion: Organizing solver feedback into generation, verification, and repair roles enables more scalable and faithful annotation-free symbolic planning.

title: ViSMoE: Visual-Aware Sparse Mixture-of-Experts for Embodied Referring Expression Grounding
summary: Embodied Referring Expression Grounding is the task of enabling an agent to navigate in real environments and to localize a remote object based on natural language instructions. In this scenario, the agent needs to select one view for navigation at each step and identify a specific object among all candidate objects at the destination. However, most of the previous approaches fail to distinguish between views and objects, instead processing them using the vanilla vision encoder, which results in ambiguous representations of both views and objects. To address the above issues, we propose ViSMoE, which equips sparse Mixture-of-Experts with a visual-aware routing policy for the embodied agent. This framework processes different types of visual information specifically, resulting in discriminative visual representations for both views and objects. Experimental results on REVERIE and SOON datasets demonstrate that ViSMoE outperforms the previous state-of-the-art methods, showing the superiority of our proposed method.

AI.tldr: ViSMoE introduces a sparse Mixture-of-Experts framework with a visual-aware routing policy for Embodied Referring Expression Grounding, enabling distinct representations for views and objects. It achieves state-of-the-art results on REVERIE and SOON benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Previous approaches treat views and objects with the same vanilla vision encoder, producing ambiguous and indistinguishable representations for both types of visual information, which hurts grounding performance.
AI.method: ViSMoE equips a sparse Mixture-of-Experts network with a visual-aware routing policy, allowing different types of visual information (views and objects) to be processed by specialized expert modules, yielding discriminative visual representations.
AI.result: ViSMoE outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods on both REVERIE and SOON datasets.
AI.conclusion: The proposed visual-aware routing strategy in a sparse MoE framework effectively addresses the representation ambiguity between views and objects in embodied referring expression grounding, demonstrating superior performance.

title: The Imitator Game: Benchmarking Robot Imitative Ability Beyond Action Prediction
summary: Humans imitate at the level of intent: given a demonstration, we infer its goal and carry it out with whatever tools, objects, and layouts are at hand. Current robot policies instead learn observation-to-action mappings from visual inputs and language instructions, without explicitly inferring the demonstrated task. Learning from human video thus remains largely trajectory-level: models can replay motions in near-identical scenes, but still struggle to imitate what the demonstrator intends rather than merely what they do. We introduce The Imitator Game, a four-level benchmark (L0-L3) that progressively widens the gap between the human demonstration and the robot's own scene, isolating where trajectory replay ceases to suffice and task understanding becomes necessary. We pair it with IG-10K, the largest environment-aligned paired human-robot dataset to date and the only one instantiated across all four levels in both real and simulated settings (20,000+ paired episodes, 50+ tasks, 6 domains), and Imitator Arena, an open platform for blind A/B human evaluation. Across nine state-of-the-art models, performance is stable from L0 to L2 but collapses at L3, identifying functional substitution - achieving the same intent through a different object affordance - as the decisive barrier to intent-level imitation. Human-video-conditioned models outperform caption-conditioned ones, yet every model falls below 13% zero-shot success on unseen tasks; fine-tuning IG-10K-pretrained models with only $10$ paired human-robot demonstrations yields large gains that grow with pretraining scale. The project website and access to Imitator Arena are available at https://imitator-game.github.io.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces The Imitator Game, a four-level benchmark (L0-L3) for evaluating intent-level imitation in robots, along with IG-10K (the largest environment-aligned paired human-robot dataset with 20,000+ episodes across 50+ tasks) and Imitator Arena (an open platform for blind A/B human evaluation). Evaluations show performance collapses at L3 where functional substitution is required, and all models fall below 13% zero-shot success on unseen tasks, though fine-tuning with just 10 paired demonstrations yields large gains.
AI.motivation: Current robot policies learn observation-to-action mappings from visual inputs and language instructions without explicitly inferring the demonstrated task intent. Learning from human video remains trajectory-level—models can replay motions in near-identical scenes but struggle to imitate what the demonstrator intends rather than merely what they do. There is a need for a benchmark that isolates where trajectory replay ceases to suffice and task understanding becomes necessary.
AI.method: The paper proposes a four-level benchmark (L0-L3) that progressively widens the gap between human demonstration and robot scenes to isolate the point where trajectory replay fails. It introduces IG-10K, the largest environment-aligned paired human-robot dataset instantiated across all four levels in both real and simulated settings, and Imitator Arena, an open platform for blind A/B human evaluation. Nine state-of-the-art models are evaluated across these levels.
AI.result: Models perform stably from L0 to L2 but experience a performance collapse at L3, identifying functional substitution (achieving the same intent through a different object affordance) as the decisive barrier to intent-level imitation. Human-video-conditioned models outperform caption-conditioned ones, yet every model scores below 13% zero-shot success on unseen tasks. Fine-tuning IG-10K-pretrained models with only 10 paired human-robot demonstrations yields large gains that scale with pretraining size.
AI.conclusion: Functional substitution is the critical unmet challenge for intent-level imitation in robots. Current models cannot generalize intent across different object affordances at scale, but the combination of large-scale paired data (IG-10K) and minimal fine-tuning with paired demonstrations provides a promising path forward. The proposed benchmark, dataset, and evaluation platform serve as a foundation for future progress toward true intent-level imitation.

title: Dual-Layer Agentic Memory with Fast Write Routing and Slow Consolidation
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents operate in dynamic environments where knowledge continuously evolves. Existing memory systems typically treat external memory as a monotonically growing repository, inevitably leading to retrieval degradation and increasing computational costs over time. We argue that the core challenge is not retrieval alone, but managing the knowledge lifecycle: deciding what to externalize, update, or ultimately internalize. Inspired by Complementary Learning Systems (CLS) theory in neuroscience, we propose Dual-Layer Agentic Memory, a framework that shifts memory management to the write phase through cost-aware epistemic routing and periodic parametric consolidation. Incoming information is categorized as non-write, write-new, or write-update, and routed through a small-to-large model cascade that minimizes routing overhead while filtering redundant memories. A subsequent write-back phase selectively consolidates high-value external memories into model parameters via supervised fine-tuning. Experiments demonstrate the dual efficiency of our approach: a 1.7B/8B cascade prunes up to 68% of redundant external memory while escalating fewer than 50% of inputs, yet retains over 98% of the downstream QA Exact Match (EM) achieved by an exhaustive retention baseline. We further show that periodic consolidation successfully internalizes external knowledge, allowing the router to adaptively suppress redundant writes as the model's epistemic boundaries evolve. Overall, our framework presents a unified paradigm for agent memory: selective externalization followed by selective internalization. Code and dataset will be released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: Proposes Dual-Layer Agentic Memory, a CLS-inspired framework for LLM agent memory that manages the knowledge lifecycle through cost-aware epistemic routing (categorizing inputs as non-write, write-new, or write-update) and periodic parametric consolidation via supervised fine-tuning, achieving up to 68% external memory pruning while retaining over 98% of downstream QA EM.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent memory systems treat external memory as a monotonically growing repository, leading to retrieval degradation and increasing computational costs over time. The paper argues the core challenge is managing the full knowledge lifecycle—what to externalize, update, or internalize—rather than retrieval alone.
AI.method: The framework shifts memory management to the write phase using cost-aware epistemic routing with a small-to-large model cascade (1.7B/8B) that categorizes incoming information as non-write, write-new, or write-update and filters redundant memories while minimizing routing overhead. A subsequent write-back phase periodically consolidates high-value external memories into model parameters via supervised fine-tuning, drawing inspiration from Complementary Learning Systems (CLS) theory.
AI.result: The 1.7B/8B cascade prunes up to 68% of redundant external memory while escalating fewer than 50% of inputs, yet retains over 98% of the downstream QA Exact Match achieved by an exhaustive retention baseline. Periodic consolidation successfully internalizes external knowledge, allowing the router to adaptively suppress redundant writes as the model's epistemic boundaries evolve.
AI.conclusion: The framework presents a unified paradigm for agent memory: selective externalization followed by selective internalization, demonstrating dual efficiency in both memory pruning and retention performance.

title: Training Needs Trustworthy Worlds: Verified Synthetic Web Environments for Agent Learning
summary: Web agents promise to automate complex digital workflows, but their training remains limited by synthetic environments that look plausible while hiding broken links, inconsistent states, or infeasible tasks. We address the gap between scalable environment generation and trustworthy agent learning by constructing synthetic web environments that are executable, auditable, and grounded in backend state. Our framework represents each generated website as a structured scaffold of pages, navigation links, database records, state-change markers, and task constraints, then verifies and repairs structural, semantic, consistency, and feasibility defects before policy training. During interaction, ordinary UI transitions are executed deterministically, while persistent backend updates are invoked only through validated state-change markers, enabling dense rewards compiled from verified task-progress predicates. Across 500 synthetic environments spanning six domains, our method reduces task-blocking defects and improves feasible-task rate from 48.6% to 94.8%, while producing stronger PPO policies and improving transfer to WebArena, WebShop, and MiniWoB++ without LLM calls at evaluation time. These results show that verified synthetic environments can serve as a scalable and reliable training substrate for compact web agents, shifting synthetic webagent learning from surface-level plausibility toward executable, state-grounded supervision.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a framework for constructing synthetic web environments that are executable, auditable, and grounded in backend state, addressing the gap between scalable environment generation and trustworthy agent learning. The framework represents websites as structured scaffolds (pages, navigation links, database records, state-change markers, task constraints) and verifies/repairs defects before training. Across 500 synthetic environments in six domains, it reduces task-blocking defects, improves feasible-task rate from 48.6% to 94.8%, and produces stronger PPO policies with improved transfer to WebArena, WebShop, and MiniWoB++ without LLM calls at evaluation time.
AI.motivation: Web agents are typically trained in synthetic environments that look plausible superficially but contain broken links, inconsistent states, or infeasible tasks, limiting their usefulness for trustworthy agent learning. There is a gap between scalable environment generation and reliable, executable supervision.
AI.method: The framework constructs synthetic websites as structured scaffolds comprising pages, navigation links, database records, state-change markers, and task constraints. It verifies and repairs structural, semantic, consistency, and feasibility defects before policy training. During interaction, UI transitions are executed deterministically, and persistent backend updates only occur through validated state-change markers. Dense rewards are compiled from verified task-progress predicates.
AI.result: Across 500 synthetic environments spanning six domains, the method reduces task-blocking defects, improves feasible-task rate from 48.6% to 94.8%, produces stronger PPO policies, and improves transfer to WebArena, WebShop, and MiniWoB++, all without LLM calls at evaluation time.
AI.conclusion: Verified synthetic environments can serve as a scalable and reliable training substrate for compact web agents, shifting synthetic web agent learning from surface-level plausibility toward executable, state-grounded supervision.

title: Region-Weighted Losses and Model Fusion for Cross-Modal PET Attenuation Correction
comment: ntkhoa team submission for BIC-MAC MICCAI26 challenge (https://www.codabench.org/competitions/12555/#/results-tab)
summary: We describe our approach to the Big Cross-Modal Attenuation Correction (BIC-MAC) challenge, which asks for a pseudo-CT in Hounsfield Units to be synthesized from Non-Attenuation-Corrected PET (NAC-PET), DIXON MRI and a topogram, and scores both the pseudo-CT and the Attenuation-Corrected PET (AC-PET) reconstructed from it. Three ideas carried our improvements over the organizers' 3D U-Net baseline. The loss matters more than the architecture: we compute the $L_1$ error in the Carney attenuation-coefficient ($μ$) space that the CT metric itself uses, weighted by anatomical region. Only once that loss was in place did the unregistered DIXON MRI work as extra input channels. A fixed convex combination of two independently trained models then beat both of its members on three of the four metrics and ranks first overall on the public validation leaderboard.

AI.tldr: The paper describes a winning approach for the BIC-MAC challenge that synthesizes pseudo-CT from NAC-PET, DIXON MRI, and topogram for PET attenuation correction. Key contributions include using a loss function computed in the attenuation-coefficient space weighted by anatomical region (more important than architecture), leveraging unregistered DIXON MRI as extra input channels once the loss was fixed, and ensembling two independently trained models via fixed convex combination, achieving first place on the public validation leaderboard.
AI.motivation: The BIC-MAC challenge requires synthesizing pseudo-CT in Hounsfield Units from NAC-PET, DIXON MRI, and topogram data for PET attenuation correction. The authors aimed to improve upon the organizers' 3D U-Net baseline by identifying techniques that significantly boost performance across both pseudo-CT and reconstructed AC-PET metrics.
AI.method: The approach builds on a 3D U-Net architecture with three key innovations: (1) computing L1 loss in the Carney attenuation-coefficient (μ) space (the same space used by the CT evaluation metric) with anatomical-region weighting, rather than in Hounsfield Units; (2) incorporating unregistered DIXON MRI as additional input channels, which only became beneficial once the μ-space loss was in place; (3) ensembling two independently trained models using a fixed convex combination.
AI.result: The fixed convex combination of two independently trained models outperformed both individual members on three of the four evaluation metrics and ranked first overall on the public validation leaderboard.
AI.conclusion: The choice of loss function in the appropriate physical space (attenuation-coefficient space with regional weighting) matters more than architectural changes for pseudo-CT synthesis. Proper loss design also enabled effective use of unregistered MRI inputs, and simple model ensembling provided additional gains, collectively yielding a state-of-the-art result for the challenge.

title: GCS-Bridging: Restoring Connectivity of Disconnected Convex Sets for Graph-of-Convex-Sets Motion Planning
summary: Graph-of-Convex-Sets (GCS)-based trajectory optimization represents collision-free regions in configuration space as a finite collection of convex sets and directly performs collision-free trajectory planning over these sets, substantially simplifying the planning process. However, existing GCS-based trajectory planning methods generally assume sufficient connectivity among the convex regions and do not explicitly address cases in which the start and goal regions belong to different connected components of the initial GCS map.
