To address this limitation, we propose GCS-Bridging, which reconnects disconnected convex regions through collision-free point paths followed by convex region inflation, thereby recovering the feasibility of otherwise disconnected GCS planning problems. Extensive simulations across multiple IRIS-related algorithms and scenarios demonstrate that GCS-Bridging restores missing start-to-goal connectivity in the initial GCS map with a 99.8% success rate. In addition, a hardware experiment on a single-arm Franka platform in a real-world scenario with initially disconnected start and goal regions validates the effectiveness of the proposed method in practical motion planning. Project website: https://zhouxk1997.github.io/GCS_Bridging/

AI.tldr: The paper proposes GCS-Bridging, a method to reconnect disconnected convex regions in Graph-of-Convex-Sets (GCS) trajectory optimization by generating collision-free point paths followed by convex region inflation, achieving 99.8% success in restoring connectivity and validated on a real Franka robot.
AI.motivation: Existing GCS-based trajectory planning methods assume sufficient connectivity among convex regions and fail when the start and goal regions lie in different connected components of the initial GCS map, limiting the practical applicability of GCS-based planning.
AI.method: GCS-Bridging reconnects disconnected convex regions by generating collision-free point paths between them, followed by convex region inflation to create connectivity, thereby recovering feasibility of previously disconnected GCS planning problems.
AI.result: Extensive simulations across multiple IRIS-related algorithms and scenarios show a 99.8% success rate in restoring missing start-to-goal connectivity. A hardware experiment on a single-arm Franka platform in a real-world scenario with initially disconnected start and goal regions validates the method's practical effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: GCS-Bridging effectively addresses the connectivity limitation in GCS-based trajectory optimization by bridging disconnected convex regions, enabling practical motion planning in scenarios where start and goal regions are initially disconnected.

title: Grounded Normative Rule Generation with Structured Search
summary: Normative rules like institutional charters and workplace policies must be both human-readable and operationally verifiable against actual environment records. However, current language generation and structured-output benchmarks primarily reward surface fluency or schema compliance, leaving operational grounding weakly tested. This creates a critical vulnerability where standard language models generate plausible-sounding policies that fail during enforcement because they rely on unavailable data logs or misaligned scopes. To address this challenge, we formalize the problem as Grounded Normative Rule Synthesis (GNRS) and introduce GNRS-Search, a framework that utilizes Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling to optimize a discrete, five-slot And-Or Graph (AOG). By explicitly decoupling intermediate operational structure from final prose generation, this method isolates executable feasibility from writing style and allows rule failures to be localized prior to surface realization. We evaluate our approach on GNRS-Bench, a benchmark spanning 116 controlled goals across eight scene families, and RealCharter-Bench, which evaluates transfer to 53 real-derived policy tasks with hidden source clauses. GNRS-Search raises average rubric quality from 68.8% to 81.0% and ranks first under a disclosed executable composite metric, while systematic slot interventions confirm that performance gains stem from robust operational logic rather than rhetorical tuning. Ultimately, by transforming automated rule drafting into an inspectable search problem, this work provides a foundational paradigm for deploying verifiable and compliance-ready personal agents within regulated environments.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces GNRS-Search, a framework that uses MCMC sampling to optimize discrete And-Or Graphs for Grounded Normative Rule Synthesis (GNRS), ensuring generated policies are not only fluent but operationally verifiable against environment records. The method improves rubric quality from 68.8% to 81.0% on two benchmarks and decouples executable feasibility from prose generation.
AI.motivation: Current language generation and structured-output benchmarks reward surface fluency or schema compliance but fail to test operational grounding. Standard language models generate plausible-sounding policies that fail during enforcement because they rely on unavailable data logs or misaligned scopes, creating a critical vulnerability in regulated environments.
AI.method: The authors formalize GNRS and introduce GNRS-Search, which uses MCMC sampling to optimize a discrete five-slot And-Or Graph (AOG). The approach decouples intermediate operational structure from final prose generation, enabling executable feasibility to be isolated from writing style and rule failures to be localized before surface realization. Evaluation uses GNRS-Bench (116 controlled goals across eight scene families) and RealCharter-Bench (53 real-derived policy tasks with hidden source clauses).
AI.result: GNRS-Search raises average rubric quality from 68.8% to 81.0%, ranks first under a disclosed executable composite metric, and systematic slot interventions confirm performance gains stem from robust operational logic rather than rhetorical tuning.
AI.conclusion: By transforming automated rule drafting into an inspectable search problem, this work provides a foundational paradigm for deploying verifiable and compliance-ready personal agents within regulated environments.

title: Consistency Is Not Coherence: Orientation Search for Certified Alignments Between 4D Defence Upper Ontologies
comment: 14 pages. Long paper accepted at the Ontology Matching 2026 workshop (OM 2026), co-located with ISWC 2026. Code and data: https://github.com/fabio-rovai/ies-hqdm-crosswalk
summary: We align three upper ontologies that sit under UK and NATO defence data infrastructure: the Information Exchange Standard (IES), the Higher Quality Data Model (HQDM) that underpins the National Digital Twin, and Basic Formal Ontology (BFO). No public alignment between IES and HQDM existed. Promoting a hand-curated 17-correspondence crosswalk to OWL and reasoning over the complete merged ontologies with HermiT produces three results that we believe matter beyond this pair.

AI.tldr: The paper aligns three upper ontologies underlying UK and NATO defence data infrastructure (IES, HQDM, and BFO), introduces a hand-curated 17-correspondence crosswalk from IES to HQDM in OWL, and uses the HermiT reasoner over the fully merged ontologies, yielding three generalizable findings.
AI.motivation: No public alignment existed between IES and HQDM, both of which are foundational to defence and digital twin data infrastructures. The authors aim to bridge this interoperability gap and also surface insights that generalize beyond this specific ontology pair.
AI.method: A hand-curated crosswalk of 17 correspondences between IES and HQDM is promoted to OWL, after which the complete merged ontologies (IES, HQDM, and BFO) are subjected to automated reasoning with the HermiT reasoner.
AI.result: Reasoning over the merged ontologies produces three results that the authors believe are significant beyond this particular ontology pair.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates a practical approach to upper ontology alignment with OWL-based reasoning, yielding findings with broader implications for ontology interoperability in defence and digital twin contexts.

title: VIG: Visual Information Gain as a Reward Signal for Multimodal Chain-of-Thought Compression
summary: Multimodal large reasoning models often rely on long Chain-of-Thought (CoT) traces in which a substantial fraction of tokens, such as repeated visual descriptions, self-reflection, and other visually-disengaged filler, inflate inference cost without contributing to the answer. Existing CoT compression methods optimize output length but never measure whether a reasoning token is actually grounded in the image. We propose \textbf{VIG} (Visual Information Gain), an information-theoretic GRPO reward that scores each reasoning token by how much the image reduces its predictive uncertainty. VIG is computed online from two forward passes of the same policy, one with and one without the image, so no reference chains, external annotations, or auxiliary reward models are needed. Across six main multimodal reasoning benchmarks and three Qwen3-VL-Thinking model sizes (2B/4B/8B), plus an additional R1-Onevision-Bench evaluation on 8B, VIG consistently improves the accuracy--efficiency trade-off, supporting our central claim: \emph{efficient multimodal reasoning emerges from raising visual information density, where every reasoning token earns its place by anchoring to the image, rather than from imposing a length budget.} Our source code is available at https://github.com/chaser682/vig.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes VIG (Visual Information Gain), an information-theoretic GRPO reward that scores each reasoning token by how much the image reduces its predictive uncertainty, computed online via two forward passes (with and without the image). This improves accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across multimodal reasoning benchmarks by increasing visual information density rather than imposing length budgets.
AI.motivation: Multimodal large reasoning models generate long CoT traces with many tokens not grounded in the image (repeated visual descriptions, self-reflection, filler), inflating inference cost without contributing to accuracy. Existing compression methods optimize output length but never measure whether a reasoning token is actually visually grounded.
AI.method: VIG is an information-theoretic GRPO reward that measures how much the image reduces predictive uncertainty for each reasoning token. It is computed online from two forward passes of the same policy—one with the image and one without—requiring no reference chains, external annotations, or auxiliary reward models.
AI.result: Across six main multimodal reasoning benchmarks and three Qwen3-VL-Thinking model sizes (2B/4B/8B), plus R1-Onevision-Bench evaluation on 8B, VIG consistently improves the accuracy-efficiency trade-off compared to alternatives.
AI.conclusion: Efficient multimodal reasoning emerges from raising visual information density—where every reasoning token earns its place by anchoring to the image—rather than from imposing a length budget.

title: MotionDLO: Hybrid Event- and Frame-Based Tracking of Deformable Linear Objects
summary: Reliably tracking moving deformable linear objects (DLOs) while simultaneously ensuring robustness, accuracy, and temporally consistent state estimation remains a fundamental challenge in robot perception. We introduce MotionDLO, a real-time tracking framework specifically designed to overcome these limitations in temporal continuity and latency. The method exploits the high temporal resolution and sparsity of event-based cameras and combines segmentation with the Coherent Point Drift (CPD) algorithm under the principles of Motion Coherence Theory. This integration enables temporally consistent shape estimation while maintaining a low computational overhead. Existing event-based tracking methods are typically computationally efficient but exhibit reduced accuracy compared to frame-based approaches, or alternatively compromise event sparsity to achieve competitive performance. To resolve this trade-off, we propose a hybrid event- and frame-based tracking architecture that preserves the complementary strengths of both sensing modalities. The event stream ensures high-frequency motion updates, while frame-based information stabilizes spatial accuracy and object identity. We demonstrate that the proposed framework reliably associates DLO instances across video sequences, enabling robust perception for robotic manipulation tasks. Experimental results validate real-time performance at 12 ms update rates and accurate shape tracking with an point-to-curve error as measurement of accuracy of up to 0.43 mm, supporting dynamic path adaptation during manipulation. The source code and demonstration datasets are publicly available.

AI.tldr: MotionDLO is a real-time tracking framework for deformable linear objects that combines event-based and frame-based camera data using segmentation and Coherent Point Drift (CPD) under Motion Coherence Theory, achieving 12 ms update rates and 0.43 mm point-to-curve tracking accuracy.
AI.motivation: Tracking moving deformable linear objects (DLOs) reliably while ensuring robustness, accuracy, and temporally consistent state estimation remains a fundamental challenge. Existing event-based methods are computationally efficient but less accurate than frame-based approaches, while frame-based methods sacrifice sparsity or speed.
AI.method: The method exploits the high temporal resolution and sparsity of event-based cameras, combining segmentation with Coherent Point Drift (CPD) under Motion Coherence Theory. A hybrid event- and frame-based tracking architecture is proposed: the event stream provides high-frequency motion updates, while frame-based information stabilizes spatial accuracy and object identity.
AI.result: The framework reliably associates DLO instances across video sequences, validates real-time performance at 12 ms update rates, and achieves accurate shape tracking with a point-to-curve error of up to 0.43 mm, supporting dynamic path adaptation during manipulation.
AI.conclusion: MotionDLO resolves the accuracy-versus-efficiency trade-off in DLO tracking by leveraging complementary strengths of event and frame-based sensing, enabling robust perception for robotic manipulation tasks. Source code and demonstration datasets are publicly available.

title: Whitewashing Hate, Smearing Harmless Content: Annotator-Style Rebuttal Attacks on LLM-Based Moderation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for hate speech moderation, often within human--AI workflows in which reviewers provide feedback before a final decision. Such feedback introduces two manipulation directions: whitewashing hateful content as normal and smearing normal content as hateful. This study examines the susceptibility of initially correct model judgments to annotator-style rebuttals and analyzes whether attack effectiveness differs across manipulation directions. We introduce a rejudge protocol that extends direct contradiction with decision-boundary perturbations and adversarial rationales. Experiments with multiple LLMs on two hate speech datasets show that annotator-style rebuttals substantially degrade moderation performance, with stronger effects in multi-turn settings. The results further reveal stable, model-specific asymmetries between whitewashing and smearing across attack configurations, indicating distinct directional vulnerability patterns. Explicit reasoning prompts and defensive instructions reduce these effects but do not eliminate them. These findings highlight the need for direction-aware safeguards and dedicated feedback-robustness evaluation in human--AI moderation workflows.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how annotator-style rebuttals can manipulate LLM-based hate speech moderation by either whitewashing hateful content as normal or smearing normal content as hateful. Using a rejudge protocol with decision-boundary perturbations and adversarial rationales, experiments show that such rebuttals substantially degrade moderation performance, with stable, model-specific asymmetries between the two manipulation directions. Defensive instructions reduce but do not eliminate these effects.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in human-AI hate speech moderation workflows where reviewers provide feedback before final decisions. This feedback introduces two manipulation directions (whitewashing and smearing) that could compromise initially correct model judgments, yet systematic analysis of these vulnerabilities is lacking.
AI.method: The authors propose a rejudge protocol that extends direct contradiction with decision-boundary perturbations and adversarial rationales. They conduct experiments with multiple LLMs on two hate speech datasets, comparing attack effectiveness across whitewashing versus smearing directions and across single- versus multi-turn settings.
AI.result: Annotator-style rebuttals substantially degrade moderation performance, with stronger effects in multi-turn settings. Results show stable, model-specific asymmetries between whitewashing and smearing across attack configurations, revealing distinct directional vulnerability patterns. Explicit reasoning prompts and defensive instructions mitigate but do not eliminate these effects.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight the need for direction-aware safeguards and dedicated feedback-robustness evaluation in human-AI moderation workflows, as current defensive measures are insufficient to fully counteract annotator-style manipulation.

title: ESCRAG-R1: Retrieval-Augmented Reinforcement Learning for Emotional Support Conversation
summary: Emotional Support Conversation (ESC) systems aim to provide holistic support by balancing professional therapeutic competence with natural empathy. However, existing methods struggle to simultaneously achieve structured, stage-aware reasoning and seamless empathy-expertise alignment, often resulting in an artificial splicing of clinical strategies and generic reassurance. To overcome these limitations, we propose ESCRAG-R1, a unified framework that integrates retrieval-based psychological guidance into Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). By incorporating retrieval into the reinforcement learning loop, ESCRAG-R1 transforms external knowledge into a robust learning signal that stimulates explicit internal reasoning prior to generation and fundamentally reshapes the model's internal policy. To provide the reliable supervision required for this optimization, we construct ESC-Preference, a high-quality dataset based on a Client--Counselor--Judge evaluation framework that delivers precise, empathy-aware reward signals. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ESCRAG-R1 significantly outperforms existing baselines by mitigating superficial splicing and realizing a natural integration of professional guidance and empathetic expression. Code and datasets are released at https://github.com/Matcha-Liu/ESCRAG-R1.

AI.tldr: ESCRAG-R1 is a unified framework for Emotional Support Conversation that integrates retrieval-based psychological guidance into Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), using a newly constructed ESC-Preference dataset with a Client-Counselor-Judge evaluation framework to provide precise, empathy-aware reward signals. The framework outperforms existing baselines by achieving natural integration of professional guidance and empathetic expression rather than superficial splicing of the two.
AI.motivation: Existing Emotional Support Conversation systems struggle to simultaneously achieve structured, stage-aware reasoning and seamless empathy-expertise alignment. Current methods often result in artificial splicing of clinical strategies and generic reassurance, failing to holistically balance professional therapeutic competence with natural empathy.
AI.method: ESCRAG-R1 integrates retrieval-based psychological guidance into Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Retrieval is incorporated into the reinforcement learning loop, transforming external knowledge into a robust learning signal that stimulates explicit internal reasoning before generation and fundamentally reshapes the model's internal policy. The framework uses ESC-Preference, a high-quality dataset built on a Client-Counselor-Judge evaluation framework, to provide reliable, empathy-aware reward signals for supervision.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that ESCRAG-R1 significantly outperforms existing baselines by mitigating superficial splicing and realizing a natural integration of professional guidance and empathetic expression.
AI.conclusion: The proposed ESCRAG-R1 framework successfully addresses the long-standing challenge of balancing therapeutic competence with empathy in ESC systems, demonstrating that retrieval-augmented reinforcement learning offers an effective pathway to unified, stage-aware, and empathy-aligned conversational support.

title: Pixel-Space Diffusion via Observation Operators
summary: Pixel-space diffusion models directly model image distributions but remain difficult to optimize. Recent methods alleviate this challenge through target reparameterization, while still relying on a fixed clean-image target throughout denoising. Through empirical analysis, we identify a scale-time mismatch: image structures become predictable from coarse to fine as noise decreases, whereas existing models are forced to predict the full image even under high noise, resulting in low-SNR gradients that hinder optimization. To resolve this mismatch, we propose Observation Operator Diffusion, a unified framework that aligns both the supervision trajectory and feature refinement with the intrinsic recovery order of image structures. Specifically, we replace fixed full-image supervision along the standard flow path with a time-indexed observation trajectory that evolves from coarse structures to the full image during denoising. This trajectory is instantiated with a family of Gaussian-Lanczos operators at varying observation scales, yielding a path-consistent training objective. We further introduce GL-CoDA, a decoder that injects scale-specific Gaussian-Lanczos observations across decoding stages for coarse-to-fine feature refinement. Extensive experiments show that the proposed approach converges substantially faster while consistently improving generation quality, achieving an FID of 1.52 on ImageNet-256.

AI.tldr: A unified framework called Observation Operator Diffusion (OOD) that aligns supervision and feature refinement with the coarse-to-fine recovery order of image structures, using Gaussian-Lanczos observation operators, achieving FID 1.52 on ImageNet-256 with faster convergence.
AI.motivation: Pixel-space diffusion models are difficult to optimize due to a scale-time mismatch: existing models force prediction of the full image even under high noise, producing low-SNR gradients that hinder optimization, despite image structures becoming predictable from coarse to fine as noise decreases.
AI.method: Proposes Observation Operator Diffusion that (1) replaces fixed full-image supervision with a time-indexed observation trajectory evolving from coarse structures to full image via Gaussian-Lanczos operators, forming a path-consistent training objective, and (2) introduces GL-CoDA, a decoder that injects scale-specific Gaussian-Lanczos observations across decoding stages for coarse-to-fine feature refinement.
AI.result: The approach converges substantially faster while consistently improving generation quality, achieving an FID of 1.52 on ImageNet-256.
AI.conclusion: Aligning supervision and feature refinement with the natural coarse-to-fine recovery order of images resolves the scale-time mismatch in pixel-space diffusion models, leading to faster convergence and better generation quality.

title: LD4WAM: Learning Latent Dynamics from Human Videos for World Action Models
summary: Human video is playing an increasingly central role in training World Action Models (WAMs), owing to its diversity and low collection cost relative to teleoperated robot data. However, most WAMs learn from such video only by predicting pixel-level future frames, giving dynamics that are not directly actionable, whereas motion retargeting recovers directly actionable actions but leaves a large visual gap across embodiments. We therefore propose motion-aligned latent dynamics as an embodiment-agnostic representation to bridge video priors and low-level actions. We further present LD4WAM, which pairs a Latent Dynamics Model trained with semantic reconstruction and real motion alignment with a World Dynamics Action Model built as a mixture-of-transformers (MoT), which preserves full future-video generation and uses learnable queries to distill these latent dynamics from generated futures for action conditioning. Pretrained on our curated unified dataset of over 5{,}000 hours of human and robot data, LD4WAM performs strongly in RoboTwin simulation and on real robots equipped with both grippers and dexterous hands, while generalizing well to unseen objects and backgrounds.

AI.tldr: LD4WAM proposes motion-aligned latent dynamics as an embodiment-agnostic representation to bridge human video priors and robot actions, using a Latent Dynamics Model paired with a mixture-of-transformers World Action Model. Pretrained on 5,000+ hours of human and robot data, it achieves strong performance in simulation and on real robots with grippers and dexterous hands.
AI.motivation: Human video is abundant and cheap for training World Action Models (WAMs), but existing approaches either predict pixel-level futures (not directly actionable) or use motion retargeting (leaves large visual gaps across embodiments). A unified representation is needed to bridge video priors and low-level actions.
AI.method: The paper introduces motion-aligned latent dynamics as an embodiment-agnostic representation. LD4WAM pairs a Latent Dynamics Model trained with semantic reconstruction and real motion alignment with a World Dynamics Action Model built as a mixture-of-transformers (MoT). The MoT preserves full future-video generation and uses learnable queries to distill latent dynamics from generated futures for action conditioning.
AI.result: Pretrained on a curated unified dataset of over 5,000 hours of human and robot data, LD4WAM performs strongly in RoboTwin simulation and on real robots equipped with both grippers and dexterous hands, while generalizing well to unseen objects and backgrounds.
AI.conclusion: Motion-aligned latent dynamics effectively bridge the gap between human video priors and actionable robot control, enabling strong cross-embodiment generalization from large-scale human video data.

title: Improving Few-Step Language Flows with Untied Self-Conditioning
summary: Flow-matching language models refine all token positions in parallel and can trade sampling steps for latency, yet generation quality still degrades sharply with few sampling steps. We trace a source of this degradation to a train--inference mismatch in previous-prediction self-conditioning: during training, the self-conditioning input is computed from the current noisy state with no intervening solver step; during sampling, the solver folds the previous prediction into the latent before that same prediction reappears as the explicit self-conditioning input. This coupling, absent during training, creates redundancy that grows with step width. We show that the mismatch degrades both the self-conditioning input and the solver update, and derive a correction for each from the model's own structure. From the frozen projection weights we identify directions along which the self-conditioning input is redundant with the latent and dampen them; from the solver's integration structure we derive that a step-average prediction is needed and approximate it from prediction history, with scale set by offline trajectory statistics. The resulting sampler, Untied Self-Conditioning, requires no retraining and uses one evaluation per step. At 8 sampling steps on LangFlow, it reduces OpenWebText generative perplexity from $531$ to~$62$ ($8.6\times$); under an adapted Arena-Hard-Auto~v2 protocol, its outputs are preferred in $96\%$ of pairwise comparisons. On ELF-B it reduces generative perplexity from $71$ to~$43$. Improvements hold from 8 to 256 sampling steps.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a train-inference mismatch in previous-prediction self-conditioning for flow-matching language models, where sampling couples the previous prediction into the latent via the solver step while training does not. The authors derive two corrections (dampening redundant self-conditioning directions from projection weights, and using a step-average prediction approximated from history) to create "Untied Self-Conditioning," a training-free sampler that uses one evaluation per step, dramatically improving generation quality at few sampling steps (e.g., perplexity from 531 to 62 at 8 steps on LangFlow).
AI.motivation: Flow-matching language models can trade sampling steps for latency but generation quality degrades sharply with few sampling steps. The authors aim to trace and fix the source of this degradation.
AI.method: The authors identify a train-inference mismatch: during training, self-conditioning input is computed from the current noisy state without an intervening solver step, while during sampling the solver folds the previous prediction into the latent before it reappears as explicit self-conditioning input, creating redundancy that grows with step width. They derive two corrections from the model's own structure: (1) dampen redundant self-conditioning directions using frozen projection weights, and (2) approximate a step-average prediction from prediction history with scale set by offline trajectory statistics. This yields the "Untied Self-Conditioning" sampler requiring no retraining and one evaluation per step.
AI.result: At 8 sampling steps on LangFlow, the method reduces OpenWebText generative perplexity from 531 to 62 (8.6x). Under an adapted Arena-Hard-Auto v2 protocol, outputs are preferred in 96% of pairwise comparisons. On ELF-B, generative perplexity drops from 71 to 43. Improvements hold across 8 to 256 sampling steps.
AI.conclusion: The train-inference mismatch in self-conditioning is a key source of quality degradation at few sampling steps, and the derived training-free corrections (Untied Self-Conditioning) substantially improve generation quality while maintaining the latency benefits of parallel token refinement.

title: GuardianBench: A Same-Scene Instruction-Contrastive Benchmark for Latent Contextual Risk in Embodied AI
summary: In embodied AI, safety risk can be latent: a benign instruction and a safe scene become hazardous only when composed. Prior work has advanced embodied safety by varying visual contexts or evaluating execution-time dynamics, but the complementary axis of fixing the scene and varying only the instruction remains underexplored. We introduce GuardianBench, an instruction-contrastive benchmark grounded in international safety standards that isolates this latent contextual risk through 3,024 instruction-scene examples organized as same-scene Safe/Unsafe contrastive pairs across various hazard categories. Benchmarking state-of-the-art vision-language models (VLMs) reveals instruction-insensitive verdicts: models disproportionately approve both instructions under a given scene; across the primary models, average pair accuracy is only 24.1%. Our systematic rationale audit localizes the dominant failure: models fail to bind the instruction-relevant cues that differentiate safe from unsafe compositions. As a post-training case study, Verdict Log-Odds Supervision (VLOS), a lightweight verdict-level objective, substantially improves performance on open-weight backbones. Together, our latent contextual risk task formulation, standards-grounded contrastive benchmark construction, pair-level and rationale-level failure diagnosis, and benchmark-enabled verdict calibration establish GuardianBench as a controlled evaluation suite for exposing and improving safety reasoning over instruction-scene compositions under latent contextual risk.

AI.tldr: GuardianBench is an instruction-contrastive safety benchmark for embodied AI, comprising 3,024 instruction-scene examples as same-scene Safe/Unsafe pairs grounded in international safety standards. It exposes that state-of-the-art VLMs have instruction-insensitive verdicts (pair accuracy only 24.1%), failing to bind instruction-relevant cues that differentiate safe from unsafe compositions. A lightweight post-training objective (VLOS) substantially improves performance on open-weight models.
AI.motivation: Prior embodied safety benchmarks vary visual contexts or evaluate execution-time dynamics but ignore the complementary axis of fixing the scene and varying only the instruction. This leaves latent contextual risk—where a benign instruction and safe scene become hazardous only when composed—underexplored.
AI.method: The paper introduces GuardianBench, a benchmark constructed through same-scene Safe/Unsafe instruction-contrastive pairs across hazard categories, grounded in international safety standards. It benchmarks state-of-the-art VLMs on pair-level accuracy, performs a systematic rationale audit to localize failure modes, and introduces Verdict Log-Odds Supervision (VLOS), a lightweight verdict-level post-training objective.
AI.result: State-of-the-art VLMs achieve only 24.1% average pair accuracy, revealing instruction-insensitive verdicts where models disproportionately approve both instructions under a given scene. The rationale audit shows models fail to bind instruction-relevant cues. VLOS substantially improves performance on open-weight backbones.
AI.conclusion: GuardianBench establishes a controlled evaluation suite for exposing and improving safety reasoning over instruction-scene compositions under latent contextual risk, encompassing the latent risk task formulation, standards-grounded contrastive benchmark construction, pair-level and rationale-level diagnosis, and benchmark-enabled verdict calibration.

title: A Scalable Vector Graphics Latent Space
comment: Accepted at The 19th European Conference on Computer Vision -- ECCV 2026
summary: Scalable Vector Graphics are a fundamental medium for resolution-independent visual content, yet the deep learning community lacks a continuous, dense, and invertible latent space for vector representations, the kind of foundational building block that Variational Autoencoders and their descendants have long provided for raster images. We introduce SLS (SVG Latent Space), a Transformer-based autoencoder that learns compact dense representations of individual SVG paths, the atomic visual elements from which any SVG image can be composed. By modeling SVG commands, coordinate data, and visual properties within a unified BPE-based token vocabulary, SLS learns fixed-size latent representations that jointly capture structure and appearance, and can be decoded back into valid, style-consistent SVG paths with high fidelity. The resulting embedding space is robust, invertible, and structured: embeddings lie on a unit hypersphere, enabling efficient similarity search, composition, and downstream conditioning through simple vector-space operations. Finally, we demonstrate that SLS generalizes across diverse tasks reducing their FLOPs by over 150 times compared to token-based approaches, and establishing a general-purpose latent foundation for vector graphics research.

AI.tldr: SLS is a Transformer-based autoencoder that creates a continuous, dense, invertible latent space for individual SVG paths, enabling efficient vector graphics representation and downstream tasks with over 150x FLOP reduction compared to token-based approaches.
AI.motivation: The deep learning community lacks a continuous, dense, and invertible latent space for vector graphics representations—the kind of foundational building block that VAEs have long provided for raster images. This gap limits efficient processing and manipulation of scalable vector graphics.
AI.method: SLS employs a Transformer-based autoencoder that models SVG commands, coordinate data, and visual properties in a unified BPE-based token vocabulary. It learns fixed-size latent representations capturing both structure and appearance, with embeddings constrained to lie on a unit hypersphere for structured vector-space operations.
AI.result: The embedding space is robust, invertible, and structured, enabling efficient similarity search, composition, and downstream conditioning. SLS generalizes across diverse tasks while reducing FLOPs by over 150 times compared to token-based approaches.
AI.conclusion: SLS establishes a general-purpose latent foundation for vector graphics research, providing the missing continuous and invertible latent space for SVG representations that enables efficient, scalable downstream applications.

title: Robust Bimanual Vision-Language-Action Models via Embarrassingly Simple Modality Masking
summary: Query-based Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer low-latency inference that is attractive for bimanual robotic manipulation, but we observe that they can still exhibit discontinuous actions and execution failures in complex dual-arm tasks. We hypothesize that unstable multi-view and language fusion is one contributing factor in these failures, often coinciding with attention spreading to distracting regions. To improve robustness, we introduce the Modality Masking Mechanism (M3), an embarrassingly simple, training-only strategy that requires no architectural changes or large-scale robot pretraining. M3 stochastically masks subsets of modality channels during training, exposing the policy to controlled partial observations and encouraging it to rely less on distracting cues and more on evidence that remains reliable. We evaluate M3 on ten bimanual tasks from RoboTwin 2.0 and on three long-horizon real-world tasks. Compared with the Adapter baseline, M3 improves average success by 21.7% in the Clean setting and 11.4% in Clean2Rand, where policies are trained on clean demonstrations and evaluated on randomized scenes, while also improving averaged real-world full-task success by over 30%. These results suggest that structured training-time masking is a practical way to improve the robustness of query-based VLA policies for bimanual manipulation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Modality Masking Mechanism (M3), a training-only strategy that stochastically masks modality channels during training to improve robustness of query-based Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for bimanual robotic manipulation. M3 improves average success by up to 21.7% on RoboTwin 2.0 bimanual tasks and over 30% on real-world long-horizon tasks without architectural changes.
AI.motivation: Query-based VLA models suffer from discontinuous actions and execution failures in complex bimanual manipulation tasks, attributed to unstable multi-view and language fusion where attention spreads to distracting regions instead of reliable evidence.
AI.method: M3 is an embarrassingly simple, training-only strategy that stochastically masks subsets of modality channels during training, exposing the policy to controlled partial observations and encouraging reliance on reliable evidence rather than distracting cues. It requires no architectural changes or large-scale robot pretraining.
AI.result: Evaluated on ten bimanual tasks from RoboTwin 2.0 and three long-horizon real-world tasks. Compared to the Adapter baseline, M3 improves average success by 21.7% in the Clean setting and 11.4% in Clean2Rand, and improves averaged real-world full-task success by over 30%.
AI.conclusion: Structured training-time masking is a practical and effective way to improve robustness of query-based VLA policies for bimanual manipulation, suggesting that training-time modality masking provides a lightweight alternative to architectural or pretraining-based solutions.

title: Nürnberg NLP @ GermEval Shared Task 2026: Harmful Content Detection in German Social Media through Error-Independent LLM Voters
comment: Accepted at the GermEval 2026 Shared Task on Harmful Content Detection @ KONVENS 2026 (1st place on all four subtasks)
summary: Harmful content in German social media does real-world damage, from calls to action to criminal defamation. The GermEval 2026 shared task scores its detection in four subtasks. The technical challenge is a severe class imbalance. The harmful classes are rare and share surface language with the dominant majority class, yet under macro-F1 they decide the score. The decisive lever is then not a stronger single model but error independence. This insight becomes a per-subtask nine-voter ensemble spanning three orthogonal axes: LLM, training method and class scope. Selected mainly on internal cross-validation, the system reaches macro-F1 of 89.56 (C2A), 71.63 (DBO), 54.84 (VIO) and 83.02 (DEF) on the hidden test set, placing first on all four subtasks.

AI.tldr: A system for the GermEval 2026 German harmful content detection shared task, using a per-subtask nine-voter ensemble spanning LLM, training method, and class scope axes, achieving first place on all four subtasks (macro-F1: 89.56 C2A, 71.63 DBO, 54.84 VIO, 83.02 DEF).
AI.motivation: Harmful German social media content causes real-world damage, and its detection is challenged by severe class imbalance where rare harmful classes share surface language with the dominant majority class, yet dominate the macro-F1 score.
AI.method: A per-subtask nine-voter ensemble spanning three orthogonal axes: LLM, training method, and class scope. Voters were selected mainly via internal cross-validation, leveraging error independence rather than a single stronger model.
AI.result: Macro-F1 of 89.56 (C2A), 71.63 (DBO), 54.84 (VIO), and 83.02 (DEF) on the hidden test set, placing first on all four subtasks.
AI.conclusion: Error independence among ensemble members, rather than model strength alone, is the decisive factor for handling severe class imbalance in German harmful content detection.

title: Multimodal Prompt Learning with Irregular EHRs for Robust Monitoring of Critical Care Patients
summary: Accurate assessment of patients in intensive care units (ICUs) is essential for timely clinical intervention and improved patient outcomes. Multimodal electronic health records (EHRs), including structured physiological time series and longitudinal clinical notes, provide complementary information for critical care prediction. However, in real-world clinical settings, individual modalities may be partially observed or entirely unavailable, resulting in substantial performance degradation for existing multimodal models. To address this challenge, we propose a multimodal prompt-learning framework for robust clinical prediction under diverse missing-modality scenarios. The proposed framework introduces four complementary types of prompts: generative prompts, missing-signal prompts, missing-type prompts, and temporal prompts. Generative prompts construct surrogate latent representations for unavailable modalities, while missing-signal prompts distinguish observed representations from generated ones. Missing-type prompts condition the model on different modality-availability configurations, whereas temporal prompts perform condition-specific aggregation over temporally encoded clinical sequences. Together, these prompts enable the model to capture missingness-aware intramodal dependencies and cross-modal interactions within a unified architecture. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches across evaluation metrics on two missingness settings. Ablation and robustness analyses further verify the complementary contributions of the four prompt types and the effectiveness of the proposed framework for clinical prediction from incomplete multimodal EHR data.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multimodal prompt-learning framework for robust clinical prediction in ICUs under missing-modality scenarios, introducing four complementary prompt types (generative, missing-signal, missing-type, and temporal) to handle incomplete multimodal EHR data.
AI.motivation: Multimodal EHRs (structured physiological time series and longitudinal clinical notes) provide complementary information for ICU prediction, but in real-world settings individual modalities may be partially observed or entirely unavailable, causing substantial performance degradation in existing multimodal models.
AI.method: A multimodal prompt-learning framework with four prompt types: (1) generative prompts to construct surrogate latent representations for unavailable modalities, (2) missing-signal prompts to distinguish observed from generated representations, (3) missing-type prompts to condition the model on modality-availability configurations, and (4) temporal prompts for condition-specific aggregation over temporally encoded clinical sequences. These prompts enable missingness-aware intramodal dependencies and cross-modal interactions in a unified architecture.
AI.result: The method outperforms existing approaches across evaluation metrics on two missingness settings. Ablation and robustness analyses confirm the complementary contributions of all four prompt types and the framework's effectiveness for clinical prediction from incomplete multimodal EHR data.
AI.conclusion: The proposed prompt-learning framework effectively addresses the missing-modality challenge in multimodal ICU prediction by leveraging complementary prompt types within a unified architecture, enabling robust clinical prediction from incomplete EHR data.

title: Entity-Constrained CBCT Retrieval for Low-Resource Dental Record Completion
comment: Accepted at the ODIN 2026 Workshop, MICCAI 2026
summary: Completing dental records from cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) is difficult when annotation is scarce and individual clinical fields are supported by different types of evidence. MMDental Task 3 requires seven-field record completion from only 50 labeled CBCT cases and scores the correctness of structured FDI positions and ICD codes; consequently, a visually plausible retrieved record can still be harmful when it introduces an unsupported entity. We propose Entity-Constrained CBCT-Guided Retrieval (ECCR), a parameter-free framework that separates evidence availability from evidence authority. A corpus-derived prior first supplies the complete record. A frozen 3D encoder retrieves image-conditioned Diagnosis evidence, which is appended only if it does not expand the prior FDI or ICD entity set, so the asserted entity set is invariant by construction. On public validation, ECCR reaches a weighted score of 0.3134, improving on both full-record multimodal retrieval (0.2237) and a static text-only prior (0.2915); the guard blocks 63.3% of retrieved candidates, each of which would otherwise have injected an FDI position or ICD code absent from the prior. On the final test evaluation, ECCR obtains 11.37 of a 97.4-point attainable maximum, securing second place overall. The result indicates that, in an extreme low-resource setting, controlling what multimodal evidence is allowed to modify can be more reliable than transferring an entire retrieved record.

AI.tldr: ECCR is a parameter-free retrieval framework for dental record completion from CBCT that separates evidence availability from evidence authority, using a corpus prior for the complete record and a frozen 3D encoder for image-conditioned evidence that is only appended if it does not expand the prior entity set, achieving second place in MMDental Task 3.
AI.motivation: Completing dental records from CBCT is difficult with only 50 labeled cases and seven-field annotation. A visually plausible retrieved record can be harmful when it introduces unsupported entities (FDI positions or ICD codes), so controlling what multimodal evidence is allowed to modify is critical in low-resource settings.
AI.method: ECCR is a parameter-free framework that separates evidence availability from evidence authority. A corpus-derived prior supplies the complete record. A frozen 3D encoder retrieves image-conditioned diagnosis evidence, which is appended only if it does not expand the prior FDI or ICD entity set, making the asserted entity set invariant by construction.
AI.result: On public validation, ECCR achieves 0.3134 weighted score, improving on full-record multimodal retrieval (0.2237) and static text-only prior (0.2915). The guard blocks 63.3% of retrieved candidates that would inject unsupported entities. On the final test, ECCR obtains 11.37 of a 97.4-point attainable maximum, securing second place.
AI.conclusion: In extreme low-resource settings, controlling what multimodal evidence is allowed to modify (via entity-set invariance) is more reliable than transferring an entire retrieved record, suggesting that evidence authority should be explicitly constrained even when evidence is available.

title: EMPIRE: Explicit Manipulation Planning as a Learnable Intermediate Representation for Egocentric Hand-Motion Forecasting
summary: Forecasting dexterous hand motions from egocentric observations is fundamental to intelligent interactive systems. Existing VLM-based methods typically map observations directly to future motions, overlooking the underlying manipulation process that governs hand-object interactions. Moreover, end-to-end optimization couples manipulation learning with motion synthesis, causing motion-generation gradients to interfere with the pre-learned manipulation-aware representations. To overcome these limitations, we propose EMPIRE, a two-stage framework that introduces Explicit Manipulation Planning as an Intermediate Representation for Egocentric hand-motion forecasting. Stage I: Learn to Plan. EMPIRE first learns explicit manipulation plans from multimodal context to capture the progression of hand-object interactions. Stage II: Learn to Act. A motion generator synthesizes future bimanual hand motions conditioned on frozen planner representations, preventing motion-generation gradients from affecting manipulation planning. To support our method, we further construct EMPIRE-651K, a bimanual hand-motion forecasting dataset comprising 650,910 training windows across 111 tasks, each paired with an explicit per-hand manipulation plan. Under identical training and evaluation protocols, EMPIRE achieves state-of-the-art forecasting accuracy, with an MPJPE of 84.53 mm and a finger-relative error of 38.97mm. We release the code and dataset at https://github.com/wangwen-banban/EMPIRE.

AI.tldr: EMPIRE is a two-stage framework for egocentric dexterous hand-motion forecasting that first learns explicit manipulation plans from multimodal context, then synthesizes future bimanual hand motions conditioned on frozen planner representations to avoid gradient interference. It introduces EMPIRE-651K dataset and achieves state-of-the-art performance with MPJPE of 84.53mm and finger-relative error of 38.97mm.
AI.motivation: Existing VLM-based methods directly map observations to future motions, overlooking the underlying manipulation process governing hand-object interactions. End-to-end optimization couples manipulation learning with motion synthesis, causing motion-generation gradients to interfere with pre-learned manipulation-aware representations.
AI.method: EMPIRE is a two-stage framework: Stage I (Learn to Plan) learns explicit manipulation plans from multimodal context to capture the progression of hand-object interactions; Stage II (Learn to Act) uses a motion generator to synthesize future bimanual hand motions conditioned on frozen planner representations. A large-scale dataset EMPIRE-651K is constructed, containing 650,910 training windows across 111 tasks with explicit per-hand manipulation plans.
AI.result: Under identical training and evaluation protocols, EMPIRE achieves state-of-the-art forecasting accuracy with an MPJPE of 84.53mm and a finger-relative error of 38.97mm.
AI.conclusion: Explicit manipulation planning as an intermediate representation improves egocentric hand-motion forecasting accuracy. The code and dataset are released publicly.

title: Length-Adaptive Decoding for Masked Diffusion Machine Translation
comment: Accepted to the Main Conference of EMNLP 2026. 22 pages, 7 figures. Code: https://github.com/Entropy-Valley/Entropy-Valley ; dataset and model: https://huggingface.co/collections/YanZhanPKU/entropy-valley
summary: Machine translation tests masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) because every source token must be rendered faithfully, while fixed canvas decoding must choose target length before denoising. Existing masked diffusion decoding work mainly studies token unmasking order, leaving this length decision under-explored despite its direct effect on coverage and redundancy. We introduce Entropy-Valley (EV), a training-free length selector that scores candidate target canvases by mean predictive entropy from all-mask forward passes and selects the canvas the backbone is most prepared to fill. Relative to a baseline using training corpus length statistics, EV recovers 64.9%, 65.3%, and 33.0% of the COMET-22 gain from reference target lengths on En$\to$Zh, Zh$\to$En, and En$\to$De. Our diagnostics show that denoising-friendly lengths need not match reference lengths. Evaluation by three translation experts supports the En$\leftrightarrow$Zh adequacy gains, with stronger evidence on Zh$\to$En. Compared with a LLaMA-3-8B autoregressive (AR) model trained on the same fine-tuning data, the EV system ties on En$\to$Zh and leads on Zh$\to$En; an oracle-length diagnostic further shows that, in this masked diffusion MT setting, deciding which tokens to reveal first matters less than how the target length is supplied.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Entropy-Valley (EV), a training-free length selector for masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) in machine translation. EV scores candidate target canvases using mean predictive entropy from all-mask forward passes and selects the length the backbone is most prepared to fill, recovering significant COMET-22 gains over baseline length statistics and showing that length decisions matter more than token unmasking order in masked diffusion MT.
AI.motivation: Masked diffusion language models require choosing target length before denoising, yet this length decision is under-explored in existing work. In machine translation, faithful rendering of every source token makes length choice critical, as it directly affects coverage and redundancy of the output.
AI.method: Entropy-Valley (EV) is a training-free length selector that evaluates candidate target canvas lengths by computing mean predictive entropy from all-mask forward passes through the backbone, then selects the canvas length the model is most prepared to fill. This is applied to masked diffusion MT across En→Zh, Zh→En, and En→De.
AI.result: EV recovers 64.9%, 65.3%, and 33.0% of the COMET-22 gain from oracle reference target lengths on En→Zh, Zh→En, and En→De respectively. The EV system ties with a LLaMA-3-8B autoregressive baseline on En→Zh and leads on Zh→En. Diagnostics show denoising-friendly lengths need not match reference lengths, and oracle-length analysis shows that length supply matters more than token unmasking order.
AI.conclusion: Length selection is a critical and under-explored component of masked diffusion MT. Entropy-Valley provides an effective training-free solution, and the finding that length decisions outweigh unmasking-order decisions has important implications for future dLLM decoding research in MT and potentially other generation tasks.

title: TessIndex: Capability Verified Identity System for the Agent Economy
summary: Software systems have traditionally been organized around applications where human users act as principal decision-makers. Recent developments in agentic capabilities alter this paradigm: software agents now autonomously translate high-level goals into structured tasks, orchestrating tools, services and sub-agents to execute complex workflows. This evolution gives rise to an agent economy where these autonomous agents capture real economic value. However, the infrastructure required to support the agent economy fails across three critical dimensions: the absence of persistent identity infrastructure prevents systemic accountability in agentic workflows; capability claims remain self-declared not backed by verifiable execution evidence; and the disconnect between creator identities, agent performance, and project value hinders the economic valuation of agents as assets. While existing registries provide naming and discovery, unifying these features around a persistent identity anchor remains largely unaddressed. TessIndex is a capability-verified identity system for agent primitives that utilizes a dual-plane architecture: the blockchain records compact commitments for identity, ownership, and verification, while centralized servers maintain dynamic metadata for discovery, commerce, and reputation. It establishes: persistent identities across agent primitives to enforce systemic accountability in autonomous workflows; a predicate-based verification process replacing self-declared claims with cryptographic capability proof; an identity infrastructure that links agent performance to both project and creator identities while capturing value through tokenization. Ultimately, TessIndex serves as an integrated infrastructure that binds an agent's existence across capabilities, execution, and reputation into a single persistent identity.

AI.tldr: TessIndex is a capability-verified identity system for the emerging "agent economy" that uses a dual-plane architecture (blockchain for compact identity/ownership/verification commitments, centralized servers for dynamic metadata) to provide persistent identities, cryptographic capability verification, and economic valuation for autonomous software agents.
AI.motivation: The rise of autonomous software agents creating real economic value lacks the infrastructure to support them across three critical dimensions: (1) no persistent identity infrastructure for systemic accountability, (2) capability claims are self-declared without verifiable execution evidence, and (3) the disconnect between creators, agent performance, and project value hinders economic valuation of agents as assets. Existing registries offer naming and discovery but do not unify these features around a persistent identity anchor.
AI.method: TessIndex employs a dual-plane architecture: a blockchain layer records compact cryptographic commitments for identity, ownership, and verification, while centralized servers maintain dynamic metadata for discovery, commerce, and reputation. It implements a predicate-based verification process that replaces self-declared capability claims with cryptographic capability proofs, and links agent performance to project and creator identities through tokenization.
AI.result: The system establishes persistent identities across agent primitives for systemic accountability, replaces self-declared claims with cryptographic capability proof via predicate-based verification, and provides identity infrastructure linking agent performance to project/creator identities with value capture through tokenization.
AI.conclusion: TessIndex serves as integrated infrastructure that binds an agent's existence across capabilities, execution, and reputation into a single persistent identity, addressing the accountability, verifiability, and economic valuation gaps in the emerging agent economy.

title: AirAlign: Geometry-Aware Relative Pose Alignment for UAV Last-Meter Navigation
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) navigation in modern low-altitude environments requires more accurate pose alignment in the final approach stage for target information acquisition or manipulation, making "last-meter" navigation increasingly important. However, severe viewpoint and appearance variations make this task challenging. To tackle this problem, we propose AirAlign, a framework for RGB-only image-pair relative pose alignment for UAVs. AirAlign uses a pretrained visual geometry reconstruction model as the backbone to extract geometry-aware features from source-target image pairs. In addition, to better utilize the limited training data, we split the training set into multiple scene-disjoint folds for unseen cross-validation and model selection. During inference, the predictions of the selected models are averaged to form the ensemble output of the overall framework. Experiments on the PairUAV challenge at the ACMMM 2026 Workshop on UAVs in Multimedia demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of our method, while comprehensive ablation studies validate the contribution of each component.

AI.tldr: AirAlign is an RGB-only framework for UAV relative pose alignment in final approach ("last-meter") navigation, using a pretrained visual geometry reconstruction backbone for geometry-aware feature extraction, scene-disjoint cross-validation for model selection with limited data, and ensemble inference. It achieves effective results on the PairUAV challenge at ACM MM 2026.
AI.motivation: UAV navigation in low-altitude environments requires precise pose alignment during the final approach stage ("last-meter" navigation) for target acquisition or manipulation. This is challenging due to severe viewpoint and appearance variations between source-target image pairs, making accurate relative pose estimation difficult.
AI.method: AirAlign uses a pretrained visual geometry reconstruction model as its backbone to extract geometry-aware features from source-target image pairs. To address limited training data, the training set is split into multiple scene-disjoint folds for unseen cross-validation and model selection. During inference, predictions from the selected models are averaged to form an ensemble output.
AI.result: Experiments on the PairUAV challenge at the ACMMM 2026 Workshop on UAVs in Multimedia demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the method, with comprehensive ablation studies validating the contribution of each component.
AI.conclusion: AirAlign provides an effective and robust solution for RGB-only UAV relative pose alignment in final approach navigation, leveraging geometry-aware pretrained features and ensemble-based inference to handle viewpoint and appearance variations while making efficient use of limited training data.

title: A Unified Neural-Aided Alignment and Calibration Method for AUVs
summary: Autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) rely on the fusion of inertial navigation systems (INS) and Doppler velocity logs (DVL) for accurate navigation. Before deployment, this fusion requires a DVL initialization pipeline consisting of two stages: alignment, which estimates the rotation between the INS and DVL frames, and calibration, which estimates the DVL error terms. Conventionally, both stages are solved with model-based algorithms that demand complex vehicle maneuvers, surface-level satellite reference measurements, and simplified error models, making initialization time-consuming, trajectory-dependent, and sensitive to sensor quality. In this work, we propose a fully neural- aided DVL initialization pipeline that replaces both stages with two complementary neural networks: ResAlignNet for alignment and DCNet for calibration. The unified pipeline operates in situ on a single nearly constant-velocity trajectory and uses the same inputs as the model-based baseline. Using real-world data recorded across five distinct sensor error-term combinations, the proposed pipeline reduces the velocity root mean squared error by an average of 68.7% over the model-based baseline, using only 25s of data for initialization.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a fully neural-aided DVL initialization pipeline for AUVs, replacing both stages (alignment via ResAlignNet and calibration via DCNet) of conventional model-based methods. Using real-world data from five sensor configurations, the pipeline achieves a 68.7% average reduction in velocity root mean squared error compared to the model-based baseline, using only 25 seconds of data from a single nearly constant-velocity trajectory.
AI.motivation: Conventional model-based DVL initialization requires complex vehicle maneuvers, surface-level satellite reference measurements, and simplified error models, making it time-consuming, trajectory-dependent, and sensitive to sensor quality. A more efficient and robust initialization approach is needed.
AI.method: A fully neural-aided pipeline replaces both initialization stages with two complementary neural networks: ResAlignNet for alignment (estimating rotation between INS and DVL frames) and DCNet for calibration (estimating DVL error terms). The pipeline operates in situ on a single nearly constant-velocity trajectory and uses the same inputs as the model-based baseline.
AI.result: Using real-world data recorded across five distinct sensor error-term combinations, the proposed pipeline reduces velocity root mean squared error by an average of 68.7% over the model-based baseline, using only 25 seconds of data for initialization.
AI.conclusion: The neural-aided DVL initialization pipeline significantly outperforms the model-based baseline in accuracy and efficiency, requiring far less data (25s) and a simpler trajectory while demonstrating robustness across multiple sensor error configurations.

title: LLM Evaluation on Unseen Questions: Contextual Multidimensional IRT Model
summary: Evaluation of large language models (LLMs) increasingly requires predicting how a model will perform on new questions or tasks before collecting large amounts of new annotations. This problem is challenging because question difficulty, scenario, and underlying capability demands can vary substantially. Simple retrospective averages may confound model ability with item characteristics. In this paper, we study a model-based evaluation framework that combines multidimensional item response theory model with question contexts to predict LLM performance on unseen questions. The framework represents LLMs through latent capability profiles while using question content to inform item characteristics, allowing information to transfer beyond previously observed items. Empirically, we find that for within-scenario evaluation, incorporating question embeddings improves prediction relative to model-free baselines, and that multidimensional latent structure provides a richer description of capability variation than unidimensional alternatives. At the same time, our results reveal an important limitation that the generalizability does not necessarily translate into reliable prediction under cross-scenario shift. These findings suggest that context-aware psychometric modeling is a promising direction for efficient and interpretable LLM evaluation, while also highlighting cross-scenario generalization as a central open challenge.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a model-based evaluation framework combining multidimensional item response theory (IRT) with question context embeddings to predict LLM performance on unseen questions. The framework works well within scenarios, capturing richer capability variation via multidimensional latent structures, but struggles with cross-scenario generalization.
AI.motivation: Predicting LLM performance on new questions before collecting extensive annotations is increasingly important, but naive retrospective averages confound model ability with item characteristics (difficulty, scenario, capability demands). A framework that accounts for both latent model capabilities and question contexts is needed.
AI.method: The framework integrates multidimensional item response theory with question context embeddings. LLMs are represented via latent capability profiles, while question content (via embeddings) informs item characteristics, enabling information transfer beyond previously observed items. The approach is evaluated for within-scenario prediction and cross-scenario generalizability.
AI.result: Within-scenario evaluation, incorporating question embeddings outperforms model-free baselines, and multidimensional latent structure provides richer capability descriptions than unidimensional models. However, the generalizability does not reliably translate to prediction under cross-scenario shift.
AI.conclusion: Context-aware psychometric modeling is a promising direction for efficient and interpretable LLM evaluation within scenarios, but cross-scenario generalization remains a central open challenge that must be addressed for broader applicability.

title: SSDi8: Accurate and Efficient 8-bit Quantization for State Space Duality
summary: Recent advances in sequence modeling have highlighted Mamba as a state space architecture offering efficient long-range dependency modeling and providing a viable alternative to Transformers. Building upon this, Mamba-2 introduces the Structured State Space Duality (SSD), which integrates recurrent and attention modes to achieve efficiency and scalability. However, this architectural expansion substantially increases memory and latency overhead, underscoring the need for efficient compression strategies tailored to SSD. In this work, we present SSDi8, the first post-training quantization framework specifically designed for SSD to maintain a persistent INT8 path. SSDi8 introduces a reformulation that decouples element-wise multiplications from matrix multiplications, enabling reuse of quantized activations across modules. Moreover, SSDi8 adaptively quantizes channel-varying activations at cost-effective points, further reducing latency. On the accuracy side, SSDi8 explicitly leverages the intrinsic dimensional decomposition of SSD, exploiting distinct outlier distributions across axes, and incorporates an error correction term based on per-channel error statistics. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that SSDi8 achieves accuracy comparable to FP16 while delivering up to 1.4x speedup in W4A8 and W8A8 settings. We further validate its robustness in resource-constrained environments by deploying it on the Orin NX device.

AI.tldr: SSDi8 is the first post-training quantization framework specifically designed for Mamba-2's Structured State Space Duality (SSD) architecture, maintaining a persistent INT8 path while achieving accuracy comparable to FP16 and up to 1.4x speedup in W4A8 and W8A8 settings, validated on both standard benchmarks and the Orin NX edge device.
AI.motivation: Mamba-2's SSD architecture, which integrates recurrent and attention modes, significantly increases memory and latency overhead compared to its predecessor. There is a pressing need for efficient compression strategies tailored specifically to SSD, as existing quantization approaches are not designed to handle the unique structure of this architecture.
AI.method: SSDi8 introduces three key techniques: (1) a reformulation that decouples element-wise multiplications from matrix multiplications, enabling reuse of quantized activations across modules; (2) adaptive quantization of channel-varying activations at cost-effective points to reduce latency; and (3) exploitation of SSD's intrinsic dimensional decomposition to handle distinct outlier distributions across axes, incorporating an error correction term based on per-channel error statistics.
AI.result: SSDi8 achieves accuracy comparable to FP16 while delivering up to 1.4x speedup in both W4A8 and W8A8 quantization settings. The framework's robustness was also validated in resource-constrained environments through deployment on the Orin NX device.
AI.conclusion: SSDi8 demonstrates that effective post-training quantization for SSD architectures is achievable by leveraging the structural properties of the model, providing both accuracy preservation and substantial speedup gains, with practical viability confirmed on edge hardware.

title: C$^2$Path: Class-Conditional Pathway Decoupling for Vision-Language Incremental Object Detection
summary: Incremental Object Detection (IOD) aims to enable detectors to continuously learn novel categories while preserving previously acquired knowledge. However, existing methods suffer from two forms of \textbf{class knowledge coupling}: class boundary erosion induced by shared parameter updates and class representation entanglement arising from mixed feature encoding. We argue that effective incremental learning requires class-specific computational pathways that enable isolated parameter updates and separated class-wise injection. To this end, we propose \textbf{C$^2$Path}, a class-conditional pathway decoupling framework for vision-language incremental object detection that leverages token-level class cues to establish dedicated and updatable computational pathways for different categories. Specifically, C$^2$Path introduces a category expert library and a class-conditional decoupling module. The expert library consists of learnable low-rank computational nodes that capture category-specific knowledge, while the decoupling module generates class-aware routing signals to dynamically compose \textit{ClassLoRA} adapters from these experts, thereby forming class-specific computational pathways for isolated updates and separated injection across categories. Extensive experiments on COCO 2017 under multiple incremental learning settings demonstrate that C$^2$Path consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, providing an effective and scalable solution for continual category expansion in vision-language detectors.

AI.tldr: C²Path is a class-conditional pathway decoupling framework for vision-language incremental object detection. It uses a category expert library and a class-conditional decoupling module to generate dynamic ClassLoRA adapters, creating class-specific computational pathways that enable isolated parameter updates and separated class-wise injection, thereby overcoming class knowledge coupling (boundary erosion and representation entanglement).
AI.motivation: Existing Incremental Object Detection (IOD) methods suffer from class knowledge coupling in two forms: (1) class boundary erosion caused by shared parameter updates across categories, and (2) class representation entanglement arising from mixed feature encoding. The authors argue that effective incremental learning requires class-specific computational pathways to decouple these issues.
AI.method: C²Path introduces two key components: (1) a category expert library comprising learnable low-rank computational nodes that capture category-specific knowledge, and (2) a class-conditional decoupling module that leverages token-level class cues to generate class-aware routing signals. These routing signals dynamically compose ClassLoRA adapters from the expert library, forming dedicated and updatable computational pathways for different categories, enabling isolated parameter updates and separated class-wise injection.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on COCO 2017 under multiple incremental learning settings demonstrate that C²Path consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, providing an effective and scalable solution for continual category expansion in vision-language detectors.
AI.conclusion: C²Path effectively addresses class knowledge coupling in incremental object detection by establishing class-specific computational pathways via expert-routed LoRA adapters, achieving superior performance and scalability for continual category expansion in vision-language detectors.

title: What is the effect of running-specific prostheses on long jumps? Optimization-based prediction and analysis using biomechanical models
comment: This work has been submitted to Scientific Reports and it is currently under review
summary: Long jumpers with below the knee amputation (BKA) that take off from their running-specific prosthesis (RSP) improved performances significantly over the last years. The long jump biomechanics differs compared to athletes without BKA and the question arises whether the spring-like properties of the RSP facilitate achieving long jumping distances. The aim of this work is to propose a long jump model for athletes with and without BKA, to evaluate it and to apply it for comparing long jump motions with and without RSP. We establish rigid multi-body system models of one athlete with and one athlete without below the knee amputation (BKA). Long jump motions are computed by solving a specific optimal control problem (OCP) with constraints enforcing a physically correct dynamics, both for motion reconstruction or motion synthesis. With the proposed long jump model, we are able to compute realistic long jump motions. We discuss the causes of differences in measured long jumps and show directions for eliminating them. For both athletes, the synthesized solutions reveal potential for performance improvement. The jumping distance of the athlete without BKA is 64cm (6.9%) longer than the one of the athlete with BKA in the synthesized solutions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a long jump model for athletes with and without below-knee amputation (BKA) using rigid multi-body systems and optimal control problems to reconstruct and synthesize long jump motions. The model produces realistic motions and reveals that in synthesized optimal solutions, the non-amputee athlete jump is 64 cm (6.9%) longer than the amputee athlete using a running-specific prosthesis.
AI.motivation: Long jumpers with BKA using running-specific prostheses (RSP) have improved significantly, yet it remains unclear whether the spring-like properties of the RSP facilitate achieving long jump distances, since the biomechanics differ from able-bodied athletes. A modeling approach is needed to systematically compare and understand these differences.
AI.method: Rigid multi-body system models are established for one athlete with BKA and one without. Long jump motions are computed by solving specific optimal control problems (OCPs) with constraints enforcing physically correct dynamics, used for both motion reconstruction and motion synthesis.
AI.result: The proposed long jump model computes realistic long jump motions. The causes of measured jump differences are discussed with directions for elimination. Synthesized solutions show performance improvement potential for both athletes, with the non-BKA athlete jumping 64 cm (6.9%) farther than the BKA athlete.
AI.conclusion: The model successfully captures and compares long jump biomechanics between athletes with and without BKA. The synthesized results suggest the RSP does not provide a facilitative advantage in achieving long jump distances, as the non-amputee athlete outperforms the amputee athlete in optimized solutions.

title: Text-Anchored Semantic Perturbations for Transferable Jailbreak Attacks on Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in vision-language interaction, yet their safety alignment remains vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. A key challenge is that safety behavior learned in the textual space does not reliably transfer to fused cross-modal representations, leaving multimodal inputs exploitable through latent semantic cues. We propose Text-Anchored Semantic Perturbation Attack (TA-SPA), a black-box jailbreak framework that optimizes transferable perturbations in a text-anchored semantic space. TA-SPA integrates Text-Anchored Semantic Factorization (TASF), which encourages the separation of cross-modal semantic factors from modality-specific residuals, with Semantic-Preserving Augmentation (SPA), which diversifies harmful target anchors while preserving semantic consistency. Experiments show strong attack effectiveness and transfer to commercial MLLMs, with competitive performance under representative defenses.
