Additional controls and probing support the intended factorization without implying perfect disentanglement, motivating representation-level safety alignment beyond input-level filtering.

AI.tldr: TA-SPA is a black-box jailbreak framework for MLLMs that optimizes transferable adversarial perturbations in a text-anchored semantic space using Text-Anchored Semantic Factorization (TASF) and Semantic-Preserving Augmentation (SPA), demonstrating strong attack effectiveness and transferability to commercial MLLMs while performing competitively under defenses.
AI.motivation: Safety alignment learned in textual space does not reliably transfer to fused cross-modal representations in MLLMs, leaving multimodal inputs exploitable through latent semantic cues and vulnerable to jailbreak attacks.
AI.method: TA-SPA integrates two components: (1) Text-Anchored Semantic Factorization (TASF) which separates cross-modal semantic factors from modality-specific residuals, and (2) Semantic-Preserving Augmentation (SPA) which diversifies harmful target anchors while maintaining semantic consistency. The attack operates in a text-anchored semantic space as a black-box framework.
AI.result: The framework demonstrates strong attack effectiveness, transfers successfully to commercial MLLMs, and achieves competitive performance under representative defense mechanisms. Control experiments and probing support the intended factorization of semantic factors, though not implying perfect disentanglement.
AI.conclusion: The findings motivate representation-level safety alignment beyond input-level filtering, as the imperfect but effective factorization reveals vulnerabilities that persist despite existing defenses.

title: Sparse Multi-Stage Expert-Agent Routing for Complex Clinical Reasoning
summary: Complex clinical reasoning requires models to update diagnostic hypotheses as new evidence emerges and to coordinate different medical specialities under limited consultation resources. Existing LLM-based clinical reasoning systems typically perform single-pass prediction or rely on fixed multi-agent workflows, making expert participation either static or unnecessarily exhaustive. We propose Sparse Multi-Stage Expert-Agent Routing, a language-based clinical reasoning framework that models diagnosis as a stage-wise routing process. Given progressively available clinical evidence derived from multiple modalities, the framework maintains an evolving case state and adaptively activates a sparse set of medical expert agents, supported by expert-specific memory across stages. To evaluate free-text diagnostic conclusions beyond surface similarity, we further introduce ClinFEScore, a fact-aware semantic evaluation protocol for clinical reasoning outputs. On reconstructed multi-stage cases from MAC and AgentClinic-NEJM, our framework reduces the average number of activated experts from 17.0 to 3.0 whilst maintaining strong fact-level diagnostic quality. On 200 real-world hospital MDT cases, ClinFEScore correlates strongly with clinician judgements (Spearman's $ρ=0.81$; Pearson's $r=0.87$), whilst our method achieves 91.5\% clinician-verified diagnostic accuracy with approximately five expert-agent/LLM calls per case. These results support sparse stage-wise coordination as an efficient and clinically relevant approach to LLM-based clinical reasoning.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Sparse Multi-Stage Expert-Agent Routing, a clinical reasoning framework that models diagnosis as a stage-wise routing process with adaptively activated sparse expert agents. It also introduces ClinFEScore, a fact-aware semantic evaluation metric. The framework reduces activated experts from 17.0 to 3.0 while maintaining diagnostic quality, achieves 91.5% clinician-verified accuracy on real-world cases, and ClinFEScore strongly correlates with clinician judgments.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based clinical reasoning systems either perform single-pass prediction or rely on fixed multi-agent workflows, making expert participation static or unnecessarily exhaustive. This fails to reflect real clinical practice where hypotheses are updated as evidence emerges and specialist involvement should be adaptive based on current case state.
AI.method: The framework models diagnosis as a stage-wise routing process: (1) it maintains an evolving case state as progressively available multi-modal clinical evidence arrives; (2) it adaptively activates a sparse set of medical expert agents at each stage rather than invoking all specialists; (3) expert-specific memory is maintained across stages to retain information; (4) ClinFEScore is introduced as a fact-aware semantic evaluation protocol for free-text diagnostic conclusions, going beyond surface similarity metrics.
AI.result: On reconstructed multi-stage cases from MAC and AgentClinic-NEJM, the framework reduces average activated experts from 17.0 to 3.0 while maintaining strong fact-level diagnostic quality. On 200 real-world hospital MDT cases, ClinFEScore correlates strongly with clinician judgments (Spearman's ρ=0.81; Pearson's r=0.87), and the method achieves 91.5% clinician-verified diagnostic accuracy with approximately five expert-agent/LLM calls per case.
AI.conclusion: Sparse stage-wise coordination is an efficient and clinically relevant approach to LLM-based clinical reasoning, demonstrating that adaptively activating only the necessary experts across diagnostic stages maintains quality while drastically reducing computational cost and resource usage.

title: WorldToken: Time-First Sequence Modeling for Robotic Imitation Learning
summary: Robot policies receive heterogeneous observations at each decision step, yet sequence models differ in how they organize these inputs over time. We introduce WorldToken, a time-first policy instantiation that fuses multiview images, proprioception, and task conditioning within each policy timestep into one world token. A causal temporal Transformer models the resulting world-token sequence, and a diffusion action head generates action chunks. On 23 RoboCasa tasks, an 85.3M-parameter policy trained from scratch apart from a frozen pretrained CLIP text encoder achieves 59.45% mean closed-loop success using 2,900 generated demonstrations per task. A complete factorial sweep over five dataset sizes, five model sizes, and two training seeds shows consistent gains from additional target-domain data and diminishing returns beyond moderate model size. Under same-checkpoint history truncation, reducing visible history to one or two policy timesteps lowers closed-loop success for all 50 RoboCasa policies. On RMBench Blocks Ranking, reducing visible history from 146 to 8 seconds lowers evaluator success from 95% to 28%, while an exploratory extended rollout sustains the reference swap sequence for over 850 seconds. These results establish the empirical feasibility of the complete WorldToken instantiation and characterize its data-scaling and temporal-context behavior under the tested recipes. They do not establish superiority over alternative sequence organizations or isolate which components of the complete implementation drive the observed performance.

AI.tldr: WorldToken is a time-first policy architecture that fuses multimodal observations (multiview images, proprioception, task conditioning) within each policy timestep into a single world token, processed by a causal temporal Transformer with a diffusion action head. It achieves 59.45% mean closed-loop success on 23 RoboCasa tasks with an 85.3M-parameter model, while systematic ablations reveal data-scaling benefits and temporal-context sensitivity.
AI.motivation: Robot policies receive heterogeneous observations at each decision step, but sequence models differ in how they organize these inputs over time. The motivation is to explore a time-first policy architecture that integrates all observation modalities within each policy timestep into a unified token representation.
AI.method: The paper introduces WorldToken, a time-first policy that: (1) fuses multiview images, proprioception, and task conditioning into one world token per policy timestep; (2) uses a causal temporal Transformer to model the world-token sequence; (3) employs a diffusion action head to generate action chunks. The policy is trained from scratch (except a frozen CLIP text encoder) on generated demonstrations, with systematic factorial sweeps over dataset sizes, model sizes, and training seeds.
AI.result: On 23 RoboCasa tasks, an 85.3M-parameter model achieves 59.45% mean closed-loop success using 2,900 generated demos per task. Factorial sweeps show consistent gains from additional target-domain data and diminishing returns beyond moderate model size. History truncation to 1-2 timesteps lowers success for all 50 RoboCasa policies. On RMBench Blocks Ranking, reducing visible history from 146 to 8 seconds drops evaluator success from 95% to 28%, while an extended rollout sustains the reference swap sequence for over 850 seconds.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes the empirical feasibility of the complete WorldToken instantiation and characterizes its data-scaling and temporal-context behavior. However, it does not claim superiority over alternative sequence organizations, nor does it isolate which specific components drive the observed performance.

title: Semantics or Structure? Auditing Text Sensitivity in Multimodal Time-Series Forecasting
summary: Multimodal time-series forecasting has emerged as a promising paradigm in which natural-language context is expected to improve predictive performance. Recent multimodal foundation models, including Aurora, as well as early- and late-fusion approaches such as MM-TSFlib and TaTS, report substantial gains over unimodal baselines on the Time-MMD benchmark, attributing these improvements to textual information. However, whether these models are actually sensitive to the semantic content of the text remains unverified. We address this question through controlled text perturbations, attribution analyses, and probes of Aurora's text pathway. On Time-MMD, swapping each row's text for any other real text (empty, constant, within-domain shuffled, or cross-domain) moves mean MSE by less than $0.5\%$ on all three architectures. The improvement reported in the literature is recovered when a co-shipped numeric column is removed without touching text. We conclude that, on this benchmark and within this family of frozen-encoder architectures, text content is not the operative signal behind the reported gains. To support future work on text integration in multimodal foundation models for structured data, we release our perturbation protocol and evaluation harness as a reusable diagnostic toolkit.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether multimodal time-series forecasting models (e.g., Aurora, MM-TSFlib, TaTS) are actually sensitive to the semantic content of text on the Time-MMD benchmark. Through controlled text perturbations, attribution analyses, and probes of Aurora's text pathway, the authors show that text content has essentially no effect on performance (mean MSE changes <0.5%), and that reported gains are instead attributable to a co-shipped numeric column. A reusable diagnostic toolkit is released.
AI.motivation: Recent multimodal foundation models claim substantial improvements from integrating textual context in time-series forecasting, but it is unverified whether these models actually use the semantic content of the text. The authors aim to rigorously test whether reported gains are genuinely due to text understanding or to confounding factors.
AI.method: Controlled text perturbation experiments (swapping text with empty, constant, within-domain shuffled, or cross-domain variants) across three architectures; attribution analyses; and probing of Aurora's text pathway. Evaluation on the Time-MMD benchmark, measuring mean MSE sensitivity to text perturbations.
AI.result: Swapping text with any other real text changes mean MSE by less than 0.5% across all three architectures. The reported improvements from literature are only recovered when a co-shipped numeric column is removed, with no changes to the text.
AI.conclusion: On the Time-MMD benchmark and within frozen-encoder multimodal architectures, text content is not the operative signal behind reported performance gains. The authors release a perturbation protocol and evaluation harness as a reusable diagnostic toolkit for future work.

title: Closed-loop AI achieves certifiable engineering design
summary: Agentic AI has automated parts of scientific discovery, including paper generation, expert-level coding, therapeutic proposal, and autonomous experimentation. Complex physical engineering design remains a gap, because candidates must satisfy simultaneous constraints in fluid dynamics, solid mechanics, and structural stability. We introduce The AI Engineer, an agentic framework that couples large language models (LLMs) to deterministic engineering backends in a closed loop: natural-language requirements are converted into design-domain geometry and mesh; topology is optimized with bi-directional evolutionary structural optimization (BESO) coupled to the CalculiX solver; and member sizes are refined with particle swarm optimization (PSO) coupled to Zwind under offshore aero-hydro-servo-elastic load cases. To explore many designs without per-candidate certification cost, an Automated Reviewer scores each candidate on five dimensions (capacity, steel intensity, unit cost, constructability, and fatigue life) using piecewise-linear functions calibrated on 11 real floating-wind projects. Search terminates only when a candidate reaches a composite score $S \ge 85$ (grade A) with no subscore below 60. We validated this gate by submitting the top-scoring design to the China Classification Society (CCS) for Approval in Principle (AIP), which it passed; AIP is thus an external check that the reviewer tracks professional judgment, not the daily objective. The certified design outperforms the human-optimized TuQiang baseline, reducing steel mass and unit capital cost by 8.1% each while meeting all AIP criteria. This verification-closed regime, in which every proposal is judged by deterministic physics and codified limit states, distinguishes The AI Engineer from open-ended generative systems. Remaining limits include detailed design and fabrication-hard constraints.

AI.tldr: The AI Engineer is an agentic framework that couples LLMs with deterministic engineering backends (BESO + CalculiX for topology optimization, PSO + Zwind for member sizing) to automatically design complex physical engineering structures. It uses an Automated Reviewer scoring candidates on five dimensions calibrated on 11 real floating-wind projects, and terminates when a candidate achieves grade A (composite score ≥85, no subscore below 60). The top design passed Approval in Principle from the China Classification Society and outperformed the human-optimized TuQiang baseline by reducing steel mass and unit capital cost by 8.1% each.
AI.motivation: Complex physical engineering design remains a gap for agentic AI because candidates must simultaneously satisfy constraints across fluid dynamics, solid mechanics, and structural stability—unlike other scientific discovery domains that have been automated.
AI.method: The framework converts natural-language requirements into design geometry and mesh; performs topology optimization via BESO coupled to the CalculiX solver; refines member sizes via PSO coupled to Zwind under offshore aero-hydro-servo-elastic load cases; and uses an Automated Reviewer with piecewise-linear scoring functions calibrated on 11 real floating-wind projects to score candidates on capacity, steel intensity, unit cost, constructability, and fatigue life.
AI.result: The top-scoring design passed Approval in Principle (AIP) from the China Classification Society, an external validation that the reviewer tracks professional judgment. The certified design outperforms the human-optimized TuQiang baseline, reducing steel mass and unit capital cost by 8.1% each while meeting all AIP criteria.
AI.conclusion: This verification-closed regime, where every proposal is judged by deterministic physics and codified limit states, distinguishes The AI Engineer from open-ended generative systems. Remaining limits include detailed design and fabrication-hard constraints.

title: Noise Floor Audit for Agent Benchmarks
summary: We audit measurement variability for 3 native tool-calling endpoints across 2 providers on the official BFCL multiple and parallel categories, using matched AST grading. At temperature 0, reruns are nearly deterministic across Groq endpoints and a thinking-enabled Gemini setting: ever-flip fractions are 0.7%, 2.0%, and 2.7%, with mean run correlations of 0.997, 0.966, and 0.961. Semantics-preserving prompt perturbations create the larger floor on all endpoints, with median perturbation paired SDs 11x to 58x larger than rerun paired SDs. The failure character also shifts: malformed-output failures account for 30%, 7%, and <1% of task failures, so marginal accuracy hides not only stability but also failure mode.

AI.tldr: This paper audits measurement variability in tool-calling LLM endpoints across two providers using the BFCL benchmark. It finds near-deterministic reruns at temperature 0 but much larger variability from semantics-preserving prompt perturbations (11x-58x higher SDs), while also revealing that marginal accuracy masks differences in failure modes (30%, 7%, <1% malformed-output failures across endpoints).
AI.motivation: To assess the reliability and stability of tool-calling benchmark evaluations, distinguishing between intrinsic rerun variability and perturbation-induced variability, and to expose how aggregate accuracy metrics hide failure-mode differences.
AI.method: Auditing 3 native tool-calling endpoints from 2 providers on BFCL multiple and parallel categories with matched AST grading, comparing rerun variability at temperature 0 against semantics-preserving prompt perturbation variability using paired SDs and ever-flip fractions.
AI.result: Reruns are nearly deterministic (ever-flip fractions 0.7-2.7%, mean correlations 0.961-0.997), while prompt perturbations produce 11x-58x larger paired SDs. Malformed-output failure proportions differ substantially across endpoints: 30%, 7%, and <1%.
AI.conclusion: Tool-calling evaluation results are highly reproducible under identical conditions but sensitive to prompt phrasing, and standard accuracy metrics conceal significant differences in failure mode composition across endpoints.

title: Beyond Similarity: Heterogeneous Graph Learning for Multi-Objective Food Substitution in Charitable Food Agencies
summary: Charitable food agencies play an important role in alleviating food insecurity by distributing donated food to people in need. However, they rely on ad hoc in-kind donations and often face shortages of specific foods, so they offer substitutes. A good food substitution requires matching household preferences, nutritional needs, and item similarity. Agencies have limited direct records of consumption behavior due to resource constraints, making it challenging to make an appropriate substitution decision that meets multiple criteria. In this study, we propose a heterogeneous graph neural network (HeteroGNN), a source-grounded recommendation framework for food substitution in charitable food agencies. We first build a unified relational graph from large-scale public data sources, combining household behavior on food consumption and food nutrient information in the United States (US) context. We treat the substitution recommendation as a multi-objective ranking problem with three targets, including behavior affinity, health suitability, and substitution similarity. We train and validate the proposed framework under standard graph relationship and adverse cold-start settings by removing relational edges from the graph. Our results show that the proposed framework leverages relational information beyond node features in predicting consumption behavior. Additionally, the proposed framework remains robust with sparsity when the model receives incomplete information about behavior and nutrient features. Finally, we show the weak correlation among different objectives, thereby justifying the multi-objective framing as a replacement for an aggregated decision. The proposed framework can help downstream charitable agency decision-makers make contextspecific substitution recommendations with limited information available.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network (HeteroGNN) framework for food substitution recommendations in charitable food agencies, leveraging public data on household consumption behavior and food nutrition to rank substitute foods against multiple objectives: behavior affinity, health suitability, and substitution similarity.
AI.motivation: Charitable food agencies face shortages of specific foods and must offer substitutes, but lack direct consumption records due to resource constraints. Making appropriate substitution decisions that simultaneously match household preferences, nutritional needs, and item similarity is challenging without adequate behavioral data.
AI.method: The authors construct a unified relational graph from large-scale public US data sources combining household food consumption behavior and food nutrient information. They frame substitution recommendation as a multi-objective ranking problem with three targets (behavior affinity, health suitability, substitution similarity) and train a HeteroGNN under both standard graph relationship settings and adverse cold-start settings (achieved by removing relational edges).
AI.result: The HeteroGNN leverages relational information beyond node features in predicting consumption behavior, remains robust under sparsity when behavior and nutrient features are incomplete, and the weak correlation among the three objectives justifies the multi-objective framing over an aggregated single-decision approach.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides context-specific substitution recommendations to charitable agency decision-makers even with limited available information, offering a practical tool to improve food substitution quality in charitable food distribution settings.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Visual Prompting: Guiding Foundation Models in Two-Photon Imaging
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Supplementary material included
summary:
Two-photon calcium imaging presents a challenging setting for foundation models: image appearance varies substantially across recordings and experimental conditions, annotations are scarce, and rapid adaptation is often needed. Rather than adapting model weights through fine-tuning, we ask whether a foundation model can be guided at inference time by injecting external visual memory directly into its input. We implement this idea with SAM 3 and introduce Retrieval-Augmented Visual Prompting (RAVP), a framework in which each target tile is augmented with a retrieved annotated exemplar whose bounding box is used as a concept prompt.
  RAVP turns retrieval into a form of visual prompting and enables adaptation through input design alone. We study multiple exemplar selection strategies, including fluorescence-guided heuristics and a lightweight recall predictor trained to estimate which exemplar is most informative for a target tile. Experiments on the Allen Brain Observatory show that exemplar-augmented inference consistently strengthens zero-shot neuron detection and instance segmentation. Ablation studies further show that a single carefully selected exemplar is more effective than prompting with multiple retrieved examples. These results position inference-time visual memory injection as a simple and effective alternative to parameter adaptation for foundation models in specialized biomedical imaging.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Retrieval-Augmented Visual Prompting (RAVP), a method that adapts SAM 3 to two-photon calcium imaging without fine-tuning by injecting retrieved annotated exemplars directly into the model's input as visual prompts. Experiments on the Allen Brain Observatory show that a single carefully selected exemplar improves zero-shot neuron detection and instance segmentation, outperforming multi-exemplar prompting.
AI.motivation: Foundation models face significant challenges in specialized domains like two-photon calcium imaging due to high variability in image appearance across recordings, scarce annotations, and the need for rapid adaptation. Traditional fine-tuning of model weights is impractical in this setting, motivating a need for alternative adaptation strategies.
AI.method: RAVP augments each target tile with a retrieved annotated exemplar whose bounding box serves as a concept prompt, enabling inference-time adaptation purely through input design. The framework studies multiple exemplar selection strategies including fluorescence-guided heuristics and a lightweight recall predictor trained to estimate which exemplar is most informative for a given target tile.
AI.result: Experiments on the Allen Brain Observatory demonstrate that exemplar-augmented inference consistently improves zero-shot neuron detection and instance segmentation. Ablation studies reveal that a single carefully selected exemplar is more effective than prompting with multiple retrieved examples.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time visual memory injection via retrieval-augmented prompting is a simple and effective alternative to parameter adaptation for foundation models in specialized biomedical imaging, positioning RAVP as a practical solution for rapid domain adaptation scenarios.

title: Physical Agentic AI: An Architecture for Orchestrating a Robot Crew with LLMs
summary: Agentic AI frameworks interpret open-ended task goals and decompose them into multi-step plans. Richer information about embodiment-specific capabilities, physical preconditions, and cross-robot coordination improves grounding, but does not eliminate infeasible, mistimed, or unsafe physical actions. Physical robot crews therefore require an explicit architectural interface between semantic planning and execution, where every planned action is verified against robot capabilities, system state, and workflow constraints before actuation. This paper introduces Physical Agentic AI, a framework for skill-grounded robot agent orchestration, in which each robot exposes a typed library of executable skills while a foundation model planner decomposes a task into phases and assigns each phase to a robot-skill pair. A Robot Orchestration layer exposes the skill library, robot state, named locations, and workflow contracts to a non-actuating Mission Planner, while a deterministic Robot Orchestrator validates and authorizes one skill at a time. We evaluate on a drone-UGV search-and-dispatch mission, where every mission in every condition is executed live in Gazebo, and on a humanoid-quadruped transportation task using hardware-equivalent skill interfaces plus two physical trials on a Unitree G1 and Go2. Varying planner knowledge and runtime enforcement independently, we find that retrieval raises skill grounding from 51% to 96% yet leaves informed planners dispatching 23-29% of faulted steps. Per-dispatch enforcement reduces false dispatch to 0% with no false blocks, and a held-plan ablation confirms that the gate, not plan variation, is responsible. Live execution makes the difference physical: without enforcement all eight injected faults crossed the orchestration boundary and six produced robot motion; with enforcement all eight were refused before motion.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Physical Agentic AI, a framework for skill-grounded robot agent orchestration that inserts a deterministic gate between semantic planning and physical execution. Each robot exposes a typed library of executable skills, and a Robot Orchestrator validates and authorizes one skill at a time against robot capabilities, state, and workflow contracts before actuation. Evaluated on drone-UGV search-and-dispatch (in Gazebo) and humanoid-quadruped transportation (hardware-equivalent + physical trials on Unitree G1/Go2), the framework shows that retrieval raises skill grounding from 51% to 96% but planners still dispatch 23-29% faulted steps, while per-dispatch enforcement reduces false dispatch to 0% with no false blocks and prevents all eight injected faults from crossing the orchestration boundary.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI frameworks can decompose open-ended goals into multi-step plans, but richer semantic grounding does not eliminate infeasible, mistimed, or unsafe physical actions. Robot crews therefore need an explicit architectural interface between semantic planning and physical execution—a deterministic verification gate that catches faults before actuation.
AI.method: The framework separates a non-actuating Mission Planner (foundation model) from a deterministic Robot Orchestrator. Each robot exposes a typed skill library with executable skills; a Robot Orchestration layer exposes skill libraries, robot state, named locations, and workflow contracts to the planner. The orchestrator validates and authorizes one skill at a time against capabilities, system state, and workflow constraints. Evaluation independently varies planner knowledge (retrieval) and runtime enforcement, using live Gazebo missions and hardware-equivalent interfaces plus physical trials on Unitree G1 and Go2.
AI.result: Retrieval raises skill grounding from 51% to 96% but informed planners still dispatch 23-29% faulted steps. Per-dispatch enforcement reduces false dispatch to 0% with no false blocks; a held-plan ablation confirms the gate (not plan variation) is responsible. In live execution, without enforcement all eight injected faults crossed the orchestration boundary and six produced robot motion; with enforcement all eight were refused before motion.
AI.conclusion: Semantic planning alone is insufficient for safe physical robot orchestration; a deterministic execution gate between planning and actuation is necessary and effective. The Physical Agentic AI architecture eliminates false dispatches and physically unsafe actions across heterogeneous robot crews.

title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning via Sequential Activation Patching
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable problem-solving capabilities when guided by Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, yet the internal mechanisms underlying these improvements remain poorly understood. In this work, we investigate where CoT-related causal effects emerge across the generated reasoning trajectory and which attention heads carry signals that contribute to final-answer computation. Because CoT reasoning unfolds over multiple generated tokens, standard activation patching at a single static token position is insufficient to characterize these temporally distributed effects. To address this limitation, we introduce a sequential activation patching framework that traces CoT-conditioned attention-head activations across token positions and aggregates their effects using Part-of-Speech-guided analysis. We further introduce Sequential Multi-Head Patching to evaluate the joint contribution of distributed head sets, together with cross-question and random activation controls. Targeted zero-ablation experiments show that the identified heads are functionally important for successful answer generation and affect several overlapping mechanisms, including reasoning-trajectory maintenance, answer anchoring, exemplar-target separation, and numerical generation. Overall, our results provide evidence for distributed reasoning-support sub-circuits associated with CoT-conditioned computation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a sequential activation patching framework to trace Chain-of-Thought (CoT)-related causal effects across generated reasoning trajectories in LLMs, identifying distributed attention-head sub-circuits that support final-answer computation through overlapping mechanisms such as reasoning-trajectory maintenance, answer anchoring, exemplar-target separation, and numerical generation.
AI.motivation: While LLMs show strong problem-solving under CoT prompting, the internal mechanisms behind these improvements are poorly understood. Standard activation patching at a single static token position is insufficient because CoT reasoning unfolds across multiple generated tokens, requiring a temporally distributed analysis approach.
AI.method: The authors propose a sequential activation patching framework that (1) traces CoT-conditioned attention-head activations across token positions, (2) aggregates their effects using Part-of-Speech-guided analysis, (3) introduce Sequential Multi-Head Patching to evaluate the joint contribution of distributed head sets, and (4) use cross-question and random activation controls, followed by targeted zero-ablation experiments.
AI.result: The identified attention heads are functionally important for successful answer generation and affect multiple overlapping mechanisms including reasoning-trajectory maintenance, answer anchoring, exemplar-target separation, and numerical generation.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide evidence for distributed reasoning-support sub-circuits associated with CoT-conditioned computation, advancing understanding of how CoT prompts improve LLM problem-solving capabilities.

title: Redteaming Leading Arabic LLMs with ASAS
summary: As the adoption of large language models (LLMs) grows in Arabic-speaking regions, ensuring their safety and cultural alignment is increasingly critical. However, Arabic LLM safety remains underexplored, especially in adversarial evaluation settings. We introduce the Arabic Safety Index (ASAS), the first fully human-curated Arabic benchmark for redteaming LLMs. ASAS contains 801 prompts spanning 8 safety categories and 8 attack strategies, with ideal responses in Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). We conduct a redteaming evaluation across seven leading models with Arabic capabilities, including GPT-4o, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, and regional models such as ALLaM and FANAR. Human annotators rate responses using a structured 4-point safety scale, revealing that most models fail to defend against 50% of unsafe prompts. Our findings highlight major safety gaps in high-harm categories such as weapons and illicit substances, with direct and obfuscation-based attacks proving most effective. The results also show that language alignment does not readily transfer across languages, and that automated safety judges (e.g., GPT-4o) perform poorly compared to human annotators. ASAS provides a culturally grounded benchmark and redteaming protocol to drive progress in Arabic LLM safety.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ASAS (Arabic Safety Index), the first fully human-curated Arabic benchmark for redteaming LLMs, containing 801 prompts across 8 safety categories and 8 attack strategies. Evaluation of seven leading models reveals most fail to defend against 50% of unsafe prompts, with major gaps in high-harm categories and limitations of automated safety judges.
AI.motivation: Arabic LLM safety is underexplored despite growing adoption in Arabic-speaking regions. The lack of culturally aligned, human-curated adversarial benchmarks for Arabic leaves safety evaluation gaps unaddressed.
AI.method: The authors construct ASAS, a 801-prompt benchmark in Modern Standard Arabic spanning 8 safety categories and 8 attack strategies, with ideal responses. They conduct redteaming across seven LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, ALLaM, FANAR, etc.), using human annotators with a structured 4-point safety scale, and compare against automated safety judges.
AI.result: Most models fail to defend against over 50% of unsafe prompts. Weapons and illicit substances show major safety gaps. Direct and obfuscation-based attacks are most effective. Safety alignment does not transfer across languages, and automated judges like GPT-4o underperform compared to human annotators.
AI.conclusion: ASAS provides a culturally grounded benchmark and redteaming protocol to drive progress in Arabic LLM safety, highlighting the need for language-specific safety evaluation and improved automated judging.

title: Improved denoising diffusion probabilistic models with efficient non-diagonal covariance modeling
summary: The sampling process of Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) can be accelerated by leveraging second-order information in the form of approximations to the denoising posterior covariance -- allowing samples of acceptable quality to be produced in fewer but larger sampling steps. Previous attempts at using such information have used drastic (e.g.\ diagonal) simplifications of the covariance. These do not do justice to the peculiar statistical structure of natural images, which exhibit strong non-diagonal correlations between pixels and color channels, and a slow-decaying power-law frequency spectrum. Here, we develop a novel covariance model that captures these features. Our Kronecker-DCT (K-DCT) model uses a Kronecker-factored decomposition of inter-color covariances and spatial covariances modeled in the frequency domain using the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT). The use of the DCT reduces the computational complexity from quadratic to log-linear, resulting in negligible computational and memory overhead in each denoising step. By learning K-DCT-structured amortizations of the denoising posterior covariance using pre-trained score models on CIFAR-10, Celeb-A, ImageNet and LSUN datasets, we show improved performance compared to previous SOTA denoising samplers, both in terms of FID and likelihoods, especially in the regime of few denoising steps.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a Kronecker-DCT (K-DCT) covariance model for DDPM sampling acceleration, capturing non-diagonal inter-color and spatial correlations in natural images while reducing computational complexity from quadratic to log-linear via the Discrete Cosine Transform, achieving SOTA performance on FID and likelihood measures particularly in few-step regimes.
AI.motivation: DDPM sampling can be accelerated using second-order denoising posterior covariance approximations, allowing larger sampling steps. However, previous attempts used drastic simplifications (e.g., diagonal covariance) that fail to capture the strong non-diagonal correlations between pixels and color channels and the slow-decaying power-law frequency spectrum characteristic of natural images.
AI.method: The authors propose a Kronecker-DCT (K-DCT) covariance model that uses a Kronecker-factored decomposition of inter-color covariances and spatial covariances modeled in the frequency domain via the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT). This reduces computational complexity from quadratic to log-linear. The K-DCT-structured amortizations of denoising posterior covariance are learned using pre-trained score models.
AI.result: The method demonstrates improved performance over previous state-of-the-art denoising samplers on CIFAR-10, Celeb-A, ImageNet, and LSUN datasets, in terms of both FID and likelihood scores, especially notable in the few denoising steps regime. The computational and memory overhead per denoising step is negligible.
AI.conclusion: The K-DCT covariance model effectively captures the statistical structure of natural images for DDPM sampling acceleration, providing a computationally efficient way to leverage second-order information, leading to better sample quality with fewer sampling steps than previous approaches.

title: Exact Finite-Length Theory of Uniform Car Parking: Spatial Laws, Absorption, and Aggregation
summary: The uniform car-parking process is the one-dimensional random sequential adsorption of unit cars on a segment of finite length $s$: cars arrive at uniformly random positions and park wherever they fit, until no gap admits another. This paper develops the exact finite-$s$ theory. The joint density of the parked positions is resolved into jamming cells, on each of which it is a rational function, and evaluated by a subset recursion in $O(2^n n)$ operations; the marginal and gap order statistics are obtained as hyperlogarithms whose weight is fixed by the number of coordinates integrated out; and the absorption count and the aggregate quantities are treated through the integral equation descending from Rényi.

AI.tldr: This paper develops the exact finite-segment theory of the uniform car-parking process (one-dimensional random sequential adsorption), resolving the joint density of parked positions into jamming cells with rational-function structure, computable via subset recursion in O(2^n n) operations, and deriving marginal/gap order statistics as hyperlogarithms with weights fixed by integrated coordinates, plus treatment of absorption count and aggregate quantities via Rényi's integral equation.
AI.motivation: To provide exact finite-length results for the uniform car-parking process, moving beyond asymptotic or heuristic treatments and establishing rigorous analytic structure for the joint density, order statistics, and absorption statistics on a segment of length s.
AI.method: Resolves the joint density of parked positions into jamming cells where it takes rational form; evaluates these via a subset recursion requiring O(2^n n) operations; obtains marginal and gap order statistics as hyperlogarithms with weight equal to the number of integrated-out coordinates; treats absorption count and aggregate quantities through Rényi's integral equation.
AI.result: An exact finite-s theory is developed: joint densities are rational on jamming cells and computed efficiently by recursion; marginals and gap statistics are expressed as hyperlogarithms with prescribed weights; absorption and aggregate quantities follow from the Rényi integral equation.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a complete exact framework for the finite-segment uniform car-parking process, providing computable closed-form expressions for joint distributions and statistics, thereby extending Rényi's classical approach to full finite-length detail.

title: Register Shifts Break LLM Safety: A Bengali Benchmark with Culturally Grounded Harms
summary: Bengali is the seventh-most-spoken language globally, yet LLM safety evaluation remains overwhelmingly English-centric. We introduce BanglaSafe, a benchmark of 879 Bengali prompts combining 309 natively authored prompts with 570 expert-reviewed prompts, spanning 17 culturally grounded harm categories and five prompting conditions that vary language, writing style, and authority framing. Evaluating 18 frontier LLMs, we find that over half of all responses are unsafe or partially unsafe (53.6%) while 14.7% contains strictly harmful content, and that the strongest observed effect is not the switch from English to Bengali but the choice of writing style within Bengali: the same harmful request phrased as a formal newspaper investigation succeeds 17 percentage points more often than the same request phrased as a casual message, with no adversarial engineering involved. We further show that existing safety classifiers struggle to reliably evaluate Bengali content, with even frontier models failing on nearly half of all cases.

AI.tldr: BanglaSafe is a benchmark of 879 Bengali prompts spanning 17 culturally grounded harm categories and five prompting conditions. Evaluating 18 LLMs reveals that over half of responses contain unsafe content, with formal writing style being the strongest attack vector (17pp success increase over casual style) without adversarial engineering. Existing safety classifiers also struggle with Bengali content.
AI.motivation: LLM safety evaluation is overwhelmingly English-centric despite Bengali being the seventh-most-spoken language globally, leaving a critical gap in non-English safety assessment.
AI.method: Constructed BanglaSafe with 879 Bengali prompts (309 natively authored + 570 expert-reviewed) across 17 culturally grounded harm categories and five prompting conditions varying language, writing style, and authority framing. Evaluated 18 frontier LLMs for safety response rates and tested existing safety classifiers on Bengali content.
AI.result: 53.6% of responses are unsafe or partially unsafe, and 14.7% contain strictly harmful content. The strongest effect is writing style within Bengali—formal newspaper investigation phrasing succeeds 17pp more than casual messaging. Frontier safety classifiers fail on nearly half of Bengali cases.
AI.conclusion: Non-English safety evaluation is severely lacking; LLM safety is dramatically weaker in Bengali, with even benign style variations substantially increasing harm rates, and current safety classifiers are unreliable for Bengali content.

title: DynaContext: Self-Improving Dynamic Contextualization of Optimized Prompts for Heterogeneous Parameter Extraction
summary: Automated prompt and skill optimization typically produces a single static instruction that is reused across inference instances until the next optimization cycle. However, this approach cannot adapt when the required context, constraints, and evidence vary from one instance to another. For instance, parameter extraction from electronic component descriptions breaks this assumption: resistors, capacitors, transistors, and connectors require different fields, unit constraints, and demonstrations, and each input provides a different evidence state. We introduce DynaContext, a framework that combines an offline-optimized extraction core, learned with GEPA or SkillOpt, with inference-time contextual adaptation and validation-gated self-improvement. DynaContext routes each item through internal, external, or fallback evidence paths and composes an item-specific prompt from the core, schema, evidence, unresolved fields, and validated demonstrations. Deterministic validation and an LLM judge gate every output, uncertain cases go to human review, and only human-verified corrections enter the demonstration memory. On a single-category benchmark, average accuracy increases from 86.6% for the base prompt to 96.9% for standalone SkillOpt and 98.6% for the best DynaContext configuration. Across 850 heterogeneous gold parameter facts, average field-level F1 increases from 51.8% for an unoptimized, demonstration-free control to 59.2% with dynamic demonstrations alone, 66.9% with the optimized core alone, and 71.0% with both. Holding the model fixed, the full configuration outperforms the deployed static-prompting pipeline by 17.3 F1 points on average.

AI.tldr: DynaContext is a framework for adaptive, instance-specific prompt optimization in parameter extraction tasks. It combines an offline-optimized extraction core with inference-time contextual adaptation, evidence routing, validation gating, and human-verified self-improvement. It achieves up to 98.6% accuracy on a single-category benchmark and 71.0% field-level F1 on heterogeneous data, outperforming static prompting by 17.3 F1 points.
AI.motivation: Standard automated prompt and skill optimization produces a single static instruction reused across all inference instances. This fails when context, constraints, and evidence vary per instance—as in parameter extraction from electronic component descriptions, where different component types require different fields, unit constraints, and demonstrations, and each input has a unique evidence state.
AI.method: DynaContext combines an offline-optimized extraction core (learned with GEPA or SkillOpt) with inference-time contextual adaptation and validation-gated self-improvement. It routes each item through internal, external, or fallback evidence paths and constructs an item-specific prompt from the core, schema, evidence, unresolved fields, and validated demonstrations. Deterministic validation and an LLM judge gate every output; uncertain cases go to human review, and only human-verified corrections enter demonstration memory.
AI.result: On a single-category benchmark, average accuracy rises from 86.6% (base prompt) to 96.9% (standalone SkillOpt) and 98.6% (best DynaContext). Across 850 heterogeneous gold parameter facts, field-level F1 increases from 51.8% (unoptimized control) to 59.2% (dynamic demonstrations), 66.9% (optimized core alone), and 71.0% (both). The full configuration outperforms a deployed static-prompting pipeline by 17.3 F1 points with the model held fixed.
AI.conclusion: Instance-specific, context-aware prompt composition substantially outperforms static optimized prompting. DynaContext demonstrates that combining offline optimization with inference-time adaptation, evidence routing, and validation-gated self-improvement yields large gains in structured extraction accuracy, especially under heterogeneous input conditions.

title: Close Shortcut Wins Long: Seeking Diverse and Stable Generators for Data-Free Knowledge Distillation
summary: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (DFKD) preserves privacy by transferring knowledge without real data access. However, existing generator-based DFKD methods suffer from over-reliance on teacher preferences and pattern collapse, exhibiting "generative shortcut learning" in the frequency domain: dependent on specific frequency components and frequency positions, resulting in inconsistent synthetic image quality and class diversity. In this paper, we propose a CSWL framework aimed at introducing insights from the frequency domain perspective to improve generator diversity and training stability to Close the phenomenon of Shortcut learning to Win in the Longer term. To address the issue of generative shortcut learning, we introduce frequency-domain augmentation at the feature level, encouraging the generator to attend to the full frequency spectrum and thereby suppress shortcut learning behavior. To tackle training instability, we propose a Cross-Stage Frequency Reconstruction (CSFR) auxiliary task, which implicitly constructs an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) mechanism to promote long-term optimization and stability. Extensive experiments, including downstream tasks and various image recognition datasets at multiple resolutions, validate the effectiveness of CSWL in improving both diversity and stability from the frequency view.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CSWL, a frequency-domain framework for Data-Free Knowledge Distillation that addresses "generative shortcut learning" (over-reliance on specific frequency components/positions) by introducing feature-level frequency augmentation and a Cross-Stage Frequency Reconstruction (CSFR) auxiliary task with an implicit EMA mechanism, improving generator diversity and training stability.
AI.motivation: Existing generator-based DFKD methods suffer from generative shortcut learning in the frequency domain, where generators depend on specific frequency components and positions, leading to inconsistent synthetic image quality and class diversity. This undermines the effectiveness of data-free knowledge transfer.
AI.method: CSWL introduces two key components: (1) feature-level frequency-domain augmentation that encourages the generator to attend to the full frequency spectrum, suppressing shortcut learning; (2) a Cross-Stage Frequency Reconstruction (CSFR) auxiliary task that implicitly builds an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) mechanism to promote long-term optimization and training stability.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on downstream tasks and multiple image recognition datasets at various resolutions validate that CSWL improves both generator diversity and training stability from a frequency-domain perspective.
AI.conclusion: The frequency-domain insights provide an effective means to close the shortcut learning phenomenon in DFKD, achieving improved synthetic image quality, class diversity, and stable long-term training—with the framework named CSWL to reflect "closing shortcut learning to win in the longer term."

title: VikPath: A Vision Kansformer Framework for Effective Obstacle Avoidance in Self-Supervised Pathfinding
summary: Pathfinding is a fundamental problem in artificial intelligence and autonomous systems. Traditional heuristic-based algorithms, such as A*, rely on predefined heuristic functions to guide the search process. Although effective in structured environments, their search efficiency can degrade substantially in complex, obstacle-rich scenarios, where handcrafted heuristics may provide limited guidance. Recent studies have explored learning-based approaches to improve pathfinding efficiency; however, most existing methods rely on supervised learning and require labels generated by conventional planners or obtained through manual annotation. As a result, their performance is inherently influenced by the quality of the underlying supervision and may degrade when the labeling heuristics fail to capture complex environmental structures. Moreover, existing methods primarily optimize for path length while paying limited attention to obstacle clearance and trajectory smoothness, which can lead to paths that are difficult or unsafe to execute in real-world environments. To address these limitations, we propose $\Design$, a self-supervised pathfinding framework that jointly considers obstacle proximity and path smoothness. At its core, our novel \textit{Vision Kansformer} module learns representations of obstacle distributions without relying on labeled trajectories, enabling the model to better adapt to complex environments. We further introduce a sharp-turn penalty to encourage smoother and more practically executable paths. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, compared with state-of-the-art (SOTA) approaches, $\Design$ achieves an average of 3.28\% greater obstacle clearance and 87.07\% lower inference latency while maintaining smooth path generation.

AI.tldr: Design, a self-supervised pathfinding framework, jointly optimizes obstacle clearance and path smoothness using a novel Vision Kansformer module and sharp-turn penalty, achieving 3.28% greater obstacle clearance, 87.07% lower inference latency, and smoother paths compared to SOTA methods.
AI.motivation: Traditional heuristic-based pathfinding (e.g., A*) degrades in complex, obstacle-rich environments. Existing learning-based methods rely on supervised labels from conventional planners, inheriting their limitations, and primarily optimize path length while neglecting obstacle clearance and trajectory smoothness, leading to paths that are unsafe or difficult to execute in real-world settings.
AI.method: Design is a self-supervised pathfinding framework featuring a novel Vision Kansformer module that learns representations of obstacle distributions without labeled trajectories, and a sharp-turn penalty to encourage smoother, more practical paths.
AI.result: Compared to SOTA approaches, Design achieves an average of 3.28% greater obstacle clearance and 87.07% lower inference latency while maintaining smooth path generation.
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised representation learning of obstacle distributions, combined with smoothness-aware optimization, can produce safer, faster, and more executable paths without relying on planner-generated labels, overcoming key limitations of supervised pathfinding methods.

title: When Not to Imitate: Boundary-Aware Skill Memory for Reliable Tool-Use LLM Agents
summary: Extracting skills from past successes is critical for the efficient evolution of Large Language Model (LLM) agents. Prevailing agent self-evolution paradigms typically rely on a core assumption: equipping LLMs with skill memories derived from successful trajectories will monotonically improve their problem-solving capabilities. However, probe analyses reveal that extracting skills solely from successful trajectories traps the model in a \textbf{Skill Imitation Trap}. For tasks that resemble past successes but require different tools, retrieving more skills paradoxically increases the model's confidence in wrong tool calls---procedure skills raise the wrong-tool margin by $47\%$ over a memory-free baseline. To overcome this limitation, we propose \textbf{Boundary-Aware Skill Memory} (BASM), which augments each skill with explicit boundary fields---applicability conditions, risk cues, avoidance rules, and recovery notes. These fields transform each retrieved skill from an unconditional action template into state-conditioned guidance: the agent applies the skill when its conditions hold, suppresses inapplicable tool calls when they do not, and issues targeted repairs when execution fails. Across three agent benchmarks and four model scales, BASM consistently outperforms success-distilled skill-memory baselines: it improves task success rate by up to $23.8\%$ on AppWorld, accuracy by up to $5.0\%$ on BFCL, and reduces attack success rate by $4.6\%$ on AgentDojo, while simultaneously reducing average AppWorld steps by up to $6.6\%$ relative to the memory-free baseline.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies the "Skill Imitation Trap" where extracting skills solely from successful LLM agent trajectories can paradoxically harm performance on tasks that resemble past successes but require different tools, increasing wrong-tool confidence by up to 47%. The authors propose Boundary-Aware Skill Memory (BASM), which augments each skill with explicit boundary fields (applicability conditions, risk cues, avoidance rules, recovery notes), transforming skills from unconditional action templates into state-conditioned guidance. BASM consistently outperforms success-distilled baselines across three benchmarks (AppWorld, BFCL, AgentDojo) and four model scales, improving success rates by up to 23.8%.
AI.motivation: Prevailing agent self-evolution paradigms assume that equipping LLMs with skill memories from successful trajectories monotonically improves problem-solving. However, probe analyses reveal this assumption is flawed: extracting skills solely from successful trajectories traps models in a "Skill Imitation Trap" — for tasks similar to past successes but requiring different tools, retrieving more skills increases the model's confidence in wrong tool calls rather than reducing it.
AI.method: BASM augments each extracted skill with explicit boundary fields: (1) applicability conditions, (2) risk cues, (3) avoidance rules, and (4) recovery notes. These transform skills from unconditional action templates into state-conditioned guidance — the agent applies a skill when conditions hold, suppresses inapplicable tool calls when they do not, and issues targeted repairs on execution failure.
AI.result: Across three agent benchmarks and four model scales, BASM outperforms success-distilled skill-memory baselines: improving task success rate by up to 23.8% on AppWorld, accuracy by up to 5.0% on BFCL, and reducing attack success rate by 4.6% on AgentDojo, while reducing average AppWorld steps by up to 6.6% relative to the memory-free baseline.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that boundary-aware skill augmentation is essential for reliable agent self-evolution — naive success-distilled skill memory can actively harm performance by inducing overconfident wrong tool calls, and explicit boundary information is needed to make retrieved skills safely conditional on state rather than blindly imitative.

title: SPAR-Hate: An Auditor-Guided Multi-Agent Framework for Bilingual Hate Speech Parsing
summary: Hate speech detection has recently shifted from coarse-grained classification to structured parsing, where systems must jointly identify hateful targets, arguments, and target-level labels. However, existing studies primarily emphasize benchmark evaluation while paying less attention to the cultural, linguistic, and social-group challenges involved in structured hate speech parsing. To address these challenges, we propose SPAR-Hate, an auditor-guided multi-agent framework for bilingual hate speech parsing. The framework first decomposes documents into clause-level decision units and then generates evidence-grounded judgments from three complementary perspectives: Victim, Moderator, and Cultural Bystander. An evidence-constrained arbitration process resolves conflicts among role-specific predictions and aggregates them into structured sample-level outputs. Experiments on the STATE-ToxiCN and TBO benchmarks show that SPAR-Hate consistently improves bilingual hate parsing across diverse large language models. The framework achieves state-of-the-art results on bilingual multi-tuple extraction tasks, with the largest gains observed under stricter structural evaluation metrics.

AI.tldr: SPAR-Hate is an auditor-guided multi-agent framework for structured bilingual (Chinese-English) hate speech parsing that decomposes text into clause-level units, generates judgments from three complementary role perspectives (Victim, Moderator, Cultural Bystander), and uses evidence-constrained arbitration to produce structured sample-level outputs. It achieves state-of-the-art results on STATE-ToxiCN and TBO benchmarks, with largest gains under stricter structural evaluation metrics.
AI.motivation: Existing structured hate speech parsing research focuses primarily on benchmark evaluation while neglecting cultural, linguistic, and social-group challenges inherent in the task, particularly in bilingual contexts.
AI.method: The framework decomposes documents into clause-level decision units, generates evidence-grounded judgments from three complementary perspectives (Victim, Moderator, Cultural Bystander), and employs an evidence-constrained arbitration process to resolve conflicts and aggregate predictions into structured sample-level outputs.
AI.result: SPAR-Hate consistently improves bilingual hate parsing across diverse LLMs, achieving state-of-the-art results on bilingual multi-tuple extraction tasks on STATE-ToxiCN and TBO benchmarks, with the largest improvements under stricter structural evaluation metrics.
AI.conclusion: A multi-perspective, auditor-guided approach effectively addresses cultural and linguistic challenges in structured hate speech parsing, demonstrating robust gains over existing methods on bilingual benchmarks.

title: ORBIT++: Benchmarking SfM in the Wild with 360° Video
comment: A revision was Accepted at CVPR 2026
summary: Structure-from-Motion (SfM) is a cornerstone of 3D perception, yet current methods often fail when applied to complex videos involving challenging camera motions or dynamic scenes. Compounding the problem, the field lacks reliable ground-truth benchmarks for such difficult scenarios, making it hard to gauge real-world progress or to pinpoint where improvements are most needed. To address this gap, we introduce a new benchmark for evaluating camera pose estimation. Our key insight is to leverage online panoramic 360° video as a source of data from which to construct challenging clips, while still enabling robust ground-truth trajectory recovery. The panoramic nature of these videos provides richer visual context for tracking camera motion, even when parts of the view are affected by blur, motion, or dynamic objects. After tracking camera motion across full 360° videos, we crop and reproject selected portions to generate perspective-view clips that serve as our benchmark, called ORBIT. Experiments show that COLMAP, as well as recent optimization-based and feed-forward SfM methods struggle to accurately estimate camera poses on our benchmark. Hence, ORBIT provides a valuable testbed where researchers can meaningfully measure progress on truly challenging, real-world SfM problems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ORBIT, a new benchmark for camera pose estimation built from online panoramic 360° videos. By leveraging the rich visual context of panoramic footage, the authors construct challenging perspective-view clips with reliable ground-truth trajectories, demonstrating that existing SfM methods (COLMAP, optimization-based, and feed-forward approaches) struggle on this benchmark.
AI.motivation: Current Structure-from-Motion methods fail on complex videos with challenging camera motions or dynamic scenes, and the field lacks reliable ground-truth benchmarks for such difficult scenarios, making it hard to gauge real-world progress or identify where improvements are most needed.
AI.method: The authors introduce ORBIT, a benchmark built from online panoramic 360° videos. They track camera motion across full 360° videos (which provide richer visual context robust to blur, motion, or dynamic objects), then crop and reproject selected portions to generate perspective-view clips. This pipeline enables the construction of challenging clips while still allowing robust ground-truth trajectory recovery.
AI.result: Experiments show that COLMAP, recent optimization-based, and feed-forward SfM methods all struggle to accurately estimate camera poses on ORBIT, confirming that the benchmark presents truly challenging, real-world problems.
AI.conclusion: ORBIT provides a valuable testbed for researchers to meaningfully measure progress on challenging, real-world SfM problems, filling a critical gap in the benchmarking landscape.

title: RACO: Reliability-Aware Coarse-Goal Optimization for Inspection-Oriented UAV Vision-Language Navigation
summary: UAV vision-language navigation (UAV-VLN) is commonly evaluated as goal reaching, but inspection-oriented deployment requires the agent to stop within a valid inspection region and avoid falsely confirming visually or semantically similar distractors. This requirement exposes a key weakness in existing coarse-to-fine UAV-VLN policies: the coarse goal predicted before local refinement is often treated as reliable, although it may drift toward plausible but incorrect object regions and limit the ability of the local stage to recover. To systematically evaluate this problem, we introduce LG-UVI, an object-centric inspection evaluation setting derived from CityNav/CityRefer. LG-UVI extends standard UAV-VLN episodes with target objects, hard distractors, type-aware inspection regions, and diagnostics for inspection-region arrival and object-level confirmation. To address this inspection-oriented setting, we further propose RACO, a reliability-aware adaptive coarse-to-fine navigation framework. Instead of treating the predicted coarse goal as a fixed waypoint, RACO views it as a runtime hypothesis and uses object-level candidate anchors to check and correct coarse localization before Stage 1 and at the Stage 1-to-Stage 2 boundary. RACO also applies scale-adaptive terminal refinement to handle terminal near-miss cases using runtime-observable geometric and anchor-based evidence. Under a unified online evaluation protocol, RACO improves SR over the reproduced HETT baseline by 9.53 and 7.98 percentage points on validation-unseen and test-unseen, respectively. It also improves inspection-region arrival and reduces false verification risk, showing that coarse-goal reliability optimization is an effective complement to existing coarse-to-fine UAV-VLN policies.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a key weakness in coarse-to-fine UAV-VLN policies for inspection-oriented tasks: coarse goals predicted before local refinement may drift toward incorrect object regions and limit recovery. The authors introduce LG-UVI, an object-centric inspection evaluation benchmark derived from CityNav/CityRefer, and propose RACO, a reliability-aware adaptive coarse-to-fine navigation framework that treats coarse goals as runtime hypotheses, uses object-level candidate anchors for correction, and applies scale-adaptive terminal refinement.
AI.motivation: Traditional UAV-VLN evaluation focuses on goal reaching, but real inspection-oriented deployment requires agents to stop within valid inspection regions and avoid false confirmation of visually or semantically similar distractors. Existing coarse-to-fine UAV-VLN policies treat the coarse goal as reliable, even though it can drift toward plausible but incorrect object regions, limiting the local stage's ability to recover.
AI.method: The paper introduces LG-UVI, an object-centric inspection evaluation setting extending standard UAV-VLN episodes with target objects, hard distractors, type-aware inspection regions, and diagnostics. It proposes RACO, which: (1) treats the predicted coarse goal as a runtime hypothesis rather than a fixed waypoint; (2) uses object-level candidate anchors to check and correct coarse localization before Stage 1 and at the Stage 1-to-Stage 2 boundary; (3) applies scale-adaptive terminal refinement using runtime-observable geometric and anchor-based evidence for terminal near-miss cases.
AI.result: Under a unified online evaluation protocol, RACO improves Success Rate over the reproduced HETT baseline by 9.53 and 7.98 percentage points on validation-unseen and test-unseen splits, respectively. It also improves inspection-region arrival and reduces false verification risk.
AI.conclusion: Coarse-goal reliability optimization is an effective complement to existing coarse-to-fine UAV-VLN policies. RACO demonstrates that treating coarse goals as hypotheses subject to correction, rather than fixed waypoints, significantly improves inspection-oriented navigation performance.

title: One-Step Evolution for Long-Time Extrapolation: An Error-Bound-Informed and Prior-Guided Neural Residual Framework for Autonomous PDEs
summary: Accurate simulation of the long-time evolution of systems governed by partial differential equations (PDEs) is central to scientific computing. Among existing deep learning?based approaches for solving PDEs, neural operators typically rely on extensive trajectory data, whereas physics-informed meth?ods often exhibit limited stability during long-time extrapolation. For a well-posed autonomous PDE, long-time trajectories can be generated by repeated composition of a fixed-step evolution operator; hence, long-time extrapolation depends on controlling the approximation error of this operator and the propagation of that error under recursive composition. Accordingly, we propose a numerical-prior-guided, physics-constrained method trained without ground-truth trajectory supervision: a low-cost numerical prior reduces the difficulty of approximating the one?step evolution operator, while a weak-form PDE residual provides a computable proxy for the one-step error term in the error?propagation bound. We validate the method on five benchmark cases spanning four PDE classes and compare it with ten physics?informed learning methods under a unified protocol that excludes ground-truth trajectories from training and model selection. The results indicate that, in all five cases, the proposed method reduces long-time extrapolation error relative to the numerical prior and outperforms the best competing baseline in each case, thereby improving long-time simulation accuracy across different PDEs without ground-truth trajectory supervision. The source code developed for this paper will be made publicly available upon acceptance of the manuscript.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a numerical-prior-guided, physics-constrained deep learning method for solving PDEs that achieves accurate long-time trajectory simulation without ground-truth trajectory supervision. By combining a low-cost numerical prior to ease one-step evolution operator approximation and a weak-form PDE residual as a proxy for the one-step error in the error-propagation bound, the method reduces long-time extrapolation error across five benchmark cases spanning four PDE classes, outperforming ten physics-informed baselines.
AI.motivation: Long-time simulation of PDE-governed systems is central to scientific computing, but existing approaches have significant limitations: neural operators require extensive trajectory data, while physics-informed methods suffer from poor stability during long-time extrapolation. Since long-time trajectories can be generated by recursively composing a fixed-step evolution operator, controlling both the one-step approximation error and its propagation under composition is key—motivating a method that addresses both without needing ground-truth trajectory supervision.
AI.method: The proposed approach is a numerical-prior-guided, physics-constrained framework: (1) a low-cost numerical prior is used to reduce the difficulty of approximating the one-step evolution operator, and (2) a weak-form PDE residual serves as a computable proxy for the one-step error term appearing in the error-propagation bound. Training is conducted without ground-truth trajectory supervision, and model selection follows the same constraint.
AI.result: Validated on five benchmark cases spanning four PDE classes, the method is compared against ten physics-informed learning baselines under a unified protocol excluding ground-truth trajectories from training and selection. In all five cases, the proposed method reduces long-time extrapolation error relative to the numerical prior and outperforms the best competing baseline.
AI.conclusion: The method consistently improves long-time simulation accuracy across different PDEs without relying on ground-truth trajectory supervision, demonstrating a robust and generalizable alternative to existing neural operator and physics-informed approaches for long-time PDE evolution.

title: Physics Filtering Favors the Generalization of Robot Learning
summary: Living organisms exhibit extraordinary adaptability to unseen environments through their intrinsic physical structures and lifelong feedback-driven learning. Endowing robots with comparable generalization is critical for reliable operation in the real world. While recent approaches attempt to improve generalization by scaling training data, such strategies remain impractical for robotics, where collecting real-world demonstrations at the scale of large language models is prohibitively costly and slow. Contrary to this reliance on massive datasets, we show that robots can generalize effectively under dynamics uncertainties even with limited training data by leveraging a feedback mechanism, namely PhyFilter, that corrects learning outputs with physics-filtered learning residuals. PhyFilter operates as a lightweight, model-agnostic module whose parameters can be automatically optimized through an auto-learning algorithm, eliminating manual tuning and enabling seamless integration with diverse robot policies. We validate PhyFilter across four representative robotic systems, demonstrating that it enables quadruped robots to generalize to unseen terrains, payload variations, and speed ranges; drones to flight under unseen wind disturbances; aerial manipulators to achieve centimeter-level in-air capture despite wind and mass uncertainties; and acceleration differentiators to remain robust with distribution shift. These results show that physics-filtered feedback can serve as a powerful alternative to massive data scaling.

AI.tldr: PhyFilter is a lightweight, model-agnostic feedback module that corrects robot learning outputs with physics-filtered learning residuals, enabling effective generalization under dynamics uncertainties without relying on massive training data.
AI.motivation: Robots need to generalize to unseen environments, but scaling training data (as done in large language models) is impractical for robotics due to the prohibitive cost and slowness of collecting real-world demonstrations. The paper challenges the data-scaling paradigm by seeking an alternative mechanism for generalization.
AI.method: PhyFilter operates as a lightweight, model-agnostic module that corrects learning outputs using physics-filtered learning residuals. Its parameters are automatically optimized via an auto-learning algorithm, eliminating manual tuning and enabling seamless integration with diverse robot policies.
AI.result: Validation across four robotic systems: quadruped robots generalize to unseen terrains, payload variations, and speed ranges; drones fly under unseen wind disturbances; aerial manipulators achieve centimeter-level in-air capture despite wind and mass uncertainties; and acceleration differentiators remain robust under distribution shift.
AI.conclusion: Physics-filtered feedback can serve as a powerful alternative to massive data scaling for achieving robot generalization under dynamics uncertainties.

title: Can Large Language Models "Hyper-Thread"?
summary: Large language models generate tokens sequentially, but can they execute multiple tasks concurrently while forming each token? Broader attention allocation may provide a mechanism for such task concurrency. Existing approaches to scaling inference primarily rely on longer generations, more samples, or additional verification stages, while attention dispersion is often treated as a signal of interference or error. Task concurrency within serial generation therefore remains underexplored. We propose the Model Hyper-Threading Hypothesis and evaluate its predictions using multiple coordinated tasks that share state within the same problem. We design three conditions (Baseline, Serial Functional Scheduling, and Concurrent Functional Loading) and evaluate their benefits and costs using accuracy, output-token distributions, and attention metrics. On an AIME 2025 development set, Concurrent Functional Loading achieves the highest accuracy. Relative to Serial Functional Scheduling, its typical output length is similar and it is shorter on most problems, while exhibiting greater attention dispersion and higher task-relevant coverage, albeit with a heavier output-length tail. Within-step concurrency and its causal mechanism still require direct tests. Our results show that more dispersed attention can coexist with higher accuracy, providing preliminary behavioral and correlational evidence for the hyper-threading hypothesis. These findings motivate a shift in perspective on inference scaling from "generating more tokens" toward "having each generation step carry more tasks," pointing to a new avenue for improving reasoning performance.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the Model Hyper-Threading Hypothesis, suggesting that large language models can execute multiple concurrent tasks while generating each token, analogous to CPU hyper-threading. Through experiments with coordinated multi-task problems on an AIME 2025 development set, the authors find that Concurrent Functional Loading achieves the highest accuracy compared to baseline and serial approaches, with more dispersed attention and higher task-relevant coverage, providing preliminary evidence for task concurrency within serial generation.
AI.motivation: Existing inference scaling approaches rely on longer generations, more samples, or additional verification stages, while attention dispersion is typically treated as a sign of interference or error. Task concurrency within serial generation—where multiple tasks execute simultaneously while forming each token—remains largely unexplored, motivating an investigation into whether broader attention allocation can enable concurrent task execution and improve reasoning performance.
AI.method: The authors formalize the Model Hyper-Threading Hypothesis and test its predictions using multiple coordinated tasks that share state within the same problem. They design three experimental conditions: (1) Baseline, (2) Serial Functional Scheduling (executing tasks sequentially), and (3) Concurrent Functional Loading (executing tasks concurrently). They evaluate the three conditions using accuracy, output-token distributions, and attention metrics on an AIME 2025 development set.
