AI.result: Concurrent Functional Loading achieves the highest accuracy on the AIME 2025 development set. Compared to Serial Functional Scheduling, it produces similar typical output length, shorter lengths on most problems, greater attention dispersion, and higher task-relevant coverage, though with a heavier output-length tail. This demonstrates that more dispersed attention can coexist with higher accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The results provide preliminary behavioral and correlational evidence for the hyper-threading hypothesis, suggesting a paradigm shift in inference scaling from "generating more tokens" to "having each generation step carry more tasks." This opens a new avenue for improving reasoning performance, though direct tests of within-step concurrency and its causal mechanism remain for future work.

title: More Accurate or More Efficient? Evaluating Locally Deployed Compact Open-Weight Language Models for Mathematical Reasoning
summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed on local hardware for privacy, cost, and accessibility reasons. Yet many evaluations emphasize accuracy while fewer quantify local runtime and energy, characterize failure modes, or apply paired statistical comparisons under controlled conditions. This paper presents a controlled, documented procedure for evaluating locally hosted LLMs on mathematical reasoning. It combines fixed inference settings, hierarchical answer extraction and verification, explicit failure-mode classification, and per-question resource measurement, and reports accuracy with paired significance tests and effect sizes. We demonstrate it in a preliminary study of three compact open-weight models under five billion parameters, Gemma3:4b (Google), Phi3:3.8b (Microsoft), and Qwen3:4b (Alibaba), across datasets spanning Grade 8 Math, Calculus I, and Advanced Probability and Statistics. All models ran through the same local inference server on one workstation, using a shared prompt template, controlled settings, and a matched question set per dataset. No single model dominates. Qwen3:4b is most accurate on two datasets and Gemma3:4b on Calculus I, yet Gemma3:4b returns roughly three times more correct answers per watt-hour than Qwen3:4b on every dataset while generating far fewer output tokens; Qwen3:4b requires substantially more generation time, energy, and output per question. Phi3:3.8b is substantially less accurate on all three datasets; its low extraction-failure rate indicates incorrect answers rather than unparsed output, though we caveat possible prompt-format effects. These preliminary findings indicate that accuracy alone is an insufficient basis for selecting a local model.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a controlled, documented evaluation procedure for locally hosted LLMs on mathematical reasoning, combining fixed inference settings, hierarchical answer extraction, failure-mode classification, and per-question resource measurement with paired significance tests. A preliminary study of three sub-5B parameter models (Gemma3:4b, Phi3:3.8b, Qwen3:4b) across three math datasets shows no single model dominates: Qwen3:4b is most accurate on two datasets and Gemma3:4b on Calculus I, but Gemma3:4b achieves roughly 3× more correct answers per watt-hour with far fewer output tokens, while Phi3:3.8b is substantially less accurate overall.
AI.motivation: Most LLM evaluations emphasize accuracy while neglecting local runtime, energy consumption, failure-mode characterization, and rigorous paired statistical comparisons under controlled conditions. This gap is increasingly important as models are deployed on local hardware for privacy, cost, and accessibility reasons.
AI.method: A controlled evaluation procedure featuring: fixed inference settings, hierarchical answer extraction and verification, explicit failure-mode classification, per-question resource measurement, and paired significance tests with effect sizes. Demonstrated on three compact open-weight models (<5B parameters) using a shared prompt template, a single local inference server, matched question sets, and datasets spanning Grade 8 Math, Calculus I, and Advanced Probability and Statistics.
AI.result: No single model dominates. Qwen3:4b is most accurate on two datasets and Gemma3:4b on Calculus I. Gemma3:4b returns roughly 3× more correct answers per watt-hour than Qwen3:4b across all datasets while generating far fewer output tokens. Qwen3:4b requires substantially more generation time, energy, and output per question. Phi3:3.8b is substantially less accurate on all datasets, with a low extraction-failure rate indicating incorrect responses rather than unparsed output (with caveats about prompt-format effects).
AI.conclusion: Accuracy alone is an insufficient criterion for selecting a local model; energy efficiency and token generation characteristics must also be considered. The proposed procedure provides a reproducible framework for evaluating locally hosted LLMs that captures both quality and resource trade-offs.

title: Competitive Memory Readout for Robust Video Object Segmentation: 2nd Place Technical Report for the MOSEv2 Track of the 8th LSVOS Challenge
summary: We present our solution for the MOSEv2 track of the 8th Large-scale Video Object Segmentation (LSVOS) Challenge at ECCV 2026. The challenge evaluates robust video object segmentation under complex temporal dynamics, including long-term occlusion, disappearance and reappearance, large appearance changes, and strong interference from visually similar objects. Our method builds on SAM~3 and focuses on its memory readout. Standard target-only memory retrieval can confuse the annotated target with same-class non-target objects because such distractors are represented only implicitly as background. Our method introduces Competitive Memory Readout, which explicitly incorporates same-class competitor evidence when retrieving target information from memory. To prevent excessive suppression of weak or reappearing targets, we further apply a lightweight adaptive restoration rule after competition. The resulting system retains the original SAM~3 tracking pipeline while improving target identity preservation in challenging videos. Our submission achieves 66.20 on the primary challenge score and ranks 2nd in the MOSEv2 track.

AI.tldr: A MOSEv2 track solution for the LSVOS Challenge at ECCV 2026 that introduces Competitive Memory Readout on top of SAM 3 to handle same-class distractor interference, plus an adaptive restoration rule to avoid over-suppression, achieving 2nd place with a primary score of 66.20.
AI.motivation: Standard target-only memory retrieval in SAM 3 can confuse the annotated target with same-class non-target objects because these distractors are only implicitly represented as background, causing identity confusion in videos with complex temporal dynamics such as occlusion, reappearance, appearance changes, and similar-looking object interference.
AI.method: The method builds on SAM 3 and modifies its memory readout mechanism. Competitive Memory Readout is introduced to explicitly incorporate same-class competitor evidence when retrieving target information from memory, rather than relying on implicit background representation. A lightweight adaptive restoration rule is applied after competition to prevent excessive suppression of weak or reappearing targets. The rest of the SAM 3 tracking pipeline is kept intact.
AI.result: The system achieves a primary challenge score of 66.20 and ranks 2nd in the MOSEv2 track of the 8th LSVOS Challenge.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling same-class competitors in memory readout improves target identity preservation in challenging video object segmentation scenarios without requiring major architectural changes, as demonstrated by competitive performance at the challenge level.

title: ProBel: Propaganda Detection with Techniques, Spans, and Explanations
summary: Propaganda detection includes several related prediction levels, ranging from sentence-level decisions to technique classification and span identification. However, it remains unclear how supervision at these levels interacts when learned jointly across Arabic and English. We present ProBel, an Arabic and English resource that aligns binary labels, multi-label annotations over 23 propaganda techniques grouped into six coarse categories, technique-labeled spans, and reference explanations for the same news sentences. It includes a substantially larger English collection and supports matched binary, coarse-grained, multi-label, and span-level tasks in both languages. We evaluate zero-shot prompting, task-specific fine-tuning, and joint training under a shared setup. A single bilingual multi-task model achieves the best overall performance and remains competitive across tasks and languages. Cross-task analysis shows that transfer depends on the supervision level. Joint classification training preserves binary performance, whereas span-only training can weaken sentence-level prediction. Joint bilingual training yields the most stable results, while monolingual fine-tuning can reduce transfer to the other language. We will release the data, code, and evaluation scripts.

AI.tldr: ProBel is a new Arabic-English propaganda detection resource that aligns binary labels, multi-label technique annotations (23 techniques in 6 coarse categories), technique-labeled spans, and reference explanations for the same news sentences. A single bilingual multi-task model achieves the best overall performance, with results showing that transfer depends on supervision level—joint classification preserves binary performance while span-only training can weaken sentence-level prediction.
AI.motivation: Propaganda detection spans multiple prediction levels (sentence-level decisions, technique classification, span identification), but it is unclear how supervision at these levels interacts when learned jointly across Arabic and English. Existing resources do not align all these annotation levels for the same sentences in a bilingual setting.
AI.method: The authors construct ProBel, a bilingual (Arabic and English) resource aligning binary labels, multi-label annotations over 23 propaganda techniques grouped into six coarse categories, technique-labeled spans, and reference explanations. They evaluate zero-shot prompting, task-specific fine-tuning, and joint training under a shared setup, and perform cross-task analysis.
AI.result: A single bilingual multi-task model achieves the best overall performance and remains competitive across tasks and languages. Joint classification training preserves binary performance, while span-only training can weaken sentence-level prediction. Joint bilingual training yields the most stable results, whereas monolingual fine-tuning can reduce transfer to the other language.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that supervision level interaction matters in joint learning for propaganda detection: bilingual multi-task training is the most effective and stable approach, and the authors will release the data, code, and evaluation scripts to support further research.

title: GenCoord: Skill-Path Commitments under Private Information
comment: 25 pages, 10 figures, and 23 tables, including supplementary material. Peng He and Junning Zhu contributed equally. Paper source and compact evidence: https://github.com/JulianZJN/GenCoord
summary: Suppose one embodied agent knows what must be built, while its teammate alone knows which transformation its workcell can perform. Neither local view determines who should act, what should be handed off, or how the joint task should continue. We introduce GenCoord, which turns the task consequence of such private facts into an executable skill-path commitment. A local Qwen3.5-0.8B model emits a multi-step SELF plan and peer REQ; bounded feedback conditions route revision when the deciding capability is peer-local. The resolved commitment is parsed, checked, canonically materialized, compiled to Mineflayer skills, and verified by handoff and terminal state. Counterfactual interventions that hold the world, call schedule, and executor unchanged make requester revision and receiver execution follow the injected task consequence in both directions. Across three independently trained seeds, correct capability feedback closes the paired local-information gap from 50% to 100%. Multi-step commitments improve held-out-template success by 6.9 points while reducing model decisions by 32%. At matched closed-loop quality on 128 held-out semantic clusters, Short DSL reduces peer traffic by 92.8% and median time-to-commitment by 68.2% relative to controlled free-form communication. These results identify executable task consequences as the coordination unit connecting distributed local reasoning to verified joint action.

AI.tldr: GenCoord enables two embodied agents with asymmetric knowledge (one knows the goal, the other knows the workcell capability) to coordinate by converting private task consequences into an executable skill-path commitment, achieving 100% coordination success and significantly reducing communication overhead.
AI.motivation: In multi-agent embodied tasks, agents may hold private information that is individually insufficient for joint action: one knows what to build while the other knows what transformations are possible. Neither local view determines who should act, what to hand off, or how to continue, creating a coordination gap between distributed local reasoning and joint execution.
AI.method: GenCoord uses a local Qwen3.5-0.8B model to emit a multi-step SELF plan and peer REQ. Bounded feedback conditions route revision when the deciding capability is peer-local. The resolved commitment is parsed, checked, canonically materialized, compiled to Mineflayer skills, and verified by handoff and terminal state. Counterfactual interventions are used to test that requester revision and receiver execution follow injected task consequences.
AI.result: Correct capability feedback closes the paired local-information gap from 50% to 100% across three seeds. Multi-step commitments improve held-out-template success by 6.9 points while reducing model decisions by 32%. A Short DSL reduces peer traffic by 92.8% and median time-to-commitment by 68.2% vs. free-form communication at matched quality on 128 held-out semantic clusters.
AI.conclusion: Executable task consequences serve as the coordination unit that bridges distributed local reasoning to verified joint action, offering a scalable and efficient paradigm for multi-agent embodied coordination under asymmetric information.

title: ADMIL: Attention-Distilled Multiple Instance Learning for Selective Foundation Model Inference in Pathology
summary: Attention-based multiple instance learning (ABMIL) using pathology foundation model embeddings is effective for slide-level tasks, but exhaustive inference requires applying a large image encoder to every foreground tile despite the subsequent attention distribution often concentrating over a small subset of informative regions. We introduce ADMIL (Attention-Distilled Multiple Instance Learning), a selective-compute framework that distills an ABMIL teacher's attention into a lightweight tile-selection model, PriorNet. Using an EfficientNet architecture, PriorNet learns the teacher attention distribution from raw tile pixels with KL divergence; at inference, it scores the foreground pool, selects the top-K tiles, and invokes the expensive foundation model only on that subset before a selected-bag ABMIL student predicts the slide label. Across BRACS, PANDA, and CAMELYON16, ADMIL matches full-teacher headline performance at K=4, 8, and 128 tiles, respectively, avoiding >98% of foundation model (Virchow2) tile embeddings and model inference FLOPs. Random and teacher-attention oracle controls show that this result depends on task-relevant selection rather than tile-count reduction alone. Quantitative and qualitative analyses suggest that PriorNet recovers the teacher's tile ordering with high fidelity while focusing on task-relevant morphological regions. ADMIL shows that nearly all expensive tile encodings can be removed without sacrificing slide-level performance, providing a potential path for more efficient deployment in clinical settings where latency and compute costs are key considerations.

AI.tldr: ADMIL is a selective-compute framework that distills an ABMIL teacher's attention into a lightweight tile-selection model (PriorNet), allowing only a small subset of tiles (K=4-128) to be encoded by the expensive pathology foundation model while matching full-teacher performance on BRACS, PANDA, and CAMELYON16, avoiding >98% of embedding and inference FLOPs.
AI.motivation: Exhaustive inference in ABMIL requires applying a large image encoder to every foreground tile, which is computationally expensive, even though the attention distribution typically concentrates over a small set of informative regions. The goal is to reduce compute and latency for clinical deployment.
AI.method: ADMIL distills an ABMIL teacher's attention distribution into PriorNet, a lightweight EfficientNet-based tile-selection model trained with KL divergence against teacher attention from raw tile pixels. At inference, PriorNet scores foreground tiles, selects top-K, invokes the expensive foundation model (Virchow2) only on that subset, and a selected-bag ABMIL student predicts the slide label. Random and oracle controls validate that performance gains stem from task-relevant selection.
AI.result: ADMIL matches full-teacher headline performance at K=4, 8, and 128 tiles on BRACS, PANDA, and CAMELYON16 respectively, avoiding >98% of Virchow2 tile embeddings and model inference FLOPs. Quantitative and qualitative analyses show PriorNet recovers teacher tile ordering with high fidelity and focuses on task-relevant morphology.
AI.conclusion: Nearly all expensive tile encodings can be removed without sacrificing slide-level performance, offering a practical path for efficient deployment in latency- and compute-constrained clinical settings.

title: Triplet2Track: A Hierarchical System with Object-Centric Representations for Reliable Long-Horizon Manipulation
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures. Accepted for presentation at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics (SMC 2026)
summary: Ensuring reliability in uncertain environments remains difficult for long-horizon robotic manipulation. End-to-end VLA models are data-heavy and opaque, making diagnosis and verification difficult. Hierarchical pipelines are more interpretable, but their plans are often weakly grounded in observations, weakly aligned with low-level actions, and computed without online feedback, leading to open-loop behavior and hallucinations. To address these issues, we introduce the Triplet-to-Track System (TTS), a closed-loop long-horizon imitation learning system that uses human videos to reduce reliance on robot-collected data. TTS represents high-level subgoals as instance-grounded triplets, translates them into continuous track priors for execution, and monitors task progress from observations for online replanning. Across diverse real-world long-horizon tasks, TTS achieves a 74.8\% average success rate and supports object-level and compositional generalization.

AI.tldr: TTS is a closed-loop long-horizon imitation learning system for robotic manipulation that uses human videos to reduce reliance on robot-collected data. It represents high-level subgoals as instance-grounded triplets, translates them into continuous track priors for execution, and monitors task progress from observations for online replanning, achieving a 74.8% average success rate across diverse real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: End-to-end VLA models are data-heavy and opaque, making diagnosis and verification difficult. Hierarchical pipelines are more interpretable but their plans are weakly grounded in observations, weakly aligned with low-level actions, and computed without online feedback, leading to open-loop behavior and hallucinations.
AI.method: TTS represents high-level subgoals as instance-grounded triplets, translates them into continuous track priors for execution, and monitors task progress from observations for online replanning. The system uses human videos to reduce reliance on robot-collected data.
AI.result: Across diverse real-world long-horizon tasks, TTS achieves a 74.8% average success rate and supports object-level and compositional generalization.
AI.conclusion: TTS addresses the reliability challenges in long-horizon robotic manipulation by providing a closed-loop, interpretable alternative that is both data-efficient (via human videos) and capable of online replanning, demonstrating strong success rates and generalization capabilities.

title: SchemaGUI: A Schema-Driven Benchmark for Controllable GUI Generation Evaluation
comment: 18 pages, 6 figures, and 7 tables. Code is available at https://github.com/xdong2002/SchemaGUI
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong potential in graphical user interface (GUI) generation, but reliable evaluation remains challenging due to uncontrolled data distributions, noisy annotations, and limited layout scenario coverage. To address this, we propose SchemaGUI, a template-based benchmark for controllable GUI generation evaluation. By synthesizing paired natural language instructions and deterministic function-call references from parameterized interface schemas, SchemaGUI can generate thousands of deterministically annotated tasks in seconds without human labeling. Based on 1,000 evaluated instances per scenario and language across six representative bilingual scenarios, we benchmark five mainstream models, including the Qwen3.5 family, Qwen3-Coder-30B, and DeepSeek-R1. Our extensive analysis reveals three key insights. First, precise geometric spatial control remains an important bottleneck; while scaling Qwen3.5 from 4B to 27B improves Schema Feasibility from 91.56% to 99.63%, the Geometry score improves more modestly (from 67.05% to 75.30%). Second, generation difficulty is highly sensitive to layout complexity, with current LLMs excelling at simple sequential arrangements but suffering severe coordinate drift in dense grids and multi-region compositions. Third, thinking mode increases token consumption while generally reducing GUI Score, particularly for smaller models.

AI.tldr: SchemaGUI is a template-based benchmark for controllable GUI generation evaluation that synthesizes paired natural language instructions and deterministic function-call references from parameterized interface schemas, producing thousands of deterministically annotated tasks without human labeling. Benchmarking five mainstream LLMs across six bilingual scenarios reveals that precise geometric spatial control remains a key bottleneck, generation difficulty is highly sensitive to layout complexity, and thinking mode increases token consumption while generally reducing GUI quality.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluation of LLM-based GUI generation suffers from uncontrolled data distributions, noisy annotations, and limited layout scenario coverage, making reliable assessment difficult. A controllable, scalable, and annotation-free benchmark is needed to properly evaluate and diagnose GUI generation capabilities.
AI.method: SchemaGUI synthesizes paired natural language instructions and deterministic function-call references from parameterized interface schemas, enabling automated generation of thousands of deterministically annotated tasks in seconds without human labeling. The benchmark evaluates five mainstream models (Qwen3.5 family, Qwen3-Coder-30B, DeepSeek-R1) across 1,000 instances per scenario and language in six representative bilingual scenarios.
AI.result: Scaling Qwen3.5 from 4B to 27B improves Schema Feasibility from 91.56% to 99.63% but only modestly improves Geometry score (67.05% to 75.30%). LLMs excel at simple sequential layouts but suffer severe coordinate drift in dense grids and multi-region compositions. Thinking mode increases token consumption while generally reducing GUI Score, especially for smaller models.
AI.conclusion: Precise geometric spatial control remains the primary bottleneck in LLM-based GUI generation, and layout complexity significantly affects generation difficulty. The finding that thinking mode degrades GUI performance suggests current reasoning strategies are misaligned with the spatial precision requirements of GUI generation tasks.

title: MEMORY Wins All: Indirect Bias Injection Attacks via Social Media Feeds
summary: Personal AI agents routinely consume external content while performing tasks such as web browsing, email processing, and SNS feed summarization, and they retain selected information or execution results in persistent memory for later use. We show that this ordinary ingestion of external content opens an indirect path for manipulating subsequent agent behavior. Based on this observation, we present IBIA, an Indirect Bias Injection Attack that plants an adversary-aligned stance on a specific topic into a victim agent's memory through external content, without direct access to the agent, its memory, or future user queries. For this, IBIA combines three mechanisms: comment cloaking, which keeps the crafted content consistent with the surrounding discussion, comment watermarking, which enables lightweight identification during curation, and category anchoring, which makes the retained stance salient under later related requests. We evaluate IBIA on BiasBench, a benchmark of 6,000 adversary-crafted social comments and 120 email instances. The watermark-based curation identifies 95.9% of the injected comments. Under the OpenClaw setting, IBIA achieves adversary-aligned response rates (AARs) of 91.2% on average across four downstream tasks, including 86.6% on the frontier GPT-5.5. We further propose a memory boundary defense that detects the injected bias and reduces AARs to 80.6%.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces IBIA (Indirect Bias Injection Attack), which exploits the routine ingestion of external content by personal AI agents to plant adversarial stances into persistent memory without direct access. Using comment cloaking, watermarking, and category anchoring, IBIA achieves 91.2% adversary-aligned response rates on average across four tasks in the OpenClaw setting, with an 86.6% rate on GPT-5.5. A proposed memory boundary defense reduces AARs to 80.6%.
AI.motivation: Personal AI agents routinely ingest external content (web browsing, emails, SNS feeds) and store selected information in persistent memory. This creates an indirect attack surface where adversaries can manipulate agent behavior by injecting malicious content through ordinary external sources, without needing direct access to the agent, its memory, or future queries. The paper aims to demonstrate and characterize this novel security vulnerability.
AI.method: IBIA combines three mechanisms: (1) comment cloaking to keep crafted content consistent with surrounding discussion, (2) comment watermarking enabling lightweight identification during memory curation, and (3) category anchoring to make the retained stance salient under later related requests. The attack is evaluated on BiasBench, a benchmark of 6,000 adversary-crafted social comments and 120 email instances. A memory boundary defense is also proposed to detect injected bias.
AI.result: The watermark-based curation identifies 95.9% of injected comments. IBIA achieves adversary-aligned response rates (AARs) of 91.2% on average across four downstream tasks, including 86.6% on GPT-5.5. The proposed memory boundary defense detects the injected bias and reduces AARs to 80.6%.
AI.conclusion: Indirect bias injection through external content ingestion is a practical and effective attack vector against personal AI agents with persistent memory. While a memory boundary defense can mitigate some risk, it is only partially effective, indicating that stronger safeguards are needed to protect agent behavior from adversarial content manipulation.

title: Spiking Neural Networks for Energy-Efficient Object Detection in Forward-Looking Sonar Imagery
summary: Autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) are increasingly important tools in industries ranging from research, to energy, to defense. AUVs are power-constrained platforms operating in remote environments with fixed battery capacities, where propulsion competes with compute and sensors for power over lengthy mission durations. AUVs frequently operate in dark or turbid waters where optical sensing is of limited value, and rely on sonar as their primary sensing modality. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are the state-of-the-art solution for object detection in forward-looking sonar imagery, but are energy expensive (e.g. YOLOv8m: 322 mJ/inference). Spiking neural networks (SNNs) rely on binary spike activations and thus sparse accumulate-only operations, allowing them to be remarkably energy efficient, particularly when paired with dedicated neuromorphic hardware. The sparse, high-contrast structure of forward-looking sonar (FLS) returns is structurally matched to spike coding in a way that optical imagery is not. No prior work has assessed the suitability of SNNs for object detection in FLS imagery. SpikeYOLO, a fully spiking network trained with surrogate gradients, was benchmarked against state-of-the-art CNN baselines on three FLS object detection datasets. Key results: SpikeYOLO T=2 achieves 3.3$\times$ lower theoretical compute energy on UATD (97 vs 322 mJ) at competitive accuracy (0.529 mAP@0.5:0.95 vs. YOLOv8m's 0.575); SpikeYOLO matches YOLOv8m on mAP@0.5 and outperforms YOLO-SONAR and Fast R-CNN baselines on the sparse Marine-Debris-FLS dataset at 4.4$\times$ lower energy; SpikeYOLO demonstrates superior robustness to multiplicative speckle noise (3.0% degradation at $σ{=}0.4$ vs. 8.9% for YOLOv8m), outperforming YOLOv8m outright at $σ{=}0.6$, directly relevant to real-world FLS deployment.

AI.tldr: This paper presents SpikeYOLO, the first spiking neural network (SNN) for object detection in forward-looking sonar (FLS) imagery, demonstrating 3.3-4.4x lower theoretical compute energy than CNN baselines while achieving competitive or superior accuracy, and showing better robustness to speckle noise.
AI.motivation: AUVs are power-constrained platforms where CNNs for sonar object detection are energy-expensive (e.g., YOLOv8m at 322 mJ/inference). SNNs offer sparse accumulate-only operations with potential for remarkable energy efficiency, and the sparse, high-contrast structure of FLS imagery is structurally matched to spike coding. However, no prior work has assessed SNNs for object detection in FLS imagery.
AI.method: SpikeYOLO, a fully spiking network trained with surrogate gradients, was benchmarked against state-of-the-art CNN baselines (YOLOv8m, YOLO-SONAR, Fast R-CNN) on three FLS object detection datasets.
AI.result: SpikeYOLO T=2 achieves 3.3x lower theoretical compute energy on UATD (97 vs 322 mJ) at competitive accuracy (0.529 mAP@0.5:0.95 vs YOLOv8m's 0.575); matches YOLOv8m on mAP@0.5 and outperforms YOLO-SONAR and Fast R-CNN on Marine-Debris-FLS at 4.4x lower energy; demonstrates superior robustness to multiplicative speckle noise (3.0% degradation at sigma=0.4 vs 8.9% for YOLOv8m), outperforming YOLOv8m outright at sigma=0.6.
AI.conclusion: SpikeYOLO is a viable energy-efficient alternative to CNNs for FLS object detection in power-constrained AUV deployments, offering competitive accuracy, substantial energy savings, and superior robustness to real-world FLS noise conditions.

title: UniMem: Unifying Multimodal Memory and Control for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: While Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have leveraged internet-scale pretraining and task-focused finetuning to achieve strong performance on long-horizon tasks, they often struggle with non-Markovian tasks that require memory. Existing approaches to memory typically involve additional Vision-Language-Models (VLMs) for long-term memory management, introducing a memory bottleneck and a fractured training pipeline. Conditioning on multiple historical frames can provide the VLA with access to more descriptive features of past scenes, but can degrade performance if frames are chosen at arbitrary, fixed intervals. To address these limitations, we present UniMem, a framework that unifies high-level, multimodal memory and low-level control under one backbone. UniMem employs an event classifier for memory updates, a keyframe encoder for dense spatial memory, and a keyframe caching technique to minimize overhead during policy rollouts. We evaluate UniMem across five simulation and four hardware tasks targeting sequential and spatial memory, demonstrating that our unified, single-model system outperforms fixed-interval image sampling baselines (93.4% vs. 68.2%) in simulation and hierarchical baselines (80.0% vs. 43.5%) in hardware, while offering faster inference and a simple training pipeline for easy adoption. Project website: https://losterberg3.github.io/unimem-vla/

AI.tldr: UniMem is a unified VLA framework that integrates high-level multimodal memory and low-level control into a single backbone, using an event classifier for memory updates, a keyframe encoder for spatial memory, and keyframe caching to reduce overhead, outperforming fixed-interval baselines and hierarchical methods across simulation and hardware tasks.
AI.motivation: VLA models struggle with non-Markovian tasks requiring memory. Existing memory solutions rely on separate VLMs, creating a memory bottleneck and fractured training pipeline. Fixed-interval historical frame conditioning degrades performance due to poorly chosen frame timing.
AI.method: UniMem unifies memory and control in one backbone. It employs an event classifier for memory updates, a keyframe encoder for dense spatial memory, and a keyframe caching technique to minimize policy rollouts' overhead.
AI.result: UniMem achieves 93.4% vs. 68.2% in simulation (vs. fixed-interval image sampling) and 80.0% vs. 43.5% in hardware (vs. hierarchical baselines), with faster inference and a simple training pipeline.
AI.conclusion: A unified memory-and-control system provides superior performance, faster inference, and simpler adoption over hierarchical or fixed-interval alternatives for memory-demanding VLA tasks.

title: Don' t Box Me In: Dynamic Cultural Adaptation and Cognitive Tracking for Social Understanding
summary: Social interaction increasingly takes place in multicultural settings, where individuals may draw on multiple cultural influences and adapt their communicative behavior across contexts. Despite recent advances in equipping Large Language Models (LLMs) with social understanding capabilities, existing approaches often model culture as a static demographic attribute, limiting their ability to accommodate hybrid and dynamically expressed communicative preferences. Therefore, in this paper, we propose \textbf{DyCAC}, a training-free framework that achieves fluid social alignment by incorporating \underline{Dy}namic \underline{C}ultural \underline{A}daptation with continuous \underline{C}ognitive tracking. Rather than inferring a fixed cultural identity, DyCAC models culturally relevant communicative preferences as a time-varying mixture of population-level cultural reference profiles. This reference-based representation is further calibrated using dialogue-style signals observed in the ongoing interaction, enabling the model to capture both composite cultural influences and turn-level shifts in communicative behavior. In parallel, a memory module driven by Theory of Mind (ToM) continuously tracks the cognitive states of the interlocutor. Extensive experiments on interactive social and cultural benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our approach. The proposed framework outperforms existing baselines, exhibiting enhanced social intelligence and broad adaptability across varied multicultural contexts.

AI.tldr: Proposes DyCAC, a training-free framework for LLMs that achieves fluid social alignment in multicultural settings by modeling dynamic cultural adaptation as a time-varying mixture of cultural reference profiles, calibrated by dialogue-style signals, alongside Theory of Mind-driven cognitive tracking of the interlocutor.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM approaches model culture as a static demographic attribute, which fails to capture hybrid cultural influences and dynamically expressed communicative preferences in multicultural social interactions.
AI.method: DyCAC models culturally relevant communicative preferences as a time-varying mixture of population-level cultural reference profiles, calibrated by observed dialogue-style signals to capture composite cultural influences and turn-level shifts. A parallel Theory of Mind (ToM)-driven memory module continuously tracks the interlocutor's cognitive states.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on interactive social and cultural benchmarks show DyCAC outperforms existing baselines, exhibiting enhanced social intelligence and broad adaptability across varied multicultural contexts.
AI.conclusion: The training-free, dynamic cultural adaptation approach demonstrates that modeling culture as an evolving mixture of references rather than a fixed attribute yields superior social alignment and adaptability in multicultural LLM interactions.

title: When More References Hurt: Contamination-Aware DINOv2 Memory Banks for Few-Shot Steel Defect Detection
summary: Patch-memory anomaly detectors assume that their reference bank is normal, an assumption that is difficult to guarantee when additional industrial images are unverified. We study whether a few trusted normal images can safely recover useful normal patches from such references without defect masks. Starting from the DINOv2 patch-memory formulation used by AnomalyDINO, we score candidate patches by distance to a clean seed bank, discard the most suspicious 20%, merge the retained patches with the seed, and enforce a fixed budget by greedy coreset selection. On Severstal, naive additional references contain 9.46% anomalous patches; the proposed trim rejects 78.1\% of them and reduces residual contamination to 2.59%. At an equal 51,200-patch development budget, the proposed bank reaches 0.1084 AUPRC versus 0.0950 for naive expansion, 0.0952 for random removal, and 0.1030 for eight clean images. Injecting only 0.5\% anomalous patches into a clean bank reduces AUPRC from 0.1030 to 0.0759. On all five completed held-out pairs, the proposed bank improves over naive expansion, with a mean gain of 0.0142 AUPRC. Reference purity is therefore a first-order design variable, and unverified images are useful only when their contribution is filtered explicitly.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the problem of impure reference banks in patch-memory anomaly detection. It proposes a method to safely recover useful normal patches from unverified industrial images using a few trusted normal images, by scoring candidate patches against a clean seed bank, trimming suspicious patches, and merging with greedy coreset selection. The method reduces anomalous patch contamination from 9.46% to 2.59% and improves AUPRC from 0.0950 to 0.1084 on Severstal compared to naive expansion.
AI.motivation: Patch-memory anomaly detectors assume their reference bank contains only normal samples, but this assumption fails when additional industrial images are unverified. The authors investigate whether a small set of trusted normal images can safely filter and recover useful normal patches from such unverified references without requiring defect masks.
AI.method: Starting from the DINOv2 patch-memory formulation (as in AnomalyDINO), the method scores candidate patches by distance to a clean seed bank, discards the most suspicious 20%, merges retained patches with the seed, and enforces a fixed budget via greedy coreset selection.
AI.result: On Severstal, naive references contain 9.46% anomalous patches; the proposed trim rejects 78.1% of them, reducing residual contamination to 2.59%. At a 51,200-patch budget, the proposed bank achieves 0.1084 AUPRC vs 0.0950 (naive), 0.0952 (random removal), and 0.1030 (eight clean images). Injecting only 0.5% anomalous patches drops AUPRC from 0.1030 to 0.0759. Across five held-out pairs, the proposed bank improves over naive expansion with a mean gain of 0.0142 AUPRC.
AI.conclusion: Reference purity is a first-order design variable in patch-memory anomaly detection. Unverified images are only useful when their contribution is explicitly filtered, suggesting that contamination filtering is essential for leveraging large-scale unverified industrial data.

title: SuperMap: A Spatio-Temporal SLAM System for Visual-Language Navigation
summary:
Robotic navigation in human environments requires a spatio-temporal semantic representation that can rec- oncile open-vocabulary perception with long-term environmental changes. While foundation models provide strong zero-shot recognition, their predictions are intermittent and view-dependent, and naively integrating them into mapping pipelines leads to identity drift and stale semantics over time. We present SuperMap, a 4D spatio-temporal mapping framework for language-guided navigation that integrates high-frequency geometric SLAM with asynchronous open-vocabulary perception. Our core contribution is a consistency-driven mapping engine that combines 3D-aware instance association/re-activation with a principled existence-and-label confidence update to maintain stable object identities and prune outdated map content under occlusions and scene changes. SuperMap produces a queryable 4D scene-graph representation that interfaces naturally with Vision-Language Models by supporting compositional queries over object semantics, relations,
  We demonstrate SuperMap on benchmarks and real robots, including dynamic scenes with appearance/disappearance and relocation, and provide ablations and runtime analysis. We release the full system as open-source to provide the community with a deployable baseline for open-vocabulary spatio-temporal mapping. Project website: superodometry.com/supermap.

AI.tldr: SuperMap is a 4D spatio-temporal mapping framework for language-guided robotic navigation that integrates high-frequency geometric SLAM with asynchronous open-vocabulary perception. It uses a consistency-driven mapping engine with 3D-aware instance association/re-activation and existence-and-label confidence updates to maintain stable object identities and handle dynamic scene changes, producing a queryable 4D scene-graph representation compatible with Vision-Language Models.
AI.motivation: Robotic navigation in human environments requires a spatio-temporal semantic representation that reconciles open-vocabulary perception with long-term environmental changes. Foundation models provide strong zero-shot recognition but their predictions are intermittent and view-dependent, and naive integration into mapping pipelines causes identity drift and stale semantics over time.
AI.method: SuperMap integrates high-frequency geometric SLAM with asynchronous open-vocabulary perception through a consistency-driven mapping engine. The core mechanism combines 3D-aware instance association/re-activation with a principled existence-and-label confidence update to maintain stable object identities and prune outdated map content under occlusions and scene changes. The system produces a queryable 4D scene-graph that supports compositional queries over object semantics and relations for Vision-Language Model interfacing.
AI.result: SuperMap is demonstrated on benchmarks and real robots, including dynamic scenes with object appearance/disappearance and relocation. The paper provides ablations and runtime analysis, showing the system's effectiveness in maintaining stable object identities and handling long-term environmental changes.
AI.conclusion: The authors release the full system as open-source to provide the community with a deployable baseline for open-vocabulary spatio-temporal mapping.

title: Rank Reversal in Multilingual LLM Judges: A Label-Free Double-Centering Calibrator
summary: Multilingual LLM judges produce different evaluator-backbone rankings depending on the prompt language: on an eight-language Agent-as-a-Judge benchmark, the top-ranked backbone alternates across English, Arabic, Chinese, Hindi, Japanese, Spanish, Turkish, and Swahili, and 7 of 15 backbone pairs show statistically significant pairwise rank reversal. We treat this as a measurement problem. The multilingual judge score decomposes additively into task difficulty, backbone skill, and a language-backbone interaction term, the last of which is recoverable without human labels by double-centering the cell-mean score matrix. We make this estimator (\textbf{Consensus-Based Calibration}, CBC) explicit, give an $O(1/\sqrt{n})$ finite-sample concentration bound with variance constant $(1-\tfrac{1}{m})(1-\tfrac{1}{k})$, and show that it is unbiased even when task-language interactions are present. Across 7{,}920 judge runs (6 backbones, 8 languages, 55 tasks, 3 frameworks), CBC raises held-out cross-task rank consistency $τ$ from 0.650 to 0.902 and agrees with the held-out additive-model oracle in 100\% of per-language decisions versus 68.5\% raw; these are consistency diagnostics, not human-grounded correctness measures. On a separately collected M-RewardBench panel (7 languages, 1{,}500 items per language, 10{,}500 language-item instances, 5 evaluators), panel agreement with the public human gold preferences rises from 68.7\% to 76.6\% (gain 7.9 percentage points, 95\% CI $[6.0, 9.9]$), our strongest external evidence of downstream usefulness. The estimator is the standard two-way ANOVA interaction-recovery operation under sum-to-zero contrasts; our contribution is its application as a label-free post-hoc calibrator for multilingual LLM judges, an explicit finite-sample concentration bound, and an unbiasedness result that holds even under task-language misspecification.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a systematic language-dependent bias in multilingual LLM judges that causes evaluator-backbone rankings to reverse across prompt languages. The authors propose Consensus-Based Calibration (CBC), a label-free estimator that recovers the language-backbone interaction term via double-centering of the score matrix (standard two-way ANOVA interaction recovery). CBC improves held-out cross-task rank consistency from τ=0.650 to 0.902 and panel agreement with human gold preferences from 68.7% to 76.6%, with theoretical guarantees including O(1/√n) concentration bounds and unbiasedness under task-language misspecification.
AI.motivation: Multilingual LLM judges produce inconsistent evaluator rankings across different prompt languages, with 7 of 15 backbone pairs showing statistically significant pairwise rank reversals on an eight-language benchmark. This is framed as a measurement problem: the judge score conflates task difficulty, backbone skill, and a systematic language-backbone interaction that must be separated for reliable multilingual evaluation.
AI.method: The multilingual judge score is decomposed additively into task difficulty, backbone skill, and a language-backbone interaction term. The interaction term is estimated without human labels by double-centering the cell-mean score matrix, which is equivalent to standard two-way ANOVA interaction recovery under sum-to-zero contrasts. The estimator (CBC) is provided with an O(1/√n) finite-sample concentration bound with variance constant (1−1/m)(1−1/k) and is proven unbiased even under task-language interaction misspecification. Experiments span 7,920 judge runs (6 backbones, 8 languages, 55 tasks, 3 frameworks) plus a separate M-RewardBench panel (7 languages, 1,500 items per language, 10,500 instances, 5 evaluators).
AI.result: CBC raises held-out cross-task rank consistency τ from 0.650 to 0.902 and agrees with the held-out additive-model oracle in 100% of per-language decisions (vs. 68.5% raw). On M-RewardBench, panel agreement with human gold preferences rises from 68.7% to 76.6% (gain of 7.9 percentage points, 95% CI [6.0, 9.9]). Concentration bounds and unbiasedness are established theoretically.
AI.conclusion: The language-backbone interaction in multilingual LLM judges is a significant, measurable source of bias that can be corrected post-hoc without human labels. The contribution is the application of two-way ANOVA interaction recovery as a label-free calibration method for multilingual judges, backed by explicit finite-sample concentration bounds and robustness guarantees under task-language misspecification, with moderate-scale external evidence of downstream usefulness.

title: From SQL Generation to Tool Selection: A Domain-Oriented Pattern for MCP Servers
summary: Agents built on Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly reach enterprise data through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and many MCP database servers maximize flexibility by exposing a single generic SQL execution tool. This paper proposes the Domain-Oriented Tooling Pattern: instead of generating SQL at query time, the model selects from a small set of domain-aligned tools whose parameterized queries encapsulate schema navigation, joins and business rules on the server side. We formalize the pattern around three architectural invariants and introduce Model Demotion, the observation that replacing SQL synthesis with intent classification lowers the model tier required to serve routine requests. As a reference implementation we present MCP Blueprint, an open-source framework in which domain tools are defined declaratively as YAML metadata plus external parameterized SQL files. We evaluate the pattern with a public reproducibility benchmark comparing three MCP server designs - raw SQL execution, a thin generic tool pack, and a verticalized domain pack - on four local models (3B-8B) across seventeen customer-facing tasks over the Sakila database (609 completed cells; temperature 0; three repetitions per cell). The verticalized pack reaches a pooled mean score of 0.939 versus 0.666 for raw SQL and 0.605 for the generic pack; the smallest model improves from 0.583 to 0.929, matching or exceeding every larger configuration while cutting cost per correct answer by an order of magnitude. All harness code, prompts, gold answers, frozen packs and per-cell results are publicly available.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the Domain-Oriented Tooling Pattern for MCP-based LLM agents accessing enterprise databases, where instead of generating SQL at query time, the model selects from a small set of domain-aligned parameterized tools. The reference implementation, MCP Blueprint, uses YAML metadata plus external SQL files. A reproducibility benchmark on the Sakila database shows the verticalized domain pack achieves 0.939 pooled mean score versus 0.666 for raw SQL and 0.605 for a thin generic pack, with the smallest 3B model improving from 0.583 to 0.929—matching or exceeding larger configurations while cutting costs by an order of magnitude.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents increasingly access enterprise databases through MCP servers, many of which expose a single generic SQL execution tool for maximum flexibility. However, generating correct SQL at query time is error-prone and requires high-capability models, which is costly and unreliable for production use. The authors aim to address this by proposing a pattern that shifts responsibility from SQL synthesis to intent classification.
AI.method: The paper formalizes the Domain-Oriented Tooling Pattern around three architectural invariants and introduces the concept of "Model Demotion" — replacing SQL synthesis with intent classification to lower the model tier required for routine requests. The pattern is implemented as MCP Blueprint, an open-source framework defining domain tools declaratively via YAML metadata plus external parameterized SQL files. Evaluation compares three MCP server designs (raw SQL, thin generic tool pack, verticalized domain pack) across four local models (3B-8B) on seventeen tasks over the Sakila database, with 609 completed cells at temperature 0 and three repetitions per cell.
AI.result: The verticalized domain pack achieves a pooled mean score of 0.939 versus 0.666 for raw SQL and 0.605 for the thin generic pack. The smallest model improves from 0.583 to 0.929, matching or exceeding every larger configuration. Cost per correct answer is reduced by an order of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: The Domain-Oriented Tooling Pattern demonstrates that constraining LLM agents to domain-aligned parameterized tools—rather than free-form SQL generation—substantially improves accuracy while enabling the use of smaller, cheaper models without sacrificing quality. The authors release all code and data publicly for reproducibility and further research.

title: Three-Phase Scribble-Adaptive Curriculum Learning for autoPETV Grand Challenge
summary: This report describes Libo Zhang's algorithmic solution to autoPETV Grand Challenge on interactive lesion segmentation in whole-body PET/CT. Interaction is encoded as two additional input channels that rasterize the accumulated foreground and background scribbles, and a residual-encoder U-Net of about 140 million parameters is trained with a three-phase curriculum over 4000 epochs: the network first learns fully automatic segmentation with silent interaction channels, then observes ground-truth-derived scribbles under randomly sampled visibility modes, and finally adapts to its own mistakes through online simulation of up to five error-driven correction steps. Training draws on 1811 autoPET and DeepPSMA studies, and the submission ensembles the best and final checkpoints of five folds by logit averaging. In interactive five-fold cross-validation with six interaction steps, the final checkpoints reach a mean AUC-Dice of 3.836 and a mean AUC-DMM of 3.869, improving monotonically in every fold, with roughly half of the total gain delivered by the first corrective scribble. Our code and trained model checkpoints are available on https://github.com/Libo1023/autoPETV-Curriculum.

AI.tldr: This report describes an interactive lesion segmentation solution for whole-body PET/CT, using a residual-encoder U-Net (~140M parameters) that encodes scribble interactions as extra input channels and is trained via a three-phase curriculum with online error-driven correction simulation, achieving monotonic performance gains across five folds.
AI.motivation: To develop an effective interactive segmentation approach for whole-body PET/CT imaging that leverages user scribbles to iteratively refine lesion segmentation, addressing the challenge of segmenting lesions in a grand challenge setting.
AI.method: The method encodes foreground/background scribbles as two additional rasterized input channels to a residual-encoder U-Net (~140M parameters). The network is trained with a three-phase curriculum over 4000 epochs: (1) fully automatic segmentation with silent interaction channels, (2) training with ground-truth-derived scribbles under randomly sampled visibility modes, and (3) adapting to its own mistakes through online simulation of up to five error-driven correction steps. Training uses 1811 autoPET and DeepPSMA studies, and the final submission ensembles the best and final checkpoints of five folds via logit averaging.
AI.result: In interactive five-fold cross-validation with six interaction steps, the final checkpoints achieve a mean AUC-Dice of 3.836 and a mean AUC-DMM of 3.869, with monotonic improvement across all folds and roughly half of the total gain delivered by the first corrective scribble.
AI.conclusion: The curriculum-based interactive segmentation approach with online error-driven correction simulation yields strong and consistently improving interactive lesion segmentation performance, with code and model checkpoints publicly released.

title: Aligned Alone, Misaligned Together: Forecasting Adversarial Capture in LLM Agent Populations
summary: The unit of AI safety evaluation is still the individual model, yet language-model agents are increasingly deployed in interacting populations that read and write one another's decisions. This raises a question no single-agent audit can answer: an agent that is well-calibrated on its own may still be pulled toward a different decision by the agents around it. We study this on a security-triage task, where populations of language-model monitors decide whether to escalate or dismiss alerts, and into which we can inject a committed minority that always pushes one way. We find that two alerts a single agent judges almost identically on its own can drive collective behavior far apart, so auditing any one member need not reveal what the population will do. Yet that collective behavior can be predicted in advance. From a population's benign, adversary-free operation alone, we calibrate a response function that forecasts, before any attack is run, how far a committed minority will later move it. We then ask what shifts the outcome and find that letting agents see each other's reasoning neutralizes a weak attack, while only delaying it against a strong one, turning the question from whether the population converges on the adversaries' choice into when. Finally, we exclude the hypothesis of capture being an irreversible trap: once the committed agents are removed, the population drifts back toward where it began, so capture is a temporary state. Alignment in isolation is not alignment in a population, yet what a population will do under attack can be read in advance, from how it behaves before any adversary arrives.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that single-agent AI safety audits are insufficient for language-model agents deployed in interacting populations, and that a population's vulnerability to a committed adversarial minority can be forecast in advance from its benign operation alone.
AI.motivation: AI safety evaluation typically audits individual models, but agents increasingly operate in populations that influence one another's decisions. A well-calibrated agent may be pulled toward different decisions by neighboring agents, raising questions no single-agent audit can answer.
AI.method: The authors study security-triage tasks where populations of language-model monitors decide whether to escalate or dismiss alerts, injecting a committed minority that always pushes one way. They calibrate a response function from benign, adversary-free population operation to forecast how far a committed minority will move the population, and test interventions like exposing reasoning to other agents.
AI.result: Two alerts a single agent judges nearly identically can drive collective behavior far apart, so single-agent audits miss population behavior. The response function predicts collective outcomes in advance. Sharing reasoning neutralizes weak attacks but only delays strong ones. Capture is not irreversible: removing committed agents lets the population drift back toward its original state.
AI.conclusion: Alignment in isolation is not alignment in a population, yet population behavior under attack can be read in advance from how it behaves before any adversary arrives.

title: Learning Implicit Constitutive Laws for Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting from Monocular Videos
summary: We present GCA (Gaussian Constitutive Alignment), a framework for learning implicit constitutive laws from monocular dynamic video of deformable objects represented by 3D Gaussians. Given a static multi-view scan for geometric initialization, our method learns intrinsic physical dynamics solely from a single fixed-viewpoint video of the moving object. Existing implicit methods often suffer from local minima under noisy supervision and lack physical interpretability, while explicit approaches rely on predefined constitutive equations, limiting generalizability and becoming unstable in monocular settings. To address these challenges, our framework unifies LoRA-based adaptation with two key alignment modules. First, we propose Rank-based Depth-Geometric Anchors (RDGA) to establish robust geometric constraints from monocular dynamic observations via scale-invariant rank-based depth alignment, reducing the reliance on unreliable pixel-level color supervision. Second, a Constitutive Prior Regularizer (CPR) integrates classical constitutive models as soft differentiable priors, regularizing the optimization while preserving the flexibility of implicit modeling---even when the actual material is absent from the hypotheses. Extensive experiments on synthetic, real-to-sim, and real-world datasets demonstrate that GCA outperforms existing methods, achieving 48% lower Chamfer Distance than the strongest baseline on synthetic benchmarks while remaining robust under monocular supervision.

AI.tldr: GCA introduces a framework for learning implicit constitutive laws of deformable objects from monocular video using 3D Gaussian representations. It combines LoRA-based adaptation with two key modules: Rank-based Depth-Geometric Anchors (RDGA) for robust geometric constraints and a Constitutive Prior Regularizer (CPR) for physics-informed regularization, achieving 48% lower Chamfer Distance than the strongest baseline.
AI.motivation: Existing implicit methods for learning constitutive laws from video suffer from local minima under noisy supervision and lack physical interpretability, while explicit approaches rely on predefined constitutive equations that limit generalizability and become unstable in monocular settings. The goal is to learn intrinsic physical dynamics of deformable objects from a single fixed-viewpoint video.
AI.method: GCA unifies LoRA-based adaptation with two alignment modules: (1) Rank-based Depth-Geometric Anchors (RDGA) establishes robust geometric constraints via scale-invariant rank-based depth alignment from monocular dynamic observations, reducing reliance on unreliable pixel-level color supervision; (2) Constitutive Prior Regularizer (CPR) integrates classical constitutive models as soft differentiable priors to regularize optimization while preserving implicit modeling flexibility even when the actual material is absent from hypothesis set. The framework starts from a static multi-view scan for geometric initialization.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic, real-to-sim, and real-world datasets show GCA outperforms existing methods, achieving 48% lower Chamfer Distance than the strongest baseline on synthetic benchmarks while maintaining robustness under monocular supervision.
AI.conclusion: GCA effectively bridges the gap between physical interpretability and modeling flexibility for learning implicit constitutive laws from monocular video, demonstrating superior accuracy and robustness over existing approaches.

title: Figurative Justice: Detecting metaphors in Hindi judgements with qualitative assessment and transformers
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Dataset available at https://osf.io/z398e/
summary:
Metaphors are figurative use of words for conceptual mapping. Metaphor detection in the legal context has been crucial as metaphors are persuasive juridical means of creating legal meaning and concepts resulting in significant consequences. Metaphorical framing in legal discourse by judges, lawyers, and legislators brings about real-time implications upon individuals and influences judicial decision-making, argumentation and interpretation of laws. This is crucial in Human Rights infringement cases where language determines severity of punishment, public perception and judicial outcomes.
  While automatic metaphor detection in major languages like English, Spanish, Polish, Lithuanian have aided in understanding inherent intentions of metaphorical use of language, there is no such attempt in low-resource languages like Hindi. The dearth of annotated legal corpora in Hindi makes it difficult to develop NLP models and detect metaphors in judicial proceedings. In the Indian context, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have been used for classification of bail judgements, however there are no existing models designed for metaphor detection.
  We present a Hindi Legal Metaphor Corpus (HiLeMe) by isolating judgements from Hindi Legal Data Corpus (HLDC). Legal experts annotated HiLeMe to classify metaphorical constructions using the MIPVU schema. We downstreamed an mBERT on Hindi legal metaphor detection task. We built a transformer-based architecture for metaphor detection that are known to outperform traditional models in legal classification tasks. This model provides insights into the judicial psyche for decoding judicial decisions. Our research contributes to advancing automated models in legal discourse in low-resource languages like Hindi and envisages adoption into 22 Indian schedule languages.

AI.tldr: This paper presents HiLeMe, the first Hindi Legal Metaphor Corpus, created by annotating judgements from the Hindi Legal Data Corpus (HLDC) using the MIPVU schema. The authors fine-tune mBERT for metaphor detection in Hindi legal text, providing the first automated metaphor detection model for Hindi judicial discourse and aiming to extend this approach to all 22 scheduled Indian languages.
AI.motivation: Metaphor detection in legal discourse is crucial because metaphorical framing influences judicial decision-making, argumentation, and legal interpretation—particularly in Human Rights cases where language affects punishment severity and judicial outcomes. While metaphor detection systems exist for major languages like English, Spanish, Polish, and Lithuanian, there is no such attempt for Hindi, a low-resource language, due to the dearth of annotated legal corpora.
AI.method: The authors construct a Hindi Legal Metaphor Corpus (HiLeMe) by isolating judgements from the Hindi Legal Data Corpus (HLDC). Legal experts annotate the corpus to classify metaphorical constructions following the MIPVU (Metaphor Identification Procedure Vrije Universiteit) schema. They then fine-tune a multilingual BERT (mBERT) model for the Hindi legal metaphor detection task using a transformer-based architecture.
AI.result: The mBERT-based transformer model successfully performs metaphor detection in Hindi legal texts, providing the first automated system for this task in a low-resource Indian language. The model offers insights into the judicial psyche and aids in decoding judicial decisions.
AI.conclusion: This research advances automated NLP models for legal discourse in Hindi and other low-resource Indian languages, with a vision to extend the approach to all 22 scheduled languages of India.

title: Vehicle speed dataset for the major European road network derived from Sentinel-2 imagery, 2022-2026
summary: The dataset provides individual vehicle speed observations on European E-roads: motorways, trunk roads, primary and secondary roads, as tagged in OpenStreetMap as e-road, for the years 2022-2026. Speeds are derived from Copernicus Sentinel-2 Level-2A satellite optical imagery using a processing pipeline that exploits the short, well-characterized acquisition delays between the blue (B02_10m), green (B03_10m), and red bands (B04_10m) of the Sentinel-2 push-broom instrument. A moving vehicle appears at slightly displaced positions in the three bands, forming a moving echo. The detected displaced intensity peaks are linked into per-vehicle trajectories through a prediction-and-matching procedure. The resulting displacements are converted into ground speeds using publicly accessible inter-band time delays. Each record contains the trajectory geometry, per-channel displacements and headings, internal quality indicators, the estimated speed, the acquisition timestamp, and the source Sentinel-2 product identifier. The dataset is distributed as GeoPackage files, with one record per detected vehicle, and can support studies of traffic patterns, speed behavior, transport modeling, and the calibration of road network attributes at a continental scale.

AI.tldr: A dataset of per-vehicle speed observations on European E-roads (2022-2026), derived from Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellite imagery by exploiting inter-band acquisition delays to detect moving vehicle echoes and estimate ground speeds.
AI.motivation: To provide a continental-scale, satellite-derived dataset of individual vehicle speeds on European E-roads, enabling studies of traffic patterns, speed behavior, transport modeling, and road network attribute calibration.
AI.method: Vehicle speeds are extracted from Sentinel-2 Level-2A optical imagery by exploiting short, well-characterized delays between the blue, green, and red bands of the push-broom instrument. Displaced intensity peaks (moving echoes) are detected and linked into per-vehicle trajectories via a prediction-and-matching procedure, then converted to ground speeds using publicly accessible inter-band time delays.
AI.result: A dataset distributed as GeoPackage files with one record per detected vehicle, containing trajectory geometry, per-channel displacements and headings, quality indicators, estimated speed, acquisition timestamp, and source Sentinel-2 product identifier.
AI.conclusion: The dataset supports large-scale studies of traffic patterns, speed behavior, transport modeling, and calibration of road network attributes at a continental scale across European E-roads.

title: TRACE: Artifact-Robust Statistical Shape Modeling from Imperfect Surface Scans - A Case Study in Craniosynostosis 3D Photography
comment: Accepted at ShapeMI workshop at MICCAI 2026
summary: Craniosynostosis severity analysis increasingly relies on statistical shape models (SSMs) to quantify cranial morphology, but most existing workflows depend on computed tomography or heavily curated three-dimensional (3D) photographs. Raw clinical 3D photographs provide a radiation-free and repeatable alternative, yet often contain shoulders, hands, hair, clothing, scanner noise, and incomplete boundaries that corrupt correspondences. We introduce the Template-constrained Robust Artifact-aware Correspondence Estimation (TRACE) framework, an unsupervised method for constructing SSMs directly from artifact-contaminated clinical 3D head photographs. TRACE predicts sparse anatomically corresponding head-surface control points from the raw point cloud, refines them through a coarse-to-fine Surface-Aware Deformation cascade, and uses thin-plate spline warping to deform a clean template mesh into a subject-specific head reconstruction. This template-constrained formulation keeps dense correspondences on clinically relevant head anatomy while suppressing non-head artifacts. The correspondence module is decoupled from the point-cloud encoder, enabling the same deformation pipeline to be paired with different backbones, including PointNet, DGCNN, and Point Transformer V3. Across all backbones, TRACE substantially improves surface sampling, topology preservation, and shape-model quality over prior SSM methods, providing a scalable foundation for photograph-based craniosynostosis shape analysis and a framework that may extend to other artifact-contaminated surface scans when an appropriate clean template is available.

AI.tldr: TRACE is an unsupervised framework for constructing statistical shape models directly from artifact-contaminated clinical 3D head photographs, using a template-constrained robust correspondence estimation approach with a decoupled deformation pipeline that improves surface sampling and topology preservation across multiple backbone architectures.
AI.motivation: Existing SSM workflows for craniosynostosis analysis depend on CT scans or heavily curated 3D photographs, which are either radiation-exposing or require extensive manual curation. Raw clinical 3D photographs offer a radiation-free alternative but contain artifacts (shoulders, hands, hair, clothing, scanner noise, incomplete boundaries) that corrupt point correspondences needed for SSM construction.
AI.method: TRACE predicts sparse anatomically corresponding head-surface control points from raw point clouds, refines them via a coarse-to-fine Surface-Aware Deformation cascade, and uses thin-plate spline warping to deform a clean template mesh into a subject-specific head reconstruction. The correspondence module is decoupled from the point-cloud encoder, allowing pairing with different backbones including PointNet, DGCNN, and Point Transformer V3.
AI.result: Across all backbones tested (PointNet, DGCNN, Point Transformer V3), TRACE substantially improves surface sampling, topology preservation, and shape-model quality compared to prior SSM methods.
AI.conclusion: TRACE provides a scalable, radiation-free foundation for photograph-based craniosynostosis shape analysis, with a template-constrained framework that can potentially extend to other artifact-contaminated surface scans when an appropriate clean template is available.

title: GTA-RAG: Graph-Trajectory-Augmented Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures. Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Fundings
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enables LLMs to access external knowledge for answering knowledge-intensive questions. For complex multi-hop questions, multi-turn retrieval-augmented reasoning extends RAG into an iterative process that repeatedly searches for and integrates evidence across documents. However, existing reinforcement-learning (RL) approaches for agentic RAG are typically optimized with final-answer rewards, which provide sparse supervision and overlook whether the model actually retrieves the required evidence chain. We present \textsc{GTA-RAG}, a graph-trajectory-augmented RL framework for multi-turn retrieval-augmented reasoning. From an entity--document graph, we sample connected document paths, synthesize multi-hop QA trajectories, and validate them with the deployed retriever to obtain executable trajectory-level supervision. We then optimize the retrieval policy with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and a trajectory-guided reward that encourages both accurate answers and acquisition of target evidence documents, followed by answer-reward training on natural QA instances. Experiments on three multi-hop and two simple QA benchmarks show that \method{} consistently outperforms RL-based RAG baselines with both Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen2.5-7B backbones, while substantially improving evidence-chain coverage. Our code is available at https://github.com/cjcj46262/GTA-RAG.

AI.tldr: GTA-RAG is a graph-trajectory-augmented reinforcement learning framework for multi-turn retrieval-augmented reasoning that uses entity-document graph sampling to synthesize validated multi-hop QA trajectories, providing dense trajectory-level supervision for optimizing retrieval policies with GRPO and trajectory-guided rewards.
AI.motivation: Existing RL approaches for agentic RAG rely on sparse final-answer rewards, which fail to supervise whether the model actually retrieves the required evidence chain for multi-hop questions.
AI.method: GTA-RAG samples connected document paths from an entity-document graph, synthesizes multi-hop QA trajectories, and validates them with the deployed retriever to obtain executable trajectory-level supervision. The retrieval policy is optimized with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and a trajectory-guided reward encouraging both accurate answers and target evidence document acquisition, followed by answer-reward training on natural QA instances.
AI.result: GTA-RAG consistently outperforms RL-based RAG baselines on three multi-hop and two simple QA benchmarks with both Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen2.5-7B backbones, while substantially improving evidence-chain coverage.
AI.conclusion: Providing dense trajectory-level supervision via graph-sampled and retriever-validated trajectories significantly improves multi-turn RAG policy learning, yielding better answer accuracy and evidence-chain coverage compared to final-reward-only RL training.

title: Development and Feasibility Evaluation of an Edge AI as Medical Device System for Breast Cancer Multidisciplinary Team Meetings
summary: Breast Cancer Multidisciplinary Team (MDT) meetings manage increasingly complex cases under considerable time pressure, and documentation requirements can reduce clinical efficiency and decision quality. Existing AI based MDT workflows rely on cloud-based processing, limiting their use because patient discussions contain identifiable information. We developed a fully on-device AI pipeline using open-source Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Large Language Models (LLMs) that transcribes breast cancer MDT discussions, structures clinical information, and generates treatment recommendations using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounded in National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidance. The pipeline runs on a single NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, ensuring that patient audio, transcripts, and outputs remain within institutional infrastructure. Evaluation included two recorded simulated MDT discussions, ten clinically validated synthetic discussions, and 1,270 acoustically augmented recordings. Optimisation of Whisper large-v3 reduced word error rate by 20.7% and 24.4% on the recorded discussions and achieved performance within 0.58% WER and 1.58% word information lost of a commercial clinical ASR benchmark on augmented audio. MedGemma-RAG identified 2.3 times more MDT-concordant interventions than a proprietary cloud comparator (p = 0.020), with no significant difference in overall accuracy. Stakeholders identified automated documentation, treatment recommendation support, and case triage as the most credible near-term applications while highlighting workflow integration, governance, and clinician trust as key implementation challenges. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of privacy-preserving, fully on-device AI for MDT documentation and guideline-informed decision support, providing a foundation for prospective clinical evaluation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a fully on-device AI pipeline for breast cancer MDT meetings that transcribes discussions, structures clinical information, and generates NICE guideline-grounded treatment recommendations using open-source ASR (Whisper large-v3) and LLMs (MedGemma-RAG) on a single NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. It achieves competitive performance against commercial cloud benchmarks while keeping all patient data within institutional infrastructure.
AI.motivation: Breast cancer MDT meetings face increasing complexity and time pressure, and documentation requirements reduce clinical efficiency. Existing AI-based MDT workflows rely on cloud processing, which is problematic because patient discussions contain identifiable information, limiting their practical adoption in clinical settings.
AI.method: The pipeline uses open-source ASR (Whisper large-v3) and LLMs (MedGemma with retrieval-augmented generation grounded in NICE guidance) running entirely on a single NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin edge device. Whisper was optimized for transcription, and evaluation included two recorded simulated MDT discussions, ten clinically validated synthetic discussions, and 1,270 acoustically augmented recordings for benchmarking.
AI.result: Whisper optimization reduced word error rate by 20.7% and 24.4% on recorded discussions, achieving performance within 0.58% WER and 1.58% word information lost of a commercial clinical ASR benchmark on augmented audio.
