MedGemma-RAG identified 2.3 times more MDT-concordant interventions than a proprietary cloud comparator (p=0.020) with no significant difference in overall accuracy. Stakeholders identified documentation, recommendation support, and case triage as credible applications but noted workflow integration, governance, and clinician trust as key challenges.
AI.conclusion: The findings demonstrate the feasibility of privacy-preserving, fully on-device AI for MDT documentation and guideline-informed decision support, providing a foundation for prospective clinical evaluation.

title: When Does Visual Generation Help Visual Understanding in Unified Multimodal Models?
summary: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) can perform both understanding and generation, raising a central question: can visual generation improve understanding? Existing evaluations provide mixed evidence, but confound task difficulty, reasoning paradigms, and the closed-loop interaction between generation and understanding. We introduce VGAU-Diag, a fine-grained evaluation framework for vision generation-assisted understanding. It stratifies samples by difficulty, enables unified evaluation of multiple reasoning paradigms, and uses Oracle-Assisted Reference Protocols. Our analysis shows that generated visual aids help on easier instances but become unreliable as reasoning complexity increases. Oracle-assisted diagnosis further reveals that the main bottleneck often lies on the visual-understanding side rather than the visual-generation side, as current UMMs struggle to leverage even faithful visual aids. We also show that effective visual generation should target visual-understanding bottlenecks rather than add more reasoning steps, and identify a three-stage transition from task-irrelevant noise, to misleading plausible guidance, and finally to useful assistance. These findings would be useful to guide the development of better UMMs.The code is available at https://github.com/zyb1029/VGAU-Diag.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces VGAU-Diag, a fine-grained evaluation framework that disentangles task difficulty, reasoning paradigms, and closed-loop interaction to assess whether visual generation helps understanding in unified multimodal models. Findings show generated visual aids help on easier tasks but become unreliable with complexity; the bottleneck is more often visual understanding than generation; and effective generation should target understanding bottlenecks rather than add reasoning steps.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of whether visual generation improves understanding in UMMs provide mixed evidence due to confounds from task difficulty, reasoning paradigms, and the closed-loop interaction between generation and understanding.
AI.method: VGAU-Diag stratifies samples by difficulty, enables unified evaluation of multiple reasoning paradigms, and uses Oracle-Assisted Reference Protocols for fine-grained diagnosis.
AI.result: Generated visual aids help on easier instances but become unreliable as reasoning complexity increases. Oracle-assisted diagnosis reveals the main bottleneck is visual understanding rather than generation; current UMMs fail to leverage even faithful visual aids. A three-stage transition from task-irrelevant noise to misleading plausible guidance to useful assistance is identified.
AI.conclusion: Effective visual generation should target visual-understanding bottlenecks rather than add more reasoning steps, guiding the future development of better UMMs.

title: VERDICT: Agreement Beats Pixel-Space Verification in Real-Document OCSR
summary: Optical Chemical Structure Recognition (OCSR) converts 2D molecular depictions in the published literature into SMILES, and is increasingly important for constructing large-scale chemical training datasets. Automation at that scale requires identifying unreliable predictions in the absence of ground truth. Three families of label-free signals were compared on $263$ ACS journal depictions with verified ground truth: model confidence, re-rendering similarity, and agreement among recognizers. Pixel-space re-rendering performed little better than chance (AUROC $0.547$, $95\%$ CI $[0.465,0.629]$), and an oracle-tuned threshold on it reduced correct labels per image from $0.745$ to $0.205$. Agreement among four architecturally distinct recognizers instead reached an AUROC of $0.916$ ($[0.880,0.952]$). The two-of-four rule accepted $81.7\%$ of images at $88.8\%$ precision, the three-of-four rule $52.1\%$ at $98.5\%$. The same pattern held on CLEF-IP, UOB, and USPTO. This distinction is obscured on synthetic benchmarks, where re-rendered predictions naturally resemble their inputs. A substance filter removed $2{,}193$ false agreements on wildcards and R-group fragments, after which the three-of-four rule rejected all $68$ generic depictions. VERDICT was then applied to PMC Open Access, producing $6{,}146$ structure labels for $4{,}833$ molecules; chemist adjudication of $400$ released labels in two independent samples yielded precisions of $0.995$ for the three-of-four tier and $0.958$ for the two-of-four tier. VERDICT therefore enables validated labels for multimodal molecular databases linking structure images, machine-readable representations, and source-publication information. In SES AI's Molecular Universe platform, VERDICT further serves as an image-based interface for searching and retrieving molecular records.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces VERDICT, a label-free quality-control method for OCSR that uses agreement among multiple architecturally distinct chemical structure recognizers to validate predicted SMILES labels. It outperforms re-rendering similarity (AUROC 0.916 vs 0.547) and model confidence, scales to PubMed Central Open Access (6,146 labels with up to 99.5% chemist-verified precision), and is deployed in SES AI's Molecular Universe platform.
AI.motivation: As OCSR becomes essential for building large-scale chemical datasets, there is a critical need to identify unreliable predictions at scale without ground truth labels. Existing label-free signals (model confidence, re-rendering similarity, recognizer agreement) have not been systematically compared on real published literature.
AI.method: Three families of label-free signals were compared on 263 ACS journal depictions with verified ground truth: (1) model confidence, (2) re-rendering similarity (pixel-space), and (3) agreement among four architecturally distinct recognizers. Validated by applying a two-of-four and three-of-four voting rule, with a substance filter to remove false agreements on wildcards and R-group fragments, followed by chemist adjudication.
AI.result: Agreement among recognizers achieved AUROC 0.916 vs 0.547 for re-rendering similarity. The two-of-four rule accepted 81.7% of images at 88.8% precision; three-of-four accepted 52.1% at 98.5%. Pattern held across CLEF-IP, UOB, and USPTO. Applying VERDICT to PMC Open Access produced 6,146 structure labels for 4,833 molecules with chemist-adjudicated precisions of 0.995 (three-of-four) and 0.958 (two-of-four).
AI.conclusion: VERDICT enables validated structure labels for multimodal molecular databases at scale, without requiring ground truth, by leveraging cross-recognizer agreement. It is deployed in SES AI's Molecular Universe platform as an image-based search and retrieval interface. Re-rendering similarity is shown to be unsuitable for real literature due to natural similarity between re-rendered predictions and inputs, a confound absent in synthetic benchmarks.

title: From Diagnosis to Redesign: Using Quantitative Ethnography to Improve Multi-Agent LLM Reasoning
comment: Accepted at ICQE 2026 (to appear in Springer CCIS)
summary: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems are designed to improve reasoning by decomposing tasks across multiple agents with specialized functions, but the presence of multiple agents does not inherently guarantee coherent reasoning or outputs that align with task objectives. This paper introduces a quantitative ethnographic (QE) approach for diagnosing and redesigning multi-agent LLM systems based on the discourse produced through agent interactions. We test this approach using automated essay scoring as an example context, applying Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) to model a five-agent multi-agent debate system and examine differences between debates that produced correct versus incorrect scoring decisions. Results show that, in the initial system, correct scoring decisions were characterized by rubric-grounded justification, agreement, and elaboration. Incorrect scoring decisions, in contrast, were characterized by extended proposition-challenge-response exchanges that were less consistently tied to rubric criteria. We then used the findings to revise the agents' prompts. The revised system improved exact scoring accuracy from 27.78% to 40.28% and shifted the discourse of incorrect debates toward the rubric-grounded pattern of correct ones, making the two nearly indistinguishable. Based on these results, we argue that QE can support a diagnostic-to-redesign loop for AI reasoning by tracing how patterns of agent interaction relate to system performance, informing prompt redesign, and evaluating whether those redesigns change both outcomes and interaction patterns.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a quantitative ethnographic (QE) approach for diagnosing and redesigning multi-agent LLM systems by analyzing agent interaction discourse. Using automated essay scoring and Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA), the authors show that correct scoring decisions were characterized by rubric-grounded justification, agreement, and elaboration, while incorrect decisions exhibited extended proposition-challenge-response exchanges less tied to rubric criteria. After redesigning agent prompts based on these findings, exact scoring accuracy improved from 27.78% to 40.28%, and the discourse of incorrect debates became nearly indistinguishable from correct ones. The authors argue QE supports a diagnostic-to-redesign loop for AI reasoning.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems do not inherently guarantee coherent reasoning or outputs aligned with task objectives. There is a need for methods to diagnose why such systems fail and guide their redesign based on the actual discourse produced through agent interactions.
AI.method: The authors apply a quantitative ethnographic (QE) approach using Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) to model a five-agent multi-agent debate system in an automated essay scoring context. They compare discourse patterns between debates yielding correct versus incorrect scoring decisions, then use findings to revise agent prompts and re-evaluate outcomes and discourse patterns.
AI.result: Correct scoring decisions were initially characterized by rubric-grounded justification, agreement, and elaboration, whereas incorrect decisions exhibited prolonged proposition-challenge-response exchanges less consistently tied to rubric criteria. Prompt redesign improved exact scoring accuracy from 27.78% to 40.28% and shifted the discourse of incorrect debates toward the rubric-grounded pattern of correct ones, making the two nearly indistinguishable.
AI.conclusion: QE can support a diagnostic-to-redesign loop for AI reasoning by tracing how agent interaction patterns relate to system performance, informing prompt redesign, and evaluating whether redesigns change both outcomes and interaction patterns.

title: Role-Specialized Mixture-of-Agents with Open-Weight LLMs for Clinical Prediction
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to clinical prediction tasks such as in-hospital mortality and readmission from electronic health records (EHRs). Privacy and compliance constraints motivate systems that can be deployed locally, which has increased interest in open-weight multi-agent designs. However, most medical multi-agent systems are evaluated as a single block, leaving unclear which agent role contributes to prediction and whether retrieval drives observed gains. We study a role-specialized Mixture-of-Agents (MoA) that combines medical knowledge retrieval with contrastive similar-patient reasoning. By varying the role design while holding the retrieval setup fixed, we localize the main effect to the final integrator. Pairing large open-weight analysts with a small open-weight integrator matches closed-model prompting on F1 for mortality prediction while flagging substantially more true high-risk patients. Mechanism analysis shows the role assignment directly yields a high-recall operating point without threshold tuning. The effect is task-dependent, with smaller gains for readmission because the available records correlate weakly with this longer-horizon outcome. These results position role design as a key factor in privacy-constrained, training-free clinical LLM prediction.

AI.tldr: This paper studies a role-specialized Mixture-of-Agents (MoA) framework for clinical prediction from EHRs using open-weight LLMs, localizing the main predictive contribution to the final integrator role rather than retrieval, and showing that pairing large analysts with a small integrator matches closed-model F1 for mortality prediction while flagging more true high-risk patients—all without training or threshold tuning.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for clinical prediction tasks like in-hospital mortality and readmission from EHRs, but privacy and compliance motivate local deployment of open-weight multi-agent systems. However, existing medical multi-agent systems are evaluated as a single block, leaving unclear which agent roles contribute to prediction and whether retrieval drives gains.
AI.method: The authors study a role-specialized Mixture-of-Agents (MoA) that combines two components: medical knowledge retrieval and contrastive similar-patient reasoning. They vary the role design while keeping the retrieval setup fixed to isolate the effect of the integrator. They also perform mechanism analysis to understand how role assignment affects the operating point.
AI.result: The main predictive effect is localized to the final integrator role. Pairing large open-weight analysts with a small open-weight integrator matches closed-model prompting on F1 for mortality prediction while flagging substantially more true high-risk patients. Role assignment directly yields a high-recall operating point without threshold tuning. The effect is task-dependent, with smaller gains for readmission because available records correlate weakly with this longer-horizon outcome.
AI.conclusion: Role design is a key factor in privacy-constrained, training-free clinical LLM prediction, positioning the architectural choice of agent roles as central to achieving strong predictive performance under local-deployment constraints.

title: Targeted Iterative Filtering
summary: The assessment of image denoising results depends on the respective application area, i.e. image compression, still-image acquisition, and medical images require entirely different behavior of the applied denoising method. In this paper we propose a novel, nonlinear diffusion scheme that is derived from a linear diffusion process in a value space determined by the application. We show that application-driven linear diffusion in the transformed space compares favorably with existing nonlinear diffusion techniques.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a novel nonlinear diffusion scheme derived from a linear diffusion process in an application-specific transformed value space, showing it outperforms existing nonlinear diffusion techniques across different application areas like image compression, still-image acquisition, and medical imaging.
AI.motivation: Image denoising quality assessment differs depending on the application area (e.g., image compression, still-image acquisition, medical images), each requiring different behavior from the denoising method. Existing approaches do not sufficiently account for this application-dependent variation in denoising requirements.
AI.method: The authors propose a nonlinear diffusion scheme that is derived from a linear diffusion process conducted in a value space that is specifically determined by the target application. The nonlinearity emerges from transforming the image into this application-specific space before applying linear diffusion.
AI.result: The proposed application-driven linear diffusion in the transformed space is shown to compare favorably with existing nonlinear diffusion techniques across the different application contexts.
AI.conclusion: Application-driven diffusion in a transformed value space provides a principled way to tailor image denoising to specific application requirements, outperforming generic nonlinear diffusion methods.

title: WnW: Waxing-and-Waning KV Cache for Long-Form Speech LLMs
comment: Accepted at EMNLP 2026 Main Conference. 8 pages, 5 figures
summary: Long-form audio inputs make the KV cache the dominant memory cost of speech LLMs. Prefill-only KV compression methods permanently discard audio KV positions once evicted, with no pathway to recover them during decoding. We show this is fragile on long-form audio: prefill attention concentrates near the audio start (an attention-sink effect), while decode-time attention distributes broadly, and the two rankings overlap weakly. We propose WnW (Waxing-and-Waning KV cache), which classifies KV-heads into anchor, tidal, and fixed roles via offline calibration. Anchor heads remain on GPU and serve as a decode-time importance observer; tidal heads keep a CPU-resident complement that is recalled chunk-by-chunk based on aggregated anchor-head scores; fixed heads keep only an on-GPU subset, with the rest permanently discarded. On LibriSpeech-Long with two 3B backbones (Voxtral-mini-3b and Qwen2.5-Omni-3B), WnW preserves near-Full-Cache accuracy while keeping only 20% of audio tokens on GPU, where prefill-only baselines fail to terminate. Results generalize across language, task, and domain shifts, and CPU-GPU recall adds little decode-time overhead in our measurements.

AI.tldr: WnW (Waxing-and-Waning KV cache) is a method for speech LLMs that adaptively manages KV cache across GPU and CPU by classifying attention heads into anchor, tidal, and fixed roles via offline calibration, preserving near-Full-Cache accuracy on long-form audio while keeping only 20% of audio tokens on GPU.
AI.motivation: Long-form audio inputs make the KV cache the dominant memory cost in speech LLMs. Existing prefill-only KV compression methods permanently evict audio KV positions with no recovery pathway during decoding, which is fragile because prefill attention concentrates near the audio start (attention-sink effect) while decode-time attention distributes broadly, and the two positional attention rankings overlap only weakly.
AI.method: WnW classifies KV-heads into three roles via offline calibration: (1) anchor heads remain on GPU and act as a decode-time importance observer; (2) tidal heads keep a CPU-resident complement that is recalled chunk-by-chunk based on aggregated anchor-head scores; (3) fixed heads keep only an on-GPU subset with the rest permanently discarded.
AI.result: On LibriSpeech-Long with two 3B backbones (Voxtral-mini-3b and Qwen2.5-Omni-3B), WnW preserves near-Full-Cache accuracy while keeping only 20% of audio tokens on GPU, whereas prefill-only baselines fail to terminate. Results generalize across language, task, and domain shifts, and CPU-GPU recall adds little decode-time overhead.
AI.conclusion: WnW demonstrates that a hybrid CPU-GPU KV cache management strategy with role-specialized heads effectively addresses the attention distribution mismatch between prefill and decode phases in long-form speech LLMs, offering a scalable solution that outperforms prefill-only compression approaches.

title: Disagree to Explore, Agree to Commit: Routing-Guided Test-Time Scaling for Software Agents
summary: Software-engineering agents solve repository-level tasks through long, stochastic tool-use trajectories, and repeated attempts often find fixes missed by one run. Test-time scaling is difficult because patches lack canonical answer forms, while sibling actions from a shared prefix are correlated. We study whether native MoE router traces can guide steering and selection without an external judge or selection-time test execution. Our analysis shows that routing provides a robust behavioral role signal; token-granular readouts and decision-matched comparison sets turn it into effective control. We therefore introduce Risa (Routing-Informed Steering and Arbitration): within trajectories, routing encourages diverse exploration and controlled convergence during patch commitment; across separately sampled trajectories, agreement at informative patch positions selects a final candidate. We evaluate on SWE-bench Verified using open-weight sparse MoE agents across scales and reasoning-effort settings. Risa's routing arbitration raises the macro-average resolved rate from 44.9% under uniform sampling to 48.2% on the gpt-oss family, matching text consensus without answer-string matching, and it transfers to Qwen3.6, where it improves on uniform choice and matches text consensus on the full 500-task benchmark.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Risa, a method that uses native Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) router traces to steer and select software-engineering agent trajectories without external judges or test execution. Routing provides a behavioral role signal; token-granular readouts and decision-matched comparison sets enable effective control. Within trajectories, routing encourages diverse exploration and controlled convergence; across trajectories, agreement at informative patch positions selects final candidates. On SWE-bench Verified, Risa raises macro-average resolved rate from 44.9% to 48.2% on gpt-oss, matching text consensus without answer-string matching, and transfers to Qwen3.6.
AI.motivation: Software-engineering agents solve repository-level tasks through long, stochastic tool-use trajectories, and repeated attempts can find fixes missed in a single run. Test-time scaling is challenging because patches lack canonical answer forms and sibling actions from a shared prefix are correlated, making external judges or selection-time test execution difficult.
AI.method: Risa (Routing-Informed Steering and Arbitration) leverages native MoE router traces. Within trajectories, routing signals encourage diverse exploration and controlled convergence at patch commitment; across separately sampled trajectories, agreement at informative patch positions selects the final candidate. It uses token-granular readouts and decision-matched comparison sets rather than external judges or test execution.
AI.result: On SWE-bench Verified with open-weight sparse MoE agents across scales and reasoning-effort settings, Risa's routing arbitration improves the macro-average resolved rate from 44.9% (uniform sampling) to 48.2% on the gpt-oss family, matching text consensus without answer-string matching. It also transfers to Qwen3.6, improving over uniform choice and matching text consensus on the full 500-task benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Router traces provide a robust behavioral role signal that can guide test-time scaling for software-engineering agents. Risa effectively replaces external judges and selection-time test execution with routing-informed steering and arbitration, yielding consistent improvements and transfer across model families.

title: Self-Calibrating Dense Displacement Fields for Reliable Co-Registration of Large Optical Satellite Imagery
summary: Co-registration underlies nearly every multi-temporal and multi-sensor use of optical satellite imagery, and operational products still carry documented offsets well above the fraction-of-a-pixel scale at which change detection, time series, and data fusion degrade. Real image pairs differ along several axes at once (sensor response, scene content, viewing geometry, resolution, mosaic seams), and the last of these is not a single global motion. Existing tools embed a motion model and constants tuned to their development data; a pair that fits is registered precisely, while one that does not either fails to match or returns a result wrong by tens of pixels with no failure reported. Learned matchers add a GPU requirement and carry no accuracy guarantee outside their training distribution. We present SCDF (self-calibrating displacement fields), a training-free, GPU-free estimator whose motion model is the dense per-pixel displacement field itself, so no scene motion falls outside the model. A single predict--measure--filter loop runs over a resolution pyramid: the accumulated field predicts where each patch of the moving image falls in the reference, RootSIFT matching and a correlation pass measure the displacement there to sub-pixel precision, and filters whose thresholds are all calibrated on the image pair itself decide what survives. One configuration, with no per-dataset tuning, processes full $8192^2$ scenes on a single CPU core. On 584 constructed-ground-truth pairs built from real Sentinel-2, Landsat-8/9, and NAIP imagery, against seven classical baselines and two zero-shot pretrained matchers, SCDF registers every pair with zero failures, reduces the best baseline's real-pair median end-point error from 6.83 to 4.17m, and cuts its 90th percentile from 17.8 to 7.77m.

AI.tldr: SCDF is a training-free, GPU-free image co-registration estimator using dense per-pixel displacement fields with a predict-measure-filter loop over a resolution pyramid, achieving zero failures and superior accuracy on real satellite imagery.
AI.motivation: Existing co-registration tools embed fixed motion models and constants tuned to development data, causing failures or large errors (tens of pixels) on pairs outside their assumed distribution. Learned matchers require GPUs and lack accuracy guarantees outside training distribution. Real imagery pairs differ along multiple axes simultaneously (sensor response, content, geometry, resolution, mosaic seams), and seam-induced motion is not a single global translation.
AI.method: SCDF uses a training-free, GPU-free approach where the motion model is the dense per-pixel displacement field itself, ensuring no scene motion falls outside the model. It runs a single predict-measure-filter loop over a resolution pyramid: the accumulated field predicts patch locations, RootSIFT matching and correlation measure displacements to sub-pixel precision, and pair-calibrated filters decide which measurements survive.
AI.result: On 584 constructed-ground-truth pairs from real Sentinel-2, Landsat-8/9, and NAIP imagery, SCDF outperforms seven classical baselines and two zero-shot pretrained matchers: zero registration failures, median end-point error reduced from 6.83m to 4.17m (vs best baseline), and 90th percentile reduced from 17.8m to 7.77m. One configuration processes full 8192^2 scenes on a single CPU core with no per-dataset tuning.
AI.conclusion: By making the motion model equivalent to the dense displacement field itself and calibrating all filter thresholds on the image pair at hand, SCDF achieves robust, accurate, training-free registration for arbitrary real imagery pairs across sensors and resolutions, including cases where existing tools fail or err silently.

title: Reward-Free Continual Adaptation for Resilient Space Robots
comment: Accepted for publication at the Third Conference on AI in and for Space (SPAICE 2026) | The source code is available at https://github.com/AndrejOrsula/space_robotics_bench
summary: Space robots operate in extreme environments where hardware degradation can critically compromise traditional control strategies. While continual reinforcement learning offers a promising mechanism for online adaptation, it inherently requires access to a reward signal during deployment. However, precise reward computation in space is often infeasible due to the lack of external tracking systems and the overall complexity of the environment. To address the challenge of unobservable rewards, we introduce a reward-free continual learning framework that leverages latent-state world models. By pre-training a model-based agent across diverse simulations, the world model learns a robust predictor of the reward structure within its latent space. Upon deployment to an environment with severe hardware degradation, we freeze the observation encoder and reward predictor to update only the transition dynamics of the world model through unsupervised rollouts. By training the policy entirely on imagined trajectories generated by this updated world model, the agent adapts to altered dynamics without receiving new rewards. We demonstrate our approach across simulated planetary traversal, orbital navigation, and precision assembly tasks subjected to severe morphological failures.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a reward-free continual learning framework for space robots that uses latent-state world models to adapt to hardware degradation without requiring reward signals during deployment. The agent pre-trains a model-based policy across diverse simulations, then updates only the world model's transition dynamics via unsupervised rollouts while freezing the encoder and reward predictor, enabling adaptation to altered dynamics on imagined trajectories alone.
AI.motivation: Space robots face hardware degradation that breaks traditional control strategies, and continual RL requires reward signals that are often infeasible to compute in space due to lack of external tracking systems and environmental complexity. This creates a need for adaptation without observable rewards.
AI.method: A reward-free continual learning framework leveraging latent-state world models. Key steps: (1) pre-train a model-based agent across diverse simulations so the world model learns a robust latent reward predictor, (2) upon deployment with hardware degradation, freeze the observation encoder and reward predictor while updating only the transition dynamics through unsupervised rollouts, (3) train the policy entirely on imagined trajectories from the updated world model.
AI.result: The approach is demonstrated across simulated planetary traversal, orbital navigation, and precision assembly tasks subjected to severe morphological failures, showing adaptation to altered dynamics without new reward signals.
AI.conclusion: By decoupling reward prediction (frozen) from transition dynamics (updated), the framework enables space robots to continually adapt to hardware degradation in a reward-free manner, providing a viable mechanism for online adaptation in extreme environments where rewards are unobservable.

title: A Source-Grounded Framework for Constructing and Evaluating Progressive Multimodal Diagnostic Dialogues from Clinical Case Reports
comment: Accepted to IEEE HealthCom 2026, Distinguished Invited Papers Track
summary: Clinical diagnosis requires progressive integration of patient history, physical examination, laboratory findings, medical images, and diagnostic-informative tests. However, most multimodal medical benchmarks evaluate fixed inputs or endpoint answers, while fully interactive diagnostic agents conflate evidence selection with evidence interpretation. We present a source-grounded framework to construct progressive multimodal diagnostic dialogues from case reports and an evaluation strategy for assessing MLLMs on final diagnosis, diagnostic reasoning, and image-finding interpretation. Evaluation on 24 internal medicine case reports showed that our framework can accurately convert case reports into reference dialogues, achieving a diagnosis F1 of 0.99 and a reasoning-quality score of 4.79 out of 5. Evaluation on two frontier MLLMs (o4-mini and Claude Haiku 4.5) achieved reasoning-quality scores of 2.75 and 2.50, respectively, with substantially lower diagnosis, reasoning, and image-finding F1 scores. The results demonstrate that fluent responses do not necessarily reflect evidence-grounded clinical reasoning and highlight the utility of the proposed framework for evaluating multimodal diagnostic reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a source-grounded framework for constructing progressive multimodal diagnostic dialogues from case reports, plus an evaluation strategy for assessing MLLMs on final diagnosis, diagnostic reasoning, and image-finding interpretation. The framework achieves high reference-dialogue quality (diagnosis F1 0.99, reasoning 4.79/5), while two frontier MLLMs score much lower (reasoning 2.75/2.50), revealing that fluent responses do not guarantee evidence-grounded clinical reasoning.
AI.motivation: Clinical diagnosis requires progressive multimodal evidence integration, yet existing benchmarks either evaluate fixed inputs/endpoints or conflate evidence selection with interpretation in fully interactive agents. A gap exists for a framework that separates and assesses these distinct cognitive processes in progressive diagnostic dialogues.
AI.method: A source-grounded framework converts case reports into progressive multimodal diagnostic dialogues, providing an evaluation strategy covering three dimensions: final diagnosis correctness, diagnostic reasoning quality, and image-finding interpretation. Tested on 24 internal medicine case reports against two frontier MLLMs (o4-mini and Claude Haiku 4.5).
AI.result: The framework itself achieved diagnosis F1 of 0.99 and reasoning-quality of 4.79/5 in converting case reports to reference dialogues. Frontier MLLMs scored reasoning-quality of 2.75 and 2.50 respectively, with substantially lower diagnosis, reasoning, and image-finding F1 scores compared to the reference.
AI.conclusion: Fluent multimodal responses from frontier MLLMs do not necessarily reflect evidence-grounded clinical reasoning. The proposed source-grounded framework provides a useful tool for evaluating multimodal diagnostic reasoning, separating evidence selection from interpretation.

title: Query-Driven Multimodal Information Extraction from Long Documents
summary: In domain-specific multimodal long documents, images and text jointly convey complex knowledge that cannot be fully captured by plain text alone. However, existing paradigms like DocVQA primarily focus on generating textual answers or localizing evidence regions, rather than outputting query-specific textual attribute values and corresponding images. To address this gap, we propose query-driven image-text joint extraction from long documents, requiring models to output query-requested textual attribute values and corresponding image bounding boxes. Based on challenges related to both user intent and document content, we designed a two-level taxonomy that operates at the query and instance levels. Further, we construct ITJoint, the first high-quality, manually annotated benchmark for this new task, comprising 2,455 pages of domain-specific documents with numerous non-decorative images, 316 queries, and 910 answer instances. Finally, we evaluate representative standalone Vision-Language Models from different providers and further design Q2IT, a multi-agent collaborative framework consisting of three progressively collaborating agents for evidence collection, page selection, and target-image localization. Using a joint evaluation approach that assesses both text extraction and image localization, our experiments show that standalone VLMs struggle with this task, while Q2IT significantly improves performance on ITJoint, although a substantial gap remains toward perfect results.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a new task called query-driven image-text joint extraction from long documents, where models must output query-requested textual attribute values along with corresponding image bounding boxes. The authors construct ITJoint, the first manually annotated benchmark for this task (2,455 pages, 316 queries, 910 answers), and propose Q2IT, a multi-agent framework with three collaborating agents. Experiments show standalone VLMs struggle on this task while Q2IT significantly improves performance, though a substantial gap to perfect results remains.
AI.motivation: Existing paradigms like DocVQA only generate textual answers or localize evidence regions, but fail to jointly output query-specific textual attribute values AND corresponding images, which is necessary for complex domain-specific multimodal long documents where knowledge is conveyed across both modalities.
AI.method: The authors design a two-level taxonomy (query-level and instance-level) based on challenges in user intent and document content, construct a manually annotated benchmark called ITJoint, and propose Q2IT—a multi-agent collaborative framework comprising three progressively collaborating agents for evidence collection, page selection, and target-image localization.
AI.result: Standalone Vision-Language Models perform poorly on the new task, while the proposed Q2IT framework significantly improves performance on ITJoint under a joint evaluation assessing both text extraction and image localization. However, a substantial gap toward perfect results remains.
AI.conclusion: The new task of query-driven image-text joint extraction is challenging and underexplored; the ITJoint benchmark provides a foundation for future work, and the Q2IT multi-agent framework demonstrates a promising direction, though further improvements are needed to close the remaining performance gap.

title: On Tensor-Based PDEs and their Corresponding Variational Formulations with Application to Color Image Denoising
summary: The case when a partial differential equation (PDE) can be considered as an Euler-Lagrange (E-L) equation of an energy functional, consisting of a data term and a smoothness term is investigated. We show the necessary conditions for a PDE to be the E-L equation for a corresponding functional. This energy functional is applied to a color image denoising problem and it is shown that the method compares favorably to current state-of-the-art color image denoising techniques.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates conditions under which a PDE can be expressed as an Euler-Lagrange equation of an energy functional with data and smoothness terms, then applies the resulting functional to color image denoising, demonstrating competitive performance against state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: To establish necessary conditions for a PDE to be derived from a variational energy functional (E-L equation), enabling the use of variational optimization frameworks for PDE-based image processing tasks.
AI.method: Derives necessary conditions for a PDE to be an Euler-Lagrange equation of an energy functional consisting of a data term and a smoothness term, then applies this energy functional formulation to a color image denoising problem.
AI.result: The proposed energy functional-based method for color image denoising compares favorably to current state-of-the-art color image denoising techniques.
AI.conclusion: PDEs satisfying the derived necessary conditions can be reformulated as E-L equations of variational energy functionals, and this approach yields competitive color image denoising performance.

title: Act with Intent: Distilling Behavior Intent for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can turn multimodal context into robot actions, but their action decoders are still trained largely by behavior cloning. This supervises which motor command was demonstrated while leaving implicit the local objective served by the behavior under the instruction. Future-based supervision enriches action learning with frames, latent observations, trajectories, or motion representations, but these signals capture particular realizations of what may happen rather than the shared semantic objective of the forthcoming behavior. We propose Intention Distillation (INDI), which distills behavior-level intent into the action decoder. During training, a frozen teacher VLM interprets a demonstrated segment from the current observation, instruction, coarse action summary, and corresponding execution video. From its standard inputs, the deployed VLA recovers the resulting multimodal intent representation at an intermediate decoder layer and uses it to organize action prediction together with representations of how the behavior unfolds and what it achieves. On SimplerEnv-Bridge, INDI improves GR00T-N1.7 from 64.3% to 84.7%, and on RoboCasa Kitchen it improves the controlled GR00T-N1.7 baseline from 64.1% to 70.3%, with consistent gains on $π_{0.5}$ across both benchmarks. In real-world tasks, INDI improves average success from 62.0% to 68.7%, with gains of up to 12.0 pp on longer-horizon tasks. Further analyses show that the recovered latent is used by the decoder, captures behavior objective and execution progress, and organizes downstream predictions in an objective-dependent manner. These results show that action decoders benefit from explicitly modeling the semantic objective of the behavior they generate.

AI.tldr: INDI (Intention Distillation) improves VLA action decoders by distilling behavior-level intent from a frozen teacher VLM into the action decoder, using multimodal intent representations to organize action prediction. It achieves substantial gains (e.g., GR00T-N1.7 from 64.3% to 84.7% on SimplerEnv-Bridge) across benchmarks and real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: VLA action decoders are largely trained via behavior cloning, which supervises which motor command was demonstrated but fails to capture the local objective served by the behavior under instruction. Existing future-based supervision signals (frames, latent observations, trajectories, motion representations) only capture particular realizations of what may happen rather than the shared semantic objective of the forthcoming behavior.
AI.method: INDI distills behavior-level intent into the action decoder. During training, a frozen teacher VLM interprets a demonstrated segment from the current observation, instruction, coarse action summary, and corresponding execution video. At inference, the deployed VLA recovers the resulting multimodal intent representation at an intermediate decoder layer and uses it to organize action prediction alongside representations of how the behavior unfolds and what it achieves.
AI.result: On SimplerEnv-Bridge, INDI improves GR00T-N1.7 from 64.3% to 84.7%; on RoboCasa Kitchen, it improves the controlled GR00T-N1.7 baseline from 64.1% to 70.3%, with consistent gains on π0.5 across both benchmarks. In real-world tasks, INDI improves average success from 62.0% to 68.7%, with gains up to 12.0 percentage points on longer-horizon tasks. Analyses show the recovered latent captures behavior objective and execution progress and organizes downstream predictions in an objective-dependent manner.
AI.conclusion: Action decoders benefit from explicitly modeling the semantic objective of the behavior they generate, as demonstrated by consistent improvements across simulation benchmarks and real-world tasks.

title: DiaRelay: Relaying Dialogue Context with a Constant-Size Memory for Emotion Recognition in Conversation
summary: Emotion Recognition in Conversation (ERC) requires models to identify subtle emotional cues that are often distributed across distant dialogue turns. Existing methods typically incorporate dialogue history through a fixed context window. However, short windows discard potentially useful long-range evidence, while enlarging the window repeatedly re-encodes overlapping utterances, increases computational and memory costs, and may introduce irrelevant context. Moreover, commonly used parameter-efficient adaptation methods, such as LoRA, mainly introduce fixed low-rank transformations in the feature space and do not explicitly maintain a dialogue-level state or condition their transformations on the evolving conversational context. To address these limitations, we propose a lightweight adapter, DiaRelay, to enable LLMs to explicitly maintain a dialogue-level memory for accurate ERC. Based on LoRA, DiaRelay introduces two extra tightly collaborative components, Selective Relay Memory Transition and Dual-axis Relay Memory Read. Selective Relay Memory Transition progressively aggregates useful historical evidence into a bounded relay memory and propagates it across successive utterance predictions. This allows earlier emotional cues to influence later predictions after they leave the local context window, without re-encoding the complete dialogue history or expanding the backbone context length. Dual-axis Relay Memory Read uses the propagated memory to dynamically modulate low-rank feature transformations, enabling context-dependent representation adaptation without test-time gradient updates. Extensive experiments show that DiaRelay can achieve SOTA weighted F1 and accuracy on MELD while obtaining competitive results on IEMOCAP with only an extra 7.1M trainable parameters, indicating the effectiveness and generalizability of our DiaRelay in enhancing LLM-based emotional understanding.

AI.tldr: DiaRelay is a lightweight adapter that enables LLMs to maintain explicit dialogue-level memory for Emotion Recognition in Conversation. It augments LoRA with a Selective Relay Memory Transition module that propagates useful historical emotional cues across turns, and a Dual-axis Relay Memory Read module that dynamically modulates low-rank transformations based on the accumulated context. It achieves SOTA on MELD and competitive results on IEMOCAP with only 7.1M extra trainable parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing ERC methods rely on fixed context windows that either discard long-range emotional evidence or incur high computational costs when enlarged. Additionally, parameter-efficient methods like LoRA introduce static low-rank transformations that do not explicitly model dialogue-level state or adapt to evolving conversational context.
AI.method: DiaRelay builds on LoRA with two collaborative components: (1) Selective Relay Memory Transition, which aggregates useful historical evidence into a bounded relay memory and propagates it across successive utterance predictions, allowing earlier cues to influence later predictions without re-encoding full history; and (2) Dual-axis Relay Memory Read, which uses the propagated memory to dynamically modulate low-rank feature transformations for context-dependent adaptation without test-time gradient updates.
AI.result: DiaRelay achieves state-of-the-art weighted F1 and accuracy on MELD, and competitive results on IEMOCAP, requiring only an additional 7.1M trainable parameters.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate that explicit dialogue-level memory maintenance via lightweight adapters can effectively enhance LLM-based emotional understanding, offering both effectiveness and generalizability while remaining parameter-efficient.

title: Beyond What Meets the Eye: Unveiling Situational Illusions for Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Real-world situation appearances can deviate from their underlying physical states, challenging the reliability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) in practical applications. In this paper, we term this phenomenon situational illusions and investigate: (1) how MLLMs perform under such illusions, and (2) how to mitigate the limitations. We first develop a comprehensive where-what-how taxonomy that characterizes where situational illusions occur, what targets they take, and how they arise. Building on this taxonomy, we introduce MSIBench, a benchmark designed to assess the discrimination, understanding, and reasoning capabilities of MLLMs under situational illusions. Evaluations of 27 model configurations reveal that current MLLMs are highly vulnerable to these illusions and exhibit 6 typical failure modes related to visual observation, grounding, and reasoning. To mitigate the limitations, we build on the core idea of systematically inspecting and reasoning over visual evidence for contextual understanding, developing prompting for closed-source models and supervised fine-tuning for open-source models, respectively. These two simple yet effective methods improve model performances by 20% at most, suggesting a practical path toward more reliable multimodal perception and reasoning in complex real-world environments.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the concept of "situational illusions"—where real-world appearances deviate from underlying physical states—and presents MSIBench, a taxonomy-based benchmark for evaluating MLLMs under such illusions. Evaluations of 27 model configurations reveal 6 typical failure modes, and the authors propose prompting and supervised fine-tuning methods that improve performance by up to 20%.
AI.motivation: MLLMs often fail when real-world situations appear differently from their underlying physical states, but this phenomenon has not been systematically studied. The authors aim to characterize these "situational illusions" and develop a benchmark to assess and improve MLLM reliability in such scenarios.
AI.method: The authors develop a where-what-how taxonomy categorizing where situational illusions occur, what targets they affect, and how they arise. Based on this taxonomy, they construct MSIBench to evaluate MLLM discrimination, understanding, and reasoning. They also develop two mitigation strategies: prompting for closed-source models and supervised fine-tuning for open-source models, both built on the principle of systematically inspecting and reasoning over visual evidence.
AI.result: Evaluation of 27 model configurations shows current MLLMs are highly vulnerable to situational illusions, exhibiting 6 typical failure modes related to visual observation, grounding, and reasoning. The proposed mitigation methods (prompting and supervised fine-tuning) improve model performance by up to 20%.
AI.conclusion: Situational illusions pose a significant challenge to MLLM reliability in real-world applications. The proposed taxonomy and benchmark enable systematic evaluation, and the simple yet effective mitigation strategies offer a practical path toward more reliable multimodal perception and reasoning in complex environments.

title: Adapting Dense Vision-Language Relationships for Multi-label Classification with Partial Label
summary: Learning multi-label image classification with incomplete annotations is a challenging task that has been widely studied for its superior trade-off between high efficiency and less labor consumption on large-scale datasets. Predominant methods rely on strong prior assumptions to recover the missing semantics from partial annotations. However, these statistic priors suffer from unstable semantic mistakes and thus lead to catastrophic overfitting. Toward this end, we propose a Language-driven Dense Semantic Adaptor (LDSA) that excavates prior-adaptive relationships from multimodal pretrained CLIP models. In our approach, the densely contrastive adaptor is first proposed to construct dense visual contrastive constraints, transferring the task-specific knowledge to visual domains. We then propose a language-driven interactive decoder with the help of class-specific prompt tuning, which adapts language proxies with visual domains. With the collaborative learning of proposed modules, experimental results demonstrate our proposed LDSA achieves a new state of the art on public multi-label classification benchmarks, and interpretable analyses reveal that our LDSA discovers implicit semantic relationships with the prior-adaptive learning scheme.

AI.tldr: LDSA is a language-driven dense semantic adaptor leveraging CLIP models for multi-label image classification with incomplete annotations, achieving state-of-the-art results on public benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for multi-label classification with incomplete annotations rely on statistical priors to recover missing semantics, but these priors suffer from unstable semantic mistakes leading to catastrophic overfitting.
AI.method: LDSA consists of two main components: (1) a densely contrastive adaptor that constructs dense visual contrastive constraints to transfer task-specific knowledge to visual domains, and (2) a language-driven interactive decoder with class-specific prompt tuning that adapts language proxies to visual domains.
AI.result: Experimental results show LDSA achieves a new state of the art on public multi-label classification benchmarks, with interpretable analyses revealing that it discovers implicit semantic relationships through the prior-adaptive learning scheme.
AI.conclusion: The collaborative learning of the dense contrastive adaptor and language-driven interactive decoder effectively mitigates overfitting by leveraging multimodal CLIP priors adaptively, outperforming previous statistical prior-based approaches.

title: Beyond Factual Knowledge: Benchmarking and Learning Step-Level Procedural Rule Reasoning in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) excel at text understanding and generation, yet still struggle to reliably understand and apply externally provided procedural rules at scale. To evaluate this capability, we introduce RuleWorld, a large-scale benchmark that reformulates rules as globally reusable abstract units rather than instance-specific facts. In RuleWorld, several scenarios, including single-rule, parallel multi-rule, and multi-hop reasoning, are settled for comprehensive evaluation. We further propose DynaRule, an end-to-end framework that injects the given rules into the KV cache and turns retrieval into an internal, learnable, step-wise process. Specifically, DynaRule employs Stacked Step-Level Attention Training with a special <search> token to enable dynamic rule re-attention and updating during inference. In this way, the model can re-attend to the most relevant rules at each step, dynamically replacing outdated ones to support more stable multi-step reasoning. Experiments on RuleWorld show that existing LLMs face challenges under large rule pools, while DynaRule improves average QA accuracy by up to 19 points and achieves over 85% Recall@1 at 10K rules, outperforming strong baselines by large margins. We make our code and dataset available here: https://github.com/SharkSpicy-NLP/Beyond-Factual-Knowledge.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RuleWorld, a large-scale benchmark for evaluating LLMs' ability to apply externally provided procedural rules, and proposes DynaRule, an end-to-end framework that injects rules into the KV cache with dynamic, step-wise rule retrieval via Stacked Step-Level Attention Training and a special <search> token. DynaRule improves QA accuracy by up to 19 points and achieves over 85% Recall@1 at 10K rules.
AI.motivation: LLMs excel at text understanding and generation but struggle to reliably understand and apply externally provided procedural rules at scale. Existing approaches treat rules as instance-specific facts, failing to capture their globally reusable abstract nature.
AI.method: DynaRule is an end-to-end framework that injects given rules into the KV cache, converting retrieval into an internal, learnable, step-wise process. It employs Stacked Step-Level Attention Training with a special <search> token, enabling dynamic rule re-attention and updating during inference so the model can re-attend to the most relevant rules at each step.
AI.result: On RuleWorld, existing LLMs face challenges under large rule pools, while DynaRule improves average QA accuracy by up to 19 points and achieves over 85% Recall@1 at 10K rules, outperforming strong baselines by large margins.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that LLMs struggle with large-scale procedural rule application, and DynaRule's dynamic rule attention mechanism significantly improves performance in this setting, with code and dataset publicly available.

title: Read Less, Solve More: Token-Efficient Sparse Reading for AI Agents
summary: Long-horizon agents increasingly rely on repeated access to external artifacts, yet current reading interfaces often expose entire objects even when only sparse evidence is needed. This over-reading increases token and latency costs and can dilute task-relevant evidence, while existing context-reduction methods mainly intervene after broad content has already entered the trajectory. We present SparseRead, a training-free, model-transparent reading layer that controls content admission before unnecessary evidence reaches the model context. SparseRead combines a regime-aware Read Gate, extensible Reader Backends, and a stateful protocol for bounded, source-anchored evidence acquisition with explicit refinement, verification, stopping, and fallback. Across six frontier models, including Claude Opus 5, and five workload scenarios, SparseRead reduces token volume by up to 92.9% and wall time by up to 89.0%, while preserving or improving task quality. Its consistent gains across three agent frameworks further demonstrate broad portability.

AI.tldr: SparseRead is a training-free, model-transparent reading layer that controls content admission before unnecessary evidence reaches the model context, reducing token volume by up to 92.9% and wall time by up to 89.0% while preserving or improving task quality across six frontier models and five workload scenarios.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon agents frequently over-read external artifacts, exposing entire objects when only sparse evidence is needed. This incurs high token and latency costs, dilutes task-relevant evidence, and existing context-reduction methods act too late—after broad content has already entered the trajectory.
AI.method: SparseRead combines a regime-aware Read Gate, extensible Reader Backends, and a stateful protocol for bounded, source-anchored evidence acquisition with explicit refinement, verification, stopping, and fallback mechanisms. It is training-free and model-transparent, intervening early in the content admission pipeline.
AI.result: Across six frontier models (including Claude Opus 5) and five workload scenarios, SparseRead reduces token volume by up to 92.9% and wall time by up to 89.0%, while preserving or improving task quality. Consistent gains were observed across three agent frameworks, demonstrating broad portability.
AI.conclusion: SparseRead demonstrates that proactive, early-stage content filtering through a lightweight reading layer can deliver substantial efficiency gains in long-horizon agent systems without sacrificing task performance, and it generalizes well across models, workloads, and agent frameworks.

title: On the Choice of Tensor Estimation for Corner Detection, Optical Flow and Denoising
summary: Many image processing methods such as corner detection, optical flow and iterative enhancement make use of image tensors. Generally, these tensors are estimated using the structure tensor. In this work we show that the gradient energy tensor can be used as an alternative to the structure tensor in several cases. We apply the gradient energy tensor to common image problem applications such as corner detection, optical flow and image enhancement. Our experimental results suggest that the gradient energy tensor enables real-time tensor-based image enhancement using the graphical processing unit (GPU) and we obtain 40% increase of frame rate without loss of image quality.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the gradient energy tensor as an alternative to the conventional structure tensor for image processing tasks such as corner detection, optical flow, and iterative image enhancement. Experimental results show that the gradient energy tensor enables real-time GPU-based image enhancement with a 40% frame rate increase and no loss in image quality.
AI.motivation: Structure tensors are widely used in image processing methods but may have computational or quality limitations. The authors seek a cheaper and equally effective alternative tensor estimation method.
AI.method: The authors apply the gradient energy tensor to common image processing problems including corner detection, optical flow, and iterative image enhancement, comparing its performance against the standard structure tensor.
AI.result: The gradient energy tensor achieves a 40% increase in frame rate for GPU-based real-time tensor-based image enhancement without sacrificing image quality.
AI.conclusion: The gradient energy tensor is a viable and more efficient alternative to the structure tensor for several image processing applications.

title: XTC: Head-Aware Sampling by Excluding Top Choices
summary: Standard decoding rules for autoregressive language models promote diversity by rescaling the full next-token distribution or truncating its low-probability tail. These strategies overlook a common regime of open-ended generation in which several continuations are plausible but too much probability mass remains concentrated on the most generic choice. We introduce XTC (Exclude Top Choices), a lightweight head-aware decoding operator that targets this regime directly. XTC identifies tokens whose probabilities exceed an absolute plausibility threshold $τ$: when at least two qualify, it removes the dominant eligible choices with probability $ρ$ and retains only the weakest plausible alternative before renormalization. Across 60 experiments on Gemma 3 27B Q4, Gemma 3 12B Q6, and DeepSeek R1 14B Q6, with scaling validation on Llama 3.3 70B Q4, XTC improves the diversity-repetition Pareto frontier. On creative generation, Distinct-2 increases by 11--15% and repeat trigrams decrease by 27--47% across the four models. Combined with temperature scaling, gains reach 38% in Distinct-2 and 71% in repeat-trigram reduction over baseline. A blinded Amazon Mechanical Turk study with 150 Master raters yields a 62.3% creativity preference for XTC ($p<10^{-4}$) without reduced fluency, while a GPT-4o control judge reproduces the Anthropic-judge direction on every measure. On IFEval with Llama 3.3 70B Q4, XTC preserves prompt-level strict accuracy within 1.7 percentage points of baseline while recovering most of the diversity gain; a temperature setting matched on Distinct-2 reduces IFEval by 8.8 points. The effect is additive with temperature and repetition penalties, robust across quantization levels and model families, and consistent across twelve prompt genres. XTC has been adopted by llama.cpp, ExLlamaV2, and text-generation-webui.

AI.tldr: XTC is a head-aware decoding operator that improves diversity-repetition tradeoffs in open-ended generation by excluding dominant token choices above an absolute plausibility threshold, retaining only the weakest plausible alternative. It improves Distinct-2 by 11-38% and reduces repeat trigrams by 27-71% across four models, wins 62.3% creativity preference in human evaluation, preserves IFEval accuracy within 1.7 points, and has been adopted by llama.cpp, ExLlamaV2, and text-generation-webui.
AI.motivation: Standard decoding rules (rescaling, truncation) target the low-probability tail, but overlook the common regime where several continuations are plausible yet probability mass is overly concentrated on the most generic choice. Existing methods fail to address this concentration-on-generic-token problem directly.
AI.method: XTC identifies tokens exceeding an absolute plausibility threshold τ; when at least two qualify, it removes dominant eligible choices with probability ρ and retains only the weakest plausible alternative before renormalization. It operates head-aware (targets the top of the distribution) and is combined with temperature scaling.
AI.result: Across 60 experiments on Gemma 3 27B Q4, Gemma 3 12B Q6, DeepSeek R1 14B Q6, and Llama 3.3 70B Q4, XTC improves the diversity-repetition Pareto frontier: Distinct-2 +11-15% and repeat trigrams -27-47% across four models; +38% Distinct-2 and 71% repeat-trigram reduction with temperature scaling. Human study: 62.3% creativity preference (p<10^-4) without reduced fluency. IFEval preserved within 1.7 points (vs 8.8-point drop for temperature-matched setting).
AI.conclusion: XTC is additive with temperature and repetition penalties, robust across quantization levels and model families, and consistent across twelve prompt genres. Its adoption by llama.cpp, ExLlamaV2, and text-generation-webui confirms practical utility for creative open-ended generation.

title: Clarify User Expertise: Towards Proactive Conversational Agents Tailoring Responses to User Proficiency
summary: In the context of information seeking, conversational agents are undergoing an evolution from reactive tools to proactive, personalized assistants. A critical aspect of this evolution is the ability to tailor strategic interactions to a user's unique needs and expectations. Unlike existing studies that focus on proactively clarifying query ambiguities, we center on clarifying the user's expertise in order to tailor responses for better user comprehension. We find that existing agents struggle to determine user expertise from queries alone, a limitation that prevents them from dynamically adapting their responses. To address this gap, we introduce PASSING to empower the agent to proactively clarify a user's expertise through targeted inquiries. This is achieved by our What-to-ask and How-to-ask strategies, induced by LLM self-play. Our extensive experiments also show our superiority. We believe that PASSING represents a crucial step towards creating more human-centric conversational agents.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PASSING, a framework that empowers conversational agents to proactively clarify a user's expertise level through targeted inquiries, using LLM self-play to generate What-to-ask and How-to-ask strategies, enabling agents to tailor responses for better user comprehension.
AI.motivation: Existing conversational agents focus on clarifying query ambiguities but fail to determine user expertise from queries alone, preventing them from dynamically adapting responses to match the user's comprehension level. There is a need to move beyond reactive tools toward proactive, personalized assistants that tailor strategic interactions to individual user needs.
AI.method: The framework PASSING uses a What-to-ask and How-to-ask strategy induced by LLM self-play to enable agents to proactively clarify user expertise through targeted inquiries, rather than relying solely on query-based inference.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of PASSING over existing approaches in enabling conversational agents to effectively determine user expertise and adapt responses accordingly.
AI.conclusion: PASSING represents a crucial step toward more human-centric conversational agents capable of tailoring responses based on clarified user expertise, moving beyond reactive clarification of query ambiguities.

title: MedReaMM: Evaluating Large Multimodal Models on Expert-Level Clinical Diagnostic Synthesis
summary: The application of Large Language Models (LLMs) to diagnostic decision-making has garnered growing interest. However, existing benchmarks largely focus on textual reasoning or isolated visual question-answering (VQA) tasks, lacking holistic integration of clinical narratives and medical imaging, and thus failing to assess the multimodal diagnostic synthesis capability central to expert clinical judgment. To bridge this gap, we introduce MedReaMM, a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate models' ability to synthesize heterogeneous clinical evidence consisting of detailed patient histories alongside multiple medical images into accurate differential diagnoses under a complete-information paradigm. Constructed from case reports sourced from top-tier medical journals and curated clinical case databases, MedReaMM comprises 625 expert-validated cases with an average of 2.79 medical images per case and a total of 1,042 standardized diagnoses annotated with ICD-11 codes. These cases predominantly represent rare, atypical, or multi-system presentations that demand expert-level evidence integration beyond routine pattern recognition. We evaluate 23 Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) and find that most achieve diagnostic accuracy scores below 50%, underscoring a substantial gap in multimodal diagnostic synthesis capability. Further analysis reveals that medical knowledge proficiency, medical image understanding, and evidence integration are all highly correlated with diagnostic performance.

AI.tldr: Introduces MedReaMM, a benchmark of 625 expert-validated clinical cases with 1,742 medical images and ICD-11-coded diagnoses, designed to evaluate LLMs on holistic multimodal diagnostic synthesis. Evaluation of 23 LMMs shows most score below 50% accuracy, revealing a substantial gap in integrating clinical narratives with imaging for differential diagnosis.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for LLM diagnostic decision-making are fragmented—focusing either on textual reasoning or isolated visual QA—and fail to assess the integrated multimodal synthesis of clinical narratives and medical imaging that is central to expert clinical judgment.
AI.method: Constructed MedReaMM from case reports in top-tier medical journals and curated clinical databases, yielding 625 expert-validated cases with an average of 2.79 medical images per case and 1,042 standardized ICD-11-coded diagnoses. The benchmark emphasizes rare, atypical, and multi-system presentations requiring expert-level evidence integration. 23 Large Multimodal Models were evaluated under a complete-information paradigm.
AI.result: Most of the 23 evaluated LMMs achieved diagnostic accuracy below 50%. Medical knowledge proficiency, medical image understanding, and evidence integration were each found to be highly correlated with diagnostic performance.
AI.conclusion: Current LMMs fall far short of expert-level multimodal diagnostic synthesis, and MedReaMM provides a rigorous benchmark to measure and drive progress in this capability, highlighting that performance is tied to knowledge, imaging comprehension, and evidence integration jointly.

title: Don't Repeat Yourself: Stopping Verbatim Loops at Sampling Time
summary: Large Language Models generate text autoregressively, but open-ended generation is prone to verbatim looping, in which models repeat spans already present in context. Standard defenses such as repetition, presence, and frequency penalties and n-gram blocking act on token recurrence rather than the sequential structure of a loop, and often suppress looping only at strengths that also degrade formatting or fluency. We propose Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY), a sampling-time logit adjustment that penalizes a candidate token only when generating it would extend the current suffix into an exact continuation of a span seen earlier in the context. Sequence breakers protect chat templates and formatting tokens. Across models from 1.5B to 120B parameters, nine prompt families, and a 600-pair human study, DRY reduces suffix-extension rate by 47% while improving lexical diversity. An intervention-matched placebo produces no comparable reduction, identifying suffix matching as the operative mechanism. On AWQ-quantized 70B and 120B models, DRY reduces loop rate by roughly half while preserving MT-Bench, MMLU, and GSM8K performance, whereas standard alternatives lose measurable ground. DRY has been adopted by popular open-source LLM inference frameworks including llama.cpp, ExLlamaV2, and text-generation-webui, highlighting its practical impact on text generation.

AI.tldr: DRY is a sampling-time logit adjustment that prevents verbatim looping in LLM text generation by penalizing a token only when it would extend the current suffix into an exact continuation of a previously seen span. It reduces suffix-extension rate by 47% across models from 1.5B to 120B parameters and is adopted by popular inference frameworks like llama.cpp and ExLlamaV2.
AI.motivation: Open-ended LLM generation is prone to verbatim looping where models repeat spans already in context. Standard defenses (repetition, presence, frequency penalties, n-gram blocking) act on token recurrence rather than the sequential structure of a loop, and only suppress looping at strengths that degrade formatting or fluency. A mechanism targeting the actual loop structure at sampling time is needed.
AI.method: DRY applies a logit adjustment at sampling time that penalizes a candidate token only when generating it would extend the current suffix into an exact continuation of a span seen earlier in the context. Sequence breakers are used to protect chat templates and formatting tokens. The method is evaluated via an intervention-matched placebo to isolate suffix matching as the operative mechanism.
AI.result: Across models from 1.5B to 120B parameters, nine prompt families, and a 600-pair human study, DRY reduces suffix-extension rate by 47% while improving lexical diversity. A placebo produces no comparable reduction, confirming suffix matching as the mechanism. On AWQ-quantized 70B and 120B models, DRY reduces loop rate by roughly half while preserving MT-Bench, MMLU, and GSM8K performance, unlike standard alternatives which lose measurable ground.
AI.conclusion: DRY is a targeted, effective defense against verbatim looping that outperforms standard penalties without degrading quality metrics. Its adoption by major open-source inference frameworks (llama.cpp, ExLlamaV2, text-generation-webui) demonstrates significant practical impact in real-world text generation.

title: HERO: Human-profile Enhanced Retrieval Optimization Framework for Long-term Agent Memory
summary: Long-term memory is crucial for personalized responses and long-horizon agent interactions. Existing methods often rely on LLMs to compress or rewrite dialogue histories and use the transformed memories as retrieval evidence. Despite the progress in organizing fragmented contexts, two major drawbacks persist: (1) information loss from compression, which discards fine-grained but later useful details, and (2) semantic drift from rewriting, which erodes the original tone and situated context. In this work, we propose a novel Human-profile Enhanced Retrieval Optimization framework for long-term agent memory (HERO). Specifically, HERO converts the dialogue history into a traceable heterogeneous memory graph that preserves raw dialogue text as evidence for reasoning, thereby mitigating information loss. For retrieval, HERO extracts initial anchors from the current query and incorporates human profiles via an iterative graph traversal; these anchors and profiles provide guidance signals that adaptively activate the most informative regions of the graph. Experiments on two benchmark datasets show that HERO outperforms strong baselines on both factual and personalized reasoning, while providing more faithful access to raw dialogue evidence.

AI.tldr: HERO is a Human-profile Enhanced Retrieval Optimization framework for long-term agent memory that converts dialogue history into a traceable heterogeneous memory graph preserving raw text, and uses human profiles with iterative graph traversal to activate informative regions, outperforming baselines on factual and personalized reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing long-term memory methods rely on LLM-based compression or rewriting of dialogue histories, which suffer from (1) information loss that discards fine-grained but later useful details, and (2) semantic drift that erodes original tone and situated context.
AI.method: HERO constructs a traceable heterogeneous memory graph from dialogue history that preserves raw dialogue text as retrieval evidence. For retrieval, it extracts initial anchors from the current query and incorporates human profiles via iterative graph traversal, using these signals to adaptively activate the most informative graph regions.
AI.result: Experiments on two benchmark datasets show HERO outperforms strong baselines on both factual and personalized reasoning, while providing more faithful access to raw dialogue evidence.
AI.conclusion: Preserving raw dialogue text through a heterogeneous memory graph combined with human-profile-guided graph traversal can mitigate information loss and semantic drift, improving both factual accuracy and personalization in long-term agent memory.

title: AcroMELD: Recovering Interactive PDF Forms with Structure-Aware Graph Set Transformers
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. Source compiles to a tagged PDF 2.0 document with MathML embedded as associated files
summary: Interactive PDF form fields are often absent from documents that visually resemble forms, leaving users unable to enter data without printing or external editing tools. Detecting the missing widgets is difficult because a field may be indicated by several overlapping cues, born-digital PDFs expose useful but incomplete drawing structure, and dense pages can contain hundreds of fields. We introduce AcroMELD (AcroForm Multi-source Evidence Linking Decoder), a 39.4M-parameter detector that combines a high-resolution visual transformer with label-free PDF primitives. Its 896-query set comprises 384 visual proposals, 384 structure-seeded proposals, and 128 learned recovery queries. Four graph-set layers exchange information over geometry-biased sparse neighborhoods and cross-attend to PDF structure. A learned same-field relation links co-referent candidates, while a localization-quality head is trained on the containment-aware overlap used by the downstream recovery decision. We define a hash-bound evaluation protocol with disjoint development, calibration, internal-test, and quarantined external-holdout roles. The sealed, single-seed candidate reaches native containment micro-$F_1$ 0.9344 on the internal test and 0.8477 on the one-shot external holdout (95% PDF-cluster bootstrap interval [0.8339, 0.8605]). This passes the registered historical FFGBT-v8 reference by 0.0186 absolute $F_1$. Under the stricter external adapter, however, performance is 0.7786 IoU-$0.5$ $F_1$ and 0.2900 COCO mAP, below a locally evaluated CommonForms-L reference; the signature class receives no prediction at the selected threshold. Thus the result supports the registered operational gate while exposing substantial domain and rare-class limitations.

AI.tldr: AcroMELD is a 39.4M-parameter detector for locating missing interactive PDF form fields (AcroForm widgets) in born-digital documents, combining a high-resolution visual transformer with PDF primitives and a 896-query set. It achieves native containment micro-F1 of 0.9344 internally and 0.8477 on external holdout, passing a registered baseline reference, yet shows substantial degradation under stricter adapters and fails on rare classes.
AI.motivation: Interactive PDF form fields are frequently missing from documents that visually resemble forms, preventing users from entering data without printing or external tools. Detecting these missing widgets is challenging due to overlapping visual cues, incomplete PDF drawing structure, and dense pages containing hundreds of fields.
AI.method: AcroMELD employs a hybrid architecture: a high-resolution visual transformer combined with label-free PDF primitives. It uses 896 queries (384 visual proposals, 384 structure-seeded proposals, 128 learned recovery queries) processed through four graph-set layers with geometry-biased sparse neighborhoods and cross-attention to PDF structure. A learned same-field relation links co-referent candidates, and a localization-quality head is trained on containment-aware overlap. Evaluation uses a hash-bound protocol with separated development, calibration, internal-test, and quarantined external-holdout roles.
