AI.result: The model achieves native containment micro-F1 of 0.9344 on internal test and 0.8477 on one-shot external holdout (95% bootstrap CI [0.8339, 0.8605]), surpassing the registered FFGBT-v8 reference by 0.0186 absolute F1. However, under the stricter external adapter, performance drops to 0.7786 IoU-0.5 F1 and 0.2900 COCO mAP, below a local CommonForms-L reference, with no predictions for the signature class at the selected threshold.
AI.conclusion: The results support passing the registered operational gate but expose substantial domain-shift and rare-class limitations, indicating that while AcroMELD works well under native protocols, its generalization to stricter external conditions and signature-type fields remains a significant challenge.

title: DelistBench: Evaluating Search-Enabled LLMs for Auditable Corporate-Event Database Completion
summary: Financial institutions need an independent way to detect missing, stale, and misclassified corporate-event records in vendor databases. We introduce Search-to-Record, a database-assurance task in which search-enabled large language models reconstruct institution-defined event records from public sources for a known security universe and historical cutoff, and DelistBench, a 1,200-record benchmark for security-level delisting announcements. We evaluate five models in paired closed-book and web-enabled conditions. Web access raises announcement-date accuracy within seven days by 34.0 to 48.0 percentage points and event-status accuracy by approximately 2.8 to 21.7 points; the best system achieves 81.5% overall joint accuracy within seven days. Economy web systems achieve 75.9-78.3% overall joint accuracy within seven days at 4.5-6.6% of the API cost of the most expensive web system. Risk-based triage identifies low-error subsets, although the highest-coverage operating point still sends 27.3% of the balanced test set to review. The evaluation identifies web retrieval as the main source of timing gains and shows that low-cost systems can approach the best system's accuracy. Together, Search-to-Record, DelistBench, and the evaluation provide concrete deployment guidance: calibrate triage to local event prevalence and market mix, preserve positive-event recall, and route positive and ambiguous cases to targeted review.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Search-to-Record, a database-assurance task for detecting missing, stale, and misclassified corporate-event records using search-enabled LLMs, along with DelistBench, a 1,200-record benchmark for security-level delisting announcements. Web access significantly improves accuracy (34.0-48.0 points for announcement dates within seven days, 2.8-21.7 points for event status), with the best system achieving 81.5% joint accuracy. Economy systems achieve near-parity at 4.5-6.6% of the cost, and risk-based triage reduces review workload while providing concrete deployment guidance.
AI.motivation: Financial institutions require an independent mechanism to verify the completeness and correctness of corporate-event records in vendor databases, as missing, stale, or misclassified records can have significant operational and financial consequences.
AI.method: The authors define Search-to-Record (S2R), a task where search-enabled LLMs reconstruct institution-defined event records from public sources given a known security universe and historical cutoff. They build DelistBench with 1,200 records of security-level delisting announcements and evaluate five models in paired closed-book and web-enabled conditions, measuring announcement-date accuracy and event-status accuracy within defined windows.
AI.result: Web access raises announcement-date accuracy within seven days by 34.0-48.0 percentage points and event-status accuracy by ~2.8-21.7 points. The best system achieves 81.5% overall joint accuracy within seven days. Economy systems achieve 75.9-78.3% at 4.5-6.6% of the API cost of the most expensive system. Risk-based triage identifies low-error subsets, though the highest-coverage operating point still routes 27.3% of the balanced test set to review.
AI.conclusion: Web retrieval is the main source of timing gains, low-cost systems can approach the best system's accuracy, and deployment requires calibrating triage to local event prevalence and market mix, preserving positive-event recall, and routing positive/ambiguous cases to targeted review.

title: Where Cognition Lives: Dissecting Emergent from Computed Function in a Minimal Complete Cognitive Architecture
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures. Code, preregistrations and results: https://github.com/fmarrabal/miuracognitive
summary: A cognitive architecture is more than the module that reasons: it must also decide how long to think and what deserves the effort. We built a minimal but complete system - a recurrent reasoner with adaptive halting, a homeostatic control field, and a value module - and asked of each part: does this function emerge from gradient descent, or must it be computed? Competence emerges. Stopping appears to emerge too, and to be worth more than everything decidable in advance, but that appearance is instrumentation: payoff at matched mean compute climbs from 0.467 (uniform) through 0.546 (difficulty) to 0.698 (ex-ante value), and the further climb to 0.921 (posterior self-observation) does not survive audit. PonderNet-style halting returns a halting-weighted mixture of hidden states while forced-depth baselines return one, and the language head is trained on the mixture alone; equalizing the readout annihilates the apparent advantage of native execution (residual +0.000 [0.000, 0.000]). Value does not emerge: trained couplings capture zero of a payoff an explicit allocator captures completely (+0.151, routing correlation +0.79), so the second-order decisions that pay must be computed, at least where value is orthogonal to content, as here by construction. On a frozen LLM actuator the same instruments show self-consistency voting to be a measured bound (+0.0236 [+0.0150, +0.0326]) and inter-sample agreement nearly worthless as a stopping signal, its mass concentrating on wrong answers. Every null we assert carries a mechanism and a positive control, and the protocol is part of the contribution. Executing our own falsifiable prediction, value under commitment pays +0.1312 [+0.1124, +0.1502] in a cliff-cost family, some seven times the smooth-family estimate - not because the cliff shifts information ex ante, but because it multiplies the attainable range fivefold (5.1x [3.4, 8.2]).

AI.tldr: This paper systematically tests whether compute allocation (how long to think, what deserves effort) in a recurrent reasoner emerges from gradient descent or must be explicitly computed. Stopping behavior appears to emerge but survives audit only for computable signals (difficulty, ex-ante value), not for posterior self-observation. Value estimation does not emerge—trained couplings capture zero of payoff that an explicit allocator captures completely. On frozen LLMs, self-consistency voting is a measured bound, and inter-sample agreement is nearly worthless as a stopping signal. Complete protocols, positive controls, and null results are part of the contribution.
AI.motivation: A cognitive architecture must not only reason but also decide how long to think and where to invest effort. The paper asks whether these second-order, compute-allocation decisions emerge through gradient descent or require explicit mechanisms, using a minimal but complete architecture.
AI.method: Builds a minimal recurrent reasoner with adaptive halting, a homeostatic control field, and a value module. Tests each component against null hypotheses using matched-mean-compute payoff comparisons, forced-depth baselines, equalized readouts, and a cliff-cost family for commitment effects. Also probes frozen LLMs with self-consistency voting and inter-sample agreement as stopping signals.
AI.result: Competence and apparent stopping emerge, but the posterior self-observation advantage (0.921 vs 0.698) fails audit—equalized readout yields residual +0.000. Value does not emerge: trained couplings capture zero of payoff that an explicit allocator captures (+0.151, routing correlation +0.79). On frozen LLMs, self-consistency voting yields +0.0236, and inter-sample agreement concentrates on wrong answers. Under commitment in a cliff-cost family, value pays +0.1312, roughly seven times the smooth-family estimate, due to 5.1x expansion in attainable range rather than ex-ante information shifts.
AI.conclusion: Which second-order decisions emerge and which must be computed depends on the specific function. Apparent emergent stopping can be an instrumentation artifact that vanishes under equalized readouts. Value estimation requires explicit computation when orthogonal to content. The paper's protocol—null results with mechanisms and positive controls—is itself a contribution, and its falsifiable prediction is experimentally executed.

title: TransHands: Repurposing Human Pose Encoders as Hand Pose Encoders
summary: Lifting 3D hand poses from 2D monocular representations remains challenging due to the limited availability of large-scale, diverse 3D-annotated hand datasets, in contrast to the abundance of human body motion data. We address this limitation by transferring motion representations learned from large body pose corpora to the hand domain. We introduce TransHands, a backbone-agnostic transfer learning framework that enables pre-trained human motion encoders to be effectively adapted for 3D hand pose estimation from 2D pose inputs. Rather than training hand-specific biomechanical models from scratch, TransHands combines a two-stage training and fine-tuning strategy with a lightweight hand-specific input adaptation module that aligns hand kinematics with the representation space learned for full-body motion. We evaluate TransHands across four state-of-the-art motion modeling architectures, including transformer-based, graph-based, and frequency- domain models. Results demonstrate that motion priors learned from body pose data transfer consistently across architectures, yielding consistent accuracy gains, strong cross-domain generalization, particularly in challenging egocentric settings, and applicability for downstream tasks in real-world contexts.

AI.tldr: TransHands is a backbone-agnostic transfer learning framework that adapts pre-trained human body motion encoders for 3D hand pose estimation from 2D inputs, using a two-stage training strategy and a lightweight hand-specific input adaptation module. It demonstrates consistent accuracy gains and strong cross-domain generalization across transformer, graph, and frequency-domain architectures.
AI.motivation: 3D hand pose estimation from monocular 2D representations is limited by the scarcity of large-scale, diverse 3D-annotated hand datasets, unlike the abundance of available body motion data. The authors aim to leverage this asymmetry by transferring motion representations learned from large body pose corpora to the hand domain.
AI.method: TransHands combines a two-stage training and fine-tuning strategy with a lightweight hand-specific input adaptation module. The input adaptation module aligns hand kinematics with the representation space learned for full-body motion, enabling pre-trained human motion encoders to be effectively adapted for 3D hand pose estimation from 2D pose inputs.
AI.result: Evaluation across four motion modeling architectures (transformer-based, graph-based, and frequency-domain models) shows that body motion priors transfer consistently across architectures, yielding consistent accuracy gains, strong cross-domain generalization particularly in egocentric settings, and applicability for downstream real-world tasks.
AI.conclusion: Motion priors learned from body pose data can successfully transfer to the hand domain, providing a viable alternative to training hand-specific biomechanical models from scratch and demonstrating practical utility for real-world 3D hand pose estimation applications.

title: WAM-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for World Action Models
summary: World action models (WAMs) couple visual future prediction with robot action generation, but accelerated students can lose task capabilities during distillation and later encounter states that are poorly represented by offline data. We study whether on-policy distillation (OPD) can repair such a student without requiring sparse-reward reinforcement learning. We introduce WAM-OPD, a deployment-consistent post-training recipe for a video-first WAM. The student acts in the environment and therefore determines the history distribution. A frozen teacher labels those student histories with coherent video and action targets, while the student action branch is trained under its own generated video plan, as it is at deployment. Joint video and action losses update lightweight adapters in the shared backbone, together with an action flow-matching regularizer. In preliminary RoboTwin 2.0 studies on two tasks, the released one-video/one-action-step Flash-WAM improves from 0.0% to 58.3% success on HANDOVER MIC, and from 16.7% to 33.3% on PUT OBJECT CABINET. These task-specific results are an initial capability proof rather than evidence of broad or uniform generalization. They nevertheless suggest that dense teacher supervision on student-induced histories is a promising post-training interface for video-first WAMs.

AI.tldr: WAM-OPD applies on-policy distillation to repair a distilled video-first World Action Model by having the student act in the environment, letting a frozen teacher label student-induced histories, and training lightweight adapters under deployment-consistent video plans, improving task success from 0% to 58.3% and 16.7% to 33.3% on two RoboTwin 2.0 tasks.
AI.motivation: Distilled "student" World Action Models can lose task capabilities during accelerated distillation, and later encounter states poorly covered by offline training data, leaving them unable to recover without sparse-reward RL.
AI.method: The student acts in the environment to determine the history distribution. A frozen teacher labels these student histories with coherent video and action targets. The student action branch is trained under its own generated video plan (deployment-consistent). Joint video and action losses update lightweight adapters in the shared backbone, augmented by an action flow-matching regularizer.
AI.result: On two RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, Flash-WAM improved from 0.0% to 58.3% success on HANDOVER MIC and from 16.7% to 33.3% on PUT OBJECT CABINET, serving as a capability proof rather than evidence of broad generalization.
AI.conclusion: Dense teacher supervision on student-induced histories is a promising post-training interface for video-first WAMs, though results are task-specific and not yet demonstrations of uniform generalization.

title: SPOC-SQL: Stage-wise Preference Optimization for Controllable Text-to-SQL
summary: Text-to-SQL aims to translate natural language questions into executable SQL queries over relational databases, requiring multi-stage structured reasoning over database schemas and query constraints. However, existing methods treat this task as single-step generation, where models optimize entire SQL sequences without targeted feedback at key decision points and lack support for interacting with and controlling the intermediate generation process. To address this issue, we propose SPOC-SQL, which decomposes Text-to-SQL into four sequential subtasks following standard SQL execution logic and designs stage-specific optimization strategies for the model to learn key decisions. Specifically, we propose the implementation of fine-grained preference optimisation at key decision points across SQL stages, with the objective of enhancing structured decision-making during query construction. Furthermore, a structured decomposition strategy is designed, facilitating stage-wise intervention and correction through explicit intermediate representations. This results in more controllable and reliable SQL generation. Experiments demonstrate that incorporating stage-wise human knowledge consistently improves performance, validating the effectiveness of stage perception controllable generation.

AI.tldr: SPOC-SQL decomposes Text-to-SQL into four sequential subtasks following standard SQL execution logic, with stage-specific preference optimization and structured decomposition for controllable and reliable query generation.
AI.motivation: Existing Text-to-SQL methods treat the task as single-step generation, optimizing entire SQL sequences without targeted feedback at key decision points and lacking support for interacting with and controlling the intermediate generation process.
AI.method: SPOC-SQL decomposes Text-to-SQL into four sequential subtasks following standard SQL execution logic, implements fine-grained preference optimization at key decision points across SQL stages, and designs a structured decomposition strategy enabling stage-wise intervention and correction through explicit intermediate representations.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that incorporating stage-wise human knowledge consistently improves performance, validating the effectiveness of stage-perception controllable generation.
AI.conclusion: Stage-wise decomposition with targeted preference optimization at key decision points yields more controllable and reliable SQL generation compared to single-step approaches.

title: Addressing the Selection Problem in Explainable AI
comment: Accepted to the Workshop on Explainable Artificial Intelligence at the International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence 2026 (XAI@IJCAI26)
summary: Explainable AI (XAI) research has produced a plethora of explanation techniques, yet user studies repeatedly show that available explanations are not effective in practice. We argue that, given the siloed nature of conventional XAI, users are struggling to select the appropriate XAI technique. Viewing XAI through a philosophical lens, we offer a formalization of what we call the selection problem: the systematic failure of XAI interfaces to bridge the gap between a user's natural-language uncertainty and the explanation technique that resolves it. Following a logical premise-conclusion format, we show that conventional interfaces require users to translate their uncertainty into a technique selection, a challenging prerequisite to meet. We also propose a structural solution: a multi-agent LLM orchestration tool that translates the user's query to the proper XAI explanation technique. We provide an example of how this structural solution could be instantiated to address the selection problem.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes the "selection problem" in Explainable AI (XAI)—the systematic failure of XAI interfaces to bridge users' natural-language uncertainty with appropriate explanation techniques—and proposes a multi-agent LLM orchestration tool as a structural solution that translates user queries into the proper XAI technique selection.
AI.motivation: Despite an abundance of XAI explanation techniques, user studies consistently show that available explanations are ineffective in practice. The authors argue this stems from the siloed nature of conventional XAI, which forces users to select the appropriate technique themselves—a challenging prerequisite given the gap between users' natural-language uncertainty and the technical selection process.
AI.method: The paper (1) views XAI through a philosophical lens to offer a formalization of the selection problem, (2) demonstrates via a logical premise-conclusion format that conventional interfaces impose an unreasonable translation burden on users, and (3) proposes a structural solution: a multi-agent LLM orchestration tool that automatically translates user queries into the appropriate XAI explanation technique, with an illustrative instantiation example.
AI.result: The paper establishes a formal definition of the selection problem, logically demonstrates why conventional XAI interfaces fail, and presents a concrete architectural proposal (multi-agent LLM orchestration) with an example instantiation showing how the structural solution could be implemented.
AI.conclusion: The selection problem is a fundamental barrier to XAI effectiveness, and a structural—rather than incremental—solution is needed. A multi-agent LLM orchestration system that bridges natural-language uncertainty to technique selection offers a promising pathway to make XAI explanations actually useful in practice.

title: Fast and Compact 3D Gaussian Splatting with Polarized Opacity Prior
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) achieves state-of-the-art rendering quality at real-time speeds but suffers from "model bloat" - a large number of redundant, low-opacity Gaussians that inflate memory usage and training costs. This inefficiency stems from the standard "densify-then-prune" paradigm, which expands the model aggressively before relying on pruning to achieve compactness. To mitigate this problem, we present an efficient training framework that builds an intrinsically compact representation, replacing the conventional densify-then-prune cycle. Our method leverages a synergistic design: an L2 reconstruction loss to provide error-proportional gradients that stabilize optimization, and a novel Polarized Opacity Prior (POP) to actively manage the Gaussian population. POP steers informative primitives toward full opacity and uninformative ones toward transparency, enabling natural pruning and accelerating rendering through Early Ray Termination. Experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently achieves accelerated 3DGS training with significantly fewer Gaussians while maintaining comparable visual reconstruction quality. These results show that the proposed framework provides a simple and effective path toward fast and inherently compact 3DGS training.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an efficient training framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that builds an intrinsically compact representation, replacing the conventional densify-then-prune cycle. It uses an L2 reconstruction loss and a novel Polarized Opacity Prior (POP) to manage the Gaussian population, steering informative primitives toward full opacity and uninformative ones toward transparency, enabling natural pruning and Early Ray Termination.
AI.motivation: 3DGS achieves state-of-the-art rendering quality at real-time speeds but suffers from "model bloat" - a large number of redundant, low-opacity Gaussians that inflate memory usage and training costs, stemming from the standard "densify-then-prune" paradigm.
AI.method: The framework synergistically combines an L2 reconstruction loss (providing error-proportional gradients for stabilized optimization) with a Polarized Opacity Prior (POP) that actively manages the Gaussian population, steering informative primitives toward full opacity and uninformative ones toward transparency. This enables natural pruning and accelerates rendering via Early Ray Termination.
AI.result: Experiments on three public datasets show the approach consistently achieves accelerated 3DGS training with significantly fewer Gaussians while maintaining comparable visual reconstruction quality.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a simple and effective path toward fast and inherently compact 3DGS training.

title: Contextrast++: Robust Multi-Scale Contextual Contrastive Learning for Semantic Segmentation
comment: Accepted to IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence (TPAMI), 2026
summary: Semantic segmentation has rapidly advanced with deep learning; however, challenges remain in effectively capturing local and global contexts as well as addressing the long-tailed distribution problem. To tackle these issues, we present Contextrast++, a robust contrastive learning method for semantic segmentation that improves multi-scale feature integration and mitigates class imbalance issues. Our method consists of two key components: 1) contextual contrastive learning (CCL) and 2) boundary-aware negative (BANE) sampling. CCL includes three subcomponents: adaptive fusion module, pixel-to-anchor (PA) loss, and anchor-to-anchor (AA) loss. The adaptive fusion module dynamically balances local and global feature integration, resulting in a more context-aware representation. While the PA loss leverages the fused multi-scale features to improve feature representation learning, the AA loss focuses on addressing the long-tailed distribution problem by utilizing a memory bank that stores a fixed number of class-balanced representative anchors. Meanwhile, BANE sampling enhances segmentation precision by selecting hard negatives from misclassified boundary regions, which refines fine-grained details during contrastive learning. As verified in extensive experiments using public datasets, we demonstrate that Contextrast++ substantially improves semantic segmentation performance over existing contrastive learning-based state-of-the-art approaches, while introducing no additional computational overhead during inference.

AI.tldr: Contextrast++ is a contrastive learning framework for semantic segmentation that combines contextual contrastive learning (CCL) with boundary-aware negative (BANE) sampling to improve multi-scale feature integration and mitigate long-tailed distribution problems without adding inference-time overhead.
AI.motivation: Existing semantic segmentation methods struggle with capturing local and global contexts effectively and suffer from long-tailed distribution problems (class imbalance), limiting their performance.
AI.method: Contextrast++ comprises two main components. (1) Contextual contrastive learning (CCL) includes an adaptive fusion module that dynamically balances local and global feature integration, a pixel-to-anchor (PA) loss for improved feature representation learning using fused multi-scale features, and an anchor-to-anchor (AA) loss that addresses long-tailed distributions via a memory bank of class-balanced representative anchors. (2) Boundary-aware negative (BANE) sampling selects hard negatives from misclassified boundary regions to refine fine-grained details during contrastive learning.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on public datasets show that Contextrast++ substantially improves semantic segmentation performance over existing contrastive learning-based state-of-the-art approaches, while introducing no additional computational overhead during inference.
AI.conclusion: Contextrast++ effectively handles multi-scale feature integration and class imbalance in semantic segmentation through contextual contrastive learning and boundary-aware hard negative sampling, achieving superior results at no extra inference cost.

title: TRACE: A Self-Evolving Skill Bank for Consistent, Limit-Aware LLM Agents
summary: Reliable deployment of LLM agents in user-facing products depends not on raw task-solving ability but on consistency and limit-awareness: behaving the same way across repeated trials, and recognizing when a request cannot, or cannot yet, be safely fulfilled. CAR-bench exposes this reliability gap in the domain of in-car assistants: an LLM-simulated user issues incomplete or ambiguous requests, requiring the agent to resolve uncertainty through multi-turn dialogue and tool use while strictly adhering to domain policies. Even frontier models show a substantial gap between what they can solve at least once (Pass@3) and what they solve consistently across trials (Pass^k). We bridge this gap with TRACE (TRAjectory-Contrastive Evolution), which iteratively improves a skill-based agent's behavioral knowledge without modifying model weights. This knowledge is organized as a Skill Bank of modular, retrievable skills, each encoding a self-contained set of tool-use rules and behavioral guidelines. TRACE evolves this bank through an agentic self-evolution loop: after each evaluation round, it groups trajectories by the skills invoked and refines each skill by contrasting successful and failed behaviors. The updated bank then guides subsequent rounds, while during deployment the Actor performs state-conditioned skill orchestration at every turn. On GPT-5.5, TRACE improves consistency (Pass^3) by 34.6 points, from 59.9% to 94.5%, while shrinking the gap between potential and reliable performance to just 4.0 points. On the official hidden set, TRACE achieved first place using GPT-5.6-Sol, attaining a Pass^3 score of 70%-a 40% relative improvement over the baseline. These results show that TRACE converts high model potential into stable, consistent performance gain. Project homepage: https://darwin-agent.github.io/Car-bench-TRACE.

AI.tldr: CAR-bench exposes the reliability gap in LLM agents for in-car assistants, showing a substantial difference between what agents can solve at least once versus consistently across trials. The paper introduces TRACE, a trajectory-contrastive evolution method that improves a skill-based agent's behavioral knowledge through a Skill Bank of modular, retrievable skills without modifying model weights. TRACE improves consistency on GPT-5.5 from 59.9% to 94.5% Pass^3, shrinking the potential-to-reliable gap to just 4.0 points, and achieved first place on the official hidden set with a 40% relative improvement over baseline.
AI.motivation: Reliable deployment of LLM agents in user-facing products depends not on raw task-solving ability but on consistency and limit-awareness: behaving consistently across repeated trials and recognizing when a request cannot be safely fulfilled. The paper identifies that even frontier models show a significant gap between what they can solve at least once and what they solve reliably across trials, which is critical for domains like in-car assistants where dependability is paramount.
AI.method: TRACE (TRAjectory-Contrastive Evolution) iteratively improves a skill-based agent's behavioral knowledge without modifying model weights. The knowledge is organized as a Skill Bank of modular, retrievable skills, each encoding a self-contained set of tool-use rules and behavioral guidelines. TRACE evolves this bank through an agentic self-evolution loop: after each evaluation round, it groups trajectories by the skills invoked and refines each skill by contrasting successful and failed behaviors. During deployment, the Actor performs state-conditioned skill orchestration at every turn.
AI.result: On GPT-5.5, TRACE improves consistency (Pass^3) by 34.6 points, from 59.9% to 94.5%, shrinking the gap between potential and reliable performance to just 4.0 points. On the official hidden set, TRACE achieved first place using GPT-5.6-Sol, attaining a Pass^3 score of 70%—a 40% relative improvement over the baseline.
AI.conclusion: TRACE effectively converts high model potential into stable, consistent performance gains by using trajectory-contrastive evolution to improve a skill-based agent's behavioral knowledge without modifying model weights. The results demonstrate that the gap between potential and reliable performance can be substantially closed in safety-critical domains like in-car assistants.

title: Analyzing and Mitigating Cross-Lingual Degradation in Multilingual Medical VQA
summary: Medical visual question answering (VQA) is a crucial task in clinical AI, yet its evaluation has so far centered almost exclusively on English, limiting its relevance to linguistically diverse patients and clinicians. Recent multilingual medical VQA benchmarks show that large vision-language models (LVLMs) degrade in non-English languages, but lack a fine-grained analysis of how cross-lingual variation affects the distinct capabilities that medical VQA requires. To this end, we construct a multilingual medical VQA benchmark over eight languages, organized into four representative scenarios that isolate the core capabilities medical VQA requires. Evaluating five open- and closed-source LVLMs, we find that cross-lingual degradation is not uniform but highly scenario-dependent. We therefore propose MedVL-XLRepE, a training-free scenario-aware representation engineering method, leveraging LVLMs' superior English medical VQA capability to steer non-English representations toward their English counterparts at inference time. Across three LVLMs and eight languages, MedVL-XLRepE consistently mitigates cross-lingual degradation, with gains of up to 6.33\%.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a multilingual medical VQA benchmark across eight languages with four scenario-based tasks, revealing that cross-lingual performance degradation in LVLMs is scenario-dependent rather than uniform. It proposes MedVL-XLRepE, a training-free representation engineering method that steers non-English representations toward English counterparts at inference time, consistently improving performance by up to 6.33%.
AI.motivation: Existing medical VQA evaluation is almost exclusively English-centric, limiting relevance to linguistically diverse populations. Prior multilingual medical VQA benchmarks show LVLMs degrade in non-English languages but lack fine-grained analysis of how cross-lingual variation impacts distinct capabilities required by medical VQA.
AI.method: The authors construct a multilingual medical VQA benchmark over eight languages, organized into four representative scenarios that isolate core capabilities. They evaluate five open- and closed-source LVLMs and propose MedVL-XLRepE, a training-free, scenario-aware representation engineering method that leverages LVLMs' superior English medical VQA capability to steer non-English representations toward English counterparts at inference time.
AI.result: Cross-lingual degradation is not uniform but highly scenario-dependent across LVLMs. MedVL-XLRepE consistently mitigates cross-lingual degradation across three LVLMs and eight languages, achieving gains of up to 6.33%.
AI.conclusion: Cross-lingual degradation in medical VQA is scenario-specific, and representation engineering using English capabilities as a reference provides an effective, training-free approach to improving multilingual medical VQA performance.

title: Multimodal examination answer data with expert-designed Outcome-Based Education rubrics for criterion-level assessment
summary: This data article describes a multimodal collection of scanned examination answers paired with expert-designed Outcome-Based Education (OBE) grading metadata. The collection contains 485 answer submissions from 415 consenting students at four academic institutions. Eight faculty contributors supplied examination materials covering nine subjects and 12 distinct question templates. Each answer-level item links a scanned PDF to a randomized identifier, subject label, question, model answer, criterion definitions, performance-level descriptions, criterion marks, and a total mark. The 12 rubrics contain 47 criteria in total. The scans retain realistic academic content, including handwriting, printed text, equations, tables, code, figures, sketches, and diagrams. CamScanner, Adobe Scan, and conventional scanners contributed variation in illumination, contrast, orientation, compression, and resolution. Diverse handwriting, crossed-out work, revised calculations, and inserted corrections add further visual variability for robustness and generalization studies. Preparation involved heterogeneous-source consolidation, label and text standardization, score validation, identifier randomization, filename randomization, and JSON-to-PDF integrity checks. An answer-level audit confirmed 485 unique identifiers, 485 unique PDF filenames, agreement between each total mark and its criterion-mark sum, and scores within the applicable rubric maximum. The data can support rubric-aware automated evaluation, multimodal document understanding, criterion-level feedback, score prediction, and privacy-aware OBE assessment research. Access is restricted to research use and is available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a multimodal dataset of 485 scanned student examination answers from 415 students across four institutions, paired with expert-designed Outcome-Based Education (OBE) grading rubrics. The dataset includes 8 faculty contributors, 9 subjects, 12 question templates, and 47 rubric criteria across 12 rubrics. Each item links a scanned PDF to randomized identifiers, subject labels, questions, model answers, criterion definitions, performance descriptions, criterion marks, and total marks. The scans contain realistic academic content with varied handwriting and scanning device variations, supporting research in automated evaluation, multimodal document understanding, and score prediction.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to create a privacy-aware, multimodal dataset that supports Outcome-Based Education (OBE) research, enabling automated evaluation, criterion-level feedback generation, score prediction, and multimodal document understanding. The dataset addresses the gap in accessible academic data that pairs authentic scanned examination answers with expert-designed rubric-based grading metadata.
AI.method: The dataset was constructed through heterogeneous-source consolidation from four academic institutions, with label and text standardization, score validation, identifier randomization, filename randomization, and JSON-to-PDF integrity checks. Scans were captured using CamScanner, Adobe Scan, and conventional scanners to introduce natural variation in illumination, contrast, orientation, compression, and resolution. Each answer-level item pairs a scanned PDF with metadata including randomized identifiers, subject labels, questions, model answers, criterion definitions, performance-level descriptions, criterion marks, and total marks.
AI.result: The final dataset contains 485 answer submissions from 415 consenting students, created by 8 faculty contributors covering 9 subjects and 12 question templates. It comprises 12 rubrics with 47 criteria total. An answer-level audit confirmed 485 unique identifiers, 485 unique PDF filenames, agreement between total marks and criterion-mark sums, and scores within rubric maximums, validating data integrity.
AI.conclusion: The multimodal OBE grading dataset provides a realistic, validated resource for research in rubric-aware automated evaluation, multimodal document understanding, criterion-level feedback, score prediction, and privacy-aware assessment. Access is restricted to research purposes and available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.

title: LLM-Based Selection of Incongruent Verbal and Nonverbal Behavior for Virtual Humans
summary: Nonverbal behavior generation systems for virtual agents often take an utterance as input and generate nonverbal behaviors that emphasize or illustrate the content of the verbal channel. However, human nonverbal behavior is shaped by more than the content of the speech. It is also influenced by speaker roles, interpersonal relationships, social context, and the cognitive and emotional states of the interactants. As a result, the nonverbal channel may reinforce, weaken, qualify, or even contradict the verbal channel. It may also reveal internal states that are hidden or only indirectly implied in speech, including emotional "leakage" that may be incidental to the immediate interaction. Modeling this richer relationship between verbal and nonverbal behavior is important for designing virtual agents that exhibit realistic, human-like behavior. It is especially critical in training contexts that require nuanced social interpretation, such as counseling simulations involving virtual patients. Drawing on Ekman's framework of verbal nonverbal relationships, we propose a taxonomy of categories in which mismatches between verbal and nonverbal behavior can occur. We then examine alternative approaches for realizing these behaviors using large language models, focusing on whether LLMs can select contextually appropriate mismatched verbal and nonverbal behaviors from a given dialogue and social interaction context. Finally, we evaluate the resulting behaviors in a human-subject study, assessing whether context-driven nonverbal behavior, when embodied in a virtual human, produces the intended effects on observers.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a taxonomy based on Ekman's framework for categorizing mismatches between verbal and nonverbal behavior in virtual agents, explores how large language models can generate contextually appropriate mismatched behaviors from dialogue and social context, and evaluates these behaviors through a human-subject study with embodied virtual humans.
AI.motivation: Current nonverbal behavior generation systems for virtual agents only consider speech content, ignoring that human nonverbal behavior is also shaped by speaker roles, relationships, social context, and cognitive/emotional states. This limits realism in virtual agents, especially for training contexts like counseling simulations that require nuanced social interpretation.
AI.method: The authors propose a taxonomy of verbal-nonverbal mismatch categories drawing on Ekman's framework, examine approaches for LLMs to generate contextually appropriate mismatched behaviors from dialogue and social context, and evaluate the outcomes in a human-subject study with embodied virtual humans.
AI.result: The paper presents a taxonomy of verbal-nonverbal mismatches, demonstrates LLM-based approaches for generating such behaviors, and reports findings from a human-subject study assessing whether embodied context-driven nonverbal behavior produces intended observer effects.
AI.conclusion: Modeling the richer relationship between verbal and nonverbal behavior—including mismatches driven by social context and internal states—is important for realistic virtual agents, and LLMs show potential for generating contextually appropriate mismatched behaviors, which can be evaluated for effectiveness through human studies.

title: SDoH-Aware Narrative Anchoring Bias in Medical LLMs for Trustworthy Clinical Decision Support
comment: Accepted for publication at 10th International Artificial Intelligence and Data Processing Symposium (IDAP'26)
summary: Medical large language models are often judged by how many clinical questions they answer correctly. That view is useful, but it misses a practical risk. A model may know the right answer and still change its response when the same case is written in a different patient voice. This paper evaluates that risk as SDoH aware narrative anchoring bias. We use NarrativeShield SDoH MedQA, a counterfactual medical question answering dataset in which each case appears in persona based narratives while the answer key remains fixed. The dataset is reshaped from wide format into case grouped persona rows. We evaluate three open source instruction tuned LLMs from the Qwen2.5 family: 1.5B, 3B, and 7B. The final experiment uses 300 clinical cases and produces 8,100 model responses across three prompting conditions. We report persona level accuracy, counterfactual consistency, correct consistency, and narrative sensitivity error. Qwen2.5 7B achieves the best accuracy at 56.33 percent and the best correct consistency at 40.33 percent. Paired McNemar exact tests show significant accuracy gains for 7B over 3B in all prompt settings. Even so, narrative sensitivity remains, with the lowest error still at 31.67 percent. These results suggest that trustworthy clinical decision support should be evaluated by both average correctness and stability across medically equivalent patient narratives.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces and evaluates SDoH-aware narrative anchoring bias in medical LLMs using the NarrativeShield SDoH MedQA dataset, where clinical cases with fixed answer keys are presented in persona-based narratives. Three Qwen2.5 models (1.5B, 3B, 7B) are tested across 300 cases and 8,100 responses. The 7B model achieves the best accuracy (56.33%) and correct consistency (40.33%), but the lowest narrative sensitivity error remains at 31.67%, demonstrating that stability across equivalent patient narratives is an important but unmet evaluation dimension.
AI.motivation: Standard accuracy-based evaluation of medical LLMs misses a critical practical risk: a model may know the correct answer but change its response when the same clinical case is expressed in different patient voices (persona-based narratives). This paper formalizes this risk as SDoH-aware narrative anchoring bias and proposes evaluating both correctness and stability.
AI.method: The paper constructs NarrativeShield SDoH MedQA, a counterfactual medical QA dataset where each case is rewritten into persona-based narratives with a fixed answer key, reshaped from wide to case-grouped persona rows. Three open-source instruction-tuned LLMs from the Qwen2.5 family (1.5B, 3B, 7B) are evaluated across 300 clinical cases, producing 8,100 responses under three prompting conditions. Metrics include persona-level accuracy, counterfactual consistency, correct consistency, and narrative sensitivity error. Paired McNemar exact tests assess significance of accuracy differences.
AI.result: Qwen2.5 7B achieves the best accuracy at 56.33% and the best correct consistency at 40.33%. Paired McNemar exact tests reveal significant accuracy gains for 7B over 3B across all prompt settings. However, narrative sensitivity error persists, with the lowest value still at 31.67%, indicating substantial instability in responses across medically equivalent patient narratives.
AI.conclusion: Trustworthy clinical decision support systems should be evaluated not only by average correctness but also by stability across medically equivalent patient narratives. The persistent narrative sensitivity error even in the best-performing model suggests that current instruction-tuned LLMs remain vulnerable to SDoH-aware narrative anchoring bias, warranting further mitigation efforts.

title: Pre-Decoding Acoustic Triage for Budgeted Vision-Language Captioning of Untrimmed Egocentric Video
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, 9 tables. Under review at IEEE BigData 2026, Industrial and Government Track. Code: https://github.com/masjalayer/PreDecoding-AcousticTriage
summary: Automatically analyzing hours-long egocentric video is increasingly essential for progress monitoring, quality control, and safety in logistics, construction, and manufacturing. Yet current pipelines that process short, fixed-size windows with a vision-language model (VLM) are prohibitively expensive because cost scales with the number of model calls. To reduce this cost, prior work proposes triage policies to select which windows merit a VLM invocation. However, these policies either sample uniformly or rank windows using visual features, which ironically requires the video decoding that the budget constraints are meant to avoid. We propose audio-first triage: select windows using the lightest modality, scored before any video frame is decoded, so the approach composes naturally with token compression or quantization. The novelty lies in the objective, not the representation: rather than a per-frame sound-event detector, we train the selector to trigger once per action. This objective shift improves action coverage by 4.0-10.8 percentage points across all evaluated call rates, using frozen AudioSet-pretrained features without domain-specific sound-event labels. Using fewer than half of the available calls, the triage cuts 9-20% of VLM calls at matched coverage on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 (EK-100), surpasses uniform sampling through the mid-range on Ego4D over 247 clips, and outperforms two recent visual keyframe selectors. Code, the reference implementation and every results file this manuscript reads are at https://github.com/masjalayer/PreDecoding-AcousticTriage.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes audio-first triage for egocentric video analysis, selecting which windows merit vision-language model (VLM) invocation using only lightweight audio features before any video frame is decoded, reducing VLM call costs while improving action coverage.
AI.motivation: Analyzing hours-long egocentric video with VLMs is prohibitively expensive because cost scales with the number of model calls. Prior triage policies either sample uniformly or rank windows using visual features, which ironically requires video decoding that budget constraints aim to avoid.
AI.method: The approach selects windows using the lightest modality (audio) scored before any video frame is decoded, composing naturally with token compression or quantization. The key novelty is in the objective: rather than a per-frame sound-event detector, the selector is trained to trigger once per action (one activation per action). It uses frozen AudioSet-pretrained features without domain-specific sound-event labels.
AI.result: The objective shift improves action coverage by 4.0-10.8 percentage points across all evaluated call rates. Using fewer than half of available calls, triage cuts 9-20% of VLM calls at matched coverage on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 (EK-100), surpasses uniform sampling through the mid-range on Ego4D over 247 clips, and outperforms two recent visual keyframe selectors.
AI.conclusion: Audio-first triage provides an effective, low-cost alternative to visual-based window selection for egocentric video analysis, improving coverage while reducing VLM invocations, and avoiding the very video decoding that budget constraints seek to prevent.

title: MIVIFI: Bridging Perspective and Fisheye Domains for Training Multi-View Fisheye Image Generation Models
comment: Accepted at the IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSC) 2026
summary: Achieving 360° coverage is critical for the visual perception systems of autonomous vehicles. Fisheye cameras offer a cost-effective solution by enabling full surround coverage with as few as two sensors. However, existing multi-view fisheye datasets are limited, and synthesizing rare corner cases typically requires computationally expensive 3D simulations, hindering the training. While generative models have achieved significant success in standard perspective imagery, their application to wide-angle distortion remains unexplored. In this work, we formally introduce the novel problem of multi-view fisheye image generation conditioned on volumetric semantic representations and present two distinct methods. We first propose SyntheOcc-FE, which adapts the SyntheOcc architecture to fisheye data. While effective, this method is constrained by the scarcity of fisheye datasets, which limits its generalization. To overcome these limitations, we propose our second method, MIVIFI (multi-view fisheye), which leverages cross-domain learning with Equirectangular Projections. By bridging the gap between dataset domains using KITTI-360 fisheye images alongside nuScenes multi-view standard images, our approach enables high-fidelity manipulation of scene content. This framework enables the structural modification of semantic occupancy inputs to introduce or eliminate specific actors and facilitates the rendering of diverse meteorological conditions and illumination scenarios absent in the limited fisheye datasets. Quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that our methods achieve robust photorealistic multi-view fisheye image generation and highlight the specific advantages of our cross-domain strategy for handling data scarcity.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces multi-view fisheye image generation conditioned on volumetric semantic representations for autonomous driving. Two methods are proposed: SyntheOcc-FE (adapting SyntheOcc to fisheye data) and MIVIFI (cross-domain learning with Equirectangular Projections), which bridges dataset domains using KITTI-360 fisheye and nuScenes standard images to enable photorealistic fisheye image generation despite data scarcity.
AI.motivation: 360° coverage is critical for autonomous vehicle perception, and fisheye cameras enable this cost-effectively with minimal sensors. However, multi-view fisheye datasets are scarce, and synthesizing rare corner cases requires computationally expensive 3D simulations. While generative models have succeeded for standard perspective imagery, wide-angle distortion has not been explored.
AI.method: Two methods are proposed: (1) SyntheOcc-FE, which adapts the SyntheOcc architecture to fisheye data but is limited by fisheye dataset scarcity; (2) MIVIFI (multi-view fisheye), which leverages cross-domain learning with Equirectangular Projections, bridging dataset domains using KITTI-360 fisheye images alongside nuScenes multi-view standard images. The framework enables structural modification of semantic occupancy inputs to introduce/eliminate actors and renders diverse meteorological and illumination conditions.
AI.result: Quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate robust photorealistic multi-view fisheye image generation, highlighting the advantages of the cross-domain strategy (MIVIFI) for handling data scarcity compared to the direct adaptation approach (SyntheOcc-FE).
AI.conclusion: Cross-domain learning via Equirectangular Projections effectively addresses fisheye data scarcity, enabling high-fidelity multi-view fisheye image generation and manipulation of scene content, which is crucial for training autonomous vehicle perception systems with rare corner cases.

title: DIAG: Diagnostic Iterative Alignment and Generation for Data-Efficient Mathematical Preference Distillation
summary: Iterative preference optimization is essential for aligning Large Language Models on mathematical reasoning tasks, yet its efficiency is often throttled by signal scarcity: as the model improves, static problem sets become increasingly mismatched to the model's evolving competence, producing rollouts that are either too easy or too hard and therefore non-informative, which leads to a scarcity of valid preference pairs. We propose DIAG, a Diagnostic Iterative Alignment and Generation framework that adaptively reshapes the practice distribution to increase informative supervision and focus training near the student's current competence boundary. DIAG consists of two phases: (1) diagnosing valid preference-pair yield to calibrate the exploration-exploitation trade-off and allocate topic quotas via an Empirical Bayes shrinkage estimator, thereby prioritizing high-yield concepts; and (2) generating targeted practice, where a teacher synthesizes variants from the student's failure traces. We further provide a theoretical view interpreting DIAG as a teacher-mediated approximation to KL-regularized reweighting of the practice distribution toward the student's competence boundary, where valid preference-pair yield is maximized. Experiments show that DIAG boosts yield across iterations and delivers stronger reasoning performance under an iso-effective training budget, demonstrating that it can distill more informative preference supervision for mathematical reasoning.

AI.tldr: DIAG is a diagnostic iterative alignment and generation framework that adaptively reshapes the practice distribution for LLM preference optimization on mathematical reasoning by prioritizing high-yield concepts and synthesizing targeted practice problems from student failure traces, leading to more informative preference supervision and stronger reasoning performance under a fixed training budget.
AI.motivation: Iterative preference optimization for mathematical reasoning suffers from signal scarcity: as the model improves, static problem sets become mismatched to the model's evolving competence, producing rollouts that are either too easy or too hard and thus non-informative, leading to a scarcity of valid preference pairs.
AI.method: DIAG consists of two phases: (1) diagnosing valid preference-pair yield to calibrate the exploration-exploitation trade-off and allocate topic quotas via an Empirical Bayes shrinkage estimator, prioritizing high-yield concepts; and (2) generating targeted practice where a teacher synthesizes variants from the student's failure traces. A theoretical interpretation frames DIAG as a teacher-mediated approximation to KL-regularized reweighting of the practice distribution toward the student's competence boundary where valid preference-pair yield is maximized.
AI.result: Experiments show DIAG boosts preference-pair yield across iterations and delivers stronger reasoning performance under an iso-effective training budget, demonstrating more informative preference supervision for mathematical reasoning.
AI.conclusion: DIAG effectively addresses signal scarcity in iterative preference optimization by adaptively reshaping the practice distribution toward the model's competence boundary, distilling more informative preference supervision and improving mathematical reasoning performance under constrained training budgets.

title: LLMs for Survey Text Analysis - A Performance Comparison Between Humans and GPT-5 on Inductive Content Analysis
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support text analysis in qualitative research, yet evidence on their performance in inductive content analysis remains limited. This study compares human and LLM-based inductive coding of open-ended survey responses from 903 answers across six variables from a European PhD student survey. Five human coders performed inductive content analysis following a standardized coding scheme, while an LLM (GPT-5.4) conducted the same task using an established prompting procedure. Agreement between human and LLM outputs was assessed using the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI). Results showed an alignment between humans and the LLM, with ARI values of 0.61 for coding and 0.54 for theme generation. These values were close to the internal consistency of coding and theme results within humans (ARI = 0.68) and the LLM (ARI = 0.76). Agreement varied widely across variables, with low within-entity consistency consistently linked to low between-entity agreement, underscoring the role of data characteristics and individual performance in reliability. Overall, the findings suggest that LLMs can approximate human coding in this case-specific setting, particularly at the coding level, and may serve as a scalable support tool for inductive qualitative analysis.

AI.tldr: This study compares human and GPT-5.4-based inductive coding of 903 open-ended survey responses across six variables from a European PhD student survey. Using the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI), the authors found moderate alignment between human and LLM outputs (ARI = 0.61 for coding, 0.54 for theme generation), approaching human internal consistency (ARI = 0.68) and LLM internal consistency (ARI = 0.76). Agreement varied widely across variables, with low within-entity consistency linked to low between-entity agreement. The findings suggest LLMs can approximate human inductive coding, particularly at the coding level, and may serve as scalable support tools.
AI.motivation: There is limited evidence on how well large language models perform in inductive content analysis for qualitative research, despite their increasing use as text analysis support tools. This study aims to fill that gap by systematically comparing human and LLM performance in inductive coding using standardized methods within a realistic research setting.
AI.method: The study analyzed 903 open-ended survey responses across six variables from a European PhD student survey. Five human coders performed inductive content analysis following a standardized coding scheme, while an LLM (GPT-5.4) performed the same task using an established prompting procedure. Agreement between human and LLM outputs was quantified using the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI), and internal consistency for humans (ARI = 0.68) and the LLM (ARI = 0.76) was also computed. Agreement was analyzed both overall and across variables.
AI.result: Human-LLM alignment was ARI = 0.61 for coding and ARI = 0.54 for theme generation, close to within-entity consistency for humans (ARI = 0.68) and the LLM (ARI = 0.76). Agreement varied substantially across the six variables, and low within-entity consistency predicted low between-entity agreement.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can approximate human inductive coding in this specific research setting, particularly at the coding level, and may serve as a scalable support tool for inductive qualitative analysis. Data characteristics and individual coder performance play important roles in reliability, suggesting LLMs are best used as augmentative tools rather than full replacements.

title: When Do VLMs Help Arabic Manuscript OCR? A Cross-Dataset Study
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly being used for document understanding, yet their role in Arabic and Islamic manuscript recognition remains underexplored. To address such a gap in this paper, we evaluate traditional OCR, general-purpose VLMs, Arabic-specialized VLMs, and OCR-conditioned VLM correction across eight Arabic text datasets spanning historical manuscripts, aged printed books, clean print, multi-domain documents, and handwriting. The results show that no single approach dominates across setups. On line-level historical manuscripts, VLMs are close to Tesseract; on page-level manuscript images, they perform better; and in several settings, an OCR-conditioned corrector improves over both standalone OCR and standalone VLMs. The central finding is an OCR-prior recoverability principle: OCR conditioning helps when the OCR output remains visually and textually recoverable, providing anchors that the VLM can refine against the image. It improves recognition on aged print, clean print, mixed-domain Arabic, and some Naskh manuscripts, but degrades performance when the prior is script-mismatched or systematically misleading, as in Maghribi manuscripts and realistic student handwriting. Additional diagnostics show that Arabic VLM-OCR is sensitive to diacritics, preprocessing, generation budget, and repetition loops. These findings support an adaptive OCR-VLM workflow that routes pages according to script, OCR-prior recoverability, length diagnostics, and failure-mode indicators.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates traditional OCR, general-purpose VLMs, Arabic-specialized VLMs, and OCR-conditioned VLM correction across eight Arabic text datasets spanning historical manuscripts to handwriting. It finds that no single approach dominates, and introduces an "OCR-prior recoverability principle" showing that OCR conditioning helps when the OCR output is visually and textually recoverable as anchors for the VLM, but degrades when the prior is mismatched or misleading. The authors propose an adaptive OCR-VLM workflow that routes pages based on script, recoverability, and failure diagnostics.
AI.motivation: VLMs are increasingly used for document understanding, but their role in Arabic and Islamic manuscript recognition remains underexplored. The paper addresses this gap by systematically evaluating how different recognition approaches perform across diverse Arabic text types.
AI.method: The authors evaluate four approaches—traditional OCR, general-purpose VLMs, Arabic-specialized VLMs, and OCR-conditioned VLM correction—across eight Arabic text datasets covering historical manuscripts, aged printed books, clean print, multi-domain documents, and handwriting. They conduct comparative benchmarking and diagnostic analyses on factors like diacritics, preprocessing, generation budget, and repetition loops.
AI.result: No single approach dominates across all settings. VLMs approach Tesseract on line-level historical manuscripts, outperform it on page-level manuscripts, and OCR-conditioned correction beats both standalone methods in several settings. The OCR-prior recoverability principle holds: conditioning helps with aged print, clean print, mixed-domain Arabic, and some Naskh manuscripts, but hurts with Maghribi scripts and realistic student handwriting. Arabic VLM-OCR is sensitive to diacritics, preprocessing, generation budget, and repetition issues.
AI.conclusion: The findings motivate an adaptive OCR-VLM workflow that dynamically routes pages based on script type, OCR-prior recoverability, length diagnostics, and failure-mode indicators, rather than relying on a single recognition approach.

title: MomADv2: Reliable Temporal Memory for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
summary: Long-horizon planning is critical for safe autonomous driving in complex scenarios. Existing methods improve planning continuity with temporal memory, but such memory may become invalid and mislead decisions when the driving command changes. Thus, selectively leveraging useful history while suppressing command-inconsistent memory remains a key challenge. To address this issue, we propose MomADv2, a reliable state-space memory framework for long-horizon end-to-end autonomous driving. At its core, MomADv2 introduces a Selective State-Space Planning Memory Query Module, which filters historical planning queries based on temporal continuity and command consistency, selects planning modes relevant to the current command, and models the evolution of planning intentions through a selective state-space mechanism. To further alleviate local trajectory deviations and error accumulation in long-horizon planning, we design a Flow-Matching Trajectory Residual Refiner. It learns a continuous residual correction field from the refined planning output to the expert trajectory, enabling fine-grained trajectory refinement while preserving the stability of anchor-based planning. Extensive experiments on closed-loop NAVSIM and Bench2Drive, as well as open-loop nuScenes, demonstrate that MomADv2 improves long-horizon planning consistency and reduces the average collision rate by 15.6% over MomAD under 6-second planning.

AI.tldr: MomADv2 is a state-space memory framework for long-horizon autonomous driving planning that selectively filters historical planning queries based on temporal continuity and command consistency, using a Selecti ve State-Space Planning Memory Query Module and a Flow-Matching Trajectory Residual Refiner. It reduces average collision rate by 15.6% over MomAD under 6-second planning on closed-loop NAVSIM, Bench2Drive, and open-loop nuScenes benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon planning is critical for safe autonomous driving, but existing temporal memory-based methods may become invalid and mislead decisions when driving commands change. The key challenge is selectively leveraging useful history while suppressing command-inconsistent memory.
AI.method: The paper proposes MomADv2, which introduces a Selective State-Space Planning Memory Query Module that filters historical planning queries based on temporal continuity and command consistency, selects planning modes relevant to the current command, and models planning intention evolution via a selective state-space mechanism. Additionally, a Flow-Matching Trajectory Residual Refiner learns a continuous residual correction field from refined planning output to expert trajectories, enabling fine-grained refinement while preserving anchor-based planning stability.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on closed-loop NAVSIM and Bench2Drive, and open-loop nuScenes demonstrate improved long-horizon planning consistency and a 15.6% reduction in average collision rate over MomAD under 6-second planning.
AI.conclusion: MomADv2 effectively addresses command-inconsistent memory issues in long-horizon planning through selective state-space memory filtering and flow-matching residual refinement, achieving safer and more consistent autonomous driving planning.

title: Industrial-Instruction: An End-to-End Framework for Building Instruction-Tuning and Benchmark Datasets from Industrial Technical Reports
comment: 29 pages, 8 figures, 18 tables, 5 listings. Datasets available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Parssky/industrial-instruction-dataset ; code at https://github.com/parssky/industrial-instruction
summary: Industrial technical reports contain high-value knowledge for maintenance, troubleshooting, and product engineering, but their heterogeneous structure (dense prose, specifications, tables) makes them difficult to index and reason over with standard retrieval and QA pipelines, and no public instruction-tuning or benchmark datasets are built from such documents. We address this gap with Industrial-Instruction, contributing (i) two open QA datasets built from real industrial technical reports and (ii) the end-to-end pipeline that produces them. Using 906 public Panasonic documents (7,525 pages), we apply layout-aware extraction, build a semantic retrieval index, and synthesize multiple-choice QA grounded in retrieved evidence under five query-document relationships (irrelevant retrieval, single-/multi-document support, single-/multi-document answer). After filtering an initial 23.9k generated samples, each dataset provides approximately 13.6k QA pairs with source documents and a held-out benchmark split. Fine-tuning small open LLMs (under 10B parameters) improves Set-Match Accuracy from 28.5% to 42.0% and F1 from 46.6% to 63.5% on the Panasonic benchmark. We release two parallel versions built by the same pipeline: one generated with the open-weight Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct model and one with the closed, API-based Claude-Opus-4.6 model, enabling a direct comparison of open- versus frontier-model data generation. The Claude-Opus-4.6 dataset yields a cleaner raw corpus and larger fine-tuning gains, at roughly two orders of magnitude higher cost. MMLU evaluation shows models trained on the Claude-Opus-4.6 data retain essentially all general knowledge, versus a small but measurable forgetting effect for the Qwen-generated data. Together, these datasets and pipeline offer a practical, reproducible path toward scalable industrial benchmarks and training data from real-world documentation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Industrial-Instruction, a pipeline and two open QA datasets built from 906 real Panasonic industrial technical reports (7,525 pages), producing ~13.6k QA pairs each via layout-aware extraction, semantic retrieval, and synthetic multi-choice QA generation. Fine-tuning small LLMs (<10B) improves Set-Match Accuracy from 28.5% to 42.0% and F1 from 46.6% to 63.5% on the Panasonic benchmark. Datasets generated with Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct and Claude-Opus-4.6 are compared, with Claude offering cleaner data and larger gains at ~100x higher cost but no general-knowledge forgetting.
AI.motivation: Industrial technical reports contain high-value knowledge but their heterogeneous structure (dense prose, specs, tables) makes them hard to index and reason over with standard retrieval/QA pipelines, and no public instruction-tuning or benchmark datasets exist for such documents.
AI.method: Applying layout-aware extraction on 906 Panasonic documents, building a semantic retrieval index, and synthesizing multiple-choice QA grounded in retrieved evidence under five query-document relationship types (irrelevant retrieval, single/multi-document support, single/multi-document answer). An initial 23.9k generated samples are filtered down to ~13.6k QA pairs per dataset. Datasets are generated using two models: Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct (open-weight) and Claude-Opus-4.6 (closed API).
AI.result: Fine-tuning small open LLMs (<10B parameters) improves Set-Match Accuracy from 28.5% to 42.0% and F1 from 46.6% to 63.5% on the Panasonic benchmark. The Claude-Opus-4.6 dataset yields cleaner raw corpus and larger fine-tuning gains at roughly two orders of magnitude higher cost. MMLU results show Claude-trained models retain essentially all general knowledge, while Qwen-generated data causes small but measurable forgetting.
AI.conclusion: The datasets and pipeline provide a practical, reproducible path toward scalable industrial benchmarks and training data from real-world documentation, enabling direct comparison of open versus frontier-model data generation quality and cost.

title: Where World Models Break: Natural-Input Failure Discovery
summary: World models predict action-conditioned futures and serve as critical internal simulators for downstream planning and control. However, catastrophic prediction failures of world models could dangerously propagate through the control pipeline, as subsequent agent or model training and decision-making depend heavily on the continuous environment evolution forecasted by these world models. Existing evaluations overlook this systemic risk: by aggregating average errors over benign generations from general queries, they fail to stress-test the model against catastrophic collapses under rare or unobserved condition-action combinations. To bridge this gap, we formalize the natural-input failure discovery problem: under a finite query budget, finding environment-valid conditions and action prefixes that induce severe prediction risk, verifying whether these failures reproduce on fresh seeds, and testing their persistence under nearby valid edits. Discovering such critical failures is computationally challenging, as valid condition-action combinations explode exponentially, rendering exhaustive search or standard sampling infeasible given the high cost of noisy rollouts. To tackle this, we propose BasinLens, which exploits the underlying structure of valid inputs, where each coordinate possesses environment-defined semantic types and admissible domains, by pairing uncertainty-guided global search with typed local replacements. Across diverse benchmarks and world-model families, BasinLens exposes reproducible and locally persistent failure modes that conventional evaluations fail to reveal, showing that average-case benchmarks can mask important vulnerabilities in world-model-driven control.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces BasinLens, a framework for discovering catastrophic prediction failures in world models by formalizing the natural-input failure discovery problem—finding environment-valid conditions and action prefixes that induce severe prediction risk within a finite query budget, verifying reproducibility, and testing persistence under valid edits.
AI.motivation: World models predict action-conditioned futures and serve as internal simulators for downstream planning and control. Catastrophic prediction failures can dangerously propagate through the control pipeline, yet existing evaluations only aggregate average errors over benign generations, failing to stress-test the model against catastrophic collapses under rare or unobserved condition-action combinations.
AI.method: BasinLens exploits the underlying structure of valid inputs, where each coordinate has environment-defined semantic types and admissible domains, by pairing uncertainty-guided global search with typed local replacements to efficiently discover critical failures within a finite query budget.
AI.result: Across diverse benchmarks and world-model families, BasinLens exposes reproducible and locally persistent failure modes that conventional evaluations fail to reveal, demonstrating that average-case benchmarks can mask important vulnerabilities in world-model-driven control.
AI.conclusion: Average-case evaluation metrics are insufficient for assessing the safety of world-model-driven systems; structured search over the valid input space is necessary to uncover hidden catastrophic failure modes, and BasinLens provides an effective approach for this critical stress-testing.

title: DiD It in 87 Minutes: A Label-Free Softmax-to-Linear Adaptation of Vision Transformers for Object Detection
summary: While linear attention is a compelling mechanism for high-resolution object detection due to its reduced cost for global token mixing, converting the Softmax-attention ViT backbone of a trained detector into a linear-attention one is not a trivial drop-in replacement. Directly swapping the attention operator leads to severe performance degradation, and generic label-free distillation, though effective for classification, often fails on detection tasks. We argue that the central challenge is \textit{detector-interface preservation}: the converted backbone must reproduce the exact feature tensors expected by the fixed downstream detector, rather than merely imitating internal Softmax hidden states. To address this, we introduce Detector-Interface Distillation (DiD), a label-free conversion method that exclusively trains the linear-attention backbone by aligning detector-facing interface tensors with those of a frozen Softmax teacher. On DOTA-v1.5, DiD substantially outperforms established baselines and matches supervised, fully trained linear models. Adaptation completes in roughly 87 minutes on 4 GPUs, and the linearized backbone cuts inference latency by ~62% and peak memory by ~49%. We hope our findings offer the community a simple, label-free route to reusing trained Softmax detectors as efficient linear ones, and encourage interface-aware objectives in future architecture-conversion work.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Detector-Interface Distillation (DiD), a label-free method for converting Softmax-attention ViT detector backbones into linear-attention ones by aligning detector-facing interface tensors with a frozen Softmax teacher, outperforming baselines on DOTA-v1.5 and achieving ~62% inference latency reduction and ~49% peak memory savings in ~87 minutes of adaptation.
AI.motivation: Linear attention offers reduced cost for global token mixing in high-resolution object detection, but converting a trained Softmax-attention ViT backbone to linear attention is not a trivial drop-in replacement—direct swaps cause severe performance degradation, and generic label-free distillation that targets hidden Softmax states often fails on detection tasks. The key challenge is detector-interface preservation: the converted backbone must reproduce exact feature tensors expected by the fixed downstream detector.
AI.method: DiD is a label-free conversion method that exclusively trains the linear-attention backbone by aligning detector-facing interface tensors (i.e., the features consumed by the downstream detector head) with those of a frozen Softmax attention teacher, rather than imitating internal hidden states.
AI.result: On DOTA-v1.5, DiD substantially outperforms established baselines and matches supervised fully trained linear models. Adaptation completes in ~87 minutes on 4 GPUs, and the linearized backbone reduces inference latency by ~62% and peak memory by ~49%.
AI.conclusion: The paper offers a simple, label-free route to reuse trained Softmax detectors as efficient linear ones, and encourages interface-aware objectives in future architecture-conversion work.

title: GeoWAM: Visual Geometry World Action Models for Autonomous Driving
summary: World action models (WAMs) have recently gained increasing attention as a framework for jointly modeling scene evolution and ego actions in autonomous driving. Most existing WAMs learn scene dynamics in pixel space by combining a video-generation backbone for future-observation prediction with an action head for ego-trajectory prediction. Pixels, however, provide only an indirect representation of these dynamics: they entangle geometry and motion with appearance, texture, and illumination, forcing the model to infer three-dimensional transformations from two-dimensional observations. We argue that geometry, represented by point clouds, offers a more natural state space for driving because it explicitly captures spatial structure and the rigid and non-rigid transformations that govern scene evolution while directly aligning with the space in which driving actions are executed.
