Building on this insight, we introduce \textbf{GeoWAM}, a visual geometry world action model for autonomous driving. Rather than predicting future images, GeoWAM is pretrained to forecast future scene geometry, yielding representations that jointly encode spatial structure and temporal evolution. A geometry-conditioned action head then leverages these learned geometric dynamics to predict future ego trajectories. Extensive open-loop and closed-loop evaluations show that visual geometry world modeling yields substantially stronger driving policies than image-based alternatives, establishing future-geometry prediction as an effective pretraining objective for autonomous driving.

AI.tldr: GeoWAM is a visual geometry world action model for autonomous driving that predicts future scene geometry (point clouds) instead of future images, yielding representations that jointly encode spatial structure and temporal evolution. A geometry-conditioned action head leverages these learned geometric dynamics for ego-trajectory prediction, outperforming image-based alternatives in both open-loop and closed-loop evaluations.
AI.motivation: Existing world action models (WAMs) learn scene dynamics in pixel space, but pixels only indirectly represent dynamics by entangling geometry and motion with appearance, texture, and illumination, forcing models to infer 3D transformations from 2D observations. The authors argue that point clouds offer a more natural state space for driving because they explicitly capture spatial structure and rigid/non-rigid transformations while aligning directly with the space where driving actions are executed.
AI.method: GeoWAM is pretrained to forecast future scene geometry (point clouds) rather than future images, producing representations that jointly encode spatial structure and temporal evolution. A geometry-conditioned action head then uses these learned geometric dynamics to predict future ego trajectories.
AI.result: Extensive open-loop and closed-loop evaluations show that visual geometry world modeling yields substantially stronger driving policies than image-based alternatives, establishing future-geometry prediction as an effective pretraining objective for autonomous driving.
AI.conclusion: Future-geometry prediction in point cloud space is a more effective pretraining objective for autonomous driving than image-based future prediction, as it provides a natural and direct representation of scene dynamics and driving action space.

title: SAVER: Selective Auditing of Verbal Evidence for Error Recovery in VLM Change Reasoning
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) frequently fail at visual change reasoning, even when their vision encoders contain sufficient information. We observe that correct VLM outputs tend to contain explicit verbal evidence (object names, colors, spatial locations) that supports the claimed change, while incorrect outputs often lack such evidence. We propose SAVER (Selective Auditing of Verbal Evidence for Error Recovery), a lightweight, rule-based method that parses VLM responses for this evidence and triggers structured reprompting only when evidence is missing or inconsistent. Across three change detection benchmarks and four VLMs, SAVER significantly improves accuracy on tasks where errors stem from the model failing to articulate what it saw (expression failures), with gains up to +25.8% on CLEVR-Change. The evidence patterns can also be generated by an LLM in a single call, matching the hand-tuned gate on CLEVR-Change. Ablation experiments confirm that the evidence gate, not reprompting alone, drives the improvement.

AI.tldr: SAVER is a lightweight, rule-based method that parses VLM responses for explicit verbal evidence of visual changes and triggers structured reprompting only when evidence is missing or inconsistent, improving change detection accuracy by up to +25.8% on CLEVR-Change.
AI.motivation: VLMs frequently fail at visual change reasoning despite having sufficient information in their vision encoders. A key observation is that correct outputs contain explicit verbal evidence while incorrect outputs lack it, suggesting that errors stem from expression failures rather than perception failures.
AI.method: SAVER (Selective Auditing of Verbal Evidence for Error Recovery) is a rule-based method that parses VLM responses for verbal evidence such as object names, colors, and spatial locations. It triggers structured reprompting only when evidence is missing or inconsistent. Evidence patterns can also be generated by an LLM in a single call.
AI.result: Across three change detection benchmarks and four VLMs, SAVER significantly improves accuracy on tasks where errors stem from expression failures, with gains up to +25.8% on CLEVR-Change. LLM-generated evidence patterns match the hand-tuned gate on CLEVR-Change. Ablations confirm the evidence gate, not reprompting alone, drives the improvement.
AI.conclusion: Selective evidence auditing is an effective and efficient strategy for recovering from VLM expression failures in visual change reasoning, and the evidence gate is the critical component responsible for the performance gains.

title: Think with Structured Grounding: Perceptual Reinforcement Learning for Chart and Visual-Tabular Understanding
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) capable of thinking with images often rely on external tools for fine-grained perception. However, this reliance introduces significant inference latency and fails to effectively resolve the spatial-structural gap-a fundamental challenge in text-dense and structurally relational visuals (e.g., charts and visual tables) where strict relative spatial arrangements bind textual elements. Without external tools, standard MLLMs struggle with such fine-grained visual reasoning tasks. To address these issues, we propose Think with Structured Grounding (TwSG), a novel fine-grained image perception framework designed to internalize complex images's tool-use capabilities within the model. TwSG distills the benefits of multi-step reasoning and micro-cropping into a single efficient forward pass during inference. Specifically, we use an MLLM to identify key regions guided by ground-truth answers, and then prompt a teacher model to generate high-quality visual question-answering (VQA) data. These fine-grained, region-based supervisory signals are subsequently distilled back into the full-image representation. Our training pipeline consists of two stages: (1) a cold-start supervised fine-tuning (SFT) phase using multi-turn data with focused area descriptions to foster complex reasoning and error recovery; and (2) a reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) phase driven by a novel process reward mechanism, TL-GRPO, which encourages strategic reasoning. Extensive experiments across various MLLM architectures demonstrate that TwSG reduces inference latency while substantially improving accuracy and robustness, endowing models with native fine-grained region description and flexible reasoning capabilities.

AI.tldr: TwSG is a fine-grained image perception framework that distills external tool-use capabilities (multi-step reasoning and micro-cropping) into MLLMs via a single efficient forward pass, using two-stage training (cold-start SFT + TL-GRPO reinforcement fine-tuning) to internalize structured grounding for text-dense visuals like charts and tables.
AI.motivation: Standard MLLMs rely on external tools for fine-grained perception, which introduces significant inference latency and fails to resolve the spatial-structural gap in text-dense and structurally relational visuals where strict relative spatial arrangements bind textual elements. Without external tools, standard MLLMs struggle with fine-grained visual reasoning tasks.
AI.method: TwSG uses an MLLM to identify key regions guided by ground-truth answers, then prompts a teacher model to generate high-quality VQA data. These region-based supervisory signals are distilled into the full-image representation. The training pipeline has two stages: (1) cold-start SFT using multi-turn data with focused area descriptions for complex reasoning and error recovery, and (2) RFT driven by a novel process reward mechanism called TL-GRPO for strategic reasoning.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across various MLLM architectures demonstrate that TwSG reduces inference latency while substantially improving accuracy and robustness, endowing models with native fine-grained region description and flexible reasoning capabilities.
AI.conclusion: TwSG effectively internalizes tool-use capabilities within MLLMs, eliminating external tool dependency during inference while improving fine-grained visual reasoning performance on text-dense and structurally relational visuals.

title: LiST: Local-Simplex Test-Time LoRA Fusion
summary: Task-specific LoRA adapters offer a modular way to specialize large language and vision-language models. However, existing adapter composition methods are mostly static and cannot adapt to individual test inputs. To address these issues, we propose \textbf{LiST}, a label-free test-time LoRA fusion framework that converts an existing LoRA bank into a target-conditioned local simplex and searches sample-specific fusion weights at inference time. LiST builds joint task representations from LoRA parameter anchors and prompt-level behavior vectors, retrieves neighboring adapters as a local search space, and performs branch-preserving fusion without updating the backbone or adapters. Candidate weights are selected by a prompt-level energy with prior, geometric, and stochastic-consistency constraints, and are deployed only when they pass a safe acceptance rule. Otherwise, LiST falls back to a target-conditioned prior. Experiments on multimodal and language benchmarks show that LiST outperforms static LoRA merging and conventional test-time adaptation baselines, while preserving task-specific adapter utility and improving robustness on unseen tasks.

AI.tldr: LiST is a label-free test-time LoRA fusion framework that converts a LoRA bank into a target-conditioned local simplex, searches sample-specific fusion weights at inference, and only deploys fused weights when they pass a safe acceptance rule, outperforming static merging and test-time adaptation baselines on multimodal and language benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing LoRA adapter composition methods are static and cannot adapt to individual test inputs, limiting their effectiveness when tasks or distributions vary at inference time.
AI.method: LiST converts a LoRA bank into a target-conditioned local simplex by building joint task representations from LoRA parameter anchors and prompt-level behavior vectors. It retrieves neighboring adapters as a local search space and performs branch-preserving fusion without updating the backbone or adapters. Candidate weights are selected via a prompt-level energy with prior, geometric, and stochastic-consistency constraints, and deployed only when passing a safe acceptance rule; otherwise it falls back to a target-conditioned prior.
AI.result: Experiments on multimodal and language benchmarks show LiST outperforms static LoRA merging and conventional test-time adaptation baselines, while preserving task-specific adapter utility and improving robustness on unseen tasks.
AI.conclusion: LiST demonstrates that label-free, sample-specific LoRA fusion at inference time is a viable and superior alternative to static adapter composition, offering both better performance and robustness on unseen tasks.

title: Better Retrieval, Worse Robustness: How Multi-hop RAG Amplifies Upstream ASR Errors
summary: Speech-based applications pass spoken queries through automatic speech recognition (ASR) before any retrieval module, so ASR errors enter the pipeline as a fixed upstream constraint. We empirically test whether two extensions to standard retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), entity-graph linking and iterative reformulation, absorb or amplify these errors. Using four English accents synthesized through neural TTS, we evaluate four RAG configurations on three multi-hop QA benchmarks (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA and MuSiQue) against a clean-text oracle. Although the structurally richer configurations generally retain higher absolute F1 under ASR input, both extensions amplify the error: the F1 gap from clean text to the highest-WER accent is 36-67% larger under their combination than under naive dense retrieval, on all three benchmarks. The dominant failure mode is corruption of one or more query entities, accounting for 87-96% of degradation cases on 2WikiMultiHopQA across all four methods. Two lightweight surface-form mitigations leave most of the gap intact, indicating that downstream retrieval structure amplifies remaining entity errors. We release code and data at https://github.com/Continuum-AI-Corp/spoken-multihop-rag .

AI.tldr: This paper empirically investigates how ASR errors propagate through multi-hop retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines for spoken queries. Testing entity-graph linking and iterative reformulation across four English accents and three multi-hop QA benchmarks, the authors find that while richer RAG configurations retain higher absolute F1, both extensions amplify ASR-induced errors—the F1 gap from clean text to the highest-WER accent increases by 36-67% when both extensions are combined. Query entity corruption is the dominant failure mode (87-96% of degradation cases), and lightweight surface-form mitigations fail to close the gap.
AI.motivation: Speech-based applications must pass spoken queries through ASR before retrieval, meaning ASR errors act as a fixed upstream constraint. Since standard RAG was designed for clean text, it is unknown whether more sophisticated RAG extensions (entity-graph linking, iterative reformulation) absorb or amplify these speech-to-text errors in multi-hop QA settings.
AI.method: The authors synthesize four English accents via neural TTS to create spoken query inputs. They evaluate four RAG configurations (combining entity-graph linking and iterative reformulation as extensions) against a clean-text oracle across three multi-hop QA benchmarks: HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue. They measure F1 degradation under varying WER and analyze failure modes, followed by testing lightweight surface-form mitigations.
AI.result: Structurally richer RAG configurations maintain higher absolute F1 under ASR input, but both extensions amplify ASR errors. The F1 gap from clean text to the highest-WER accent grows 36-67% larger under the combined extensions than under naive dense retrieval across all three benchmarks. Query entity corruption accounts for 87-96% of degradation cases on 2WikiMultiHopQA. Lightweight surface-form mitigations leave most of the gap intact.
AI.conclusion: Downstream retrieval structure amplifies remaining entity errors introduced by ASR, even when richer configurations achieve higher absolute performance. Surface-level fixes are insufficient, indicating that ASR robustness must be addressed at a deeper architectural level for spoken multi-hop RAG systems.

title: When Persona Simulations Are Informative: Graph-Structured Signals for Pluralistic Opinion Sensing
summary: Persona-conditioned large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate survey responses across diverse domains. However, apparent response variation can reflect unconditioned model priors or token sampling noise rather than systematic persona conditioning. We argue that persona-conditioned variation is informative when semantically similar personas exhibit concordant response shifts. To operationalize this principle, we introduce Persona-Conditioned Informativeness (PCI), an unsupervised diagnostic metric that measures whether semantically similar personas deviate in concordant directions relative to item-level sample baselines. By modeling personas as a similarity graph, PCI uses Local Moran's I to quantify local spatial coherence and extract compact persona subsets without using construct labels. To evaluate PCI without external human benchmarks, we test its ability to recover established latent value structure using the 57-item Portrait Values Questionnaire-Revised (PVQ-RR). Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) shows that a PCI-selected 10% subset substantially improves overall construct recovery relative to response-stability and random selection. These findings support PCI as a principled internal diagnostic for screening synthetic respondents in survey pipelines.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Persona-Conditioned Informativeness (PCI), an unsupervised diagnostic metric that identifies whether semantically similar personas produce concordant response shifts in LLM-based survey simulations. PCI models personas as a similarity graph and uses Local Moran's I to quantify local spatial coherence, enabling the selection of compact persona subsets without construct labels. Evaluated on the PVQ-RR (57 items), a PCI-selected 10% subset substantially improved construct recovery via CFA compared to response-stability and random selection baselines.
AI.motivation: Persona-conditioned LLMs are widely used for survey simulation, but apparent response variation may stem from unconditioned model priors or token sampling noise rather than genuine persona conditioning. The paper argues that informative personas should exhibit concordant response shifts among semantically similar groups, motivating a principled diagnostic to distinguish systematic persona effects from noise.
AI.method: The authors formalize persona-conditioned variation as informative when semantically similar personas deviate in concordant directions from item-level sample baselines. They propose PCI, which constructs a similarity graph of personas and applies Local Moran's I to measure local spatial coherence, extracting compact subsets of informative personas without relying on construct labels. Validation uses the 57-item PVQ-RR, with confirmatory factor analysis comparing construct recovery of PCI-selected subsets against response-stability and random selection baselines.
AI.result: CFA shows that a PCI-selected 10% persona subset substantially improves overall construct recovery on the PVQ-RR relative to response-stability-based selection and random selection baselines, demonstrating PCI's effectiveness as an internal diagnostic for screening synthetic respondents.
AI.conclusion: PCI is a principled, unsupervised internal diagnostic for identifying genuinely informative persona-conditioned responses in LLM survey pipelines, offering a scalable screening mechanism that improves latent construct recovery without external human benchmarks or construct labels.

title: M$^3$ISR: A Multi-Modal Multi-View Benchmark for 3D/4D Gaussian Splatting and Feedforward Compression
summary: High-fidelity free-viewpoint video (FVV) and interactive rendering increasingly rely on explicit Gaussian representations, yet practical deployment remains constrained by representation size, dynamic updates, and computational cost. Existing multi-view video benchmarks provide valuable real-captured content, but they make it difficult to isolate the effects of controlled camera geometry, representation efficiency, and temporal redundancy. We introduce M$^3$ISR, a controlled synthetic benchmark for 3D and 4D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS/4DGS). The benchmark contains 25 scenes from five indoor and outdoor scene groups, two camera/motion configurations, six synchronized 1080p views, and dense ground-truth annotations including RGB, camera parameters, depth, semantic and instance segmentation, and static--dynamic masks. The shared-center camera design intentionally isolates angular view variation and enables controlled evaluation of novel-view synthesis and representation efficiency. We organize M$^3$ISR into five complementary tracks covering 3DGS synthesis, 4DGS synthesis, 4DGS streaming, 3DGS compression, and 4DGS compression. Representative baseline results show small differences in static reconstruction quality but substantial differences in representation storage, while the evaluated streaming methods exhibit substantially higher reported training or reconstruction cost than the corresponding offline dynamic reconstruction baselines. We further define feedforward compression tasks for 3DGS and 4DGS and provide reference rate--distortion formulations and preliminary baseline evaluations. The benchmark is intended as a controlled and complementary testbed for systematic study of Gaussian-based FVV reconstruction, compression, and streaming.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces M³ISR, a controlled synthetic benchmark for 3D and 4D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS/4DGS) research. It contains 25 scenes across five indoor/outdoor scene groups, two camera configurations, six synchronized 1080p views, and dense ground-truth annotations. The benchmark is organized into five tracks covering 3DGS synthesis, 4DGS synthesis, 4DGS streaming, 3DGS compression, and 4DGS compression, aiming to isolate variables like camera geometry, representation efficiency, and temporal redundancy that are difficult to control in real-captured benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-view video benchmarks provide real-captured data but make it difficult to isolate the effects of controlled camera geometry, representation efficiency, and temporal redundancy on Gaussian-based free-viewpoint video reconstruction.
AI.method: The authors construct M³ISR as a synthetic benchmark with 25 scenes from five scene groups, two camera/motion configurations, six synchronized 1080p views, and dense annotations (RGB, camera parameters, depth, semantic/instance segmentation, static-dynamic masks). The shared-center camera design isolates angular view variation. The benchmark is partitioned into five tracks: 3DGS synthesis, 4DGS synthesis, 4DGS streaming, 3DGS compression, and 4DGS compression, with feedforward compression tasks and reference rate-distortion formulations defined.
AI.result: Representative baseline results show small differences in static reconstruction quality across methods but substantial differences in representation storage. Streaming methods exhibit significantly higher training or reconstruction cost compared to offline dynamic reconstruction baselines. Preliminary baseline evaluations for the compression tracks are also provided.
AI.conclusion: M³ISR serves as a controlled and complementary testbed for systematic study of Gaussian-based free-viewpoint video reconstruction, compression, and streaming, enabling researchers to isolate and evaluate specific aspects of representation efficiency and dynamic behavior.

title: AraDetox: A Multi-Dialect Arabic Detoxification Dataset
summary: Arabic harmful-language detection has received considerable attention, yet Arabic text detoxification remains underexplored. We introduce AraDetox, a multi-dialect Arabic detoxification dataset comprising 10,500 harmful social-media posts and 84,000 detoxified rewrites generated using GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 Flash across Modern Standard Arabic, Gulf, Levantine, and Egyptian Arabic. The generated outputs were assessed through human evaluation and automatic analyses of lexical change, semantic preservation, sentiment, and dialectal style. Results show that detoxification is primarily a meaning-preserving rewriting task: substantial lexical and structural reformulation is accompanied by consistently high semantic similarity. Human evaluation confirms successful harmful-language removal while largely preserving the original meaning. Dialectal analyses further indicate that the generated variants exhibit measurable stylistic alignment with reference Arabic dialect corpora. Comparison with existing resources highlights two complementary approaches to detoxification: minimal-edit lexical substitution and meaning-preserving reformulation. Our findings demonstrate that large-scale Arabic detoxification resources can be constructed through LLM-assisted generation and human verification. The dataset is publicly available at https://github.com/ArabicNLP-UK/AraDetox to support future research on Arabic detoxification, safe text generation, and multi-dialect Arabic NLP.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AraDetox, a multi-dialect Arabic detoxification dataset with 10,500 harmful posts and 84,000 detoxified rewrites across MSA, Gulf, Levantine, and Egyptian Arabic, generated via GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 Flash and verified through human evaluation and automatic analyses.
AI.motivation: While Arabic harmful-language detection has been extensively studied, Arabic text detoxification remains underexplored, motivating the creation of a dedicated multi-dialect detoxification resource.
AI.method: The authors constructed AraDetox by generating detoxified rewrites of 10,500 harmful social-media posts using GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 Flash, covering four Arabic dialects. Outputs were assessed via human evaluation and automatic analyses of lexical change, semantic preservation, sentiment, and dialectal style alignment.
AI.result: Detoxification is primarily a meaning-preserving rewriting task: substantial lexical and structural reformulation occurs with consistently high semantic similarity. Human evaluation confirms successful harmful-language removal with meaning largely preserved. Generated variants show measurable stylistic alignment with reference dialect corpora. Comparisons reveal two complementary detoxification approaches: minimal-edit lexical substitution and meaning-preserving reformulation.
AI.conclusion: Large-scale Arabic detoxification resources can be reliably constructed through LLM-assisted generation combined with human verification, and AraDetox is publicly released to support future research on Arabic detoxification, safe text generation, and multi-dialect Arabic NLP.

title: Small Reasoning Models are Instruction Followers in Function Calling
summary: Function calling represents the core capability of agentic large language models (LLMs). Existing research has focused on enhancing LLMs function-calling accuracy through fine-tuning, reinforcement learning (RL), and multi-agent frameworks, particularly for native function-calling LLMs. This work demonstrates that LLMs achieve superior accuracy in function calling in instruction-following contexts (i.e., standard user-assistant interactions) rather than a tool calling context. We introduce Instruction-Followed Function Calling (IFFC), a novel framework that decouples function-calling logic from the primary LLM and delegates it to a dedicated smaller model operating within the instruction-following paradigm. Our method consistently outperforms both native function calling (NFC) and prompt-based function calling (PFC) baselines, with particularly strong gains on reasoning-oriented LLMs. Furthermore, we demonstrate that IFFC maintains robust performance under aggressive quantization, enabling efficient on-device deployment without significant accuracy degradation. This work establishes a new paradigm for reliable, resource-efficient function calling in edge-computing scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that LLMs perform better at function calling in standard instruction-following contexts than in dedicated tool-calling contexts, and introduces IFFC—a framework that decouples function-calling logic from the main LLM by delegating it to a smaller dedicated model operating in the instruction-following paradigm. IFFC outperforms native and prompt-based function-calling baselines and remains robust under aggressive quantization for efficient on-device deployment.
AI.motivation: Existing research has focused on improving function-calling accuracy through fine-tuning, RL, and multi-agent frameworks, yet this work reveals that LLMs actually demonstrate superior function-calling accuracy in standard instruction-following contexts rather than in tool-calling contexts, motivating a paradigm shift.
AI.method: The proposed IFFC framework decouples function-calling logic from the primary LLM and delegates it to a dedicated smaller model operating within the instruction-following paradigm, rather than a tool-calling context.
AI.result: IFFC consistently outperforms both native function calling (NFC) and prompt-based function calling (PFC) baselines, with particularly strong gains on reasoning-oriented LLMs. It also maintains robust performance under aggressive quantization.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a new paradigm for reliable, resource-efficient function calling in edge-computing scenarios, demonstrating that instruction-following paradigms combined with delegated small models enable efficient on-device deployment without significant accuracy degradation.

title: HeatTok: Enhancing Remote Sensing Image Understanding via Thermodiffusion-based Tokenization
comment: 19 pages (10 pages main text + appendix), 10 figures. Accepted at the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM 2026), Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, November 10--14, 2026
summary: Current visual tokenizers in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) predominantly rely on patch-based partitioning, which causes severe semantic mixture and object fragmentation in remote sensing imagery due to the irregular contours of geo-objects. Moreover, existing adaptive methods struggle to extract precise object-level tokens and lack dedicated geometric positional encodings for irregular regions. In this paper, we propose HeatTok, a semantic-aware tokenizer driven by thermodiffusion aggregation. Inspired by the physical principles of heat conduction, HeatTok adaptively merges adjacent homogeneous regions to generate semantically independent, object-aligned irregular tokens. To enable MLLMs to perceive these irregular shapes, we design the Gaussian Multimodal Rotary Positional Embedding (G-MRoPE), which models token spatial distributions via 2D Gaussians and explicitly injects center, scale, and orientation cues. Extensive evaluations on the VRSBench and EarthVQA datasets demonstrate that HeatTok effectively preserves object-level semantic integrity and achieves state-of-the-art performance under a reasonable token budget. The code is available: https://github.com/YingyingYan1/HeatTok.

AI.tldr: HeatTok is a semantic-aware visual tokenizer for MLLMs that uses thermodiffusion aggregation to merge homogeneous regions into object-aligned irregular tokens, avoiding the semantic mixture and fragmentation problems of patch-based partitioning. It introduces G-MRoPE to encode irregular token shapes via 2D Gaussians with center, scale, and orientation cues, achieving SOTA on VRSBench and EarthVQA.
AI.motivation: Patch-based visual tokenization in MLLMs causes severe semantic mixture and object fragmentation when applied to remote sensing imagery, because geo-objects have irregular contours. Existing adaptive tokenization methods fail to extract precise object-level tokens and lack dedicated geometric positional encodings for irregular regions.
AI.method: HeatTok employs a heat-conduction-inspired thermodiffusion aggregation mechanism that adaptively merges adjacent homogeneous regions to produce semantically independent, object-aligned irregular tokens. To make MLLMs aware of these irregular shapes, it introduces Gaussian Multimodal Rotary Positional Embedding (G-MRoPE), which models token spatial distributions using 2D Gaussians and explicitly injects center, scale, and orientation cues.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations on VRSBench and EarthVQA datasets show that HeatTok preserves object-level semantic integrity and achieves state-of-the-art performance under a reasonable token budget. Code is publicly released.
AI.conclusion: HeatTok demonstrates that physics-inspired aggregation (thermodiffusion) combined with geometry-aware positional encodings (G-MRoPE) effectively addresses the limitations of patch-based tokenization for remote sensing MLLMs, improving object-level semantic integrity and pushing state-of-the-art results.

title: SelFusion: Self-distillation for Diffusion Language Models
comment: Published as a main conference paper at ACL 2026
summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) alleviate the inherent latency bottleneck of autoregressive (AR) large language models (LLMs), but their degraded generation quality limits practical applicability. Although knowledge distillation (KD) can be a promising direction for improving performance, we empirically find that naively applying conventional KD yields only marginal gains, or even degrades generation quality. Based on these observations, we propose a novel self-distillation framework for DLMs, namely SelFusion. To enable effective KD without an external teacher model, SelFusion performs two forward passes with different masking levels, defining the hard mode with a larger masking probability and the easy mode with a smaller masking probability. However, the easy mode is not always more accurate than the hard mode and can be overconfident on incorrect tokens. Thus, we introduce bidirectional KD between the two modes, which can dynamically determine the distillation direction based on token-level correctness. Experimental results on instruction-following tasks show that the proposed self-distillation substantially outperforms other KD methods with external LLM and DLM teachers. In many configurations, the student trained with SelFusion even surpasses the performance of the LLM teacher, providing a practical path toward improving DLM generation quality. Source code can be found at https://github.com/scai-research/SelFusion_official

AI.tldr: SelFusion is a self-distillation framework for diffusion language models (DLMs) that performs two forward passes with different masking levels (hard and easy modes) and applies bidirectional knowledge distillation between them, dynamically determining distillation direction based on token-level correctness. It outperforms KD methods using external DLM and LLM teachers and often surpasses the LLM teacher's performance.
AI.motivation: DLMs address the latency bottleneck of autoregressive LLMs but suffer from degraded generation quality. While knowledge distillation (KD) could improve performance, naively applying conventional KD yields only marginal gains or even degrades quality, motivating the need for a more effective distillation approach without relying on external teachers.
AI.method: SelFusion performs two forward passes with different masking levels during training: a hard mode with larger masking probability and an easy mode with smaller masking probability. Since the easy mode is not always more accurate and can be overconfident on incorrect tokens, bidirectional KD is introduced between the two modes, dynamically determining the distillation direction based on token-level correctness.
AI.result: On instruction-following tasks, SelFusion substantially outperforms other KD methods with external LLM and DLM teachers. In many configurations, the student trained with SelFusion even surpasses the performance of the LLM teacher.
AI.conclusion: Self-distillation without an external teacher provides a practical path toward improving DLM generation quality, addressing the quality gap that has limited DLM applicability.

title: When Does AI for PDEs Yield Scientific Evidence?
summary: Existing AI-for-PDE benchmarks primarily assess models in terms of predictive or approximation accuracy. In physics research, however, AI outputs often serve as evidence for scientific claims. These two objectives are not equivalent: the former measures an output's agreement with a reference target or satisfaction of governing constraints; the latter asks whether, given a specified object of study, scientific claim, assumptions, and evidence standard, the output provides sufficient evidence for that claim. To bridge this gap, we extend a widely used PDE-simulation benchmark and a comprehensive benchmark for PDE inverse problems to enable, for the first time in AI for PDEs, evaluation of whether and to what extent model outputs support specified scientific claims. Our results show that numerical accuracy and evidential support can rank models differently, explain when and why they do so, and reveal that existing benchmarks can favor methods whose outputs provide weaker support for the scientific claims of interest. Together, we formalize, empirically demonstrate, and explain this evaluation--use mismatch in AI for PDEs.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a gap in AI-for-PDE benchmarks: existing benchmarks evaluate predictive/approximation accuracy, but in physics research AI outputs serve as evidence for scientific claims, and these two objectives are not equivalent. The authors extend two PDE benchmarks (forward simulation and inverse problems) to enable evidential-support evaluation, showing that numerical accuracy and evidential support can rank models differently, and existing benchmarks can favor methods whose outputs provide weaker scientific evidence.
AI.motivation: Existing AI-for-PDE benchmarks only measure predictive or approximation accuracy, but in physics research AI outputs serve as evidence for scientific claims. These two objectives are not equivalent: accuracy measures agreement with a reference target or constraint satisfaction, while evidential support asks whether the output provides sufficient evidence for a specified scientific claim given assumptions and evidence standards. This evaluation-use mismatch has not been addressed.
AI.method: The authors extend a widely used PDE-simulation benchmark and a comprehensive benchmark for PDE inverse problems to add evidential-support evaluation—for the first time in AI for PDEs. They formalize the distinction between predictive accuracy and evidential support and enable systematic comparison of models under both criteria.
AI.result: Numerical accuracy and evidential support can rank models differently. The analysis explains when and why such ranking divergence occurs and reveals that existing benchmarks can favor methods whose outputs provide weaker support for scientific claims of interest.
AI.conclusion: The paper formalizes, empirically demonstrates, and explains the evaluation-use mismatch in AI for PDEs, advocating for evidential-support evaluation as a complementary benchmark criterion alongside numerical accuracy.

title: Learning Sample-wise Rank-aware Interpolation Weights for Composed Visual Data Retrieval
summary: At the heart of composed visual data retrieval is the fusion of a reference visual input and a textual modification into a single query. While current state-of-the-art methods utilize multimodal large language models for this fusion, their complexity introduces prohibitive querytime latency, limiting their scalability. We instead revisit the efficacy of simple linear interpolation within an embedding space, and introduce SRAIN, the first framework that dynamically predicts query-specific interpolation weights. The key challenge lies in the fact that the quality of an interpolation weight should be measured by the interpolated embedding's discriminability from negatives as well as its proximity to true targets; this makes collecting and predicting optimal weights intractable. We overcome this bottleneck through two key innovations: batch-wise rank-aware weight estimation during training, and a compact memory bank that synthesizes hard negatives during inference. SRAIN achieves the best in composed video retrieval and matches the current state of the art in composed image retrieval, all while substantially reducing querytime latency compared to MLLM-based alternatives.

AI.tldr: SRAIN is a lightweight framework for composed visual retrieval that dynamically predicts query-specific interpolation weights in embedding space, achieving state-of-the-art results in composed video retrieval and matching SOTA in composed image retrieval while dramatically reducing query-time latency compared to MLLM-based methods.
AI.motivation: Current state-of-the-art composed visual retrieval methods rely on multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for fusing reference visual input with textual modifications, but their complexity introduces prohibitive query-time latency that limits scalability.
AI.method: SRAIN revisits linear interpolation in embedding space and introduces dynamic, query-specific interpolation weight prediction. It overcomes the intractability of collecting/predicting optimal weights via two innovations: (1) batch-wise rank-aware weight estimation during training, and (2) a compact memory bank that synthesizes hard negatives during inference.
AI.result: SRAIN achieves the best performance in composed video retrieval and matches the current state of the art in composed image retrieval, while substantially reducing query-time latency compared to MLLM-based alternatives.
AI.conclusion: Simple linear interpolation with dynamically predicted weights can rival complex MLLM-based fusion approaches in composed visual retrieval, offering a more scalable and efficient alternative without sacrificing accuracy.

title: Do Spoken Language Models Hear Speech as They Read Text? Bridging Structural Gaps Between Speech and Text
summary: Spoken Language Models (SLMs) generate textual responses directly from speech, offering an alternative to cascaded systems. Despite recent advances, existing SLMs still exhibit weaker instruction-following behavior and limited generalization across diverse tasks compared to text-based language models. Our analysis shows that speech and text representations in current SLMs remain weakly aligned despite strong downstream performance, indicating that structural differences between continuous, temporally varying speech and discrete text remain insufficiently addressed. To address this, we propose a simple framework that decouples length mismatch from semantic alignment and encourages closer correspondence between speech and text representations. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate competitive performance against strong baselines, underscoring the importance of explicitly addressing structural differences between speech and text in SLM training. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/jaykim9870/Do_SLMs_Hear_Speech_as_They_Read_Text.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a simple framework for spoken language models (SLMs) that decouples length mismatch from semantic alignment to improve speech-text representation alignment, achieving competitive performance on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing SLMs exhibit weaker instruction-following and limited generalization across tasks than text-based models, despite strong downstream performance. Analysis reveals that speech and text representations remain weakly aligned in current SLMs due to insufficiently addressed structural differences between continuous, temporally varying speech and discrete text.
AI.method: A simple framework that decouples length mismatch from semantic alignment, explicitly encouraging closer correspondence between speech and text representations during SLM training.
AI.result: Competitive performance against strong baselines across multiple benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly addressing structural differences between speech and text in SLM training is important, as demonstrated by the proposed framework's competitive results.

title: ClawProBench: Trace-Aware Evaluation of AI Agents with Runtime Coverage and Frozen Workplace-Style Holdouts
summary: Agent benchmarks often evaluate only final answers even when agents run on stateful runtimes. We argue this under-specifies what is being evaluated: the proper unit is a declared model-plus-runtime configuration whose failures can occur in evidence acquisition, runtime routing, safety boundaries, or repeated execution. We present ClawProBench, a trace-aware benchmark for runtime-native agent evaluation instantiated on OpenClaw, a live agent runtime with workspace tools and native surfaces for browsing, memory, messaging, scheduling, skills, and subagents. ClawProBench defines two tracks: a 102-scenario full profile with live workspace and native-runtime routing tasks, and a frozen 68-scenario holdout with closed-world JSON output contracts for robust ranking. Trials are scored from execution traces via a safety-gated formula combining correctness, process quality, and efficiency, preserving failure evidence for audit. Our anonymous artifact includes benchmark definitions, scoring code, manifests and sanitized traces. We evaluate 68 configurations on the full profile and 37 on holdout. The top safety-gated average trace score is 0.7671. Native-runtime tasks underperform workspace-live tasks (0.5238 vs. 0.6415). On holdout, pass@k-any outperforms strict three-trial pass (0.6638 vs. 0.2890), while full-profile and holdout rankings show weak alignment (Spearman 0.1300). Rankings based purely on correctness differ substantially from process-aware, safety-gated and strict-pass views. Final-answer leaderboards may hide native-surface weaknesses, one-off successes and trace-local agent failure modes.

AI.tldr: ClawProBench is a trace-aware benchmark for runtime-native agent evaluation on the OpenClaw agent runtime, with 102 full-profile and 68 frozen holdout scenarios. It demonstrates that process-aware, safety-gated scoring from execution traces reveals agent failures that final-answer leaderboards miss, with native-runtime tasks underperforming workspace-live tasks and weak ranking alignment between full-profile and holdout tracks.
AI.motivation: Agent benchmarks typically evaluate only final answers even when agents run on stateful runtimes, under-specifying what is being evaluated. The proper unit of evaluation should be a declared model-plus-runtime configuration, with failures potentially occurring in evidence acquisition, runtime routing, safety boundaries, or repeated execution.
AI.method: ClawProBench is instantiated on OpenClaw, a live agent runtime with workspace tools and native surfaces for browsing, memory, messaging, scheduling, skills, and subagents. It defines two tracks: a 102-scenario full profile with live workspace and native-runtime routing tasks, and a frozen 68-scenario holdout with closed-world JSON output contracts. Trials are scored from execution traces via a safety-gated formula combining correctness, process quality, and efficiency.
AI.result: 68 configurations were evaluated on the full profile and 37 on holdout. The top safety-gated average trace score is 0.7671. Native-runtime tasks underperform workspace-live tasks (0.5238 vs. 0.6415). Pass@k-any outperforms strict three-trial pass on holdout (0.6638 vs. 0.2890), and full-profile and holdout rankings show weak alignment (Spearman 0.1300). Rankings based purely on correctness differ substantially from process-aware, safety-gated, and strict-pass views.
AI.conclusion: Final-answer leaderboards may hide native-surface weaknesses, one-off successes, and trace-local agent failure modes. Trace-aware evaluation is necessary for accurately assessing runtime-native agents.

title: TRACE: Temporal Retrieval with Anchored and Convergent Evidence for Long-Horizon Video Understanding
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Main Conference. 19 pages, 5 figures, 6 tables. Project page: https://buaa-colalab.github.io/TRACE/
summary: A long-video answer is evidence-supported only when the frames decoded from the video cover every event the answer depends on. Existing evaluations score final-answer correctness or predicted evidence intervals, but the frames a method decodes before answering are rarely audited, so correct answers can still rest on incomplete observation. We introduce VES-Bench, a 600-question benchmark of Temporal Ordering and Event Counting items over 348 public long videos. Each item carries a jointly necessary set of evidence intervals, letting us audit at three strictness levels whether a method's decoded frames cover every one of them. We also propose TRACE, a training-free agent that grounds answers in raw visual clips, builds an evidence bundle round by round, and stops only when the answer stabilises as the bundle grows and a final pass over the same clips returns the same answer. Under a same-backbone audit, TRACE answers 50.7% of questions correctly with at least two decoded frames inside every evidence interval, at 98.7 frames per question: over 10 points above uniform decoding at 128 frames (40.2%), and within 2.6 points of uniform decoding at 256 frames at 0.39x its frame cost, while reaching the highest answer accuracy in the audit (63.5%). TRACE also stays competitive on Video-MME (86.1), LVBench (75.6), and LongVideoBench (75.1).

AI.tldr: This paper introduces VES-Bench, a 600-question benchmark for auditing whether decoded video frames cover the jointly necessary evidence intervals for long-video answers, and TRACE, a training-free agent that grounds answers in raw clips and stops only when the answer stabilizes. TRACE achieves 50.7% accuracy with two decoded frames per evidence interval at 98.7 frames/question, beating uniform decoding at 128 frames by >10 points and matching 256-frame decoding at 0.39x frame cost, while staying competitive on Video-MME (86.1), LVBench (75.6), and LongVideoBench (75.1).
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of long-video question answering score final-answer correctness or predicted evidence intervals but never audit whether the frames a method actually decodes cover all evidence required by the answer. This means a correct answer can rest on incomplete observation, and current benchmarks cannot detect such gaps.
AI.method: The authors build VES-Bench, a 600-question benchmark with Temporal Ordering and Event Counting items over 348 public long videos, where each question has a jointly necessary set of evidence intervals. They propose three strictness levels to audit whether a method's decoded frames cover every interval. They also introduce TRACE, a training-free agent that grounds answers in raw visual clips, builds an evidence bundle round by round, and stops only when the answer stabilizes as the bundle grows and a final pass over the same clips reproduces the same answer.
AI.result: Under a same-backbone audit, TRACE answers 50.7% of questions correctly with at least two decoded frames inside every evidence interval at 98.7 frames per question, which is over 10 points above uniform decoding at 128 frames (40.2%) and within 2.6 points of uniform decoding at 256 frames at 0.39x its frame cost. TRACE also achieves the highest answer accuracy in the audit (63.5%) and stays competitive on Video-MME (86.1), LVBench (75.6), and LongVideoBench (75.1).
AI.conclusion: Evidence-coverage auditing reveals that correct long-video answers can rest on incomplete observation, and the proposed TRACE agent shows that training-free, adaptive decoding can achieve both higher answer accuracy and stronger evidence coverage than uniform decoding at a fraction of the frame cost.

title: Exploring Dowker Homology for Sentence Similarity
comment: 12 pages; accepted at "Workshop on Insights from Negative Results in NLP 2026"
summary: Dowker homology is a topological tool that may be used to analyze the relative position of two point clouds living in a common space. We investigate whether Dowker homology captures sentence similarity information by treating the embeddings of the tokens that constitute a sentence pair as a pair of point clouds in the latent space of a transformer model, using both models that have and have not been fine-tuned for sentence similarity. We find that Dowker homology captures sentence similarity information, as measured by regressing Dowker homology features onto ground-truth similarity scores, and that it can be used for visual inspection of similarity data and models. In an attempt to make Dowker homology readily applicable, we derive from it single-number summaries that we expect to capture sentence similarity directly. These turn out to work reasonably well, but without outperforming standard sentence similarity measures based on established pooling methods.

AI.tldr: This paper applies Dowker homology, a topological data analysis tool for comparing two point clouds, to sentence similarity by treating token embeddings of sentence pairs as point clouds in transformer latent space. Dowker homology features capture sentence similarity information (validated via regression onto ground-truth scores) and enable visual inspection, but single-number summaries derived from it perform reasonably yet do not surpass standard pooling-based similarity measures.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether Dowker homology, a topological tool designed for analyzing the relative positioning of two point clouds, can capture sentence similarity information when applied to token embeddings in transformer latent space, potentially offering a novel topologically-grounded approach to semantic similarity.
AI.method: Treat the token embeddings of each pair of sentences as two point clouds in the latent space of transformer models (both fine-tuned and not fine-tuned for sentence similarity). Compute Dowker homology features between the pair of point clouds, regress these features onto ground-truth similarity scores to assess informativeness, use them for visual inspection, and derive single-number summaries from Dowker homology for direct sentence similarity scoring.
AI.result: Dowker homology captures sentence similarity information as shown by regression of its features onto ground-truth scores, and supports visual inspection of similarity data and models. The derived single-number summaries work reasonably well but do not outperform standard pooling-based sentence similarity measures.
AI.conclusion: Dowker homology provides a meaningful topological lens for sentence similarity that is useful for analysis and visualization, though it does not yet surpass established pooling-based methods for direct similarity scoring.

title: HANSARD: A Reference Architecture for Forensic Readiness, Runtime Witnessing, and Graded Attribution in Autonomous Multi-Agent AI Systems
summary: Autonomous multi-agent systems nowadays act in finance, software supply chains, and security operations. Already, the first largely AI-orchestrated intrusion campaigns have been reported. Yet, when such a system causes harm, no method can robustly establish what happened, what caused it, or who is accountable. This is because provenance forensics works at the wrong abstraction, formal causality assumes the causal model, and agent auditing trusts self-recording. The target failure mode is, thus, attribution laundering, i.e., spreading an act across redundant agents until none is a but-for cause. Worse, the record is produced by the suspects, which comprises the assumption adopted throughout this work. Agents may therefore anticipate the investigation and the part of logging infrastructure may itself collude. In this paper, HANSARD is proposed, a reference architecture treating accountability as a life-cycle property. First, a readiness profile sealed before operation bounds what later findings may claim. Second, capturing at five choke points beyond the agents' reach makes omissions detectable, not only tampering. Third, a typed PROV-DM-aligned causal graph accrues as the system runs, and three indicators read it live to gate oversight without adjudicating. Fourth, post-incident replay yields contingent effects under the modified Halpern-Pearl definition, together with a compensation-set size. Finally, a synergy residual measures harm due to the combination rather than to individuals, making laundering visible. Cause, responsibility and accountability are then reported separately, each capped by an evidentiary tier, while a future research agenda is also provided.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes HANSARD, a reference architecture for accountability in autonomous multi-agent systems that addresses "attribution laundering"—where harmful acts are spread across redundant agents so no single agent is a but-for cause. It introduces five choke-point capture points beyond agents' reach, a typed PROV-DM-aligned causal graph with live indicators, post-incident replay using modified Halpern-Pearl causality, and a synergy residual metric to detect collusive diffusion of responsibility. The system separates cause, responsibility, and accountability reporting with evidentiary tiers.
AI.motivation: Autonomous multi-agent systems increasingly operate in critical domains (finance, software supply chains, security). The first AI-orchestrated intrusion campaigns have already occurred, yet no robust method can establish what happened, who caused it, or who is accountable when harm occurs. Existing approaches fail because provenance forensics operates at the wrong abstraction level, formal causality assumes the causal model is given, and agent auditing trusts self-recorded data. The adversarial setting—where agents may anticipate investigation and collude with logging infrastructure—demands a fundamentally different approach.
AI.method: HANSARD is a five-part reference architecture treating accountability as a life-cycle property: (1) a readiness profile sealed before operation bounds what later findings may claim; (2) capture at five choke points beyond agents' reach makes omissions detectable in addition to tampering; (3) a typed PROV-DM-aligned causal graph accrues at runtime with three live indicators gating oversight (without adjudicating); (4) post-incident replay computes contingent effects under the modified Halpern-Pearl definition plus a compensation-set size; and (5) a synergy residual metric measures harm attributable to agent combinations rather than individuals, making laundering visible.
AI.result: The architecture reports cause, responsibility, and accountability separately, each capped by an evidentiary tier to prevent overclaiming. The synergy residual makes attribution laundering detectable by exposing harm due to agent combinations. The design ensures that even when suspects produce the record and may collude with logging infrastructure, omissions at externally-anchored choke points remain detectable.
AI.conclusion: HANSARD provides a viable reference architecture for accountability in adversarial multi-agent environments, treating it as a life-cycle property rather than a post-hoc forensic activity. The paper concludes with a future research agenda, acknowledging the evolving nature of AI-orchestrated threats and the need for continued refinement of these mechanisms.

title: VISTA: Test-Time Compositional Alignment for Visual Autoregressive Generation
summary: Visual autoregressive (VAR) models have emerged as a fast, high-quality alternative to diffusion for text-to-image generation, but like diffusion models they exhibit persistent compositional failures, producing images that violate the attribute bindings and spatial relations specified in the prompt. While a rich line of test-time alignment methods has developed for diffusion, no comparable approach exists for next-scale VAR generation, whose stateful, discrete, multi-resolution sampling process makes existing techniques inapplicable. We close this gap with \textbf{VISTA} (\textbf{Vi}sual Autoregressive \textbf{S}emantic \textbf{T}est-time \textbf{A}lignment), the first gradient-based test-time alignment framework for next-scale autoregressive image generation. Built on Infinity, VISTA intervenes directly in the generation process, optimizing intermediate representations through the frozen transformer to steer visual predictions toward compositional constraints, without modifying model parameters or requiring additional training. VISTA introduces the mechanisms needed to make such optimization stable across scales, together with an extensible objective space that any differentiable constraint on cross-attention can plug into. Across two benchmarks and two model scales, VISTA improves every targeted compositional category, raising the mean targeted score by nearly 20\% on a 2B backbone and almost 6\% on an 8B backbone, with the largest gains on spatial relations. Image quality is preserved: an independent preference model VISTA never optimizes scores its outputs nearly 20\% higher. Notably, the 2B model with VISTA surpasses a backbone four times its size, indicating that a substantial part of the compositional gap between model scales is recoverable at test time.

AI.tldr: VISTA is the first gradient-based test-time alignment framework for next-scale visual autoregressive (VAR) image generation, enabling compositional constraint optimization during inference without retraining, improving compositional accuracy by up to ~20% on targeted metrics while preserving image quality.
AI.motivation: Visual autoregressive (VAR) models, while fast and high-quality alternatives to diffusion for text-to-image generation, suffer from persistent compositional failures (attribute binding and spatial relation errors). Although test-time alignment methods exist for diffusion, none apply to next-scale VAR generation due to its stateful, discrete, multi-resolution sampling process.
AI.method: VISTA intervenes directly in the generation process of the Infinity model, optimizing intermediate representations through the frozen transformer to steer predictions toward compositional constraints. It introduces stability mechanisms for optimization across scales and an extensible objective space where any differentiable constraint on cross-attention can be plugged in, without modifying model parameters or requiring additional training.
AI.result: Across two benchmarks and two model scales, VISTA improves every targeted compositional category, raising mean targeted scores by nearly 20% on a 2B backbone and almost 6% on an 8B backbone, with the largest gains on spatial relations. Image quality is preserved, with an independent preference model scoring outputs nearly 20% higher. The 2B model with VISTA surpasses a backbone four times its size.
AI.conclusion: VISTA demonstrates that a substantial portion of the compositional gap between model scales is recoverable at test time for VAR generation, offering a training-free, parameter-free solution to compositional failures in visual autoregressive models.

title: Knowing Isn't Always Saying: When Do Spatial Encodings Reach Answers in Vision-Language Models?
comment: Accepted to appear in the EMNLP 2026 Main Conference
summary: Vision-language models are known to encode spatial information in their hidden states, yet often fail to use it when answering. However, it remains unclear when and where this encoded information reaches the answer. We address this with direction patching, a class-conditioned causal intervention applied across layers, token positions, and prompt formats. Using spatial-ID directions constructed following prior encoding evidence, we find that causal influence on answer logits emerges only at mid-to-deep depths. Text chain-of-thought suppresses immediate object-word argmax-level transport in most models, while visually grounded prompts keep it open. Positive target-logit gain can remain below the argmax threshold, and transport can re-emerge at the final prefix token or at the answer step in deeper layers. Across the ten VLMs we study, these local effects form descriptive transport patterns. Complementary experiments characterize how these patterns shift across datasets, attributes, and encoding amplitudes. Together, these results reframe the encoding-grounding gap as a problem of conditional transport in VLMs.

AI.tldr: This paper uses direction patching, a class-conditioned causal intervention, to investigate when and where spatial information encoded in vision-language model hidden states causally influences answer logits. The authors find that causal influence emerges only at mid-to-deep depths, text chain-of-thought suppresses immediate object-word transport while visually grounded prompts preserve it, and transport can re-emerge at final prefix or answer tokens in deeper layers across ten VLMs, reframing the encoding-grounding gap as conditional transport.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models encode spatial information in their hidden states but often fail to use it when answering questions. Previous work has established the "encoding-grounding gap," but it remains unclear when (at which layers/token positions) and how this encoded spatial information actually reaches the final answer. Understanding this temporal and spatial pathway of information flow is critical for diagnosing and potentially fixing grounding failures.
AI.method: The authors propose "direction patching," a class-conditioned causal intervention applied systematically across layers, token positions, and prompt formats. They construct spatial-ID directions based on prior encoding evidence and intervene on these directions to measure their causal influence on answer logits. Experiments are conducted across ten vision-language models, with complementary analyses varying datasets, attributes, and encoding amplitudes.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) causal influence on answer logits emerges only at mid-to-deep model depths; (2) text chain-of-thought suppresses immediate object-word argmax-level transport in most models, while visually grounded prompts keep it active; (3) positive target-logit gain can remain below the argmax threshold; (4) transport can re-emerge at the final prefix token or at the answer step in deeper layers; (5) local effects across ten VLMs form descriptive transport patterns that shift with datasets, attributes, and encoding amplitudes.
AI.conclusion: The paper reframes the encoding-grounding gap as a problem of conditional transport in VLMs—i.e., the issue is not whether spatial information is encoded, but whether and when it is causally transported to the answer under different conditions (prompt formats, layers, token positions). This provides a more nuanced mechanistic understanding of VLM spatial reasoning failures and opens avenues for targeted interventions.

title: CONTRAMEM: Learning Self-Evolving Procedural Memory from Contrasting Multi-Model Trajectories
summary: Autonomous computer-use agents are increasingly applied to long-horizon tasks requiring coordinated application calls, persistent state tracking, and verifier-sensitive writes, yet they remain prone to procedural failures: misreading application state, tool semantics, or task progress. Procedural memory promises more consistent decisions and less redundant exploration, but constructing high-quality memory without model training remains challenging. We introduce CONTRAMEM, a source-flexible, training-free framework for self-evolving procedural memory that treats same-task outcome variation as supervision: differences in correctness, efficiency, recovery, and failure modes expose outcome-relevant procedural distinctions, distilled into a compact bank of app-level Function Cards and task-level Skill Cards that evolves through localized curation rather than append-only accumulation or whole-bank rewriting. On held-out GAIA2/ARE computer-use tasks, CONTRAMEM more than doubles the success rate across the three source-model targets (26.2% to 55.3%), with consistent per-model gains (GPT-5.5: 27.5 to 61.0; Claude Sonnet 4.6: 28.0 to 52.5; DeepSeek V4 Pro: 23.0 to 52.5). The same bank transfers unchanged to the unseen Qwen3.7 Plus (18.5 to 35.5), indicating transferable procedural knowledge rather than model-specific behavior. The same construction carries over unchanged to AppWorld, beating both no memory and its own single-source self-memory variant for all three mid-tier agents on both public test splits. Under a matched trajectory budget, heterogeneous multi-model trajectories yield stronger memory than self- or same-model multi-rollout memory: the margin comes from contrastive behavioral diversity, not stronger source agents or more sampling.

AI.tldr: CONTRAMEM is a training-free framework for self-evolving procedural memory in autonomous computer-use agents. It leverages same-task outcome variation (differences in correctness, efficiency, recovery, failure modes) as implicit supervision to distill compact app-level Function Cards and task-level Skill Cards. It more than doubles success rates on GAIA2/ARE tasks (26.2% to 55.3%), transfers to unseen models, and outperforms single-source memory on AppWorld benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Computer-use agents prone to procedural failures (misreading app state, tool semantics, task progress). Procedural memory could improve decision consistency and reduce redundant exploration, but building high-quality memory without model training remains challenging.
AI.method: CONTRAMEM treats same-task outcome variation as supervision, distilling procedural distinctions into a compact bank of app-level Function Cards and task-level Skill Cards. It uses localized curation (evolving bank) rather than append-only accumulation or whole-bank rewriting. Memory is generated from heterogeneous multi-model trajectories under a matched budget.
AI.result: On GAIA2/ARE: success rate more than doubled from 26.2% to 55.3% across three source-model targets (GPT-5.5: 27.5→61.0; Claude Sonnet 4.6: 28.0→52.5; DeepSeek V4 Pro: 23.0→52.5). The same bank transfers to unseen Qwen3.7 Plus (18.5→35.5). On AppWorld, it beats no-memory and single-source self-memory variants for three mid-tier agents on both public test splits. Under matched trajectory budget, heterogeneous multi-model trajectories outperform self- or same-model multi-rollout memory due to contrastive behavioral diversity.
AI.conclusion: Contrastive procedural distinctions derived from outcome variation across heterogeneous models yield transferable, model-agnostic procedural memory. The margin comes from behavioral diversity in source trajectories rather than stronger source agents or more sampling.

title: RS$^3$-Prune: Read-Sparse, Store-Sparse Token Pruning for Video Object Segmentation
summary: We introduce RS$^3$-Prune, a training-free token-pruning recipe that instantiates as a small set of inference time hooks atop existing video object segmentation (VOS) networks. Modern VOS models have converged on a common, expensive design: an image encoder produces a dense token grid for every frame, and a memory bank accumulates these tokens across all previously processed frames to condition future predictions. As a video grows longer, the resulting token budget governs both per-frame latency and peak GPU memory. Hence these models break on use cases such as --- long-form video or real-time deployment on memory-bounded accelerators. In this work we argue that the right axis along which to compress memory-bank VOS is the token budget itself. RS$^3$-Prune operates in two precise locations within an arbitrary memory-bank VOS pipeline: at the boundary between the image encoder and the memory-attention readout, where we restrict the queries that participate in the cross-frame attention to only a small, geometrically informed subset; and at the boundary between the memory encoder and the memory bank, where we restrict which tokens are ever permitted to enter the bank to those that lie within the object's spatial extent. Over various established benchmarks, RS$^3$-Prune delivers up to $38.8\%$ FPS speedup and reduces $13.1\%$ peak memory usage, while preserving a competitive $\mathcal{J}$&$\mathcal{F}$ compared to the unmodified VOS networks.

AI.tldr: RS$^3$-Prune is a training-free token-pruning method for memory-bank video object segmentation (VOS) that accelerates inference by restricting cross-frame attention queries to a geometrically informed subset and limiting memory bank entries to tokens within the object's spatial extent, achieving up to 38.8% FPS speedup and 13.1% peak memory reduction while maintaining competitive segmentation quality.
AI.motivation: Modern VOS models rely on dense per-frame token grids and memory banks that accumulate tokens across all frames, causing per-frame latency and peak GPU memory to scale with video length. This breaks deployment on long-form video and memory-bounded accelerators. The paper argues the token budget itself is the correct compression axis for memory-bank VOS.
AI.method: RS$^3$-Prune operates as a set of training-free inference-time hooks at two precise locations in any memory-bank VOS pipeline: (1) between the image encoder and memory-attention readout, restricting cross-frame attention queries to a small, geometrically informed subset; and (2) between the memory encoder and the memory bank, restricting which tokens may enter the bank to only those within the object's spatial extent.
AI.result: Across established benchmarks, RS$^3$-Prune achieves up to 38.8% FPS speedup and 13.1% peak memory reduction while preserving a competitive J&F score compared to unmodified VOS networks.
AI.conclusion: Token pruning at strategic pipeline boundaries—queries for attention and entries to the memory bank—is an effective, training-free approach to making memory-bank VOS viable for long-form and real-time deployments without sacrificing segmentation quality.

title: TSWAP: A Multilingual Retrieval-Augmented Thai Wellness Advisor
comment: 8 pages, 2 tables. Data and evaluation logs: https://huggingface.co/datasets/iapp/tswap-wellness-benchmark
summary: We present TSWAP, a deployed eight-language conversational wellness advisor grounded, via retrieval-augmented generation, in a verified knowledge base of Thai traditional medicine and certified wellness providers. An unmodified open-weight LLM (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on vLLM) is grounded on a ~30.6K-chunk Thai index by a hybrid dense-sparse retriever with cross-encoder reranking; a first-turn query classifier forces tool-based retrieval for entity lookups; a rule-based safety layer enforces medical scope and Thai emergency routing; and all eight languages are served zero-shot with translate-then-retrieve. We release the first Thai traditional-medicine/wellness retrieval benchmark (50 questions with gold document IDs; Recall@5 = 0.88), production QA logs (91.1% test-retest pass over 259 cases), and a 71-question frontier no-retrieval probe showing what each grounding pillar contributes: without the safety prompt the backend model family produced a full drug-dosing schedule and complied with out-of-scope requests, and without the knowledge base it produced zero verifiable provider recommendations. We further report two transferable deployment findings: English-calibrated 4-bit AWQ quantization corrupts Thai tone marks, and forced-retrieval routing is necessary for reliable grounding.

AI.tldr: TSWAP is a deployed eight-language conversational wellness advisor grounded in Thai traditional medicine via RAG, using an unmodified open-weight LLM, hybrid retrieval, safety layers, and translate-then-retrieve. It releases a new retrieval benchmark, production QA logs, and ablation probes showing the contributions of each grounding pillar, plus transferable findings on quantization and forced-retrieval routing.
AI.motivation: To provide a reliable, multilingual conversational wellness advisor for Thai traditional medicine that is safely grounded in a verified knowledge base, while addressing the lack of benchmarks and deployment insights for such low-resource, high-stakes domains.
AI.method: RAG pipeline: unmodified Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on vLLM grounded on a ~30.6K-chunk Thai index via hybrid dense-sparse retrieval with cross-encoder reranking; first-turn query classifier forces tool-based retrieval; rule-based safety layer enforces medical scope and Thai emergency routing; eight languages served zero-shot via translate-then-retrieve.
AI.result: Releases a 50-question Thai traditional-medicine/wellness retrieval benchmark (Recall@5=0.88), production QA logs (91.1% test-retest pass over 259 cases), and a 71-question no-retrieval probe showing the safety prompt and knowledge base are critical. Also finds English-calibrated 4-bit AWQ corrupts Thai tone marks, and forced-retrieval routing is necessary for reliable grounding.
AI.conclusion: TSWAP demonstrates that a fully grounded, multilingual wellness advisor is deployable with an unmodified open-weight LLM, and that safety prompt design, verified knowledge grounding, quantization calibration language, and forced retrieval routing are key determinants of reliability.

title: STAGE: Stateful Translation to Agentic Graph Execution with Policy-Scoped Context and Deterministic Control
summary: Policy-governed agents must interpret case evidence while following an authorized procedure. We present \textsc{Stage}, an executable-graph framework that confines model judgment to policy-scoped nodes while placing procedural control in deterministic code. At each node, the model receives task-relevant policy context and returns a typed result, while the coordinator enforces the reviewed execution contract. We evaluate \textsc{Stage} on SOP-Bench Referral Abuse, two $τ^2$-bench domains, and Smart Dispute, a proprietary banking benchmark. Compared with monolithic full-policy execution, \textsc{Stage} generally improves task success and repeated-run reliability across workflows of varying procedural complexity. The largest gains occur on the deeper Telecom and Smart Dispute workflows, where $\mathrm{Pass}^3$ increases by 7.5--55.0 and 57.2--65.7 percentage points, respectively, depending on the model. These results show that combining policy-scoped context with deterministic procedural control can improve the reliability of policy execution.

AI.tldr: Stage is an executable-graph framework for policy-governed agents that confines model judgment to policy-scoped nodes while placing procedural control in deterministic code. It improves task success and repeated-run reliability over monolithic full-policy execution across multiple benchmarks, with the largest gains on deeper workflows.
AI.motivation: Policy-governed agents need to interpret case evidence while following authorized procedures, but monolithic full-policy execution is less reliable, especially for complex or deep workflows.
AI.method: Stage uses an executable-graph architecture where the model operates only at policy-scoped nodes with task-relevant policy context and returns typed results, while a deterministic coordinator enforces the reviewed execution contract for procedural control.
AI.result: Evaluated on SOP-Bench Referral Abuse, two τ²-bench domains, and Smart Dispute. Stage generally improves task success and repeated-run reliability. Largest gains on deeper Telecom and Smart Dispute workflows, with Pass³ improving by 7.5-55.0 and 57.2-65.7 percentage points respectively depending on the model.
AI.conclusion: Combining policy-scoped context with deterministic procedural control improves the reliability of policy execution.

title: SymmAdapt: Symmetrical Flow Matching for Source-Free Domain Adaptation in Medical Image Segmentation
comment: Accepted at SASHIMI 2026, held in conjunction with MICCAI 2026. To appear in the Springer LNCS proceedings of the MICCAI 2026 Satellite Events
summary: Domain shift across imaging modalities and acquisition sites remains a significant barrier to the clinical deployment of segmentation models. Source-free unsupervised domain adaptation (SFUDA) addresses this by adapting a pretrained model to an unlabeled target domain without requiring access to sensitive source data. We introduce a novel SFUDA framework built on Symmetrical Flow Matching, a unified generative model that segments an input image and synthesizes a source-like image from a mask within the same learned flow.
