By initializing inference from a domain-agnostic Gaussian origin, the model preserves structural consistency across domains and grounds predictions in learned anatomy rather than shifted texture statistics. Our pipeline leverages this symmetry to generate reliable pseudo-labels and corresponding source-like synthetic images from unlabeled target data, creating a generative replay buffer that anchors source knowledge during a generative self-training stage that fine-tunes on a joint set of real target and synthetic source-like images. We evaluate on abdominal multi-organ and cardiac segmentation, covering cross-modality MRI<->CT shifts, and multi-site prostate segmentation. Our approach outperforms SFUDA baselines and is competitive with conventional UDA methods.

AI.tldr: A novel source-free unsupervised domain adaptation framework using Symmetrical Flow Matching to jointly segment images and synthesize source-like images, enabling generative self-training for cross-modality and multi-site medical image segmentation.
AI.motivation: Domain shift across imaging modalities and acquisition sites hinders clinical deployment of medical segmentation models. SFUDA is needed to adapt pretrained models to unlabeled target domains without accessing sensitive source data, but existing methods struggle with structural consistency across domains.
AI.method: A unified generative model based on Symmetrical Flow Matching that both segments input images and synthesizes source-like images from masks within the same learned flow. Inference is initialized from a domain-agnostic Gaussian origin to preserve structural consistency. The pipeline generates reliable pseudo-labels and source-like synthetic images from unlabeled target data, creating a generative replay buffer for generative self-training on a joint set of real target and synthetic source-like images.
AI.result: Evaluated on abdominal multi-organ and cardiac segmentation with cross-modality MRI<->CT shifts, plus multi-site prostate segmentation. The method outperforms SFUDA baselines and is competitive with conventional UDA methods.
AI.conclusion: Symmetrical Flow Matching with domain-agnostic initialization provides an effective SFUDA solution that grounds predictions in learned anatomy while using generative replay to anchor source knowledge, achieving state-of-the-art performance among SFUDA approaches.

title: HelaBERT: Enhancing Sinhala Language Understanding with Dual Pooling Classification Head
summary: We present HelaBERT, a family of two BERT-based masked language models pre-trained from scratch on approximately 1 billion tokens of Sinhala text sourced from MADLAD-400, CulturaX, and a custom corpus comprising news articles, Sinhala Wikipedia, and web crawl data. HelaBERT-Small (~23.3M parameters, 6 layers) and HelaBERT-Large (~110M parameters, 12 layers) both use a SentencePiece Unigram tokenizer (vocabulary size 32,000) tailored to Sinhala's agglutinative morphology and complex script. We evaluate both models on four downstream Sinhala text classification tasks: news category classification, news source classification, sentiment analysis, and writing style classification, using 5 independent seed runs with stratified 80/20 train/test splits. We additionally propose a dual pooling classification head and evaluate it systematically across all four tasks, finding consistent improvements on sentiment analysis and a moderate gain on news category classification for HelaBERT-Small, while the standard [CLS]-linear head remains competitive on news source classification, a headline-level task with short average input length. We release both models to support further research in Sinhala NLP.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces HelaBERT, two BERT-based masked language models (Small ~23.3M params/6 layers and Large ~110M params/12 layers) pre-trained from scratch on ~1B tokens of Sinhala text, using a SentencePiece Unigram tokenizer (vocab size 32,000) tailored to Sinhala's agglutinative morphology. The models are evaluated on four downstream text classification tasks, and a novel dual pooling classification head is proposed, showing consistent improvements on sentiment analysis and moderate gains on news category classification for HelaBERT-Small.
AI.motivation: To address the gap in Sinhala NLP resources by pre-training BERT-based language models from scratch on Sinhala text, and to explore architecture improvements (e.g., a dual pooling classification head) for downstream text classification in this under-resourced language.
AI.method: Two BERT-based masked language models (HelaBERT-Small and HelaBERT-Large) are pre-trained from scratch on ~1B Sinhala tokens from MADLAD-400, CulturaX, and a custom corpus. Both use a SentencePiece Unigram tokenizer with a 32,000 token vocabulary. Evaluation is performed on four downstream tasks (news category, news source, sentiment analysis, and writing style classification) using 5 independent seed runs with stratified 80/20 train/test splits. A dual pooling classification head is proposed and systematically compared against the standard [CLS]-linear head.
AI.result: The dual pooling classification head consistently improves sentiment analysis and provides moderate gains on news category classification for HelaBERT-Small, while the standard [CLS]-linear head remains competitive on news source classification (a headline-level task with short average input length).
AI.conclusion: HelaBERT models and the proposed dual pooling head are released to support further research in Sinhala NLP, demonstrating effective pre-trained language models and task-specific classification head improvements for this low-resource language.

title: Scaling Curriculum Learning For Autonomous Driving
comment: 31 pages, 18 figures. Under review at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Batched simulators for autonomous driving have recently enabled training reinforcement learning (RL) agents at scale, encompassing thousands of traffic scenarios and billions of interactions within a matter of days. Although such high-throughput feeds RL algorithms faster than ever, their sample-efficiency has not kept pace: As the standard training scheme, domain randomization uniformly samples scenarios, thereby consuming a vast number of interactions on cases that contribute little to learning. Curriculum learning offers a remedy by adaptively prioritizing scenarios that matter most to policy improvement. We present CL4AD, the first integration of curriculum learning into batched autonomous driving simulators by framing scenario selection as an unsupervised environment design problem. We introduce utility functions that shape curricula based on success rates and the realism of the agent's behavior, in addition to existing regret-estimation functions. Large-scale experiments in GPUDRIVE demonstrate that curriculum learning achieves a 99% success rate a billion steps earlier than domain randomization, reducing wall-clock time by 77%, and outperforms heuristic curricula with static and dynamic attributes, with only one exception at the largest scale. An ablation under limited compute shows that curriculum learning improves sample efficiency by 67%. We also investigate how utility functions behave at scale, and how prioritized scenarios evolve during training. We release an implementation of CLForAD in GPUDRIVE.

AI.tldr: CL4AD integrates curriculum learning into batched autonomous driving simulators by framing scenario selection as unsupervised environment design, achieving 99% success rate a billion steps earlier than domain randomization (77% less wall-clock time) and 67% sample efficiency gains under limited compute.
AI.motivation: While batched simulators (e.g., GPUDRIVE) enable large-scale RL training for autonomous driving, uniform scenario sampling (domain randomization) wastes vast numbers of interactions on low-information cases. Curriculum learning can adaptively prioritize scenarios most beneficial to policy improvement, yet it had not been integrated into batched autonomous driving simulators.
AI.method: The authors frame scenario selection as an unsupervised environment design problem and introduce utility functions that shape curricula based on (1) success rates, (2) realism of agent behavior, and (3) existing regret-estimation functions. This is implemented as CL4AD within the GPUDRIVE batched simulator.
AI.result: Large-scale experiments show curriculum learning reaches a 99% success rate a billion steps earlier than domain randomization, reducing wall-clock time by 77%. It outperforms heuristic curricula with static and dynamic attributes (except one case at the largest scale). An ablation under limited compute shows 67% sample efficiency improvement. Analysis of utility function behavior at scale and scenario evolution during training is provided.
AI.conclusion: Curriculum learning is an effective and scalable alternative to domain randomization in batched autonomous driving simulators, and the authors release CLForAD as an open-source implementation in GPUDRIVE.

title: Vision-Language Models for Occupational Physical Exposure Assessment: Estimating External Hand Forces in Manual Material Handling Tasks from RGB Video
summary: External hand forces are important inputs to biomechanical analyses of occupational physical exposure and injury risk, yet continuous force measurements during manual material handling (MMH) typically requires instrumented objects or specialized sensing. We evaluated a vision-language model (VLM)-based pipeline that combines task-specific textual cues, visual representations, and known box mass to estimate dynamic, triaxial, bilateral external hand forces from RGB video. Thirty-five healthy young adults performed five MMH tasks involving lifting, carrying, pushing, and pulling with box masses of 6, 9, and 12 kg. The pipeline used text-guided localization of participant and handled-object regions of interest (ROIs), pretrained vision-transformer feature extraction, and transformer-based temporal regression. Performance was evaluated using leave-one-subject-out validation across seven camera-view conditions (three single-view and four multi-view conditions) and four ROI strategies. Overall, root mean square error was ~4.7-5.6 N for the horizontal and mediolateral force components and ~10.6-11.0 N for the vertical component. Including the handled object as a second ROI generally improved force estimation, with some of the largest benefits under single-camera conditions, whereas pixel-level segmentation provided little additional improvement. Multi-camera capture provided the clearest benefit for peak-force estimation, particularly for the vertical component, whereas differences in overall frame-level error among camera configurations were comparatively modest. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of estimating continuous, bilateral, directional hand-force estimates from RGB video and known load mass without requiring sensors on the worker or handled objects as model inputs, supporting the development of more scalable occupational physical exposure and risk assessments.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a vision-language model (VLM)-based pipeline that estimates continuous, dynamic, triaxial bilateral external hand forces during manual material handling tasks from RGB video and known box mass, achieving RMSE of ~4.7-5.6 N for horizontal/mediolateral components and ~10.6-11.0 N for vertical components across 35 participants and five MMH tasks.
AI.motivation: External hand forces are critical for biomechanical analyses of occupational physical exposure and injury risk, but continuous force measurement during manual material handling typically requires instrumented objects or specialized sensing equipment, limiting scalability of workplace assessments.
AI.method: A VLM-based pipeline combining task-specific textual cues, visual representations, and known box mass. The pipeline uses text-guided localization of participant and handled-object ROIs, pretrained vision-transformer feature extraction, and transformer-based temporal regression. Evaluated with leave-one-subject-out validation across seven camera-view conditions and four ROI strategies on 35 healthy young adults performing five MMH tasks with 6, 9, and 12 kg box masses.
AI.result: Overall RMSE was ~4.7-5.6 N for horizontal and mediolateral force components and ~10.6-11.0 N for vertical components. Including the handled object as a second ROI improved force estimation, especially under single-camera conditions. Pixel-level segmentation provided little additional benefit. Multi-camera capture benefited peak-force estimation most, particularly for the vertical component, though frame-level errors among camera configurations were comparatively modest.
AI.conclusion: Continuous, bilateral, directional hand-force estimation from RGB video and known load mass is feasible without requiring sensors on workers or handled objects, supporting the development of more scalable occupational physical exposure and risk assessments.

title: What Proves You Wrong: Benchmarking Language Models on Falsifiable Research Ideation
comment: Equal contribution by Ziyue Wang, Aomufei Yuan and Yiran Yao. Corresponding authors: Tong Yang and Xu Sun
summary: Large language models are increasingly used to propose research ideas, yet the prevailing ways of judging such ideas supply no shared decision rule: free-form judging sways with style and position, and scoring against a later paper rewards recovery of one realized trajectory. We introduce a benchmark that carries a proposal from Literature to Test: the Lit2Test benchmark centers on a six-field contract organized around a falsifying outcome, so that every proposal precommits the observation that would prove it wrong, making its quality decidable in the first place rather than merely arguable. Built prospectively from 200 real-paper neighborhoods, Lit2Test elicits proposals from four frontier models and compares them through 1,200 pairwise comparisons judged blind in both presentation orders. The protocol audits its own reliability through diagnostic controls and bounded human calibration, with three annotators corroborating the conclusions within explicitly stated reliability bounds. Lit2Test recovers a strict ranking of the four models in all 10,000 bootstrap replicates, and the separation comes from the quality of the proposed tests and metrics rather than from surface fluency. We release the benchmark, construction pipeline, and audit artifacts for public use.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Lit2Test, a benchmark for evaluating research proposals from LLMs that ties each proposal to a precommitted falsifying outcome via a six-field contract, making proposal quality decidable rather than arguable. Built prospectively from 200 real-paper neighborhoods, it compares four frontier models through 1,200 blind pairwise comparisons with reliability auditing via diagnostic controls and bounded human calibration. Lit2Test recovers a strict model ranking across all 10,000 bootstrap replicates, with separation driven by test and metric quality rather than surface fluency.
AI.motivation: Current methods for judging LLM-proposed research ideas lack a shared decision rule: free-form judging is swayed by style and position, and scoring against realized papers rewards only one specific trajectory. This makes research proposal quality merely arguable rather than decidable.
AI.method: The Lit2Test benchmark centers on a six-field contract organized around a falsifying outcome, so every proposal precommits the observation that would prove it wrong. Built prospectively from 200 real-paper neighborhoods, it elicits proposals from four frontier models and compares them through 1,200 pairwise comparisons judged blind in both presentation orders. Reliability is audited through diagnostic controls and bounded human calibration, with three annotators corroborating conclusions within stated reliability bounds.
AI.result: Lit2Test recovers a strict ranking of the four models in all 10,000 bootstrap replicates, and the observed separation comes from the quality of proposed tests and metrics rather than surface fluency of the proposals.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark, construction pipeline, and audit artifacts are publicly released. Lit2Test provides a principled, reproducible way to evaluate research proposals from LLMs by making falsifiability the central contract.

title: ExecRubrics: Executable Tool-Augmented Rubrics for Verifiable and Efficient Long-Form Evaluation
summary: Rubrics aim to make language-model evaluation transparent by decomposing response quality into interpretable criteria. However, natural-language rubrics are often ambiguous, require black-box LLM judges, and typically assume criteria aggregate independently through linear weighted sums, limiting their ability to capture dependencies, alternatives, penalties, and override conditions. We propose ExecRubrics, a framework for representing rubrics as compact executable programs. ExecRubrics encodes evaluation logic as verifiable Python scoring functions, giving natural-language rubric intent an operational semantics: a fixed decision procedure that can be inspected, executed, and edited. On three long-form response benchmarks-HealthBench, HelpSteer, and ArgQuality-we show that ExecRubrics can substitute for expensive black-box judges in ranking preferred over dispreferred responses, matching or improving NL rubric baselines with best preference accuracies of 53%, 78%, and 92%, respectively, while reducing evaluation latency by up to 320 times. We show that incorporating external logic and resources from text processing libraries such as NLTK and spaCy further improves preference accuracy. Our results suggest a novel way of looking at evaluation, by offering a faster, more explainable, and less ambiguous alternative to black-box rubric evaluation, particularly in high-stakes domains such as healthcare and banking where precision and auditability are critical.

AI.tldr: ExecRubrics represents evaluation rubrics as compact executable Python programs instead of natural-language descriptions, providing an operational semantics that can be inspected, executed, and edited. On three long-form response benchmarks (HealthBench, HelpSteer, ArgQuality), it matches or improves NL rubric baselines with preference accuracies of 53%, 78%, and 92% respectively, while reducing evaluation latency by up to 320x.
AI.motivation: Natural-language rubrics suffer from ambiguity, require expensive black-box LLM judges, and typically assume criteria aggregate independently through linear weighted sums—limiting their ability to capture dependencies, alternatives, penalties, and override conditions in evaluation.
AI.method: ExecRubrics encodes evaluation logic as verifiable Python scoring functions, translating natural-language rubric intent into a fixed decision procedure (operational semantics) that can be inspected, executed, and edited. The framework leverages text processing libraries such as NLTK and spaCy to incorporate external logic and resources.
AI.result: On HealthBench, HelpSteer, and ArgQuality, ExecRubrics achieves best preference accuracies of 53%, 78%, and 92%, respectively, matching or improving NL rubric baselines while reducing evaluation latency by up to 320 times. Incorporating external text-processing resources further improves preference accuracy.
AI.conclusion: ExecRubrics offers a faster, more explainable, and less ambiguous alternative to black-box rubric evaluation, particularly valuable in high-stakes domains such as healthcare and banking where precision and auditability are critical.

title: AI-based worker guidance in assembly and disassembly operations using multimodal ego/exo-centric data capture and structured task knowledge
comment: 5 pages. Published in CIRP Annals - Manufacturing Technology
summary: Assembly and disassembly processes rely on expert knowledge that is difficult to document, reuse, and transfer. This paper presents a data-centric approach for extracting structured task knowledge from expert demonstrations using egocentric and exocentric recordings. Temporal and multimodal information from video and narration is jointly encoded to derive structured task representations that enable procedural documentation and context-aware worker guidance. The approach is evaluated on a real-world disassembly case study, demonstrating that video-based representations capture procedural structure and execution context beyond static image-based methods. The results highlight the potential of egocentric video understanding for repair, training, and circular manufacturing applications. Project website: https://indego-assistant.github.io/

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a data-centric approach to extract structured task knowledge from expert demonstrations using both egocentric and exocentric video recordings. Temporal and multimodal information from video and narration are jointly encoded to derive structured task representations for procedural documentation and context-aware worker guidance, evaluated on a real-world disassembly case study.
AI.motivation: Assembly and disassembly processes rely on expert knowledge that is difficult to document, reuse, and transfer, creating a need for automated ways to capture and structure this knowledge from demonstrations.
AI.method: The approach jointly encodes temporal and multimodal information from egocentric/exocentric video recordings combined with narration to derive structured task representations.
AI.result: Evaluation on a real-world disassembly case study demonstrates that video-based representations capture procedural structure and execution context beyond what static image-based methods achieve.
AI.conclusion: The results highlight the potential of egocentric video understanding for applications in repair, training, and circular manufacturing.

title: The Illusion of Control: Why Bare Classifier Inversion Silently Fails in Concept-Bottleneck Text Generation
summary: Concept-bottleneck controllable generation routes multi-attribute control through a low-dimensional concept code that, at deployment, must be synthesised from a target attribute configuration. We study this problem in concept-bottleneck text generation under multi-axis compositional generalisation, comparing three ways to obtain the inference-time code: classifier inversion against the encoder heads, reference-text encoding, and a post-hoc label-conditioned prior. Since a concept code admits no direct LM-fluency term, regularising inversion must instead constrain the code toward the encoder's training distribution. We therefore test bare inversion and three regularised variants: label-agnostic and label-conditioned Mahalanobis penalties, and a conditional normalising-flow density baseline. Every inversion variant we test underperforms a simple post-hoc prior fitted to per-combination encoder means on the same checkpoints, across three backbone families spanning $124$M to $8$B parameters. The bare form of classifier inversion also silently collapses to chance, traceable to a directly measured off-manifold code. We validate this diagnosis on real-world benchmarks and under external evaluators, enabling fair comparison with published baselines.

AI.tldr: This paper studies concept-bottleneck controllable text generation under multi-axis compositional generalization, comparing three ways to obtain inference-time concept codes: classifier inversion, reference-text encoding, and a post-hoc label-conditioned prior. The study finds that all classifier inversion variants underperform a simple post-hoc prior fitted to per-combination encoder means across three backbone families (124M to 8B parameters). Bare classifier inversion silently collapses to chance due to off-manifold codes, a diagnosis validated on real-world benchmarks.
AI.motivation: In concept-bottleneck controllable generation, a low-dimensional concept code must be synthesized from a target attribute configuration at deployment time. Since the concept code admits no direct LM-fluency term, regularizing inversion must instead constrain the code toward the encoder's training distribution. The paper aims to systematically study how to obtain inference-time codes under multi-axis compositional generalization.
AI.method: The paper compares three approaches for obtaining inference-time concept codes: (1) classifier inversion against encoder heads, including bare inversion and three regularized variants (label-agnostic Mahalanobis penalty, label-conditioned Mahalanobis penalty, and a conditional normalizing-flow density baseline); (2) reference-text encoding; and (3) a post-hoc label-conditioned prior fitted to per-combination encoder means. Experiments span three backbone families from 124M to 8B parameters.
AI.result: Every classifier inversion variant underperforms the simple post-hoc prior fitted to per-combination encoder means on the same checkpoints, across all three backbone families. Bare classifier inversion silently collapses to chance, a failure traceable to a directly measured off-manifold code. The diagnosis is validated on real-world benchmarks and under external evaluators, enabling fair comparison with published baselines.
AI.conclusion: Classifier inversion is consistently inferior to a simple post-hoc prior for concept-code synthesis in concept-bottleneck controllable text generation. Bare inversion collapses due to off-manifold codes, and even with regularization it cannot match the prior-based approach, highlighting the difficulty of constraining inversion toward the encoder's training distribution without a direct fluency term.

title: CausalCache: Conditional High-Fidelity Restoration for Long-Horizon GUI Agents
summary: Long-horizon GUI agents can retain complete action histories as compact text, but only a few historical screenshots fit in active context. We formulate this as budgeted fidelity restoration: every event remains summarized, while a fixed budget $B$ determines which events regain their archived screenshots. Recent-$B$ assigns all visual slots to the latest events. CausalCache instead scores the complete history and swaps in an older event only when its predicted utility exceeds that of a recent event. A history-gated key/value adapter modifies only restored history-image tokens and is exactly bypassed when no history image is active, preserving current-screen processing. The adapter and selector are trained with matched-budget interventions on desktop trajectories and evaluated zero-shot on mobile. On OSWorld-Verified, activating historical screenshots improves success by about $13$ percentage points over summary-only memory. Under the official $15$-step limit, CausalCache and Recent-$4$ are statistically indistinguishable; in a $30$-step diagnostic, CausalCache achieves $46.7\%$ success versus $42.4\%$ ($+4.3$ points). Zero-shot on $117$ MobileWorld tasks, CausalCache improves over Recent-$4$ from $30.2\%$ to $36.8\%$. The gain is concentrated on a pre-defined cross-app memory-candidate split ($30.6\%$ vs. $19.4\%$, $+11.2$ points), while single-app controls show no detectable difference ($43.6\%$ vs. $42.4\%$). These results show that selecting which past events regain pixels is more effective than spending a fixed visual budget entirely on recency.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses long-horizon GUI agent memory by proposing budgeted fidelity restoration: all events are summarized as text, but a fixed budget B determines which events regain their archived screenshots. The CausalCache method scores the full history and swaps in older events when their predicted utility exceeds recent ones, using a history-gated key/value adapter. On OSWorld-Verified, this improves success by ~13 points over summary-only memory; on a 30-step diagnostic, CausalCache achieves 46.7% vs. 42.4% for Recent-4, and zero-shot on 117 MobileWorld tasks improves from 30.2% to 36.8%, with gains concentrated on cross-app memory-candidate splits.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon GUI agents can retain full action histories as compact text, but only a few historical screenshots fit in active context due to context window limits. The key question is how to spend a fixed visual budget—entirely on recency, or by intelligently selecting which past events deserve pixel-level fidelity.
AI.method: The paper formulates budgeted fidelity restoration where every event is text-summarized while a fixed budget B decides which events regain screenshots. Recent-B allocates all visual slots to the most recent events. CausalCache scores the entire history and swaps in an older event when its predicted utility exceeds a recent event's. A history-gated key/value adapter modifies only restored history-image tokens and is exactly bypassed when no history image is active, preserving current-screen processing. The adapter and selector are trained with matched-budget interventions on desktop trajectories and evaluated zero-shot on mobile.
AI.result: On OSWorld-Verified, activating historical screenshots improves success by ~13 percentage points over summary-only memory. Under the official 15-step limit, CausalCache and Recent-4 are statistically indistinguishable; in a 30-step diagnostic, CausalCache achieves 46.7% vs. 42.4% (+4.3 points). Zero-shot on 117 MobileWorld tasks, CausalCache improves over Recent-4 from 30.2% to 36.8%. Gains concentrate on a cross-app memory-candidate split (30.6% vs. 19.4%, +11.2 points), while single-app controls show no detectable difference (43.6% vs. 42.4%).
AI.conclusion: Selecting which past events regain pixels is more effective than spending a fixed visual budget entirely on recency, particularly for cross-app memory-candidate scenarios. CausalCache demonstrates that utility-based historical screenshot selection improves long-horizon GUI agent performance without degrading current-screen processing.

title: OmniCAD: A Large-Scale Benchmark for 3D Spatial Reasoning in Robotics Assemblies
summary: Recent vision-language models (VLMs) show strong capabilities in robotic perception and spatial reasoning, yet their ability to reason about complex mechanical assemblies remains underexplored. We introduce OmniCAD, a large-scale benchmark for assembly-aware 3D spatial reasoning across diverse industrial systems, including robotic mechanisms, automotive components, aerospace structures, and agricultural machinery. OmniCAD contains 25k mechanical assemblies, with an average of 12 parts per assembly and 21 types of mate relationships. Each assembly includes a human-verified ground-truth 3D model and renderings from 20 viewpoints. The benchmark evaluates three capabilities: (1) component-level 3D spatial reasoning, requiring prediction of part positions and orientations; (2) part-to-part relational reasoning, requiring identification of mating relationships and assembly constraints; and (3) tool-augmented agentic reasoning, where models iteratively select viewpoints, inspect visual evidence, and refine predictions. Experiments show that current VLMs struggle with industrial assembly reasoning, often producing inaccurate poses, invalid mating relationships, part interpenetration, and degraded performance as assembly complexity increases. We will open-source the benchmark, evaluation code, and tool interfaces to support research on accurate, physically valid, and scalable 3D assembly reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces OmniCAD, a large-scale benchmark with 25k mechanical assemblies (avg. 12 parts, 21 mate relationship types) for evaluating vision-language models on assembly-aware 3D spatial reasoning across industrial domains. It assesses three capabilities—component-level spatial reasoning, part-to-part relational reasoning, and tool-augmented agentic reasoning—and finds current VLMs struggle with industrial assembly reasoning, producing inaccurate poses, invalid mating relationships, and part interpenetration that worsen with assembly complexity.
AI.motivation: While vision-language models demonstrate strong robotic perception and spatial reasoning capabilities, their ability to reason about complex mechanical assemblies—a critical skill for real-world industrial applications—remains largely unexplored. This gap motivates the need for a comprehensive benchmark to systematically evaluate and drive progress in this area.
AI.method: The paper constructs OmniCAD, a benchmark containing 25k mechanical assemblies spanning robotic mechanisms, automotive components, aerospace structures, and agricultural machinery. Each assembly has an average of 12 parts, 21 types of mate relationships, human-verified ground-truth 3D models, and renderings from 20 viewpoints. The benchmark evaluates three capability levels: (1) component-level 3D spatial reasoning (predicting part positions and orientations), (2) part-to-part relational reasoning (identifying mating relationships and assembly constraints), and (3) tool-augmented agentic reasoning (iterative viewpoint selection, visual evidence inspection, and prediction refinement).
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that current VLMs perform poorly on industrial assembly reasoning tasks. They frequently produce inaccurate part poses, invalid mating relationships, and part interpenetration. Performance further degrades as assembly complexity increases.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark and its open-sourced evaluation code and tool interfaces will support future research toward accurate, physically valid, and scalable 3D assembly reasoning in VLMs.

title: Closed-Loop Bayesian Molecular Inverse Design with Semantic LLM Surrogates
summary: Practical molecular inverse design is rarely a one-shot generation problem; it often takes the form of closed-loop candidate-pool enrichment, where under a limited oracle budget the goal is to \emph{increase the fraction of generated molecules that match a desired property profile}. Bayesian optimization (BO) offers a natural framework for this setting, yet standard Gaussian-process surrogates typically operate in compressed continuous embeddings, which discard the substructural and reference-similarity signals that chemists naturally use to decide where to look next. We propose \textbf{\method}, a closed-loop framework in which the surrogate, rather than the generator, is treated as the locus of design choice, and instantiate it with a frozen large language model that reasons directly over the task instruction, SMILES-level optimization history, and oracle feedback in their native textual form. At each iteration, the surrogate returns a structured decision signal that selects informative reference molecules under an exploration and exploitation principle, optionally with a concise guidance sentence. This signal is converted into next-round conditioning text for a frozen molecular generator, yielding an inspectable optimization trace in natural language. Experiments on MolQA drug and material design tasks show that \method improves over one-shot prompting, is competitive with or stronger than GP-based BO baselines, and reveals a domain-dependent interface: reference-only transfer works best for binary drug targets, while adding a concise surrogate summary is more beneficial for continuous material

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a closed-loop molecular inverse design framework called \method, where a frozen large language model serves as the surrogate that reasons directly over task instructions, SMILES optimization history, and oracle feedback in native textual form, outputting structured decision signals (reference molecule selection under exploration-exploitation, optionally with guidance sentences) that condition a frozen molecular generator for next-round candidate generation. Experiments on MolQA drug and material design tasks show it improves over one-shot prompting, matches or beats GP-based BO baselines, and reveals domain-dependent transfer interfaces.
AI.motivation: Standard Bayesian optimization surrogates operate in compressed continuous embeddings that discard the substructural and reference-similarity signals chemists naturally use to guide exploration. Practical molecular inverse design is an iterative candidate-pool enrichment problem under limited oracle budget, yet existing one-shot or embedding-based approaches fail to leverage rich textual chemical reasoning present in optimization history and oracle feedback.
AI.method: A closed-loop framework where the surrogate (not the generator) is the locus of design choice. It is instantiated with a frozen LLM that reasons over task instruction, SMILES-level history, and oracle feedback in native text. Each iteration, the surrogate outputs a structured decision signal: selected informative reference molecules under exploration/exploitation, optionally with a concise guidance sentence. This signal becomes conditioning text for a frozen molecular generator, producing an inspectable natural-language optimization trace.
AI.result: On MolQA drug and material design tasks, \method improves over one-shot prompting, is competitive with or stronger than GP-based BO baselines. It also reveals a domain-dependent interface: reference-only transfer works best for binary drug targets, while adding a concise surrogate summary is more beneficial for continuous material property optimization.
AI.conclusion: Treating the surrogate as the design choice and leveraging a frozen LLM to reason over native textual optimization history provides an effective, inspectable alternative to embedding-based BO for closed-loop molecular inverse design, with performance varying by task domain and interface type.

title: Weakly supervised concept Bottleneck Learning for Robust Two stage Object centric visual reasoning
summary: Two-stage neuro-symbolic architectures provide an elegant paradigm for visual problem solving by cleanly separating connectionist perception of predefined symbols from possibly later defined relational reasoning thereon. However, anchoring high-level predicates into visual frames typically necessitates annotations that are expensive to acquire. In this work, we introduce the Dynamic Orthogonal Concept Bottleneck (D-OCB), an object-centric slot- VAE framework designed to extract human-aligned symbolic predicates under extremely weak supervision. D-OCB eliminates the arduous manual tuning of loss-balancing coef- ficients by dynamically learning optimal hyperparameter allocations during training. To infuse prior knowledge on independence of concept categories, in addition to standard re- construction self-supervision we penalize correlation across concept subspaces. Crucially, to combat the instability of very low supervision regimes, D-OCB incorporates a dynamic di- mensionality allocation mechanism; this adaptive formulation allows well-represented con- cepts to yield latent dimensions to underperforming concepts that are lagging behind, effectively preventing representation collapse and significantly improving overall concept accuracy. Through an extensive empirical evaluation, we demonstrate that our framework achieves high concept alignment and downstream visual reasoning accuracy using minimal label budgets, matching or outperforming end-to-end paradigms.

AI.tldr: Introduces D-OCB, an object-centric slot-VAE framework that extracts human-aligned symbolic predicates under extremely weak supervision using dynamic hyperparameter learning, concept subspace decorrelation, and adaptive dimensionality allocation to prevent representation collapse.
AI.motivation: Two-stage neuro-symbolic architectures separate perception from reasoning, but anchoring high-level predicates into visual frames requires expensive annotations. Existing methods need manual tuning of loss-balancing coefficients and suffer from instability under very low supervision.
AI.method: D-OCB is an object-centric slot-VAE that (1) dynamically learns optimal hyperparameter allocations during training to eliminate manual coefficient tuning, (2) penalizes correlation across concept subspaces to enforce independence prior, and (3) uses a dynamic dimensionality allocation mechanism that transfers latent dimensions from well-represented concepts to lagging ones, preventing representation collapse.
AI.result: Extensive empirical evaluation shows D-OCB achieves high concept alignment and downstream visual reasoning accuracy with minimal label budgets, matching or outperforming end-to-end paradigms.
AI.conclusion: D-OCB provides an effective solution for extracting symbolic predicates from vision under extremely weak supervision, eliminating manual tuning while improving robustness and concept accuracy without sacrificing downstream reasoning performance.

title: Multiple View Neural Regression of a Facial Shape Model
summary:
Creating re-topologized 3D facial meshes is essential for high-quality facial animation but remains labor-intensive and time-consuming. This dissertation explores more efficient approaches for capturing production-ready facial meshes through: (1) the development of VarIS, a custom light sphere for capturing high-resolution stereo geometry and reflectance maps; (2) analysis of camera parameters affecting automatic 2D and 3D landmarking; (3) synthetic-data methods for training neural face regression; and (4) techniques for improving neural multi-view face-shape regression.
  While VarIS enables photorealistic face capture, its operational and processing costs motivate a more scalable approach. A deep learning framework is therefore proposed to directly predict re-topologized facial meshes from synthetic multiview images generated with Visage Craft, an in-house physically based rendering system using an Appearance 3D Morphable Model (A3DMM). The system produces standardized meshes ready for rigging and animation with minimal human supervision. Results show that incorporating accurate camera intrinsics and extrinsics improves landmark accuracy and geometric consistency, while 3D landmark regularization further improves reconstruction quality.

AI.tldr: This dissertation presents a scalable deep learning framework for automatically generating production-ready, re-topologized 3D facial meshes from synthetic multi-view images. It combines VarIS (a custom light sphere for photorealistic capture), analysis of camera parameters for landmarking, and neural face-shape regression trained on synthetic data from an Appearance 3D Morphable Model rendered via Visage Craft. Incorporating accurate camera intrinsics/extrinsics and 3D landmark regularization improves reconstruction quality.
AI.motivation: Traditional re-topologized 3D facial mesh creation is labor-intensive and time-consuming, making it impractical for high-volume production needs. The goal is to reduce human supervision and cost while maintaining production-ready quality.
AI.method: The approach combines: (1) VarIS, a custom light sphere capturing high-resolution stereo geometry and reflectance maps; (2) analysis of camera parameters affecting 2D/3D landmarking; (3) synthetic-data generation using Visage Craft, an in-house physically based renderer with an Appearance 3D Morphable Model (A3DMM); and (4) a deep learning framework for direct prediction of re-topologized meshes from synthetic multiview images, incorporating camera intrinsics/extrinsics and 3D landmark regularization.
AI.result: The framework produces standardized meshes ready for rigging and animation with minimal human supervision. Accurate camera intrinsics and extrinsics improve landmark accuracy and geometric consistency, and 3D landmark regularization further enhances reconstruction quality. VarIS enables photorealistic capture but has high operational and processing costs that motivated the scalable deep learning approach.
AI.conclusion: A deep learning-based pipeline trained on physically rendered synthetic multiview data can effectively replace costly photorealistic capture systems for producing production-ready re-topologized facial meshes, with camera parameter accuracy and 3D landmark regularization serving as key quality levers.

title: What Does Activation Steering Control? Attribution Across Answer Encodings and Output-Sensitive Subspaces
summary: Activation steering is often evaluated under the answer encoding used to construct the direction. A reported gain may reflect the intended judgment or compatibility with answer identifiers seen during construction. We introduce Cross-Encoding Steering Evaluation, which freezes an intervention while re-encoding answers to the same held-out items. On NormBank, after A/B/C identifiers are reassigned, contrastive activation addition (CAA) induces larger target-versus-source score changes for the extraction indices than for the semantic labels under the new mapping. We call this extraction-index following. Varying identifier vocabulary (A/B/C, X/Y/Z, or 1/2/3) and row order shows that the effect tracks extraction index rather than row position. After matching direction norms across layers, extraction-index following emerges mainly at later depths. A low-rank output-sensitive component containing 15.4% of the direction's squared norm retains 96.3% of this effect. An Inference-Time Intervention (ITI)-style method also favors extraction-index over semantic-label following on NormBank in three models. In aggregate, MNLI favors extraction-index following, whereas Social Chemistry 101 (SC101) favors semantic-label following. Multiple-choice and open-ended evaluations can yield different behavioral conclusions. Thus, a steering gain under one answer encoding does not by itself identify what the intervention controls.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that activation steering evaluations can be misleading: a steering direction may track answer extraction indices (e.g., A/B/C positions) rather than the semantic labels they encode. The authors introduce Cross-Encoding Steering Evaluation to detect this, showing that extraction-index following dominates under CAA and ITI on NormBank and MNLI, while SC101 favors semantic-label following.
AI.motivation: Activation steering gains are typically evaluated under the same answer encoding used to construct the steering direction. This conflates genuine judgment control with mere compatibility with answer identifiers (e.g., A/B/C tokens) seen during construction, making it unclear what the intervention actually controls.
AI.method: The authors freeze the intervention while re-encoding answers to the same held-out items, reassigning identifiers (A/B/C to X/Y/Z or 1/2/3) and varying row order. They measure whether score changes track extraction indices or semantic labels. They also analyze direction norms across layers, identify low-rank output-sensitive components, and test both CAA and ITI-style methods across multiple models and benchmarks (NormBank, MNLI, SC101), including multiple-choice and open-ended settings.
AI.result: CAA on NormBank induces extraction-index following rather than semantic-label following. The effect tracks extraction index rather than row position, emerges mainly at later depths after layer-wise direction norm matching, and a low-rank component containing 15.4% of squared norm retains 96.3% of the effect. ITI-style methods also favor extraction-index following on NormBank. MNLI favors extraction-index following, while SC101 favors semantic-label following. Multiple-choice and open-ended evaluations yield different behavioral conclusions.
AI.conclusion: A steering gain under one answer encoding does not by itself identify what the intervention controls. Evaluations must cross-check across answer encodings to distinguish between genuine semantic control and spurious extraction-index following.

title: Coalition-Aware Skill Reliability for Self-Evolving Agents
summary: Agent skills, structured artifacts distilled from interaction trajectories and dynamically reused from skill banks, have become a central mechanism for enabling large language model (LLM)-based self-evolving agents to learn from past experience. Yet existing work has largely focused on the operational aspects of skills, such as acquisition, evolution, and retrieval, while leaving a more fundamental reliability question unresolved: Do accumulated skills in an agent's skill bank actually make positive mechanistic contributions? We investigate this question through systematic skill-bank audits across alternative bank compositions and deployment domains, measuring the resulting changes in agent behavior. These audits reveal two recurring reliability failures: coalition pollution, where bank-level gains conceal negative coalition-level skill contributions, and cross-domain utility reversal, where source-beneficial skills reverse their effects after transfer. These findings motivate two reliability interventions: coalition-aware skill selection during skill accumulation and label-free skill masking after transfer. Coalition-Aware Skill Selection (CASS) selects more reliable candidate skills for the current bank using sampled Shapley marginals. Unsupervised Skill-Masked Coalition Optimizer (u-SMCO) masks transferred skills whose exclusion improves retrieval quality on unlabeled target-domain data. Agentic experiments on LoCoMo, LongMemEval, HotpotQA, and ALFWorld show that CASS and u-SMCO consistently improve task performance and cross-domain generalization over strong skill-based self-evolving agent baselines. Beyond accuracy, coalition-conditioned reliability modeling reduces sensitivity to noisy outcome-reward fluctuations during reinforcement learning and exposes the limits of isolation-based skill evaluation.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether accumulated skills in LLM-based self-evolving agents' skill banks make positive mechanistic contributions, revealing two reliability failures (coalition pollution and cross-domain utility reversal) and proposing two interventions (CASS and u-SMCO) that consistently improve task performance and cross-domain generalization.
AI.motivation: Existing work on agent skills focuses on operational aspects (acquisition, evolution, retrieval) but leaves the fundamental reliability question unresolved: do accumulated skills actually make positive mechanistic contributions to agent behavior? This paper systematically audits skill banks to answer this question.
AI.method: The paper conducts systematic skill-bank audits across alternative bank compositions and deployment domains, measuring behavioral changes. It proposes two interventions: (1) Coalition-Aware Skill Selection (CASS) using sampled Shapley marginals for reliable candidate skill selection during accumulation, and (2) Unsupervised Skill-Masked Coalition Optimizer (u-SMCO) which masks transferred skills whose exclusion improves retrieval quality on unlabeled target-domain data.
AI.result: Experiments on LoCoMo, LongMemEval, HotpotQA, and ALFWorld show that CASS and u-SMCO consistently improve task performance and cross-domain generalization over strong skill-based self-evolving agent baselines. Additionally, coalition-conditioned reliability modeling reduces sensitivity to noisy outcome-reward fluctuations during RL and exposes limits of isolation-based skill evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Skill bank reliability is not guaranteed by operational effectiveness alone; coalition effects and cross-domain transfer can cause skills to be harmful despite appearing beneficial. Coalition-aware selection and masking provide practical fixes, and reliability must be assessed coalition-conditionally rather than in isolation.

title: Hyperbolic Hierarchical Clustering for Visual Representation Learning
summary: We investigate the token mixer in vision backbones by revisiting clustering, one of the most classic approaches in machine learning. An effective token mixer is a fundamental component of modern vision backbones like vision Transformers, facilitating information exchange between image patches. Mainstream token mixers, which rely on convolution, attention, MLP, or their hybrids, primarily focus on navigating the trade-off between accuracy and computational cost. However, a significant drawback of these methods is their black-box nature; their encoding process is opaque and lacks interpretability. Diverging from these opaque designs, we introduce ClusterMixer, a transparent token mixer that is grounded in a clustering paradigm and interpretable by design. ClusterMixer explicitly formulates the token mixing process through a hierarchical clustering mechanism. To model the natural, tree-like relationships inherent in visual data, the clustering is performed in hyperbolic space, which is well-suited for embedding hierarchies with low distortion. Building on this innovation, we present HCFormer, a new backbone architecture that integrates ClusterMixer with a series of meticulously designed clustering strategies to ensure robust performance across tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HCFormer consistently outperforms its counterparts across diverse tasks, including image classification, object detection, instance segmentation, and semantic segmentation. Considering its transparency and efficacy, we hope HCFormer can facilitate a paradigm shift toward interpretable backbones.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ClusterMixer, a transparent token mixer grounded in hierarchical clustering in hyperbolic space, and HCFormer, a new vision backbone architecture built on it. HCFormer outperforms counterparts across image classification, object detection, instance segmentation, and semantic segmentation while being interpretable by design, in contrast to opaque convolution/attention/MLP-based token mixers.
AI.motivation: Mainstream token mixers (convolution, attention, MLP, or hybrids) are black-box and lack interpretability in their encoding processes. The authors aim to address this gap by revisiting clustering—a classic machine learning approach—to design a token mixer that is both effective and inherently interpretable.
AI.method: ClusterMixer explicitly formulates the token mixing process through a hierarchical clustering mechanism performed in hyperbolic space, which is well-suited for embedding the natural tree-like hierarchical relationships in visual data with low distortion. This mixer is integrated into a new backbone called HCFormer, which includes a series of meticulously designed clustering strategies to ensure robust performance across tasks.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that HCFormer consistently outperforms its counterparts across diverse tasks, including image classification, object detection, instance segmentation, and semantic segmentation.
AI.conclusion: By combining transparency with efficacy, the authors hope HCFormer can facilitate a paradigm shift toward interpretable vision backbones, proving that interpretability does not have to come at the cost of performance.

title: LLM Pedagogical Behavior in AI Tutoring Interactions
summary: Students increasingly use LLMs as tutors for coursework and problem solving. Little is known about the level of assistance LLMs provide when students use them as tutors in authentic learning interactions. This matters because tutoring responses can differ substantially in how directly they help students complete a task. We operationalize this dimension as scaffolding level and develop a five-level scale, validated against human annotations, that characterizes responses according to the degree of direct assistance they provide. We apply the scale to 14,637 LLM responses from 203 students in a university AI course. Responses are overwhelmingly concentrated at high levels of assistance, with more than 95% classified as either Explaining or Solving. Scaffolding level is systematically associated with students' subsequent conversational behavior, but provides little additional predictive information about performance on three subsequent exams beyond prior achievement and dialogue behavior. These findings provide an empirical baseline for LLM assistance in tutoring interactions and a measurement framework for evaluating how alternative tutoring designs change that assistance.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a five-level scaffolding scale to measure how directly LLM tutors assist students, applies it to 14,637 responses from 203 students in a university AI course, and finds that over 95% of responses are at high assistance levels (Explaining or Solving). Scaffolding level correlates with subsequent dialogue behavior but adds little predictive value for exam performance beyond prior achievement and dialogue behavior.
AI.motivation: Students increasingly use LLMs as tutors, but little is known about the level of assistance LLMs provide in authentic learning interactions. Since tutoring responses can vary substantially in how directly they help students, understanding this dimension is crucial for evaluating educational outcomes.
AI.method: The authors operationalize assistance directness as "scaffolding level" and develop a five-level scale validated against human annotations. They apply the scale to 14,637 LLM responses collected from 203 students in a university AI course and analyze relationships between scaffolding levels, subsequent conversational behavior, and exam performance.
AI.result: Responses are overwhelmingly concentrated at high assistance levels, with more than 95% classified as either Explaining or Solving. Scaffolding level is systematically associated with students' subsequent conversational behavior, but provides little additional predictive information about exam performance beyond prior achievement and dialogue behavior.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide an empirical baseline for LLM assistance in tutoring interactions and offer a measurement framework for evaluating how alternative tutoring designs might change the level of assistance provided to students.

title: DeepSAGE: Stage-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Structured CBT Counseling Dialogue
summary: Large Language Model (LLM)-based counseling agents can generate fluent and supportive responses, but they often lack the structured, goal-directed progression required to conduct a coherent therapeutic session. We present DeepSAGE (Strategic AI Guidance Engine), a hybrid LLM--Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) framework for stage-aware counseling dialogue grounded in the first session of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT). DeepSAGE represents the session as eleven stages with explicit therapeutic objectives, with an external controller determines stage completion and the DRL model selects therapeutic intentions that guide LLM response generation. We evaluate DeepSAGE against six retrieval-, prompting-, stage-, and policy-based alternatives. DeepSAGE elicits higher simulated client engagement and openness and achieves the strongest balance of stage-goal completion and dialogue efficiency among stage-structured systems. Domain expert review further indicates that the generated conversations exhibit broadly plausible emotional trajectories and recognizable CBT processes. Because the evaluation relies primarily on simulated clients and model-based metrics, these findings demonstrate comparative dialogue-control improvements rather than clinical effectiveness. These results suggest that combining stage-structured dialogue with learned strategy selection is a promising approach for AI counseling, though clinical effectiveness, safety, and real-world utility require further human evaluation.

AI.tldr: DeepSAGE is a hybrid LLM-Deep Reinforcement Learning framework for stage-aware counseling dialogue grounded in the first CBT session, representing therapy as eleven stages with explicit objectives. An external controller detects stage completion while a DRL model selects therapeutic intentions to guide LLM response generation. It outperforms six alternatives in simulated client engagement, openness, and balance of stage-goal completion versus dialogue efficiency, though clinical effectiveness requires further human evaluation.
AI.motivation: LLM-based counseling agents can produce fluent, supportive responses but lack the structured, goal-directed progression necessary for coherent therapeutic sessions, motivating the need for a framework that enforces therapeutic structure while maintaining generative flexibility.
AI.method: DeepSAGE combines an LLM for response generation with a Deep Reinforcement Learning controller within a hybrid framework. The CBT first session is modeled as eleven discrete stages with explicit therapeutic objectives. An external controller identifies stage completion, and the DRL model selects the therapeutic intentions that steer the LLM's response generation at each turn.
AI.result: DeepSAGE was evaluated against six retrieval-, prompting-, stage-, and policy-based alternatives. It elicited higher simulated client engagement and openness, achieved the strongest balance of stage-goal completion and dialogue efficiency among stage-structured systems, and domain expert review found broadly plausible emotional trajectories and recognizable CBT processes in generated conversations.
AI.conclusion: Combining stage-structured dialogue with learned strategy selection is a promising approach for AI counseling. However, since evaluation relied primarily on simulated clients and model-based metrics, results demonstrate comparative dialogue-control improvements rather than clinical effectiveness. Clinical effectiveness, safety, and real-world utility require further human evaluation.

title: Unlearning Is Not Just Erasing: Temporal Decoupling via Generation Inequality
summary: Large language models (LLMs) require effective unlearning to address privacy regulations and safety concerns. However, achieving precise forgetting without compromising general utility remains challenging. Existing sequence- and token-level methods penalize target outputs without modeling their context-dependent retrieval paths, which can disrupt linguistic structure or suppress benign knowledge. We present ADU, a fine-grained, training-based framework that shifts unlearning from token erasure to contextual attention-pathway decoupling. Exploiting the functional distinction between local and global attention heads, ADU identifies preplan positions that retrieve persistent sensitive anchors and fixes their candidate paths under the original model. It then trains attention-projection adapters to suppress attention mass along these paths while preserving local-attention structure and retain-set language modeling. Post-training activation exchange tests whether the modified attention-output module transmits the learned forgetting effect. ADU achieves the strongest aggregate performance among evaluated baselines on the TOFU and WMDP benchmarks, including a Forget Quality of (0.93) on TOFU. It preserves 87--98% of model utility (92.9% on average versus 81.9% for baselines) while reducing side effects in benign contexts.

AI.tldr: ADU is a fine-grained, training-based framework for LLM unlearning that decouples contextual attention-pathways rather than erasing tokens, achieving strong forgetting performance on TOFU and WMDP while preserving 92.9% average model utility.
AI.motivation: Existing sequence- and token-level unlearning methods penalize target outputs without modeling their context-dependent retrieval paths, which can disrupt linguistic structure or suppress benign knowledge. A more precise approach is needed that avoids compromising general utility.
AI.method: ADU exploits the functional distinction between local and global attention heads to identify preplan positions that retrieve persistent sensitive anchors. It fixes candidate paths under the original model, trains attention-projection adapters to suppress attention mass along these paths while preserving local-attention structure and retain-set language modeling, and uses post-training activation exchange to test whether the modified attention-output module transmits the learned forgetting effect.
AI.result: ADU achieves the strongest aggregate performance among evaluated baselines on TOFU and WMDP benchmarks, including a Forget Quality of 0.93 on TOFU. It preserves 87-98% of model utility (92.9% on average versus 81.9% for baselines) while reducing side effects in benign contexts.
AI.conclusion: Shifting unlearning from token erasure to contextual attention-pathway decoupling enables precise forgetting with minimal collateral damage, outperforming existing baselines in both forget quality and utility preservation.

title: CAI-DLLM: Convergence Aware Inference for Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion language models can generate many tokens in parallel, but they still require repeated denoising steps during inference. This makes generation costly, especially when the model continues to recompute tokens that are already stable. To address these limitations, we propose CAI-DLLM, a training-free inference method that uses first-step confidence to guide denoising and reduce inference time. Specifically, CAI-DLLM commits easy tokens earlier, allocates more denoising steps to harder tokens, and adjusts decoding schedules across output blocks. As it relies only on first-step confidence signals, it does not require retraining, extra predictors, or weight updates. We evaluate CAI-DLLM on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct across math, code, reasoning, commonsense, and long-context tasks. CAI-DLLM achieves up to 18.2x wall clock inference speedup on LLaDA GSM8K while improving accuracy from 76.27% to 77.41%, and up to 13.1x speedup on Dream HumanEval while achieving higher pass@1 than no-cache inference, 48.17% compared with 46.95%. On harder reasoning tasks, speedups reach 44.8x, with a largest accuracy drop of 4.4 points, while energy consumption is reduced by up to 95.3%.

AI.tldr: CAI-DLLM is a training-free inference acceleration method for diffusion language models that uses first-step confidence signals to commit stable tokens early, allocate more denoising steps to harder tokens, and adjust decoding schedules, achieving up to 18.2x wall-clock speedup on LLaDA GSM8K and 44.8x on harder reasoning tasks with minimal accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: Diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel but require repeated denoising steps during inference, making generation costly. A key inefficiency is that models continue recomputing tokens that are already stable across denoising iterations.
AI.method: CAI-DLLM is a training-free inference method that leverages first-step confidence to guide denoising. It commits easy tokens earlier (freezing stable tokens), allocates more denoising steps to harder tokens, and adjusts decoding schedules across output blocks. It requires no retraining, extra predictors, or weight updates.
AI.result: Evaluated on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct across math, code, reasoning, commonsense, and long-context tasks. Achieves up to 18.2x wall-clock speedup on LLaDA GSM8K with accuracy improvement from 76.27% to 77.41%, up to 13.1x speedup on Dream HumanEval with pass@1 improved to 48.17% vs 46.95%, up to 44.8x speedup on harder reasoning tasks with a largest accuracy drop of 4.4 points, and energy consumption reduced by up to 95.3%.
AI.conclusion: CAI-DLLM demonstrates that confidence-guided denoising with early token commitment enables substantial inference acceleration and energy savings for diffusion language models without sacrificing accuracy in most cases, making it a practical and efficient solution for deployment.

title: MorphoCLIP: Text-Supervised Contrastive Learning for Perturbation Matching in Cell Painting Images
summary: Cell Painting microscopy captures how cells change after a chemical or genetic perturbation. Connecting these images to the perturbations that produced them could make large imaging screens easier to search and interpret, but the task remains difficult because biological effects are subtle and technical variation is substantial. We introduce MorphoCLIP, a contrastive model that links Cell Painting profiles with text descriptions of compounds, CRISPR knockouts, and ORF overexpressions. The model keeps its vision and language backbones frozen and trains only a compact cross-channel module and projection layers, so it can be trained on a single consumer GPU. On held-out CPJUMP1 data, MorphoCLIP searches in both directions: from a cell image to its perturbation description and from a description to matching cell images. In both cases, a correct match appears among the top ten results much more often than expected by chance. Adding a replicate-alignment loss makes profiles from repeated experiments more consistent, although this improvement does not yet translate into reliable gene-compound matching. Gene-aware labels and plate correction also show no consistent retrieval benefit. These findings suggest that text supervision can help organize chemical and genetic Cell Painting data. Matching compounds with genetic perturbations, however, remains an open problem.

AI.tldr: MorphoCLIP is a contrastive model that links Cell Painting images with text descriptions of chemical and genetic perturbations using frozen vision and language backbones with only a lightweight trainable module, achieving bidirectional retrieval on held-out CPJUMP1 data despite several proposed enhancements (replicate-alignment loss, gene-aware labels, plate correction) providing limited improvement.
AI.motivation: Connecting Cell Painting microscopy images to the perturbations that produced them could make large imaging screens easier to search and interpret, but this remains difficult due to subtle biological effects and substantial technical variation.
AI.method: MorphoCLIP is a contrastive model that keeps vision and language backbones frozen and trains only a compact cross-channel module and projection layers, enabling training on a single consumer GPU. It links Cell Painting profiles with text descriptions of compounds, CRISPR knockouts, and ORF overexpressions, with additional experiments on replicate-alignment loss, gene-aware labels, and plate correction.
AI.result: On held-out CPJUMP1 data, MorphoCLIP achieves bidirectional retrieval (image-to-description and description-to-image) with correct matches appearing in top-10 results much more often than chance. Replicate-alignment loss improves profile consistency but does not translate to reliable gene-compound matching. Gene-aware labels and plate correction show no consistent retrieval benefit.
AI.conclusion: Text supervision can help organize chemical and genetic Cell Painting data, but matching compounds with genetic perturbations remains an open problem.

title: Most of the LLM Routing Gap Is Task Type
summary: An LLM router picks which model should answer each query. The appeal is that models fail on different questions. Whatever single model is best overall still gets some wrong, and another model in the pool gets many of those right. Getting that choice right every time is the ceiling, and a router is an attempt to approach it. However, recent work reports that routers do not get close. Across 21 routing methods on five benchmarks, sharply different designs land within a fraction of a point of each other, and all of them stay far below that ceiling. Learned routers often fail to beat simply always calling the strongest model. We ask what those missed questions have in common. We set fourteen models to answer all 294 questions, with 7 task types across 3 languages: Korean, English and Hindi. We ran the whole matrix twice, changing nothing, but 5.37% of the 4,116 model-question pairs came out scored differently anyway. Run-to-run movement like that is normal, and we argue that a small win does not show that routing did anything, ours or anyone else's. Counting an answer correct only when the model got it right in both runs, 29 questions on this matrix can be improved with routing. Every correct-answer count here is on that rule. Task type accounts for most of them: assigning each task type one model in advance, chosen once and never updated, improves 21 of the 29. Splitting each task type by language improves 2 more and leaves 6 of 294 unoptimized. That handful is what a learned router would have been built for, and it is smaller than the run-to-run movement above, which is a share of pairs rather than of questions. The static table we adopted answers 262 of 294 questions at \$3.33 per run, against the best single model's 245 at \$7.69. All of this is fitted and scored on the same 294 questions with no holdout.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the efficacy of learned LLM routing. Across 14 models × 294 questions (7 task types, 3 languages), routers fail to significantly outperform always calling the strongest model. The authors show that most routing gains can be captured by a static rule (one model per task type, optionally split by language), which improves 21–23 of 29 optimizable questions, leaving only ~6 questions where a learned router would matter—smaller than run-to-run scoring noise (5.37% of pairs). The static table answers 262/294 questions at $3.33 vs. the best single model's 245 at $7.69, though all results are in-sample with no holdout.
AI.motivation: Recent work reports that LLM routers fail to approach the theoretical ceiling of choosing the best model per query, often not even beating always calling the strongest model. This paper asks what the missed questions have in common, to understand whether routing failures stem from missing structure or from the task itself not offering much headroom above simple static rules.
AI.method: The authors ran a full matrix of 14 models answering 294 questions (7 task types across Korean, English, Hindi), twice, to measure run-to-run scoring variance (5.37% of 4,116 pairs changed score). They count an answer correct only if both runs agree. They then construct a static routing table: assign each task type one model in advance, never updated, and evaluate its coverage of the 29 optimizable questions, optionally splitting by language.
AI.result: Static per-task-type assignment improves 21 of 29 optimizable questions; splitting by language improves 2 more, leaving only 6 out of 294 questions that would require a learned router. This remainder is smaller than the run-to-run noise (which is a share of pairs, not questions). The static table answers 262/294 questions at $3.33 per run, versus the best single model's 245 at $7.69.
AI.conclusion: Learned routers offer negligible gains over a simple, static routing table because most routing headroom is captured by task-type structure. Small apparent router wins are likely attributable to run-to-run scoring noise. The ceiling for learnable routing is very low—about 6/294 questions—so router research should account for static baselines and measurement noise. The authors also note all results are in-sample with no holdout, implying caution in interpretation.

title: A-CPES: A Reference Framework for Agentic AI in Cyber-Physical Energy Systems
summary: Energy system operation contains a loop of work that automation has never taken over: posing the optimization problem the current cycle should solve, disposing of infeasibility, sequencing a solution into interlocked switching orders, assembling evidence no single model holds, negotiating adjustable capacity with many parties, and settling experience into practice. Licensed dispatchers carry all of it in person, and the rising share of variable renewable generation is making that loop turn faster than their number can grow. Agentic AI supplies the abilities it requires, but enters as the outer loop of control: it calls SCED and the other decision models rather than being called by them. We propose A-CPES, three nested rings, an authorization and accountability frame around an agentic control outer loop around a six-layer CPES core. We argue the loop is indivisible, tune where and how tightly it may close, state eight structural failure modes as falsifiable predictions, and specify six governance modules that rebuild the authorization frame until it covers the loop, before the loop starts turning.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes A-CPES, a three-ring architecture where agentic AI operates as the outer control loop in energy system operation, surrounding a six-layer CPES core, with an authorization and accountability frame to manage the human-work loop that automation has not yet covered.
AI.motivation: Energy system operation still requires licensed human dispatchers to handle a work loop—posing optimization problems, resolving infeasibility, sequencing switching orders, negotiating capacity, and settling practice—that automation has never taken over. The growing share of variable renewable generation is accelerating this loop's cycle time faster than the dispatcher workforce can grow, creating a critical need for agentic AI to fill the gap.
AI.method: The paper proposes A-CPES, an architecture with three nested rings: an authorization and accountability frame, an agentic control outer loop, and a six-layer CPES core. Instead of being called by decision models like SCED, the agentic AI acts as the caller/outer loop of control. The paper argues the work loop is indivisible, specifies where and how tightly the loop may close, states eight structural failure modes as falsifiable predictions, and specifies six governance modules to rebuild the authorization frame.
AI.result: The paper presents a structural architecture (A-CPES) with three nested rings and six governance modules, along with eight falsifiable structural failure-mode predictions for the agentic control outer loop in energy system operation.
AI.conclusion: The work loop in energy system operation is indivisible and must be covered end-to-end by an authorization and accountability frame that is rebuilt before the agentic control loop begins turning, positioning agentic AI as the outer loop that calls decision models rather than being called by them.

title: Hybrid Generative-Discriminative Object Placement
summary: As an important operation of image composition, object placement aims to predict the plausible placement (location, scale) for the inserted foreground object. Previous object placement methods can be divided into generative methods and discriminative methods, both of which cannot balance efficiency and effectiveness well. In this work, we propose a semi-generative method in the middle ground between them. In particular, we assign uniformly distributed anchors on the background. Then, we fuse foreground and background features to predict the rationality score for each anchor and predict plausible placement sets for positive anchors. Extensive experiments on the OPA dataset show that our method can strike a good balance between efficiency and effectiveness.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a semi-generative method for object placement that balances efficiency and effectiveness by using uniformly distributed anchors on the background, fusing foreground and background features to predict rationality scores for each anchor, and predicting plausible placement sets for positive anchors.
AI.motivation: Previous object placement methods fall into generative or discriminative categories, neither of which achieves a good balance between efficiency and effectiveness.
AI.method: A semi-generative approach that places uniformly distributed anchors on the background, fuses foreground and background features to compute a rationality score for each anchor, and predicts plausible placement sets for positive anchors.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on the OPA dataset demonstrate that the proposed method strikes a good balance between efficiency and effectiveness.
