AI.tldr: The paper proposes LiteraryBigFive, a framework that represents authorial writing characteristics as coordinates in a unified five-dimensional interpretable space (inspired by the Big Five personality model). It derives stylistic axes from activation-space contrasts between author-written and neutral text, and introduces a steering mechanism for author-personalized text generation that improves authorial expressiveness while preserving semantic fidelity.
AI.motivation: Existing author modeling and personalization approaches represent writing behavior as independent labels, requiring large-scale corpus collection or per-author fine-tuning. These methods are costly, hard to interpret, and generalize poorly across authors.
AI.method: LiteraryBigFive reframes authorial writing characteristics as coordinates in a five-dimensional interpretable space. Each axis (e.g., Classicism, Emotionality) is derived from activation-space contrasts between author-written and neutral passages. An interpretable steering mechanism is introduced to guide text generation toward target author coordinates.
AI.result: Experimental results show that LiteraryBigFive improves authorial expressiveness while preserving semantic fidelity. Derived author per-axis scores strongly correlate with real-world literary consensus.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers transparent and interpretable explanations of author-specific generation behavior, providing a unified and efficient alternative to label-based personalization without requiring per-author fine-tuning or large corpora.

title: TailSieve: Partial-Rollout-Guided Tail Routing for LLM Rollouts
summary:
Large-scale rollouts have become a core component of modern LLM systems, spanning reinforcement learning (RL) post-training, on-policy distillation (OPD), and sampling-heavy evaluation pipelines. Unlike online serving, which is typically optimized for request-level latency and throughput, a small number of long-tail generations can dominate the end-to-end makespan of an entire rollout step. In practice, rollout requests are often routed uniformly across replicas, which can place extremely long generations inside high-concurrency decoding batches.
  To address this, we present TailSieve, a partial-rollout-guided framework that jointly controls tail routing and replica allocation for LLM rollouts. In an idealized setting with known completion lengths, we show that makespan-optimal routing in the long-tail regime combines tail isolation with load balancing, and that a simple top-k policy closely approximates this offline optimum. Leveraging the observation that long-tail prompts tend to remain long-tailed across policy updates, TailSieve uses partial rollouts as a training-free signal for identifying candidate tail groups. A hierarchical controller then jointly adapts the number of isolated groups and the replica split between the tail and bulk pools using collected response-work history and a measured concurrency-throughput model. TailSieve achieves up to 1.67x routing-only speedup over uniform group routing. The resulting low-concurrency tail pool further enables route-specialized speculative decoding with MTP or DFlash, achieving up to 2.59x speedup over uniform routing. Selected prompts are regenerated under the current policy, preserving on-policy generation and avoiding additional routing-induced length bias in steady state.

AI.tldr: TailSieve is a partial-rollout-guided framework that jointly controls tail routing and replica allocation for LLM rollouts, achieving up to 1.67x routing-only speedup and 2.59x total speedup via route-specialized speculative decoding.
AI.motivation: Large-scale LLM rollouts (used in RL post-training, on-policy distillation, and evaluation pipelines) suffer from long-tail generations that dominate end-to-end makespan. Uniform routing can place extremely long generations inside high-concurrency decoding batches, creating stragglers that slow down the entire rollout step.
AI.method: TailSieve uses (1) a top-k routing policy that approximates the offline makespan-optimal routing in the long-tail regime by combining tail isolation with load balancing; (2) partial rollouts as a training-free signal to identify candidate tail groups, exploiting the observation that long-tail prompts remain long-tailed across policy updates; (3) a hierarchical controller that jointly adapts the number of isolated groups and the replica split between tail and bulk pools using response-work history and a concurrency-throughput model; (4) route-specialized speculative decoding (MTP or DFlash) in the low-concurrency tail pool; and (5) regeneration of selected prompts under the current policy to preserve on-policy generation.
AI.result: TailSieve achieves up to 1.67x routing-only speedup over uniform group routing, and up to 2.59x total speedup when combined with route-specialized speculative decoding (MTP or DFlash) in the low-concurrency tail pool.
AI.conclusion: Partial-rollout-guided tail routing with adaptive replica allocation effectively mitigates long-tail stragglers in large-scale LLM rollout systems, and the resulting low-concurrency tail pool creates additional opportunities for speculative decoding acceleration without compromising on-policy generation quality.

title: VersaDB: A High-Performance AI Storage Database for Unifying Mutimodal Datasets
summary: The AI field has been rapidly developing, leading to the emergence of a large number of AI training datasets of various types. These datasets contain different modalities, including text, images, audio, etc., and may come in various data storage formats. With the advancement of AI hardware, AI computation units like GPUs, TPUs, and NPUs can greatly accelerate the training speed of AI models, which in turn increases the demand for faster data processing. When using existing AI processing frameworks to handle datasets with different modalities and storage formats, processing speeds may be suboptimal due to issues such as data layout and the way users handle the data. Therefore, using a unified database to store multiple data formats can better manage and optimize data access. In this paper, we introduce VersaDB, a database designed specifically for AI datasets with various modalities. We implemented a page-based storage system, separating structured and unstructured data. Additionally, we generated B+ tree-based index files to accelerate data access. VersaDB supports automatic sharding and maintains a hierarchical metadata management system, with corresponding metadata maintained at the page, shard, and global levels, forming the foundation for the efficient operation of the database. We also focused on ease of use by providing APIs for directly converting datasets into VersaDB, as well as APIs for converting popular AI data storage formats (e.g., CSV, TFRecord, .bin) into VersaDB.Our experiments show that using VersaDB can achieve up to 5.35x acceleration and maintain consistent performance across different parallelism levels.

AI.tldr: VersaDB is a purpose-built database for AI training datasets that handles multiple modalities (text, images, audio) and storage formats via a page-based storage system with separated structured/unstructured data, B+ tree index files, automatic sharding, and hierarchical metadata management. It achieves up to 5.35x acceleration over existing frameworks with consistent performance across parallelism levels.
AI.motivation: Existing AI processing frameworks handle heterogeneous datasets (different modalities and storage formats) suboptimally due to data layout issues and user handling patterns. As AI hardware (GPUs, TPUs, NPUs) accelerates model training, the demand for faster data processing has increased, creating a need for a unified database that can efficiently store and manage diverse AI dataset formats.
AI.method: VersaDB implements a page-based storage system that separates structured and unstructured data. It generates B+ tree-based index files to accelerate data access, supports automatic sharding, and maintains hierarchical metadata management at the page, shard, and global levels. It also provides APIs for converting datasets directly into VersaDB and for converting popular AI storage formats (CSV, TFRecord, .bin) into VersaDB.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that VersaDB achieves up to 5.35x acceleration compared to existing frameworks and maintains consistent performance across different levels of parallelism.
AI.conclusion: A unified database approach for multi-modal AI datasets can significantly improve data processing performance and manageability, with VersaDB serving as an effective solution for accelerating AI training data pipelines.

title: Language Chain in Alignment: Cross-Lingual Ranking Preference Optimization
summary: The alignment of Large Language Models heavily relies on English-centric high-quality preference data, which often leads to suboptimal performance in other languages. In this paper, we propose Cross-Lingual Ranking Preference Optimization (CRPO), a novel framework that leverages robust preference knowledge from English to facilitate preference alignment in the target language. We design a hierarchical structure within parallel preference pairs across the target language and English to jointly optimize intra- and inter-lingual preferences, thereby enhancing language adaptation and output quality. Building on the LambdaLoss framework, CRPO goes beyond the binary comparison based optimization by providing a relative ranking signal across multiple candidate responses. Our experiments across five languages with varying resource scales demonstrate that CRPO consistently outperforms standard approaches in both instruction-following and knowledge utilization capability. Notably, the robust performance gains observed across various weighting schemes further validate the empirical effectiveness of our hierarchical design in a multilingual setup. Furthermore, our findings highlight that CRPO significantly improves both reward margins and the log-probability of desirable responses, contributing to a more stable preference manifold for cross-lingual alignment.

AI.tldr: CRPO is a novel framework for cross-lingual preference alignment in LLMs that transfers preference knowledge from English to target languages through a hierarchical ranking structure across parallel preference pairs, using the LambdaLoss framework to provide relative ranking signals beyond binary comparisons.
AI.motivation: LLM alignment relies heavily on English-centric preference data, resulting in suboptimal performance in other languages due to the scarcity of high-quality multilingual preference data.
AI.method: CRPO uses a hierarchical structure within parallel preference pairs across target languages and English to jointly optimize intra- and inter-lingual preferences. It builds on the LambdaLoss framework to provide relative ranking signals across multiple candidate responses, going beyond binary comparison-based optimization.
AI.result: Experiments across five languages with varying resource scales show CRPO consistently outperforms standard approaches in both instruction-following and knowledge utilization. It shows robust performance gains across various weighting schemes and significantly improves reward margins and log-probability of desirable responses.
AI.conclusion: CRPO effectively enables cross-lingual preference alignment by leveraging English preference knowledge, producing a more stable preference manifold and better multilingual LLM performance.

title: Performance of a domain-specific large language model in answering patient questions in psychiatry
summary: Background This study was designed to evaluate whether a domain-specific large language model (LLM) trained exclusively on patient education resources can answer questions about psychiatric medications, in a manner superior to LLM chatbots. We developed an LLM ("MIND") fine-tuned for clinical fidelity, trained on patient education resources from authoritative medical organizations. Methods We compared the responses of MIND, ChatGPT, and OpenEvidence to patient questions about escitalopram, using two methods: (1) computer analysis according to a rubric measuring accuracy, clarity, completeness, nuance, safety, and referral appropriateness; (2) ratings from N=10 board-licensed psychiatrists on similar metrics. Results When rated by rubric, MIND was rated highest in all domains (p<0.001). When rated by psychiatrists, ChatGPT was rated accurate more often than MIND with a negligible effect size (p=0.021, r=0.073); MIND was rated complete more often than ChatGPT with a small effect size (p<0.001, r=0.160); and MIND and ChatGPT were rated safe with the same frequency (p=0.955, r=0.002). The majority of psychiatrists preferred the responses generated by ChatGPT (57.6%) compared to MIND (42.4%, p=0.003). Conclusions MIND was able to answer many questions about escitalopram in a manner deemed accurate, complete, and safe by psychiatrists the majority of the time. However, despite MIND's ability to provide more complete responses, psychiatrists preferred ChatGPT's responses. MIND represents a step towards building safe LLM systems to enhance patient education in psychiatry.

AI.tldr: This study developed "MIND," a domain-specific LLM fine-tuned on patient education resources for psychiatric medications, and compared its responses to ChatGPT and OpenEvidence on questions about escitalopram. MIND scored highest on automated rubric analysis across all domains, but psychiatrists rated ChatGPT's responses as preferred more often (57.6% vs 42.4%), despite MIND being rated more complete. Both models were rated safe with equal frequency.
AI.motivation: To evaluate whether a domain-specific large language model trained exclusively on authoritative patient education resources can answer psychiatric medication questions better than general-purpose LLM chatbots, addressing the need for safe, clinically faithful AI patient education tools in psychiatry.
AI.method: MIND was developed by fine-tuning an LLM on patient education resources from authoritative medical organizations. Its responses to patient questions about escitalopram were compared against ChatGPT and OpenEvidence using two evaluation methods: (1) automated rubric-based computer analysis measuring accuracy, clarity, completeness, nuance, safety, and referral appropriateness; (2) ratings from N=10 board-licensed psychiatrists on similar metrics.
AI.result: MIND outperformed all models on the automated rubric across all domains (p<0.001). Psychiatrist ratings showed ChatGPT was rated accurate more often than MIND with negligible effect size (p=0.021, r=0.073); MIND was rated more complete than ChatGPT with small effect size (p<0.001, r=0.160); both were rated safe with equal frequency (p=0.955, r=0.002). A majority of psychiatrists preferred ChatGPT's responses (57.6%) over MIND's (42.4%, p=0.003).
AI.conclusion: MIND can answer psychiatric medication questions in a manner psychiatrists deem accurate, complete, and safe most of the time. However, despite generating more complete responses, psychiatrists preferred ChatGPT's responses, suggesting that completeness alone does not determine clinician preference. MIND represents a step toward building safe, domain-specific LLM systems for patient education in psychiatry.

title: Direct, Parallel, or Sequential? A Comparative Study of Training-Free Multi-Subject Image-to-Video Generation
summary: Text-conditioned image-to-video (I2V) generation has advanced rapidly, yet generating videos with multiple subjects remains challenging. A model must simultaneously preserve the appearance of each subject, assign distinct motions, and maintain coherent spatial and temporal interactions. This paper presents a systematic study of three representative paradigms for training-free multi-subject I2V generation: direct, parallel, and sequential generation. Direct generation applies a pretrained I2V model to the complete reference image and prompt, requiring all subjects and motions to be synthesized jointly. Parallel and sequential generation instead decompose the reference image and prompt into subject-specific visual and textual conditions. Parallel generation synthesizes each subject independently and subsequently composes the resulting videos, reducing the complexity of each generation step at the cost of weaker inter-subject context. Sequential generation first synthesizes a background video and then progressively introduces individual subjects. This preserves accumulated scene context but introduces sensitivity to subject ordering and error propagation. We empirically evaluate the three paradigms across diverse multi-subject scenes, comparing appearance preservation, motion fidelity, temporal consistency, and inter-subject coherence, while also characterizing their distinct failure modes. Our findings reveal the strengths and limitations of each paradigm and offer practical insights for designing controllable multi-subject video generation systems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a systematic comparative study of three training-free paradigms for multi-subject text-conditioned image-to-video (I2V) generation: direct, parallel, and sequential. It evaluates them across appearance preservation, motion fidelity, temporal consistency, and inter-subject coherence, characterizing their distinct failure modes and offering practical design insights.
AI.motivation: Multi-subject I2V generation is challenging because a model must simultaneously preserve each subject's appearance, assign distinct motions, and maintain coherent spatial and temporal interactions. Despite advances in I2V generation, there is a lack of systematic understanding of how different decomposition paradigms handle these competing requirements.
AI.method: The authors systematically study three training-free paradigms: (1) direct generation, which applies a pretrained I2V model to the full reference image and prompt, synthesizing all subjects jointly; (2) parallel generation, which decomposes the reference image and prompt into subject-specific conditions, generates each subject independently, then composes the resulting videos; (3) sequential generation, which first generates a background video and progressively introduces subjects one by one, preserving accumulated scene context.
AI.result: The empirical evaluation across diverse multi-subject scenes compares appearance preservation, motion fidelity, temporal consistency, and inter-subject coherence. The findings reveal the strengths and limitations of each paradigm: direct generation benefits from full inter-subject context but suffers from joint synthesis complexity; parallel generation reduces per-step complexity at the cost of weaker inter-subject context; sequential generation preserves scene context but is sensitive to subject ordering and prone to error propagation.
AI.conclusion: The paper offers practical insights for designing controllable multi-subject video generation systems by characterizing the trade-offs between the three paradigms, helping researchers choose the appropriate decomposition strategy based on their specific requirements for subject fidelity, motion quality, and inter-subject coherence.

title: Counter with Evidence! A Multi-Agent Memory Efficient Reasoning Framework for Hate Category Informed Counterspeech Generation
summary: Counterspeech effectively neutralizes the impact of online hate. Although prior work explores automated counterspeech generation, it largely emphasizes stylistic control while treating hate speech as homogeneous, overlooking that distinct forms of abuse require fundamentally different counterspeech strategies. To address this gap, we introduce FIRE (Factuality Informed Multi-Agent Reasoning Framework) that first decomposes hate speech into one of the five distinct categories (misinformation, stereotype, conspiracy, dehumanizing, non-factual), and then maps it to a targeted counterspeech style. To facilitate FIRE, we curate FactualCS, a novel dataset of $4,784$ instances that provides the annotations regarding hate categories, reasoning traces, and evidence mappings, which are critical elements for grounded generation that are missing in prior work. A comprehensive evaluation across $28$ baseline configurations demonstrates that FIRE significantly surpasses existing methods, despite using compact agents ($<$2B). FIRE achieves a $\sim$ $12 \%$ and $\sim$ $11 \%$ improvements in factual and category-specific accuracy respectively, while simultaneously reducing toxicity by $\sim$ $11 \%$ relative to the strongest baselines. Further human evaluation confirms that responses generated by FIRE are significantly preferred over the strongest baselines, underscoring its effectiveness for real-world deployment. These findings show that decomposing the underlying intent of hate speech is essential for generating safe, effective, and contextually precise counterspeech.

AI.tldr: FIRE is a factuality-informed multi-agent reasoning framework that decomposes hate speech into five distinct categories (misinformation, stereotype, conspiracy, dehumanizing, non-factual) and maps each to a targeted counterspeech style, outperforming 28 baseline configurations with compact (<2B) agents.
AI.motivation: Prior automated counterspeech generation treats hate speech as homogeneous and focuses primarily on stylistic control, overlooking that distinct forms of abuse require fundamentally different counterspeech strategies.
AI.method: FIRE first decomposes hate speech into one of five categories (misinformation, stereotype, conspiracy, dehumanizing, non-factual), then maps each to a targeted counterspeech style. The authors curate FactualCS, a 4,784-instance dataset with hate category labels, reasoning traces, and evidence mappings for grounded generation.
AI.result: Across 28 baseline configurations, FIRE achieves ~12% improvement in factual accuracy and ~11% in category-specific accuracy while reducing toxicity by ~11% relative to the strongest baselines, using compact agents (<2B parameters). Human evaluation confirms significant preference for FIRE-generated responses.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing the underlying intent of hate speech is essential for generating safe, effective, and contextually precise counterspeech, making FIRE suitable for real-world deployment.

title: Beyond the Harness: End-to-End Optimization of Context Artifacts for Enterprise Text-to-SQL
summary: Deploying LLMs for enterprise Text-to-SQL is bottlenecked less by the model than by what context reaches it: business logic spans thousands of tables, and no model can ingest a full catalog at once. We argue that the most effective place to intervene is therefore the \emph{knowledge-base context} the model consumes, and that this context should be \emph{constructed} from historical usage rather than tuned for as a fixed input. Using a query-DAG decomposition--the same family of intermediates that enterprise benchmarks like BEAVER annotate, here recovered from production SQL--we compare the value of oracle query graphs versus retrieved knowledge-base context. In this ablation, retrieved knowledge-base context provides the largest marginal improvement when added to the full oracle graph. Building on this, we optimize a distillation procedure that turns historical query profiles into reusable SQL reference cards. On a benchmark of 5176 production queries from a major online retailer, optimizing these context artifacts yields larger gains (${\sim}12$--$25\%$ AST similarity) than optimizing the retrieval harness (${\sim}3$--$12\%$). On the public BEAVER benchmark, which lacks the production-usage signals available in our internal setting, the picture is more mixed: table cards alone perform about the same as raw historical SQL. The best optimized variant retrieves both cards and raw SQL, scoring $9.00\%$ versus $6.33\%$ (p-value $0.12$) for the comparable baseline on a held-out $N{=}300$ subset, using retrieved context and harness changes but no agentic loop.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that enterprise Text-to-SQL performance is bottlenecked by the knowledge-base context provided to LLMs, not the model itself. The authors construct context artifacts from historical production query usage (query-DAG decompositions and SQL reference cards) rather than treating context as a fixed input, demonstrating gains of ~12-25% AST similarity over retrieval-harness optimization alone on 5176 production queries, with more mixed results on the public BEAVER benchmark.
AI.motivation: Enterprise Text-to-SQL is limited by the volume of context (thousands of tables in business logic) that no model can ingest at once. The authors argue the most effective intervention point is the knowledge-base context, which should be constructed from historical usage patterns rather than being a fixed, tuned input.
AI.method: The paper uses query-DAG decomposition (intermediates recovered from production SQL rather than annotated) to compare oracle query graphs versus retrieved knowledge-base context. They optimize a distillation procedure that converts historical query profiles into reusable SQL reference cards, and compare gains from optimizing context artifacts versus optimizing the retrieval harness.
AI.result: On 5176 production queries from a major online retailer, optimizing context artifacts yields larger gains (~12-25% AST similarity) than optimizing the retrieval harness (~3-12%). On BEAVER (lacking production signals), table cards perform on par with raw historical SQL; the best variant retrieves both cards and raw SQL, scoring 9.00% vs 6.33% (p=0.12) on a held-out N=300 subset without an agentic loop.
AI.conclusion: Constructing knowledge-base context from historical query usage is more effective for enterprise Text-to-SQL than tuning retrieval mechanisms alone. However, gains depend on having production-usage signals; where such signals are absent (e.g., public benchmarks), the advantage becomes less clear, though combining reference cards with raw SQL still shows directional improvement.

title: SiZeUp: Fast 3D Proxy from Aerial Images via Depth Ordinal Loss
summary: We present SiZeUp, a fast and scalable approach for constructing large-scale 3D urban proxy models directly from calibrated oblique aerial imagery. Our method adopts a height-from-footprint representation, reducing 3D building abstraction to a low-dimensional optimization problem in which building footprints are extruded by a single height parameter. To enable efficient and robust height estimation, we introduce an ordinal depth consistency loss that enforces agreement between the relative depth ordering of rendered proxies and depth priors predicted by a monocular depth model. This is realized through a differentiable renderer that maps parametric building proxies into multi-view depth images, allowing gradients to be propagated from depth supervision to building heights. Our ordinal formulation produces stable optimization in practice and avoids explicit feature matching or dense point cloud reconstruction. Rather than relying on metric depth, which can be unreliable under monocular scale ambiguity, our ordinal depth consistency loss operates on relative depths, providing a more reliable signal across views. Combined with an efficient dynamic view selection, our approach achieves a 23-52$\times$ speedup over state-of-the-art proxy reconstruction pipelines while maintaining comparable proxy-level coverage and volume consistency, making it well suited for large-scale urban modeling tasks.

AI.tldr: SiZeUp is a fast and scalable method for constructing large-scale 3D urban proxy models from oblique aerial imagery. It reduces 3D building abstraction to a low-dimensional height-from-footprint optimization problem, using an ordinal depth consistency loss with a differentiable renderer to estimate building heights from monocular depth priors. The approach achieves 23-52x speedup over state-of-the-art methods while maintaining comparable coverage and volume consistency.
AI.motivation: Large-scale 3D urban proxy model construction from aerial imagery is computationally expensive and complex. Existing methods rely on feature matching or dense point cloud reconstruction, which are slow and unreliable for large-scale deployment. There is a need for a fast, scalable approach that simplifies the 3D abstraction problem while maintaining quality.
AI.method: SiZeUp adopts a height-from-footprint representation that reduces building abstraction to a low-dimensional optimization problem where footprints are extruded by a single height parameter. It introduces an ordinal depth consistency loss that enforces agreement between relative depth ordering of rendered proxies (via a differentiable renderer producing multi-view depth images) and depth priors from a monocular depth model. The ordinal formulation avoids metric depth scale ambiguity and explicit feature matching or dense reconstruction, combined with efficient dynamic view selection.
AI.result: SiZeUp achieves a 23-52x speedup over state-of-the-art proxy reconstruction pipelines while maintaining comparable proxy-level coverage and volume consistency, making it suitable for large-scale urban modeling.
AI.conclusion: The ordinal depth consistency loss, operating on relative depth ordering rather than metric depth, provides a more reliable supervision signal across views. Combined with the low-dimensional height-from-footprint representation and dynamic view selection, SiZeUp offers an efficient and scalable solution for constructing large-scale 3D urban proxy models.

title: Accelerating Diffusion Language Models via Structured Suffix Modeling
summary: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) exhibit strong parallel decoding capabilities by denoising multiple tokens in a single generation step. However, this parallelism comes with substantial computational overhead, as each step requires interactions with all suffix tokens. Existing methods typically reduce this cost by retaining only a local suffix window as a substitute for the full suffix. Despite their effectiveness, these methods overlook the structural heterogeneity across suffix regions and re-initialize suffix tokens with identical representations at each timestep. To this end, we propose a structured suffix modeling method for efficient DLM inference. Specifically, we divide the suffix into three regions, i.e., the local, middle, and tail regions, and retain different numbers of suffix tokens in each region according to their structural roles. Moreover, we incorporate the decoding results from the previous step into the suffix token representations at the current step, allowing them to carry evolving denoising information across generation steps. Notably, our method is training-free and orthogonal to several existing acceleration techniques, such as parallel decoding strategies and KV cache. Empirical results across multiple benchmarks on three DLMs demonstrate that our method can further accelerate DLM inference and improve performance in most cases. In particular, in long-sequence inference, our method achieves up to a \(72.81\times\) speedup when combined with other acceleration techniques. Our code is available at https://github.com/zifengcheng/SSM.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a structured suffix modeling (SSM) method for efficient diffusion language model (DLM) inference. It divides the suffix into local, middle, and tail regions with different token retention counts based on structural roles, and incorporates previous-step decoding results into current suffix representations. The method is training-free, orthogonal to existing acceleration techniques, achieving up to 72.81x speedup in long-sequence inference.
AI.motivation: DLMs offer parallel decoding but incur high computational overhead since each denoising step requires interactions with all suffix tokens. Existing methods reduce cost by retaining only a local suffix window but overlook structural heterogeneity across suffix regions and re-initialize suffix tokens with identical representations at each timestep, leading to suboptimal efficiency and performance.
AI.method: The method divides the suffix into three regions—local, middle, and tail—and retains different numbers of suffix tokens per region according to their structural roles. Additionally, it incorporates decoding results from the previous step into current suffix token representations to carry evolving denoising information across generation steps. The approach is training-free and orthogonal to parallel decoding strategies and KV cache.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations across multiple benchmarks on three DLMs show the method further accelerates DLM inference and improves performance in most cases. In long-sequence inference, it achieves up to a 72.81x speedup when combined with other acceleration techniques.
AI.conclusion: Structured suffix modeling with region-specific token retention and cross-step information flow provides an effective, training-free acceleration for DLM inference that complements existing techniques and improves both speed and quality.

title: Let the Bullets Fly: Multimodal Fake News Detection with Temporal-Aligned Generative Danmaku
summary: The social interactions among crowds via \textit{Danmaku} (a.k.a., bullet comments) on modern multimedia platforms can facilitate both viewpoint conflicts and consensus, providing fine-grained discriminative social signals that can benefit fake news detection. However, the inherent accumulation latency of \textit{Danmaku} in real-world scenarios violates the real-time necessity of fake news detection, making the studies of \textit{Danmaku}-related fake news detection underexplored. To break this violation, we simulate this temporal-aware user interactive process by proposing a novel temporal \textbf{Gen}erative \textbf{da}nmaku framework, called \textbf{Genda}, which consists of: (1) a \textit{Danmaku} Trigger for predicting the timing and intensity of user reactions; and (2) a \textit{Danmaku} Generator for synthesizing corresponding semantic and emotional expressions, thereby mutually constructing a temporally aligned and human-like pseudo \textit{Danmaku} streams. To make the generated \textit{Danmaku} useful for identifying fake news videos, we further design a \textit{Danmaku}-guided Temporal Multimodal fake news detection model - \textbf{DM-FEND}, which enables fine-grained multimodal interactions among video, audio, text, and \textit{Danmaku}, enhancing dynamic modalities alignment and semantic noise inhibition. The experimental results demonstrate that \emph{DM-FEND} consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across both Chinese (FakeSV) and English (FakeTT) benchmarks. Further ablations validate the crucial role of temporal \textit{Danmaku} modeling in enhancing robustness and discriminative capability. Finally, this study offers a bright and robust solution for multimodal fake news detection in modern social interactive fashions by bridging the temporal inconsistency between news and user behaviors.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a temporal generative Danmaku framework called Genda to synthesize time-aligned, human-like bullet comments, and a Danmaku-guided multimodal fake news detection model (DM-FEND) that leverages these pseudo Danmaku streams to enhance fake news detection in videos, outperforming SOTA baselines on Chinese (FakeSV) and English (FakeTT) benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Social interactions via Danmaku (bullet comments) provide fine-grained discriminative signals for fake news detection, but the inherent accumulation latency of real Danmaku violates the real-time necessity of fake news detection, making Danmaku-related studies underexplored.
AI.method: Two main components: (1) Genda, a temporal generative Danmaku framework with a Danmaku Trigger (predicts timing and intensity of user reactions) and a Danmaku Generator (synthesizes semantic and emotional expressions) to build temporally aligned pseudo Danmaku streams; (2) DM-FEND, a Danmaku-guided Temporal Multimodal fake news detection model enabling fine-grained interactions among video, audio, text, and Danmaku, with dynamic modality alignment and semantic noise inhibition.
AI.result: DM-FEND consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on both Chinese (FakeSV) and English (FakeTT) benchmarks. Ablation studies confirm the crucial role of temporal Danmaku modeling for robustness and discriminative capability.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a robust solution for multimodal fake news detection in modern social interactive platforms by bridging the temporal inconsistency between news content and user behaviors through generative Danmaku simulation.

title: VeCAS: Vessel-Focused Contrast-Free Angiogram Synthesis for Vascular Interventions
summary: X-ray angiography relies on iodinated contrast agents to visualize vascular structures during image-guided interventions. However, contrast administration carries risks of adverse events, motivating the development of contrast-free alternatives. Generating X-ray angiograms directly from non-contrast X-ray images offers a potential solution, but existing approaches remain limited by (i) insufficient control over vascular localization and (ii) inefficient modeling of redundant background content. To address these challenges, we propose VeCAS, a two-stage vessel-focused contrast-free angiogram synthesis framework that separates vascular structure localization from angiographic appearance synthesis. In Stage I, a discriminative model localizes vascular structures in non-contrast X-ray images, while cross-modality latent distillation transfers vessel-sensitive knowledge from X-ray angiograms during training. In Stage II, a vessel-focused inpainting model synthesizes angiographic appearance within the localized vascular regions while preserving the non-vascular background. Experiments on an in-house lower-limb vascular intervention dataset show that VeCAS outperforms the comparison methods in terms of vascular structural fidelity and image quality. Visual Turing tests and physician assessments indicate the perceptual realism of the synthesized angiograms. In addition, robotic guidewire navigation experiments in vascular phantoms show that VeCAS guidance reduces the time to target by 41.4% and the number of operation steps by 40.7% compared with non-contrast guidance. Together, these results suggest the potential of VeCAS to serve as ``meta contrast agent'' for vascular interventions.

AI.tldr: VeCAS is a two-stage contrast-free X-ray angiogram synthesis framework that first localizes vascular structures via a discriminative model with cross-modality latent distillation, then synthesizes angiographic appearance within localized regions using a vessel-focused inpainting model. It outperforms baselines on an in-house lower-limb dataset and demonstrates practical utility: reducing robotic guidewire navigation time by 41.4% and operation steps by 40.7% in vascular phantoms, acting as a "meta contrast agent."
AI.motivation: Iodinated contrast agents used in X-ray angiography carry risks of adverse events. Existing contrast-free angiogram synthesis approaches suffer from (i) insufficient control over vascular localization and (ii) inefficient modeling of redundant background content, motivating the need for a better framework.
AI.method: VeCAS employs a two-stage vessel-focused framework. Stage I uses a discriminative model to localize vascular structures in non-contrast X-ray images, augmented by cross-modality latent distillation that transfers vessel-sensitive knowledge from X-ray angiograms during training. Stage II uses a vessel-focused inpainting model to synthesize angiographic appearance within the localized vascular regions while preserving the non-vascular background.
AI.result: On an in-house lower-limb vascular intervention dataset, VeCAS outperforms comparison methods in vascular structural fidelity and image quality. Visual Turing tests and physician assessments confirm perceptual realism. Robotic guidewire navigation experiments in vascular phantoms show VeCAS guidance reduces time-to-target by 41.4% and operation steps by 40.7% compared to non-contrast guidance.
AI.conclusion: VeCAS demonstrates the potential to serve as a "meta contrast agent" for vascular interventions, offering a safe, contrast-free alternative with strong synthesis quality and tangible clinical benefit for interventional guidance.

title: CaRGo-T: Causal Reasoning Graph-of-Thought improves Multimodal Humor Comprehension
summary: Large-scale vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable versatility across a wide range of multimodal tasks. However, understanding humor remains challenging because humorous content often depends on subtle interactions among entities, events, context, and implicit relationships across image and text modalities. These interactions can involve complex chains of reasoning that are difficult to capture through conventional prompting or linear chain-of-thought reasoning. In this work, we propose CaRGo-T (Causal Reasoning Graph-of-Thought), a reasoning framework that represents the causal and contextual relationships underlying multimodal humor as a lightweight graph-based reasoning structure. The graph is serialized into a code-based representation generated by a VLM, which can subsequently be interpreted by the same or a different VLM to produce the final prediction in zero-shot or in-context learning settings. We evaluate CaRGo-T on humor understanding and humor detection across four datasets spanning diverse forms of comedic content, including satire, sarcasm, and memes. Experiments with state-of-the-art commercial and open-source VLMs show that CaRGo-T consistently improves performance over existing reasoning-based baselines, achieving gains of approximately 1-20% on humor understanding and 1-3% on humor detection. Further analysis using mutual information indicates that the reasoning representations produced by CaRGo-T contain more information relevant to the target output than those generated by baseline reasoning approaches. Code is available at https://github.com/abhi1nandy2/CaRGo-T.

AI.tldr: CaRGo-T is a novel reasoning framework that represents causal and contextual relationships underlying multimodal humor as a lightweight graph structure, serialized into a code-based representation that VLMs can interpret for humor understanding and detection tasks.
AI.motivation: Humor understanding in VLMs remains challenging because comedic content relies on subtle, implicit interactions across image and text modalities that involve complex reasoning chains not easily captured by conventional prompting or linear chain-of-thought approaches.
AI.method: The framework constructs a lightweight graph representing causal and contextual relationships in multimodal humor, serializes it into a code-based representation generated by a VLM, and uses the same or a different VLM to interpret the serialized graph for final predictions in zero-shot or in-context learning settings.
AI.result: Evaluated on four datasets spanning satire, sarcasm, and memes, CaRGo-T consistently outperforms existing reasoning-based baselines, achieving gains of approximately 1-20% on humor understanding and 1-3% on humor detection across state-of-the-art commercial and open-source VLMs. Mutual information analysis confirms the reasoning representations contain more target-relevant information than baseline approaches.
AI.conclusion: CaRGo-T demonstrates that graph-structured reasoning, serialized into interpretable code, is an effective approach for improving VLM performance on complex multimodal tasks like humor comprehension, and the framework enables this capability in both zero-shot and in-context learning settings.

title: FinixDoc: Rethinking Financial Document Parsing Beyond Saturated Benchmarks
summary: Financial document parsing requires accuracy, structural consistency, and verifiability that current benchmarks often fail to reflect. We present FinixDoc, an end-to-end agentic parsing system for real-world financial documents, with FinixDoc-VL, a 4B-scale vision-language model built on Qwen3-VL-4B, as its core parser. To characterize the gap between benchmark and deployment performance, we introduce a Document Parsing Capability Matrix organized along two practical axes: visual quality and document scale. Guided by this matrix, FinixDoc-VL is trained with a domain-adapted recipe combining homoglyph-aware contrastive learning and multi-stage reinforcement learning with composite domain-specific rewards. To better leverage our accumulated advantage in low-quality financial-document data and support large-scale, high-quality data production, we further build a human-in-the-loop Data Factory pipeline with confidence-aware expert review. For evaluation, we construct FinixDocBench, a financial-domain evaluation suite covering digital-native, camera-captured, ultra-large-page, and internal-workflow scenarios, with a compliance-reviewed subset released alongside this technical report. On its main subsets, FinixDoc-VL achieves the highest overall score (81.43) among evaluated baselines, outperforming the next-best open-source model by 5.13 points, with the largest gains on internal financial workflows (FinixInner: 84.08 vs. 78.73).

AI.tldr: FinixDoc is an end-to-end agentic parsing system for financial documents, featuring FinixDoc-VL, a 4B-scale vision-language model built on Qwen3-VL-4B. The paper introduces a Document Parsing Capability Matrix (organized by visual quality and document scale), a domain-adapted training recipe (homoglyph-aware contrastive learning + multi-stage RL with composite rewards), a human-in-the-loop Data Factory pipeline, and FinixDocBench evaluation suite. FinixDoc-VL achieves the highest overall score (81.43) on FinixDocBench, outperforming the next-best open-source model by 5.13 points, with the largest gains on internal financial workflows (84.08 vs. 78.73).
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks fail to reflect the accuracy, structural consistency, and verifiability required for real-world financial document parsing, creating a gap between benchmark and deployment performance.
AI.method: The paper proposes (1) a Document Parsing Capability Matrix along two axes (visual quality and document scale) to characterize benchmark-to-deployment gaps; (2) FinixDoc-VL, a 4B-scale VL model based on Qwen3-VL-4B, trained with homoglyph-aware contrastive learning and multi-stage reinforcement learning with composite domain-specific rewards; (3) a human-in-the-loop Data Factory pipeline with confidence-aware expert review for large-scale data production; and (4) FinixDocBench, a financial-domain evaluation suite covering digital-native, camera-captured, ultra-large-page, and internal-workflow scenarios with a compliance-reviewed subset.
AI.result: FinixDoc-VL achieves the highest overall score (81.43) on FinixDocBench among evaluated baselines, outperforming the next-best open-source model by 5.13 points. The largest gains are on internal financial workflows (FinixInner: 84.08 vs. 78.73).
AI.conclusion: The FinixDoc system demonstrates that domain-adapted training guided by a capability matrix, combined with a confidence-aware data production pipeline, can significantly improve financial document parsing performance, particularly for real-world deployment scenarios such as internal financial workflows.

title: Following Motion for Sequential Modeling in Video Frame Interpolation
summary: State Space Models (SSMs) have surfaced as a promising architecture in Video Frame Interpolation (VFI), as they can capture long-range dependencies with linear computational complexity. However, their predefined scanning order limits their effectiveness in modeling the dynamic motion trajectories inherent in VFI problems. To tackle this challenge, we propose Motion-Guided Mamba for Video Frame Interpolation (MGMVFI), an adaptation of the selective state space model tailored explicitly for VFI. MGMVFI introduces Motion-Guided Serialization (MGS), which leverages optical flow to define a motion-adaptive 1D input order for the SSM. This aligns the causal state updates with semantically related tokens, enabling motion-consistent feature propagation, particularly for large and dynamic motions. Additionally, to mitigate the unreliable feature representations caused by inaccurate optical flow estimates, we introduce contextual synthesis that utilizes the surrounding spatial context for robust inter-frame feature synthesis. These components are seamlessly integrated within our tailored Mamba architecture, which also employs a lightweight refinement block to enhance local detail reconstruction at a reduced computational cost. Extensive experiments on standard VFI benchmarks demonstrate that MGMVFI achievesstate-of-the-artperformance,particularly on complex and dynamic motions, thereby establishing a new direction for sequence modeling in video interpolation.

AI.tldr: MGMVFI is a selective state space model (Mamba) adaptation for Video Frame Interpolation that uses optical flow to define motion-adaptive serialization orders, enabling SSMs to better capture dynamic motion trajectories while handling unreliable flow estimates via contextual synthesis.
AI.motivation: SSMs promise linear-complexity long-range dependency modeling for VFI, but their fixed, predefined scanning order fails to align with the dynamic and irregular motion trajectories inherent in video interpolation, limiting effectiveness.
AI.method: Introduces Motion-Guided Serialization (MGS) using optical flow to create a motion-adaptive 1D input order for the SSM, aligning causal state updates with semantically related tokens. Adds contextual synthesis to counter unreliable optical flow estimates by leveraging surrounding spatial context, integrated within a tailored Mamba architecture featuring a lightweight refinement block for local detail reconstruction at reduced cost.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard VFI benchmarks, particularly excelling on complex and dynamic motion scenarios.
AI.conclusion: MGMVFI validates motion-guided sequence ordering for SSMs in video interpolation and opens a new direction for sequence modeling in VFI.

title: LongWoF-Bench: Evaluating EvoMap Genes for Verifiable Long-Workflow Tasks
summary: Large language models are increasingly expected to execute complex workflows whose success depends on maintaining interdependent constraints and producing artifacts that satisfy strict end-to-end verification. Yet successful execution experience is typically lost after a single run, forcing subsequent models to rediscover strategies and failure modes from scratch. We study whether such experience can instead be externalized and reused through EvoMap, where verifier-confirmed execution trajectories are consolidated into structured Gene. To evaluate this setting, we introduce the Long-Workflow Benchmark (LongWoF-Bench), comprising 778 machine-verifiable tasks across code generation, agent-environment synthesis, mathematical reasoning, and rule following. On the 252 tasks with verifier-confirmed Opus trajectories, evolved EvoMap Gene outperform Skill across all seven evaluated models by 8.7-15.5 percentage points, with the gains extending to consumer models from different model families. In contrast, reference-distilled Gene do not exhibit the same advantage, indicating that compact representation alone is insufficient and that Gene utility is closely associated with verified experience provenance. For Claude Opus, Gene reuse also completes 39 more tasks than Skill while reducing solve-time token consumption by 9.9%. Together, these results show that verified execution experience can be retained and shared as a reusable external resource, enabling models to improve long-workflow completion without repeatedly paying the full cost of experience discovery.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces EvoMap, a framework that externalizes and consolidates verifier-confirmed execution trajectories into structured "Gene" representations that can be reused across models, along with LongWoF-Bench, a benchmark of 778 machine-verifiable long-workflow tasks. EvoMap Gene outperform Skill baselines by 8.7-15.5 percentage points across seven models and reduce token consumption by 9.9% for Claude Opus, demonstrating that verified execution experience can be retained, shared, and reused as an external resource.
AI.motivation: Large language models often fail to maintain interdependent constraints in complex long workflows, and successful execution experiences are discarded after each run. This forces subsequent models to rediscover strategies and failure modes from scratch, resulting in inefficient repeated trial-and-error. The paper asks whether verified execution experience can instead be externalized and reused.
AI.method: The authors propose EvoMap, which consolidates verifier-confirmed execution trajectories into structured Gene representations. They also introduce LongWoF-Bench, comprising 778 machine-verifiable tasks spanning code generation, agent-environment synthesis, mathematical reasoning, and rule following. They evaluate evolved Gene against Skill baselines and reference-distilled Gene across seven models, including consumer models from different families and Claude Opus.
AI.result: On 252 tasks with verifier-confirmed Opus trajectories, evolved EvoMap Gene outperform Skill by 8.7-15.5 percentage points across all seven evaluated models. Reference-distilled Gene do not show the same advantage, indicating compact representation alone is insufficient and Gene utility depends on verified experience provenance. For Claude Opus, Gene reuse completes 39 more tasks than Skill while reducing solve-time token consumption by 9.9%.
AI.conclusion: Verified execution experience can be retained and shared as a reusable external resource, enabling models to improve long-workflow completion without repeatedly paying the full cost of experience discovery. The provenance of experience (verified vs. distilled) is critical to Gene utility, and the benefits generalize across different model families.

title: GSAR: Goal-State-Anchor Rewards for Mobile GUI Agents with Self-Evolving Data Synthesis
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) based GUI agents stand to benefit significantly from online reinforcement learning (RL). However, their training is bottlenecked by two fundamental issues: current data synthesis methods for GUI Agents rely on specific environments and struggle to generate diverse data, while existing evaluators either suffer from limited scalability or provide inaccurate and unreliable reward signals. To overcome these challenges, we introduce GSAR (Goal-State-Anchor Reward), a RL reward framework that supports scalable task generation and delivers reliable reward signals for stable and efficient policy optimization. Our approach features self-evolving data synthesis, which produces multiple environments through task execution and generates diverse tasks and goal states. Complementing this, a state-anchor mechanism automatically annotates task-relevant UI elements in successful goal states as reference anchors. During RL training, these reference anchors provide accurate, scalable reward signals that substantially enhance efficiency. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our framework achieves over 90% accuracy on offline trajectory verification and performs closest to rule-based methods. Furthermore, agents trained using our reward framework exhibit strong performance on both AndroidWorld and our constructed benchmark, establishing a scalable approach for GUI agent training.

AI.tldr: GSAR (Goal-State-Anchor Reward) is a reinforcement learning reward framework for GUI agents that combines self-evolving data synthesis with a state-anchor mechanism to generate diverse training data and provide accurate, scalable reward signals, achieving over 90% accuracy on offline trajectory verification and strong performance on AndroidWorld.
AI.motivation: Online RL for VLM-based GUI agents is bottlenecked by two issues: existing data synthesis methods are environment-specific and lack diversity, while current evaluators either have limited scalability or provide inaccurate/unreliable reward signals.
AI.method: GSAR features two key components: (1) a self-evolving data synthesis approach that generates multiple environments through task execution and produces diverse tasks and goal states, and (2) a state-anchor mechanism that automatically annotates task-relevant UI elements in successful goal states as reference anchors, which serve as accurate and scalable reward signals during RL training.
AI.result: The framework achieves over 90% accuracy on offline trajectory verification, performs closest to rule-based methods among evaluated approaches, and agents trained with GSAR demonstrate strong performance on both AndroidWorld and the authors' constructed benchmark.
AI.conclusion: GSAR establishes a scalable approach for GUI agent training by providing reliable reward signals and diverse data generation, overcoming the scalability and reliability limitations of existing methods.

title: Toward Sub-1 kB Identity-Preserving Face Compression: A Benchmark of Codecs, a Custom Learned Codec, and Studies of Resolution, Demographic Fairness, Recompression, and Adversarial Robustness
summary:
Storing face images under a hard sub-kilobyte budget, as required for identity documents, smart-card biometrics and bandwidth-constrained verification, forces a codec to discard most of the signal while keeping what a face matcher actually reads: identity. Generic codecs optimize pixel fidelity, not the embedding distances that drive verification, so which codec, resolution and setting best preserve identity at 1024 bytes or less, and how that degrades at 512, is unclear.
  We benchmark ten general and face-specific codecs across resolutions, byte budgets, two datasets (controlled Color FERET, in-the-wild AI-Solutions-KK) and four anchor face matchers, with a fourteen-model ViT and CNN roster confirming the ranking is backbone-invariant. We then train a custom identity-preserving codec that hits the byte budget exactly via binary search over a frozen gain table, and run four studies: resolution, demographic fairness, recompression, and no-box adversarial robustness.
  Sub-kilobyte identity preservation is feasible, but which codec to deploy depends entirely on the budget. At 1024 bytes and the 112 px working resolution the problem is close to solved: modern codecs hold Color FERET equal-error rate under 0.35 percent on the ArcFace anchor. At 512 bytes the field re-sorts: AVIF, HEIF, JPEG XL and legacy JPEG collapse to 28 to 98 percent false-non-match rate at FMR 1e-4, while WebP, JPEG-AI and our byte-budgeted learned codecs stay out of that band, with 24.3 percent for WebP against 6.9 percent for our accurate variant in the wild. That re-sort, not the 1024-byte ranking, is the operational result: a codec chosen at 1 kB is not the codec to deploy at half that.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks ten face codecs at sub-kilobyte budgets (1024 and 512 bytes) across multiple resolutions, datasets, and face matchers, revealing that codec performance rankings shift dramatically between byte budgets. The authors train a custom identity-preserving codec that hits byte budgets exactly via binary search over a frozen gain table, and show that while sub-kilobyte identity preservation is feasible (EER under 0.35% at 1024 bytes on Color FERET/ArcFace), the codec ranking re-sorts at 512 bytes—with WebP and learned codecs surviving while AVIF, HEIF, JPEG XL, and legacy JPEG collapse to 28-98% FNMR.
AI.motivation: Generic image codecs optimize pixel fidelity rather than embedding distances used by face matchers, yet identity documents and smart-card biometrics require storing face images under hard sub-kilobyte budgets. It is unclear which codec, resolution, and settings best preserve identity at 1024 bytes or less, and how performance degrades at 512 bytes, motivating a systematic benchmark and a purpose-built identity-preserving codec.
AI.method: The authors benchmark ten general and face-specific codecs across resolutions, byte budgets, two datasets (Color FERET and AI-Solutions-KK), and four anchor face matchers, confirmed by a fourteen-model ViT/CNN roster for backbone-invariance. They additionally train a custom identity-preserving codec that exactly hits byte budgets via binary search over a frozen gain table, and run four studies: resolution, demographic fairness, recompression, and no-box adversarial robustness.
AI.result: At 1024 bytes and 112px resolution the problem is nearly solved—modern codecs achieve Color FERET EER under 0.35% on the ArcFace anchor. At 512 bytes the ranking re-sorts: AVIF, HEIF, JPEG XL, and legacy JPEG degrade to 28-98% FNMR at FMR 1e-4, while WebP, JPEG-AI, and the byte-budgeted learned codecs stay out of that band (WebP at 24.3% FNMR versus the accurate variant at 6.9% in the wild).
AI.conclusion: Sub-kilobyte identity preservation is feasible, but codec selection is budget-dependent: a codec chosen at 1 kB is not necessarily the right choice at half that budget. The re-sort at 512 bytes is the key operational finding rather than the 1024-byte ranking.

title: Aligning Biomedical Texts and Knowledge Graphs: A Systematic Comparison of Lightweight Alignment Strategies
comment: Accepted at the Third Workshop on Knowledge Graphs and Neurosymbolic AI (KG-NeSy 2026) co-located with ISWC 2026
summary: Biomedical knowledge exists in two complementary but distinct forms: unstructured scientific literature and structured knowledge graphs (KGs). Aligning them is essential for knowledge grounding, evidence retrieval, and KG completion, yet existing methods do not explicitly align free-text evidence with KG triples. We present a unified framework for systematically studying design choices for aligning biomedical text and KGs. With a text encoder and a KG embedding model both frozen, we learn only a lightweight projection between their spaces via a contrastive objective. This enables a fair comparison across six design dimensions: text encoder, KG embedding model, projection head, triple composition, training direction, and hard-negatives sampling. We construct CTD-Align, a corpus of over 22K one-to-one tripledocument pairs linking chemical-gene interactions from the Comparative Toxicogenomics Database to supporting PubMed passages. We evaluate alignment on it in two retrieval settings: document-to-triple and triple-to-document. We find that the triple composition and the training direction (i.e., shared retrieval space) have the greatest impact, whereas the text encoder and hard-negatives sampling matter little. Overall, simple choices win: projecting text into the KG space with a linear head over concatenated subject, predicate, and object embeddings performs best. These findings establish lightweight contrastive alignment as an effective, practical foundation for bridging biomedical text and KGs.

AI.tldr: A lightweight contrastive alignment framework for bridging biomedical literature and knowledge graphs, evaluated on a new corpus of over 22K chemical-gene interaction triples paired with PubMed passages, finding that simple design choices (linear projection into KG space with concatenated triple embeddings) work best.
AI.motivation: Biomedical knowledge exists in two complementary forms—unstructured literature and structured knowledge graphs—but existing methods fail to explicitly align free-text evidence with KG triples, which is essential for knowledge grounding, evidence retrieval, and KG completion.
AI.method: A unified framework that freezes a text encoder and KG embedding model, learns only a lightweight projection between their spaces via contrastive objective, and systematically compares six design dimensions: text encoder, KG embedding model, projection head, triple composition, training direction, and hard-negatives sampling. A new benchmark corpus, CTD-Align, is constructed with over 22K one-to-one triple-document pairs linking chemical-gene interactions to PubMed passages.
AI.result: Triple composition and training direction (shared retrieval space) have the greatest impact on alignment quality, while text encoder choice and hard-negatives sampling matter little. The best configuration projects text into the KG space using a linear head over concatenated subject, predicate, and object embeddings.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight contrastive alignment is an effective and practical foundation for bridging biomedical text and KGs, with simple design choices outperforming more complex alternatives.

title: Your AI, On a Dial: Controlling Investment Bias in LLMs with a Single Neuron
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in investment decision-making, yet prior work shows that they exhibit systematic, model-specific investment preferences. We study whether a model's overall investment stance can be calibrated to a specified direction and strength. We introduce an investment-bias dial, an inference-time intervention on a single neuron that continuously adjusts a model-level decision prior---its overall tendency toward buying or selling---without targeting specific firms or investment attributes. Using matched positive and negative evidence, we evaluate five open-weight LLMs and find that the dial produces monotonic changes in investment stance without modifying prompts or model parameters. At the response level, the dial shifts both investment decisions and the evidential emphasis of generated rationales under identical inputs. In an agentic retrieval setting, the dial also changes what information the model searches for, which evidence it selects, and which evidence is reflected in its final analysis. In a long-context evaluation, the dial maintains stable stance control as context length increases, whereas a matched system-prompt instruction progressively attenuates. We further show that changes in the dial propagate to security rankings and downstream portfolio composition in an exploratory backtest. Overall, our results show that an LLM's aggregate investment stance can be calibrated toward a specified target at inference time.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an "investment-bias dial"—an inference-time intervention on a single neuron that continuously adjusts an LLM's overall tendency toward buying or selling—and demonstrates its effectiveness across five open-weight LLMs, including shifts in investment decisions, rationales, information retrieval, long-context stability, and downstream portfolio outcomes.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in investment decision-making but exhibit systematic, model-specific investment preferences. The authors aim to determine whether a model's overall investment stance can be calibrated to a specified direction and strength at inference time.
AI.method: The authors introduce an inference-time intervention on a single neuron acting as an "investment-bias dial" that continuously adjusts a model-level decision prior (overall buy/sell tendency) without modifying prompts or parameters. They evaluate five open-weight LLMs using matched positive and negative evidence, testing across response-level decisions, agentic retrieval settings, long-context scenarios, and an exploratory backtest.
AI.result: The dial produces monotonic changes in investment stance across all five models without prompt or parameter modification. It shifts investment decisions and evidential emphasis in rationales under identical inputs, changes what information the model searches for and selects in agentic retrieval, maintains stable stance control as context length increases (whereas system-prompt instructions attenuate), and propagates to security rankings and downstream portfolio composition.
AI.conclusion: An LLM's aggregate investment stance can be effectively calibrated toward a specified target at inference time via a single-neuron intervention, offering a more robust alternative to prompt-based calibration, particularly in long-context settings.

title: Large-Small Model Collaboration for Zero-Shot Surgical Phase Recognition
summary: Task-specific lightweight models for surgical phase recognition excel at capturing temporal dynamics but generalize poorly under domain shift. Conversely, surgical foundation models (FMs) offer superior transferability via large-scale pretraining, yet their lack of explicit temporal modeling often yields temporally inconsistent predictions, leading to degraded performance. To exploit the complementary strengths of both paradigms, we propose \textbf{La}rge-\textbf{S}mall \textbf{T}emporal adaptation (\textbf{LaST}), a novel large-small collaborative framework that enables zero-shot adaptation to unseen clinical domains. In LaST, the FM initiates the pipeline by generating frame-level phase priors that serve as initial weak supervision. To effectively utilize these noisy phase priors, we introduce an iterative temporal refinement scheme that integrates dynamic quality control to filter reliable predictions and dual-model cross-learning to mitigate confirmation bias. Simultaneously, the lightweight model leverages its intrinsic temporal modeling ability to progressively correct inconsistent predictions and enhance overall accuracy across iterations. At the end, a cycle replay strategy is employed to close the loop: the refined, more accurate predictions are utilized as upgraded supervision signals for the subsequent iterations, fostering a self-reinforcing evolution of both label quality and model capability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LaST achieves robust adaptation to unseen domains for zero-shot surgical phase recognition, outperforming the baseline (PeskaVLP) by 24.85\%-43.17\% in accuracy and even surpassing fully supervised linear probing and several state-of-the-art few-shot approaches. Codes will be released at https://github.com/YIYIZH/LaST.

AI.tldr: LaST is a large-small temporal adaptation framework for zero-shot surgical phase recognition, combining a surgical foundation model's transferability with a lightweight model's temporal modeling via iterative refinement, cycle replay, and dynamic quality control, achieving 24.85%-43.17% accuracy improvements over the baseline while surpassing fully supervised linear probing.
AI.motivation: Task-specific lightweight models excel at temporal dynamics but generalize poorly under domain shift, while surgical foundation models offer superior transferability but lack explicit temporal modeling, leading to temporally inconsistent predictions. The paper aims to exploit the complementary strengths of both paradigms.
AI.method: LaST introduces a large-small collaborative framework where the foundation model generates frame-level phase priors as weak supervision, followed by an iterative temporal refinement scheme with dynamic quality control for filtering reliable predictions and dual-model cross-learning to mitigate confirmation bias. A cycle replay strategy closes the loop by using refined predictions as upgraded supervision signals for subsequent iterations.
AI.result: LaST achieves robust zero-shot adaptation to unseen clinical domains for surgical phase recognition, outperforming the PeskaVLP baseline by 24.85%-43.17% in accuracy and surpassing fully supervised linear probing and several state-of-the-art few-shot approaches.
AI.conclusion: The proposed LaST framework demonstrates that a self-reinforcing evolution of both label quality and model capability through iterative collaboration between large foundation models and small temporal models enables effective domain-shift adaptation in surgical phase recognition.

title: A Multi-Domain and Multi-Task Generative Framework with Explicit Task and Domain Conditioning for Cross-Domain Event Extraction
summary: Event extraction aims to identify event triggers, classify event types, and extract arguments to construct structured event representations. Despite strong in-domain performance, developing models that generalize robustly across domains remains challenging due to variations in contextual expressions and event schemas. Prior unified and multi-task approaches improve in-domain accuracy but exhibit limited flexibility when applied to unseen domains. Even large language model-based methods that provide full event ontologies at inference time often underperform compared to smaller, task-specific fine-tuned models. We propose a unified multi-domain and multi-task training framework that models heterogeneous event schemas within a single model. Our approach introduces domain conditioning signals, jointly with task-specific prompts, enabling dynamic adaptation to dataset-specific schemas without requiring complete event label sets at inference time. The framework supports both pipeline and end-to-end extraction settings, facilitating efficient task- and domain-level transfer. Experiments on diverse event extraction benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves competitive performance, strong cross-domain generalization, and practical scalability, while preserving domain-specific precision.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a unified multi-domain, multi-task training framework for event extraction that models heterogeneous event schemas within a single model using domain conditioning signals and task-specific prompts, achieving competitive performance and strong cross-domain generalization without requiring complete event label sets at inference.
AI.motivation: Event extraction models struggle to generalize across domains due to variations in contextual expressions and event schemas. Prior unified and multi-task approaches improve in-domain accuracy but lack flexibility on unseen domains, and LLM-based methods providing full event ontologies often underperform smaller fine-tuned models. A unified framework enabling dynamic schema adaptation within a single model is needed.
AI.method: The proposed framework is a unified multi-domain, multi-task training approach that integrates heterogeneous event schemas into a single model. It introduces domain conditioning signals combined with task-specific prompts, allowing dynamic adaptation to dataset-specific schemas without requiring complete event label sets at inference. The framework supports both pipeline and end-to-end extraction settings to enable task- and domain-level transfer.
AI.result: Experiments on diverse event extraction benchmarks show the method achieves competitive performance, strong cross-domain generalization, practical scalability, and preserves domain-specific precision.
AI.conclusion: The unified multi-domain and multi-task training framework enables a single model to handle heterogeneous event schemas effectively, offering competitive performance and robust cross-domain generalization while maintaining domain-specific precision and practical scalability.

title: Proxy reliance in large language model decisions is uncalibrated to predictive evidence
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are entering decisions in triage and lending, where task-relevant inference must be distinguished from impermissible proxy use. Current audits ask whether decisions change when demographics change. But attributes correlated with a protected group carry predictive value, so a changed decision can be discrimination or sound inference. We measure causal proxy effects in four LLMs on a clinical-ranking task with known ground truth, where the reliance the evidence warrants can be computed exactly and used as the reference. One audit signal yields three verdicts: over-reliance, warranted and under-reliance. Under neutral labels every model relies on proxies with no information. Informative proxies draw all three. Social field names push reliance down, below the reference in one model. Two findings explain this. Reliance severely undertracks the evidence, and social-label suppression is fragile, since in-context examples raise it above zero in every model. Accuracy-based evaluation detects none of this.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a causal proxy effect audit for LLMs in high-stakes decision-making (triage, lending). Using a clinical-ranking task with exact ground truth, it measures whether LLMs over-rely, warrantedly rely, or under-rely on proxy attributes. Findings: neutral labels cause over-reliance on non-informative proxies; informative proxies produce all three outcomes; social field names suppress reliance (below reference in one model); reliance severely undertracks evidence; social-label suppression is fragile (in-context examples raise it above zero in every model); accuracy-based evaluation misses all of this.
AI.motivation: Current audits only ask whether decisions change with demographics, conflating discrimination with sound inference since demographics correlate with predictive attributes. A better causal benchmark is needed to distinguish impermissible proxy use from warranted reliance.
AI.method: The authors introduce a causal proxy effect audit measuring reliance against an exact reference computed from ground truth in a clinical-ranking task. Four LLMs are tested under neutral labels and informative/social field-name conditions, yielding per-model verdicts of over-reliance, warranted reliance, or under-reliance.
AI.result: All models over-rely on non-informative proxies under neutral labels. Informative proxies yield all three verdicts. Social field names lower reliance (below reference in one model). Reliance significantly undertracks evidence, and in-context examples raise suppressed social-label reliance above zero in every model. Accuracy-based evaluation detects none of these effects.
AI.conclusion: The proposed audit reveals nuanced proxy reliance behaviors that standard accuracy-based or change-based audits miss, highlighting fragile social-label suppression and the need for reference-anchored causal evaluations in high-stakes LLM decisions.

title: FOVEA: Focused On-Demand Visual Evidence Adaptation for Cache-Friendly Multimodal Speculative Decoding
summary: Multimodal speculative decoding accelerates vision-language models by allowing a lightweight draft model to propose candidate tokens for parallel verification by a larger target model. Existing methods typically condition the drafter on a fixed visual interface, such as a predefined visual-token budget or a static compressed representation. However, our controlled visual-budget analysis shows that visual demand varies substantially across tasks and decoding stages, which means more visual input is not always beneficial. Actually, insufficient evidence may weaken visual grounding, while excessive context adds overhead and may disrupt drafting. We propose FOVEA (Focused On-demand Visual Evidence Adaptation), a cache-friendly approach that builds a reusable visual memory and dynamically retrieves a bounded subset for a draft state. A cumulative-mass rule determines both how many and which entries are selected. The selected entries are aggregated into a visual readout and fused with the current draft hidden state through a lightweight gated residual correction. Rather than inserting visual tokens into the autoregressive context, the correction modifies only the representation passed to the language-model head. Experiments across multiple vision-language backbones and multimodal benchmarks show that FOVEA improves draft acceptance and end-to-end decoding speed, achieving up to $2.13\times$ speedup over autoregressive decoding.
