These results demonstrate that state-conditioned evidence retrieval is an effective alternative to reusing a fixed visual representation throughout multimodal generation.

AI.tldr: FOVEA is a cache-friendly multimodal speculative decoding method that dynamically retrieves a bounded subset of visual evidence conditioned on the current draft state, using a cumulative-mass rule to select both how many and which visual entries to retrieve. It aggregates selected entries into a visual readout fused with the draft hidden state via a lightweight gated residual correction, achieving up to 2.13x speedup over autoregressive decoding.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal speculative decoding methods rely on a fixed visual interface (e.g., predefined visual-token budgets or static compressed representations), but controlled visual-budget analysis shows visual demand varies substantially across tasks and decoding stages—more visual input is not always beneficial. Insufficient evidence weakens visual grounding while excessive context adds overhead and may disrupt drafting.
AI.method: FOVEA builds a reusable visual memory and dynamically retrieves a bounded subset for each draft state. A cumulative-mass rule determines both the number and identity of selected entries. Selected entries are aggregated into a visual readout and fused with the current draft hidden state through a lightweight gated residual correction, modifying only the representation passed to the language-model head rather than inserting visual tokens into the autoregressive context.
AI.result: Across multiple vision-language backbones and multimodal benchmarks, FOVEA improves draft acceptance and end-to-end decoding speed, achieving up to 2.13x speedup over autoregressive decoding.
AI.conclusion: State-conditioned evidence retrieval is an effective alternative to reusing a fixed visual representation throughout multimodal generation.

title: Credal Large Language Models for Semantic Commitment under Uncertainty
summary: Large language models (LLMs) often produce fluent but incorrect answers with unwarranted confidence. A central limitation is that standard LLMs represent uncertainty through a single predictive distribution, conflating epistemic ignorance with genuine ambiguity. We introduce Credal Large Language Models (CLLMs): an ensemble of LoRA adapters induces a credal set whose lower and upper probabilities expose the spread of plausible predictive distributions rather than collapsing to a single softmax output. From this representation we derive two complementary commitment scores. Credal Token Commitment (CTC) is a token-space score that combines lower-bound support, credal width, and intersection entropy, computed without additional generation. Semantic Commitment Consistency (SCC) extends commitment to semantic space using sampled completions, with SCC-Gap measuring the mismatch between token-level and semantic-level support. We evaluate hallucination detection, calibration, selective prediction, and reasoning on Gemma-2-9B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B across OpenBookQA, CoQA, TriviaQA, and ARC-Challenge. CLLM is the best method on QA accuracy at competitive expected calibration error, and CTC tracks the best hallucination AUROC within 1.5 pp on most settings without additional generation. On selective prediction at 80% coverage, CLLM with SCC reaches 99.0% accuracy on OpenBookQA, and on ARC-Challenge CLLM with Csem confidence achieves <= 0.6% ECE across the three backbones.

AI.tldr: Credal Large Language Models (CLLMs) use an ensemble of LoRA adapters to induce a credal set of predictive distributions, exposing uncertainty as lower/upper probabilities rather than collapsing to a single softmax output. Two commitment scores—Credal Token Commitment (CTC) and Semantic Commitment Consistency (SCC)—are derived for hallucination detection, calibration, and selective prediction. Evaluated on Gemma-2-9B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B across four QA datasets, CLLM achieves best QA accuracy at competitive ECE, near-best hallucination AUROC without extra generation, and superior selective prediction performance.
AI.motivation: Standard LLMs conflate epistemic ignorance (uncertainty due to lack of knowledge) with genuine ambiguity (inherent uncertainty in the question/answer space) by representing uncertainty through a single predictive distribution, leading to fluent but overconfident incorrect answers.
AI.method: CLLMs are constructed as an ensemble of LoRA adapters that produce a credal set of predictive distributions. From this, two scores are derived: (1) CTC, a token-space score combining lower-bound support, credal width, and intersection entropy computed without extra generation; and (2) SCC, a semantic-space score using sampled completions, with SCC-Gap measuring the mismatch between token-level and semantic-level support.
AI.result: On Gemma-2-9B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B across OpenBookQA, CoQA, TriviaQA, and ARC-Challenge: CLLM achieves the best QA accuracy at competitive expected calibration error; CTC matches the best hallucination AUROC within 1.5 percentage points on most settings without additional generation; CLLM with SCC reaches 99.0% accuracy on OpenBookQA at 80% coverage; CLLM with Csem confidence achieves ≤0.6% ECE on ARC-Challenge across all three backbones.
AI.conclusion: Modeling uncertainty via a credal set—rather than a single predictive distribution—allows LLMs to separate epistemic ignorance from genuine ambiguity, improving hallucination detection, calibration, and selective prediction while maintaining competitive accuracy.

title: CDEG: Learning Decision-Critical Evidence for Long-Horizon Diagnostic Agents
summary: Unlike static medical question answering, long-horizon diagnosis captures the sequential nature of clinical practice: evidence is progressively acquired, integrated, and evaluated over multiple rounds of interaction before reaching a final diagnosis. However, existing doctor agents often fail when critical evidence is either not acquired or not adequately incorporated into diagnostic reasoning. Recent agentic approaches attempt to address these failures by reusing historical trajectories or distilled memories. But their diagnostic gains remain constrained because such experience may contain noisy or incidental information and is typically reused without validating which evidence actually drives diagnostic decisions. To address this limitation, we introduce CDEG, a graph-based framework that learns reusable decision-critical evidence from historical diagnostic trajectories. CDEG contrasts successful and failed trajectories from the same case to identify candidate evidence, validates their diagnostic impact through controlled counterfactual interventions, and organizes the resulting diagnosis--evidence--action relations into a structured graph. During inference, CDEG tracks the evolving patient evidence state to retrieve relevant diagnostic relations and selectively guide missing evidence acquisition or overlooked evidence reappraisal. Across in-domain and out-of-distribution benchmarks with multiple doctor agent backbones, CDEG consistently improves diagnostic performance, achieving up to an 11.5% accuracy gain over vanilla agents. These results demonstrate that reliable long-horizon diagnosis requires moving beyond trajectory-level experience reuse toward evidence-level learning of the factors that truly shape clinical decisions.

AI.tldr: CDEG is a graph-based framework that learns decision-critical evidence from historical diagnostic trajectories by contrasting successful and failed cases, validating impact via counterfactual interventions, and organizing diagnosis-evidence-action relations into a structured graph to guide long-horizon diagnosis, achieving up to 11.5% accuracy gains over vanilla doctor agents.
AI.motivation: Existing doctor agents for long-horizon diagnosis fail when critical evidence is not acquired or not adequately incorporated into diagnostic reasoning. Prior agentic approaches that reuse historical trajectories or distilled memories yield limited gains because such experience may contain noisy or incidental information and is reused without validating which evidence actually drives diagnostic decisions.
AI.method: CDEG contrasts successful and failed trajectories from the same case to identify candidate evidence, validates the diagnostic impact of this evidence through controlled counterfactual interventions, and organizes the resulting diagnosis-evidence-action relations into a structured graph. During inference, it tracks the evolving patient evidence state to retrieve relevant diagnostic relations and selectively guide missing evidence acquisition or overlooked evidence reappraisal.
AI.result: Across in-domain and out-of-distribution benchmarks with multiple doctor agent backbones, CDEG consistently improves diagnostic performance, achieving up to an 11.5% accuracy gain over vanilla agents.
AI.conclusion: Reliable long-horizon diagnosis requires moving beyond trajectory-level experience reuse toward evidence-level learning of the factors that truly shape clinical decisions.

title: DRAgent: Discriminative Reasoning Agent for Referring Expression Segmentation
summary: Referring Expression Segmentation (RES) aims to generate a pixel-level mask for the object specified by a language expression. Recent methods based on multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often rely on one-pass coordinate prediction for visual localization, which serializes continuous spatial locations as discrete text tokens and may lead to localization bias and alignment errors. To address these issues, we propose DRAgent, an MLLM-driven discriminative reasoning (DR) framework for RES. Instead of requiring the MLLM to generate localization coordinates, DRAgent first constructs a detector-generated candidate space and then uses the MLLM as a visual-semantic target discriminator. Specifically, the MLLM performs reliable target selection among potential distractors through a two-stage DR mechanism, which first screens high-recall candidates and then performs instance-wise verification. The selected target box is subsequently used as a spatial prompt for a foundation segmentation model to produce the final pixel-level mask. Furthermore, we construct a self-consistency-filtered reasoning-chain data pipeline for LoRA-based fine-tuning, providing more reliable supervision for enhancing the MLLM's discriminative reasoning capability. Experiments demonstrate that DRAgent achieves competitive performance on RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg.

AI.tldr: DRAgent is an MLLM-driven discriminative reasoning framework for Referring Expression Segmentation that avoids one-pass coordinate prediction by using a detector-generated candidate space, a two-stage discriminative reasoning mechanism for target selection, and a foundation segmentation model for final mask generation.
AI.motivation: Existing RES methods based on multimodal large language models rely on one-pass coordinate prediction that serializes continuous spatial locations as discrete text tokens, leading to localization bias and alignment errors.
AI.method: DRAgent first constructs a detector-generated candidate space instead of requiring the MLLM to generate localization coordinates. The MLLM acts as a visual-semantic target discriminator through a two-stage discriminative reasoning mechanism: high-recall candidate screening followed by instance-wise verification. The selected target box is used as a spatial prompt for a foundation segmentation model. Additionally, a self-consistency-filtered reasoning-chain data pipeline is constructed for LoRA-based fine-tuning.
AI.result: DRAgent achieves competitive performance on RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: By shifting the MLLM's role from coordinate generator to target discriminator within a candidate space, DRAgent effectively mitigates localization bias and alignment errors, demonstrating that discriminative reasoning is a viable alternative to direct coordinate prediction in MLLM-based RES.

title: Future Querying: Can LLMs Serve as Implicit Medical World Models?
comment: This paper is accepted at The 1st MICCAI Workshop on Medical World Models (MICCAI-2026)
summary: Traditional clinical prediction models rely on task-specific pipelines and curated, structured data, which scale poorly and underutilize unstructured text. To address this, we introduce future querying, a paradigm that probes whether large language models (LLMs) can function as implicit medical world models by evaluating their ability to answer time-indexed clinical queries about a patient's future. Our framework operates on unstructured clinical documentation using endpoint-agnostic training, enabling a single model to answer diverse clinical queries over patient trajectories without manual feature engineering or task-specific retraining. We show that small, locally fine-tuned open-weight models can match or approach larger proprietary systems, making the framework suitable for privacy-preserving, on-premise deployment. Evaluated on a new synthetic medical reports dataset and real ICU notes from the MIMIC-IV dataset, our results provide encouraging evidence that LLMs can capture aspects of clinical dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "future querying," a paradigm for using LLMs as implicit medical world models by answering time-indexed clinical queries about a patient's future from unstructured text, trained endpoint-agnostically without task-specific feature engineering.
AI.motivation: Traditional clinical prediction models depend on task-specific pipelines and curated structured data, which scale poorly and fail to leverage unstructured clinical text. The authors aim to create a more flexible, scalable approach to clinical prediction.
AI.method: The framework uses endpoint-agnostic training on unstructured clinical documentation, enabling a single LLM to answer diverse time-indexed clinical queries about patient trajectories. Small, locally fine-tuned open-weight models are used to support privacy-preserving on-premise deployment, evaluated on a synthetic medical reports dataset and real ICU notes from MIMIC-IV.
AI.result: Small, locally fine-tuned open-weight LLMs match or approach larger proprietary systems in answering future clinical queries, providing encouraging evidence that LLMs can capture aspects of clinical dynamics from unstructured data.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can serve as implicit medical world models for clinical prediction directly from unstructured text, and the endpoint-agnostic, privacy-preserving approach offers a practical alternative to task-specific clinical prediction pipelines.

title: Beyond Observed Auxiliary Relations: Environment-Conditioned Modeling for Multi-Behavior Recommendation
comment: Accepted at CIKM 2026 (35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management). 11 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables
summary: Multi-behavior recommendation (MBR) leverages auxiliary behavioral signals, such as clicks and add-to-cart, to enhance target behavior prediction like purchases. While recent graph neural network-based approaches have achieved strong performance by systematically propagating auxiliary behavior signals, they still suffer from two fundamental challenges inherent to auxiliary behaviors: (1) missing auxiliary signals, which hinder generalization to items without auxiliary observations, and (2) unreliable auxiliary signals, which amplify noise misaligned with the target behavior. To address these challenges in a unified manner, we propose BOAR, an environment-conditioned MBR framework that addresses missing and unreliable auxiliary signals through two complementary modules conditioned on auxiliary observability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BOAR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving up to 7.82% gains in HR@10 overall and up to 44.2% gains for target items without auxiliary observations, highlighting its ability to capture hidden preferences beyond observed auxiliary relations. Our code is available at: https://github.com/LSH0411/BOAR.

AI.tldr: BOAR is an environment-conditioned multi-behavior recommendation framework that unifies handling of missing and unreliable auxiliary behavioral signals via two modules conditioned on auxiliary observability, achieving up to 7.82% HR@10 gains overall and 44.2% gains on items without auxiliary observations.
AI.motivation: Existing graph neural network-based MBR methods propagate auxiliary behavior signals effectively but suffer from two fundamental issues: (1) missing auxiliary signals hinder generalization to items lacking auxiliary observations, and (2) unreliable auxiliary signals amplify noise that is misaligned with the target behavior. These two challenges need to be addressed in a unified manner.
AI.method: BOAR is an environment-conditioned MBR framework with two complementary modules conditioned on auxiliary observability to jointly address both missing and unreliable auxiliary signals within a unified information environment.
AI.result: BOAR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving up to 7.82% gains in HR@10 overall and up to 44.2% gains for target items without auxiliary observations, demonstrating strong capability in capturing hidden preferences.
AI.conclusion: BOAR effectively handles both missing and unreliable auxiliary signals in multi-behavior recommendation through environment-conditioned modules, showing significant improvements especially for items with no auxiliary observations, and the code is publicly released.

title: NemoSplat: Feed-Forward 4D Gaussian Splatting for Media-Aware Underwater Reconstruction
summary: Reconstructing photorealistic scenes in unconstrained underwater environments remains challenging due to severe media-induced light scattering and unpredictable dynamic objects. Recent feed-forward visual foundation models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in generalized novel view synthesis and tracking. However, when directly applied to aquatic videos, optical attenuation and motion interference fatally corrupt their feature aggregation, leading to severe tracking and reconstruction failures. To overcome these limitations, we present NemoSplat, the first feed-forward 4D Gaussian Splatting framework tailored for media-aware dynamic reconstruction directly from uncalibrated marine videos. Beyond providing robust estimations of camera poses and dense scene depth, we devise a Promptable Dynamic Disentangler that utilizes a confidence-aware fusion strategy of learned dynamic probabilities and optional semantic text priors, effectively isolating massive transient entities. Furthermore, to counteract visual degradation, a Media-Aware Gaussian Predictor is formulated to jointly estimate intrinsic 3D Gaussian attributes alongside physical media parameters, rendering pristine scene appearance in a single forward pass. Additionally, we introduce a large-scale underwater dataset with massive dynamic elements to facilitate training and evaluation. Extensive experiments on our dataset demonstrate that NemoSplat achieves state-of-the-art tracking accuracy and high-fidelity rendering. Homepage: https://nemosplat.hkustvgd.com

AI.tldr: NemoSplat is the first feed-forward 4D Gaussian Splatting framework for media-aware dynamic reconstruction from uncalibrated underwater videos, addressing light scattering and dynamic object interference through a Promptable Dynamic Disentangler and a Media-Aware Gaussian Predictor.
AI.motivation: Reconstructing photorealistic scenes in unconstrained underwater environments is challenging due to severe media-induced light scattering and unpredictable dynamic objects. Existing feed-forward visual foundation models fail when applied to aquatic videos because optical attenuation and motion interference corrupt their feature aggregation, leading to tracking and reconstruction failures.
AI.method: NemoSplat introduces a feed-forward 4D Gaussian Splatting framework with three key components: (1) robust estimation of camera poses and dense scene depth, (2) a Promptable Dynamic Disentangler using confidence-aware fusion of learned dynamic probabilities and optional semantic text priors to isolate transient entities, and (3) a Media-Aware Gaussian Predictor that jointly estimates intrinsic 3D Gaussian attributes and physical media parameters in a single forward pass. A large-scale underwater dataset with massive dynamic elements is also introduced for training and evaluation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that NemoSplat achieves state-of-the-art tracking accuracy and high-fidelity rendering on the introduced underwater dataset.
AI.conclusion: NemoSplat effectively overcomes media-induced degradation and dynamic interference in unconstrained aquatic environments, delivering advanced tracking and photorealistic reconstruction capabilities through a unified feed-forward framework.

title: A Scalable Cross-Domain Event Extraction System via a Unified Generative Training Framework
summary: Event extraction is fundamental to information extraction. Prior approaches often separate event detection and argument extraction or depend on dataset-specific designs, limiting scalability and cross-domain generalization. We propose a unified generative sequence-to-sequence framework that performs event extraction subtasks jointly and supports both pipeline and end-to-end configurations. We fine-tune pretrained language models on multiple event datasets across diverse domains, enabling a single model to retain domain-specific semantics while generalizing over large and evolving label spaces. We demonstrate these capabilities through a web-based application tailored for researchers and practitioners. The platform supports document upload, schema-aware event extraction, visualization of triggers and arguments, and comparison of different extraction configurations across domains.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a unified generative sequence-to-sequence framework for event extraction that jointly handles all subtasks, supports both pipeline and end-to-end configurations, and is fine-tuned on multiple datasets across diverse domains to enable a single model to generalize over large and evolving label spaces. The authors also present a web-based application for researchers featuring document upload, schema-aware extraction, visualization, and cross-domain configuration comparison.
AI.motivation: Prior event extraction approaches either separate event detection from argument extraction or rely on dataset-specific designs, which limits scalability and cross-domain generalization.
AI.method: A unified generative seq2seq framework that jointly performs event extraction subtasks, fine-tuned on pretrained language models across multiple event datasets and domains, supporting both pipeline and end-to-end configurations.
AI.result: The framework enables a single model to retain domain-specific semantics while generalizing over large and evolving label spaces. A web-based application demonstrates capabilities including document upload, schema-aware event extraction, visualization of triggers and arguments, and comparison of extraction configurations across domains.
AI.conclusion: The proposed unified generative framework improves scalability and cross-domain generalization for event extraction by learning jointly across multiple datasets and domains, with a practical web-based tool supporting researchers and practitioners.

title: Concepts for Securing Agentic AI Coding and the Terok Environment
comment: to be published in the proceedings of the AGENSYS workshop (Workshop on Knowledge Discovery, Maintenance and Distributed Intelligence in Multi-Agent Systems) at ECML PKDD 2026 conference in Sept. 2026
summary:
Agentic AI is a fascinating new tool for software development. It is a huge step forward compared to "conventional" AI assisted coding, which in turn was a considerable breakthrough earlier. AI support through LLMs is a young and very fast-moving field. The "conventional" (non-agentic) flavor became useful and productive in early 2025 (around 18 months ago) and the agentic flavor followed in fall 2025 (approximately 9 months ago). Besides all its benefits and potential, it also carries some fundamental risks for IT security. And the agentic approach added very severe risks while making others much more dangerous.
  With all the motivation to explore this fascinating new tool we should not ignore the risks but actively address them. We present (I) an assessment of the IT security risks, (II) a concept for mitigating them without breaking its benefits, and (III) an overview about an implementation of our concept. In this very dynamic field this is likely not the final and once-and-for-all answer to the identified issues but still a substantial step forward in responsible usage of Agentic AI for software development. It should also be a contribution to the community to allow early and eager evaluation of the potential of agentic AI for software development without actually suffering from its implied IT security risks.

AI.tldr: This paper assesses IT security risks introduced by Agentic AI for software development, proposes a mitigation concept that preserves its benefits, and presents an overview of an implementation of that concept.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI for software development brings significant benefits but also introduces severe IT security risks beyond those of conventional AI-assisted coding. The authors argue these risks must be actively addressed rather than ignored, motivating a systematic risk assessment and mitigation approach.
AI.method: The paper presents three contributions: (I) an assessment of IT security risks associated with Agentic AI in software development, (II) a concept for mitigating these risks without sacrificing the benefits, and (III) an overview of an implementation of the proposed concept.
AI.result: The paper delivers a structured risk assessment for Agentic AI systems, a mitigation concept designed to preserve the tool's benefits, and an implemented proof-of-concept overview, serving as a practical step toward responsible usage of Agentic AI in software engineering.
AI.conclusion: The authors acknowledge that their work is likely not a final, definitive solution given the fast-moving nature of the field, but position it as a substantial contribution enabling early and eager adoption of Agentic AI for software development without exposing practitioners to its inherent IT security risks.

title: AquaFlow: A Monocular Gaussian Splatting SLAM for Underwater Streaming Reconstruction
summary: Recent monocular 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) streaming reconstruction methods have achieved impressive performance by balancing reconstruction quality and efficiency. However, extending these frameworks to underwater scenes remains challenging due to severe visual degradation, such as light attenuation and scattering, which degrades camera pose tracking and distorts scene geometry. To address these challenges, we propose AquaFlow, a monocular Gaussian Splatting streaming reconstruction framework for efficient and high-fidelity underwater reconstruction. Specifically, AquaFlow fine-tunes a 3D vision foundation model on large-scale underwater data for robust pose and pointmap estimation, and introduces a medium-guided incremental Gaussian initialization strategy for streaming mapping. Furthermore, we develop a streaming-compatible hybrid scene representation that integrates structured, distance-conditioned neural Gaussians with a physics-inspired optical model to compensate for underwater image formation effects, enabling accurate scene reconstruction. We evaluate AquaFlow on a comprehensive dataset of 62 diverse underwater trajectories, collected from both public benchmarks and in-the-wild web videos across various scales. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AquaFlow achieves state-of-the-art tracking and rendering performance, reducing average localization error by 13.2% and improving PSNR by 4.74 dB compared to WaterSplat-SLAM.

AI.tldr: AquaFlow is a monocular Gaussian Splatting streaming reconstruction framework that addresses underwater scene reconstruction by fine-tuning a 3D vision foundation model on underwater data for robust pose estimation, using a medium-guided incremental Gaussian initialization strategy, and integrating a physics-inspired optical model into a hybrid scene representation to compensate for underwater image formation effects. It achieves state-of-the-art results on 62 diverse underwater trajectories, reducing localization error by 13.2% and improving PSNR by 4.74 dB over WaterSplat-SLAM.
AI.motivation: Monocular 3DGS streaming reconstruction methods work well in general scenes but fail in underwater environments due to severe visual degradation (light attenuation and scattering), which degrades camera pose tracking and distorts scene geometry.
AI.method: The framework consists of three key components: (1) fine-tuning a 3D vision foundation model on large-scale underwater data for robust pose and pointmap estimation; (2) a medium-guided incremental Gaussian initialization strategy for streaming mapping; (3) a streaming-compatible hybrid scene representation combining structured, distance-conditioned neural Gaussians with a physics-inspired optical model to compensate for underwater image formation effects.
AI.result: Evaluated on 62 diverse underwater trajectories from public benchmarks and in-the-wild web videos, AquaFlow achieves state-of-the-art tracking and rendering performance, reducing average localization error by 13.2% and improving PSNR by 4.74 dB compared to WaterSplat-SLAM.
AI.conclusion: By integrating underwater-specific adaptations into the 3DGS streaming pipeline, AquaFlow enables efficient and high-fidelity real-time underwater scene reconstruction, demonstrating that domain-appropriate foundation model fine-tuning and physics-aware representations are effective for addressing visual degradation challenges in underwater environments.

title: EvoWiki: Incremental State Overwriting and Traceable Question Answering for Cross-Meeting Knowledge Evolution
summary: In long-term collaboration spanning multiple meetings, factual states such as decisions and risks are continually revised, overturned, and replaced. Existing long-context methods typically stack the entire history, while many RAG and structured-memory methods organize knowledge as static or append-only facts and rely on semantic relevance at read time. Without explicit modeling of knowledge lifecycles, these approaches may retain conflicting old and new states simultaneously or discard history, leading to stale retrieval and answers that are difficult to verify. We present EvoWiki, an incremental question-answering architecture for dynamic long-form text. EvoWiki decouples offline incremental construction (BUILD) from online structured reading (READ). BUILD captures the intra-meeting micro-evolution from proposal to decision and uses entity version chains and a fine-grained State-Overwrite Protocol to explicitly distinguish current valid states from superseded history while preserving meeting-level provenance anchors. READ bypasses relevance-based Top-k retrieval and performs deterministic entity addressing, temporal resolution, and cross-entity multi-hop aggregation over the complete Wiki to produce grounded and traceable answers. We further introduce CrossMeet, a high-fidelity bilingual benchmark designed to simulate long-term state evolution, covering factual consistency, temporal reasoning, and cross-meeting multi-hop reasoning. Across six datasets and two reader models, EvoWiki improves macro-average Judge Accuracy over the strongest baselines by 9.72 and 10.00 percentage points, respectively. Human evaluation shows that EvoWiki is more robust and factually faithful under frequent state flips, validating valid-state-oriented reading as a reliable approach to cross-meeting knowledge evolution.

AI.tldr: EvoWiki is an incremental QA architecture for dynamic long-form text that decouples offline construction (BUILD) from online reading (READ). It models knowledge lifecycles using entity version chains and a State-Overwrite Protocol to distinguish current valid states from superseded history while preserving provenance. A new bilingual benchmark (CrossMeet) is introduced, and EvoWiki outperforms strong baselines by ~10 percentage points in Judge Accuracy across six datasets and two reader models.
AI.motivation: Long-term collaborative text has frequently revised and overturned factual states (decisions, risks), but existing methods stack entire history, use static/append-only fact storage, or rely solely on semantic relevance at read time. This causes conflicting old/new states to coexist or history to be discarded, leading to stale retrieval and hard-to-verify answers.
AI.method: EvoWiki decouples offline incremental construction (BUILD) from online structured reading (READ). BUILD captures intra-meeting micro-evolution from proposal to decision using entity version chains and a fine-grained State-Overwrite Protocol, explicitly distinguishing current valid states from superseded history while preserving meeting-level provenance anchors. READ performs deterministic entity addressing, temporal resolution, and cross-entity multi-hop aggregation over the complete Wiki—bypassing relevance-based Top-k retrieval—to produce grounded and traceable answers. A new bilingual benchmark, CrossMeet, is introduced to simulate long-term state evolution.
AI.result: Across six datasets and two reader models, EvoWiki improves macro-average Judge Accuracy over the strongest baselines by 9.72 and 10.00 percentage points respectively. Human evaluation confirms EvoWiki is more robust and factually faithful under frequent state flips.
AI.conclusion: Valid-state-oriented reading is a reliable approach to cross-meeting knowledge evolution, demonstrating that explicit lifecycle modeling and deterministic structured reading outperform relevance-based retrieval for dynamic long-form question answering.

title: What Process Evaluation of Coding Agents Actually Measures: Action, Task, and Step Are Three Different Levels
summary: Coding agents are increasingly evaluated not only by whether they solve a task, but also by how they execute it. However, existing process-level evaluations often treat action prediction, task uncertainty, and step attribution as if they were the same problem, which makes it unclear what such evaluations actually measure. In this paper, we introduce a measurement framework for process evaluation in coding agents and instantiate step-level causal attribution with SCAE, a replay-based estimator derived from a structural causal model of agent execution. Our framework combines prefix-conditioned identification, replay/intervention-based estimation, and controlled judge-information manipulation to study process evaluation at the action, task, and step levels. Experiments on 499 file-localization episodes from 12 repositories show that next actions are driven primarily by execution provenance rather than code-graph transitions, execution uncertainty is structured at the task rather than step level, and full-trace judges exhibit systematic collider bias, suggesting that current process evaluation often measures semantic relevance rather than certified causal contribution.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a measurement framework for process-level evaluation of coding agents and proposes SCAE, a replay-based estimator for step-level causal attribution derived from a structural causal model. Experiments on 499 file-localization episodes across 12 repositories reveal that action prediction is driven by execution provenance, uncertainty is task-level, and full-trace judges exhibit collider bias—suggesting current process evaluations measure semantic relevance rather than causal contribution.
AI.motivation: Existing process-level evaluations of coding agents conflate action prediction, task uncertainty, and step attribution into a single problem, obscuring what such evaluations actually measure. A principled measurement framework is needed to disentangle these distinct aspects of process evaluation.
AI.method: The authors propose a measurement framework that combines (1) prefix-conditioned identification, (2) replay/intervention-based estimation instantiated via SCAE (a replay-based estimator from a structural causal model of agent execution), and (3) controlled judge-information manipulation. This framework enables studying process evaluation at action, task, and step levels separately.
AI.result: Experiments on 499 file-localization episodes from 12 repositories show: (a) next-action prediction is driven primarily by execution provenance rather than code-graph transitions; (b) execution uncertainty is structured at the task level rather than the step level; (c) full-trace judges exhibit systematic collider bias, indicating current process evaluation often measures semantic relevance rather than certified causal contribution.
AI.conclusion: Current process-level evaluations of coding agents may be measuring the wrong construct—semantic relevance rather than causal contribution. The proposed framework and SCAE estimator provide a principled foundation for disentangling action, task, and step-level process evaluation, with implications for how coding agents should be assessed and compared.

title: Results of the 1st Asynchronous CASTLE Challenge at the Joint Egocentric Vision Workshop in Conjunction with CVPR 2026
summary: This report summarizes the contributions and results of the 1st Asynchronous CASTLE Challenge at the Joint Egocentric Vision Workshop in conjunction with CVPR 2026.

AI.tldr: A summary report of the 1st Asynchronous CASTLE Challenge held at the Joint Egocentric Vision Workshop with CVPR 2026, covering the event's contributions and results.
AI.motivation: The abstract does not provide explicit motivation, but the challenge is presumably motivated by advancing asynchronous egocentric vision research through a competitive benchmarking platform.
AI.method: The abstract does not describe a specific method; it is a challenge summary rather than a technical methodology paper.
AI.result: The abstract mentions that contributions and results of the challenge are summarized, but specific results are not detailed in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The paper serves as a report documenting the outcomes of the 1st Asynchronous CASTLE Challenge at CVPR 2026's Joint Egocentric Vision Workshop.

title: Dynamic Topic Modeling for Cross-Corpus Temporal Analysis
summary: Dynamic Embedded Topic Models (D-ETM) provide an interpretable framework for modeling temporal semantic evolution, but cross-corpus comparison remains difficult because topics are often learned independently and aligned only after training, a process that does not guarantee stable topic correspondence across corpora and time. To address this problem, we propose a D-ETM framework that first learns a common dynamic topic space over a merged multi-corpus collection, which we call the shared backbone, then introduces corpus-specific residual adaptation around the frozen backbone without creating separate latent topic spaces. This design preserves a shared topic index for cross-corpus comparison while allowing each corpus to specialize lexically. We evaluate the framework on three temporally structured corpora spanning 97 years: the Corpus of Historical American English, Harvard Business Review, and International Labour Review. Residual adaptation improves corpus-specific fit relative to the shared backbone while preserving the same-index cross-corpus topic trajectories, achieving substantially stronger alignment than full fine-tuning from the same backbone, with $97.5 \pm 0.7\%$ versus $17.9 \pm 1.1\%$ trajectory Retrieval@1, as well as stronger alignment than independent training with post-hoc Hungarian matching. These results suggest that incorporating topic alignment into the model can support more stable over-time cross-corpus comparisons while retaining corpus-specific lexical variation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Dynamic Embedded Topic Model (D-ETM) framework that learns a shared backbone topic space over merged multi-corpus data, then applies corpus-specific residual adaptation around the frozen backbone to enable stable cross-corpus topic alignment while preserving lexical specialization. Evaluated on three historical corpora spanning 97 years, residual adaptation achieves 97.5% trajectory Retrieval@1 compared to 17.9% for full fine-tuning and outperforms post-hoc Hungarian matching.
AI.motivation: Dynamic Embedded Topic Models struggle with cross-corpus comparison because topics are learned independently per corpus and aligned only after training, which does not guarantee stable topic correspondence across corpora and time.
AI.method: First learn a common dynamic topic space (shared backbone) over a merged multi-corpus collection, then introduce corpus-specific residual adaptation around the frozen backbone without creating separate latent topic spaces, preserving a shared topic index for comparison while allowing lexical specialization.
AI.result: Residual adaptation achieves 97.5 ± 0.7% trajectory Retrieval@1 versus 17.9 ± 1.1% for full fine-tuning from the same backbone, and also outperforms independent training with post-hoc Hungarian matching on the same-index cross-corpus topic trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating topic alignment into the model supports more stable over-time cross-corpus comparisons while retaining corpus-specific lexical variation.

title: Buried in Textual Debt: Context Pruning with Visual Evidence Preservation for MLLM Agents
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed as multi-step agents, where explicit reasoning supports task decomposition and tool coordination but also accumulates self-generated text. Over long trajectories, this text can dominate the context and suppress visual evidence, creating textual debt. We observe that reasoning becomes redundant once task-relevant visual evidence is grounded, while stale hypotheses can misguide later inference when grounding remains uncertain. Pruning must therefore remove redundant text without discarding visual evidence. We propose SPARE, a Kullback--Leibler (KL)-guided framework for pruning accumulated reasoning in multimodal tool-use agents. SPARE uses a compact task-state summary as privileged diagnostic context. For each candidate segment, it replays the same model under the original and summary-conditioned contexts. Reverse-KL divergence from on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) then tests whether the summary sufficiently covers the segment without disrupting future reasoning. We further fine-tune the summarizer with supervised fine-tuning (SFT), enabling more compact summaries, broader coverage, and more aggressive pruning. Across multi-step visual tool-use benchmarks, SPARE achieves the highest average accuracy among pruning methods while removing 37.89--64.58\% of reasoning tokens. This favorable accuracy--context trade-off shows that reducing textual dominance restores reliance on visual evidence and mitigates over-conditioning on self-generated language.

AI.tldr: SPARE is a KL-guided framework that prunes redundant accumulated reasoning text in multimodal tool-use LLM agents by using compact task-state summaries as diagnostic context and reverse-KL divergence from on-policy self-distillation to decide what to prune, achieving high accuracy while removing 37.89–64.58% of reasoning tokens.
AI.motivation: MLLMs deployed as multi-step agents accumulate self-generated reasoning text over long trajectories, which can dominate the context and suppress visual evidence—a phenomenon termed "textual debt." Pruning must remove redundant text without discarding visual evidence, and stale hypotheses can misguide later inference when grounding is uncertain.
AI.method: SPARE uses a compact task-state summary as privileged diagnostic context. For each candidate reasoning segment, it replays the same model under both the original and summary-conditioned contexts. Reverse-KL divergence from on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) tests whether the summary sufficiently covers the segment without disrupting future reasoning. The summarizer is further fine-tuned with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for more compact summaries, broader coverage, and more aggressive pruning.
AI.result: Across multi-step visual tool-use benchmarks, SPARE achieves the highest average accuracy among pruning methods while removing 37.89–64.58% of reasoning tokens, demonstrating a favorable accuracy–context trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Reducing textual dominance in multimodal agent trajectories restores reliance on visual evidence and mitigates over-conditioning on self-generated language, showing that pruning textual debt improves both efficiency and performance.

title: Motion-Based Tokenization for Cross-Dataset Egocentric Gaze Modeling
summary: Gaze is increasingly used as an input signal for vision and multimodal models, yet no consensus exists on how to represent it across datasets. Raw traces preserve detail but are noisy and device-dependent, while coarse event labels are easy to model but can discard local motion structure. We formulate event-aligned, fixed-horizon angular displacement as an interpretable, event-conditioned motion vocabulary and compare it with event-only, spatial, absolute-angle, learned vector-quantized, and continuous representations. To assess transfer alongside target predictability and token collapse, our evaluation combines next-token prediction with target-domain regret, low-order target references, paired bootstrap, order sensitivity, motif overlap, and frozen structural probes. In an event-aligned headset benchmark, angular-motion tokens have lower target-domain regret than frozen-codebook VQ tokens in one transfer direction, while the reverse direction is inconclusive. The probes reveal complementary representation properties, and event-only tokens show that low perplexity can retain little motion information. On a third egocentric dataset, a matched comparison of I-VT, native, and frame-span interfaces shows that event construction materially changes transfer: native events have the lowest regret into EGTEA, while frame-span events have zero motif overlap and fail severely as a source. Motion-based tokenization therefore provides a compact representation for event-aligned egocentric gaze streams, while the evaluation identifies how target predictability and event construction shape cross-dataset conclusions.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the lack of consensus on gaze representation for vision and multimodal models by proposing event-aligned, fixed-horizon angular displacement as an interpretable motion vocabulary. It compares this with various alternatives (event-only, spatial, absolute-angle, VQ, continuous) using a multi-faceted evaluation including next-token prediction, target-domain regret, and structural probes. Results show angular-motion tokens have lower regret than VQ tokens in one transfer direction, event construction materially affects transfer, and low perplexity does not guarantee retained motion information.
AI.motivation: There is no consensus on how to represent gaze as an input signal across datasets. Raw traces are noisy and device-dependent, while coarse event labels discard local motion structure, motivating the need for a principled, interpretable gaze representation and rigorous cross-dataset evaluation.
AI.method: Formulates event-aligned, fixed-horizon angular displacement as an interpretable motion vocabulary. Compares it against event-only, spatial, absolute-angle, learned VQ, and continuous representations. Evaluation combines next-token prediction with target-domain regret, low-order target references, paired bootstrap, order sensitivity, motif overlap, and frozen structural probes. Conducts experiments on event-aligned headset benchmarks and a third egocentric dataset with matched I-VT, native, and frame-span event interfaces.
AI.result: Angular-motion tokens achieve lower target-domain regret than frozen-codebook VQ tokens in one transfer direction, with the reverse inconclusive. Probes reveal complementary representation properties. Native events have the lowest regret into EGTEA, while frame-span events have zero motif overlap and fail severely as a source. Event-only tokens show low perplexity can retain little motion information.
AI.conclusion: Motion-based tokenization provides a compact representation for event-aligned egocentric gaze streams. The evaluation framework identifies how target predictability and event construction shape cross-dataset conclusions, highlighting that these factors materially influence transfer outcomes.

title: Beyond the Stability-Exploration Dilemma: Environmental Regularization for LLM Policy Optimization
summary: Policy optimization (PO) for Large Language Models faces a stability--exploration trade-off, currently mediated by an action-side Policy-KL regularizer. This puts practitioners in a double bind: keeping Policy-KL constrains response behavior and consumes the action-side exploration budget, while dropping it leaves the optimization without an explicit drift control. We argue for an alternative that breaks the dilemma by moving regularization to the input side. As training progresses, the distribution over training queries induced by the current policy drifts unchecked from its pre-RL reference distribution. Concretely, Environment-Regularized Policy Optimization (ERPO) introduces a Query-KL (QKL) term that bounds this query distribution shift, together with a dataset-static reference-derived per-query weight that biases each per-query update toward queries typical under the reference. The QKL gradient flows strictly through the query likelihood; the response score function used by policy-gradient estimators does not appear in the QKL term, so QKL exerts no direct gradient pressure on the response distribution---exploration is preserved. ERPO plugs into GRPO/PPO/REINFORCE-style pipelines without additional forward passes. On six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, ERPO replaces the standard Policy-KL regularizer while achieving effective control over query distribution drift, delivering stronger accuracy and substantially more stable behavior under high-temperature decoding and long-horizon training. Our source code are available at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/ERPO

AI.tldr: ERPO moves policy optimization regularization from the action side (Policy-KL) to the input side via a Query-KL (QKL) term, bounding query distribution drift while preserving exploration, yielding stronger accuracy and improved stability across six math reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current Policy-KL regularizers create a stability-exploration trade-off: they constrain response behavior and consume the action-side exploration budget, while removing them leaves optimization without drift control. This is a double bind for practitioners.
AI.method: Environment-Regularized Policy Optimization (ERPO) introduces a Query-KL term that bounds the shift of the training query distribution from its reference, plus a dataset-static reference-derived per-query weighting that biases updates toward typical queries. The QKL gradient flows only through query likelihood, not the response score function, so no direct gradient pressure is placed on the response distribution.
AI.result: On six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, ERPO replaces the standard Policy-KL regularizer while effectively controlling query distribution drift, delivering stronger accuracy and substantially more stable behavior under high-temperature decoding and long-horizon training, without additional forward passes in GRPO/PPO/REINFORCE pipelines.
AI.conclusion: ERPO breaks the stability-exploration dilemma by regularizing the input side instead of the action side, preserving exploration while maintaining drift control, with improved accuracy and stability.

title: ParallelWorld: Test-Time Scaling for Embodied Reasoning
summary: Embodied Reasoning constitutes a fundamental capability of embodied intelligence, serving as the basis for autonomous perception, reasoning, and interaction within physical environments. Recent studies have shifted the paradigm of embodied reasoning from static perception toward dynamic exploration, where agents acquire task-relevant information through interactions with the environment. However, existing active reasoning approaches generally generate exploration trajectories incrementally without long-horizon planning. Even recently emerged test-time scaling frameworks often resort to myopic, single-step lookaheads, which struggle to resolve the delayed feedback inherent in complex, occluded spatial environments. To address this limitation, we propose ParallelWorld, a multi-horizon test-time scaling framework for embodied reasoning. Instead of greedy, single-step trials, ParallelWorld empowers agents to simulate and evaluate multi-step future trajectories in parallel before committing to an action. Specifically, we introduce a verifier-guided tree-search paradigm. Starting from the current state, ParallelWorld branches into multiple parallel trajectories and rolls them out continuously across a multi-step horizon. At each simulation step, a verifier agent evaluates the intermediate state transitions, dynamically pruning unpromising branches and prioritizing paths with the highest information gain. Once the multi-step prospective simulation is complete, the agent synthesizes the long-horizon outcomes to commit to the optimal action sequence. Finally, an answer agent performs reasoning over the selected trajectory to produce the final reasoning. Extensive experiments on ESI-Bench demonstrate that ParallelWorld consistently improves active perception and reasoning performance.

AI.tldr: ParallelWorld is a multi-horizon test-time scaling framework for embodied reasoning that uses verifier-guided tree-search to simulate and evaluate multiple parallel future trajectories before committing to an action, outperforming greedy single-step lookahead approaches on ESI-Bench.
AI.motivation: Existing active reasoning approaches generate exploration trajectories incrementally without long-horizon planning, and current test-time scaling frameworks rely on myopic single-step lookaheads that fail to handle delayed feedback in complex, occluded spatial environments.
AI.method: ParallelWorld employs a verifier-guided tree-search paradigm: (1) from the current state, it branches into multiple parallel trajectories rolled out across a multi-step horizon; (2) at each simulation step, a verifier agent evaluates intermediate state transitions, dynamically pruning unpromising branches and prioritizing high-information-gain paths; (3) after multi-step prospective simulation completes, an agent synthesizes long-horizon outcomes to commit to the optimal action sequence; (4) an answer agent performs reasoning over the selected trajectory for the final output.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on ESI-Bench demonstrate that ParallelWorld consistently improves active perception and reasoning performance compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: Multi-horizon parallel simulation with verifier-guided pruning is an effective test-time scaling strategy for embodied reasoning, enabling agents to overcome delayed feedback challenges in complex spatial environments.

title: Quality Inspection of Printed Circuit Board Pin Insertion via Semantic Segmentation and Board-Level Feature Extraction
summary: Quality control during printed circuit board (PCB) assembly is a critical step in ensuring reliable electronic products. Detecting misaligned pins during or after pin insertion remains a particularly challenging inspection task. This paper presents an automated defect detection method for identifying incorrectly inserted pins on PCBs. The proposed pipeline combines semantic segmentation using a U-Net architecture with contour-based feature extraction and logistic regression for board-level pass/fail classification. Segmentation masks are used to derive contour representations of individual pins, from which board-level features -such as average contour size- are extracted and used to train a logistic regression classifier. We evaluate the method on two datasets: an industrial collection of real-world PCB images, and a publicly available PCB pin-inspection dataset with substantially different visual characteristics. To assess the effectiveness of the proposed approach, a comparison against PatchCore, an anomaly detection technique new to be applied to pin inspection, as well as instance segmentation-based pin detection is made. The developed method achieved Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (ROC-AUC) values of 0.990 on a random test set split from the industrial data and 1.000 on the public dataset indicating strong separation between pass and fail boards. The results indicate that the proposed approach is a promising candidate for automated pin inspection in industrial environments and achieves strong performance on datasets with substantially different visual characteristics after dataset-specific training.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an automated PCB pin-inspection method combining U-Net semantic segmentation, contour-based feature extraction, and logistic regression to detect misaligned/incorrectly inserted pins, achieving ROC-AUC of 0.990 on industrial data and 1.000 on a public dataset.
AI.motivation: Quality control during PCB assembly is critical for reliable electronics, and detecting misaligned pins during/after insertion is a particularly challenging inspection task that lacks robust automated solutions.
AI.method: The pipeline uses a U-Net architecture for semantic segmentation of pins, extracts contour representations from segmentation masks to derive board-level features (e.g., average contour size), and trains a logistic regression classifier for board-level pass/fail determination. Performance is benchmarked against PatchCore anomaly detection and instance-segmentation-based pin detection.
AI.result: The method achieved ROC-AUC values of 0.990 on a random test split from industrial data and 1.000 on the public dataset, demonstrating strong separation between pass and fail boards across datasets with substantially different visual characteristics after dataset-specific training.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach is a promising candidate for automated pin inspection in industrial environments, achieving strong performance across visually diverse datasets after dataset-specific training.

title: Flesch-Kincaid Readability Depends Only on the Topic Distribution in Long Texts under Topic Models
summary: Flesch Reading Ease (FRE) and the Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL) are widely used readability scores for English computed from the same two document statistics, yet their stability on long documents need not imply invariance to lexical composition. Surprisingly, under a topic model with an explicit sentence-boundary token, both scores converge almost surely to deterministic functions of the document topic distribution through just two scalar rates: in the long-text limit, all score variation is mediated by topical composition rather than any residual readability signal. The theory covers both formulae, while the experiments evaluate FKGL. In a fixed admixture with rank[1, q, s] = 3, fibres through interior topic vectors are locally (K-3)-dimensional, whereas regular iso-score level sets are locally (K-2)-dimensional and curved. In out-of-fold evaluation on two balanced corpora, Brown and the written BNC, a topic vector inferred from one document half's content words predicts the other half's FKGL at r = 0.779 and 0.884, respectively. On Brown, adding the topic prediction to genre and mean content-word syllable count yields $ΔR^2$ = 0.002, with a confidence interval spanning zero; on the BNC, the corresponding split-half increment is 0.024, positive in four of five K = 100 fits (median 0.021). Because inferred topics may also absorb genre, register, and style, we do not interpret these results as evidence about human readability or causal effects.

AI.tldr: Under a topic model with sentence-boundary tokens, FRE and FKGL converge almost surely to deterministic functions of document topic distribution in the long-text limit, meaning all score variation is mediated by topical composition. Cross-validation shows topic vectors predict FKGL at r=0.779–0.884, but adding topic prediction to genre and syllable counts yields negligible incremental variance explained.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates whether readability scores (FRE, FKGL), despite being computed from the same two document statistics (word and sentence lengths), are invariant to lexical composition or implicitly sensitive to topic. This matters because if readability scores are dominated by topical structure rather than residual readability, their interpretation as readability measures is called into question.
AI.method: The authors develop a theoretical framework using a topic model with an explicit sentence-boundary token, proving that both FRE and FKGL converge almost surely to deterministic functions of the document topic distribution via two scalar rates. They characterize the geometry of iso-score level sets (locally (K-2)-dimensional for interior topic vectors with rank[1,q,s]=3) and evaluate FKGL empirically using out-of-fold prediction on Brown and written BNC corpora, comparing topic-based predictions against genre and syllable-count baselines.
AI.result: Topic vectors inferred from one half of a document's content words predict the other half's FKGL at r=0.779 (Brown) and r=0.884 (BNC). On Brown, adding topic prediction to genre and mean content-word syllable count yields ΔR²=0.002 with CI spanning zero; on BNC, the increment is 0.024, positive in four of five K=100 fits (median 0.021).
AI.conclusion: In the long-text limit, FRE and FKGL variation is entirely mediated by topical composition, not residual readability. However, because inferred topics may absorb genre, register, and style, the results should not be interpreted as evidence about human readability or causal effects.

title: Toward Effective and Reliable LLM Agents via Dynamic Ontology
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents rely heavily on knowledge encoded in model parameters or presented as unstructured context. In domain-specific tasks, this leaves important semantic connections implicit. This often results in incomplete evidence use and brittle multi-step decisions. Ontologies offer a way to externalize domain concepts and relations as machine-interpretable structures, but constructing task-usable ontologies traditionally requires substantial effort from domain experts and is difficult to scale. Automatic construction is also challenging: an ontology that appears semantically plausible may not contain the relational structures needed for actual decision making. We present OaK, an ontology-as-a-kernel framework that dynamically constructs and refines task-oriented ontologies for LLM agents. Given task requirements and training data, OaK constructs an ontology and its knowledge graph, generates task-adaptation functions for graph reasoning, and uses judge feedback to iteratively refine both. By making relevant concepts and relations explicit, the ontology grounds knowledge retrieval and multi-step decision making. We evaluate OaK on TravelPlanner, CRMArenaPro, and ToolQA. Results show that OaK improves standard LLM agents, strengthens evidence grounding, and boosts the reliability of multi-step reasoning.

AI.tldr: OaK is an ontology-as-a-kernel framework that dynamically constructs and refines task-oriented ontologies for LLM agents, grounding knowledge retrieval and multi-step decision making with explicit semantic structures, showing improvements on TravelPlanner, CRMArenaPro, and ToolQA.
AI.motivation: LLM agents rely on implicit knowledge in parameters or unstructured context, leading to incomplete evidence use and brittle multi-step decisions in domain-specific tasks. Constructing task-usable ontologies manually is expensive and hard to scale, while automatic construction may yield semantically plausible but decision-irrelevant structures.
AI.method: OaK dynamically constructs task-oriented ontologies and knowledge graphs from task requirements and training data, generates task-adaptation functions for graph reasoning, and uses judge feedback to iteratively refine both the ontology and adaptation functions.
AI.result: OaK improves standard LLM agents, strengthens evidence grounding, and boosts the reliability of multi-step reasoning on TravelPlanner, CRMArenaPro, and ToolQA benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Making domain concepts and relations explicit via ontologies effectively grounds knowledge retrieval and multi-step decision making in LLM agents, addressing the gap between semantic plausibility and decision utility in automated ontology construction.

title: WADE: A Reasoning-Annotated Benchmark for Multi-Instance Floating-Waste Grounding with Compact Vision-Language Models
summary: Floating waste in inland waterways threatens aquatic ecosystems and requires timely monitoring under cluttered, multi-object conditions. Existing aquatic-waste datasets provide limited geographic coverage, sparse multi-instance annotations, and little supervision beyond boxes and labels. Compact vision-language models (VLMs) therefore remain insufficiently evaluated for jointly localizing, classifying, counting, and explaining floating waste. We introduce WADE, a reasoning-annotated benchmark containing 2,167 images from rural Bangladesh, 13,608 bounding boxes, and ten waste categories. Each annotation is associated with class-level recognition rules covering visual cues, likely confusions, and discriminative features. We evaluate six VLMs under zero-shot, two-shot, reasoning-guided, and fine-tuned settings using detection, counting, and hallucination metrics. For resource-efficient adaptation, we jointly fine-tune Qwen3-VL-2B on boxes, labels, and reasoning chains using QLoRA. Fine-tuning increases recall from 0.0248 to 0.2339 and F1 from 0.0257 to 0.2163, while reducing image-level hallucination from 0.6836 to 0.0883. However, over three-quarters of instances remain undetected, establishing WADE as a challenging benchmark for dense floating-waste grounding with compact VLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces WADE, a reasoning-annotated benchmark of 2,167 images with 13,608 bounding boxes across ten floating-waste categories from rural Bangladesh, and evaluates compact vision-language models under multiple settings. Fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-2B with QLoRA improves recall from 0.0248 to 0.2339 and reduces hallucination, yet over 75% of instances remain undetected, marking WADE as a challenging dense-grounding benchmark.
AI.motivation: Floating waste in inland waterways needs timely monitoring but existing aquatic-waste datasets lack geographic diversity, dense multi-instance annotations, and supervisory signals beyond boxes and labels. Compact VLMs are insufficiently evaluated for joint localization, classification, counting, and explanation of floating waste under cluttered conditions.
AI.method: The authors construct WADE with 2,167 images from rural Bangladesh, 13,608 bounding boxes, ten waste categories, and class-level recognition rules per annotation. They evaluate six VLMs under zero-shot, two-shot, reasoning-guided, and fine-tuned settings using detection, counting, and hallucination metrics, and apply QLoRA-based joint fine-tuning of Qwen3-VL-2B on boxes, labels, and reasoning chains.
AI.result: Fine-tuning improves recall from 0.0248 to 0.2339 and F1 from 0.0257 to 0.2163, while reducing image-level hallucination from 0.6836 to 0.0883. However, over three-quarters of instances remain undetected, showing the benchmark's difficulty.
AI.conclusion: WADE serves as a challenging benchmark for dense floating-waste grounding with compact VLMs, revealing significant room for improvement despite notable gains from resource-efficient fine-tuning.

title: The Emergence of Relevance Through Axiomatic Attention Patterns During LoRA Fine-Tuning
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Findings. 17 Pages. 25 Figures. 5 Tables
summary: LoRA fine-tuning is standard for adapting LLMs to reranking, but it remains unclear where in the network task-specific relevance behavior is learned and what attention-level changes accompany that learning. Through ablation and attention experiments, we identify where LoRA attention updates to RankLLaMA improve performance and whether those gains coincide with interpretable relevance-oriented attention patterns such as lexical matching, rarity sensitivity, and query-document interaction. We find that given LoRA fine-tuned MLPs throughout the network, restricting LoRA attention updates to a compact mid-network region is sufficient for recovering over half of the performance gained by applying LoRA to all attention layers, and that omitting attention fine-tuning in this region hurts performance more than elsewhere in the network. Additionally, we show that regions where applying LoRA affects performance the most overlap with regions where fine-tuning increased attention to axiomatic IR features. Rarity sensitivity, document-query interaction, and several compositional features are highly correlated with gains in ranking performance. Our results support an interpretable, correlational account of how relevance-oriented behavior emerges during LoRA fine-tuning and point toward improved strategies for adapting rerankers.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates where LoRA attention updates in RankLLaMA contribute to reranking performance and whether these gains align with interpretable relevance-oriented attention patterns (lexical matching, rarity sensitivity, query-document interaction). The authors find that restricting LoRA attention updates to a compact mid-network region recovers over half the performance of full attention LoRA, and that regions of high performance impact overlap with regions where fine-tuning increased attention to axiomatic IR features.
AI.motivation: LoRA fine-tuning is the standard approach for adapting LLMs to reranking, but it is unclear where task-specific relevance behavior is learned in the network and what attention-level changes accompany that learning. Understanding this could lead to more efficient and interpretable adaptation strategies.
AI.method: The authors conduct ablation experiments on LoRA attention updates across different network regions of RankLLaMA, and perform attention-level analysis to identify whether performance gains coincide with interpretable relevance-oriented attention patterns such as lexical matching, rarity sensitivity, and query-document interaction.
AI.result: Restricting LoRA attention updates to a compact mid-network region recovers over half of the performance gained from applying LoRA to all attention layers. Omitting attention fine-tuning in this region hurts performance more than elsewhere. Regions where LoRA affects performance most overlap with regions where fine-tuning increased attention to axiomatic IR features. Rarity sensitivity, document-query interaction, and compositional features are highly correlated with ranking performance gains.
AI.conclusion: The results support an interpretable, correlational account of how relevance-oriented behavior emerges during LoRA fine-tuning, and point toward improved strategies for adapting rerankers by focusing fine-tuning on specific network regions.

title: Budget-Constrained Embodied Perception: Four Resource Walls and a Pre-Registered Evaluation of Access-Structured Perception on Open Models at less than 31B
summary: Embodied multimodal agents must answer from growing observation streams under a fixed per-decision token budget. We formalize this constraint through four resource walls: a perceptual Shannon wall for bounded state, a horizon wall for query-independent frame selection, a round wall for non-adaptive retrieval, and a conditional composition wall for fixed-depth inference. We introduce ASP, a training-free wrapper for frozen multimodal models that combines a capped structured state, a verbatim episodic index, and query-conditioned budget allocation with iterative access. Following a pre-registered protocol, we evaluate seven open-weight models from 3B to 31B on SEW-Bench, a license-free synthetic long-horizon walkthrough benchmark constructed to instantiate these walls. The registered natural-video benchmarks were not run because their frames require dataset agreements; our evidence therefore concerns access mechanisms, not natural-scene perception. Under a 4,096-token decision budget, ASP reaches 75 to 94% episodic retrieval accuracy, compared with 3 to 19% for equal-budget query-independent sampling, and budget reallocation outperforms quadrupling the sampling budget on every backbone. However, the full three-component architecture does not validate channel duality: removing the compressive state raises the flagship mean from 35.4 to 58.0, ASP does not outperform the verbatim-only baseline on any backbone, and two of four pre-registered falsification criteria fire. These results show that query-conditioned access, rather than parameter count or context growth alone, is decisive under a fixed budget, while prompted online compression does not earn its cost in this setting.

AI.tldr: ASP is a training-free wrapper for frozen multimodal models that improves query-conditioned access under fixed token budgets via a capped structured state, verbatim episodic index, and iterative budget allocation. It achieves 75–94% episodic retrieval accuracy vs 3–19% for query-independent sampling on SEW-Bench, but the full architecture fails pre-registered falsification tests—removing the compressive state boosts the flagship mean from 35.4 to 58.0, and ASP never beats the verbatim-only baseline.
AI.motivation: Embodied multimodal agents must process growing observation streams under a fixed per-decision token budget, creating four resource walls (perceptual Shannon, horizon, round, and conditional composition) that prior methods do not systematically address.
AI.method: Introduces ASP, a training-free wrapper combining (1) a capped structured state, (2) a verbatim episodic index, and (3) query-conditioned budget allocation with iterative access, evaluated on seven open-weight models (3B–31B) from a pre-registered protocol on SEW-Bench synthetic long-horizon walkthroughs under a 4,096-token decision budget.
AI.result: ASP achieves 75–94% episodic retrieval accuracy vs 3–19% for query-independent sampling, and budget reallocation beats quadrupling the sampling budget on every backbone. However, the full three-component architecture fails to validate channel duality: removing the compressive state raises flagship mean from 35.4 to 58.0, ASP does not outperform verbatim-only baselines, and two of four pre-registered falsification criteria fire. Natural-video benchmarks were excluded due to dataset agreement constraints.
AI.conclusion: Query-conditioned access is decisive under fixed token budgets, not parameter count or context growth alone. However, prompted online compression does not earn its cost in this setting, and the compressive state component should likely be dropped or redesigned.

title: WildHandBench: A Benchmark for Handwritten Text Understanding that Challenges MLLMs and Humans
summary:
While the top model on OmniDocBench now reaches 96.34% overall on printed-document parsing, the ability of current models to handle challenging handwritten documents remains largely uncharacterized. Existing benchmarks focus on isolated text or formulas, overlook handwritten tables and real-world degradation, and report aggregate accuracy without explaining why models fail.
  We present WildHandBench, a benchmark containing 500 handwritten documents across three structures (free text, tables, formulas), four languages, and nine real-world scenarios. We introduce a Prior-Driven Error (PDE) metric that quantifies whether errors originate from language priors rather than visual evidence. Evaluating 18 state-of-the-art models together with calibrated human baselines, we find: (1) the best model achieves only 71.85% overall; (2) humans outperform all models yet the gap is narrow (77.09% vs. 71.85%); and (3) model errors are qualitatively different from human errors -- 63-91% of model errors are prior-driven versus only 49% for humans, exposing systematic reliance on language priors that conventional accuracy metrics cannot capture.

AI.tldr: WildHandBench is a benchmark for evaluating handwritten document parsing across 500 documents spanning three structures, four languages, and nine real-world scenarios. It introduces a Prior-Driven Error (PDE) metric to quantify whether errors stem from language priors versus visual evidence. Evaluating 18 state-of-the-art models against calibrated human baselines, the best model achieves only 71.85% overall (humans: 77.09%), and 63-91% of model errors are prior-driven versus 49% for humans—exposing a systematic reliance on language priors that conventional accuracy metrics miss.
AI.motivation: While printed-document parsing models reach 96.34% on OmniDocBench, their performance on challenging handwritten documents remains uncharacterized. Existing benchmarks neglect handwritten tables and real-world degradation, and report only aggregate accuracy without diagnosing why models fail.
AI.method: The authors build WildHandBench with 500 handwritten documents covering three structures (free text, tables, formulas), four languages, and nine real-world scenarios. They introduce the Prior-Driven Error (PDE) metric to distinguish errors originating from language priors versus visual evidence, and evaluate 18 state-of-the-art models together with calibrated human baselines.
AI.result: The best model achieves only 71.85% overall accuracy versus 77.09% for humans—a narrow gap. Notably, 63-91% of model errors are prior-driven versus only 49% for humans, revealing a qualitative difference in failure modes that aggregate accuracy metrics cannot expose.
AI.conclusion: Current document-parsing models perform far worse on handwritten documents than on printed ones and systematically rely on language priors rather than visual evidence, a failure pattern that conventional accuracy metrics fail to capture. The PDE metric provides a principled tool to diagnose this issue and guide future improvements in handwritten document understanding.

title: FormuEvo: LLM-Guided Evolution for Discovering Solver-Efficient Mixed-Integer Programming Formulations
comment: 27 pages, 6 figures, and 9 tables. To appear in the Proceedings of EMNLP 2026
summary: Mixed-integer programming (MIP) lies at the core of operations research and industrial optimization. While large language models (LLMs) have recently shown promise in automated MIP modeling from natural language, they prioritize semantic correctness but overlook formulation strength, severely bottlenecking the efficiency of downstream solvers. We propose FormuEvo, an LLM-guided evolutionary framework for automated discovery of solver-efficient MIP formulations.
