FormuEvo frames MIP formulation design as evolutionary optimization over the symbolic space of MIP formulations, represented as executable modeling programs, by iteratively generating, evaluating, and selecting stronger candidates via LLM-driven crossover, mutation, and repair operations. To move beyond blind exploration, FormuEvo introduces a solver-informed diagnosis mechanism that exploits fine-grained solver statistics as verbal gradients for targeted refinement. Additionally, a structured memory abstracts prior experience into reusable modeling strategies, avoiding redundant exploration while enabling zero-shot transfer to unseen problems and bootstrapping smaller LLMs. Experiments across diverse linear and non-linear problems demonstrate that FormuEvo discovers formulations that significantly outperform both expert-designed formulations and existing LLM-based approaches, accelerating solvers by up to 5.5$\times$, with distilled knowledge transferring effectively across problems and model scales.

AI.tldr: FormuEvo is an LLM-guided evolutionary framework that automatically discovers solver-efficient mixed-integer programming (MIP) formulations by evolving executable modeling programs through crossover, mutation, and repair, guided by solver statistics as verbal gradients and structured memory for knowledge reuse, achieving up to 5.5x solver speedup over expert and LLM baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based approaches for automated MIP modeling prioritize semantic correctness over formulation strength, producing valid but computationally weak formulations that bottleneck downstream solver efficiency. The paper addresses the gap between creating correct MIP models and creating solver-efficient ones.
AI.method: FormuEvo frames MIP formulation design as evolutionary optimization over a symbolic space of formulations represented as executable modeling programs. It iteratively generates, evaluates, and selects candidates using LLM-driven crossover, mutation, and repair operations. Key innovations include: (1) a solver-informed diagnosis mechanism using fine-grained solver statistics as verbal gradients for targeted refinement, and (2) a structured memory that abstracts prior experience into reusable modeling strategies, enabling zero-shot transfer to unseen problems and bootstrapping smaller LLMs.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse linear and non-linear problems show FormuEvo discovers formulations that significantly outperform both expert-designed formulations and existing LLM-based approaches, accelerating solvers by up to 5.5x. Distilled knowledge transfers effectively across problems and model scales.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that combining LLM-guided evolutionary search with solver-informed feedback signals can effectively discover strong MIP formulations beyond human expertise, and the structured memory enables scalable knowledge transfer across problem domains and model sizes.

title: SA-RSQ: A Versatile Sparse Representation Framework for Multi-modal Recommender Systems
summary: Deploying high-dimensional multimodal features in industrial recommender systems incurs substantial storage and latency overhead. Hard quantization is compact but introduces boundary distortion, whereas dense soft quantization couples representation quality to the limited storage budget. We propose Sparse Activation-based Residual Soft Quantization (SA-RSQ), which uses Top-K sparse routing and softmax weights to store compact (Index, Probability) tuples. The stored tuples decouple per-item storage from codebook dimensionality; for a fixed selected support, gradients propagate through the routing weights and weighted reconstruction without relying on a straight-through estimator. Experiments on a proprietary food-delivery advertising dataset show favorable reconstruction-performance and CTR trade-offs across storage budgets of 8-48 bytes per item. A preliminary Next-Distribution Prediction study and a one-week online A/B test further demonstrate the practical potential of SA-RSQ, with relative lifts of +2.51% in CTR and +3.66% in CPM.

AI.tldr: SA-RSQ is a sparse activation-based residual soft quantization method for high-dimensional multimodal features in industrial recommender systems, storing compact (Index, Probability) tuples via Top-K sparse routing to decouple per-item storage from codebook dimensionality, achieving favorable reconstruction-performance and CTR trade-offs with +2.51% CTR and +3.66% CPM lifts in online A/B testing.
AI.motivation: High-dimensional multimodal features in industrial recommender systems demand substantial storage and latency overhead. Hard quantization is compact but suffers boundary distortion, while dense soft quantization ties representation quality directly to the limited storage budget, motivating a method that is both compact and high-fidelity.
AI.method: SA-RSQ employs Top-K sparse routing with softmax weights to store compact (Index, Probability) tuples. This decouples per-item storage from codebook dimensionality. For a fixed selected support, gradients propagate through routing weights and weighted reconstruction without relying on a straight-through estimator, enabling end-to-end training.
AI.result: Experiments on a proprietary food-delivery advertising dataset show favorable reconstruction-performance and CTR trade-offs across storage budgets of 8-48 bytes per item. A preliminary Next-Distribution Prediction study and a one-week online A/B test demonstrate practical potential with relative lifts of +2.51% in CTR and +3.66% in CPM.
AI.conclusion: SA-RSQ effectively addresses the storage-distortion trade-off in industrial recommendation systems by combining sparse activation routing with residual soft quantization, showing strong offline and online performance gains while maintaining practical storage efficiency.

title: Simplified Cross-Modal Calibration for Heterogeneous Event-RGB Stereo Systems
comment: Accepted to the 37th British Machine Vision Conference (BMVC) 2026
summary: Accurate extrinsic calibration between event-based and frame-based cameras remains a practical bottleneck for heterogeneous stereo systems. Existing approaches often require sensor or target motion, precise synchronization, or computationally expensive event-to-image reconstruction. We propose a simple, motion-free cross-modal calibration framework that uses a temporally modulated, blended ChArUco target presented on standard consumer displays. By alternating between the original pattern and a partially blended version, the target reliably triggers events while remaining continuously observable to a frame-based camera, avoiding blank frames and reducing synchronization constraints to a coarse, trigger-based alignment. We discretize events into frames coarsely aligned with the RGB images, apply lightweight denoising, and perform ChArUco-based intrinsic and stereo extrinsic calibration. Extensive experiments assess robustness to blending opacity, display brightness, external illumination, viewing angle, and handheld acquisition. Compared to the strongest motion-based reference (E2Calib + Kalibr) and a non-motion-based reference (Plasberg et al.), our approach reduces the mean reprojection error by $44\%$ and $6\%$, respectively, while substantially simplifying the calibration procedure. Finally, we demonstrate practical utility in a robotic eye-to-hand calibration case study, showing consistent transformations and stable downstream geometric measurements even under partial occlusions. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/nhessenthaler/simple-evrgb-cal.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a simple, motion-free cross-modal calibration framework for event-based and frame-based cameras using a temporally modulated, blended ChArUco target displayed on standard consumer screens. The method alternates between original and blended patterns to trigger events while keeping the target continuously visible to frame cameras, reducing synchronization requirements to coarse trigger-based alignment. It reduces mean reprojection error by 44% and 6% compared to motion-based (E2Calib + Kalibr) and non-motion-based (Plasberg et al.) baselines, respectively, and is validated in a robotic eye-to-hand calibration case study.
AI.motivation: Accurate extrinsic calibration between event-based and frame-based cameras remains a practical bottleneck for heterogeneous stereo systems. Existing approaches require sensor or target motion, precise synchronization, or computationally expensive event-to-image reconstruction, making them cumbersome in real-world settings.
AI.method: The framework uses a temporally modulated, blended ChArUco target on consumer displays, alternating between the original pattern and a partially blended version to reliably trigger events while remaining continuously observable to a frame camera. Events are discretized into frames coarsely aligned with RGB images, lightweight denoising is applied, and ChArUco-based intrinsic and stereo extrinsic calibration is performed.
AI.result: Compared to the strongest motion-based reference (E2Calib + Kalibr), the approach reduces mean reprojection error by 44%, and by 6% compared to a non-motion-based reference (Plasberg et al.). Experiments assess robustness to blending opacity, display brightness, external illumination, viewing angle, and handheld acquisition. A robotic eye-to-hand calibration case study shows consistent transformations and stable downstream geometric measurements under partial occlusions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed motion-free cross-modal calibration approach substantially simplifies the calibration procedure while achieving superior accuracy. It provides robust and practical calibration for heterogeneous event-frame camera systems, with code publicly available.

title: The Geometry of Low-Resource Language Representations
summary: The performance gap between low- and high-resource languages in LLMs is widely known, but it remains unclear which internal model factors drive these disparities. In this paper, we characterise this gap through the lens of representational geometry. Comparing the geometric properties of hidden representations across 30 languages reveals that LLM geometry is systematically related to language data availability. The most consistent effect is in final layers, where low-resource languages exhibit representational degeneration. To counter this, we investigate the effectiveness of regularisation terms to penalise degeneration during continued pretraining (CPT). Experiments monolingually adapting 9 base LLMs to 10 African languages show that geometric regularisation successfully reduces representational degeneration during CPT. For larger models, cosine similarity-based regularisation marginally improves performance over vanilla CPT, with more consistent gains on the most challenging tasks. We establish that the representational geometry of low- and high-resource languages in LLMs is measurably distinct, and that targeted geometric intervention is a viable strategy for improving CPT for low-resource languages.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes the performance gap between low- and high-resource languages in LLMs through representational geometry, finding that low-resource languages exhibit representational degeneration in final layers. The authors propose geometric regularisation during continued pretraining (CPT) and show it reduces degeneration across 10 African languages and 9 base LLMs, with marginal performance gains for larger models.
AI.motivation: The performance gap between low- and high-resource languages in LLMs is well-documented, but the internal model factors driving these disparities remain unclear. The authors aim to precisely characterise this gap through representational geometry and explore whether targeted geometric interventions can mitigate it.
AI.method: The authors compare geometric properties of hidden representations across 30 languages to relate LLM geometry to language data availability. They then apply regularisation terms penalising representational degeneration during continued pretraining (CPT), monolingually adapting 9 base LLMs to 10 African languages, using cosine similarity-based regularisation for larger models.
AI.result: Low-resource languages exhibit systematic representational degeneration in final layers. Geometric regularisation successfully reduces this degeneration during CPT. For larger models, cosine similarity-based regularisation yields marginal improvements over vanilla CPT, with more consistent gains on the most challenging tasks.
AI.conclusion: The representational geometry of low- and high-resource languages in LLMs is measurably distinct, and targeted geometric intervention is a viable strategy for improving continued pretraining for low-resource languages.

title: PatchWrite: One Line, Not One Section -- Compile-Gated, Validity-Preserving Editing for AI-Drafted Manuscripts
summary: Automated manuscript pipelines often regenerate an entire section to repair a local defect, allowing unrelated metrics and citations to change even when the resulting PDF still builds. PatchWrite instead constrains how candidate edits become committed manuscript states: it reuses bounded EDIT N M editing and rollback, but tightens compilation acceptance with fatal-log checks and adds evidence locks that require every cited key and experimental numeric token to be attested by a reference registry or experimental log. Candidates that fail either check are rejected and the previous HEAD is retained. On a 24-manuscript x 8-fault oracle stress test (768 jobs, evenly split between compile-breaking and content-only faults), whole-slot rewriting mutated an unrelated "12-layer" line in every case (0/192 preserved; numeric Jaccard 0.6667), whereas PatchWrite preserved it in 192/192 cases. Removing the compile gate reduced acceptance to 0, while removing the evidence gate allowed a hallucinated citation to pass. The same pattern held across all eight faults. To test the protocol with generation rather than oracle edits, we reran the 192 jobs with the writer model proposing the edits. The model's candidates were accepted in 75% of cases; nearly all rejections came from one reproducible failure mode in which the model attempted to delete a line using an empty replacement unsupported by the current grammar. Every accepted candidate passed both gates, and 93.75% fixed the injected fault; the remaining cases involved a technically valid but sentence-inappropriate citation and one markup-changing near-miss. In a blind evaluation of sixteen PDF pairs, both raters preferred PatchWrite for preserving lab-grounded facts (C1 Likert 5.0 vs. 2.0), while rating prose quality nearly identically. Logs from 193 in-product drafting tasks show the same classes of failures occurring in practice.

AI.tldr: PatchWrite is a manuscript-patch editing protocol that constrains candidate edits via bounded EDIT N M operations, fatal-log compilation checks, and evidence locks requiring all cited keys and numeric tokens to be attested by reference registries or experimental logs. On a 768-job oracle stress test it preserved unrelated content 192/192 times vs. 0/192 for whole-slot rewriting, and passed both gates for every accepted candidate.
AI.motivation: Automated manuscript pipelines typically regenerate entire sections to fix local defects, causing unrelated metrics and citations to silently change in the final PDF. This undermines lab-grounded fact preservation and scientific integrity.
AI.method: PatchWrite combines bounded EDIT N M editing and rollback with tightened compilation acceptance via fatal-log checks and evidence locks. Evidence locks require every cited key and experimental numeric token to be attested by a reference registry or experimental log. Candidates failing either check are rejected; the previous HEAD is retained. The protocol was tested with oracle edits and with writer-model-generated edits.
AI.result: On a 24-manuscript x 8-fault oracle test (768 jobs), whole-slot rewriting mutated an unrelated "12-layer" line in every case (0/192 preserved; numeric Jaccard 0.6667), while PatchWrite preserved it in 192/192 cases. Removing the compile or evidence gate badly degraded results. Writer-model candidates were accepted 75% of the time; every accepted candidate passed both gates and 93.75% fixed the injected fault. Blind evaluation favored PatchWrite for fact preservation (C1 Likert 5.0 vs. 2.0) with near-identical prose quality.
AI.conclusion: PatchWrite demonstrates that targeted, tightly-gated patching outperforms wholesale section rewriting at preserving lab-grounded facts while maintaining manuscript quality. The main remaining limitation is a reproducible grammar-supported-deletion failure mode in the writer model, plus occasional technically-valid-but-inappropriate citations.

title: Optimize Surgical Triplet Recognition: A Knowledge-Driven Mixture-of-Experts Solution
summary: Surgical action triplet recognition constitutes a critical task in context-aware robot-assisted surgery, facilitating automatic surgical action perception by identifying instrument, verb, target, and their association. However, existing works struggle to analyze such complex surgical scenes due to three main issues: (1) component-level optimization conflicts caused by entangled feature spaces, (2) category-level optimization conflicts arising from severe data imbalance, and (3) lack of domain knowledge guidance that limits model interpretability and robustness. To address these challenges, we propose a Mixture-of-Experts-guided Co-Optimization (\textit{MoeCo}) framework powered by knowledge-driven learning. Within the co-optimization pipeline, to first mitigate component-level conflicts, we introduce a component-tailored adapter that disentangles task-specific features across spatial-temporal regimes, facilitating effective component specialization. Next, we develop a coordinated gradient learning strategy to handle category-level conflicts, which adaptively rebalances positive-negative gradients to enhance the perception of rare categories. Notably, inspired by surgical domain expertise, we introduce a knowledge-driven mixture-of-experts mechanism that dynamically integrates multimodal large language model-guided knowledge via activated experts, thereby enriching the co-optimization pipeline with more expressive and robust representations. Extensive experiments on the public CholecT45 and CholecT50 datasets confirm the effectiveness of the proposed co-optimization pipeline and the superiority of dynamic priors integration via the knowledge-driven mixture-of-experts mechanism.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MoeCo, a Mixture-of-Experts-guided Co-Optimization framework for surgical action triplet recognition that addresses three key challenges: component-level optimization conflicts via component-tailored adapters for feature disentanglement, category-level conflicts via coordinated gradient learning for rare category handling, and lack of domain knowledge via a knowledge-driven mixture-of-experts mechanism integrating multimodal LLM-guided priors. Experiments on CholecT45 and CholecT50 validate its effectiveness.
AI.motivation: Existing surgical action triplet recognition methods struggle due to (1) component-level optimization conflicts from entangled feature spaces, (2) category-level optimization conflicts from severe data imbalance, and (3) lack of domain knowledge guidance limiting interpretability and robustness.
AI.method: The MoeCo framework employs a co-optimization pipeline with three key components: (1) a component-tailored adapter that disentangles task-specific features across spatial-temporal regimes to mitigate component-level conflicts, (2) a coordinated gradient learning strategy that adaptively rebalances positive-negative gradients to handle category-level conflicts, and (3) a knowledge-driven mixture-of-experts mechanism that dynamically integrates multimodal large language model-guided knowledge via activated experts for enriched representations.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on the public CholecT45 and CholecT50 datasets confirm the effectiveness of the proposed co-optimization pipeline and demonstrate the superiority of dynamic priors integration via the knowledge-driven mixture-of-experts mechanism.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MoeCo framework effectively addresses the three identified challenges in surgical action triplet recognition, achieving superior performance through co-optimization and knowledge-driven expert integration.

title: Cross-lingual Biography Enrichment via Claim Extraction and Alignment
summary: English Wikipedia is often treated as the default encyclopedic source, yet non-English Wikipedia editions can contain richer locally grounded information for long-tail figures. We study cross-lingual biography enrichment: enriching an existing English biography with facts supported by a non-English biography about the same person. Focusing on women from non-English-speaking contexts, we introduce \textsc{CLAW-4L}, a benchmark consisting of 300 Wikipedia biography pairs linking an English biography with its French, Chinese or Azerbaijani counterpart, along with claim annotations and a fine-grained claim-pair relation corpus. We propose a claim-based enrichment framework that extracts English claims from both biographies, aligns them to identify enrichment evidence from the non-English biography, and rewrites the English biography using the selected claims. Our results show that non-English Wikipedia biographies provide valuable evidence for improving English biography coverage, while lower-resource settings remain challenging.

AI.tldr: This paper studies cross-lingual biography enrichment—adding facts from non-English Wikipedia biographies to English biographies. It introduces CLAW-4L, a benchmark of 300 biography pairs (English paired with French, Chinese, or Azerbaijani) with claim annotations and a claim-pair relation corpus, and proposes a claim-based enrichment framework that extracts, aligns, and rewrites claims. Results show non-English biographies provide valuable enrichment evidence, though lower-resource languages remain challenging.
AI.motivation: English Wikipedia is often treated as the default encyclopedic source, but non-English editions can contain richer locally grounded information for long-tail figures. The authors aim to address the gap where enriching English biographies with facts from non-English biographies (especially for women from non-English-speaking contexts) could improve coverage.
AI.method: The paper introduces CLAW-4L, a benchmark of 300 Wikipedia biography pairs linking English biographies with French, Chinese, or Azerbaijani counterparts, annotated with claims and a fine-grained claim-pair relation corpus. A claim-based enrichment framework is proposed that (1) extracts English claims from both biographies, (2) aligns them to identify enrichment evidence from the non-English biography, and (3) rewrites the English biography using the selected claims.
AI.result: The proposed framework demonstrates that non-English Wikipedia biographies provide valuable evidence for improving English biography coverage. However, lower-resource settings (e.g., Azerbaijani vs. French/Chinese) remain challenging for the enrichment task.
AI.conclusion: Cross-lingual biography enrichment from non-English Wikipedia editions is a viable approach for improving English biography coverage, particularly for long-tail figures. While the method shows promise, resource availability across languages significantly affects performance, indicating a need for further work on lower-resource scenarios.

title: PsychJail: Exploring Psychological Jailbreaks via Multi-Turn Persuasion of LLM Policies
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in education, healthcare, policy advising, and other interactive settings, where users engage them as sustained social interlocutors rather than one-shot query engines. This shift makes jailbreaks a growing safety threat, yet most research emphasizes single-turn prompt optimization or iterative attack refinement, leaving psychologically grounded multi-turn vulnerabilities underexplored. We present PsychJail, a psychology-guided framework for red teaming aligned LLMs through theory-grounded, multi-turn persuasion. PsychJail maps established social-psychological persuasion techniques into a tactic-conditioned attack policy. It factorizes each attacker action into a Change-of-Meaning analysis, tactic selection, and victim-visible message, operationalizing the Persuasion Knowledge Model (PKM). The policy is refined with trajectory-level reinforcement learning using a PKM-gated reward that credits early jailbreak success only when every turn contains a well-formed Change-of-Meaning analysis. Across four aligned victim models, PsychJail achieves the highest average attack success rate (87.3%) and outperforms strong single-turn and multi-turn baselines on every model. We also measure susceptibility at the action that breaks each victim, revealing four distinct model-level fingerprints that identify which persuasion levers affect each model and how broadly. These fingerprints help explain cross-model transfer asymmetry. We interpret them as four candidate psychological profiles-rationalist, credibility-driven, narrative-monoculture, and broadly persuadable-while treating this interpretation as a conjecture requiring future validation. Our findings establish psychological jailbreaks as a distinct red-teaming frontier for increasingly interactive LLMs.

AI.tldr: PsychJail is a psychology-guided framework for red teaming aligned LLMs via multi-turn persuasion attacks, grounded in the Persuasion Knowledge Model (PKM). It achieves 87.3% average attack success rate across four victim models and reveals four model-level psychological susceptibility fingerprints.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used in sustained interactive settings, making jailbreaks a growing threat. However, most jailbreak research focuses on single-turn prompt optimization or iterative attack refinement, leaving psychologically grounded multi-turn vulnerabilities largely unexplored.
AI.method: PsychJail maps established social-psychological persuasion techniques into a tactic-conditioned attack policy. Each attacker action is factorized into a Change-of-Meaning analysis, tactic selection, and victim-visible message, operationalizing the Persuasion Knowledge Model (PKM). The policy is trained via trajectory-level reinforcement learning with a PKM-gated reward that only credits early jailbreak success when every turn contains a well-formed Change-of-Meaning analysis.
AI.result: Across four aligned victim models, PsychJail achieves the highest average attack success rate (87.3%) and outperforms strong single-turn and multi-turn baselines on every model. The framework identifies four distinct model-level susceptibility fingerprints (rationalist, credibility-driven, narrative-monoculture, broadly persuadable) that explain cross-model transfer asymmetry.
AI.conclusion: Psychological jailbreaks constitute a distinct red-teaming frontier for increasingly interactive LLMs. The identified fingerprints serve as candidate psychological profiles requiring future validation, but establish that psychology-guided multi-turn persuasion is a powerful and under-explored attack vector.

title: ENCORE: Entropy-Guided Cropping and Attention Regularization for Robust Vision--Language Understanding
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) perform well on diverse vision-language tasks, but transformer-based visual encoders split images into fixed-resolution sub-images, compromising object integrity in lightweight VLMs. Existing methods only focus on the visual modality and fail to dynamically preserve the integrity of prompt-relevant regions, limiting performance. In this work, we observe that the early-layer image-text entropy of cross-modal attention strongly correlates with answer grounding quality and task accuracy. Building on this finding, we propose \textbf{ENCORE}, an entropy-guided framework with two components: At inference, an \textbf{Entropy-based Cropping Strategy} (ECS) evaluates a small set of candidate crops and selects the one with minimal entropy, preserving contiguous regions relevant to the prompt. At training, \textbf{Entropy Regularization Training} (ERT) augments next-token prediction with an entropy term that sharpens attention on key visual tokens while down-weighting irrelevant ones. Experiments on ten VQA benchmarks show that ENCORE, fine-tuning only 0.14\% of parameters, achieves an average 1.43\% accuracy gain and state-of-the-art performance among recent 2B-parameter VLMs. Our code is released in https://github.com/baokou-fw2/ENCORE.

AI.tldr: ENCORE is an entropy-guided framework for lightweight Vision-Language Models that dynamically preserves prompt-relevant image regions via an entropy-based cropping strategy at inference and entropy regularization at training, achieving +1.43% average accuracy on ten VQA benchmarks with only 0.14% of parameters fine-tuned.
AI.motivation: Transformer-based visual encoders split images into fixed-resolution sub-images, which compromises object integrity in lightweight VLMs. Existing methods only focus on the visual modality and fail to dynamically preserve the integrity of prompt-relevant regions, limiting performance.
AI.method: The paper first observes that early-layer image-text entropy of cross-modal attention strongly correlates with answer grounding quality and task accuracy. Based on this, ENCORE has two components: (1) Entropy-based Cropping Strategy (ECS) at inference—evaluates a small set of candidate crops and selects the one with minimal entropy to preserve contiguous prompt-relevant regions; (2) Entropy Regularization Training (ERT)—augments next-token prediction with an entropy term that sharpens attention on key visual tokens while down-weighting irrelevant ones.
AI.result: On ten VQA benchmarks, ENCORE achieves an average 1.43% accuracy gain while fine-tuning only 0.14% of parameters, and achieves state-of-the-art performance among recent 2B-parameter VLMs.
AI.conclusion: Cross-modal attention entropy in early layers serves as a reliable signal for object grounding quality, and entropy-guided cropping and regularization can effectively improve lightweight VLM performance with minimal parameter overhead.

title: Cross-Domain, Multi-Task Data-to-Text Generation without In-Domain Training Data
summary: Structured data exists in many forms (tables, knowledge graphs, charts, and time series), and converting it into text may involve different generation tasks. However, most prior work on data-to-text (D2T) generation has focused on specific tasks and datasets, relying either on task-specific training data or on the zero-shot capabilities of large language models. We study cross-domain D2T generation in a setting where neither in-domain training text nor test references are available, and where domains, generation goals, and input structures vary substantially. We compare data-driven knowledge distillation (DDKD) against zero-shot inference and fine-tuning on out-of-domain D2T data, and introduce structure-preserving augmentation via structural subsampling and perturbation. Experiments on five benchmarks show that, at constant model size (1.7B parameters), DDKD consistently outperforms both fine-tuning and zero-shot inference. Moreover, the resulting small models outperform a much larger finetuned model on two of the five domains, achieving comparable performance on the remaining three. We further construct QUINTD-5, a fivefold extension of QUINTD-1, and show that simply scaling real target-domain inputs yields only modest gains, whereas our augmentation strategy remains more effective and more cost-efficient for cross-domain distillation.

AI.tldr: This paper studies cross-domain data-to-text (D2T) generation where neither in-domain training text nor test references are available. It compares data-driven knowledge distillation (DDKD) against zero-shot inference and out-of-domain fine-tuning, and introduces structure-preserving augmentation via structural subsampling and perturbation. Experiments on five benchmarks show DDKD at 1.7B parameters consistently outperforms both baselines, and even beats a much larger fine-tuned model on two domains. The paper also constructs QUINTD-5 (a fivefold extension of QUINTD-1) and demonstrates that scaling real target-domain inputs yields only modest gains compared to the proposed augmentation strategy.
AI.motivation: Most prior D2T generation work focuses on specific tasks and datasets, relying on task-specific training data or zero-shot LLM capabilities. The authors aim to address cross-domain D2T generation in a more challenging and realistic setting where no in-domain training text or test references exist, and where domains, generation goals, and input structures vary substantially.
AI.method: The paper compares data-driven knowledge distillation (DDKD) against zero-shot inference and fine-tuning on out-of-domain D2T data. It introduces structure-preserving augmentation via structural subsampling and perturbation. Additionally, it constructs QUINTD-5, a fivefold extension of QUINTD-1, and evaluates the effect of scaling real target-domain inputs versus the proposed augmentation strategy.
AI.result: At a constant model size (1.7B parameters), DDKD consistently outperforms both fine-tuning and zero-shot inference across five benchmarks. The resulting small models outperform a much larger fine-tuned model on two of five domains and achieve comparable performance on the remaining three. Scaling real target-domain inputs yields only modest gains, while the augmentation strategy remains more effective and cost-efficient.
AI.conclusion: Data-driven knowledge distillation with structure-preserving augmentation is an effective and cost-efficient approach for cross-domain D2T generation in low-resource, domain-agnostic settings, outperforming both zero-shot inference and out-of-domain fine-tuning while enabling small models to rival or exceed much larger models.

title: Artificial Empathy: Towards a Framework for Unsupervised Agency Detection and Policy Reconstruction
summary: We study how an AI system can identify and model other agents in its environment from observation alone, which is a capability necessary for cooperative behaviour in the real world. This problem is less constrained than inverse reinforcement learning and remains largely unexplored. We propose a framework that uses a reinforcement learning agent, trained on an independent task as a prior about agentic dynamics, to perform agency detection and policy reconstruction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a framework for agency detection and policy reconstruction, where an AI system identifies and models other agents in its environment from observation alone, using a reinforcement learning agent trained on an independent task as a prior about agentic dynamics.
AI.motivation: The ability to identify and model other agents from observation is necessary for cooperative behavior in the real world. This problem is less constrained than inverse reinforcement learning and remains largely unexplored.
AI.method: A framework that leverages a reinforcement learning agent trained on an independent task as a prior about agentic dynamics to perform agency detection and policy reconstruction.
AI.result: No specific results are provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: No explicit conclusion is provided in the abstract, but the implication is that using RL priors enables effective agency detection and policy reconstruction from observation alone.

title: Coarse Indexing, Fine Evidence: Decoupling Temporal Granularity in Long-Video RAG
summary: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) provides a scalable paradigm for long-video understanding, but existing systems typically inherit a fixed temporal granularity from video segmentation when constructing their retrieval index. We argue that this design unnecessarily couples indexing granularity with evidence granularity: coarse representations can often suffice for locating relevant temporal regions, while fine-grained evidence remains important for downstream reasoning. We propose \textbf{Density-Aware Graph Construction (DAGC)}, a training-free approach that decouples a query-independent coarse retrieval index from the original fine-grained evidence space. DAGC constructs a compact, density-adaptive graph index by merging visually redundant neighboring chunks, while preserving mappings to the original temporal units. Retrieved coarse regions are subsequently expanded back to the original chunk granularity for fine-grained evidence refinement and answer generation. Experiments on MLVU, VideoMME, and LongVideoBench show that DAGC retains only about 40--50\% of the original graph nodes and achieves $1.3$--$1.7\times$ end-to-end wall-clock acceleration while preserving approximately 99\% of the original QA performance. The gains transfer across different LVLM backbones and video RAG pipelines, suggesting that long-video RAG need not maintain the same temporal granularity for indexing and evidence reasoning.

AI.tldr: DAGC is a training-free method for long-video RAG that decouples indexing granularity from evidence granularity by constructing a compact, density-adaptive graph index that merges visually redundant neighboring chunks while preserving mappings to original temporal units. It retains only 40-50% of graph nodes, achieves 1.3-1.7x wall-clock acceleration, and preserves ~99% of QA performance across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing graph-based RAG systems for long-video understanding couple indexing granularity with evidence granularity, inheriting a fixed temporal resolution from video segmentation. This design is suboptimal because coarse representations can suffice for locating relevant temporal regions, while fine-grained evidence is still needed for downstream reasoning—yet current systems maintain a single granularity throughout.
AI.method: DAGC is a training-free approach that (1) decouples a query-independent coarse retrieval index from the original fine-grained evidence space, (2) constructs a compact density-adaptive graph index by merging visually redundant neighboring chunks while preserving mappings back to original temporal units, and (3) expands retrieved coarse regions back to the original chunk granularity for fine-grained evidence refinement and answer generation.
AI.result: On MLVU, VideoMME, and LongVideoBench, DAGC retains only about 40-50% of the original graph nodes, achieves 1.3-1.7x end-to-end wall-clock acceleration, and preserves approximately 99% of the original QA performance. The gains transfer across different LVLM backbones and video RAG pipelines.
AI.conclusion: Long-video RAG need not maintain the same temporal granularity for indexing and evidence reasoning; decoupling these granularities via density-aware graph construction provides substantial efficiency gains without sacrificing answer quality.

title: STONIC: A Layered Measurement Contract for LLM Value Profiling
summary: LLM value studies often merge questionnaire ratings, pairwise choices, and values inferred from generated text into one profile. That merge assumes that the three observations describe the same stable preference. STONIC tests this assumption on 5,144 situations from four banks and 35 fixed model configurations. It compares responses rated in isolation, choices made under counterbalanced conflict, spontaneous answers, and later choices between a model's own answer and authored alternatives. 10 of 17 configurations with usable behavioral data preserve the endorsement-choice relation across banks. Every one of the 17 eligible configurations prefers its own earlier answer (median effect 0.790), although option position changes the choice rate in every eligible configuration. Profile shape transfers most strongly from ratings to conflict choices and weakens for spontaneous text. Three-way annotation of 200 L3 responses provides a task-local check of the semantic audit: FULCRA agrees most closely with the human majority, while DeBERTa retains useful rank information after calibration. Hidden states encode the completed decision more clearly than the prompt alone. Thus the models show reproducible behavioral continuity, but the evidence does not support one scorer-independent value identity across interfaces.

AI.tldr: STONIC tests whether LLM value measurements from ratings, choices, and text reflect a single stable preference, finding behavioral continuity across some configurations but no single scorer-independent value identity across interfaces.
AI.motivation: LLM value studies commonly aggregate questionnaire ratings, pairwise choices, and text-inferred values into one profile, assuming these observations capture the same stable preference. STONIC systematically tests this foundational assumption.
AI.method: STONIC evaluates 5,144 situations across four banks and 35 fixed model configurations, comparing isolated ratings, counterbalanced conflict choices, spontaneous answers, and later choices between a model's own answer and authored alternatives. It also performs three-way annotation of 200 L3 responses and analyzes hidden states.
AI.result: 10 of 17 configurations with usable behavioral data preserve the endorsement-choice relation across banks. All 17 eligible configurations prefer their own earlier answer (median effect 0.790), though option position affects choice rate in every configuration. Profile shape transfers most strongly from ratings to conflict choices but weakens for spontaneous text. FULCRA aligns closest with human majority annotation; DeBERTa retains useful rank information after calibration. Hidden states encode completed decisions better than the prompt alone.
AI.conclusion: Models exhibit reproducible behavioral continuity, but the evidence does not support the existence of a single, scorer-independent value identity across different interfaces.

title: MobilePA-Bench: Benchmarking Mobile Planner Agents on Complex Real-World Tasks
summary: As on-device LLM agents evolve into personal copilots, the mobile operating system has become a key testbed for this paradigm, making rigorous capability evaluation essential. Yet existing benchmarks fall into two camps, each with a critical blind spot: GUI-centric benchmarks test surface-level screen manipulation while overlooking background tool use and long-horizon planning, whereas static function-calling benchmarks rely on offline API matching that is detached from real runtime constraints. To close this gap, we present \textbf{MobilePA-Bench}, an interactive, stateful, and tool-centric benchmark for evaluating the tool-calling and planning abilities of mobile planning agents. MobilePA-Bench runs on an executable sandbox that maintains live application databases and returns structured feedback, spanning $13$ functional domains and $212$ realistic mobile tools. Beyond basic tool use, it evaluates a central planning agent along three advanced dimensions: \emph{(1)~Sub-agent Collaboration}---decomposing a complex task and delegating specialized work to capable sub-agents; \emph{(2)~Memory Usage}---recalling stored memories, user profiles, and past preferences to resolve implicit requests; and \emph{(3)~Skill Usage}---invoking pre-packaged composite skills instead of planning every step from scratch. Extensive experiments show that current frontier LLMs remain unreliable in mobile settings: performance drops sharply under strict tool ordering, permission limits, and unexpected runtime errors. By pairing an interactive function-calling sandbox with evidence-based verification, MobilePA-Bench serves as both a practical diagnostic benchmark and an interactive foundation for agentic reinforcement learning---accelerating the development of dependable mobile agents.

AI.tldr: MobilePA-Bench is an interactive, stateful, tool-centric benchmark for evaluating tool-calling and planning abilities of on-device LLM agents in mobile operating systems, spanning 13 functional domains and 212 realistic mobile tools.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks fall into two camps with critical blind spots: GUI-centric benchmarks test surface-level screen manipulation while overlooking background tool use and long-horizon planning, whereas static function-calling benchmarks rely on offline API matching detached from real runtime constraints. There is a need for a benchmark that captures real mobile agent capabilities.
AI.method: MobilePA-Bench runs on an executable sandbox that maintains live application databases and returns structured feedback, spanning 13 functional domains and 212 realistic mobile tools. It evaluates a central planning agent along three advanced dimensions: Sub-agent Collaboration (decomposing complex tasks and delegating to sub-agents), Memory Usage (recalling stored memories, user profiles, and past preferences), and Skill Usage (invoking pre-packaged composite skills).
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that current frontier LLMs remain unreliable in mobile settings: performance drops sharply under strict tool ordering, permission limits, and unexpected runtime errors.
AI.conclusion: By pairing an interactive function-calling sandbox with evidence-based verification, MobilePA-Bench serves as both a practical diagnostic benchmark and an interactive foundation for agentic reinforcement learning, accelerating the development of dependable mobile agents.

title: Misanthrope: A Privacy-Preserving Keypoint Detector
comment: Accepted to Privacy preserving Visual Localization (PPVLM) workshop at the European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV) 2026
summary: Image matching is a core component of applications such as Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM), Visual Localization, and Structure from Motion (SfM). However, the local image features central to this task are vulnerable to inversion attacks, which enable adversaries to reconstruct privacy-sensitive scene content from local features. These attacks pose a particular threat in distributed computing scenarios where the pre-computed features leave edge devices to be processed by remote servers. In this work, we introduce Misanthrope, a novel privacy-preserving keypoint detector trained through self-distillation to avoid detecting keypoints on people---a predominant source of privacy-sensitive content in most localization scenarios---thus mitigating inversion attacks at the source rather than through post-hoc obfuscation. We demonstrate how inverted images from traditional feature detection pipelines can be used to detect and re-identify people in the scene, while Misanthrope is able to mitigate these attacks. Furthermore, Misanthrope maintains image matching performance on par with the state of the art and even surpasses it in challenging settings where people act as distractors, such as phototourism and in-the-wild odometry. On the Image Matching Challenge 2021 Phototourism test set, Misanthrope is the top-performing sparse feature extractor in 7 out of 9 scenes. We make our model and its evaluation script available here: https://github.com/fratopa/misanthrope

AI.tldr: Misanthrope is a privacy-preserving keypoint detector trained via self-distillation to avoid detecting keypoints on people, mitigating inversion attacks at the source in image matching pipelines.
AI.motivation: Local image features used in SLAM, Visual Localization, and SfM are vulnerable to inversion attacks that can reconstruct privacy-sensitive scene content, particularly in distributed computing where features are processed by remote servers.
AI.method: The model is trained through self-distillation to avoid detecting keypoints on people, thereby preventing inversion attacks at the source rather than using post-hoc obfuscation.
AI.result: Misanthrope mitigates inversion attacks that can detect and re-identify people from inverted features, while maintaining state-of-the-art matching performance and surpassing existing methods in challenging distractor scenarios. It is the top-performing sparse feature extractor in 7 out of 9 scenes on the Image Matching Challenge 2021 Phototourism test set.
AI.conclusion: Misanthrope demonstrates that privacy-preserving feature detection can be achieved without sacrificing image matching performance, offering a scalable solution to mitigate inversion attacks in distributed localization and mapping systems.

title: A Comprehensive Analysis of Arabic Natural Language Processing Research: Trends, Topic Evolution, and Research Gaps -- A Bibliometric and Topic-Based Study
summary: Arabic Natural Language Processing (NLP) has grown rapidly over the past decade, driven by digital transformation in the Arab world, social media, and large language models (LLMs). Despite this growth, a comprehensive quantitative meta-analysis remains absent. This study presents a bibliometric and topic-based analysis of 7,120 Arabic NLP papers published between 1960 and 2026, sourced from five platforms (arXiv, ACL Anthology, Semantic Scholar, Crossref, OpenAlex) plus an additional targeted OpenAlex subset. We employ BERTopic for topic modeling, regression analysis, social network analysis, and geographic mapping. Our findings show a significant publication surge after 2020, driven by transformer models and LLMs. Topic modeling identifies 19 themes, the largest centered on text, speech, translation, and recognition (2,942 papers). Citation analysis reveals a positive correlation between paper age and citations (r = 0.245, p < 0.001); regression (R^2 = 0.105) shows that indexing in OpenAlex or Semantic Scholar and institutional affiliation are associated with higher citations. Saudi Arabia, the United States, and Egypt lead in research output. A task-dialect gap matrix identifies understudied areas, including summarization for Maghrebi, Iraqi, and Sudanese dialects. The largest topic has the highest H-index (90), followed by sentiment analysis (57). Our quantitative approach complements existing qualitative surveys and offers recommendations to prioritize under-resourced dialects and develop culturally aligned benchmarks.

AI.tldr: A bibliometric and topic-based meta-analysis of 7,120 Arabic NLP papers (1960–2026) from five platforms, using BERTopic, regression, social network analysis, and geographic mapping to reveal a post-2020 publication surge, 19 research themes, citation patterns, leading countries, and under-researched dialect-task combinations.
AI.motivation: Despite rapid growth in Arabic NLP driven by digital transformation, social media, and LLMs, no comprehensive quantitative meta-analysis of the field exists. This study fills that gap by providing a large-scale bibliometric and topic-based overview to complement existing qualitative surveys.
AI.method: Analyzed 7,120 papers from five platforms (arXiv, ACL Anthology, Semantic Scholar, Crossref, OpenAlex) plus a targeted OpenAlex subset. Used BERTopic for topic modeling, regression analysis for citations, social network analysis, and geographic mapping. Constructed a task-dialect gap matrix to identify understudied areas.
AI.result: Found a significant publication surge after 2020 driven by transformer models and LLMs; identified 19 topics with the largest centered on text, speech, translation, and recognition (2,942 papers). Citation analysis showed positive correlation between paper age and citations (r=0.245, p<0.001); regression (R²=0.105) indicated indexing in OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar and institutional affiliation boost citations. Saudi Arabia, the US, and Egypt lead in output. The largest topic has the highest H-index (90), followed by sentiment analysis (57).
AI.conclusion: The quantitative approach complements qualitative surveys and offers recommendations to prioritize under-resourced dialects (e.g., Maghrebi, Iraqi, Sudanese summarization) and develop culturally aligned benchmarks.

title: AutoSaddler: Automatic Harness Optimization with Durable Updates from Agent Execution Traces
comment: 44 pages, 15 figures. Project website and code: https://aka.ms/AutoSaddler-website
summary: LLM agents remain unreliable on long-horizon tasks, where small local failures can compound over extended interactions and lead to overall task failure. Although external harnesses can substantially improve robustness, harness design remains a manual and expensive process that requires searching over a large space of prompts, tool configurations, and control logic. We propose AutoSaddler, an automatic harness optimization framework that formulates harness improvement as an offline learning problem and iteratively updates the harness using failure signals from mini-batches. AutoSaddler combines failure-trace diagnosis, structured patch generation that treats the harness as code, and validation-based update selection. Experiments on GAIA2, SWE-Bench Pro, and Terminal-Bench 2.0 show that AutoSaddler substantially improves agent performance over the corresponding base harnesses, achieving gains of 9.0, 9.6, and 10.0 percentage points, respectively. Ablation studies further suggest that effective harness optimization benefits from three ingredients: deep debugging rather than shallow reflection, targeted modifications rather than unconstrained editing, and generalization-aware selection rather than trajectory-specific repair. Together, these results suggest that automatic harness optimization is a promising path toward more performant and reliable agent systems.

AI.tldr: AutoSaddler is an automatic harness optimization framework that treats harness improvement as an offline learning problem, iteratively updating external agent harnesses using failure signals, achieving 9-10 percentage point gains on GAIA2, SWE-Bench Pro, and Terminal-Bench 2.0.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are unreliable on long-horizon tasks because small local failures compound over extended interactions. While external harnesses can improve robustness, harness design is manual, expensive, and requires searching over a large space of prompts, tool configurations, and control logic.
AI.method: AutoSaddler formulates harness improvement as an offline learning problem and iteratively updates the harness using failure signals from mini-batches. It combines three components: failure-trace diagnosis, structured patch generation that treats the harness as code, and validation-based update selection.
AI.result: AutoSaddler improves agent performance by 9.0, 9.6, and 10.0 percentage points on GAIA2, SWE-Bench Pro, and Terminal-Bench 2.0 respectively. Ablations show three key ingredients are necessary: deep debugging over shallow reflection, targeted modifications over unconstrained editing, and generalization-aware selection over trajectory-specific repair.
AI.conclusion: Automatic harness optimization is a promising path toward more performant and reliable agent systems, offering a scalable alternative to manual harness engineering.

title: AnaDiffusion: Anatomically CompositionalLatent Diffusion for Controllable 3D Brain MRI Generation
summary: 3D brain MRI generation has made significant advances in medical imaging, simulation, and controllable anatomical analysis. However, existing generative models typically synthesize 3D volumes monolithically, often overlooking regional anatomical structures and limiting local controllability. To address these limitations, we introduce AnaDiffusion, an anatomically compositional latent diffusion framework that factorizes the generation process into distinct, anatomically meaningful regions, followed by part-to-whole assembly and global refinement. Our approach first trains part diffusion models to capture local structural priors. We then inject an assembled anatomical composite of the parts into the whole-brain latent representation and continue denoising. This mechanism enables the model to resolve global context while preserving the injected anatomy. As a result, AnaDiffusion produces both explicit part assets and a globally coherent volume, thereby enabling controllable part editing without requiring subject-specific dense segmentation maps at inference time while maintaining consistent part-to-whole brain structure. On the subject-disjoint ADNI test split, AnaDiffusion achieves the lowest FID across the whole brain, left and right hemispheres, cerebellar-brainstem complex, and seam regions. It also achieves the best cerebellar and second-best ventricular and brainstem absolute Cohen's d values among the evaluated methods. In localized editing experiments, paired MS-SSIM demonstrates high target transfer and off-target preservation, supporting controllable part replacement with minimal unintended anatomical alterations.

AI.tldr: AnaDiffusion is an anatomically compositional latent diffusion framework for 3D brain MRI generation that factorizes synthesis into distinct anatomical regions, assembles them into a whole-brain volume, and continues denoising for global refinement. It enables controllable part editing without dense segmentation maps at inference, achieving state-of-the-art FID scores across whole brain and regional structures on the ADNI dataset.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D brain MRI generative models synthesize volumes monolithically, overlooking regional anatomical structures and lacking local controllability for editing specific brain regions.
AI.method: AnaDiffusion uses a two-stage approach: (1) trains part diffusion models on anatomically distinct brain regions to capture local structural priors, and (2) injects an assembled anatomical composite of the parts into the whole-brain latent representation and continues denoising to resolve global context while preserving the injected anatomy.
AI.result: On the ADNI test split, AnaDiffusion achieves the lowest FID across the whole brain, left/right hemispheres, cerebellar-brainstem complex, and seam regions. It achieves the best cerebellar and second-best ventricular and brainstem Cohen's d values. In editing experiments, it demonstrates high target transfer and off-target preservation via paired MS-SSIM.
AI.conclusion: AnaDiffusion enables controllable part editing and replacement with minimal unintended anatomical alterations while maintaining globally coherent brain structure, without requiring subject-specific dense segmentation maps at inference time.

title: How Useful are LLMs for Grammar Engineering? Cantonese ParGram Resources and Controlled Experimental Evaluation with English Baselines
comment: Accepted to Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026
summary: This paper presents new Cantonese ParGram resources and evaluates LLMs for knowledge-driven grammar engineering within a controlled experimental paradigm. Using Cantonese ParGram resources as gold standards, with corresponding English baselines, we investigate whether OpenAI's gpt-oss-120b and GPT-5.4 can generate machine-processable grammars from sentences and target formal structures under systematically varied prompting conditions. GPT-5.4 outperformed gpt-oss-120b, while grammars generated from target formal structures generally outperformed those generated from sentences. Although both models could generate locally plausible phrase-structure rules, lexical entries, and templates, they often struggled to coordinate interacting formal constraints, especially in multi-construction settings. The results characterize both the capabilities and limitations of current LLMs for potential integration into AI-assisted expert workflows: LLMs may support intermediate stages of grammar development, but human linguistic expertise remains central to analysis, validation, and refinement. The study also contributes new Cantonese symbolic grammatical resources.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces new Cantonese ParGram resources and evaluates LLMs (gpt-oss-120b and GPT-5.4) for knowledge-driven grammar engineering, finding GPT-5.4 superior overall, with grammars from target formal structures outperforming those from sentences, though both models struggle with coordinating interacting formal constraints in multi-construction settings.
AI.motivation: To systematically evaluate the capabilities and limitations of current LLMs for knowledge-driven grammar engineering, specifically assessing whether they can generate machine-processable grammars from sentences and target formal structures, and to contribute new Cantonese symbolic grammatical resources to the field.
AI.method: Using Cantonese ParGram resources as gold standards with English baselines, the study employs a controlled experimental paradigm where two LLMs (gpt-oss-120b and GPT-5.4) generate grammars under systematically varied prompting conditions, comparing outputs from sentences versus target formal structures across single- and multi-construction settings.
AI.result: GPT-5.4 outperformed gpt-oss-120b. Grammars generated from target formal structures generally outperformed those from sentences. Both models succeeded at generating locally plausible phrase-structure rules, lexical entries, and templates but failed to coordinate interacting formal constraints, especially in multi-construction settings.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can support intermediate stages of grammar development in AI-assisted expert workflows, but human linguistic expertise remains essential for analysis, validation, and refinement of generated grammars. The study also contributes new Cantonese symbolic grammatical resources.

title: From Inertia to Objectivity: Improving Deep Research Agents with Noise Isolation
summary: Web search agents powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) show strong promise, but deep research tasks expose a recurring failure mode: once an agent has produced a query, plan, or intermediate conclusion, it becomes less objective when later judging the consequences of that same action. We term this phenomenon \textbf{inertia bias}. To make it measurable, we introduce the IBIS benchmark, which controls the search observations while varying whether the model is evaluating the outcome of its own prior action. We find that models are substantially worse when they ``own'' the preceding search step, showing that self-authored action history can systematically distort subsequent judgment. We further show that this bias propagates into two forms of system-level degradation: search noise at the worker level and contextual noise at the manager level. To address this problem, we propose NIS-Agent, which applies context isolation at the two decision points most vulnerable to inertia bias: webpage triage and final-answer validation. Across GAIA, WebWalkerQA, BrowseComp, and BrowseComp-zh, NIS-Agent achieves competitive performance while reducing token cost by 33\% compared to our baseline. We further train an 8B model to be intrinsically more resistant to inertia bias; under the same NIS-Agent framework, it attains average performance comparable to GPT-4o on deep research benchmarks.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies "inertia bias" in LLM-powered web search agents—where models become less objective when evaluating outcomes of their own prior actions—and introduces the IBIS benchmark to measure it. The authors propose NIS-Agent, a framework applying context isolation at two vulnerable decision points, achieving competitive performance on multiple benchmarks with 33% token cost reduction, and further train an 8B model with intrinsic resistance to this bias achieving GPT-4o-comparable performance.
AI.motivation: Deep research web search agents powered by LLMs exhibit a systematic failure: once a model has produced a query, plan, or intermediate conclusion, its subsequent judgment of that same action becomes less objective. This self-authored action history distortion is termed inertia bias, and the authors aim to make it measurable and addressable.
AI.method: The paper introduces the IBIS benchmark that controls search observations while varying whether the model evaluates its own prior action to measure inertia bias. To address it, they propose NIS-Agent, which applies context isolation at two decision points most vulnerable to the bias: webpage triage and final-answer validation. Additionally, they train an 8B model to be intrinsically more resistant to inertia bias.
AI.result: Models perform substantially worse when they "own" the preceding search step, confirming systematic judgment distortion from self-authored history. Inertia bias propagates into system-level degradation (search noise at worker level, contextual noise at manager level). NIS-Agent achieves competitive performance on GAIA, WebWalkerQA, BrowseComp, and BrowseComp-zh while reducing token cost by 33%. The trained 8B model with NIS-Agent attains average performance comparable to GPT-4o on deep research benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Inertia bias is a measurable and addressable failure mode in LLM web search agents. Context isolation via NIS-Agent effectively mitigates this bias while improving efficiency (33% token savings), and smaller models can be trained to be intrinsically resistant, achieving GPT-4o-level performance at lower cost.

title: When the Edit Changes the Patient: Measuring Identity Preservation in Counterfactual Retinal Images
summary: Counterfactual medical image generation aims to modify an existing image to reflect a hypothetical scenario in which certain characteristics of the imaged subject are altered, while keeping their identity fixed. Most existing works repurpose established image editing methods, which do not directly supervise identity preservation. Instead, they assume that identity is implicitly preserved by anchoring generation to the source image. This assumption is rarely tested and may fail in domains where biometric cues are subtle, such as retinal optical coherence tomography (OCT). In this work, we explicitly measure identity preservation for three groups of text-conditioned editing methods - source-anchored, structured-prompt, and paired-training - using referee classifiers, embedding alignment scores, and a blind reader study. We find that all methods produce high-quality OCT images with comparable editing success, yet their identity preservation differs markedly. Source-anchored editing frequently alters the depicted subject, while paired-training preserves it best. We argue that future work on medical counterfactual generation must explicitly measure and report identity preservation alongside image realism and editing success.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates identity preservation in counterfactual medical image generation for retinal OCT, finding that source-anchored editing methods frequently alter the subject's identity while paired-training methods preserve it best, despite all methods achieving comparable image quality and editing success.
AI.motivation: Existing counterfactual medical image generation methods repurpose general image editing techniques that assume identity is implicitly preserved by anchoring to the source image, but this assumption is rarely tested and may fail in domains with subtle biometric cues like retinal OCT.
AI.method: The authors systematically evaluate three groups of text-conditioned editing methods (source-anchored, structured-prompt, and paired-training) using three evaluation approaches: referee classifiers, embedding alignment scores, and a blind reader study, applied to retinal OCT counterfactual generation.
AI.result: All methods produce high-quality OCT images with comparable editing success, but identity preservation differs significantly across method groups. Source-anchored editing frequently alters the depicted subject, while paired-training methods preserve identity best.
AI.conclusion: Future work on medical counterfactual generation must explicitly measure and report identity preservation alongside image realism and editing success, as implicit assumptions about identity preservation are insufficient.

title: What's the Catch? Evaluating Temporal Consistency in Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) achieve strong performance on video and image-sequence benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether they capture temporal structure. To study this question, we formulate temporal grounding as an anomaly detection problem, providing a simple and controlled evaluation that directly tests sensitivity to temporal consistency. We introduce TimeCatch, where temporal anomalies are created by swapping consecutive frames and frame-level anomalies by replacing a frame with Gaussian noise. Models are evaluated on anomaly detection and localization tasks across four synthetic and real-world datasets, alongside a human study. Our evaluation reveals a substantial gap between frame-level and temporal anomaly detection. While VLMs consistently detect frame-level anomalies and often localize them accurately, they perform near chance on temporal anomaly detection and only modestly above chance on localization. Humans, in contrast, achieve near-ceiling performance on both tasks. Additional analyses across model scales, prompting strategies, sequence lengths, and visual similarity suggest that these failures cannot be explained solely by limitations in perception or model capacity. Together, these findings indicate that current VLMs can identify anomalies within individual frames but struggle to integrate information across frames to reason about temporal consistency. TimeCatch provides a controlled benchmark for evaluating temporal grounding in vision-language models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TimeCatch, a benchmark for evaluating temporal grounding in vision-language models (VLMs) by framing it as an anomaly detection problem. It reveals that while VLMs excel at detecting frame-level anomalies (e.g., Gaussian noise), they perform near chance on temporal anomalies (swapped consecutive frames), whereas humans achieve near-ceiling performance on both.
AI.motivation: Despite strong performance on video benchmarks, it is unclear whether VLMs truly capture temporal structure. The authors aim to provide a controlled, simple evaluation that directly tests sensitivity to temporal consistency in VLMs.
AI.method: The paper formulates temporal grounding as an anomaly detection task. Temporal anomalies are created by swapping consecutive frames, and frame-level anomalies by replacing a frame with Gaussian noise. Models are evaluated on anomaly detection and localization across four synthetic and real-world datasets, alongside a human study. Additional analyses vary model scales, prompting strategies, sequence lengths, and visual similarity.
AI.result: VLMs consistently detect and localize frame-level anomalies but perform near chance on temporal anomaly detection and only modestly above chance on temporal anomaly localization. Humans achieve near-ceiling performance on both tasks. The failures persist across model scales, prompting strategies, sequence lengths, and visual similarity, suggesting they are not solely due to perception limits or model capacity.
AI.conclusion: Current VLMs can identify anomalies within individual frames but struggle to integrate information across frames to reason about temporal consistency. TimeCatch serves as a controlled benchmark for evaluating temporal grounding in vision-language models.

title: LLM-based Agents for Forecasting and Prediction: Methods, Training, Evaluation, and Applications
summary: Large language models (LLMs) now support forecasting systems that combine language-based reasoning with temporal data, evidence retrieval, external tools, and iterative prediction. We investigate LLM-based forecasting agents, meaning systems in which a language model contributes to a scored prediction about a future or currently unobserved target. We organize architectures into three groups. Standalone LLM workflows operate on encoded time series or event context. Tool- and retrieval-augmented agents incorporate external evidence. Hybrid systems pair LLMs with statistical or foundation models. We then review training methods and evaluation protocols. We examine negative as well as positive evidence, including sensitivity to small input perturbations, ablations in which the LLM component does not improve accuracy, and benchmark gains that may reflect contamination instead of temporal reasoning. We cover applications in finance, weather, health, energy, and operations, and we summarize the benchmarks and datasets used for evaluation. The evidence indicates that measurement is a central limitation. Future work requires calibration under distribution shift, contamination-resistant live evaluation, explicit reporting of cost and accuracy together, and methods for handling feedback between deployed forecasts and the outcomes being forecast.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a comprehensive survey of LLM-based forecasting agents, categorizing them into standalone workflows, tool/retrieval-augmented agents, and hybrid systems with statistical or foundation models. It reviews training methods, evaluation protocols, and applications across finance, weather, health, energy, and operations, while critically examining negative evidence and identifying measurement as the central limitation requiring future work on calibration under distribution shift, contamination-resistant evaluation, cost-accuracy reporting, and feedback handling.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used in forecasting systems, but there is a need to systematically organize the growing body of work on LLM-based forecasting agents, understand their architectural variations, and critically assess both their capabilities and limitations—particularly whether apparent gains reflect genuine temporal reasoning or artifacts like dataset contamination.
AI.method: The paper surveys LLM-based forecasting agents by organizing architectures into three groups: (1) standalone LLM workflows operating on encoded time series or event context, (2) tool- and retrieval-augmented agents incorporating external evidence, and (3) hybrid systems pairing LLMs with statistical or foundation models. It reviews training methods, evaluation protocols, negative evidence (perturbation sensitivity, ablation failures, contamination), and catalogs applications and benchmarks.
AI.result: The survey finds that measurement is the central limitation in LLM forecasting. Evidence shows sensitivity to input perturbations, ablations where the LLM component fails to improve accuracy, and benchmark gains that may reflect contamination rather than temporal reasoning. Applications span finance, weather, health, energy, and operations, with a catalog of relevant benchmarks and datasets provided.
AI.conclusion: Future work in LLM-based forecasting must prioritize calibration under distribution shift, contamination-resistant live evaluation, explicit joint reporting of cost and accuracy, and methods for handling feedback between deployed forecasts and the outcomes being forecast.

title: Cultural Moment Benchmark: Evaluating Video Cultural Reasoning and Grounding in Southeast Asia
summary: Cultural understanding in video means more than recognizing what is visible; it requires grasping the symbolic and temporal significance of cultural concepts. We decompose this into three abilities: naming what a concept symbolizes, visually recognizing it on video, and locating its sub-events in time. Existing video-cultural benchmarks tend to test what is seen, collapsing these three abilities into a single score that hides the bottleneck. We introduce the Cultural Moment Benchmark (CMB): 306 expert-curated concepts from seven countries in Southeast Asia across five categories. We evaluate each concept through three stages, one per ability. Given a description, Stage 1 (S1) selects from four candidate concept names, Stage 2 (S2) selects from four candidate video moments, and Stage 3 (S3) predicts the start and end times of the moment in a video. To keep each stage focused on a distinct ability, we use three design choices: semantic-similarity distractors (S1, S2), unlabeled video moments (S2), and free-form localization on a different example video (S3). Across six vision-language models, failure modes vary by ability and modality. i) Even the strongest closed-source models score below 30% when all three stages must be correct; ii) The three abilities do not fully cascade: naming a concept correctly helps half the models recognize it on video, but recognizing it has little effect on locating the sub-event in time; iii) Audio is complementary, redundant, or distracting depending on the concept, more often distracting in non-Latin-script countries; removing both audio and subtitles hurts Games and Music the most. Our 14-rater human study shows that even Expert raters score below chance on concepts from a neighboring country, indicating that CMB requires country-specific cultural knowledge. CMB acts as a diagnostic harness, attributing failures to a specific ability or modality.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Cultural Moment Benchmark (CMB), which decomposes video cultural understanding into three distinct abilities: naming a cultural concept, visually recognizing it in video, and temporally localizing its sub-events. Evaluated on 306 expert-curated concepts from seven Southeast Asian countries, CMB reveals that current vision-language models fail dramatically (below 30% on all three stages), that abilities do not fully cascade, and that audio can help, complement, or distract depending on the concept and culture.
AI.motivation: Existing video-cultural benchmarks collapse three distinct abilities (naming, visual recognition, temporal localization) into a single score, hiding which capability is the actual bottleneck in models' cultural understanding. There is a need for a diagnostic benchmark that isolates each ability to attribute failures to specific skills.
AI.method: CMB evaluates each concept through three staged tasks: S1 selects a concept name from four candidates given a description, S2 selects the correct video moment from four candidates, and S3 predicts start/end times of the moment in a video. Three design choices isolate abilities: semantic-similarity distractors, unlabeled video moments, and free-form localization on a different example video. The benchmark covers 306 concepts across five categories from seven Southeast Asian countries, evaluated on six vision-language models plus a 14-rater human study.
AI.result: Even the strongest closed-source models score below 30% when all three stages must be correct. The three abilities do not fully cascade—naming helps half the models recognize concepts on video, but recognition does not help temporal localization. Audio is complementary, redundant, or distracting depending on the concept, more often distracting in non-Latin-script countries; removing audio and subtitles hurts Games and Music most. Expert raters score below chance on concepts from neighboring countries, confirming country-specific cultural knowledge is required.
AI.conclusion: CMB serves as a diagnostic harness that attributes model failures to specific abilities (naming, recognition, localization) or modalities (audio, vision, subtitles), revealing that cultural understanding in video remains a major unsolved challenge for current models and requires country-specific knowledge that even human experts lack for foreign cultures.

title: On the Threat Model of Weird Generalization and Emergent Misalignment
