summary: Narrow fine-tuning on small, domain-specific datasets can produce broad and surprising changes in model behavior-a phenomenon called weird generalization (WG). Yet, it remains unclear what features of the fine-tuning data are necessary for WG to arise. Here, we address this question by investigating a range of plausibly relevant features, including dataset size, composition, language, presentation style, and novelty relative to a model's parametric knowledge. Further, since WG evaluations rely on small question sets that assess the extent of the generalization, we also analyze how sensitive this measurement is to the set of questions used. Experiments with three open-weight models on four datasets show that the degree of WG (1) depends heavily on dataset composition and language (more than on size); (2) is greater for data familiar from pretraining than for novel data; and (3) is sensitive to the set of evaluation questions used. Collectively, these results indicate that WG is a product of quite fragile properties of both training and evaluation data. As such, we argue that WG is more plausible as an adversarial threat-requiring careful data engineering-rather than as a significant hazard inherent to routine fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates "weird generalization" (WG)—where narrow fine-tuning on small domain-specific datasets causes broad, surprising model behavior changes. It systematically tests which features of fine-tuning data (size, composition, language, presentation, novelty) drive WG, and how sensitive WG measurement is to evaluation question sets. Experiments across three open-weight models and four datasets reveal WG depends heavily on dataset composition and language, is stronger for pretraining-familiar data, and is sensitive to evaluation questions—suggesting WG is an adversarial threat requiring careful data engineering rather than an inherent hazard of routine fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: While weird generalization has been observed, it remains unclear what features of the fine-tuning data are necessary for WG to arise. The authors aim to systematically identify these features and also assess the reliability of WG measurement itself.
AI.method: The study varies plausibly relevant data features—dataset size, composition, language, presentation style, and novelty relative to parametric knowledge—across experiments with three open-weight models on four datasets. It also analyzes measurement sensitivity by varying the set of evaluation questions used to assess generalization extent.
AI.result: Three main findings: (1) WG depends heavily on dataset composition and language, more than on dataset size; (2) WG is greater for data familiar from pretraining than for novel data; (3) WG measurements are sensitive to the set of evaluation questions used.
AI.conclusion: WG arises from fragile properties of both training and evaluation data. Consequently, it is more plausibly characterized as an adversarial threat requiring deliberate data engineering than as a significant hazard inherent to routine fine-tuning.

title: Improving O-RADS Risk Stratification from Ultrasound Reports: A Comparative Evaluation of Hybrid versus End-to-End LLM Reasoning Strategies
comment: Main manuscript: 20 pages, 5 figures, and 2 tables; supplemental material: 11 pages, 1 figure, and 3 tables
summary: Background: Automating clinical guideline-based decision-making with large language models (LLMs) remains challenging because of reliability, hallucination, and limited interpretability. We compared the performance of LLMs and reasoning strategies for automated Ovarian-Adnexal Reporting and Data System (O-RADS) classification from free-text pelvic ultrasound reports. Methods: In this retrospective study, consecutive patients with ovarian masses who underwent pelvic ultrasound were included. Eight LLMs were tested with three reasoning strategies: implicit-knowledge end-to-end, rule-informed end-to-end, and a feature-based hybrid architecture that decoupled feature extraction from rule-based classification. The reference standard was O-RADS categorization established by expert consensus. Results: A total of 310 women with 390 ovarian masses were evaluated. The feature-based hybrid architecture using Gemini 3.6 Flash demonstrated the best performance, achieving an accuracy of 99.2% (387 of 390) and almost perfect agreement with the reference standard (weighted kappa = 1.00; 95% CI: 0.99-1.00). Its performance surpassed that of original clinical reports (accuracy, 87.7% [342 of 390]; weighted kappa = 0.94; 95% CI: 0.91-0.96) and end-to-end LLM strategies (accuracy range, 65.6% [256 of 390] to 95.9% [374 of 390]). For structured feature extraction, Gemini 3.6 Flash demonstrated higher overall accuracy than Claude Fable 5 (98.9% vs 97.8%; P < 0.001). The hybrid architecture reduced misclassification errors and mitigated the overstaging tendency observed in original reports. Conclusion: The feature-based hybrid LLM architecture that separates clinical feature extraction from deterministic guideline execution enables highly accurate, reliable, and interpretable automated O-RADS classification, providing a promising approach for standardized, guideline-based clinical decision-making.

AI.tldr: A retrospective study of 310 women (390 ovarian masses) comparing eight LLMs and three reasoning strategies for automated O-RADS classification from pelvic ultrasound reports. The feature-based hybrid architecture using Gemini 3.6 Flash achieved the best accuracy (99.2%, weighted kappa = 1.00), surpassing original clinical reports (87.7%) and all end-to-end LLM strategies (65.6-95.9%).
AI.motivation: Automating clinical guideline-based decision-making with LLMs is challenged by reliability issues, hallucination, and limited interpretability. This study compares LLM performance and reasoning strategies for O-RADS classification from free-text ultrasound reports to find a more reliable and interpretable approach.
AI.method: Retrospective study including consecutive patients with ovarian masses undergoing pelvic ultrasound. Eight LLMs were evaluated using three reasoning strategies: (1) implicit-knowledge end-to-end, (2) rule-informed end-to-end, and (3) a feature-based hybrid architecture that separates feature extraction from rule-based classification. The reference standard was expert consensus O-RADS categorization. Performance metrics included accuracy and weighted kappa.
AI.result: The feature-based hybrid architecture using Gemini 3.6 Flash achieved the best performance with 99.2% accuracy and weighted kappa = 1.00 (95% CI: 0.99-1.00), outperforming original clinical reports (87.7%, kappa = 0.94) and end-to-end strategies (accuracy 65.6-95.9%). Gemini 3.6 Flash also outperformed Claude Fable 5 in structured feature extraction (98.9% vs 97.8%; P < 0.001). The hybrid approach reduced misclassification errors and mitigated overstaging.
AI.conclusion: The feature-based hybrid LLM architecture that decouples clinical feature extraction from deterministic guideline execution provides highly accurate, reliable, and interpretable automated O-RADS classification, representing a promising paradigm for standardized, guideline-based clinical decision-making.

title: Grounding Isn't Knowing: Do VLMs Need Object Localization for Spatial Reasoning?
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can answer spatial questions, yet the mechanisms connecting object grounding to spatial reasoning remain poorly understood. It is underexplored whether spatial reasoning internally requires precise objects localization, or can bypass explicit localization through global layout cues. In this work, we investigate two representative model families, LLaVA-1.5 and Qwen2.5-VL, using a suite of mechanistic interpretability tools, including token ablation, layer-wise probing, attention knockout, and causal mediation analysis. We find that spatial relation prediction follows a staged grounding-to-reasoning process in which object-aligned tokens establish coarse target-reference anchors, while precise bounding-box boundaries are not required. Positional information becomes decodable before relation decisions emerge, and a small set of attention heads mediates the causal effects of both localization and spatial reasoning. The two tasks share early grounding-related processing but ultimately rely on partially distinct specialized pathways. Through rigorous experiments, we provide a token-, layer-, and head-level account of how VLMs transform object grounding into spatial relations, showing that knowing where objects are is not equivalent to knowing how they relate.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how vision-language models (VLMs) perform spatial reasoning, finding that spatial relation prediction follows a staged grounding-to-reasoning process where coarse object anchors (not precise bounding boxes) are sufficient. A small set of attention heads mediates both localization and reasoning, and the two tasks share early processing but rely on partially distinct pathways.
AI.motivation: The mechanistic connection between object grounding and spatial reasoning in VLMs is poorly understood. It is unclear whether spatial reasoning requires precise object localization or can operate on global layout cues, which has implications for model interpretability and design.
AI.method: The authors analyze LLaVA-1.5 and Qwen2.5-VL using mechanistic interpretability tools: token ablation, layer-wise probing, attention knockout, and causal mediation analysis.
AI.result: Spatial reasoning uses coarse target-reference anchors rather than precise bounding-box boundaries. Positional information becomes decodable before relation decisions emerge. A small set of attention heads causally mediates both localization and reasoning. Grounding and reasoning share early processing but rely on partially distinct specialized pathways.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a token-, layer-, and head-level account of how VLMs transform object grounding into spatial relations, demonstrating that knowing where objects are is not equivalent to knowing how they relate.

title: When Names Cross Scripts: A Source-Grounded Benchmark for Historical Entity Reconciliation in the Mongol World
summary:
Historical people may appear under different languages, scripts, and transcription traditions, while distinct individuals may share highly similar or even identical names. This makes historical identity reconciliation more than a problem of string matching or transliteration. We introduce MHER, a provenance-controlled benchmark for pairwise reconciliation of person-name attestations from the Mongol world. MHER contains a balanced 396-pair Name-only core over 84 primary historical persons and a stricter 160-pair Source-grounded subset constructed from mention-by-source evidence, with entity-disjoint development and test splits.
  Across five generative systems, correctly Source-grounded evidence improves paired TEST accuracy by 12.96 to 94.44 percentage points relative to Name-only input. On five identical-surface different-person cases, all models fail under names alone (0/25 model-item decisions), whereas Source-grounded evidence yields 24/25 correct resolutions, with the remaining output an abstention. Context-only ablations show that historical descriptions often carry substantial identity information, while explicitly signaled misgrounding controls produce substantially lower performance. We also find that names are not uniformly beneficial: for Qwen3-8B, restoring surface forms converts ten otherwise correct Context-only distinctions into false identity merges.
  These results show that historical entity reconciliation depends not only on surface correspondence, but on whether identity judgments respond appropriately to provenance-controlled historical evidence. MHER therefore provides a controlled framework for studying evidence use, abstention, and failure modes in historical NLP.

AI.tldr: MHER is a provenance-controlled benchmark for reconciling historical person-name attestations from the Mongol world, showing that source-grounded evidence dramatically improves identity disambiguation compared to name-only input, while names alone fail on identical-surface different-person cases.
AI.motivation: Historical identity reconciliation is more complex than string matching or transliteration because the same person may appear under different languages/scripts/transcription traditions, while distinct individuals may share highly similar or identical names. Existing approaches lack provenance-controlled benchmarks to disentangle these challenges.
AI.method: MHER contains a balanced 396-pair Name-only core over 84 primary historical persons and a stricter 160-pair Source-grounded subset built from mention-by-source evidence, with entity-disjoint development and test splits. The benchmark is tested across five generative systems with controlled ablations including name-only, source-grounded, context-only, and explicitly misgrounded conditions.
AI.result: Correct Source-grounded evidence improves paired TEST accuracy by 12.96-94.44 percentage points over Name-only input. On five identical-surface different-person cases, all models fail under names alone (0/25 correct), while source-grounded evidence yields 24/25 correct resolutions. Context-only ablations show descriptions carry substantial identity info, and for Qwen3-8B restoring surface names converts ten correct context-only distinctions into false identity merges.
AI.conclusion: Historical entity reconciliation depends not only on surface correspondence but on whether identity judgments respond appropriately to provenance-controlled historical evidence. MHER provides a controlled framework for studying evidence use, abstention, and failure modes in historical NLP.

title: From Generation to Simulation: How Far Are World Models from Being True Simulators?
summary: With the rapid progress of diffusion models and large-scale video generation, generative world models are increasingly expected to replace traditional simulators, including physics engines, game engines, and reinforcement-learning environments. Yet the remaining distance from generation to simulation lacks a systematic assessment. We present a capability-based study using an external yardstick: eight capabilities of a traditional simulator, namely asset construction, physics engine, interaction, controllability, stability, state feedback, diversity, and evaluation metrics. We trace three main technical routes--latent dynamics, video generation, and joint-embedding prediction--and map exactly 200 representative works published from 2018 to June 2026 onto these capabilities. Our analysis shows that world models have achieved functional substitution in interaction and controllability for specific scenarios, but remain short of traditional simulators in formal guarantees of physical laws, structured state feedback, and reproducible long-horizon evolution. State feedback is the most neglected cross-route shortcoming: only 6 of 163 implementation papers expose a runtime interface for querying entity states or physical parameters. We identify six research directions: formalized physics, a unified action interface, first-class state feedback, long-horizon stability, downstream-utility evaluation, and cross-route hybridization. Project page: https://github.com/AtongWang/world-model-simulators

AI.tldr: This paper presents a capability-based systematic assessment of generative world models as replacements for traditional simulators (physics engines, game engines, RL environments), mapping 200 representative works (2018-2026) across three technical routes onto eight simulator capabilities, finding partial functional substitution but persistent gaps in physical law guarantees, structured state feedback, and long-horizon stability.
AI.motivation: As generative world models rapidly advance, there is growing expectation that they will replace traditional simulators, yet no systematic framework exists to assess how far generation has come from simulation. The gap between "generation" and "simulation" needs a capability-based evaluation using an external yardstick.
AI.method: The authors define eight capabilities of traditional simulators (asset construction, physics engine, interaction, controllability, stability, state feedback, diversity, evaluation metrics) and trace three technical routes (latent dynamics, video generation, joint-embedding prediction), mapping exactly 200 representative works published from 2018 to June 2026 onto these capabilities for cross-route comparison.
AI.result: World models achieve functional substitution in interaction and controllability for specific scenarios but fall short in formal physical law guarantees, structured state feedback, and reproducible long-horizon evolution. State feedback is the most neglected shortcoming across routes—only 6 of 163 implementation papers expose a runtime interface for querying entity states or physical parameters.
AI.conclusion: Six research directions are identified: formalized physics, unified action interface, first-class state feedback, long-horizon stability, downstream-utility evaluation, and cross-route hybridization, guiding future efforts to close the remaining gap between world models and traditional simulators.

title: Loopy: Seamless Video Loop Generation via Anchored Looping Shift of Positional Embedding
comment: 15 pages, 21 figures, accepted by ACM TOG
summary: Looping videos are essential for practical applications such as web graphics, game development, and social media. However, existing approaches typically fail to generate high-quality looping videos due to the neglect of how video generation models perceive temporal order and how this relates to the looping behavior. In this work, we are the first to reveal that position embedding at different attention layers within DiT exhibits varying levels of positional control, with the most pronounced layer acting as an anchor. We formulate this anchored layer as the reference point of the looping video, offering strong contextual priors for the remaining layers to facilitate the generation of seamless and coherent video content. Based on this insight, we propose an anchored position embedding shifting strategy that applies layer-specific shift lengths according to each layer's temporal control effect, effectively transforming DiT's temporal perception from a straight line to a circle. Leveraging this strategy, we develop a general framework, Loopy, for high-quality looping video generation, supporting both RGB and RGBA videos, while also enabling advanced AIGC features such as identity control and style transfer. Experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly improves temporal consistency and visual fidelity in generated looping videos. The released model is available on our website: https://donghaotian123.github.io/Loopy.

AI.tldr: Loopy is a framework for high-quality looping video generation that leverages the insight that position embeddings in different attention layers of DiT exhibit varying positional control, with the most dominant layer acting as an anchor. By applying layer-specific shift lengths to transform DiT's temporal perception from a line to a circle, Loopy achieves seamless looping videos supporting both RGB and RGBA formats, along with advanced features like identity control and style transfer.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches fail to generate high-quality looping videos because they neglect how video generation models perceive temporal order and how this relates to looping behavior.
AI.method: The paper reveals that position embeddings at different attention layers within DiT have varying positional control levels, with the most pronounced layer acting as an anchor. Based on this, they propose an anchored position embedding shifting strategy that applies layer-specific shift lengths according to each layer's temporal control effect, effectively transforming DiT's temporal perception from a straight line to a circle. This forms the basis of the Loopy framework for looping video generation, supporting both RGB and RGBA videos and enabling identity control and style transfer.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that the approach significantly improves temporal consistency and visual fidelity in generated looping videos.
AI.conclusion: The anchored position embedding shifting strategy is an effective general framework for high-quality looping video generation, with the released model available publicly.

title: ConvergeFlow: Language Flow with Provable Convergence to Token Embeddings
summary: Recent advances in continuous diffusion and flow-based language models (LMs) have achieved performance competitive with discrete LMs. However, existing continuous frameworks still rely on decoders supervised with cross entropy (CE) because the flow trajectories are not guaranteed to terminate at valid token embeddings. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce \textbf{ConvergeFlow}, an embedding-space flow-based LM, which constrains the data predictor to the convex hull of token embeddings and trains it solely with the mean squared error objective induced by flow matching. Under suitable regularity conditions, we prove that the resulting flow converges to valid token embeddings despite errors in the data predictor, enabling direct token prediction without a CE-supervised decoder. We further develop three sampling mechanisms for controlling the trade-off between the generative perplexity and entropy. Experiments on OpenWebText demonstrate that ConvergeFlow achieves performance competitive with existing continuous and discrete diffusion LMs. These findings demonstrate the potential of the flow-based paradigm for language modeling. Our code is available at https://github.com/Na-Li66/ConvergeFlow.

AI.tldr: ConvergeFlow is an embedding-space flow-based language model that constrains the data predictor to the convex hull of token embeddings and trains solely with MSE from flow matching, proving convergence to valid token embeddings and enabling direct token prediction without cross-entropy-supervised decoders.
AI.motivation: Existing continuous diffusion and flow-based LMs still depend on decoders supervised with cross entropy since flow trajectories are not guaranteed to terminate at valid token embeddings. This dependency limits the full potential of the flow-based paradigm for language modeling.
AI.method: ConvergeFlow constrains the data predictor to the convex hull of token embeddings and trains it solely with the mean squared error objective from flow matching. The paper provides theoretical proof that under suitable regularity conditions, the flow converges to valid token embeddings despite errors in the data predictor. It also introduces three sampling mechanisms to control the trade-off between generative perplexity and entropy.
AI.result: On OpenWebText, ConvergeFlow achieves performance competitive with existing continuous and discrete diffusion LMs, while eliminating the need for a CE-supervised decoder.
AI.conclusion: The findings demonstrate that flow-based language modeling can serve as a standalone paradigm that produces valid token embeddings directly, rivaling discrete LMs and existing continuous frameworks without requiring auxiliary cross-entropy supervision.

title: AgentWeave: Routing Before Reasoning for Efficient Function Calling in Tool-Rich Language Models
comment: 12 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Open-source implementation and reproducibility artifacts available in the AgentWeave repository
summary: Large language models increasingly operate over large collections of tools, functions, APIs, and specialized agents. As the candidate action space grows, a function-calling model must process more schemas, consume more prompt tokens, and distinguish among increasingly similar or irrelevant alternatives. We study a complementary systems strategy: reduce the candidate set before language-model inference while leaving the downstream model unchanged. We introduce AgentWeave, a deterministic pre-inference routing layer that constructs a bounded model-visible action space using eligibility, requirement, capability, and routing signals. We evaluate AgentWeave with a frozen BFCL-derived routing-pressure protocol using the public MadeAgents/Hammer2.1-1.5b model. On 48 fresh BFCL V4 multiple-function tasks, AgentWeave achieves 6/48 (12.5%) native BFCL successes, whereas all-tools, deterministic random top-8, and semantic top-8 baselines each achieve 0/48. The paired success difference is +12.5 percentage points with a 10,000-resample paired bootstrap 95% confidence interval of +4.17 to +22.92 points and exact McNemar p=0.03125. Relative to all-tools exposure, AgentWeave presents 70.18% fewer tools, uses 61.70% fewer input tokens, and exhibits 50.95% lower mean local-model latency. The result is deliberately narrow: this is a BFCL-derived routing-pressure study rather than an official full BFCL leaderboard score, and absolute task success remains low. The evidence nevertheless shows that candidate-space construction can materially affect a fixed model's function-calling behavior and motivates evaluating routing as a distinct stage before model reasoning.

AI.tldr: AgentWeave is a deterministic pre-inference routing layer that reduces the candidate tool/function set before LLM inference, improving function-calling success on BFCL V4 tasks (12.5% vs 0% for baselines) while reducing tool exposure, token usage, and latency.
AI.motivation: Large language models increasingly operate over large collections of tools, functions, APIs, and agents. As the candidate action space grows, function-calling models must process more schemas, consume more tokens, and distinguish among increasingly similar or irrelevant alternatives. The authors propose a complementary systems strategy—reducing the candidate set before LLM inference—rather than modifying the downstream model.
AI.method: AgentWeave is a deterministic pre-inference routing layer that constructs a bounded model-visible action space using four signal types: eligibility, requirement, capability, and routing signals. It was evaluated with a frozen BFCL-derived routing-pressure protocol using the MadeAgents/Hammer2.1-1.5b model across 48 fresh BFCL V4 multiple-function tasks. Baselines included all-tools exposure, deterministic random top-8, and semantic top-8.
AI.result: AgentWeave achieved 6/48 (12.5%) native BFCL successes versus 0/48 for all baselines. The paired success difference is +12.5 percentage points with a bootstrap 95% CI of +4.17 to +22.92 and exact McNemar p=0.03125. Relative to all-tools exposure, AgentWeave presents 70.18% fewer tools, uses 61.70% fewer input tokens, and exhibits 50.95% lower mean local-model latency.
AI.conclusion: The results are deliberately narrow—this is a BFCL-derived routing-pressure study rather than an official full BFCL leaderboard score, and absolute task success remains low. Nevertheless, the evidence shows that candidate-space construction can materially affect a fixed model's function-calling behavior and motivates evaluating routing as a distinct stage before model reasoning.

title: Training-Free Pseudo-Fusion for Composed Image Retrieval with Diffusion Models and Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Composed Image Retrieval (CIR) is an emerging paradigm in content-based image retrieval that enables users to formulate compositional queries by combining a reference image with an auxiliary modality, usually text-based. This approach supports fine-grained search where the target image shares structural elements with the user-provided image while incorporating the modifications specified by the auxiliary text. Conventional CIR methods rely on multimodal fusion to combine visual and textual features into a joint query embedding, which requires training modules that align composed queries with the targets. In this work, we propose PeFuse (for pseudo-fusion), a training-free framework that leverages pretrained Diffusion Models and Multimodal Large Language Models to bridge modalities via generative conversion. We introduce two novel strategies: uni-directional and bi-directional conversion, which convert CIR into four single-modality retrieval problems. These methods reformulate CIR as either intra-modal or cross-modal single-query retrieval tasks, bypassing the need for dedicated task-specific training. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that converting CIR into text-to-image retrieval tasks is more effective than alternative conversion strategies, achieving competitive or superior performance compared with state-of-the-art methods, while maintaining high flexibility thanks to replaceable components of the conversion pipeline. These results highlight the effectiveness of the pseudo-fusion paradigm for zero-shot CIR. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/StevenXuf/PeFuse4CIR.

AI.tldr: PeFuse is a training-free framework for Composed Image Retrieval that uses pretrained Diffusion Models and Multimodal Large Language Models to convert CIR into four single-modality retrieval problems via uni-directional and bi-directional generative conversion strategies, bypassing task-specific training while achieving competitive performance.
AI.motivation: Conventional CIR methods rely on multimodal fusion to combine visual and textual features into a joint query embedding, which requires training dedicated modules to align composed queries with targets. This work seeks to eliminate the need for task-specific training by leveraging pretrained generative models.
AI.method: PeFuse reformulates CIR as either intra-modal or cross-modal single-query retrieval tasks through two novel strategies: uni-directional and bi-directional conversion. The framework uses pretrained Diffusion Models and Multimodal Large Language Models to bridge modalities via generative conversion, producing four possible single-modality retrieval configurations.
AI.result: Experiments on standard benchmarks show that converting CIR into text-to-image retrieval tasks outperforms alternative conversion strategies, achieving competitive or superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods while maintaining high flexibility due to replaceable components in the conversion pipeline.
AI.conclusion: The pseudo-fusion paradigm is an effective approach for zero-shot CIR, demonstrating that generative conversion of modalities can substitute for learned fusion, eliminating the need for task-specific training while maintaining competitive performance.

title: SWE Refactor Bench: Can Coding Agents Complete a Long-Horizon, Whole-Repository Stack Migration?
summary: Modern software systems accumulate technical debt over decades of development, which makes migration expensive and largely manual. As coding agents become increasingly capable at bug fixing, can they autonomously perform such migrations? Existing benchmarks cannot answer this question because they evaluate only behavioural correctness, not whether the migration actually occurred. This leads an easy hack: agents copy the original implementation to make tests pass. We call this Blindness. To address this problem, we introduce SWE Refactor Bench, a benchmark comprising 20 whole-repository migrations, covering 4 kinds of technical debt. A three-stage evaluation protocol measures both migration completeness and behavioural correctness. (1) Migration Audit verifies that the migration occurred. (2) Behavioural Tests measure correctness with a fixed test suite. (3) Agentic Verification uses 6 independent coding agents to generate targeted tests for hidden behavioural differences. Across 520 runs from 8 frontier models and 26 model-effort configurations, only 28 of 520 runs ($5.4\%$) pass all three stages, 13 of the 20 tasks receive no accepted solution, and the best model (claude-opus-5) scores $47.0/100$. Migration completeness and behavioural correctness are distinct abilities: a few runs preserve behaviour by skipping the migration and are stopped at Migration Audit; most attempt it and break behaviour, and are stopped at Behavioural Tests. Agents cannot deliver a perfect migration: among the 340 runs that pass Migration Audit, $58\%$ reach $99\%$ of the fixed checks, yet only $26\%$ reach $100\%$. Agent capability differs across migration categories: agents score $31.4$ on build toolchain rewrites but only $5.6$ on language rewrites. Together, these findings position SWE Refactor Bench as a rigorous testbed for developing coding agents for reliable whole-repository migrations.

AI.tldr: SWE Refactor Bench is a benchmark of 20 whole-repository migrations covering 4 types of technical debt, with a three-stage evaluation protocol (Migration Audit, Behavioural Tests, Agentic Verification). Across 520 runs from 8 frontier models, only 5.4% pass all stages, revealing that current coding agents cannot reliably perform autonomous migration without hacking or breaking behavior.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks evaluate only behavioural correctness of coding agents on migrations, which allows agents to cheat by copying the original implementation to pass tests (termed "Blindness"). This fails to assess whether the migration actually occurred, making it impossible to determine if agents can autonomously perform real technical debt migrations.
AI.method: The paper introduces SWE Refactor Bench with 20 whole-repository migrations across 4 technical debt categories. A three-stage evaluation protocol is used: (1) Migration Audit verifies the migration occurred, (2) Behavioural Tests measure correctness with a fixed test suite, and (3) Agentic Verification uses 6 independent coding agents to generate targeted tests for hidden behavioural differences.
AI.result: Across 520 runs from 8 frontier models and 26 model-effort configurations, only 28/520 runs (5.4%) pass all three stages. 13 of 20 tasks receive no accepted solution, and the best model (claude-opus-5) scores 47.0/100. Migration completeness and behavioural correctness are distinct abilities. Among 340 runs passing Migration Audit, 58% reach 99% of fixed checks but only 26% reach 100%. Agents score 31.4 on build toolchain rewrites but only 5.6 on language rewrites.
AI.conclusion: Current coding agents cannot deliver perfect whole-repository migrations, as they either skip the migration (caught at Migration Audit) or attempt it and break behaviour (caught at Behavioural Tests). SWE Refactor Bench serves as a rigorous testbed for developing coding agents for reliable whole-repository migrations, and reveals that agent capability varies significantly across migration categories.

title: POOL: Propagated Uncertainty Over Lookalikes
summary: Black-box large language models need confidence scores that can separate likely-correct from likely-incorrect outputs, enabling systems to prioritize human review, route uncertain cases to stronger models, or choose abstention thresholds on development data. Yet existing confidence estimators face a cost-quality trade-off: verbal confidence is cheap but is often overconfident, while sampling-based uncertainty is more informative but scales linearly with the number of samples per query. We propose \textsc{POOL} (\emph{Propagated Uncertainty Over Lookalikes}),a cost-efficient framework that addresses this trade-off taking inspiration from group-testing.\textsc{POOL} clusters query stems with overlaps, evaluates a base estimator on representative medoids, softly propagates confidence scores to nearby queries, and selectively evaluates high-disagreement cases. We instantiate this framework with \textsc{Hy@}$p$, a hybrid estimator that combines verbal confidence with spectral answer diversity computed from the negative von Neumann entropy of sampled answer embeddings.Across six domains from three datasets and five black-box LLMs, \textsc{Hy@}5 achieves higher average AUROC than verbal confidence and \textsc{Vn@}10 sampling while using half as many samples as \textsc{Vn@}10. \textsc{POOL}-\textsc{Hy@}5 retains 93.5--97.9\% of its AUROC while saving 19.3--39.3\% of generations. On paraphrase-dense workloads, generation savings rise to 73-76\%, showing that semantic redundancy can be leveraged to lower confidence-estimation costs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes POOL (Propagated Uncertainty Over Lookalikes), a cost-efficient framework for confidence estimation in black-box LLMs that clusters query stems, propagates confidence scores from representative medoids to nearby queries, and selectively evaluates high-disagreement cases. It introduces Hy@p, a hybrid estimator combining verbal confidence with spectral answer diversity, achieving higher AUROC than verbal confidence and Vn@10 sampling while using half the samples, with substantial generation savings on paraphrase-dense workloads.
AI.motivation: Black-box LLMs need confidence scores that separate correct from incorrect outputs, but existing confidence estimators face a cost-quality trade-off: verbal confidence is cheap but overconfident, while sampling-based uncertainty is more informative yet scales linearly with the number of samples per query.
AI.method: POOL clusters query stems with overlaps, evaluates a base estimator on representative medoids, softly propagates confidence scores to nearby queries, and selectively evaluates high-disagreement cases. The framework is instantiated with Hy@p, a hybrid estimator combining verbal confidence with spectral answer diversity computed from the negative von Neumann entropy of sampled answer embeddings.
AI.result: Across six domains from three datasets and five black-box LLMs, Hy@5 achieves higher average AUROC than verbal confidence and Vn@10 sampling while using half as many samples. POOL-Hy@5 retains 93.5-97.9% of its AUROC while saving 19.3-39.3% of generations. On paraphrase-dense workloads, generation savings rise to 73-76%.
AI.conclusion: Semantic redundancy across similar queries can be leveraged to lower confidence-estimation costs, demonstrating that group-testing-inspired propagation strategies effectively address the cost-quality trade-off in LLM confidence estimation.

title: Bridge Damage Detection from Low-Light UAV Imagery via Degradation-Aware Mixture-of-Experts Enhancement
summary: Poor illumination obscures small, low-contrast defects in UAV bridge imagery, reducing the reliability and operational flexibility of automated inspection. This paper investigates whether degradation-aware image restoration can improve bridge damage detection under low-light conditions and transfer from synthetic degradations to real inspection scenes. We propose DaL- MoE, a detector-agnostic restoration front end trained with an ISP-aware low-light synthesis pipeline and equipped with degradation-aware guidance estimation and complementary experts for noise suppression, color adjustment, and structural-detail recovery. On paired synthetic data, DaL-MoE achieves 23.12 dB PSNR and 0.8482 SSIM, increasing YOLOv11m box mAP50 from 0.3097 to 0.4923 and mask mAP50 from 0.2281 to 0.3529. On real low-light UAV imagery without paired normal-light references, sim-to-real evaluation shows improved defect visibility and more complete detections than direct inference on raw low-light inputs. Future work will develop low-light-aware bridge damage detectors with stronger cross-scene generalization across bridge sites, imaging conditions, and illumination levels.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes DaL-MoE, a detector-agnostic degradation-aware image restoration front end for UAV bridge damage detection under low-light conditions. It uses an ISP-aware low-light synthesis pipeline and a mixture-of-experts architecture for noise suppression, color adjustment, and detail recovery. On synthetic data it achieves 23.12 dB PSNR and 0.8482 SSIM, boosting YOLOv11m box mAP50 from 0.3097 to 0.4923 and mask mAP50 from 0.2281 to 0.3529, with improved sim-to-real performance on real low-light UAV imagery.
AI.motivation: Poor illumination obscures small, low-contrast defects in UAV bridge imagery, compromising the reliability and flexibility of automated inspection. The paper aims to determine whether degradation-aware image restoration can improve bridge damage detection under low-light conditions and transfer from synthetic degradations to real inspection scenes.
AI.method: DaL-MoE is a detector-agnostic restoration front end trained with an ISP-aware low-light synthesis pipeline. It incorporates degradation-aware guidance estimation and complementary mixture-of-experts modules for noise suppression, color adjustment, and structural-detail recovery.
AI.result: On paired synthetic data, DaL-MoE achieves 23.12 dB PSNR and 0.8482 SSIM, increasing YOLOv11m box mAP50 from 0.3097 to 0.4923 and mask mAP50 from 0.2281 to 0.3529. On real low-light UAV imagery without paired references, sim-to-real evaluation shows improved defect visibility and more complete detections than direct inference on raw low-light inputs.
AI.conclusion: Degradation-aware restoration effectively improves bridge damage detection under low-light conditions and transfers from synthetic to real scenarios. Future work will focus on developing low-light-aware bridge damage detectors with stronger cross-scene generalization across bridge sites, imaging conditions, and illumination levels.

title: Jiuge-Tuiqiao: An Interpretable Human-AI System for Classical Chinese Poetry Refinement
comment: Accepted to the System Demonstrations Program at EMNLP 2026. Code and demo: https://github.com/jiangli-va/Jiuge-Tuiqiao
summary: Classical Chinese poetry composition has long valued Tuiqiao, the iterative refinement of words, imagery, and prosody. However, many current AI poetry systems follow a one-shot generation paradigm, which reduces users to prompt providers and weakens their creative agency. We present Jiuge-Tuiqiao, an interactive human-AI collaborative system for classical Chinese poetry composition. The system is designed around a triadic model: user-driven control, ancient-guided evidence, and AI-assisted generation. Users can lock characters or lines, receive real-time prosody feedback, and obtain interpretable refinement suggestions grounded in high-frequency collocations, PPL-ranked classical lines, and structured knowledge extracted from classical encyclopedias. This design turns AI from an autonomous generator into a background assistant that supports the user's own process of poetic refinement. Preliminary experiments and user feedback suggest that Jiuge-Tuiqiao improves controllability, interpretability, and user engagement in classical poetry composition.

AI.tldr: Jiuge-Tuiqiao is an interactive human-AI collaborative system for classical Chinese poetry composition that shifts from one-shot generation to iterative refinement (Tuiqiao), using a triadic model of user-driven control, ancient-guided evidence, and AI-assisted generation to support poetic editing with real-time feedback and interpretable suggestions.
AI.motivation: Current AI poetry systems follow a one-shot generation paradigm that diminishes users' creative agency, reducing them to mere prompt providers. Classical Chinese poetry composition traditionally values Tuiqiao—the iterative refinement of words, imagery, and prosody—which existing systems fail to support.
AI.method: The system employs a triadic model: (1) user-driven control via locking characters or lines, (2) ancient-guided evidence through high-frequency collocations, PPL-ranked classical lines, and structured knowledge from classical encyclopedias, and (3) AI-assisted generation providing real-time prosody feedback and interpretable refinement suggestions. This positions AI as a background assistant rather than an autonomous generator.
AI.result: Preliminary experiments and user feedback indicate that Jiuge-Tuiqiao improves controllability, interpretability, and user engagement in classical poetry composition compared to existing one-shot approaches.
AI.conclusion: The interactive human-AI collaborative design effectively supports the iterative refinement process inherent to classical Chinese poetry composition, transforming AI from an autonomous generator into a supportive assistant that enhances user creative agency.

title: A Simulator-Grounded Framework For Constructing Verifiable Muscle-Grounded QA From 3D Tongue Meshes
summary: Existing articulatory corpora based on real-time MRI and electromagnetic articulography capture tongue shape and motion but do not provide traceable labels for the muscle-driven process that generated an observed configuration. We introduce a simulator-grounded data-construction framework and instantiate it as 3DTongueQA. Controlled 11-dimensional muscle activations are mapped to fixed-topology tongue meshes with the ArtiSynth Badin finite-element model, converted into structured biomechanical records, and rendered as deterministic QA on muscle state, geometry, and target-directed change. We screen 295,157 configurations, retain 295,115 valid meshes, and construct 891,156 QA records per language. Language naturalization changes only surface form and is verified against the source records; English and Korean instantiations demonstrate construction-level portability. A swappable SpiralNet++--Qwen3-8B baseline reaches 62.9 $\pm$ 9.2 Muscle EM, 74.0 $\pm$ 0.2 Value Accuracy, and 65.9 $\pm$ 4.7 Direction EM, while mismatching the paired mesh reduces Muscle EM to 2.2; a dataset-leakage-controlled anchor-held-out model retains 80.4--98.6\% of the full-inventory scores on unseen anchors. Task-specific structured readouts further reach 88.7 $\pm$ 0.7 Muscle EM and 93.3 $\pm$ 1.0 Direction EM. These complementary results show that the constructed supervision supports both efficient structured prediction and heterogeneous natural-language QA rather than being tied to a particular decoder architecture.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces 3DTongueQA, a simulator-grounded data construction framework for articulatory biomechanics QA. Using the ArtiSynth Badin finite-element model, 295,115 valid tongue meshes are generated from controlled 11-dimensional muscle activations, yielding 891,156 QA records per language (English and Korean). A SpiralNet++--Qwen3-8B baseline achieves 62.9±9.2 Muscle EM, 74.0±0.2 Value Accuracy, and 65.9±4.7 Direction EM, with structured readouts reaching 88.7±0.7 Muscle EM and 93.3±1.0 Direction EM, demonstrating architecture-agnostic supervision.
AI.motivation: Existing articulatory corpora (real-time MRI, EMA) capture tongue shape and motion but lack traceable labels linking observed configurations to the underlying muscle-driven biomechanical process. This prevents supervised learning of muscle-state prediction and structured biomechanical reasoning.
AI.method: Controlled 11-dimensional muscle activations are mapped to fixed-topology tongue meshes via the ArtiSynth Badin finite-element model. Structured biomechanical records are converted into deterministic QA targets covering muscle state, geometry, and target-directed change. Language naturalization (English/Korean) changes only surface form while preserving source records. Evaluated with a swappable SpiralNet++ encoder paired with Qwen3-8B, plus task-specific structured readouts.
AI.result: Screened 295,157 configurations retaining 295,115 valid meshes; 891,156 QA records per language. SpiralNet++--Qwen3-8B achieves 62.9±9.2 Muscle EM, 74.0±0.2 Value Accuracy, 65.9±4.7 Direction EM. Mesh mismatch drops Muscle EM to 2.2, confirming input-grounded reasoning. Anchor-held-out retains 80.4–98.6% of full-inventory scores. Structured readouts reach 88.7±0.7 Muscle EM and 93.3±1.0 Direction EM.
AI.conclusion: The simulator-grounded construction provides reliable, traceable biomechanical supervision that supports both efficient structured prediction and heterogeneous natural-language QA, independent of specific decoder architectures. The framework is portable across languages as demonstrated by English and Korean instantiations.

title: AI emotional support is better only when chosen, but shifts preferences even when it is not
summary: People increasingly face a novel decision when seeking emotional support: human or AI. In existing studies, AI's empathic messages are rated as well as or better than humans'. But these studies either assigned the support source or honored people's choice. In real life, support is often incongruent with choice, as people want one source and receive the other. Across three experiments (N = 1,951), participants chose whether to share an emotional experience with a human or an AI, then were randomly assigned to a congruent or incongruent partner. AI support was rated as superior only among those who had chosen it. Yet regardless of congruence, interacting with AI increased willingness to choose it again. In a 28-day study with OpenAI (N = 981), daily conversations shifted preferences toward AI and away from humans, but only when conversations turned personal. Emotional support choices are thus path-dependent, progressively redirecting away from human connection.

AI.tldr: Across three experiments (N=1,951) and a 28-day field study (N=981), AI emotional support is rated superior only by those who chose it, yet any AI interaction (congruent or incongruent with choice) increases willingness to choose AI again. Daily personal conversations with AI progressively shift preferences away from humans, revealing path-dependent dynamics in emotional support source selection.
AI.motivation: Previous studies showing AI empathy equals or exceeds human empathy either assigned the support source or honored participant choice, failing to reflect real-world scenarios where support source may be incongruent with preference. The research addresses this gap by examining how congruence between choice and actual support source affects evaluations and subsequent preferences.
AI.method: Three experiments (N=1,951) where participants chose human or AI emotional support then were randomly assigned to congruent or incongruent partners, followed by a 28-day longitudinal study with OpenAI (N=981) tracking daily conversations and preference shifts, distinguishing personal from non-personal conversations.
AI.result: AI support rated superior only among those who chose AI; incongruence did not lead to lower AI ratings. Interacting with AI increased willingness to choose it again regardless of congruence. Longitudinal data showed daily personal (but not non-personal) conversations shifted preferences toward AI and away from humans.
AI.conclusion: Emotional support source choices are path-dependent and self-reinforcing: AI interaction increases future AI preference, progressively redirecting users away from human connection, even when initial AI support was unsolicited or incongruent with prior choice.

title: Cognitive Profiling of LRMs' Reasoning Traces Using Bloom's Taxonomy
summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have revolutionized reasoning in LLMs, and the increasing public availability of reasoning traces creates valuable opportunities to study model behavior not only at the surface level but also at the granularity of individual reasoning steps. However, understanding the types of thinking employed during reasoning - which offers critical insights into models' reasoning patterns and enables actionable applications - remains underexplored. To address this gap, we introduce a framework for automatic annotation of reasoning steps through the lens of Bloom's Taxonomy, which classifies thinking into six cognitive levels, such as Remembering, Applying and Evaluating. Using this framework, we perform a large-scale analysis across models and datasets, revealing both similarities and differences in thinking patterns across models and tasks. Moreover, we demonstrate that thinking-type information derived from reasoning traces correlates with correctness, paving the way for improved reasoning. Our findings establish a fine-grained framework for analyzing thinking patterns in LRMs and provide actionable insights for enhancing reasoning quality.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a framework for automatically annotating individual reasoning steps of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) using Bloom's Taxonomy, which classifies thinking into six cognitive levels. The authors conduct large-scale analysis across multiple models and datasets, revealing similarities and differences in thinking patterns, and demonstrate that thinking-type information correlates with reasoning correctness, offering actionable insights for improving reasoning quality.
AI.motivation: While LRMs have advanced reasoning capabilities and their reasoning traces are increasingly available, there is limited understanding of the types of thinking employed during reasoning at the granularity of individual reasoning steps. Understanding these thinking patterns could provide critical insights into model behavior and enable actionable applications, yet this remains underexplored.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework for automatic annotation of reasoning steps using Bloom's Taxonomy, which categorizes thinking into six cognitive levels (e.g., Remembering, Applying, Evaluating). They apply this framework to perform a large-scale analysis of thinking patterns across different models and datasets, and investigate correlations between thinking types and correctness.
AI.result: The analysis reveals both similarities and differences in thinking patterns across models and tasks. The authors demonstrate that thinking-type information derived from reasoning traces correlates with correctness, suggesting that such information can support improved reasoning.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a fine-grained framework for analyzing thinking patterns in LRMs, providing actionable insights for enhancing reasoning quality and opening new directions for studying model behavior beyond surface-level performance.

title: How Merge-Tolerant Are Vision Transformers for Wheat Phenotyping?
comment: Accepted to the CVPPA workshop at ECCV 2026
summary: Vision-based wheat phenotyping requires repeated measurements under deployment constraints, from growth-stage recognition to wheat-head counting and organ segmentation. Plain Vision Transformers (ViTs) provide a common architecture for these tasks, but quadratic attention limits high-throughput and edge inference. Training-free token merging is attractive because it can be inserted into trained models without retraining. We provide a systematic benchmark of ToMe and Mutual Pair Merging across growth-stage classification, wheat-head detection, and wheat-organ segmentation, measuring task quality, throughput, token count, and peak GPU memory, with additional Raspberry Pi 5 measurements. The benchmark reveals a clear hierarchy: classification is highly merge-tolerant, while detection and segmentation are constrained by repeated instances, thin organs, dense boundaries, reconstruction, and runtime overhead. Optimized attention backends can erase apparent speedups, so deployment value must be profiled on the target runtime rather than inferred from token count.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks training-free token merging methods (ToMe and Mutual Pair Merging) for vision-based wheat phenotyping tasks including growth-stage classification, wheat-head detection, and wheat-organ segmentation, evaluating task quality, throughput, token count, and peak GPU memory, plus Raspberry Pi 5 measurements. Results show classification tolerates aggressive merging while detection and segmentation are constrained by repeated instances, thin organs, and dense boundaries, and that optimized attention backends can negate apparent speedups.
AI.motivation: Plain Vision Transformers (ViTs) provide a unified architecture for wheat phenotyping tasks but quadratic attention limits high-throughput and edge deployment. Training-free token merging is attractive because it can be inserted into pre-trained models without retraining, yet its effectiveness across diverse phenotyping tasks had not been systematically evaluated.
AI.method: The authors provide a systematic benchmark comparing ToMe (Token Merging) and Mutual Pair Merging across three wheat phenotyping tasks: growth-stage classification, wheat-head detection, and wheat-organ segmentation. They evaluate task quality, throughput, token count, and peak GPU memory, with additional measurements on Raspberry Pi 5 to assess edge deployment viability.
AI.result: The benchmark reveals a clear task hierarchy in merge tolerance: classification is highly merge-tolerant, while detection and segmentation are constrained by repeated instances, thin organs, dense boundaries, reconstruction quality, and runtime overhead. Additionally, optimized attention backends can erase apparent speedups from token reduction, meaning deployment value must be measured on the actual target runtime.
AI.conclusion: Training-free token merging is viable for classification tasks but requires careful evaluation for detection and segmentation in wheat phenotyping. Deployment benefits must be profiled on target hardware rather than inferred from token count alone, since attention backend optimizations can eliminate speedup gains.

title: What is mathematics now, and what should it be?
summary: Advances in neural theorem provers have been impressive, but the successes obscure a broader vision of what AI can do for mathematics and how mathematicians can engage with AI. This essay advances a more expansive and optimistic point of view.

AI.tldr: This essay argues for a broader vision of AI's role in mathematics beyond neural theorem proving, presenting an optimistic perspective on how AI and mathematicians can collaboratively engage with mathematics.
AI.motivation: While neural theorem provers have made impressive advances, these successes limit our view of AI's potential in mathematics. The author seeks to expand this perspective and highlight the greater possibilities for AI-mathematician collaboration.
AI.method: This is an essay/position paper that advances a more expansive and optimistic viewpoint on AI's role in mathematics, moving beyond the narrow focus on automated theorem proving.
AI.result: No experimental results are presented as this is an essay; the contribution is a broader conceptual framing of AI's potential in mathematics.
AI.conclusion: The essay concludes that AI's role in mathematics should be viewed more broadly and optimistically than current neural theorem proving successes suggest, opening new avenues for mathematician-AI engagement.

title: An end-to-end-trained vision-language model for native-language prostate pathology report generation
summary: Prostate cancer is among the most frequently diagnosed malignancies worldwide, and structured reporting of each biopsy core burdens pathologists. Existing tools frame this as classification, leaving pathologists to assemble coherent reports, while many slide-level vision-language models rely on English-centric encoders that transfer poorly to other clinical languages. We present a slide-level framework generating prostate biopsy reports that is language-independent by construction: tokenizer and model are trained from scratch, demonstrated here in German. To address paired-data scarcity, an automated pipeline uses a locally deployed large language model to split composite reports into core-specific image-text pairs, yielding 17,344 pairs from 2,402 historical cases without manual annotation. Evaluated for clinical attributes rather than linguistic similarity, the model achieves 96.2% F1 for malignancy detection and 65.2% for Gleason grading, competitive with an FDA-cleared classifier. Grading is further validated on three external cohorts with latent-space augmentation. Institutions can thus train native-language reporting models on their own archives.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a slide-level framework for generating prostate biopsy reports that is language-independent by construction, trained from scratch in German. Using an automated pipeline with a locally deployed LLM to split composite reports into core-specific image-text pairs (17,344 pairs from 2,402 cases), the model achieves 96.2% F1 for malignancy detection and 65.2% for Gleason grading, competitive with an FDA-cleared classifier, and validated on three external cohorts.
AI.motivation: Prostate cancer is a frequently diagnosed malignancy where structured reporting of each biopsy core burdens pathologists. Existing tools frame this as classification (leaving report assembly to pathologists), and many slide-level vision-language models rely on English-centric encoders that transfer poorly to other clinical languages, limiting deployment in non-English clinical settings.
AI.method: The framework is language-independent by construction: both tokenizer and model are trained from scratch (demonstrated in German). To address paired-data scarcity, an automated pipeline uses a locally deployed large language model to split composite reports into core-specific image-text pairs, producing 17,344 pairs from 2,402 historical cases without manual annotation. The model is evaluated on clinical attributes rather than linguistic similarity, and validated on three external cohorts with latent-space augmentation.
AI.result: The model achieves 96.2% F1 for malignancy detection and 65.2% for Gleason grading, competitive with an FDA-cleared classifier. Grading is further validated on three external cohorts with latent-space augmentation.
AI.conclusion: Institutions can train native-language reporting models on their own archives, enabling slide-level prostate biopsy report generation in non-English clinical languages without reliance on English-centric pretrained encoders or manual annotation.

title: Is Next-Chunk Reasoning RL Really Better than SFT? Revisiting Training Strategies under no-CoT Data
summary: Recent work proposes next-chunk reasoning RL for leveraging no-CoT data---corpora such as worked solutions and textbook derivations that contain reasoning-rich content but lack explicit chain-of-thought annotations. The method trains a model to generate implicit reasoning traces and rewards them by their ability to predict the next chunk of text. While promising, existing evaluations primarily compare against conventional SFT baselines, leaving open whether the gains come from the RL formulation itself or from more effectively exposing the model to no-CoT data. We address this question with a controlled study of next-chunk reasoning RL and a simple but previously overlooked alternative: Mixed SFT, a single supervised fine-tuning stage that jointly trains on no-CoT and long-CoT data. Despite its simplicity, Mixed SFT achieves a clearly higher post-RLVR performance ceiling than next-chunk reasoning RL while requiring over 60 times less training compute. The advantage is consistent across in-domain mathematical reasoning and out-of-domain reasoning tasks. Moreover, we show that higher pre-RLVR accuracy does not necessarily translate into higher post-RLVR accuracy, highlighting the need to evaluate no-CoT training strategies in the context of the full post-training pipeline.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a controlled comparison between next-chunk reasoning RL and Mixed SFT (a joint supervised fine-tuning on no-CoT and long-CoT data) for leveraging no-CoT corpora. Mixed SFT achieves higher post-RLVR performance with over 60x less training compute, and the authors find that higher pre-RLVR accuracy does not guarantee higher post-RLVR accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of next-chunk reasoning RL primarily compare against conventional SFT baselines, making it unclear whether the gains come from the RL formulation itself or from more effectively exposing the model to no-CoT data. The authors aim to disentangle these factors.
AI.method: The authors conduct a controlled study comparing next-chunk reasoning RL against Mixed SFT—a simple alternative that jointly trains on no-CoT and long-CoT data in a single supervised fine-tuning stage. They evaluate across in-domain mathematical reasoning and out-of-domain reasoning tasks, measuring both pre-RLVR and post-RLVR performance.
AI.result: Mixed SFT achieves a clearly higher post-RLVR performance ceiling than next-chunk reasoning RL while requiring over 60 times less training compute. This advantage is consistent across both in-domain and out-of-domain reasoning tasks. Additionally, higher pre-RLVR accuracy does not necessarily translate to higher post-RLVR accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The gains attributed to next-chunk reasoning RL may stem more from data exposure than the RL formulation itself, and simple SFT alternatives can be more compute-efficient. No-CoT training strategies should be evaluated within the full post-training pipeline context, as pre-RLVR metrics are not reliable predictors of final performance.

title: BenthicFlow: Generating Extensible Underwater Environments via Flow Matching
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026 in the 2nd Workshop on Marine Vision
summary: Computer vision applications for 3D scene understanding in underwater environments remain challenging due to the lack of high-quality 3D data and the inability of surface-trained models to generalize to underwater scenes. To address this challenge, an emerging trend is to employ generative models to close the data domain gap. However, existing methods assemble large scenes by stitching independently generated tiles post hoc with separately trained models, while demonstrating heterogeneous landscapes only within individual survey sites. We introduce BenthicFlow, a unified framework based on a single conditional flow-matching model that jointly generates aligned textures and depth maps. A MultiDiffusion-inspired sampling procedure reconciles overlapping windows throughout the generative trajectory, enabling spatially extensible RGBD mosaics without a separate stitching model. The generated mosaics are subsequently lifted into explicit 3D benthic environments using surface-aligned Gaussian surfels. Experiments across geographically distinct survey sites demonstrate that BenthicFlow preserves site-specific appearance while generating coherent, large-scale 3D scenes that closely match the target distributions. Code and trained models are available at https://github.com/jacomof/BenthicFlow.

AI.tldr: BenthicFlow is a unified conditional flow-matching framework that jointly generates aligned textures and depth maps for underwater 3D scene understanding, using a MultiDiffusion-inspired sampling procedure to produce spatially extensible RGBD mosaics without separate stitching, which are then lifted into explicit 3D benthic environments via surface-aligned Gaussian surfels.
AI.motivation: 3D scene understanding in underwater environments is hindered by scarce high-quality 3D data and poor generalization of surface-trained models. Existing generative approaches rely on stitching independently generated tiles with separately trained models and fail to capture heterogeneous landscapes across survey sites.
AI.method: The method employs a single conditional flow-matching model that jointly generates aligned textures and depth maps. A MultiDiffusion-inspired sampling procedure reconciles overlapping windows during generation, producing spatially extensible RGBD mosaics without needing a separate stitching model. The mosaics are then lifted into explicit 3D scenes using surface-aligned Gaussian surfels.
AI.result: Experiments across geographically distinct survey sites demonstrate that BenthicFlow preserves site-specific appearance while generating coherent, large-scale 3D scenes that closely match target distributions.
AI.conclusion: The unified framework effectively closes the data domain gap for underwater 3D scene understanding, producing spatially coherent and site-specific 3D benthic environments without the complexity of separate stitching models. Code and trained models are publicly available.

title: Automated Construction of FAIR Digital Object Knowledge Graphs from Flat Cultural Heritage Records
comment: Accepted for publication as a short paper at CIKM 2026 (The 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management)
summary: The FAIR Digital Object (FDO) framework mandates that metadata attribute values be expressed as persistent identifiers (PIDs) wherever possible, to produce a fully machine-actionable graph in which every reference is resolvable. The Europeana Data Model was designed long before the FDO specification, and it stores most metadata values as plain text. This serves human browsing well enough, but gives an automated agent nothing to follow across records or collections. We present a pipeline that transforms flat Europeana records into an FDO-compliant knowledge graph structured with CIDOC-CRM. Following the FDO specification, we model every heritage entity as a discrete FDO with its own PID, type, profile, and metadata layer. The core technical challenge is automating the FDO-prescribed distinction between values that must become PID references (resolvable entities) and those that may remain literals (terminal leaves such as notes, measurements, and dates). We address this with a large language model that classifies each metadata value, routes it to a controlled vocabulary (Getty AAT, Wikidata, VIAF, PeriodO), and links it to a shared entity FDO. We evaluate using 637 archaeological records from five Europeana providers, processing each with the LLM. The pipeline links 86% of metadata slots, resolving 58.5% of values Europeana had not already enriched. It also merges cross-lingual surface forms that byte-identical matching keeps apart, where 17 of 33 such merges are correct on manual review. Graph connectivity does not separate this from string matching; what distinguishes the FDO graph is that every node is typed and resolvable.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a pipeline that transforms flat Europeana records into FDO-compliant knowledge graphs structured with CIDOC-CRM, using a large language model to classify metadata values as either PID references or literals. Evaluated on 637 archaeological records, the pipeline links 86% of metadata slots and resolves 58.5% of previously unenriched values, while correctly merging 17 of 33 cross-lingual surface forms.
AI.motivation: The Europeana Data Model predates the FDO specification and stores most metadata as plain text, which serves human browsing but prevents automated agents from traversing records and collections. There is a need to transform these records into a fully machine-actionable, resolvable knowledge graph.
AI.method: The pipeline transforms flat Europeana records into an FDO-compliant knowledge graph structured with CIDOC-CRM. Each heritage entity is modeled as a discrete FDO with PID, type, profile, and metadata layer. An LLM classifies each metadata value, routing it to controlled vocabularies (Getty AAT, Wikidata, VIAF, PeriodO) and linking it to a shared entity FDO. The automated distinction between PID references and terminal literals follows the FDO specification.
AI.result: Using 637 archaeological records from five Europeana providers, the LLM-based pipeline links 86% of metadata slots and resolves 58.5% of values Europeana had not already enriched. It merges 17 of 33 cross-lingual surface forms correctly on manual review, improving upon byte-identical string matching.
AI.conclusion: The FDO graph's distinguishing value does not lie in graph connectivity alone (which does not separate it from string matching), but in that every node is typed and resolvable. The pipeline demonstrates a viable path toward FDO compliance for legacy cultural heritage metadata.

title: Neighbor-Aware View Synthesis for Restoring Missing Views in Light-Field Camera Arrays
summary: In light-field (LF) imaging systems, dense spatial sampling from a camera array enables powerful post-capture capabilities such as refocusing and depth estimation. However, real-world LF capture is often affected by hardware malfunctions, where one or more cameras in the array fail, leading to missing sub-aperture images and degraded reconstruction quality. This paper addresses the problem of defective or missing view restoration in light-field camera arrays. We propose a novel generative framework that synthesizes the absent views by exploiting information from a carefully selected subset of neighboring cameras. These selected images, along with a positional encoding map indicating both their locations and the desired target view, are fed into a conditional Generative Adversarial Network (cGAN) trained to generate the missing viewpoint in a geometrically consistent manner. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world LF datasets demonstrate that our method produces visually plausible and photometrically accurate reconstructions, outperforming baselines for view interpolation both quantitatively and qualitatively. The proposed framework thus offers a robust and efficient solution for fault-tolerant light-field image acquisition.

AI.tldr: A generative cGAN-based framework for restoring missing views in light-field camera arrays when hardware failures occur. The method synthesizes absent sub-aperture images using a carefully selected subset of neighboring cameras plus a positional encoding map, producing geometrically consistent reconstructions that outperform view interpolation baselines on synthetic and real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Real-world light-field camera arrays frequently suffer hardware malfunctions where one or more cameras fail, causing missing sub-aperture images and degraded reconstruction quality. Existing approaches do not adequately address this fault-tolerance problem.
AI.method: A conditional Generative Adversarial Network (cGAN) is trained to generate the missing viewpoint. Inputs consist of a carefully selected subset of neighboring camera images along with a positional encoding map that encodes both the locations of the selected views and the desired target view, enabling geometrically consistent synthesis.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world LF datasets show the method produces visually plausible and photometrically accurate reconstructions, outperforming view interpolation baselines both quantitatively and qualitatively.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a robust and efficient solution for fault-tolerant light-field image acquisition, enabling recovery of missing views in camera array systems.

title: Hidden in the Request: Explaining Unethical LLM Compliance through Token Relevance
summary: Although Large Language Models (LLMs) are aligned to optimize for both helpfulness and harmlessness, these dual objectives may conflict, inevitably leading to alignment failures. This work systematically investigates instances where LLMs fail to exhibit ethical behavior. To understand the underlying mechanics of these vulnerabilities, we introduce a probing methodology that presents unethical scenarios to LLMs in three distinct structural modalities: objective classification tasks, subjective first-person statements, and direct requests for assistance. We find that model performance degrades in the request-for-assistance-based form. Using Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP), we trace this discrepancy to an attribution bias: the model places greater emphasis on benign task-framing tokens (e.g., "Can you help me...") than on tokens signaling the underlying unethical behavior (e.g., "without getting caught"), which we term cue-tokens. We hypothesize that this under-attribution contributes to harmful compliance. To test this, we introduce two LRP-guided decoding methods that steer generation toward trajectories more relevant to cue tokens. Empirical evaluations show that these interventions promote safer responses, supporting cue-token attribution's role in compliance failures.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates why LLMs fail to exhibit ethical behavior despite alignment to be both helpful and harmless. The authors introduce a probing methodology presenting unethical scenarios in three modalities, find performance degrades in direct request-for-assistance forms, and use Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) to trace this to an attribution bias where models overweight benign task-framing tokens (e.g., "Can you help me...") over cue-tokens signaling unethical behavior (e.g., "without getting caught"). They introduce two LRP-guided decoding methods that steer generation toward cue-token-relevant trajectories, promoting safer responses.
AI.motivation: The dual objectives of helpfulness and harmlessness in LLM alignment can conflict, leading to alignment failures. The authors aim to systematically understand the underlying mechanics of why LLMs fail to exhibit ethical behavior in certain scenarios.
AI.method: The authors introduce a probing methodology that presents unethical scenarios in three structural modalities: objective classification tasks, subjective first-person statements, and direct requests for assistance. They use Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) to analyze attribution bias across tokens. They then introduce two LRP-guided decoding methods to steer generation toward trajectories more relevant to cue-tokens.
AI.result: Model performance degrades specifically in the request-for-assistance-based form. LRP reveals an attribution bias where models place greater emphasis on benign task-framing tokens than on cue-tokens signaling unethical behavior. The two LRP-guided decoding methods empirically promote safer responses.
AI.conclusion: The findings support the hypothesis that cue-token under-attribution contributes to harmful compliance in LLMs, and LRP-guided interventions can effectively mitigate this by steering generation toward cue-token-relevant trajectories.

title: EchoWM: Open and Enterable Omnimodal World Models
summary: We present EchoWM, an omnimodal world model for enterable generative media that responds to continuous navigation while jointly generating 720p video, environmental sound, music and speech. We organize interaction around camera intent: in first-person scenes, it specifies observer motion, while in third-person scenes, camera--character dynamics are learned from data without view-specific controllers. Discrete commands and continuous poses are mapped to a shared metric-scale relative 6-DoF trajectory, with dataset-level calibration preserving motion magnitude across heterogeneous data. To jointly learn audio-visual generation and trajectory control, we construct a complementary data engine and adopt progressive training followed by autoregressive post-training for long-horizon generation. Extensive evaluations show that \model achieves strong trajectory following and high visual quality on public world-model benchmarks, supporting both first- and third-person interaction across varied subjects, and maintaining synchronized environmental sound and speech over long-horizon generation.

AI.tldr: EchoWM is an omnimodal world model that generates 720p video, environmental sound, music, and speech simultaneously while responding to continuous user navigation in both first- and third-person scenes. It unifies discrete commands and continuous poses into a shared metric-scale 6-DoF trajectory representation and uses progressive training plus autoregressive post-training for long-horizon generation.
